certs.name: Claude Certified Associate – Foundations
certs.fee: $99 USD (per attempt; the price shown at checkout reflects the discount applicable to your partner tier)
certs.delivery: Proctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy — delivered by Pearson VUE (the candidate chooses online proctoring or a Pearson test center when scheduling)
certs.prerequisites: There are no mandatory prerequisites or required courses, and no software development or API experience is needed. The recommended experience (regular professional use of Claude, understanding of structured problem-solving and workflow design, business/consulting roles, practical understanding of AI's limitations) is recommended, NOT required. The credential is awarded solely based on exam performance.
certs.languages: The v1.0 exam guide doesn't list delivery languages. The exam is taken in English (all official sample items are in English). Check language availability with Pearson VUE when scheduling.
certs.audience: Professionals who use Claude as a productivity tool and build Claude Projects in their day-to-day work: operations, marketing, project management, education, communications, and knowledge work in general. Includes both internal staff who maintain and optimize AI-enabled workflows and external consultants who support implementation, use-case identification, and process redesign. They sit between the casual prompt user and the technical AI practitioner: their value lies in translating business objectives into effective AI interactions.
certs.mqc: The Minimally Qualified Candidate (MQC) is a professional who uses Claude as a core productivity tool and applies it within real workflows to improve efficiency, quality, and outcomes. They have applied, foundational knowledge of Claude's capabilities: prompt structuring, task orchestration, and familiarity with features like Projects, Artifacts, and workflow-based interactions. They go beyond basic question-and-answer use toward reimagining processes, automating tasks, and developing projects. They are aware of the organizational context: how Claude generates value, where adoption risks exist, and how to align usage with business needs and responsible AI practices. They have regular, hands-on experience using Claude in a professional setting and can independently complete common productivity and workflow tasks on the platform.
certs.notFor: It is not intended for software developers who build against APIs or design agentic systems, nor for machine learning specialists, software engineers, or advanced AI system designers. The candidate is not expected to design enterprise-scale AI architectures or integrations: that scope belongs to the Claude Architect and Claude Developer credentials, to which the Associate escalates more complex or technical work.

domains.title: Prompting and Task Execution
objectives: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
Iterate prompts to improve output quality
Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 14%

This domain measures the Associate's most elementary skill — and, precisely for that reason, not the most heavily weighted one on the exam: turning a business objective into an instruction that Claude can execute well on the first try or within a few iterations. The guide describes the candidate as someone "distinguished by their ability to translate business objectives into effective AI interactions" and to "create structured prompts." That is exactly what gets assessed here: not the eloquence of the prompt, but the architecture of the request — what context goes in, in what order, with what constraints, with what output format, and with what escape hatch for when the model doesn't have the information.

The business decision this domain represents is the entry point to the process: if the prompt is poorly formulated, everything that comes after (evaluation, workflow integration, troubleshooting) works on garbage. Anthropic is explicit on a point the exam rewards: prompt engineering is not the tool for every problem — "latency and cost can be sometimes more easily improved by selecting a different model." A competent Associate knows when the problem is a prompt problem (vague output, inconsistent formatting, hallucination about a document) and when it isn't (the model is too slow, the task exceeds scope, the source of truth is missing). The 14% reflects that this domain is a necessary but not sufficient condition: it intersects with Domain 7 (Troubleshooting: diagnosing the prompt that fails) and with Domain 2 (Evaluation: you can't iterate without success criteria).

Official Objectives

  • Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks You'll be given a business task and several prompt formulations: you must choose the one that provides explicit context, constraints, and output format — not the longest one, nor the most polite one.

  • Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests You'll be given a complex request (multiple sources, multiple audiences, multiple deliverables) and you must recognize when to split it into chained steps with inspection points, and when NOT to split it.

  • Iterate prompts to improve output quality You'll be given a prompt that produced a deficient output, and you must choose the correction that attacks the cause (missing criteria, ambiguity, absent context) — not the one that rewrites everything from scratch, nor the one that asks the model to self-correct.

  • Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming) You'll be told the task type and must apply the corresponding strategy: grounding in the document for analysis, source requirements for research, examples and audience for drafting, forced diversity for brainstorming.

Key Concepts

1. The Official Mental Model: The Brilliant New Employee

Anthropic defines the canonical analogy: "Think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows." Brilliant means you don't need to explain what a penalty clause is. New means it doesn't know your process, your audience, your internal policy, or your deliverable format — and it won't guess them.

From this comes the official golden rule, which the exam may quote almost verbatim: "Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too." The nuance that separates those who know the material: the rule doesn't say "if an expert thinks it's fine." It says colleague with minimal context. A prompt that only works because you know what you meant to say is a broken prompt.

2. Anatomy of a Business Prompt

It isn't a ritual template: it's a list of elements that, when missing, produce predictable failures.

ElementWhat it providesWhat fails if you omit it
Role / persona (in system or in the Project instructions)Focuses tone and domain. "Even a single sentence makes a difference."Generic register, tone inconsistent across sessions
Explicit taskVerb + deliverableClaude "converses" instead of delivering
Context and motivation (the why)Lets the instruction generalize to cases you didn't anticipateThe rule is applied literally and breaks on the first edge case
Delimited input dataSeparates instructions from materialThe model confuses your data with your orders
ConstraintsSets limits (audience, length, prohibitions)"Correct" but unusable output
Output formatMakes the output consumable by the next processManual reformatting, which is where the savings die
Escape hatchExplicit permission to say "I don't know"Hallucination out of compliance

The element almost no one includes, and the one the exam rewards: motivation. The documentation's canonical example isn't "NEVER use ellipses," but rather: "Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses since the text-to-speech engine will not know how to pronounce them." Official closing line: "Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation." Operative translation: when you explain the why behind a constraint, Claude extends it to cases you didn't enumerate. When you only prohibit, it doesn't.

3. Say What to Do, Not What Not to Do

Official rule and a frequent exam trap. Instead of "Do not use markdown," the effective formulation is "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs." Prohibitions leave a void: the model knows what to avoid but not what to produce. Positive instructions fix the target.

Corollary along the same axis: over-prompting is a flaw, not a precaution. Current documentation asks you to tone it down with the newer models: "Where you might have said 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...', you can use more normal prompting like 'Use this tool when...'." Writing in all caps, repeating "MANDATORY" three times, or threatening the model doesn't increase compliance; it triggers over-activation (overtriggering) of the behavior you requested, in contexts where it didn't apply.

4. Specificity, Sequential Steps, and Modifiers

  • Be specific about format and constraints. Official example: Create an analytics dashboard (weak) → Create an analytics dashboard. Include as many relevant features and interactions as possible. Go beyond the basics to create a fully-featured implementation. (strong). The second isn't longer for decoration: it adds an ambition modifier that changes the completeness level of the output.
  • Give instructions as sequential steps (numbered list or bullets) when order or completeness matters. If the task has five things to check and you write them in a paragraph, the model will do the first three well.
  • Length: ask for paragraphs or sentences, not exact word counts. The model counts tokens, not words. "Write exactly 250 words" is an instruction it can't reliably fulfill; "three short paragraphs, one per finding" it can.

5. Examples (Few-Shot / Multishot): 3–5, Diverse, Delimited

"Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output format, tone, and structure." It's the most powerful lever for format and voice — more so than any adjective you attach to style.

The three official requirements of a good example:

  • Relevant — a mirror of the real case, not a toy case.
  • Diverse — covers edge cases and varies enough that Claude doesn't learn patterns you didn't want. Three examples that all start with "Dear customer:" teach Claude that everything starts with "Dear customer:".
  • Structured — delimited and labeled (in business practice: clearly marked blocks; in official syntax, <example> tags inside <examples>).

Official number: 3–5. "Include 3–5 examples for best results." The nuance that separates those who know the material: more examples isn't better. It's the classic mistake of the candidate who believes twenty examples are four times better than five; what that actually does is inflate the context and overfit the style to a spurious pattern. And if your examples are poor, you can ask Claude to evaluate their relevance and diversity, or to generate more from a seed.

6. Structure: Separating Instructions from Data

When the prompt mixes instructions + context + examples + variable data, you need to label each type of content. The documentation uses XML tags (<instructions>, <context>, <input>, <documents>) because "XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously." For the Associate profile, the principle matters more than the syntax: the model needs to know which part of the text is an order and which part is material to process. A customer email pasted without delimiting inside a prompt can be read as an instruction.

Official best practices: consistent tag names (not <contexto> in one prompt and <background> in the next) and nested tags when there's a natural hierarchy (multiple documents inside a container, each with its source and content).

7. Long Context: Documents on Top, Question at the End

A hard, verified rule, and one of the most "free" questions in this domain:

Place long documents ABOVE the prompt, above your question, instructions, and examples. "Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests, especially with complex, multi-document inputs."

The threshold the documentation cites for "long inputs" is 20k+ tokens. Every office-work instinct pushes toward the opposite ("first I explain what I want, then I paste the file"), and that is exactly what the exam penalizes.

Additionally, each document must carry its identified source and an index, so Claude can cite where each claim came from. Without source identification, there's no possible traceability in the validation phase (Domain 2).

8. Anti-Hallucination by Prompt: The Three Real Controls

From the official Reduce hallucinations document, the three basic techniques — memorize them, they're the heart of this domain's distractors:

  1. Explicitly allow "I don't know." "Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This simple technique can drastically reduce false information." Model phrase: If you're unsure about any aspect or if the report lacks necessary information, say "I don't have enough information to confidently assess this." Without this valve, the model is implicitly obligated to produce something, and that "something" is the hallucination.
  2. Direct quotes first (grounding). For long documents: ask it to extract the relevant verbatim quotes BEFORE doing the task, and then base the analysis only on those quotes. Two-phase pattern: quotes first, then the analysis built on them.
  3. Restriction of external knowledge. Explicitly prohibit it from using its general knowledge and force it to rely only on the material provided.

And the official disclaimer the exam uses as a realism filter: "while these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions." No prompt replaces human verification. A candidate who chooses "I added 'don't hallucinate' to the prompt, it's solved now" has failed two domains at once.

9. Task Decomposition

Two levels, and you need to know which to choose:

  • Decomposition WITHIN a prompt: numbered steps in a single request. Useful when the task is a single one but has parts that can be forgotten. Cost: zero extra calls.
  • Prompt chaining: splitting into separate requests — generate → review → refine. Useful when you want to inspect the intermediate result, when each step has a different success criterion, or when a human must approve before continuing.

Criteria for splitting (this is the judgment being assessed):

  • The output mixes different genres (analysis + writing + recommendation) and the model averages across the three, doing all three halfway.
  • You need a human checkpoint in the middle (the data goes to a high-stakes audience: legal, compliance, client, leadership).
  • Step 2 depends on a decision you want to make yourself, not delegate.
  • The material exceeds what you want to review at once: if you can't audit the output, you can't use it.

Criteria for NOT splitting — and this is the one people fail: breaking a simple task into twelve micro-steps adds latency, cost, failure points, and reassembly work, without gaining quality. Decomposition is a tool, not a ritual of virtue. If the task is "classify these 30 tickets into 4 categories," splitting it into 30 calls is a lapse in judgment, not a demonstration of rigor.

10. Iteration: The Empirical Cycle

Before writing the prompt, the documentation requires three prerequisites, literally:

"1. A clear definition of the success criteria for your use case; 2. Some ways to empirically test against those criteria; 3. A first draft prompt you want to improve."

This is counterintuitive for the business profile, and that's exactly why it's tested: you first define what "good" means and how you'll verify it; only then do you write the prompt. A useful success criterion is specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant — "good-quality summaries" is not a criterion; "all five contractual deadlines appear and match the source text" is.

The cycle: define criteria → build test cases → draft prompt → test and iterate → final validation.

Rules of disciplined iteration:

  • Change one variable at a time. If you rewrite the role, add examples, and change the format in the same pass, you won't know what worked.
  • Diagnose before rewriting. The failure has a nameable cause: ambiguous instruction, absent context, undeclared success criteria, insufficiently diverse examples, inverted context order, or a problem that isn't a prompt problem at all.
  • Keep a regression set. Five real cases that represent the distribution of the work, including the ugly ones. Every version of the prompt gets re-run against the five. Without this, "improving the prompt" is superstition.
  • Self-verification at the end of the prompt (official technique): "Before you finish, verify your answer against [test criteria]." This is indeed a useful control within the prompt — but pay attention to the Domain 2 nuance: it's a control against criteria that you set, not a self-assessment of the model's confidence in its own accuracy (the latter is not a valid signal).
  • And the rule the exam loves: "Not every success criteria or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering. For example, latency and cost can be sometimes more easily improved by selecting a different model." If the problem is that it's slow or expensive, don't rewrite the prompt: switch models (Domain 3).

11. Strategy by Task Type

The official objective names four types. Each has a characteristic failure and a characteristic defense.

Task typeTypical failureDominant strategy
AnalysisInvents figures or conclusions the document doesn't supportDocument on top, question at the end; quotes first, analysis on top of the quotes; prohibit external knowledge; ask for the explicit analysis criterion, not just the verdict
ResearchCites sources that sound real but don't existRequire an identifiable source per claim; the model is not the authoritative source; verify against the original source; under high uncertainty, run the same prompt multiple times and compare (best-of-N): inconsistency across runs gives away the hallucination
DraftingGeneric, correct, voiceless text3–5 examples of approved pieces (few-shot is the real lever for tone); stated audience; length in paragraphs/sentences; a list of what must NOT appear, phrased positively when possible
BrainstormingFifteen variants of the same ideaForce explicit diversity: name the axes that must differ, require mutually exclusive categories, ban sector clichés; split into two phases — diverge first, converge after (applied decomposition). Ask for evaluation criteria afterward, not during

The cross-cutting nuance: for analysis and research, constraint is the virtue (it locks the model into the material). For drafting and brainstorming, the constraint is audience and diversity (the model has freedom, but with a defined target).

12. What Is NOT a Prompting Lever for an Associate

A hygiene block, because the exam plants technically sophisticated distractors that fall outside the scope of the credential:

  • temperature and other sampling parameters are not your tool. In claude.ai you don't touch them, and in the current high-end models (Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8) non-default values for temperature, top_p, and top_k are directly rejected by the API. Style is steered with the prompt, not with sampling.
  • Deep reasoning is requested with general instructions, not a hand-written step-by-step plan. "Prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps. A prompt like 'think thoroughly' often produces better reasoning than a hand-written step-by-step plan." Manual chain-of-thought (<thinking> … <answer>) is today a fallback for when extended reasoning is turned off.
  • Any option that sounds like an endpoint, parameter, or header in an item on this exam is suspicious by definition: the credential explicitly states that no API experience is required.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Marta, Ops Lead: The 63-Page Contract

Situation. Marta, an operations lead at a carrier company, must extract all late-delivery penalty clauses from a 63-page contract so Finance can model the quarter's risk. The amount at stake is around $400,000.

Mediocre candidate. Writes: "I'm going to send you a contract. Summarize the penalty clauses." and pastes the PDF below it. Gets back six well-written bullet points, two of which cite percentages that don't appear in the contract. Since the summary sounds professional, they forward it.

Competent candidate. Places the document first and the instruction at the end. Asks for two phases: (1) extract the verbatim quotes of every clause that mentions penalty, late fee, non-compliance discount, or service level, each with its section number; (2) only then, tabulate section / trigger / calculation formula / cap. Adds the escape valve: "If a clause is ambiguous or you can't find the information, say so explicitly instead of inferring it." And prohibits external knowledge: the analysis is based only on the extracted quotes.

Why. The document→question order is worth up to 30% quality on multi-document inputs. The quotes-first pattern makes every claim verifiable against the text: Marta can audit six quotes in ten minutes, something impossible with six unsourced bullet points. And the escape hatch is what stops the model from filling the gap of the ambiguous clause with a plausible invention.

Example 2 — Diego, Marketing: 40 Subject Lines That Are the Same Subject Line

Situation. Diego is preparing the campaign for a B2B webinar. He asks for 40 subject lines. He gets back 40 lines that are four ideas with synonyms swapped in: all of them start with a number or with "How to."

Mediocre candidate. Asks again: "Give me 40 more, but more creative." Gets another 40 from the same mold, because nothing structural changed. Concludes that "AI isn't good for creativity."

Competent candidate. Diagnoses the failure: there's no declared diversity axis and no examples. Reformulates: defines five mutually exclusive angles (avoided loss, curiosity, social proof, counterintuitive, operational urgency), requires 8 subject lines per angle, explicitly bans the patterns already seen ("don't start with a number or with 'How to'"), and attaches four historical subject lines with their real open rates as examples of the approved voice. Afterward, in a separate second request, asks it to evaluate the 40 against three business criteria and select the 6 finalists.

Why. Brainstorming fails through convergence, and convergence is countered by structuring the search space before generating. The 3–5 examples fix the voice without fixing the mold (which is why they must be diverse, not four variants of the same subject line). And separating generation from evaluation is decomposition: mixing both into a single request makes the model self-censor while generating and produce the safe option.

Example 3 — Lucía, PM: The Monolithic Quarterly Report

Situation. Lucía must produce her program's quarterly report: consolidate three sources (progress dashboard, risk meeting minutes, a 120-response satisfaction survey), analyze deviations, and draft a one-page executive summary for the leadership committee.

Mediocre candidate. Asks for everything in one giant prompt. Gets a text that analyzes superficially, writes acceptably, and mixes findings with recommendations without distinguishing them. Doesn't know which part to review first.

Competent candidate. Chains three requests with inspection in between:

  1. Extraction: from each source, the facts with their origin (figure + where it came from). Lucía reviews this table — 8 minutes — and corrects two misread figures.
  2. Analysis: on top of the now-validated table, identify deviations from the plan and their probable cause, marking what is evidence and what is hypothesis.
  3. Drafting: executive summary for the committee, with stated audience and format, based solely on the approved analysis.

Why. The three steps have different success criteria (fidelity, reasoning, tone) and can't be optimized at once. The human checkpoint after step 1 is what prevents a reading error from propagating all the way to the leadership committee, amplified and well written. Note what she didn't do: she didn't split the extraction into three separate calls, one per source. That would have been ritual, not judgment.

Example 4 — Andrés, L&D: The Rubric That Always Comes Out Generic

Situation. Andrés generates evaluation rubrics for a training program. They always come out flat: four levels, vague adjectives ("adequate," "excellent"), no observable behaviors. He has rewritten the prompt five times, changing several things each time, with no improvement.

Mediocre candidate. Writes a 900-word prompt with "IMPORTANT: the rubric MUST be specific and high-quality, DO NOT use generic language" in all caps.

Competent candidate. Stops rewriting and defines the success criterion first: "each level describes a classroom behavior that is observable, verifiable by an outside observer without knowing the student." With that criterion, the diagnosis is immediate: the prompt never said what makes a rubric good. The fix is a single variable: adding two real, already-approved rubrics from the team as examples. He sets a regression set of five distinct competencies and re-runs against all five before signing off on the new version. He adds a self-verification closer: "Before finishing, verify that each level descriptor is observable by a third party; if any isn't, rewrite it."

Why. Shouting "be specific" in all caps doesn't define specificity: it's over-prompting, and its documented effect is over-activation, not precision. Examples are the real lever for format and voice; the success criterion is what lets you know whether the iteration worked; the regression set is what keeps you from fixing one case and breaking four others without noticing.

Example 5 — Sofía, Communications: The Press Release and the Word-Count Trap

Situation. Sofía needs a launch press release. She asks: "Write a press release of exactly 400 words, with a professional but approachable tone, and make sure all the facts are correct."

Mediocre candidate. Gets back 480 words, a tone indistinguishable from any press release in the world, and a figure of "over 10,000 users" that no one gave it. She replies to Claude: "Are you sure that figure is correct?", Claude says yes, and Sofía publishes it.

Competent candidate. (a) Requests length as structure, not an exact count: "headline, lede, and four paragraphs, none longer than three sentences" — because the model counts tokens, not words. (b) Attaches three approved press releases from the company as voice examples: that defines "professional but approachable" a thousand times better than the adjective does. (c) Delivers a closed fact sheet (figures, dates, titles, verbatim spokesperson quotes) and explicitly prohibits any fact not on the sheet, with an escape valve: "if a fact is missing, leave a [PENDING: fact] marker instead of estimating it." (d) Verifies the figures against the fact sheet, not by asking Claude if it's sure.

Why. The mediocre candidate's three errors are archetypal: an exact word count (an instruction the model can't reliably meet), a tone adjective with no example (which conveys nothing), and circular self-verification — asking the model whether its own output is correct is not a control; self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy.

How the Exam Asks This

Verbs and stem signals. Items in this domain announce themselves with: "write a prompt", "which prompt would be most effective", "break down", "decompose", "the task is complex", "the output is too generic / too vague", "how should the associate structure the request", and with the explicit name of the task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming). The wording "most effective" / "most appropriate" is the tell that there will be several defensible options and only one is the best under the constraint stated in the stem.

The shape of the correct answer. As throughout the exam: the disciplined middle action. Structuring, decomposing with judgment, iterating on evidence, adapting the strategy to the task type. Neither the shortcut (sending a one-line prompt) nor maximalism (a 900-word prompt with twenty examples and all caps).

Distractors specific to this domain — connect them to the decoder's archetypes:

  • "Add 'don't make up data' / 'don't hallucinate' to the prompt." — Archetype C, the Fake Control. Instructing the model is not a governance or accuracy control. The real control is grounding in quotes + the "I don't know" escape hatch + human verification against the source. The documentation says so: the techniques reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them.
  • "Ask Claude to review its own answer and confirm it's correct." — Archetype B, Circular Self-Verification. A model is not the authoritative source about its own accuracy. Watch the fine nuance: asking it to "verify your answer against these [explicit] criteria" is a valid official technique within the prompt; asking it "are you sure?" or "rate your confidence" is not. The difference is whether the criterion comes from outside or from inside the model.
  • "Use the most capable model to fix the vague output." — Archetype F, Wrong Lever. A vague output caused by a vague prompt isn't fixed with more intelligence; it's fixed with specificity, context, and format. (And its mirror image: if the real problem is latency or cost, then yes, the lever is switching models, not rewriting the prompt — that's the official line.)
  • "Add 15–20 examples to maximize quality." — The docs say 3–5, and require diversity. More examples that lack diversity teach unwanted patterns.
  • "Paste the question first and the 60-page document at the end." — Backwards: documents on top, query at the end. Up to +30% quality.
  • "Split the task into 12 sub-prompts" when the task is a simple classification — ritual decomposition: it adds cost, latency, and reassembly work without gaining quality.
  • "Rewrite the prompt from scratch" when the output failed — the exam rewards diagnosing the cause and changing one variable, not starting over. Rewriting everything is indistinguishable from guessing.
  • "Write the prompt in all caps / repeat CRITICAL / threaten the model" — over-prompting; the docs call for the opposite tone.

Sample items, exam-style (stated in English, as on the real test):

1. An operations associate must extract all late-delivery penalty clauses from a 60-page carrier contract for the finance team. Which prompt structure is most effective? A. Ask the question first, then paste the contract below it, and request a bulleted summary. B. Place the contract at the top, then instruct Claude to first extract verbatim quotes of every penalty clause with its section number, and only then tabulate them — stating explicitly when information is missing. C. Paste the contract and add "Summarize the penalty clauses. Do not hallucinate." D. Split the contract into 60 prompts, one per page, and merge the outputs.

Correct: B. It applies three official rules at once: document on top / instruction at the end (up to +30% on complex inputs), grounding in quotes before analysis, and an escape hatch for missing information. A reverses the order. C is the Fake Control: "do not hallucinate" is not a control. D is ritual decomposition: it multiplies cost and reassembly work, and destroys the context between pages.

2. A marketing associate's brainstorming prompt keeps returning 40 subject lines that are variations of the same four ideas. What is the best next step? A. Ask for 40 more and specify "be more creative." B. Switch to the most capable, highest-cost model. C. Define mutually exclusive angles, require a quota of ideas per angle, ban the patterns already produced, and supply 3–5 diverse approved examples. D. Increase the temperature setting.

Correct: C. The failure is convergence, and it's corrected by structuring the search space + diverse examples. A changes nothing structural. B is Default Maximalism: the problem isn't capability. D is outside the Associate's scope and, in the current high-end models, non-default values for temperature are rejected by the API — style is steered with the prompt.

3. Before improving a prompt that produces generic training rubrics, what should the associate do first? A. Rewrite the prompt from scratch with more forceful language. B. Define measurable success criteria for what a good rubric contains, and a small set of real cases to test against. C. Ask Claude to rate the quality of its own rubric from 1 to 10. D. Add "IMPORTANT: be specific" in capital letters.

Correct: B. It's the official prerequisite for prompt engineering: success criteria + a way to test them empirically + a draft to improve. A and D are over-prompting (and the docs call for toning it down, not up). C is circular self-verification.

Common Mistakes

  1. Pasting the question before the long document. → Documents on top, question and examples at the end. Up to +30% quality on multi-document inputs.
  2. Believing "don't hallucinate" is a control. → The control is grounding in quotes + explicit permission to say "I don't know" + human verification against the source. And even then the risk isn't eliminated: "they don't eliminate them entirely."
  3. Asking Claude whether its answer is correct. → Self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy. Self-verification does count when the criterion is external and explicit ("verify against these criteria: …").
  4. Confusing a long prompt with a good prompt. → A good prompt is one a colleague with minimal context could execute. Length ≠ clarity.
  5. Piling up 15 examples. → 3–5, relevant, diverse, and delimited. Examples that lack diversity teach patterns you didn't want.
  6. Only prohibiting, never describing. → "Do not use markdown" → "Respond in flowing prose paragraphs." Say what to do, not what not to do.
  7. Writing in all caps and repeating "MANDATORY." → Over-prompting; it triggers over-activation, not obedience. The docs call for a normal tone.
  8. Omitting the reason behind the constraint. → With the motivation, the model generalizes the rule to cases you didn't enumerate. Without it, it applies the rule literally and fails on the first edge case.
  9. Asking for "exactly 400 words." → The model counts tokens, not words. Ask for paragraphs, sentences, or sections.
  10. Decomposing as ritual. → Splitting a simple task into twelve calls adds cost, latency, and reassembly without gaining quality. You decompose when there are distinct success criteria or a human checkpoint is needed.
  11. Iterating by changing five things at once. → One variable per iteration, against a regression set of real cases. Otherwise, you don't know what worked.
  12. Writing the prompt before knowing what "good" looks like. → Official prerequisite: success criteria + a way to test them empirically. That comes first, the prompt comes after.
  13. Trying to fix a latency or cost problem with prompting. → "Latency and cost can be sometimes more easily improved by selecting a different model." That's a Domain 3 problem, not a Domain 1 problem.
  14. Mixing data and instructions without delimiting them. → Label each block consistently. Third-party text pasted without delimiting can be read as an order.

Few-shot / multishot promptingExample-driven promptingIncluding 3–5 relevant, diverse examples to fix format, tone, and structure.
Zero-shotNo-example promptingRequesting the task without showing any sample of the desired output.
Task decompositionSplitting a task into stepsBreaking a complex request into steps, each with its own success criteria.
Prompt chainingLinked, separate requestsRunning the steps as separate requests (generate → review → refine) so the intermediate result can be inspected.
Chain of thought (CoT)Explicit reasoning before the answerRequesting explicit reasoning before the response; today it's a fallback for when extended reasoning is turned off.
GroundingAnchoring claims in the sourceRequiring every claim to be backed by verbatim quotes from the material provided.
Escape hatchPermission to say "I don't know"Explicit permission to say "I don't have enough information" instead of making something up.
HallucinationConfident, unsupported outputPlausible, confidently stated content that isn't backed by any real source.
Success criteriaDefinition of a good outputA specific, measurable definition of what makes the output good; set before the prompt.
IterationTest-diagnose-adjust cycleThe cycle of testing, diagnosing the cause, changing one variable, and re-testing against real cases.
Regression setFixed set of real test casesA fixed set of real cases you re-run every prompt version against.
Over-promptingShouted, hyper-emphatic instructionsShouted or hyper-emphatic instructions that trigger over-activation instead of precision.
Long contextLarge input handlingLarge inputs (20k+ tokens): documents on top, question at the end.
Best-of-N verificationRun-and-compare consistency checkRunning the same prompt N times and comparing; inconsistency gives away the hallucination.
Output formatRequested output structureThe structure explicitly requested (table, bullets, prose, fields) so the output is consumable.

Checklist

If you can't check off one of these, you haven't mastered Domain 1.

  • I can state the official golden rule ("show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context…") and use it to judge someone else's prompt.
  • I can name the seven elements of a business prompt and say what fails when each one is omitted.
  • I know why adding the motivation behind a constraint improves generalization, and I can give the text-to-speech example.
  • I know that a positive instruction ("respond in flowing prose") beats a prohibition ("don't use markdown"), and why.
  • I know that over-prompting (ALL CAPS, "CRITICAL," threats) degrades the result instead of reinforcing it.
  • I know the official number of few-shot examples (3–5) and their three requirements (relevant, diverse, delimited) — and why "more" isn't better.
  • I can explain why documents go on top and the question goes at the end, and cite the order of magnitude of the improvement (up to ~30%).
  • I know the three anti-hallucination prompting techniques (allow "I don't know," quotes first, restrict external knowledge), and I know that none of them eliminates the risk.
  • I can distinguish valid self-verification (against explicit external criteria) from circular self-verification (asking the model if it's sure).
  • I know when to decompose a task (distinct success criteria, human checkpoint, inspecting the intermediate result) and when not to (ritual decomposition of a simple task).
  • I can state the three official prerequisites before doing prompt engineering (success criteria, a way to test them, a draft to improve).
  • I iterate by changing one variable at a time against a regression set of real cases, and I diagnose the cause before rewriting.
  • I can recognize when the problem isn't a prompt problem (latency, cost, scope) and what the correct lever is in that case.
  • I can give the dominant strategy for each task type: analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming — and the typical failure mode of each.
  • I know that style is steered with the prompt, not with sampling parameters, and that any exam option that sounds like an API parameter is outside the scope of this credential.

domains.title: Output Evaluation and Validation
objectives: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
Determine when human review or additional verification is required
Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 21%

This is the largest domain on the exam, and that's no accident. A language model generates text that sounds correct because it's optimized to produce plausible language, not true language. When the Associate pastes that output into an email, a compliance report, or a presentation to the committee, the model disappears from the chain of accountability: the name attached to it is the human's. Domain 2 measures exactly that — whether the candidate is a filter or a conduit. The MQC's stated profile says it without mincing words: they know how to "critically evaluate AI-generated content, adapt outputs for different audiences, and recognize when human expertise, validation, or escalation is required."

The business decision this domain represents is a single one: what do I control before this leaves my hands, and how much control does this particular output deserve? Not every piece of text needs forensic verification; verifying everything with the same intensity is as costly as verifying nothing. The competent professional calibrates: they distinguish a verifiable claim from a stylistic choice; they distinguish a reversible decision from an irreversible one; they distinguish an internal audience from a regulated one. And they know that the real control lives outside the model — in the authoritative source, in the system of record, in the human reviewer — never inside the very conversation that produced the output. The three official sample items include one from this domain, and its moral is literal: the model's self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy.

Official Objectives

Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness You'll be asked to separate three axes that the mediocre candidate conflates: whether it's accurate (the facts are true), whether it's complete (nothing the task asked for is missing), and whether it's well written (fluency). An output can have all three, or only the third.

Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses Recognizing the three failure modes by their shape: a specific invented data point (citation, subsection, figure, date, URL), an internal contradiction or one between runs, and an output systematically skewed by how it was asked or by the sources used.

Apply fact-checking and validation techniques Applying the right control: cross-checking against the primary source, requiring verifiable citations, restricting to the documents provided, regenerating and comparing. Not "asking Claude not to make things up."

Determine when human review or additional verification is required Setting the threshold. Which outputs pass straight through, which need a second pair of eyes, which need a subject-matter expert, and which get escalated to an Architect or Developer because the problem is no longer editorial but technical.

Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience Rewriting the same facts for an executive, a specialist, a client, or the legal department — and comparing two versions against a rubric, not against personal taste.

Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data) Choosing between an inline response, an artifact (a reusable, editable artifact), or structured data (table / CSV / JSON), depending on what will be done with the output afterward. Curating: removing duplicates, flagging gaps, separating fact from inference.

Key Concepts

The Three Independent Axes: Accuracy, Completeness, Fluency

  • Accuracy: every verifiable claim is true against an external source.
  • Completeness: the output covers everything the task asked for. A contract summary that omits the termination clause is 100% accurate and 60% complete — and it is a failure.
  • Fluency: the prose reads well.

The nuance that separates those who know the material: fluency is the variable the model optimizes for, and the only one of the three that tells you nothing about the other two. Fluency bias is the central error this domain punishes. When you evaluate, evaluate the three axes separately, and never let rhetorical quality serve as evidence of accuracy.

A practical corollary on completeness: completeness is evaluated against an acceptance list written before prompting, not against your memory afterward. If you asked to "summarize the policy and identify the three applicable deadlines," your checklist is: (1) summary, (2) deadline A, (3) deadline B, (4) deadline C. If the model delivers two deadlines with flawless prose, one is missing.

Hallucination

Precise definition: the model produces a specific, plausible, and false claim, in the same tone of certainty it uses for true ones. It is not a random typo-like error: it is the structural consequence of generating text that "fits" rather than consulting a database.

Where it hallucinates most — the surfaces you need to check first:

  • Citations and references: subsection numbers, articles, pages, DOIs, study titles, URLs.
  • Figures: percentages, amounts, market sizes, dates.
  • Proper names: people, titles, companies, products.
  • Verbatim quotes attributed to someone.
  • Anything after the knowledge cutoff. The current frontier models (Claude Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5) have a reliable knowledge cutoff of January 2026; Claude Haiku 4.5's is February 2025. An event, price, regulation, or version released after that date is not in the model: it either comes from a source you gave it, from a real-time web search, or it's invention.

Operative rule: the more specific and verifiable a data point is, the more mandatory it is to verify it. Specificity is exactly what lends credibility to the hallucination — which is why the official sample item uses "citing a specific subsection number."

Anthropic documents that anti-hallucination techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations but don't eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions." That disclaimer is exam doctrine: no model, prompt, or configuration exists that exempts you from verifying. The option "use the more expensive model so it won't hallucinate" is a distractor.

Anti-Hallucination Controls an Associate Can Actually Apply (They're Prompts and Configuration, Not Code)

  1. Explicitly allow "I don't know." Working phrase: "If you can't find the information in the documents provided, respond: 'I don't have enough information to state this with confidence.'" The official documentation calls it a simple technique that drastically reduces false information. Without explicit permission not to know, the model tends to fill the gap.
  2. Anchoring in verbatim quotes (direct quotes for grounding). For long documents (>20k tokens ≈ dozens of pages), first ask for the word-for-word extraction of the relevant passages, and only afterward the analysis: "First extract the exact quotes from the policy relevant to X. If there are no relevant quotes, say 'No relevant quotes were found.' Then base your analysis solely on those quotes." It turns a memory task into a reading task.
  3. Post-hoc citation verification. After generating, ask it to go through each claim and attach the supporting quote; if it can't find the quote, have it withdraw the claim and flag the gap. A report with two flagged gaps is far better than one with no gaps and two fabrications.
  4. Restriction of external knowledge. Explicit instruction: "Use exclusively the attached documents. Do not use your general knowledge." It's the natural control in Projects with knowledge sources.
  5. Best-of-N verification (regenerate and compare). Run the same prompt multiple times in clean chats and compare. Inconsistencies across runs are a signal of hallucination. Critical nuance: this detects instability, it doesn't confirm truth — three matching runs can all three be wrong. It's a cheap filter, not a verification.

The Two Anti-Controls (The Exam's Favorite Distractors)

  • Circular self-verification: asking Claude how confident it is, or asking it to review its own output in the same thread, and using that as the criterion for sending. An LLM's self-reported confidence is not calibrated with its accuracy. Hard rule: a model is never the authoritative source about its own accuracy.
  • Instruction-as-control: "I told it not to make things up," "I asked it to only use real sources." It reduces the probability; it is not a verification control, and it does not substitute for cross-checking against the source. It serves as mitigation, not as evidence.

Fine-grained note, because the exam exploits it: asking Claude to critique an output in a new chat, with an explicit rubric and without the context of having written it, is indeed a valid, documented technique (LLM-as-judge; official best practice even calls for the judge to be a different model from the generator). What is circular is asking "are you sure?" in the same thread that produced the text. The difference: external rubric and separation from the generator vs. self-confidence within the same context.

Inconsistency

Three forms, and you need to be able to tell them apart:

  • Internal: the text contradicts itself — the percentages don't add up to 100, the summary says "three risks" and lists four, the conclusion doesn't follow from the body.
  • Across runs: the same prompt produces different answers. A signal that the model is guessing (see best-of-N).
  • Against the source: the output contradicts the document you yourself uploaded. It's the most serious failure in a Project with knowledge sources, and the easiest to detect: search for the phrase in the document.

Bias

On this exam, "bias" isn't a philosophical debate: it's a defect in the output that must be detected and corrected. Forms relevant to an Associate:

  • Framing bias (framing / leading prompt). "Write the reasons to choose vendor A" produces, by construction, a one-sided text. The bias was introduced by the prompt, not the model. Fix: ask for a symmetric analysis, the strongest counter-case, and the evidence that would refute the conclusion.
  • Source selection bias. Documented by Anthropic in its own research systems: the tendency to prefer SEO-optimized content over academic or authoritative sources. Translation for the Associate: if Claude searched the web, check what it cited, not just that it cited something. Five vendor blogs are not five sources.
  • Representational bias: people, examples, names, and assumptions that reproduce stereotypes in HR, marketing, or education materials. Fixed by reviewing who appears, how, and what is assumed by default.
  • User confirmation bias: accepting the output that matches what you already believed and scrutinizing the one that doesn't. It's the evaluator's bias, not the model's, and it's the one that does the most damage.

External Verification: The Evidence Hierarchy for the Associate

When a claim needs confirming, this is the order. Drop a level only if the one above doesn't exist:

  1. Authoritative primary source — the official text of the regulation, the signed contract, the system of record (ERP, CRM), the audited financial statement.
  2. Organizational knowledge source — the document in the Project's knowledge source, the approved connector (Google Drive, Gmail), the current internal policy.
  3. Reputable secondary source with a visible date.
  4. Claude's claim about itself — level zero. It is not evidence.

Separating nuance: Claude citing a link doesn't mean the link says that. Web search reduces factual hallucination, but it introduces the possibility of an incorrect attribution to a real source. Opening the link and searching for the phrase is part of the job.

When Human Review Is Required (and From Whom)

It isn't "always," nor "whenever I have time." It's a function of risk. It demands human review — normally from a subject-matter expert, not just any colleague — when the output meets one or more of the following:

  • Irreversible: it gets published, sent to a client, presented to a regulator, executed as a decision.
  • High-stakes audience: compliance, legal, finance, leadership, external client, media.
  • Consequence for people: health, employment, credit, grades, benefits.
  • Contains verifiable claims you cannot verify due to lack of access or expertise.
  • Deals with facts after the knowledge cutoff and there was no grounding in documents or search.
  • Feeds into a number: if the figure goes into a financial model, a dashboard, or a forecast, it gets verified against the system of record.

And the different kind of escalation: when the problem stops being editorial and becomes technical — API integration, designing an agentic system, architecture, automated evaluation at scale — the Associate escalates to a Claude Architect or Developer. Escalating isn't dodging: it's recognizing the boundary of scope. But if a compliant action exists within the Associate's scope, that action wins; abandoning the task is the distractor.

Success Criteria Before Evaluating (Define Success)

Anthropic defines good success criteria as Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and notes that most cases require multidimensional evaluation. The official categories: task fidelity, consistency, relevance and coherence, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, price. Latency and cost are first-class criteria, not footnotes.

Translation to the Associate's world: before prompting, write the acceptance list. "This draft works if: (a) it covers the four sections of the brief, (b) every figure has a citable, verifiable source, (c) it doesn't exceed 500 words, (d) the tone is informative, not promotional, (e) it doesn't mention clients by name." That list is the rubric you evaluate with — and it's what turns "I'm not convinced" into "it fails (b) and (e)."

Comparing Outputs: Rubric, Not Taste

Comparing two drafts by "seeing which one reads better" is fluency dressed up as evaluation. The correct technique:

  • Score both against the same written rubric, criterion by criterion, with an empirical output (pass/fail, or 1–5). Anthropic's documentation is explicit: purely qualitative evaluations "are difficult to assess quickly and at scale."
  • Ask for reasoning before the verdict, then keep only the verdict (the reasoning improves the judgment; the verdict is what you consume).
  • When you use Claude as a judge, do it in a clean chat, with the rubric pasted in, and preferably with a different model from the one that generated the text ("generally best practice").
  • Volume over polish: more cases reviewed with a simple criterion beats a few cases reviewed under a magnifying glass. It's the official evals doctrine ("prioritize volume over quality"), and it applies just as well to manually reviewing a batch of 40 emails.

Adapting for the Audience (Edit, Adapt, Refine)

Same facts, different rendering. The axes you change: register, length, admissible jargon, what goes first, what gets omitted, what gets quantified.

  • Executive: conclusion first, three bullets, the figure that decides, the risk, the ask. No process.
  • Specialist: method, assumptions, data limitations, sources.
  • Client: benefit, no internal jargon, no conditionals that scare without informing.
  • Legal/compliance: bounded claims, each with its source, no adjective that creates exposure.

Order matters, and the exam measures it: verify first, adapt second. Adapting the tone of a text that contains a false citation produces a text with a false citation and a better tone. That's the "cosmetic" archetype, and it is always wrong when the stem poses a factual problem.

Output Format: Inline, Artifact, or Structured Data

The objective names it explicitly, and it's the part of the domain most candidates wing. The rule is what will be done with the output afterward:

FormatWhenWhy
Inline (in the thread)Short, conversational, single-use response; part of a reasoning back-and-forthZero friction; it's read and discarded. Encapsulating it would be over-engineering
ArtifactSubstantial, self-contained content that will be reused, edited, versioned, exported, or delivered: a document, policy draft, plan, long table, diagram, codeLives as an editable, iterable object outside the chat flow; it can be refined without rewriting the whole conversation, and it's delivered as-is
Structured data (table, CSV, JSON)The output will be compared, sorted, filtered, aggregated, or consumed by another person or systemStructure makes the information auditable and actionable

Expert-level nuance — format is an evaluation control, not decoration: if you ask for a table with columns claim | source | verified? | page, you force the model to expose where each thing comes from and make the gaps visible. The same information in prose hides exactly those gaps. Choosing structure is choosing verifiability.

Curating and Organizing Information

Curating is not summarizing. It is: deduplicating, prioritizing by relevance to the decision, explicitly flagging gaps ("not found in the sources provided"), and separating fact from inference from recommendation. A working trick that pays off on the exam and in life: ask for every line to be labeled [Fact — source], [Inference], or [Recommendation]. As soon as you see it separated out, 90% of the evaluation is already done: facts get verified, inferences get questioned, recommendations get discussed.

Worked Examples

1. The Subsection That Doesn't Exist (Compliance)

Situation. Mariana, an operations lead at an insurance company, asks Claude for a summary of a new regulatory circular. The output is flawless: three paragraphs, executive tone, and it states that "subsection 4.3(b) requires client notification within 45 calendar days." The summary is due to the compliance team this afternoon.

Mediocre candidate. Sends it (it sounds confident, and Claude didn't hedge). Or asks Claude "how confident are you about subsection 4.3(b)?" and, given a "very confident," sends it. Or rewrites it in a more formal tone before sending.

Competent candidate. Opens the official text of the circular and looks up subsection 4.3(b) and the deadline. Finds that the subsection exists but the deadline is 30 business days, and that "4.3(b)" actually regulates something else. Redoes the summary with citation grounding: asks Claude to first extract the verbatim quotes from the circular and only then draft the summary. Delivers a table claim | subsection | verbatim quote | verified, with one row marked "not verifiable in the source — removed."

Why. The real control lives outside the model: the primary source. Self-reported confidence is not evidence (circular self-verification), and polishing the tone doesn't touch the problem (cosmetic fix). The specificity of the citation is precisely the risk signal, not a quality signal.

2. The 18% Growth Figure (Marketing)

Situation. Diego, from marketing, asks for a competitive brief. Claude states: "the B2B subscription market in LATAM grew 18% in 2025, according to a consulting firm's annual report." The brief is headed to the pricing committee.

Mediocre candidate. Leaves the figure in because "it comes with a source." Changes "18%" to "around 20%" to hedge.

Competent candidate. Knows two things: (a) a figure with a cited source is the most credible form a hallucination can take, and (b) 2025 is close to the knowledge cutoff, and annual data is usually published later. Looks up the report. If the report exists and says something else → corrects it. If the data point can't be found → withdraws the claim and replaces it with "[unverified data: cited report not located]." The brief ships with one fewer figure and zero risk of the committee setting prices on a fabrication. Also asks Claude to regenerate the same brief twice in clean chats: if the figure changes between runs, that confirms it was guessing.

Why. Rounding a false figure doesn't make it true: it makes it false and vague. The only honest output when there's no source is the flagged gap. Best-of-N as a cheap filter, the source as the verification.

3. The Vendor Who "Obviously" Wins (Procurement)

Situation. A PM asks: "Write the reasons why we should choose vendor A over vendor B." Claude delivers eight solid, well-written arguments. The PM brings them to the board.

Mediocre candidate. Presents them as "the AI's analysis." Loves that it confirms what they already thought.

Competent candidate. Recognizes that the bias was introduced by the prompt: it asked for a brief for the defense, not an analysis. Re-prompts symmetrically: decision criteria first (total cost, SLA, integration, vendor risk), then A and B evaluated against each criterion, then the strongest case against A and what evidence would refute it. Also checks what sources Claude used: if they're three marketing pages from vendor A itself, source selection bias is active and the analysis is worth little.

Why. The objective says "identify … biases in responses." The one-sided answer wasn't a model error: it was the reflection of a one-sided prompt. Fixing the prompt is fixing the evaluation.

4. Twelve Course Proposals and a Committee (Education)

Situation. An academic coordinator has 12 course proposals and needs a committee to decide within 40 minutes. Claude returns six paragraphs of prose per proposal.

Mediocre candidate. Pastes all 72 paragraphs into the committee's email.

Competent candidate. Changes the format, because the use changed: the output is going to be compared, not read. Requests a structured table with fixed columns (proposal | hours | cost | prerequisites | alignment with the plan | cited evidence | gaps), generates it as an artifact so it can be iterated on and delivered, and writes three inline bullets in the body of the email with the recommendation and the two runners-up. Before sending, verifies the three deciding figures (cost, hours, prerequisites) in the original proposals: the structure showed exactly which ones they were.

Why. It's the format objective: inline for the conversational, artifact for the reusable and deliverable, structure for the comparable. And the structure made verification possible — in prose, the three numbers would have gone through unreviewed.

5. Which of the Two Drafts? (Communications)

Situation. Two versions of an internal policy-change announcement. Version 1 is more elegant; version 2 is flatter.

Mediocre candidate. Picks version 1 because "it reads better."

Competent candidate. Writes the rubric before looking: (a) states the exact effective date, (b) explains what the employee needs to do, (c) links the full policy, (d) ≤300 words, (e) neutral, non-defensive tone. Scores both versions criterion by criterion, in a clean chat, pasting in the rubric and requesting pass / fail output with one line of reasoning per criterion. Version 1 fails (a) and (c). Takes version 2, fixes the tone, and sends it.

Why. "Comparing outputs for the audience" means comparing against explicit criteria. The rubric turns taste into evidence — and separating the judge from the generator (clean chat, external rubric) avoids circularity.

How the Exam Asks This

Verbs and stem anchors. "What is the most appropriate action?", "Before sending/sharing …", "What should the associate do first?", "Which approach best ensures accuracy?", "Select two". Words that give away Domain 2: confident, cites, specific subsection / statistic / figure / source, accuracy, complete, inconsistent, biased, and a high-stakes audience (compliance, legal, client, executive, external publication). When you see "confident summary" + "specific number" + "before sending to [high-stakes audience]", you already know the answer family: verify against an external authoritative source.

The shape of the correct answer. Always the disciplined middle action: it does the work, with the control in place, without abandoning the task and without dressing it up. It usually echoes the blueprint's objective lexically ("verify … against the official …", "have a subject-matter expert review …", "cite the source for each claim", "present the comparison as a structured table").

Distractors you'll see over and over in this domain:

  • Circular self-verification (the most dangerous one here). "Ask Claude to rate its own confidence", "Ask Claude to double-check its own answer and send it if it says it's correct". It looks like diligence, it adds a step — but the step is executed by the very system being audited. Always false.
  • Instruction-as-control. "Add 'do not hallucinate' to the prompt and resend", "Tell Claude to only use real sources". It mitigates; it doesn't verify. If the rival option cross-checks against the source, the instruction loses.
  • Cosmetic fix. "Reword it to sound more authoritative", "Reformat as a memo, then send". If the stem's problem is factual, any option about tone, format, or length is a distractor. Watch for the inverted trap: if the stem poses an audience problem (the same correct content isn't landing with the committee), then adapting format/register is the correct answer. Read what the actual problem is.
  • Maximalism. "Use the most capable model so it won't hallucinate". No model eliminates hallucination — that's official doctrine. It also burns cost and latency against the mandate to balance quality/efficiency/cost.
  • Zero-effort shortcut. Recognize it by the causal clause: "Send it as-is, since Claude expressed high confidence", "Publish it, because the tone is professional". When the distractor hands you the reason the control isn't needed, that reason is the trap.
  • Escape hatch. "Discard the output and write it manually from scratch", "Stop using Claude for research". The exam certifies the ability to apply Claude with control, not to run from it. It only wins when the stem offers no compliant middle path.
  • Wrong lever / out-of-scope technicality. "Lower the temperature", "Set a JSON schema", "Fine-tune the model". They sound sophisticated, and that's exactly why they hook people; they're outside the Associate's declared scope (which is explicitly not an API role). Be suspicious of the option that sounds like engineering.

Multiple-response. The item states how many to select. Treat each option as an independent true/false against the constraint. Two options that say the same thing in different words are almost never both correct — one is the distractor. And in this domain, a well-built multiple-response item usually combines one verification control (external source / human review) with one process control (rubric, structured format, flagging gaps), not two redundant verifications.

Common Mistakes

  1. Confusing fluency with accuracy. An elegant text with a fabricated citation is a failure. → Evaluate accuracy, completeness, and fluency separately, in that order of priority.
  2. Asking Claude if it's sure. Self-reported confidence isn't calibrated. → Verify against an external source; the only valid "self-critique" is with an explicit rubric, in a clean chat, and preferably with a different model.
  3. Believing "don't make things up" is a control. It's mitigation, not verification. → The control is cross-checking against the primary source or restricting the model to the documents provided.
  4. Verifying everything with the same intensity (or nothing). → Calibrate by risk: irreversibility, audience, consequence for people, whether the figure feeds into a decision.
  5. Accepting a figure because "it comes with a source." The citation is precisely the most credible form a hallucination can take. → Open the source and search for the phrase; the link existing doesn't mean it says that.
  6. Ignoring the knowledge cutoff. Asking about facts from the last few months without grounding or search is asking for invention. → Upload the document, enable search, or flag the data point as unverified.
  7. Adapting the tone before verifying the facts. Produces a better-written error. → Accuracy first, audience second.
  8. Evaluating completeness "from memory." → Write the acceptance list before prompting and check it off point by point.
  9. Comparing two drafts by taste. → Written rubric, pass/fail or 1–5 output, criterion by criterion.
  10. Treating bias as the model's problem when your prompt introduced it. "Give me the reasons to choose A" is a brief for the defense, not an analysis. → Symmetric prompt + strongest counter-case + review of which sources it used.
  11. Trusting that three matching runs mean it's true. Best-of-N detects instability, it doesn't confirm truth. → It's useful for ruling out, not for approving.
  12. Delivering prose when the output is going to be compared. Prose hides gaps. → A structured table with a source column; structure is an evaluation control.
  13. Leaving gaps unmarked. A report with no "not found" is indistinguishable from a complete one. → Require the model to explicitly declare what it couldn't back up.
  14. Escalating out of laziness, or not escalating out of pride. Escalating is correct when the work exceeds scope (integration, agentic system, architecture) or requires protected professional judgment; it's incorrect when a compliant action exists within the Associate's scope.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat it means, in a sentence
HallucinationConfident, unsupported claimA specific, plausible, false claim, delivered in the same tone of certainty as true ones.
GroundingAnchoring claims in a sourceRequiring every claim to rest on a provided source, typically by extracting verbatim quotes before reasoning.
Fact-checkingCross-checking claims against a sourceCross-checking every verifiable claim against the authoritative primary source.
AccuracyTruthfulness of the stated factsThe facts stated are true.
CompletenessFull coverage of the taskEvery element the task asked for is present, with no omissions.
Fluency biasMistaking polish for correctnessTaking the quality of the writing as evidence that the content is correct.
InconsistencyContradiction within or across outputAn internal contradiction, one between runs of the same prompt, or one against the source.
BiasSystematic skew in the outputA systematic tilt in the output caused by the prompt's framing, the sources chosen, or unexamined assumptions.
Source selection biasFavoring easy-to-find over authoritative sourcesPreferring easy-to-find (SEO-optimized) content over authoritative sources.
Best-of-N verificationRun-and-compare consistency checkRunning the same prompt N times and comparing; differences signal hallucination.
LLM-as-judgeUsing a model to score outputsUsing a model, with an explicit rubric and preferably different from the generator, to score outputs at scale.
RubricWritten scoring criteriaA written list of criteria with an empirical verdict (pass/fail or 1–5).
Success criteriaUpfront definition of a good outputA specific, measurable definition, set in advance, of what counts as a good output.
Human-in-the-loop / human reviewA person validating before impactA person (ideally an expert) who validates before the output takes effect.
Knowledge cutoffDate beyond which the model knows nothingThe date after which the model has no built-in information (Jan 2026 for the current frontier models; Feb 2025 for Haiku 4.5).
ArtifactReusable, editable output objectA substantial, self-contained output that lives as an editable/reusable object outside the chat thread.
Inline outputResponse given directly in the threadA short, conversational, single-use response.
Structured dataTable/CSV/JSON-shaped outputTable / CSV / JSON: output designed to be compared, filtered, aggregated, or fed into another process.
CurationDeduplicating and organizing informationDeduplicating, prioritizing, flagging gaps, and separating fact from inference from recommendation.
EscalationHanding off to an expertPassing the work to a human expert, or to a Claude Architect/Developer when the problem is technical.

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you haven't mastered the domain.

  • I can explain why the fluency of an output is not evidence of its accuracy, and evaluate accuracy, completeness, and fluency as three separate axes.
  • I can name the surfaces where the model hallucinates most (citations, subsections, figures, dates, names, URLs, facts after the cutoff) and prioritize verification there.
  • I know that the reliable knowledge cutoff of the current frontier models is January 2026 (and February 2025 for Haiku 4.5), and what that implies for any recent data.
  • I can apply the five Associate-level anti-hallucination controls: allow "I don't know," extract verbatim quotes before analyzing, require a citation per claim and withdraw anything unsupported, restrict to the knowledge provided, and best-of-N.
  • I can explain why asking Claude how confident it is is not a control, and how that differs from an LLM-as-judge with a rubric in a clean chat.
  • I can order the evidence hierarchy (primary source → organizational source → reputable secondary → the model's own claim = level zero), and I know a cited link needs to be opened.
  • I can distinguish internal inconsistency, cross-run inconsistency, and inconsistency against the source, and I know what signal each one gives.
  • I can detect framing bias in my own prompt and rewrite it symmetrically, and I know how to check the output for source selection bias.
  • I can state the human-review threshold (irreversibility, high-stakes audience, consequence for people, deciding figures, facts I can't verify myself), and I know when to escalate to an Architect/Developer instead of to a reviewer.
  • I write the acceptance list (specific, measurable success criteria) before prompting, and I evaluate against it.
  • I can compare two outputs using a written rubric, with an empirical verdict per criterion, instead of picking the one that reads better.
  • I know when an output should be inline, when it should be an artifact, and when it should be structured data, and I can justify the choice by what will be done with the output afterward.
  • I can explain why asking for a table with a source column is an evaluation control and not an aesthetic choice.
  • I can curate an output by separating [Fact — source], [Inference], and [Recommendation], and by explicitly flagging the gaps.
  • Faced with an item from this domain, I can, in under a minute, kill the "since…" shortcut, circular self-verification, instruction-as-control, the cosmetic fix, and abandonment — and settle on the disciplined action that delivers the work with the control in place.
