domains.html:
Why It's Worth 12%

This domain measures a single competency, and it's a business competency, not an engineering one: assigning the right resource to the right job. The exam guide defines the Associate as someone who "selects approaches that balance quality, efficiency, and cost." Domain 3 is where that balance stops being a marketing phrase and becomes a decision with consequences: which model you run, which product feature you open, and what you do when the conversation has filled up with context and responses start degrading.

Think of it as the domain of budget. Every task has three currencies — quality, speed, and cost — and you can't maximize all three. The mediocre candidate resolves the tension with a fixed rule ("I always use the most powerful model, that way I can't be wrong"), and the exam explicitly punishes that rule: Domain 3's official sample item declares "use the most capable, most expensive model for every response" incorrect. The competent candidate reads the constraint in the stem, translates it into a task profile (volume? latency? depth of reasoning? will the result be reused?), and picks the tool whose profile matches.

With 12% of the blueprint and 60 items, you're talking about approximately 7 questions. It's a small domain, but an extremely high-yield one per hour of study: the universe of concepts is bounded (four product features, three model families, a handful of context rules), and the correct answers are mechanical once you internalize the matching logic. There's no interpretive ambiguity here the way there is in governance. Either you know what Research mode is, or you're guessing.

Official Objectives

The guide's four task statements, verbatim in English, with what they mean in exam practice:

  • Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts) → You'll be given a work scenario and will have to say where it belongs: a loose chat, a Project with instructions and a knowledge base, Research mode, or an Artifact. The typical mistake is doing everything in a loose chat and re-pasting context into every conversation.

  • Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) → You need to know each family's profile (speed/cost vs. reasoning capability) and recognize it when the stem describes it without naming it. Note that the guide names families, not versions: the exam asks about tiers, not release numbers.

  • Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality) → The official sample item's objective. A stem with an explicit constraint ("speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning") → the fast, cheap model wins. A stem with complex reasoning, high risk, or long agentic work → the top tier wins.

  • Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist) → The three verbs in parentheses are literally the three possible correct answers. Faced with a saturated conversation, or context that will be needed again tomorrow: restart (new chat), summarize (explicit handoff), or persist (upload it to a Project). Knowing which of the three applies is the item.

Key Concepts

1. The Product Map: Where Each Type of Work Lives

Chat (loose chat / individual conversation). The basic unit. It's ephemeral in terms of configuration: it has no persistent instructions and no knowledge base of its own. Good for one-off tasks and exploration. The nuance that separates those who know: a loose chat isn't "bad" — it's the correct default for non-recurring work. It becomes wrong when the stem signals repetition ("the team does this every week", "I always have to re-explain the brand's tone"). Repetition is the signal for a Project.

Projects. Self-contained workspaces where you organize chats, upload documents, and maintain a separate knowledge base. Two configurable pieces:

  • Project instructions: rules Claude applies to every chat inside the project — tone, role, perspective, output format, quality criteria.
  • Project knowledge: the documents you upload that inform the responses.

Verified facts from the official support documentation: Projects are available to all users, including free-tier accounts, with a cap of five projects on the free plan. When a project's knowledge approaches the context window limit, on paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) Claude automatically enables RAG mode (retrieval augmented generation), which expands the project's capacity up to 10x while maintaining response quality. On Team and Enterprise plans, projects are shared with granular permissions: "Can use" (view and chat inside the project) and "Can edit" (modify instructions, knowledge, and members).

The nuance that separates those who know the material: a Project is not a folder. It's a container for reusable context. If the exam scenario describes five people copying and pasting the same brand brief into every chat, the problem isn't a prompting problem, it's a product-architecture problem, and the answer is a shared Project.

Artifacts. Substantial, self-contained content that Claude produces in a dedicated panel next to the chat, where it can be viewed, edited, and iterated on in real time. The official documentation sets the qualitative threshold: Claude creates an artifact when the content is substantial and self-contained (typically more than 15 lines), is something you'll likely want to edit, iterate on, or reuse outside the conversation, and stands on its own without needing the surrounding conversational context. They can be published (a public link, and the artifact appears in the Artifacts section of the sidebar, retrievable outside the original chat) and embedded into another site with the code generated by the Get embed code button.

The nuance: the exam won't ask you "what is an artifact?" in the abstract. It will give you a deliverable and see whether you recognize the reuse signal. A three-line email that gets sent and forgotten → inline. A report template the team will use twenty times, a table that needs editing, a document shared with another department → artifact. The stem's keyword is usually reuse, edit, share, iterate.

Research mode. Claude operates agentically: it runs multiple searches that build on one another, decides what to investigate next, explores different angles, and synthesizes multiple sources with verifiable citations. The official documentation is precise about when to choose it: research is optimal for exhaustive information gathering that requires five or more tool calls, over 1–3 minutes, producing in-depth reports. Hard requirement: web search must be enabled for research to work. Available on paid plans.

2. The Three Levers of "How to Search and How to Think" (and Not Confusing Them)

This trio comes up constantly and is the domain's favorite distractor, because all three sound like "Claude tries harder":

FeatureWhat it's designed for (official docs)Signal in the stem
Web searchDirect factual queries resolvable with one or two tool calls — the weather, a company's data, recent headlines"what's the current price of…?", "what did X announce this week?"
Extended thinkingComplex reasoning that doesn't require recent information from the web — math problems, debugging logic, analyzing concepts"reason," "analyze thoroughly," "without needing external sources"
ResearchExhaustive multi-source investigation, ≥5 tool calls, 1–3 minutes, with citations"full report," "multiple sources," "market overview"

They can be combined: the documentation explicitly mentions research + extended thinking together, so Claude can "carefully plan its approach and execute an exhaustive collection process" — for example, researching emerging technologies for a business proposal.

The exam error: choosing Research for a simple factual question. Research is not "web search, but better." It's an agentic mode that's expensive in time and consumption. Using it to find out the date of an event is the equivalent of convening a committee to choose the color of a folder.

3. The Model Ladder: Tiers, Not Versions

The guide names Haiku, Sonnet, Opus. That's the abstraction the exam tests: profiles, not release numbers. Memorize the axis, not the catalog.

FamilyOfficial positioningTask profile
HaikuThe fastest model, with near-frontier intelligenceHigh volume, minimal latency, straightforward tasks: classification, extraction, short answers, first-pass filtering
SonnetThe best combination of speed and intelligenceThe day-to-day workhorse: analysis, drafting, synthesis, most business work
OpusFor complex agentic work and enterprise workDeep reasoning, multi-step tasks, high stakes, long and difficult documents

As of July 2026 the current family also includes Claude Fable 5 (claude-fable-5), positioned by Anthropic as "next-generation intelligence for long-running agents" — the frontier reasoning tier, slower and more expensive. The current IDs are claude-fable-5, claude-opus-4-8, claude-sonnet-5, and claude-haiku-4-5-20251001. Don't memorize these for the exam: the Associate chooses from a selector in the application, not by writing IDs into an API call. The guide is explicit that no API experience is required, and that technical architecture belongs to the Architect and Developer credentials.

What you should have memorized is the relative order of cost and speed, because that's where the answers come from: from cheapest and fastest to most expensive and capable → Haiku → Sonnet → Opus → Fable. In published list prices (per million tokens): Haiku 4.5 $1 in / $5 out; Sonnet 5 $3/$15 (introductory price $2/$10 through August 31, 2026); Opus 4.8 $5/$25; Fable 5 $10/$50. Cite these only as an order of magnitude: the Associate exam does not ask about per-token pricing, it asks whether you know that a tier jump multiplies cost, and that the multiplier has to be justified.

The domain's golden rule: the model is not the first lever, it's the last. The correct escalation ladder, when an output falls short, is:

  1. Improve the prompt (explicit success criteria, format, audience, examples).
  2. Add context (upload the document, configure the Project, enable web search if facts are missing).
  3. Raise effort or turn on thinking (more reasoning with the same model).
  4. Move up a model tier (the expensive lever).

Jumping straight to step 4 at the first sign of friction is exactly the "maximalism by default" distractor archetype. And conversely: staying on Haiku for a 40-page regulatory analysis because "it's cheaper" is the symmetric error. The competency being tested is matching, not frugality or generosity.

4. Effort and Thinking: The Levers Almost No One Uses (and the Exam Does)

Alongside the model selector, the application exposes an effort setting and an extended thinking toggle. They are separate, combinable settings — the documentation says so literally: "Thinking and effort are separate settings, and you can use any combination of the two."

Effort levels and their official use:

  • Low / Medium — work well for routine tasks and stretch your usage (consume less of your limit).
  • High — the default; the best overall balance between quality and speed.
  • Extra high (xhigh) — for long coding and agentic tasks; deeper reasoning than high without the full cost of max.
  • Max — the most exhaustive option; for whatever demands the deepest possible reasoning.

Practical consequence the exam can exploit: lowering effort is a legitimate savings lever that doesn't require switching models. If the stem says "the team is running out of usage limit mid-week on routine tasks," "lower effort to low/medium on the routine tasks" is a correct, precise action; "switch platforms" or "turn off all features" are classic distractors (escape hatch and wrong lever).

5. Context and Memory: When to Restart, Summarize, or Persist

The context window is the total amount of information the model has in front of it in a given turn: instructions, the full conversation history, attached documents, tool results, and the generated output itself. Everything counts. Every project operates on a context window (documented as 200K, roughly the equivalent of a 500-page book), and when a project's knowledge approaches that limit, paid plans automatically activate RAG to expand capacity up to 10x.

Two distinct degradations, which the exam tells apart and the mediocre candidate conflates:

  • Saturation: there's no more room. It shows up as truncation or as the inability to add more documents.
  • Context rot: it does fit, but the signal gets diluted. A three-hour conversation with six failed attempts, contradictory corrections, and irrelevant documents produces worse responses even though it still fits. Context is a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns.

The three correct moves, which are literally the three verbs from the official objective:

MoveWhenHow to do it right
RestartThe conversation changed tasks, or is contaminated by failed iterations, or has run long and responses are getting worseA new chat with a clean start: don't re-paste the entire thread; bring over only what's still valid
SummarizeYou need continuity but not the full historyAsk Claude for an explicit handoff: decisions made, current constraints, present state, next step. That summary becomes the new chat's first message
PersistThe context will be needed more than once, or by more than one personUpload the document to Project knowledge and encode the rules in Project instructions. Stop re-pasting it into every chat

On memory, with official facts and its limits:

  • Claude automatically synthesizes insights from your chat history, and that synthesis refreshes every 24 hours. It focuses on working context: your role, your projects, your communication and work-style preferences.
  • Each project has its own memory space and its own summary, separate from out-of-project chats and from other projects. What Claude learns in one project does not carry over to another.
  • Chat search (searching previous chats) is a different thing from memory: it's on-demand retrieval (RAG over your conversations), it shows up as a tool call in the chat, and it's available on paid plans.
  • Controls in Settings > Capabilities: pause memory (keeps what exists, stops creating new memory) and reset memory (permanent, irreversible deletion). Enterprise can disable it at the organization level.
  • Incognito chats (ghost icon): the conversation is neither saved nor remembered.

The decisive nuance, and probably the most discriminating item in the domain: memory ≠ knowledge base. Memory is an automatic, approximate synthesis, subject to a delayed (24-hour) refresh, of how you work. It is not an authoritative store of facts. If a fact needs to be exact and citable — the current refund policy, the 2026 pricing table, the brand manual — it goes into Project knowledge as a document, not into "Claude will remember it." Any exam option that solves an accuracy problem with "ask Claude to remember it" is the decoder's Archetype C: the fake control (instruction-as-control). Don't pick it.

6. The Boundary of the Associate's Scope

The guide is blunt: the credential does not cover people who build against APIs or design agentic systems, and complex technical work gets escalated to Claude Architect and Claude Developer. Operative translation for Domain 3: your levers are the application's — model, effort, thinking, Project, Artifact, Research, web search, memory. If an answer option talks about API parameters, endpoints, batch jobs, prompt caching, or deployments, it's outside the credential's declared scope and, by the decoder's definition, is a distractor.

Worked Examples

Scenario 1 — Nordika Seguros contact center: 1,200 short responses per week. Elena, a support coordinator, needs to generate draft responses to policy inquiries. They're short, follow known templates, and latency matters because the SLA is 4 hours. The usage budget already runs out by Thursday.

  • Mediocre candidate: sets Opus with max effort "so no response comes out wrong," and ten days later the team is out of usage limit by midweek and responses are taking longer.
  • Competent candidate: Haiku, low or medium effort, inside a Project that contains the tone manual, the approved templates, and the three compliance rules. Responses the classifier flags as "atypical case / formal complaint" get routed to a chat with a higher-tier model and to human review.
  • Why: the stem names volume, speed, and cost, and describes straightforward tasks. The "align model selection with task requirements" objective is satisfied by matching profile to profile. The Project isn't a luxury: it's what keeps quality from depending on Elena remembering to paste the tone manual every time.

Scenario 2 — Vendor due diligence, with a 48-hour deadline. Marco (procurement) needs to deliver an overview of a logistics vendor: financial standing, public litigation, geographic coverage, comparison against two competitors. He needs citations because the document is going to the committee.

  • Mediocre candidate: opens a chat and asks "tell me about this company," gets a fluent text back, and sends it.
  • Competent candidate: Research mode (with web search enabled, a hard requirement), because the work requires multiple chained searches and multi-source synthesis; and then — critically — verifies the citations against the sources before the document reaches the committee (this is Domain 2, but the items overlap).
  • Why: the profile is exactly Research's (≥5 tool calls, 1–3 minutes, a report with citations). A simple one- or two-call web search doesn't cover "compare against two competitors and synthesize." And "ask Claude to confirm its citations are real" is circular self-verification: false.

Scenario 3 — The three-hour conversation that got worse. Priya has spent the whole afternoon iterating on a launch plan in a single chat: uploaded three PDFs, changed strategy twice, discarded an entire approach. The latest responses ignore constraints she set at the start and reintroduce ideas she already discarded.

  • Mediocre candidate: writes "please remember what I told you before and don't propose X again," and stays in the same thread. The conversation gets even longer and worse.
  • Competent candidate: asks for a handoff summary (firm decisions, current constraints, what was discarded and why, next step), opens a new chat with that summary as the first message, and persists the three PDFs and the stable constraints in a Project so the problem doesn't repeat tomorrow.
  • Why: it's the "when to restart, summarize, or persist" objective, with the three verbs used in sequence. Pressing the model within a degraded context doesn't fix the degradation: it increases it.

Scenario 4 — The one-pager the team is going to reuse twenty times. Grupo Aldana's HR department needs a job-description template: fixed structure, sections, inclusive language, that twelve recruiters will edit and adapt.

  • Mediocre candidate: asks for the template in the chat, gets it inline, copies it to a document by hand, and when they want to change a section, asks for the whole thing again.
  • Competent candidate: produces it as an Artifact (substantial, self-contained content meant to be edited and reused outside the conversation), iterates on it in the side panel, publishes it so the recruiters access the same object, and saves the style rules in HR's Project instructions.
  • Why: the stem's signals — edit, iterate, reuse, share — are the operative definition of an artifact. Inline is for what gets consumed and discarded.

Scenario 5 — The team that keeps running out of usage limit. A six-analyst team on the Team plan reports exhausting its weekly limit by Thursday. Reviewing their usage: extremely long conversations, repeated attachments in every chat, and everyone with effort set to max "just in case."

  • Mediocre candidate: asks to upgrade the plan, or proposes "using Claude less."
  • Competent candidate: three ordered fixes — (1) lower effort to low/medium on routine tasks, exactly what it's for, and it stretches usage; (2) move recurring documents to Project knowledge instead of attaching them in every chat (projects store and reuse documents instead of re-processing them every time); (3) close conversations that have already served their purpose instead of dragging around hours-long histories.
  • Why: the three documented usage drivers are conversation length, attachments, and model/configuration. The correct answer attacks all three, without abandoning the task or the platform.

How the Exam Asks This

The verbs you'll see. "Which choice best fits the task?" · "Which product feature is most appropriate?" · "What should the associate do?" · "Which model should be selected?". The wording "best fits" / "most appropriate" tells you there will be more than one defensible option: don't look for the only acceptable one, look for the best one under the stated constraint.

How to locate the constraint. Almost every item in this domain carries a clause that fixes the decision criterion, and that clause is the answer in disguise:

  • "…where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning" → low tier (Haiku). Any option that sacrifices speed/cost for quality is already dead.
  • "…the conversation has become long and responses are drifting" → restart / summarize.
  • "…the team repeats this analysis every week" → Project.
  • "…the output needs to be edited and shared with another department" → Artifact.
  • "…requires synthesizing multiple sources with citations" → Research (with web search enabled).
  • "…a straightforward factual lookup" → web search, not Research.

The distractors it plants, mapped to the decoder.

  • Maximalism by default (Archetype E): "Use the most capable, highest-cost model for every task." It's the domain's signature trap and appears verbatim in the official sample. It sounds like prudence; it's poor professional judgment, because it burns cost and latency budget and contradicts the mandate to "balance quality, efficiency, and cost."
  • Escape hatch (G): "Switch to a different AI platform." Almost always false. The exam certifies the ability to apply Claude.
  • Wrong lever (F): "Disable all product features to reduce cost." It reduces something, but not the variable the stem named, and it degrades the ability to do the work. Always ask yourself: does this action touch the constraint's variable?
  • Fake control (C), Domain 3 version: "Ask Claude to remember the pricing table for next week." Memory is an automatic synthesis, not an authoritative store. The real control is persisting the document in Project knowledge.
  • Circular self-verification (B): "Ask Claude which model it thinks is best for the task." Never. The model is not the authority on its own suitability.
  • Cosmetic fix (D): options that reformat, reorder, or "make the prompt longer" when the stated problem is a resource problem (saturated context, cost, latency).

A useful symmetry under pressure. Items in this domain tend to offer an expensive extreme (Opus for everything), a paralyzing extreme (abandon / switch platforms), a plausible decoy that doesn't touch the variable (turn off features, reword the prompt), and the middle action: matching the tool to the task's profile while respecting the constraint. Locate the two extremes, eliminate them, and rule out the decoy by asking whether it touches the named variable.

Multiple-response. When the item asks you to select two or three, treat each option as an independent true/false against the constraint. Watch for two options that say the same thing in different words ("use a faster model" / "select a lower-cost model"): the exam doesn't reward redundancy, and one of the two is usually the distractor.

Common Mistakes

  1. Choosing the most capable model "to be safe." Correction: on this exam, over-provisioning is a lapse in judgment, not a precaution. The correct option matches model profile to task profile, and the official sample states this explicitly.
  2. Choosing the cheapest model "to save money" on high-stakes tasks. Correction: the symmetric error. A 40-page regulatory analysis with legal consequences is not low-tier work. Frugality is not a virtue if it breaks the required quality.
  3. Confusing Research with "web search, but better." Correction: web search is for one- or two-call factual queries; Research is agentic, multi-source, with citations, and takes 1–3 minutes. Using Research for a trivial query wastes time and budget.
  4. Forgetting that Research requires web search to be enabled. Correction: it's a documented hard requirement. An item can be built right around this ("enabled research but isn't getting results").
  5. Confusing memory with a knowledge base. Correction: memory synthesizes how you work (role, projects, preferences) and refreshes every 24 hours. Facts that need to be exact go in as a document in Project knowledge.
  6. Assuming a project's memory is shared with others. Correction: each project has its own memory space and its own summary; what's learned in one does not carry over to another, or to out-of-project chats.
  7. Pressing the model within a degraded conversation. Correction: "remember what I told you before" doesn't reverse context rot. Summarize, restart, and persist.
  8. Re-pasting the same documents into every new chat. Correction: that consumes usage limit and guarantees drift between people. Recurring documents belong in Project knowledge, which stores and reuses them.
  9. Using a loose chat for recurring team work. Correction: repetition + multiple people = a shared Project (Team/Enterprise) with "Can use" / "Can edit" permissions.
  10. Treating every output as inline and copying it by hand. Correction: if it's going to be edited, iterated on, reused, or shared, it's an Artifact. That's its criterion for existing.
  11. Ignoring effort and thinking as levers. Correction: they are separate, combinable settings. Lowering effort on routine tasks stretches usage without switching models; raising it (or turning on thinking) resolves many cases the mediocre candidate tries to solve by jumping tiers.
  12. Believing "free" means no Projects. Correction: Projects are also available on free accounts, with a cap of five; what's exclusive to paid plans is automatic RAG expansion (up to 10x), Research, and searching previous chats.
  13. Wandering into API territory. Correction: if an option talks about endpoints, parameters, batching, or caching, it's outside the Associate's scope and is a distractor by definition. That work gets escalated to Architect/Developer.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat it means, in a sentence
ProjectSelf-contained recurring-work spaceA self-contained workspace with its own instructions and knowledge base, where recurring work lives.
Project instructionsPersistent rules for every chat in a projectPersistent rules (tone, role, format) that Claude applies to every chat in that project.
Project knowledgeUploaded documents backing a projectThe documents uploaded to the project that inform responses without re-pasting them into every chat.
RAG (retrieval augmented generation)Retrieval-based capacity expansionA technique that lets a project store and retrieve far more knowledge than fits in the window; activates automatically on paid plans when approaching the limit.
ArtifactReusable side-panel outputSubstantial, self-contained content in a side panel, made to be edited, iterated on, reused, or published.
Research modeAgentic multi-step search with citationsMulti-step agentic search with citations, for exhaustive investigations (≥5 tool calls, 1–3 minutes).
Web searchLive lookup for simple factual queriesA live query for factual questions resolvable in one or two calls.
Extended thinkingDeeper reasoning before respondingClaude spends more time decomposing and planning before responding; doesn't require the web.
EffortReasoning-depth settingA setting (low / medium / high / xhigh / max) that controls how much reasoning depth the model invests; high is the default.
Context windowEverything the model sees in a turnEverything the model has in front of it in a turn: instructions, history, attachments, results, and output.
Context rotQuality decay from a cluttered contextResponses get worse when the context fills with irrelevant or contradictory material, even though it still "fits."
MemoryAutomatic synthesis of your work contextAn automatic synthesis of your working context (role, projects, style), refreshed every 24 hours, with a separate space per project.
Chat searchOn-demand retrieval from past chatsOn-demand retrieval of information from previous conversations; distinct from memory.
Incognito chatA conversation that leaves no traceA conversation that is neither saved nor remembered.
Haiku / Sonnet / Opus(model families)A ladder of tiers: maximum speed and lowest cost → best balance → maximum reasoning capability.
Summarize / restart / persistThe three valid moves for a strained contextThe three valid moves when facing a saturated or degraded context.

Checklist

If you can't check off one of these, you haven't mastered Domain 3.

  1. I can explain, without looking it up, what a Project does that a loose chat doesn't — and name its two configurable pieces (instructions and knowledge).
  2. I know what signal in a stem indicates "this should be a Project" (repetition, multiple people, reusable context).
  3. I can state the criterion by which content deserves to be an Artifact rather than an inline response (substantial, self-contained, editable/reusable outside the conversation).
  4. I can distinguish web search, extended thinking, and Research by their usage profile, and I know Research requires web search to be enabled.
  5. I know why using Research for a simple factual query is a mistake, and what to use instead.
  6. I can describe the profile of Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus in one sentence each, and order the tiers by cost and speed.
  7. Faced with a stem that says "speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning," I choose the low tier without hesitation — and I can explain why the more capable model would be wrong there.
  8. I know that effort and extended thinking are separate, combinable settings, and that lowering effort is a savings lever that doesn't require switching models.
  9. I can explain what counts inside the context window (everything: instructions, history, attachments, outputs).
  10. I can distinguish context saturation (it doesn't fit) from context rot (it fits but degrades) and I know what to do in each case.
  11. I know when to restart, when to summarize, and when to persist — and I can give a concrete example of each.
  12. I can explain why "ask Claude to remember it" is not a valid control for a fact that needs to be exact, and what is.
  13. I know that each project's memory is isolated from other projects and from out-of-project chats.
  14. I recognize the domain's four signature distractors: model maximalism, switching platforms, turning off features to save money, and memory-as-database.
  15. I know which decisions in this domain fall outside my scope as an Associate (API, batching, architecture), and who they get escalated to.

domains.title: Workflow Integration and Solution Design
objectives: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 16%

Domains 1, 2, and 3 measure whether you can operate Claude within a conversation. Domain 4 measures whether you can change how an organization works with Claude inside it. It's the second-heaviest domain on the exam (16%, ~10 of 60 items), and that's no accident: the exam guide defines the Associate as someone who "identifies opportunities to improve processes with Claude," "translates business objectives into effective AI interactions," and "recognizes limitations and escalates more complex or technical work to Claude Architects and Developers." That profile is exactly this domain. The declared target audience — operations, marketing, project management, education, communications — includes both internal staff who "maintain and optimize AI-enabled workflows" and "external consultants who support implementation, use-case identification, and process redesign." Domain 4 is the part of the exam that certifies the consultant.

The business decision it represents is really just one question, repeated in different disguises: given a real process that already works somehow today, where does Claude fit in, with which feature, with what human checkpoint, and what am I promising my boss will happen? Almost every item in the domain is a variant of that question. And almost every distractor is a variant of two symmetric errors: over-automating (removing the human from where they needed to stay, doing a full rollout with no pilot, promising results you can't sustain) or under-automating (using Claude as a loose, personal chat instead of turning it into a shared, maintainable asset; or abandoning the opportunity because "AI isn't reliable"). The competent candidate does the third thing: finds the exact point where Claude should be inserted into the existing process, leaves the human gate where the risk demands it, measures against a baseline, and communicates value and limitations in the same breath.

Official Objectives

• Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases You'll be asked to use Claude as an analysis instrument (extracting requirements from an RFP, meeting minutes, or a tender document; inventorying and prioritizing use cases), not as a blind generator. The correct answer is usually: give Claude the real material as a source, ask for structure and traceability, and validate with the process owner.

• Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization Research and planning: research mode for multi-step inquiry with verifiable citations, Claude for mapping the current process (as-is), spotting bottlenecks, proposing the redesigned process (to-be), and estimating impact. What's being evaluated is whether you use the feature suited to the type of inquiry and whether the conclusions are auditable.

• Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration Designing the workflow solution (which prompts, which Project, which instructions, which output format, which review) and iterating it with evidence: testing with real cases, comparing against the baseline, correcting. "Support" is the key word: Claude assists the design; a human signs off on it.

• Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them The augment vs. redesign distinction is an explicit axis of the objective and shows up in the items: do I insert Claude into a step of the current process (augment), or do I redesign the process because the existing steps existed only because of the constraint Claude removes (redesign)? Where the work lives also matters: an ephemeral chat vs. a shared Project with instructions and knowledge sources.

• Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders Presenting to a committee, a client, or a team what they gain and what they risk with Claude. The items punish salesperson talk (only benefits, inflated figures, "replaces the team") and they punish fear talk too. The correct answer is honest and actionable: value quantified against a baseline + limitations named explicitly + the control that mitigates each one.

Key Concepts

1. Use-Case Fit Assessment (Use-Case Suitability)

Before designing anything, you decide whether the task is even a candidate. Five filters the exam uses as an implicit criterion:

  • Is it a language task? Drafting, summarizing, classifying, extracting, translating, rephrasing, comparing, structuring. If the real work is exact arithmetic over thousands of rows, a deterministic calculation, or a hard business rule, the right tool may be a spreadsheet or a system, not an LLM (or Claude executing code, not Claude "guessing" the number).
  • Is there a source of truth to validate against? If no one can say whether the output is correct, you can't iterate or measure. Cases with no verifiable success criterion are traps: the project never "finishes."
  • Is the error recoverable? A poorly drafted internal memo gets corrected. A regulatory communication sent to a client with a fabricated figure doesn't. The cost of the error determines where the human gate goes — not whether the case gets done at all.
  • Is there volume or frequency? ROI is (time saved per instance) × (instances per period) − (cost of operating and maintaining). Automating something that happens twice a year is productivity theater.
  • Is the data fit for use? If the input is regulated or sensitive data with no compliant anonymization path, the case gets reframed or escalated (this is where Domain 4 touches Domain 6).

The nuance that separates the two: the mediocre candidate asks "can Claude do this?" (almost always yes, on the surface). The competent one asks, "should this step exist at all, and if it does, who answers for the result?"

2. Augment vs. Redesign

  • Augment: the process stays as-is; Claude speeds up one or more steps. Low risk, fast adoption, bounded gain. Example: the analyst still writes the monthly report, but Claude produces the first draft from the data and the analyst edits it.
  • Redesign: the existence of the steps themselves gets questioned. Many steps in an old process exist only because a human couldn't keep up: that's why you sampled instead of reviewing everything, why you standardized the message instead of personalizing it, why you waited for month-end close instead of reviewing continuously. When Claude removes that constraint, the step stops making sense. Example: instead of "Claude drafts the monthly report faster," the monthly report disappears altogether and gets replaced by continuous alerts on deviations.

Exam rule: redesign is the ambitious, correct answer when the stem signals that the current process is an artifact of a human limitation; augment is the correct answer when the stem signals risk, organizational resistance, or a first adoption. When the stem says "the team is skeptical" or "first pilot," the exam wants the conservative, measurable step — not the revolution.

3. Human-in-the-Loop and Gate Design (Human Review in the Circuit)

Workflow design isn't defined by what Claude can do, but by where the human review point is placed. Three canonical positions:

  • Full review (hard gate): every output gets reviewed before use. Mandatory when the output goes external, has legal/financial effect, or is irreversible. This is what the official Domain 2 sample requires before sending a regulatory summary to compliance.
  • Sampling review + criteria: a percentage gets reviewed and the rejection rules get audited. Valid for high volume with recoverable error (internal drafts, ticket classification, labeling).
  • Exception-based review: Claude flags the doubtful cases (low structural confidence, missing data, conflicting sources) and only those go to a human. This requires the design to explicitly ask Claude to state what it couldn't verify; never trust that it will do this on its own.

Decisive nuance: human review is a control on the process, not an instruction to the model. "I tell Claude to only use real data" is not a gate. A gate is a named person, an acceptance criterion, and the authority to send the work back.

4. The Project as the Unit of Solution (Not the Chat)

A loose chat is a conversation; a Project is an installed workflow. The difference matters because the domain's objective is to integrate, and a solution that only exists in one person's head and chat history isn't integration — it's dependency.

What turns a use case into a maintainable solution:

  • Project instructions: the role, the business context, the required output format, the constraints (audience, tone, length), and the escalation rules ("if the data isn't in the project's sources, say so explicitly instead of estimating").
  • Knowledge sources: uploaded documents (current policy, approved templates, glossary, good examples) and connectors to the systems where the work actually lives (for example, Google Drive or Gmail, both named in the blueprint itself). Connectors eliminate copy-pasting and keep the context alive.
  • An owner and a maintenance cadence: who updates the instructions and sources when policy changes. A Project with expired knowledge produces confidently outdated outputs — the most expensive failure mode in this domain, because nobody catches it.
  • Reuse: the Project is shared with the team; the value multiplies by the number of users without redesigning anything.

(The fine mechanics of configuring instructions and sources is Domain 5. Here, what's being examined is the design decision: chat vs. Project, what goes in instructions vs. what goes in knowledge, and why the solution must outlive whoever created it.)

5. Claude Features Mapped to Workflow Phases

Workflow PhaseRight FeatureWhy
External inquiry, benchmarking, state of the art, verificationResearch mode (multi-step research with citations) + web searchReturns traceable sources; the value lies in being able to audit every claim. A summary without citations is useless for deciding anything.
Conversational design and explorationChatFast, disposable, ideal for breaking down and exploring options before committing to anything.
Deliverable with a life of its own (template, procedure, document, report, table)ArtifactsOutput separate from the chat, editable and iterable as an object — it's the deliverable, not the reply.
Recurring team workflowProjects (instructions + knowledge sources + connectors)Turns a personal technique into a shared asset.
Calculation, aggregation, charting over real dataCode Execution / data analysisWhen the number has to be exact, you run code on the data — you don't ask the model to "do it in its head."
Repeatable procedure Claude must follow the same way every timeSkillsPackages "how it's done here" (format, steps, criteria) and gets invoked when it applies.
Continuity across sessionsMemory / deliberate context persistenceAvoids re-explaining the world in every conversation.

The classic mistake: using chat for everything. The second classic mistake: requesting a Project for something that a three-line prompt used once would solve.

6. Connectors and MCP — What the Associate Needs to Know (and Where Their Scope Ends)

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that connects AI applications to the systems where data and tools actually live; Anthropic's official analogy is that "MCP is like a USB-C port for AI applications": you implement it once and it integrates everywhere, instead of building N×M custom integrations. The Claude product's connectors (for example, to Google Drive or Gmail, both named in the blueprint) are the user-facing side of that mechanism.

Scope boundary, and the exam uses it: using and configuring existing connectors is within the Associate's role. Building an MCP server, integrating via API, or designing an agentic system is NOT — the guide itself says that credential belongs to Claude Architect / Claude Developer, and that the Associate escalates that work. A typical distractor presents the technically sophisticated solution ("build a custom API integration that pipes tickets into Claude automatically") as if it were the mature answer: it's the out-of-scope answer. The correct move is to design the solution within the product and escalate the technical part with a well-specified requirement (which systems, which data, what volume, what SLA, what data policy).

7. Baseline, Success Criteria, and Pilot

The official prompt engineering documentation requires, before optimizing anything: (1) a clear definition of success criteria, (2) a way to test empirically against those criteria, (3) a first draft to improve on. That same order applies to workflow design, and it's the backbone of the "iteration" items:

  1. Measure the as-is: time per instance, volume, rework rate, cycle time, cost. Without a baseline there's no demonstrable value — only anecdote.
  2. Define the acceptance criterion for the output before generating the first one: what makes a draft "approvable" (completeness, accuracy of figures, tone, length, format). It's the same criterion the human reviewer will use.
  3. Bounded pilot: one team, a subset of cases, a defined period, with a representative set of cases (including the hard and unusual ones, not just the easy ones) to compare Claude against current practice.
  4. Iterate on evidence: failures get classified by cause (ambiguous instruction, missing context, undeclared success criterion, outdated knowledge source) — you don't "reprompt" blindly.
  5. Scale what survived and document it: Project, instructions, owner, review cadence.

Exam nuance: the pilot is the correct answer with extremely high frequency when the stem describes an organization about to deploy Claude across an entire department. The big-bang rollout is a distractor almost by definition.

8. Balancing Quality, Efficiency, and Cost in Design

The guide says this explicitly among the certified capabilities ("select approaches that balance quality, efficiency, and cost"). In workflow design, that means: the model and the feature are chosen per step, not per project. A real flow mixes: high-volume classification (fast, cheap model, Haiku family), nuanced drafting and complex analysis (Sonnet/Opus family), and human review at the step where the error is costly. Designing the entire flow around the most expensive model is the same lapse in judgment the guide's sample 2 penalizes, scaled up to the process level.

9. Communicating with Stakeholders: Value and Limitations

The objective literally says "value and limitations." The correct answer always carries both halves:

  • Value, expressed against a baseline and in business units: "the first draft of the report goes from 4 hours to 40 minutes of editing; at 12 reports/month that's ~38 hours/month freed up on the ops team," not "Claude is 10x faster."
  • Limitations, named along with their associated control, not as a decorative disclaimer:
    • it can hallucinate facts, figures, and citations in a confident tone → a verification gate against the source before publishing;
    • its knowledge has a cutoff date and it doesn't know anything internal unless you give it to it → knowledge sources and connectors;
    • the context window is finite: very long conversations or huge corpora require summarizing, segmenting, or persisting;
    • it's non-deterministic: two runs of the same prompt can differ → that's why you define an acceptance criterion, not a "literal expected output";
    • it doesn't replace protected professional judgment (clinical, legal, disciplinary, credit-related) or accountability: the human who signs off remains responsible;
    • there's a data policy: what can be uploaded and what can't.
  • What never gets said: savings figures with no measurement behind them, "reduces headcount by X%," "eliminates human error," or any promise of absolute accuracy. Overpromising is failure mode #1 for adoption: it kills the project at the first visible mistake.

10. Integration Failure Modes (the Ones the Exam Turns into Scenarios)

  • Paving the cowpath: automating a broken process just makes it a broken process that runs faster. Before inserting Claude, ask whether the step should exist at all.
  • Shadow AI: everyone with their own private prompt, no shared instructions, no single source. Result: inconsistent outputs, zero maintainability, data risk.
  • Orphaned solution: the Project has no owner and no cadence; the knowledge ages and nobody notices.
  • Missing gate: the output goes straight to the client/system. The first public error destroys trust in the entire program.
  • Missing metric: nobody measured the as-is, so the value is undemonstrable and the project dies at the next budget cut.
  • Escalation dodged or over-offered: failing to escalate what genuinely requires API/architecture work, or escalating out of laziness something a well-built Project would solve.

Worked Examples

Scenario 1 — Ops: Month-End Close at a Logistics Company

Marisol, operations coordinator at a trucking company with 140 units, produces a monthly incident report: she manually consolidates 6 spreadsheets from the regional depots, writes up 8 pages of narrative, and sends it to leadership. It takes her 11 hours, always during the last three days of the month, and it always arrives too late to decide anything.

  • Mediocre candidate: opens a chat, pastes the 6 spreadsheets, asks for "make me the monthly report." Gets 8 plausible-sounding pages with figures that sound right. The aggregate figures are wrong (the model didn't calculate, it estimated). Nobody notices until the quarter closes.
  • Competent candidate: (a) separates calculation from narrative: the aggregates are produced by running code on the files (Code Execution), not by asking the model to add them up; (b) sets up a Project with the report's approved templates, the incident-category glossary, and the explicit instruction "use only the figures in the data block; if a figure is missing, say so — don't estimate it"; (c) the narrative draft comes out as an Artifact that Marisol edits; (d) measures: 11 h → 2.5 h; (e) and then asks the important question: if the report can be produced in 2.5 hours, why is it monthly? Redesigns it into a biweekly pulse with exception-based alerts.
  • Why: the mediocre candidate automated the surface and inherited the most expensive failure mode (invented numbers in a leadership document). The competent one put every task in the right tool, left the human gate where the risk demanded it, and, in the end, gained more by redesigning the process than by merely speeding it up.

Scenario 2 — Marketing: 60 Nurture Emails a Month

A 4-person B2B marketing team produces 60 emails/month across 5 segments. They write each one from scratch; the tone drifts; legal bounces back ~15% for unsupported claims. The director wants to "bring in AI" and roll it out to all of marketing next week.

  • Mediocre candidate: gives everyone access and tells them "use Claude to write the emails." Everyone invents their own prompt. Consistency gets worse, not better, and now legal bounces 25% because the claims that show up are more eloquent — and just as unsupported.
  • Competent candidate: runs a pilot with one segment and two people for three weeks. Sets up a Project with: the brand guide, approved emails as examples, the list of permitted claims, and the instruction "never state a quantitative benefit that doesn't appear in the project's sources; if the angle requires one, flag it as [CLAIM A VALIDAR]." Measures the baseline (time per email, legal rejection rate) and compares against it. Keeps the legal gate fully intact throughout the pilot. Only once the rejection rate drops does she scale to the rest of the team, with the already-proven Project as the team standard.
  • Why: the stem has two constraints — consistency and compliance — and the immediate rollout addresses neither. The value didn't come from "writing faster" but from encoding the team standard into the configuration, which a loose, personal chat could never produce.

Scenario 3 — PM: Requirements Analysis for a 180-Page Tender

A consulting firm is responding to a public tender. The tender document runs 180 pages; the requirements are scattered and mixed in with legal boilerplate. Historically, they lose points for unanswered requirements.

  • Mediocre candidate: uploads the PDF and asks for "write me the proposal." Gets a proposal that's generic, polished, and not traced back to the tender document. They lose points again.
  • Competent candidate: uses Claude for what it's good at here: extracting and structuring. Asks for a traceability matrix — one row per requirement, with the verbatim quote and section number, classified as mandatory / desirable / informational, with ambiguous ones flagged. Spot-checks that the cited sections actually exist (fabricating section numbers is the canonical Domain 2 failure mode, and the guide itself uses it as a sample). With the matrix validated, each requirement gets assigned to a human owner who drafts the technical content; Claude assists with drafting each cell and with the final coverage review ("which rows in the matrix are still unanswered?").
  • Why: the domain's objective says "analyze requirements and use cases," not "write the proposal." The value is in auditable coverage, which is exactly where humans fail and where Claude is strong — as long as the citations get verified.

Scenario 4 — Education: Feedback on 320 Essays

An academic coordinator wants to use Claude to give feedback on 320 essays per cycle. Today, teachers take 15 minutes per essay and feedback arrives three weeks late, by which point it's useless.

  • Mediocre candidate: proposes that Claude grade the essays and publish the score automatically. Enormous savings, a decision with consequences for people made by a model, with no review, with bias risk, and probably against institutional policy.
  • Competent candidate: separates grading (a decision with consequences → protected professional judgment, stays with the teacher) from formative feedback (text aimed at improvement → an excellent case for Claude). Designs it as: the institutional rubric as a knowledge source; Claude produces a feedback draft anchored to the rubric, with evidence quoted from the essay itself; the teacher reviews, adjusts, and signs off. Also measures: feedback turnaround from 3 weeks to 3 days. Escalates the judgment call: the grade is always the teacher's.
  • Why: the exam item plays out right on the line between augmenting human work and replacing a decision that shouldn't be replaced. The correct answer preserves the value (feedback arrives on time) without crossing the line. Automation maximalism here isn't efficiency — it's a governance failure.

Scenario 5 — Communication: The Committee Wants Numbers

After a 6-week pilot in customer support (Claude drafts the first version of responses; agents edit them), the executive committee asks whether to scale to all 40 agents.

  • Mediocre candidate: presents "Claude cut response time by 70% and will let us cut 8 positions." There's no solid baseline, the figure comes from the 5 best conversations, and the headcount-cut promise declares war on the very team he needs in order to drive adoption.
  • Competent candidate: presents three blocks. (1) Measured value: average first-response time down from 14 min → 6 min across 240 pilot tickets; satisfaction with no significant change; zero tickets escalated for content error. (2) Limitations with their control: the model can confidently state policies that don't exist → every response still passes through the agent before it's sent; the Project's knowledge must be updated every time the returns policy changes, which requires a named owner; tickets with regulated data stay outside the flow entirely. (3) What she's asking for: scale to 12 more agents for one cycle, with the gate intact, and review the metric before deciding on a full rollout.
  • Why: the exam rewards whoever delivers value under constraint and says so honestly. The headcount-cut promise and the figure with no baseline are the archetype of the "shortcut with a rationalization." The correct communication makes the business case and gives the committee the real risk and its mitigation — which is exactly what the objective asks for.

How the Exam Asks This

Verbs and tells that give away the domain (per the decoder): "stakeholders", "existing process", "current workflow", "requirements", "use case", "pilot", "roll out", "redesign", "leadership", "executive committee", "explain the value/limitations", "first step", "best approach to integrate". When the stem describes an organization and a process (not a loose conversation), you're in Domain 4.

Most frequent stem shapes:

  • "What is the best first step?" → almost always: understand/measure the current process, or run a bounded pilot. Never: build the whole solution, or deploy to everyone.
  • "Which approach best integrates Claude into the existing workflow?" → the one that inserts Claude at a specific point while keeping human control where the risk demands it, and the one that turns the practice into a shared asset (Project) if the stem mentions a team or recurrence.
  • "How should the associate communicate the results to leadership?" → quantified value + named limitations + a requested next step. Kill any option that is only benefits or only warnings.
  • "The task requires connecting Claude to the company's internal ticketing system via its API…" → escalation to Claude Architect/Developer with a specified requirement. That's the legitimate exception to "escalate" in this domain.

Characteristic distractors:

  • The Big Bang. "Deploy Claude to all 40 agents immediately to maximize the savings." Skips the pilot and the measurement. Wrong, unless the stem already describes a successful pilot and is asking about scaling.
  • The Salesperson. "Present the 70% time savings and the projected headcount reduction." Only value, zero limitations, a figure with no baseline. The objective says value and limitations: an option missing the second half is dead on arrival.
  • The Over-Automator. Removes the human gate exactly where the stem planted the risk (external communication, grading, a decision about people, regulated data). Sounds efficient; is a design failure.
  • Out-of-Scope Sophistication. "Build a custom MCP server / API integration / multi-agent system." Technically respectable, outside the Associate's declared scope. Correct only when the option is to escalate it, not execute it.
  • Process Cosmetics. "Document the new workflow in a slide deck and share it." Produces artifacts, not change. If it doesn't touch the process or the measurement, it's a distractor.
  • The Escape Hatch. "Conclude that the process is too complex for Claude and keep it manual." Wrong, unless the stem offers no compliant path at all (a genuinely unsuitable case, irreparably sensitive data, a protected decision with no augmentable component).
  • The Wrong Lever. Optimizes a variable the stem never named: switches models when the problem was missing context; buys more licenses when the problem was that nobody maintains the knowledge source.

Decoder rule applied to this domain: identify the constraint in the stem (budget, team skepticism, data policy, deadline, regulatory risk), kill the lax extreme (deploy with no control) and the paralyzed extreme (do nothing), and pick the disciplined middle action: the smallest step that produces evidence and preserves control.

Common Mistakes

  1. Designing the solution before understanding the process. Correction: the first step is always to map the as-is and measure it. Without a baseline there's no design, no demonstrable value, and no possible iteration.
  2. Confusing a chat with a solution. Correction: if the workflow is recurring or team-based, the unit of delivery is a Project with instructions, knowledge sources, and an owner. A private prompt is not integration.
  3. Automating the wrong step. Correction: ask whether the step should exist at all. Speeding up a report nobody reads is zero value; eliminating it is all the value.
  4. Removing the human from the risk gate. Correction: human review goes wherever the error is irreversible or public. It can be lightened (sampling, exception-based), not eliminated.
  5. Asking the model for the exact number. Correction: aggregates, sums, and metrics get calculated by running code on the data, not by asking an LLM to "estimate." You ask the model for the narrative — not the arithmetic.
  6. Promising savings with no measurement. Correction: every figure you present must come from a comparison against the baseline using real cases. "10x faster" with nothing measured is a lie wearing a KPI's clothing.
  7. Selling AI as a replacement for people. Correction: frame it as freed-up capacity and work that didn't get done before. Besides being more honest, it's the only thing that sustains adoption from the team you depend on.
  8. Presenting limitations as a decorative disclaimer. Correction: every limitation gets named along with its control: hallucination → verification against the source; expired knowledge → the Project's update cadence; finite context → segmentation; sensitive data → anonymization or exclusion.
  9. Full rollout with no pilot. Correction: a bounded pilot, with representative cases (including the hard ones), a defined metric and period, before scaling.
  10. Escalating to Architect/Developer out of laziness. Correction: escalate what exceeds scope (API work, MCP servers, agentic systems, enterprise architecture). A well-configured Project using existing connectors is Associate-level work.
  11. Not escalating when you should. Correction: when the solution requires API integration or an agentic system, the correct answer is to escalate with a specified requirement (systems, data, volume, data policy, success criterion) — not improvise an integration.
  12. Leaving the solution with no owner and no maintenance. Correction: the design includes who updates instructions and sources, and how often. A Project with expired policy produces confidently wrong outputs that nobody audits.
  13. Iterating blindly. Correction: failures get classified by cause (ambiguous instruction, missing context, undeclared success criterion, outdated source), and the cause gets fixed. Randomly reprompting is not iteration.

Glossary

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you haven't mastered the domain.

  1. I can decide whether a task is a good use case for Claude by applying the five filters (language task, source of truth, recoverable error, volume, data fitness).
  2. I can tell when to augment a process and when to redesign it, and I can argue which one applies based on what the stem says.
  3. I can map an as-is process, identify the bottleneck, and point to the exact spot where Claude fits in.
  4. I know how to place the human gate in the right spot and choose between full, sampling, and exception-based review based on the cost of error.
  5. I can justify why a recurring workflow lives in a Project with instructions and knowledge sources, and not in a loose chat.
  6. I can map every phase of the work to the right feature: research mode, chat, Artifacts, Projects, Code Execution, Skills, Memory.
  7. I can explain what MCP is and what a connector does, and I know that using them is within the Associate's scope while building them is an escalation.
  8. I know how to design a pilot: what I measure, against what baseline, with what representative cases, for how long, and what decides whether it scales.
  9. I can define acceptance criteria for the output before generating the first one, and I know they're the same criteria the human reviewer will use.
  10. I know how to iterate by classifying failures by root cause, not by blindly reprompting.
  11. I can present value to a committee with figures derived from a real measurement, in business units.
  12. I can name five limitations of Claude and, for each one, the process control that mitigates it — without using "I ask Claude not to do it" as a control.
  13. I know when to escalate to Claude Architect/Developer and what information that escalation needs to carry to be actionable.
  14. I know how to assign an owner and a maintenance cadence to a solution, and can explain why an unmaintained Project is a risk, not an asset.
  15. Faced with an item from this domain, I identify the constraint in the stem, rule out the big-bang and the walk-away, and choose the smallest step that produces evidence while preserving control.
