domains.title: Configuration and Knowledge Management
objectives: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
Create effective system-level instructions
Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 12%

This domain measures one single thing, expressed four different ways: whether you know how to move knowledge and rules out of the prompt and into the configuration, and then keep them alive. The candidate who hasn't mastered Domain 5 writes a 900-word prompt every morning that repeats the brand's tone, pastes the client brief in again, and re-explains who the audience is. The candidate who has mastered it configures a Project once, with instructions and knowledge sources, and from then on their prompts run three lines. The difference isn't cosmetic: it's the difference between a one-off personal habit and an organizational asset that others can inherit, audit, and update.

The business decision it represents is where each piece of context lives and who owns it. The guide says this without ambiguity when it describes the MQC: someone who "builds Claude Projects day to day" and who "maintains and optimizes AI-enabled workflows." Maintain is the expensive verb. Configuring a Project is easy; what the exam is really after is the lifecycle: what happens when the refund policy changes, when the catalog gets updated, when the document uploaded six months ago now contradicts the current one. Outdated knowledge in a Project doesn't produce a visible error: it produces a confident, wrong answer, which is exactly the most expensive failure mode on the entire exam. That's why Domain 5 and Domain 2 (output evaluation, 21%) are cousins: half the hallucinations an Associate sees in production don't come from the model — they come from their own dirty knowledge base.

Official Objectives

• Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources You'll be asked to decide what goes in the Project's instructions, what goes in the knowledge base, and what stays in the chat prompt — and to recognize when a Project is the right tool versus a loose chat.

• Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail) You'll be asked to choose between uploading a file (a snapshot) or connecting the live source (a connector), to understand how permissions work when you do, and to manage which documents go in, which come out, and which should never have gone in at all.

• Create effective system-level instructions You'll be asked to write or fix system-level instructions (role, scope, format, hard constraints, escalation rules), distinguishing them from a one-off task request.

• Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions You'll be asked to define the maintenance plan: who owns it, how often it's reviewed, how outdated material gets retired, and how the Project's users get told that the configuration changed.

Key Concepts

1. Projects: The Reusable Context Container

A Project is a persistent workspace that groups together (a) a set of chats, (b) a set of instructions that apply to all of those chats, and (c) a shared knowledge base (project knowledge). It exists to solve the structural problem of the loose chat: in a chat, the context dies with the conversation. In a Project, the context is the baseline conversation every other one starts from.

Decision rule the exam expects: if you're going to do the same class of task more than once with the same background material, it's a Project. Drafting one reply to a client today is a chat. Drafting client replies every day using the same tone guide, the same catalog, and the same refund policy is a Project. Researching a one-off topic is a chat; maintaining a Project per client account (with its brief, its history, and its legal constraints) is what the competent Associate does.

The nuance that separates the people who really get it: a Project is not a folder. Don't group by topic — group by configuration. Two tasks that need different instructions or different knowledge belong in different Projects, even if they're about the same client. A Project meant to cover "everything Marketing does" ends up with generic instructions (useless) and a contradictory knowledge base (dangerous).

2. Project Instructions = the Associate's System-Level Instructions

The objective says "create effective system-level instructions." For a non-developer profile, that's not the API's system parameter — it's the Project's instructions (and, where relevant, custom styles). They're the functional equivalent: text Claude has in front of it in every conversation in that space, before the user types a single word.

What a good Project instruction contains, in this order:

  1. Role and audience. "You act as an operations analyst writing for the executive committee of an insurance company." One sentence changes the entire register.
  2. Scope and limits. Which tasks are in, which are out. "You do not draft communications to regulators; those get escalated."
  3. Source of truth. "When the Project's knowledge conflicts with your general knowledge, the Project's knowledge wins. If a fact isn't in the knowledge, say so explicitly instead of inferring it."
  4. Default output format. Table, one-page memo, bullets with a cited source. This alone eliminates half of all iterations.
  5. Hard constraints. Never invent figures. Never cite a policy without giving its file name. Never include client names in examples.
  6. Escalation rule. "If the question involves legal interpretation, respond with the draft and add a note that it requires Legal review."

What does not go in the instructions: content. Instructions say how to behave; knowledge says what is true. Pasting the entire refund policy into the instructions is the most common configuration mistake in this profile: it mixes what's stable (behavior) with what's volatile (fact), and when the fact changes you end up having to rewrite the behavior.

Advanced nuance: instructions are context, not an enforcement mechanism. They massively reduce variation, but they are not a security control. "Instruct Claude not to use personal data" is not a privacy control — the control is not uploading the data in the first place. The decoder calls this the Fake Control, and in Domain 5 it shows up disguised as configuration.

3. Knowledge Sources: Upload (Snapshot) vs. Connector (Live Source)

There are two ways to get knowledge into the workspace, and confusing them is a guaranteed exam item.

Uploaded file (uploaded knowledge). This is a freeze-frame. The content gets copied into the Project in the state it was in on the day you uploaded it. If the original document changes tomorrow, the Project has no idea. Advantage: stable, always available, doesn't depend on external permissions. Risk: it silently rots.

Connector (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail). Connects Claude to the system where the data lives and queries it at the moment of the request. Advantage: it never goes stale; it reflects the source's current state. Risks: it depends on the source being reachable, on permissions, and on whatever's in there being organized — a chaotic connected Drive produces chaotic answers.

Decision rule: content that changes → connector; stable, critical content you want to freeze and audit → a controlled upload. A signed contract gets uploaded. This week's sales pipeline gets queried through a connector. The brand style guide gets uploaded (and versioned). The support inbox gets queried through a connector.

4. Permissions and the "Copy" Effect: the Nuance Almost Nobody Sees

Connectors operate with the permissions of the user who connected them: Claude can't see anything in your Drive that you yourself can't see. That's why people consider them safe by default — and generally, they are.

The dangerous move is the other one: when you upload a document to a shared Project's knowledge, you're copying that content into the Project — and by doing so, exposing it to everyone who has access to the Project. The source system's permission boundary (the restricted HR folder, the Finance drive) does not travel with the file. A document whose access was restricted to three people ends up, after the upload, available to all fifteen members of the Project. This is the specific governance failure of Domain 5, and the exam can ask it as "what do you check before uploading the file to the team Project?" Answer: who has access to the Project, and whether that set of people actually had a right to the document.

5. Memory vs. Project Knowledge vs. Skills

The guide explicitly asks you to study "Projects, Artifacts, Memory, Skills, and Code Execution." The first three context mechanisms get confused with each other:

  • Project knowledge — what's true for this workspace. You put it there deliberately, and you can delete it. It's the authoritative source you want Claude to use.
  • Memory — what Claude retains from your work over time, so you don't have to repeat context between conversations. It's cumulative and convenient, but it is not a curated, authoritative source: don't use it as a substitute for uploading the right document. Memory remembers that you work with brand X; it doesn't guarantee it remembers clause 4.2 of the contract.
  • Skills — a packaged, reusable procedure: instructions, templates, and resources that Claude loads on demand, only when the task fits. The architectural difference from Project instructions is the moment of loading: Project instructions are always present within that Project; a Skill is available as a capability and activates when it applies, and it's reusable across Projects and chats.

Assignment rule, which is the exam's real question:

What You WantWhere It Goes
Applies to this conversation and nothing elseThe prompt
Applies to everything done in this workspaceProject instructions
A queryable fact, not a behavior ruleProject knowledge (upload or connector)
A repeatable procedure you want to use across several ProjectsSkill
An organizational obligation that can't depend on the user's judgmentPolicy / admin-managed configuration (Team/Enterprise), not an instruction

6. Knowledge Base Hygiene

A knowledge base is not a file: it's a living system with five rules.

  1. One single source of truth per topic. If politica_reembolsos_v2.pdf and politica_reembolsos_FINAL_final.pdf both exist side by side, Claude has no reliable way of knowing which one wins — and it will pick one confidently anyway. Duplicate = a scheduled hallucination.
  2. Date and version in the file name, plus an effective-date line inside the document. It gives Claude — and the human — a signal to break the tie.
  3. Upload what's used, not what exists. Dumping 300 documents in "just in case" degrades retrieval: noise gets in, and relevant material has to compete with tangential material. Fewer, well-chosen documents beat a complete archive.
  4. Retire it — don't annotate it. The way to kill an obsolete document is to remove it from the Project's knowledge, not to add an instruction that says "ignore the 2024 version." An instruction is a plea; deletion is a control.
  5. Owner and cadence. Every Project needs a responsible person and a periodic review (monthly, or whenever the policy feeding it changes), plus a notice to the Project's users whenever the configuration changes — that's exactly the objective "inform, maintain, and update."

7. Data Sensitivity in Configuration

Project knowledge is the point where Domain 5 touches Domain 6. Before uploading, ask: does the document contain regulated personal data, salary data, health data, confidential contract terms? If so, anonymization or redaction happens before the upload, at the source. Once the file has entered the Project, the data has already crossed the perimeter; no instruction written afterward reverses that. And if organizational policy prohibits that data in the tool, the correct path isn't "upload it and ask for discretion" — it's anonymize and proceed, or escalate if there's no anonymizable version.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — The Support Project That Started Lying

Situation. Marisol runs the Customer Success team at a fintech. She has a "Tier 1 Responses" Project with tone instructions and eight documents in its knowledge, including politica_reembolsos_2025.pdf. On July 1st a new policy takes effect: the refund window drops from 30 to 14 days. Marisol uploads politica_reembolsos_2026.pdf to the Project. Two weeks later, an agent notices Claude is still promising 30 days to some customers.

Mediocre candidate. Adds to the Project instructions: "Always use the most recent policy and ignore the 2025 one." And moves on.

Competent candidate. Removes politica_reembolsos_2025.pdf from the Project's knowledge, verifies that no other document (an internal FAQ, an email macro) repeats the old window, renames the current one with its effective date, and posts in the team channel that the Project was updated, and why.

Why. With both documents present, both count as "Project knowledge" and both sound authoritative: the instruction is competing against a document, and there's no guarantee it wins. The control is removing the document, not begging the model. Also, the error rarely lives in just one file — the old policy is also quoted in the FAQ.

Example 2 — The Brief That Gets Pasted Every Day

Situation. Diego, a PM at an agency, manages a hotel chain's account. Every morning he opens a new chat, pastes the 4-page brand brief, pastes the tone of voice, pastes the list of prohibited topics, and then asks for the day's post. He complains that results vary wildly from day to day.

Mediocre candidate. Writes a longer, more emphatic prompt ("IT IS CRITICAL that you respect the tone"), and saves the prompt in a Notes document so he can paste it faster.

Competent candidate. Creates one Project per account. In instructions: role (brand copywriter), audience, tone, prohibited topics, default output format (3 variants + a note on why), escalation rule (campaigns with a legal claim → Legal review). In knowledge: the brand brief, the tone guide, the history of posts that worked. The daily prompt shrinks to: "Post for the family suite launch, focused on families with young children, summer event."

Why. The variation came from the context being re-pasted by hand and never being quite identical. Moving what's stable into the configuration eliminates the variance and frees the prompt up for the one real variable each day. And it creates a transferable asset: if Diego leaves, the account keeps running.

Example 3 — An Entire Drive vs. Four Documents

Situation. Lorena, from HR, wants Claude to answer employee questions about benefits. Her "HR" Drive folder has 240 files: current policies, drafts, meeting minutes, 2023 payroll records, and a beneficios_propuesta_borrador.docx that was never approved.

Mediocre candidate. Connects the Google Drive connector to the entire "HR" folder and assumes Claude will be able to tell what's current from what isn't.

Competent candidate. Creates a "Benefits Questions" Project, uploads (or connects, if they change) only the four current benefits documents, leaves out drafts, meeting minutes, and anything with payroll data, and writes in the instructions: "Answer exclusively based on the Project's documents. If the answer isn't in them, say so and refer the person to rrhh@empresa.com." Sets a quarterly review with a named owner.

Why. An unapproved draft sitting in the knowledge base is indistinguishable, to the model, from a current policy: it will produce confident answers about a benefit that doesn't exist. Beyond that, payroll data is regulated data that should never have been within reach of a Project the team can query. And "answer only from the documents, say so if it's not there" turns silence into a valid output instead of an invention.

Example 4 — Uploading a Restricted Document to a Shared Project

Situation. Andrés is preparing a turnover analysis. The compensation report he needs sits in a Drive folder that only he, his director, and Finance can access. His "People Analytics" Project is shared with all eleven members of the operations team.

Mediocre candidate. Uploads the report to the Project's knowledge — "it's the only way for Claude to read it."

Competent candidate. Stops at the permission question. Checks who has access to the Project; that set doesn't match who actually had a right to the report. Valid options: (a) work in a private Project, or one restricted to the same people, or (b) upload an aggregated/anonymized version (salary ranges by band, no names) to the shared Project and run the analysis on that instead.

Why. Uploading a document to a shared Project copies the content into the Project; the source system's access control doesn't travel with it. This is a data leak executed with the best of intentions. Note that the correct answer is not "cancel the analysis" — it's apply the control and proceed, the pattern the exam rewards across all three official samples.

Example 5 — The Instruction That Was Actually Knowledge

Situation. A sales Project has 2,300 words of instructions: they include the full list of 40 SKUs with their prices, the discount schedule, and delivery times by region.

Mediocre candidate. When three prices change, edits the instructions by hand and adds a note: "updated in March."

Competent candidate. Pulls all the content out of the instructions and into a knowledge document (catalogo_precios_2026-07.csv, or better yet, a connector to the live pricing sheet). Leaves only behavior in the instructions: role, quote format, the policy "never invent a price; if the SKU isn't in the catalog, say so," and the escalation rule for off-table discounts.

Why. Instructions and knowledge have different lifecycles: behavior changes once a year, prices change every month. Mixing them turns every data update into a configuration edit — expensive, error-prone, and untraceable. On top of that, 2,300 words of instructions dilute the rules that actually matter.

How the Exam Asks This

Stem verbs and anchors. The decoder already gives you the domain's lexical tell: "Project instructions", "knowledge source", "upload documents", "connector", "Google Drive", "Gmail", "system-level instructions", "the knowledge is outdated", "the team keeps re-pasting…", "the policy changed last month", "who should maintain…". When you see "the same context every time" or "the document was updated but Claude still says…," you're in D5.

The shape of the correct answer. It's always: put the piece in the right place in the configuration, and maintain it. Translated into options: move what's stable into instructions, move facts into knowledge, retire what's obsolete from the base, choose a connector when the source changes, verify permissions before uploading, name an owner and a review cadence.

Canonical distractors in this domain, mapped to the decoder's archetypes:

  • Fake Control (C). "Add to the instructions to ignore the old document." "Tell Claude to only use the most recent policy." Sounds like configuration; is a plea. The real control is deleting the document.
  • Maximalism (E). "Connect the entire Drive folder / upload every available document so Claude has maximum context." More knowledge isn't better knowledge: noise and drafts compete with what's current.
  • Cosmetic Fix (D). "Rewrite the instructions with more emphatic language." Doesn't touch the cause (the stale data or the duplicate file).
  • Wrong Lever (F). "Switch to a more capable model so it can tell which policy is current." No model can guess which of two authoritative-looking documents is valid; the problem is configuration, not capability.
  • Zero-Effort Shortcut (A). "Keep pasting the brief into every chat — it already works." Usually comes with the subordinate clause "since the team is small" / "since it only takes a minute."
  • Escape Hatch (G). "Stop using Projects and do everything in loose chats." Eliminates the capability instead of managing it.
  • Circular Self-Verification (B). "Ask Claude which of the two documents is current." The model is not the authority on your policy's currency — the document owner is.

Options that "sound right and fail." Three specific to this domain: (1) "Save the instructions in a knowledge document so they're always available" — confuses behavior with fact; instructions go in the instructions field. (2) "Create a Project for every task" — proliferation: the unit isn't the task, it's the shared configuration. (3) "Upload the document and then instruct Claude not to share it with other Project members" — permission isn't managed through instructions.

Multiple-response. When an item asks you to "select two," the correct pair almost always combines an action on the configuration (retire/update/move to the right place) with a maintenance or communication action (name an owner, set a review, notify the Project's users). That second component is what the objective calls inform, and it's the one candidates forget.

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting content into the instructions. Correction: instructions = behavior (role, format, limits, escalation); knowledge = queryable facts. Different lifecycles, different places.
  2. Believing an instruction overrides an obsolete document. Correction: remove the document from the Project's knowledge. An instruction is context, not enforcement.
  3. Letting two versions of the same document coexist. Correction: one single source of truth per topic, with date and version in the name. A duplicate is a scheduled hallucination.
  4. Dumping the whole repository "just in case." Correction: upload only what's current and what's actually used. Drafts, meeting minutes, and dead versions poison retrieval.
  5. Assuming an uploaded file updates itself. Correction: an upload is a snapshot. If the source changes and you need the current state, use a connector or deliberately re-upload.
  6. Assuming a connector fixes the source's mess. Correction: a connector reflects the source exactly as it is. A chaotic connected Drive gives chaotic answers; sort out the source first, or narrow the scope.
  7. Uploading a document with restricted access to a shared Project. Correction: the source system's permission doesn't travel with the file. Check who can see the Project before uploading; use a restricted Project or an anonymized version.
  8. Putting personal or regulated data into the knowledge base and "asking Claude for discretion." Correction: anonymization happens before the upload, at the source. No prompt reverses data that has already crossed the perimeter.
  9. Configuring a Project and never looking at it again. Correction: named owner + review cadence + event-triggered review (policy change, price change, product change). Without maintenance, the configuration turns into a liability.
  10. Updating the configuration and telling no one. Correction: the objective says inform. The Project's users need to know what changed, when, and which earlier outputs might be affected.
  11. Confusing memory with the knowledge base. Correction: memory is cumulative convenience; Project knowledge is a curated, auditable source. Critical facts get uploaded — they don't get entrusted to memory.
  12. Creating a Project by topic instead of by configuration. Correction: if two tasks need different instructions or different knowledge, they're different Projects, even if they share a client or a topic.
  13. Not telling the Project what to do when the data isn't there. Correction: include in the instructions "if it's not in the Project's knowledge, say so and don't infer it." This turns a gap into an honest answer instead of a plausible invention.
  14. Escalating something that is really just configuration to a developer. Correction: configuring Projects, instructions, and connectors is within the Associate's scope. What gets escalated is API integration, agentic systems, and enterprise architecture — not the upkeep of a knowledge base.

Glossary

TermGlossMeaning
Projecta persistent shared workspaceA persistent workspace that groups chats, instructions, and shared knowledge together.
Project instructionsstanding behavior rulesBehavioral text that applies to every conversation in that Project.
System-level instructionsrules that frame every requestRules that frame Claude before any request; for the Associate, this means the Project's instructions.
Project knowledge / knowledge basethe Project's authoritative factsThe documents and sources Claude consults as the authoritative source inside the Project.
Knowledge sourceany content originAny content origin added to the Project: an uploaded file or a connector.
Uploaded knowledgea frozen copyA file copied into the Project: a freeze-frame that doesn't update on its own.
Connectora live link with your permissionsAn integration with an external system (Google Drive, Gmail) that queries the live source using your permissions.
Snapshotpoint-in-time copyA copy of the content in the state it had at the moment it was uploaded.
Source of truththe one document that decidesThe single document that decides, per topic, what is true.
Stale knowledgeoutdated but still presentA document still active in the Project but already superseded in reality: the cause of confidently wrong answers.
Memorycross-conversation retentionRetention of context across conversations; convenient, but not a curated source.
Skillon-demand reusable procedureA reusable procedure (instructions + resources) that Claude loads on demand when the task fits.
Custom stylereusable voice/format settingA reusable voice-and-formatting configuration.
Knowledge hygienekeeping the base cleanThe practice of keeping the knowledge base clean: no duplicates, nothing stale, with an owner and a cadence.
Permission boundarywho's allowed to see whatWho can see what; it breaks the moment you copy a restricted document into a shared space.
Redaction / anonymizationstripping identifiers before uploadRemoving or masking identifiers before the data enters the tool.
Owner / review cadencewho's responsible, how oftenThe person responsible for a Project and how often its configuration gets reviewed.

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you haven't mastered the domain.

  1. I can explain in one sentence when a task justifies a Project and when it stays a loose chat.
  2. I know what goes in the Project's instructions and what goes in the knowledge, and I can justify the separation by lifecycle.
  3. I can write Project instructions that include role, scope, source of truth, format, hard constraints, and an escalation rule.
  4. I know why "instruct Claude to ignore the old document" is not a control, and what to do instead.
  5. I can explain the difference between an uploaded file (snapshot) and a connector (live source), and choose between them based on the content's volatility.
  6. I know that uploading a document to a shared Project exposes it to every member of that Project, and I check permissions before uploading.
  7. I know a connector operates with the user's permissions and that it doesn't fix the source's mess.
  8. I can diagnose a confidently wrong answer as a knowledge-base problem (duplicate, stale, draft) rather than a model or prompt problem.
  9. I know why dumping the entire repository makes results worse instead of better.
  10. I can design a Project's maintenance plan: a named owner, a review cadence, event-based triggers, and a notice to users when the configuration changes.
  11. I can distinguish memory, Project knowledge, and Skill, and I know which to use for each type of context.
  12. I know how to include the "if it's not in the knowledge, say so" rule in instructions, and I can explain why it reduces hallucinations.
  13. I apply anonymization before the upload, not afterward through instructions.
  14. I can recognize the domain's distractors: instruction-as-control, knowledge maximalism, a more expensive model to fix a dirty base, asking Claude which document is current.
  15. I know that configuring and maintaining Projects is within the Associate's scope, and what actually does get escalated to Architect/Developer.

domains.title: Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use
objectives: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations
Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
domains.html:
Why it's worth 15%

This domain doesn't measure whether you know the rules. It measures whether you know how to deliver the work with the controls in place. The other six domains ask you how to get Claude to produce value; Domain 6 asks you under what conditions that value is legitimate, and what you do when the obvious path to obtaining it crosses a line. It's the domain where the organization stops seeing Claude as a personal tool and starts seeing it as a risk surface: data leaving the perimeter, decisions about people made from a model's draft, published content with no disclosure of who wrote it, a process that works fine until the day an auditor asks who reviewed what.

The business decision it represents is concrete and recurring: do I proceed, proceed with a control, or escalate? 15% of the exam — about nine items — lives in that fork. And the bias the exam punishes here is double, not single. It punishes the lax (uploads the file with account numbers "because it's internal") and it punishes the paralyzed (cancels the analysis "out of caution"). The official Domain 6 sample spells it out in the rationale: anonymizing the identifiers "allows the analysis to proceed"; abandoning the task (option D) is "unnecessary." Governance enables the work; it doesn't block it. The candidate who internalizes that gets almost the whole domain right; the one who memorizes prohibitions fails the items where the correct answer is to do the work.

Official objectives

The four task statements from the guide, verbatim:

• Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases You'll be given a use case and you'll have to decide whether Claude is the right tool, whether it is with a safeguard on top, or whether the case demands protected human judgment and falls outside. The axis isn't the topic, it's the consequence.

• Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations You'll be given data (a CSV, an email, a contract, a file) and you'll have to decide what can go into Claude, in what form, and under which plan. The correct answer is almost always to minimize or anonymize at the source and proceed.

• Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards You'll be given an internal policy in the stem and you'll have to apply it to the letter, even when another option is technically viable or faster. The policy stated in the stem is a hard constraint, not a suggestion.

• Understand the ethical implications of AI usage You'll be given bias, opacity, attribution, over-reliance, or impact on people, and you'll have to choose the action that preserves human accountability and transparency, not the one that "sounds ethical."

Key concepts

1. Appropriate vs. inappropriate: the axis is the consequence, not the topic (appropriate/inappropriate use case)

The beginner's mistake is to classify by topic: "healthcare = forbidden," "legal = forbidden," "HR = forbidden." False. Claude is used massively in healthcare, legal, and HR. What changes isn't the topic but what is done with the output. Three questions sort any case:

  1. What consequence does the output have on a person? Drafting a vacation policy ≠ deciding who gets fired.
  2. Is it reversible? An internal draft that someone will review is reversible. An email sent to a customer, a publication, a signed opinion, is not.
  3. Does it require protected professional judgment? Diagnosis, legal advice, credit decisions, academic grading: someone with a license and legal accountability answers for that.

From there comes the scale the exam uses over and over, from lower to higher control:

Case profileWhat the Associate does
Low risk, reversible, internal (summarizing notes, brainstorming, reformatting data, drafting a first pass)Use Claude directly. Validate the output (Domain 2), but with no extra ceremony
Output that gets published or sent to an external partyHuman review before sending + fact- and citation-checking
Sensitive data involvedMinimize / anonymize before uploading, and proceed
High-risk use caseMandatory human-in-the-loop + disclosure (see below). The qualified professional reviews and signs off
Use prohibited by the Usage Policy or with no compliant path under internal policyDon't use Claude. Escalate

The nuance that separates those who know: "inappropriate" almost never means "don't touch the topic"; it means "don't let the model's output be the final decision." Claude can analyze 400 résumés and extract the skills mentioned in each one; what it can't do is be the one who decides who gets hired.

2. Anthropic's Usage Policy and High-Risk Use Cases

The Usage Policy (also called the AUP) is the legal floor that no internal policy releases you from. It has three parts: Universal Usage Standards, High-Risk Use Case Requirements, and additional guidelines by case.

The Universal Usage Standards are absolute prohibitions, written as "Do Not…": violating the law, compromising critical infrastructure, compromising computer or network systems, developing or designing weapons, inciting violence or hatred, compromising privacy or identity rights, compromising child safety, creating psychologically or emotionally harmful content, creating or spreading misinformation, undermining democratic processes, prohibited uses in criminal justice / censorship / surveillance, fraudulent or predatory practices, abusing the platform, and generating explicit sexual content. For the exam you don't need to recite all fourteen: you need to recognize that no business justification ("it's for a client," "it's internal," "it's a pilot") enables one of these. If a stem describes covert surveillance of employees, identity impersonation, or generating misinformation, there is no middle-ground option: the answer is don't proceed and escalate.

The High-Risk Use Cases are the examinable heart of the domain, because there a compliant path does exist. They're defined as uses where the output materially affects an individual, and the Usage Policy requires two safeguards, simultaneous and non-optional:

  • Human-in-the-loop: "a qualified professional in that field must review the content or decision prior to dissemination or finalization" — a qualified professional in that field reviews the content or decision before disseminating or finalizing it. Note the two words the exam exploits: qualified (not just any colleague; someone with domain competence) and prior (before, not after sending it).
  • Disclosure: the affected person must be told that AI is being used to help produce the advice, decision, or recommendation.

Domains covered: legal, healthcare, insurance, finance, employment and housing, academic testing/accreditation/admissions, and professional journalistic or media content. Memorize that list: when a stem mentions employment, housing, credit, insurance, health, admissions, or journalism, you already know the correct answer will contain review by a qualified professional and transparency, not just one of the two.

Additional rule that shows up in product items: consumer-facing chatbots must disclose at the start of the session that the user is interacting with an AI, not a human. The disclosure goes up front, not buried in a footer.

3. Data sensitivity: the control is applied at the source, before upload

Minimum taxonomy you must distinguish:

CategoryWhat it isTypical example in an item
PII (personally identifiable information)Identifies a personName + account number, email, tax ID/SSN, address
PHI (protected health information)Clinical data linked to a person; regulated (HIPAA in the US)Medical record, diagnosis with the patient's name
Payment dataCards, bank accountsA transaction export with a PAN
Confidential / intellectual propertyNot "personal," but secretSource code, an NDA-covered contract, roadmap, pricing
Third-party data under contractA client's data that you're the custodian ofThe dataset a client handed you with a no-sharing clause

And the technique the exam rewards:

  • Data minimization: upload only the columns/fields the analysis needs. If you're going to analyze consumption trends, the name and the account number add nothing to the analysis: remove them.
  • Anonymization / de-identification: removing direct identifiers.
  • Pseudonymization: replacing the identifier with a stable token (CUSTOMER_001) — lets you keep the relationship between rows without exposing the person. It's the sophisticated option when the analysis needs to group by customer.
  • Redaction: removing sensitive fragments from a document before attaching it.

The decisive nuance, and the most expensive distractor in the whole exam: a data control is applied before the data crosses the perimeter, not after. Asking Claude "don't save this," "don't use this for training," "ignore the names" is not a control. By the moment of upload, the data has already left. The policy is satisfied by sanitizing the file, not by instructing the model. Every distractor built on "upload the file but tell Claude to…" is false by design.

4. Where your data lives: consumption plan vs. commercial plan

This is the block of verifiable facts, and the one that separates the candidate who understands governance from the one who just senses it. The difference does not depend on the model (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5 are all the same): it depends on the plan and the workspace you work in.

Commercial products (Claude for Work — Team and Enterprise — and the Claude API): Anthropic's documentation is explicit — "Retained data is never used for model training without your express permission." In other words, by default your data is not used for training; your express permission is required. This is the real argument an Associate brings to their risk committee, and that's why the correct answer to "where do I do this work with company data?" is usually "in the approved corporate workspace," not "on my personal Pro account."

Consumer products (Free / Pro / Max): there's a model improvement setting in Privacy Settings. If the user opts in, Anthropic may retain the data in de-identified form for up to 5 years in training pipelines. If they don't opt in, it's not retained for future training. Incognito chats are excluded from training even if the setting is on.

Retention that applies no matter what, and that the exam can use as a trap:

  • A deleted conversation disappears from the history immediately and from back-end systems within 30 days.
  • If the chat is flagged by automated trust & safety systems, inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 2 years, and classification scores for up to 7 years. Examinable corollary: deleting the chat does not undo a leak. If you uploaded regulated data by mistake, the correct act is to report it to the policy/privacy owner, not delete the conversation and stay quiet.

Governance controls the Enterprise plan provides (the ones an Associate requests, not configures alone): audit logs (logs of user actions, system events, and data access), SCIM (automated account provisioning), custom data retention controls, Compliance API (programmatic access to activity logs, chat histories, and file content, filterable by user and time range), Analytics API, customer-managed encryption keys, and US-only inference. In the Claude API there is also ZDR (zero data retention), enabled per organization through the sales team, and HIPAA readiness with a signed BAA. ZDR and HIPAA are Architect/Developer territory: the Associate should know they exist and who to ask for them, not implement them. That distinction is exactly the "recognize limitations and escalate" from the guide.

5. The perimeter extends with Projects and connectors

A Project with knowledge sources is a persistent repository: what you upload there isn't an ephemeral message, it's an asset that every member of the Project sees. A connector (Google Drive, Gmail) extends Claude's reach to the source system with the permissions of the user who connected it. Consequences the exam rewards:

  • Before sharing a Project, audit its knowledge base. A document uploaded "just for a quick question" three weeks ago is still there, and it gets shared with whoever you invite.
  • A connector doesn't create new permissions, but it does create a new route. If your Gmail inbox contains customer data, connecting it brings that data into Claude's scope even if your intent was only to search your own emails.
  • Project instructions are not a security control. Writing "never quote personal data" in the Project's instructions doesn't stop the personal data from being in the knowledge base. Instruction ≠ control. (Same principle as in §3.)

6. The policy hierarchy: the most restrictive wins

Four layers, and the most restrictive one that applies always wins:

  1. Law and regulation (GDPR, HIPAA, local data-protection laws, sector regulation).
  2. Anthropic Usage Policy — the non-negotiable floor.
  3. The organization's AI policy — allowed plan, authorized data classifications, prohibited cases, disclosure rules, human-review requirements, logging/retention.
  4. Team or client rules (an NDA clause that forbids processing the client's data in third-party tools is more restrictive than your internal policy, and it wins).

The nuance: Anthropic allowing something doesn't mean your company allows it, and your company allowing it doesn't mean your contract with your client allows it. On the exam, the restriction written into the stem is the one that rules, even if you know there's technically another path. If the stem says "organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data," no option that uploads that data survives, no matter how good the justification.

7. Applied ethics: bias, transparency, accountability, over-reliance

Four axes, each with its corresponding action:

  • Bias / fairness. The model learns from human text and can reproduce discriminatory patterns. Real risk when the output touches employment, housing, credit, or education (note: the same high-risk domains). Correct action: explicit, structured evaluation criteria, human review of decisions, and audit of aggregate results looking for disparate impact. Typical distractor: adding "be unbiased" to the prompt. Writing "don't be biased" doesn't remove bias; it's the ethical version of the "lying control."
  • Transparency / disclosure. Saying when AI was involved: mandatory in high-risk cases and consumer chatbots; good practice in general. Presenting AI-generated content as written entirely by a human, where disclosure is required, is a governance failure, not a style detail.
  • Accountability. Responsibility is not delegated to the model. Whoever signs off answers for it. "Claude said so" is not a defense before an auditor, a regulator, or a client. Corollary: there is always a named human responsible for the output.
  • Over-reliance / automation bias. The human tendency to accept the machine's output because it sounds confident. It's the bridge to Domain 2 (21%): fluency is not accuracy. Correct action: mandatory checkpoints in the workflow, not "trust it more or less."

8. Escalation: three different destinations, not one

Escalating well is an examinable competency, and the exam distinguishes who you escalate to:

  • To a human domain expert (lawyer, doctor, HR, finance) → when the case is high-risk and requires protected professional judgment.
  • To legal / compliance / privacy / the data-policy owner → when the question is whether the data can be processed at all, or when an incident has already happened.
  • To Claude Architects and Developers → when the work exceeds the Associate's scope: API integration, agentic systems, enterprise architecture, ZDR/BAA, technical controls.

Escalating is not evading. If a compliant action exists within the Associate's scope (anonymize and proceed, request approval, move the work to the corporate workspace), that action wins over escalating. Escalating is correct only when there's no compliant middle path, or when the final decision requires an authority you don't have.

Worked examples

Example 1 — The delinquency CSV

Situation. Lucía, an ops analyst at a fintech, has a 12,400-row CSV with name, account_number, email, balance, days_overdue, region, product. She was asked for an analysis of delinquency patterns by region and product for Thursday's committee. Company policy prohibits sharing regulated personal data with third-party tools.

Mediocre candidate. Two possible and symmetric failures: (a) uploads the full CSV to Claude "because the analysis is internal and no one outside will see it"; (b) cancels the analysis and does it by hand in a spreadsheet "out of caution," arriving late and worse to the committee.

Competent candidate. Removes name, account_number, and email from the file — none of those columns add anything to an analysis by region and product. If she needs to keep the "customer" unit to count unique customers, she pseudonymizes: CUSTOMER_0001…CUSTOMER_9999. Uploads the sanitized file to the approved corporate workspace, not her personal Pro account. Runs the analysis and validates the numbers against the source report before bringing them to the committee.

Why. The analysis never needed the identifiers: data minimization costs the result nothing and fully satisfies the policy. Option (a) violates the policy even with innocent intent, and "it's internal" is exactly the causal clause the exam uses as bait. Option (b) sacrifices business value needlessly: the official rationale is blunt that abandoning the task "is unnecessary when anonymization enables it." And choosing the right workspace is a real control (commercial plan → not used to train on your data by default), unlike telling Claude not to retain anything, which isn't a control at all.

Example 2 — The 380-résumé summary

Situation. Marco, an HR PM, wants to use Claude to process 380 résumés for an engineering opening: extract years of experience, technologies, and certifications, and produce a shortlist of 20 candidates to interview.

Mediocre candidate. Asks Claude to "score each résumé from 1 to 10 and give me the top 20," and takes that list to interviews. Alternatively, decides "AI in recruiting is illegal" and doesn't use it for anything.

Competent candidate. Separates two tasks that the mediocre candidate merged into one. Extraction (mechanical, low risk): Claude structures the 380 résumés into a table using objective criteria declared in advance (years in the stack, certifications, relevant experience). Decision (high-risk, employment): made by the human team, with criteria agreed on before seeing the data, and with a qualified recruiter reviewing the selection. In addition, informs candidates that AI assistance is used in the process, and reviews the final list looking for disparate impact (does the shortlist disproportionately eliminate any group?).

Why. Employment is an explicit high-risk domain of the Usage Policy: it requires human-in-the-loop by a qualified professional and disclosure. None of that prohibits using Claude — it prohibits Claude's output from being the decision. Scoring résumés 1 to 10 and acting on that list is delegating the decision to the model, unaudited bias included. And total abandonment isn't the answer either: 80% of the work (extracting and structuring 380 documents) is exactly where Claude adds value, without touching the decision.

Example 3 — The press release with the invented quote

Situation. Ana, in corporate communications, generates a press release about quarterly results with Claude. The release comes out excellent and cites "a 2025 study that found 68% of companies in the sector…" Publication is scheduled for tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.

Mediocre candidate. Publishes: the text is fluent, professional, and the figure sounds plausible. Or asks Claude "are you sure about that figure?" and, on getting a yes, publishes.

Competent candidate. Treats the figure and the study as unverified claims until the primary source is found. If the study exists, cites the original; if it doesn't turn up, removes the claim or replaces it with a number from the company's own financial report. Human review before publishing. And if the organization requires disclosing AI use in published content, discloses it per policy.

Why. Professional journalistic/media content is a high-risk domain. The fabricated quote is a classic hallucination, and the specific detail (a figure with decimals, a subsection number, a year) is precisely where models fabricate with the most confidence. Asking Claude if it's sure is circular self-verification: a model is never an authoritative source about its own accuracy. Publishing for fluency's sake is pure fluency bias. Note the domain crossover: this item could sit in D2 or D6, and the correct answer is the same — verify against the authoritative source before disseminating.

Example 4 — The client's NDA-covered contract

Situation. Diego, an external consultant, has a 90-page contract from his client (under an NDA that forbids processing the information in third-party tools without written authorization) and wants Claude to extract the termination and penalty clauses. His consulting firm does have an approved Enterprise workspace with retention controls.

Mediocre candidate. Uploads the contract to the Enterprise workspace, reasoning: "it's the corporate plan, it doesn't train on our data, I'm covered."

Competent candidate. Recognizes that the binding restriction here is not Anthropic's policy nor his firm's, but the client's NDA, which is the most restrictive layer. Requests written authorization from the client before processing the document; if the client authorizes it, proceeds in the Enterprise workspace (documenting which controls apply: retention, audit logs). If the client doesn't authorize it, escalates and does the work another way.

Why. This is the item that separates someone who understands the policy hierarchy from someone who memorized a single layer. That the commercial plan doesn't train on your data is true and relevant, but it isn't what the NDA forbids: the NDA forbids processing by a third party, period. The no-training guarantee doesn't satisfy a contractual no-processing control. The most restrictive layer wins.

Example 5 — The leak already happened

Situation. A member of Sofía's team pasted, into his personal Pro account, a list of 40 patient names and their diagnoses, to ask for help drafting appointment reminders. He realizes it half an hour later and asks Sofía what to do.

Mediocre candidate. "Delete the conversation and that's it." Or worse: "Tell Claude to forget that data."

Competent candidate. (1) Delete the conversation, yes, but understanding that it's mitigation, not remediation: it disappears from the history immediately and from the back end within 30 days, and if the chat was flagged by trust & safety systems, inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 2 years. (2) Report the incident to the privacy/compliance owner — it's PHI, there are notification obligations Sofía doesn't get to decide alone. (3) Review that personal account's model improvement setting. (4) Fix the root cause: patient-data work doesn't belong in personal accounts; it belongs in the approved environment, and reminders are drafted with pseudonymized templates (PATIENT_01, [DATE]) that don't even require the real data.

Why. The exam loves this pattern because the "delete the chat" distractor looks like a responsible action and is, in fact, insufficient on its own. Deleting doesn't undo the exposure or the regulatory obligations, and "tell Claude to forget" is the lying control in its purest form. The competent answer contains, reports, and fixes the process.

How the exam asks it

Stem verbs and wording. This domain announces itself with: "Organizational policy restricts…," "…contains customer names and account numbers," "regulated," "sensitive," "personal data," "PII," "privacy," "compliance," "appropriate use," "ethical," "before sharing/publishing/finalizing," and the names of high-risk domains (hiring, loan, patient, legal advice, admissions). The closer is almost always "What is the most appropriate action?" — wording that forces you to pick the best among several defensible options, not the only acceptable one.

The shape of the correct option. Apply the control and deliver the work. It reads lexically like: "Remove or anonymize the personal identifiers before uploading, consistent with policy," "Have a qualified [X] review the output before it is sent," "Use the approved corporate workspace," "Disclose that AI assisted in producing the recommendation." Notice that the correct option tends to echo the stem's restriction ("consistent with policy") — the item is written against the blueprint objective, and the objective leaks lexically into the correct option.

The distractors this domain always includes:

  • The Zero-Effort Shortcut with a causal clause. "Upload the file as-is, since the analysis is internal." The "since/because" clause is the tell: when a distractor hands you the reason the control isn't needed, that reason is the trap. Variants: "since it's a pilot," "since only my team sees it," "since the data is already in our CRM."
  • The Lying Control (instruction-as-control). "Upload the file but instruct Claude not to retain it." / "Add 'do not store personal data' to the Project instructions." / "Tell Claude to be unbiased." Asking the model for a behavior is not a governance control. The data already crossed the perimeter at the moment of upload. This family is Domain 6's signature distractor — recognize it and you win items.
  • The Escape Hatch. "Skip the analysis entirely." / "Don't use AI for this at all." This is the domain's real exception — here it sometimes is correct, but only when the stem offers no compliant middle path (a use prohibited by the Usage Policy, data that no anonymization can save, a decision that requires protected judgment and no qualified reviewer exists). Decisive test: if a compliant path exists among the options, abandonment is a distractor. If none exists, abandonment or escalation is the answer.
  • The half-safeguard. Specific to high-risk cases: one option offers human review but omits disclosure, or offers disclosure but lets the model decide. The Usage Policy requires both. When the scenario is legal/health/employment/credit, look for the option that brings both, or the one that brings the missing one.
  • The unqualified reviewer. "Have a teammate skim it before sending." The policy says qualified professional in that field. A marketing colleague reviewing a legal opinion doesn't satisfy the control.
  • Governance cosmetics. "Add a disclaimer at the bottom saying the content may contain errors." A disclaimer doesn't substitute for verification or review. It fixes the appearance of diligence, not the diligence.

Item symmetry, to use under pressure. This domain's items tend to be built as: a lax extreme (upload the data, publish, proceed), a paralyzing extreme (cancel, don't use AI), a sophisticated decoy (the lying control or the half-safeguard), and the disciplined middle action. Kill both extremes, distrust the one that "does something" without touching the root cause, and keep the one that applies a real control and delivers the work.

Common mistakes

  1. Believing that instructing the model is a control. "Upload the file but tell Claude not to retain it." → Correction: data controls are applied before upload, at the source: minimize, anonymize, pseudonymize, redact. An instruction to the model doesn't reverse an exposure or satisfy a policy.
  2. Classifying by topic instead of by consequence. "Health/legal/HR = forbidden." → Correction: what's regulated is the impact of the output on a person. Claude can structure 380 résumés; what it can't do is decide the hire.
  3. Cancelling the work out of caution. → Correction: the official rationale is explicit: abandoning the task is "unnecessary when anonymization enables it." Governance enables. D6 items don't reward the most fearful.
  4. Meeting only half the high-risk requirement. Adding human review and forgetting disclosure (or vice versa). → Correction: the Usage Policy requires human-in-the-loop and disclosure, simultaneously.
  5. Accepting any human reviewer. → Correction: a qualified professional in that field, and before dissemination or finalization, not after.
  6. Thinking the chosen model changes the governance posture. "I use Opus 4.8 because it's safer for sensitive data." → Correction: model choice is Domain 3 (cost/speed/quality). What changes data handling is the plan and workspace (consumer vs. Team/Enterprise vs. API), not the model.
  7. Working company data on a personal account. "It's the same app." → Correction: it isn't, in data terms. On commercial products, retained data is never used for training without express permission; on consumer products there's a model improvement setting that, if the user turns it on, allows de-identified retention for up to 5 years in training pipelines. In addition, audit logs, configurable retention, and the Compliance API only exist on the corporate side.
  8. Believing that deleting the chat undoes the leak. → Correction: deleting removes the conversation from the history immediately and from the back end within 30 days, but if the chat was flagged by trust & safety, inputs and outputs may be retained for up to 2 years (and classification scores up to 7). An incident with regulated data gets reported, not silently deleted.
  9. Assuming Anthropic's permission releases you from the client's contract. → Correction: the most restrictive layer wins: law > Usage Policy > internal policy > client NDA/contract. An NDA that forbids processing data with third parties isn't satisfied by "the commercial plan doesn't train on my data."
  10. Fighting bias with an instruction. "I add 'be unbiased' to the prompt." → Correction: bias is handled with explicit criteria defined beforehand, human review, and audit of aggregate results looking for disparate impact. A phrase in the prompt is the ethical version of the lying control.
  11. Confusing a disclaimer with a safeguard. "I add 'this content may contain errors.'" → Correction: the disclaimer verifies nothing. Verification against the authoritative source + human review are the controls; the disclaimer is cosmetic.
  12. Sharing a Project without auditing its knowledge base. → Correction: knowledge sources persist and get shared with members. Before inviting anyone, review which documents are still there. And remember that Project instructions are not an access control.
  13. Escalating out of convenience. Sending Architects/Developers something that was just anonymizing three columns. → Correction: escalating is correct when the work exceeds the Associate's scope (API, agents, architecture, ZDR/BAA) or requires an authority you don't have. If a compliant action exists within your scope, that action wins.
  14. Delegating responsibility to the model. "Claude said so." → Correction: accountability doesn't transfer. A named human answers for the output, always.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossMeaning
Usage Policy (AUP)Anthropic's rules of useAnthropic's rules on what can and can't be done with Claude; the non-negotiable floor that no internal policy releases you from.
Universal Usage StandardsAbsolute prohibitionsThe Usage Policy's absolute prohibitions ("Do Not…"): no exceptions, no business justification.
High-risk use caseMaterially affects a personA use whose output materially affects an individual (legal, health, insurance, finance, employment/housing, admissions, journalism); requires HITL and disclosure.
Human-in-the-loop (HITL)Qualified human reviewA qualified professional in that field reviews the content or decision before disseminating or finalizing it.
DisclosureTelling the affected personInforming the affected person that AI was used to produce the advice, decision, or recommendation.
PIIPersonally identifiable informationAny data that identifies a person: name, email, account number, tax ID.
PHIProtected health informationClinical data linked to a person; regulated (HIPAA).
Data minimizationUpload only what's neededProcessing only the fields the task actually needs; the rest doesn't get uploaded.
AnonymizationRemoving direct identifiersRemoving the direct identifiers from a dataset before using it.
PseudonymizationStable-token substitutionReplacing the identifier with a stable token (CUSTOMER_001) to preserve relationships without exposing the person.
RedactionBlacking out sensitive textRemoving sensitive fragments from a document before attaching it.
Model improvement settingConsumer opt-in to train on chatsSetting in consumer products (Free/Pro/Max) that, if enabled, allows chats to be used for training; de-identified retention up to 5 years.
Zero Data Retention (ZDR)No prompts/outputs storedAn organization-level arrangement in the Claude API so prompts and responses aren't stored; managed via the sales team (outside the Associate's scope).
BAABusiness Associate AgreementContract required for PHI workloads under HIPAA.
Audit logRecord of user/system actionsLog of user actions, system events, and data access; an Enterprise control.
Compliance APIProgrammatic activity accessProgrammatic (Enterprise) access to activity logs, chat histories, and file content for monitoring and policy enforcement.
Automation bias / over-relianceTrusting output because it sounds confidentAccepting the model's output because it sounds confident, without verifying it.
Disparate impactSkewed harm to one groupA seemingly neutral process that systematically harms one group; the central bias risk in employment, housing, and credit.
AccountabilityA named human answers for itA named human answers for the output; "the model said so" is not a defense.
EscalationRouting to the right authorityTaking the case to whoever has the competence or authority: domain expert, compliance/privacy, or Claude Architects/Developers.

Checklist

If you can't check off one of these, you haven't mastered Domain 6.

  1. I can classify a use case by consequence, reversibility, and protected professional judgment, not by topic.
  2. I can name the seven high-risk domains of the Usage Policy and the two mandatory safeguards they require.
  3. I know that human-in-the-loop means a qualified professional in that field, and before disseminating — not just any colleague, and not after it's sent.
  4. I can explain why an instruction to the model is never a governance control, and I recognize that distractor family in any of its disguises.
  5. I know how to apply minimization, anonymization, pseudonymization, and redaction to data before upload, and choose which one based on what the analysis needs to preserve.
  6. I can explain the difference in data handling between a consumer product (Free/Pro/Max) and a commercial product (Team/Enterprise/API), and why company data work belongs in the approved workspace.
  7. I know that deleting a chat doesn't undo a leak (30 days on the back end; up to 2 years if flagged by trust & safety) and that an incident with regulated data gets reported.
  8. I can name the governance controls Enterprise provides (audit logs, SCIM, configurable retention, Compliance API, customer-managed keys) and I know that ZDR and BAA/HIPAA exist but are escalation territory.
  9. I can order the policy hierarchy (law > Usage Policy > internal policy > client contract/NDA) and I know that the most restrictive one wins.
  10. I know that model choice (Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5) is a cost/speed/quality decision and not a data-governance decision.
  11. I can describe how bias is handled with explicit criteria, human review, and disparate-impact audits — and why "be unbiased" in the prompt doesn't work.
  12. I know when disclosure is mandatory (high-risk, consumer chatbots at session start) and when it's just good practice.
  13. I can explain why a shared Project extends the data perimeter, and why Project instructions are not an access control.
  14. I know how to distinguish escalating (no compliant path within my scope, or lack of authority) from evading (the task is just a hassle), and I know who to escalate to in each case.
  15. Faced with an item from this domain, I can, in under thirty seconds, kill both extremes (the lax one with its "since…" and the paralyzed one) and pick the action that applies the control and delivers the work.
