domains.title: Troubleshooting and Optimization
objectives: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
Adjust approach based on feedback and results
Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
domains.html:
Why it's worth 10%

The six preceding domains measure what you do when the work goes well: writing the prompt, evaluating the output, choosing the model, configuring the Project, applying the policy. Domain 7 measures the only thing left: what you do when it goes wrong, and what you do when it goes well but costs too much. It's the second-order domain. A professional can pass all the others and still be useless in production if, faced with a poor output, their only reflex is to rewrite the prompt "with more effort," move up to the more expensive model, or abandon the tool.

The business decision it represents is concrete and costly: the difference between a pilot that dies in week three and a workflow that survives a year. Every real Claude deployment produces, in its first week, generic outputs, fabricated citations, conversations that drift off course, and more time spent than promised. The organization that knows how to diagnose the cause (ambiguous instruction vs. missing input vs. saturated context vs. poorly chosen tool) fixes it in hours and keeps the process. The one that doesn't concludes "AI doesn't work for this" and throws away months of adoption. That judgment — diagnose before intervening, intervene on the cause and not the symptom, measure whether the intervention worked — is exactly what this domain certifies.

It's worth only 10% (≈6 items out of 60) because its content surface is small, not because it's peripheral. In practice, its items camouflage themselves: a troubleshooting stem looks a lot like one from Domain 1 (prompting) or Domain 3 (model selection). The difference is in the verb tense: Domain 1 asks how you build the prompt; Domain 7 asks what's broken and what you change, with evidence, in an attempt that already failed.

Official objectives

• Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs You'll be given a case where the output already went wrong (generic, incomplete, with invented data, with the wrong tone, with ignored instructions) and you'll have to name the root cause and choose the correction that acts on that cause — not on the symptom, not on the presentation.

• Adjust approach based on feedback and results You'll be given evidence (feedback from a stakeholder, test results, rejected outputs, an iteration that made things worse) and you'll have to choose the next move: which variable to change, what to keep, when to roll back, when to persist the fix in the configuration instead of repairing it by hand every time.

• Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness You'll be given a workflow that already works but is expensive, slow, or fragile (everyone uses the most powerful model for trivial tasks; someone re-pastes the same context 20 times a day; there's human review on 100% of outputs, including zero-risk ones) and you'll have to choose the lever that improves efficiency without breaking quality or control.

Key concepts

1. Diagnosis before intervention

The rule that governs the entire domain: before touching the prompt, classify the failure. A poor output has a bounded number of root causes, and each one has its own correction. Applying one cause's correction to a different cause is wasted work and, worse, noise that keeps you from learning.

Practical taxonomy of root causes, with their correction:

Root causeTypical symptomCorrect fix
Underspecified instruction (underspecified prompt)Generic output, "correct but useless," random formatSpecify format, audience, length, success criteria, and constraints
Missing input (missing context/input)Claude "invents" what it doesn't have, or answers in the abstractGive it the document/data: attach it, upload it as a knowledge source, or paste the excerpt
No success criteriaYou can't say why it's wrong, only that it's "unconvincing"Write down what "good" looks like before iterating
Task too largeSuperficial output, skips steps, covers the first part and abandons the restDecompose (task decomposition) or chain (prompt chaining)
Saturated or contaminated contextIgnores an instruction given 30 turns ago, mixes up two documents, degrades with lengthSummarize the state and restart in a clean chat; persist what's stable in the Project
Lack of groundingSpecific figures and citations that don't exist in any sourceGrounding with literal quotes + explicit permission to say "I don't know" + verification against the source
Outdated knowledgeCites the old policy, last quarter's priceUpdate the knowledge source / connector; don't patch the prompt
Poorly chosen tool or modelToo slow, too expensive, or insufficient for complex reasoningChange model or feature — not a prompt problem

The nuance that separates those who know from those who guess: Anthropic's official documentation is explicit that not every failure is fixed with prompt engineering. Literally: "Not every success criteria or failing eval is best solved by prompt engineering. For example, latency and cost can be sometimes more easily improved by selecting a different model." Iterating on a prompt when the problem is that Claude doesn't have the document — or that the task is running on a model whose latency doesn't fit the process — is the most common way to lose a week.

2. The three prerequisites before iterating

The official docs set three conditions before doing prompt engineering: (1) a clear definition of the use case's success criteria, (2) some way to empirically test against those criteria, and (3) a first draft prompt you want to improve. Translated to the Associate profile:

  • Success criterion = a verifiable sentence. "The summary is good" is not a criterion. "Five bullets, each with the ticket count and its category, ≤200 words, addressed to the director of operations, no recommendations" is. The official criteria are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and almost always multidimensional: quality and tone and privacy and latency and cost. Latency and cost are first-class criteria, not secondary metrics.
  • Way to test = a mini set of real cases, not one case. 5 to 10 inputs representative of the real work, including edge cases the docs explicitly name: irrelevant or nonexistent input, excessively long input, poor or ambiguous user input, cases where not even two humans would agree. Official test-design principle: "prioritize volume over quality" — more cases with quick evaluation is worth more than two cases evaluated lavishly.
  • Draft = the prompt that already failed. Save it. It's your baseline; without a baseline you can't know whether the iteration improved things or made them worse.

3. The golden rule of clarity

Official analogy: "Think of Claude as a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows." And the test, literally: "Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too."

From there come the first-level corrections, all verifiable against the docs:

  • Be explicit about format and constraints. "Create an analytics dashboard" produces the bare minimum; "Create an analytics dashboard. Include as many relevant features and interactions as possible. Go beyond the basics" produces a complete implementation. The model delivers the ceiling you ask for, not the ceiling it's capable of.
  • Give the motivation, not just the rule. Instead of "NEVER use ellipses," say "your response will be read by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses because the engine won't know how to pronounce them." The docs close with: "Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation." An instruction with its reasoning applies to cases you didn't anticipate; a rule with no reasoning breaks on the first odd case.
  • Say what to do, not what not to do. "Don't use markdown" is worse than "write in continuous prose paragraphs."
  • Numbered sequential instructions when order or completeness matters.

4. The intervention ladder (order it by cost, climb it as needed)

When an output fails, there's a cheap→expensive order of interventions. The competent candidate climbs one step at a time and tests; the mediocre one jumps straight to the last one.

  1. Clarify the instruction — format, audience, length, criteria, constraints. Resolves most "generic" outputs.
  2. Add context and motivation — the why, the internal norm, who's going to read it.
  3. Give examples (few-shot) — the docs recommend 3–5 examples, and require them to be relevant (a mirror of the real case), diverse (covering edge cases; poorly diverse examples teach unwanted patterns), and structured. It's the most reliable lever for fixing format, tone, and structure.
  4. Structure the prompt — separate instructions, context, data, and examples into clearly labeled sections. With long documents, the rule is documents on top, the question at the end: the docs report up to +30% quality in tests with complex multi-document inputs.
  5. Decompose or chain — break the task into inspectable steps (generate → review → refine), each in its own turn, instead of one mega-prompt that does eight things.
  6. Persist the fix — if the same tweak is needed every time, stop writing it every time: move it to the Project instructions or upload the recurring material as a knowledge source. A fix that lives in your head isn't a fix, it's a dependency on you.
  7. Change model or feature — the last rung, and the right one when the cause is cost, latency, or a reasoning ceiling. Haiku for high volume and direct tasks; Sonnet as the speed/intelligence balance; Opus (or the more capable Fable/Opus tier) for complex, agentic reasoning. Changing models doesn't fix an ambiguous instruction: it gives you the same generic output, better written.

5. One variable per iteration

The most expensive methodological error for the business profile: changing the prompt, changing the model, and attaching a new document, all at once, seeing that it improved, and having no idea why. The minimum discipline: same test case, one variable changed, side-by-side comparison. It's A/B testing without instrumentation, and it's enough at this level. If you changed three things and it got worse, you can't revert the one that broke it; you have to start from zero.

Corollary: save your versions. The version of the prompt (or of the Project instructions) that worked is an asset. The iteration that "sounded better" and broke three cases that used to pass is called a regression, and you only catch it if you rerun the old cases.

6. Hallucination: a diagnosable failure, not a whim

On the exam, "Claude invented a citation/figure/subsection" is never solved by asking Claude. The official techniques, in order of usefulness for an Associate:

  • Explicitly allow "I don't know": "Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This simple technique can drastically reduce false information." Model phrase: "If you don't have enough information, say: 'I don't have enough information to assess this with confidence.'"
  • Grounding with literal quotes: for long documents (the docs mention >20k tokens), first ask for the literal extraction of the relevant quotes, and only afterward the task, with the explicit constraint "base your analysis solely on the extracted quotes." If there's no quote, have it say so.
  • Post-hoc citation verification: review each claim in the output and demand the citation that backs it up; an unsupported claim gets removed, not softened.
  • External-knowledge restriction: forbid use of the model's general knowledge and limit it to the provided documents.
  • Best-of-N: run the same prompt multiple times and compare; inconsistencies between runs signal hallucination.

Official disclaimer, which the exam can indeed use as the correct option: these techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely. Always validate critical information, especially for high-stakes decisions." Grounding reduces; human verification of critical information is still mandatory.

7. Context drift and saturation

Symptoms: the conversation is 40 turns in; Claude repeats itself, ignores a constraint you gave at the start, mixes up project A with project B, or quality degrades without you having changed anything. Cause: the accumulated context turned into noise.

Correction (and this is exactly what D3's objective calls "when to restart, summarize, or persist"):

  • Summarize: ask Claude for a state summary — decisions made, constraints in force, open questions — and use it as a seed.
  • Restart: open a clean chat with that summary and only the documents that are still relevant.
  • Persist: if the context is permanent (company policy, style guide, catalog), it shouldn't live in the conversation: it should live in the Project instructions or as a knowledge source.

The anti-pattern: insisting. Repeating "remember the product is X" in a saturated thread burns tokens and doesn't fix the cause.

8. Workflow optimization ≠ prompt optimization

The third objective shifts scale: you're no longer optimizing an output, you're optimizing a process. Real levers within an Associate's reach:

  • Standardize what's repeated. If three people write three different prompts for the same task, the output variability isn't Claude's fault. A Project with instructions and a fill-in-the-blanks template eliminates the variance and the rework.
  • Eliminate re-explanation. Every time someone pastes the same context for the twentieth time, there's a knowledge source or a connector (Google Drive, Gmail) that hasn't been set up.
  • Match model to task. 400 short support replies a day don't get the most expensive model "for safety"; they get the fastest and cheapest one, reserving the capable model for complex escalations. The guide's official sample 2 certifies exactly this judgment.
  • Batch the work. Twenty emails classified in a single structured pass cost less time and less context than twenty separate chats.
  • Put human control where the risk is, not on everything. Mandatory review on what goes to compliance, to a client, or to a regulated decision; light review on the internal draft. Reviewing 100% of everything destroys the savings and trains the team to sign without reading.
  • Choose the right output format — artifact for what will be iterated on, reused, or exported; inline for short answers; structured data (table/CSV) when it feeds another system. A workflow where someone copies and re-pastes by hand every day has a diagnosable inefficiency.
  • Measure. Time per unit, re-edit rate (% of outputs that have to be rewritten), factual errors caught in review. Without a measurement there's no optimization: there's just a feeling.

Official warning that the exam can turn into a distractor: "It's always better to first engineer a prompt that works well without model or prompt constraints, and then try latency reduction strategies afterward. Trying to reduce latency prematurely might prevent you from discovering what top performance looks like." Quality first, then cost and speed.

9. Adjusting based on feedback: fix the configuration, not the output

When the stakeholder sends the work back, there are two possible responses. The mediocre one: fix that output by hand and move on. The competent one: classify the rejection ("it's missing the legal disclaimer," "the tone is too informal," "the closing figures are missing") and ask whether it's an isolated case or a pattern. If it's a pattern, the cause is in the configuration — the Project instructions, the knowledge source, the template — and that's where it gets fixed, once and for everyone.

This is the criterion that distinguishes patching outputs from patching the process, and it's the heart of the domain's second objective.

10. Where the Associate's scope ends

The guide is explicit: the Associate recognizes limitations and escalates more complex or technical work to Claude Architects and Developers. Escalating is correct when the problem requires an API, system integration, automated pipelines, or agentic design. Escalating is not correct when the cause is a vague prompt, an outdated knowledge source, or a poorly chosen model: that's within your scope, and the exam expects you to resolve it yourself.

Worked examples

Scenario 1 — The generic summary (cause: underspecification)

Situation. Marta, an operations manager at an insurance company, asks every Monday: "Summarize this week's support tickets." She gets six paragraphs that are correct, fluent, and useless: they don't say how many tickets, what category, or what went up compared to last week. She's already tried three times with different wording.

Mediocre candidate. Concludes the model "doesn't understand the business" and switches to the more capable model. Result: six generic paragraphs, better written.

Competent candidate. Diagnoses underspecification, not lack of capability. Writes the success criterion before touching the prompt: five bullets · each with ticket count and category · variation vs. the previous week · ≤200 words · audience: director of operations · no recommendations. Adds an example of the best report Marta wrote by hand (few-shot). Tests it against two prior weeks' tickets whose report she already knows. Once it works on both, moves the instructions and the example to the Project.

Why. The failure was in the instruction, not the model. Upgrading the model is rung 7 of the ladder applied to a rung-1 problem: it burns budget and doesn't touch the cause. And persisting the fix in the Project turns a one-off win into a process.

Scenario 2 — The statistic that doesn't exist (cause: lack of grounding)

Situation. Javier, in B2B marketing, asks Claude for a one-pager and gets: "68% of B2B buyers abandon the process after the third request for information (Report X, 2025)." The figure is perfect for the campaign. Report X exists; that figure doesn't.

Mediocre candidate. Asks Claude: "Are you sure about that figure?" Claude confirms. Javier publishes. (Or else: adds "don't invent data" to the instructions and considers it solved.)

Competent candidate. Diagnoses hallucination from lack of grounding. Uploads the real report as a knowledge source. Reformulates: "First extract the literal quotes from the report that back up each claim. If you can't find a quote, write 'no citation available.' Base the one-pager solely on those quotes." Reviews the surviving claims against the PDF. Adds a permanent rule to the Project instructions: "Don't cite figures that aren't in the knowledge sources; if they're not there, say so explicitly."

Why. The model's self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy (decoder archetype B: circular self-verification). And a "don't invent" instruction is a lying control (archetype C): the real fix is grounding + permission to say "I don't know" + verification against the source.

Scenario 3 — The thread that drifted (cause: saturated context)

Situation. Lucía, a PM, is 47 turns into a chat where she's designed the requirements for two products, Halo and Nimbus. Claude starts attributing constraints that belonged to Halo to Nimbus instead. Lucía has already corrected it three times: "Remember that Nimbus doesn't have SSO integration."

Mediocre candidate. Corrects it a fourth time, more forcefully and in all caps. The degradation continues.

Competent candidate. Recognizes context saturation. Asks for a state summary: decisions closed, constraints in force per product, open questions. Opens two clean threads — one per product — seeded with that summary and only each product's own documents. Moves what's permanent (glossary, platform constraints) to the Project instructions.

Why. Insisting is intervening on the symptom. The cause is the buildup of contradictory context in the same thread, and its official fix is restart / summarize / persist, not repeating the instruction.

Scenario 4 — The slow, expensive support team (cause: poorly chosen tool + bloated prompt)

Situation. A team processes ~400 level-1 support replies a day. Someone set everything up on the most capable model, with a three-page prompt that includes the company's history and eight examples. The team complains it's slow, and the CFO complains it's expensive. The quality of the replies is good.

Mediocre candidate. Cuts quality: eliminates human review on billing replies to save time. Or else turns off features "to save money" (archetype F: the wrong lever).

Competent candidate. Diagnoses two separate causes. (a) Poorly chosen tool: level 1 is direct, high-volume work → fast, cheap model (Haiku class), reserving the capable model for escalations and complex complaints. (b) Bloated prompt: trims it to 3–5 diverse examples (the official recommendation) and removes the padding that doesn't change the output. Keeps human review only where the risk is: replies touching billing or contractual commitments. Verifies with the same 10 test cases that quality didn't drop.

Why. Latency and cost are, by official doctrine, problems of model selection, not of the prompt. And cutting human control at the point of risk is exactly the trade-off the exam punishes: optimization can't be paid for with governance.

Scenario 5 — The improvement that broke something else (cause: regression)

Situation. Sofía tweaks the Project instructions for the client report generator: adds "Be concise. Cut the filler text." The tone improves. Two weeks later, Legal discovers that the latest reports went out without the mandatory disclaimer.

Mediocre candidate. Pastes the disclaimer in by hand on every report and moves on.

Competent candidate. Identifies a regression: the new instruction ("cut the filler") got interpreted as permission to remove the legal boilerplate. Rewrites the instruction additively and explicitly: "Be concise in the analysis. Keep the legal disclaimer in the final section intact and unmodified; it is mandatory." Reruns the six reference cases she keeps on file — including two that already passed before — and confirms none of them broke.

Why. Every configuration change is a change with side effects. Without a mini regression set, today's improvement is next month's compliance incident. And fixing each output by hand is patching the symptom while the cause (the instruction) stays alive in the Project.

How the exam asks it

Stem verbs and signals. The decoder already flags it: if the stem says "the output is vague / too generic / wrong," "the prompt isn't working," "results got worse after the change," "the associate has already tried X twice," "diagnose," "the most likely cause," "which change is most likely to improve the results," "make this workflow more efficient," you're in Domain 7. Strong, specific signal for this domain: the stem tells you what's already been tried. That detail exists so you rule out repeating it.

Shape of the correct answer. It almost always meets three conditions at once: (a) it names or attacks the root cause the stem hinted at; (b) it changes one variable, so the result is interpretable; (c) it verifies the effect against previous cases or the authoritative source. If an option does something reasonable but doesn't touch the cause named in the stem, it's a distractor by definition.

Distractors this domain uses over and over (mapped to the decoder archetypes):

  • Default maximalism (E). "Switch to the more capable model." Sounds prudent. Fails when the cause is an ambiguous instruction or a missing document: it gives you the same useless answer, better written, more expensive, and slower.
  • Circular self-verification (B). "Ask Claude to review its own answer and confirm it's correct" / "ask it to rate its confidence." Looks diligent. A model is not an authoritative source about its own accuracy.
  • Instruction-as-control (C). "Add to the instructions: 'don't hallucinate' / 'use only real data.'" Names the problem; doesn't install a control. The control is grounding, verification against the source, and explicit permission to say "I don't know."
  • Cosmetics (D). "Rephrase with a more formal tone," "change the report format." If the failure is factual or structural, touching the form doesn't fix it.
  • Zero-effort shortcut (A). "Accept the output, since the team is in a hurry because the process worked before." The causal clause is the bait.
  • Escape hatch (G). "Go back to the manual process" / "try another platform." The exam certifies the ability to apply Claude; abandoning almost never wins.
  • Premature optimization. "Trim the prompt to the bare minimum and drop to the cheaper model to gain speed" — when quality hasn't been established yet. The official docs explicitly warn against this.
  • Over-escalation. "Escalate it to a Claude Developer to build an API integration" — when the cause was an outdated knowledge source. Escalating is correct only when the problem exceeds the Associate's scope (API, integration, agentic system), not when it's simply a hassle.
  • Changing everything at once. "Rewrite the prompt, change the model, and upload new documents." Sounds decisive; destroys any chance of knowing what worked.

The option that "sounds good but fails" in this domain is almost always one of two: asking Claude to self-evaluate or upgrading the model. Both are moves a business professional makes by instinct, and the exam systematically penalizes them.

Multiple-response. When the item asks you to select two or three actions, the typical pattern is one diagnostic action + one corrective action + (sometimes) one verification action. Don't pick two options that are the same idea reworded; the exam doesn't reward redundancy, and one of the two is usually the distractor.

Common mistakes

  1. Iterating on the prompt when the input is missing. → Before rewriting anything, verify that Claude has access to the document, the figure, or the data. A perfect prompt over absent information produces invention.
  2. Changing models as the first resort. → Changing models is the lever for cost, latency, and reasoning ceiling. It doesn't fix ambiguity, doesn't fix missing context, doesn't fix nonexistent success criteria.
  3. Asking Claude if it's sure. → Self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy. Verify against the authoritative source: the document, the regulation, the system of record.
  4. Adding "don't invent data" and considering it solved. → Instruction ≠ control. The official fix is grounding with literal quotes, explicit permission to admit uncertainty, and post-hoc verification of each claim.
  5. Changing three variables at once. → One variable per iteration, on the same test case, comparing side by side. Otherwise you learn nothing and can't revert.
  6. Not having a written success criterion. → "It's wrong" is not a diagnosis. Without a verifiable definition of "good" (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant) there's no measurable improvement, only opinion.
  7. Confusing fluency with accuracy. → Flawless text with a fabricated citation is a failure, and polishing its tone makes it worse. This bias is the one the exam punishes most across the whole blueprint.
  8. Insisting in a saturated thread. → Repeating the instruction in conversation turn 47 doesn't fix the cause. Summarize the state, restart clean, and persist what's permanent in the Project.
  9. Fixing every output by hand instead of fixing the configuration. → If the same error shows up three times, the cause lives in the instructions or the knowledge source, not in the output.
  10. Optimizing cost and latency before you have quality. → Official doctrine: first get it working well with no constraints, then reduce. Optimizing beforehand keeps you from discovering what the ceiling was.
  11. Changing the Project instructions without retesting cases that already worked. → Silent regression. Keep a mini set of 5–10 reference cases and rerun them after every configuration change.
  12. Inflating the prompt indefinitely. → Stacking instructions on top of instructions generates contradictions that cancel each other out. Rewrite it clean: say what to do (not what not to do), give 3–5 diverse examples, remove what doesn't change the output.
  13. Testing the improvement with a single favorable case. → One case is not evidence. Test with representative cases and edge cases (irrelevant input, extremely long input, ambiguous case).
  14. Escalating any friction to Architect/Developer. → Escalating is for what exceeds your scope (API, integrations, agentic systems). A vague prompt, an outdated source, or a poorly chosen model are your job.
  15. Removing human control to gain speed. → Efficiency isn't paid for with governance. Trim review where the risk is low, never where the output touches compliance, clients, or regulated decisions.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossMeaning
Root causeThe real origin of a failureThe actual origin of the failure, not the symptom you see in the output.
Underperforming promptA prompt that reliably falls shortA prompt that repeatably produces outputs that don't meet the success criterion.
Success criteriaA verifiable definition of "good"A verifiable definition of "good": specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant.
BaselineThe version you compare againstThe version of the prompt/config/output that every improvement gets compared to.
IterationOne change-test-compare cycleA cycle of changing one variable, testing it, and comparing against the baseline.
RegressionA fix that breaks something elseA change that fixes one case and breaks another that used to work.
Edge caseAn atypical input that breaks thingsAn atypical input (irrelevant, extremely long, ambiguous) that reveals where the process breaks.
HallucinationA fabricated claim that looks realAn invented claim with the appearance of verifiable data (a citation, figure, subsection).
GroundingForcing answers onto real quotesForcing the response to rest on literal quotes from a provided document.
Few-shot examplesSample outputs that set the pattern3–5 relevant, diverse examples that fix format, tone, and structure.
Task decompositionSplitting a big task into stepsBreaking a large task into manageable, inspectable steps.
Prompt chainingRunning steps separately, in sequenceRunning the task in separate steps (generate → review → refine) instead of one mega-prompt.
Context saturation / driftA thread accumulating too much noiseThe thread has accumulated so much that the model loses focus or mixes up information.
Restart / summarize / persistThe three fixes for saturated contextThe three responses to saturated context: a clean chat, a state summary, or moving the stable part to the Project.
Project instructionsPersistent Project-level configurationPersistent configuration that applies to every conversation in the Project.
Knowledge sourceA document Claude can consultA document uploaded to the Project that Claude can consult across every conversation.
ConnectorA live link to an external sourceAn integration with an external source (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail) that feeds the context.
ArtifactOutput in its own iterable panelOutput rendered in its own panel, meant to be iterated on, reused, or exported.
Human-in-the-loop / review gateA mandatory human checkpointA mandatory human validation step before the output leaves the process.
ThroughputUnits of work per unit of timeHow many units of work the process dispatches per hour or per day.
LatencyTime to first/final responseHow long the response takes to arrive; a first-class success criterion, not a minor detail.
Best-of-N verificationRunning N times to catch driftRunning the same prompt multiple times; inconsistencies between runs expose hallucination.
A/B comparisonSame case, one variable changedSame case, one variable changed, two outputs compared side by side.
EscalationHanding off to Architect/DeveloperPassing work that exceeds the Associate's scope to an Architect/Developer.

Checklist

If you can't check off every statement, you haven't mastered the domain.

  1. I can classify a poor output by its root cause: underspecified instruction, missing input, absent success criteria, task too large, saturated context, lack of grounding, outdated knowledge, or poorly chosen tool.
  2. I can explain why latency and cost are not prompt-engineering problems, and which lever actually solves them.
  3. I can write a verifiable success criterion (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant) for a real business task, before touching the prompt.
  4. I know how to build a mini test set of 5–10 cases that includes edge cases (irrelevant input, extremely long input, ambiguous case) and I use it to catch regressions.
  5. I can state the golden rule of clarity ("if a colleague with little context would be confused by your prompt, Claude will be too") and apply it to a real prompt.
  6. I know why giving the motivation behind an instruction makes it generalize better than giving the bare rule, and I can give an example.
  7. I know how many examples the official docs recommend (3–5) and the three properties they must have (relevant, diverse, structured).
  8. I can order the intervention ladder from cheap to expensive and justify why you climb one rung at a time.
  9. I know why changing more than one variable per iteration destroys your ability to learn from the result.
  10. I can list the official anti-hallucination techniques (permission to say "I don't know," literal quotes before the task, verifying each claim against its citation, restricting external knowledge, best-of-N) and explain why "instruct it not to invent things" is none of them.
  11. I can recognize the symptoms of saturated context and choose between summarizing, restarting, or persisting.
  12. I can distinguish an output fix (patching the symptom) from a configuration fix (patching the cause), and I know when a repeated error requires moving the fix into the Project instructions.
  13. I can name at least four workflow-optimization levers that don't involve changing the model.
  14. I can explain why optimizing latency and cost before establishing quality is an official anti-pattern.
  15. I know where my scope as an Associate ends and when escalating to Architect/Developer is the correct answer — and when it's evasion in disguise.

certs.retakePolicy: Candidates who don't pass may retake the exam after a mandatory waiting period, which grows with each failed attempt: 14 days after the first failure, 30 days after the second, and 90 days after the third. Maximum 4 attempts of the same exam within a rolling 12-month period. Limits apply per exam: failing one doesn't stop you from registering for a different one. The $99 USD fee is paid on every attempt.
certs.recertification: The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded; it's time-limited because the underlying technology evolves fast. To renew on time, you review what's changed since you certified and complete a free, NOT proctored assessment in the Anthropic Partner Academy. The guide explicitly states there is NO cost for on-time renewal ("There is no fee for on-time renewal"). If the credential lapses, you must retake the full exam and pay the full fee to regain certified status. If the exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam instead of the renewal assessment. Holders remain subject to the conduct rules in Section 12.
examDayRules: The exam is administered in a standardized, secure, proctored environment, either online or at a Pearson VUE test center; the rules apply equally to both.
If you test online, you must remain visible to the proctor and the webcam for the entire session.
Keep your workspace free of notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, and any other materials.
Communicating with any other person during the exam is prohibited.
Capturing, copying, photographing, or reproducing exam content in any form is prohibited.
Prohibited items: mobile phones, smartwatches, headphones, study materials, and any recording device.
Permitted items — if any — such as scratch paper provided by the proctor, are defined by Pearson VUE.
You must present a current, government-issued photo ID; the name on the ID must match your registration name EXACTLY.
Before starting, you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement (NDA); if you don't accept it, the session ends and there is no refund.

Consequences of misconduct: cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban from future exams.
Not showing up (no-show) or arriving outside the allowed late-arrival window means forfeiting the fee and having to register again.
certs.scoring: Criterion-referenced evaluation: you're measured against a fixed performance standard, NOT against other candidates. You're not competing with anyone; you pass by demonstrating the knowledge and skills defined in the blueprint. The passing standard was set through a formal standard-setting study in which subject matter experts (SMEs) judged the expected performance level of the minimally qualified candidate. The result is reported as pass/fail plus a scaled score in a range of 100 to 1,000, with a cut score of 720. KEY POINT: 720/1000 is a SCALED score, not a percentage of correct answers — it does NOT mean 72% correct answers or 43 out of 60 items. The scale applies a psychometric model that adjusts for the difficulty of the exam form you received, so the number of correct answers needed varies between forms. The score report also shows the percentage correct by content domain; those per-section percentages are informational (to help you understand your performance) and are NOT used to determine pass/fail: the result depends solely on the total scaled score. Practical corollary: there are no domains with their own minimum cut score, so you can't fail by 'bombing' one domain, but you also can't freely compensate by ignoring Domain 2 (21% of the exam, the highest-weighted domain).
howToPrepare: There is no single mandatory course. Anthropic does not guarantee that any particular resource ensures a passing result; the recommendation is to combine hands-on experience with official resources.
Study the Section 6 blueprint and self-assess objective by objective.
Review Anthropic's official documentation and help articles on Claude features like Projects, Artifacts, Memory, Skills, and Code Execution.
Practice structuring prompts, task decomposition, and iterating to improve outputs.
Build real workflows: configure a Project with instructions and knowledge sources, and evaluate outputs for accuracy and bias.
Practice responsible-use judgment: data sensitivity, appropriate use cases, and when to escalate or request human review.
Complete the Section 8 sample questions to get familiar with the item style.
registrationSteps: Go to your exam's certification page in the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
Download the Exam Guide and review the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy BEFORE registering.
Register for the exam and complete checkout. The fee shown at checkout already reflects any discount applicable to your partner tier.
Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account, then log in to schedule your exam session.
Choose an available date and select online proctoring or a Pearson test center. The exam is delivered by Pearson VUE.
You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment. Changes within the 24 hours prior mean forfeiting the exam fee.

certs.decoderHtml:
CCAO-F Exam Decoder

Analysis of how the items of the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations (v1.0, July 2026) are constructed, derived from the three official sample items, the blueprint's language, and the stated profile of the Minimally Qualified Candidate (MQC). This is not a content guide: it's an item architecture guide. It's here to help you answer correctly even when you're unsure about the content.

1. The central rule of answering

The guide defines the Associate as someone who "applies Claude to complete business tasks with minimal guidance," "selects approaches that balance quality, efficiency, and cost," and "recognizes limitations and escalates more complex work." That's the standard every item is written against. From it comes the rule that governs the entire exam:

The option that executes the task while applying the correct control wins — not the one that avoids it, not the one that maximizes it, not the one that dresses it up.

The three official samples converge on the same shape: the correct answer is always the disciplined middle action. Verify the citation before sending it (not send it, not polish it, not ask the model). Use the fast, cheap model for high-volume work (not the more expensive one, not turning off features, not switching platforms). Anonymize the identifiers and run the analysis (not upload the raw file, not cancel the analysis). In all three, the correct candidate is someone who delivers value under constraint.

Operative corollaries, in order of usefulness:

  1. The correct answer respects the constraint stated in the stem. If the stem says "speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning," any option that sacrifices speed/cost for quality is already dead, no matter how "more professional" it sounds. If it says "policy restricts sharing regulated personal data," any option that uploads the regulated data is dead, no matter how reasonable the pretext.
  2. The correct answer preserves business value. "Skip the analysis entirely" and "Switch to a different AI platform" are almost always false. The exam doesn't reward paralysis or flight.
  3. The correct answer uses a real control, not a request to the model. Verifying against the authoritative source is a control. Instructing Claude "don't retain this" is not. Asking Claude how confident it is is not.
  4. The correct answer usually contains the word that anchors it to the blueprint objective. "Verify … against the official regulation text" ≈ Apply fact-checking and validation techniques. "Faster, lower-cost model suited to … high-volume tasks" ≈ Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality). "Remove or anonymize the personal identifiers … consistent with policy" ≈ Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations. Items are written against the objectives, and the objective leaks lexically into the correct option. If you recognize the objective, you recognize the option.

2. Distractor archetypes

Every incorrect option plays an assigned role. In a 60-item exam with 4 options each, you'll see these seven archetypes over and over. Name them and you eliminate them on sight.

A. The Zero-Effort Shortcut. Do nothing and move on, justified by a rationalization that sounds reasonable. "Send it as-is, since Claude expressed high confidence." "Upload the file as-is, since the analysis is internal." Tell: the "since…" / "because…" clause. When a distractor hands you the reason the control isn't needed, that reason is the trap. The exam uses the causal subordinate clause as bait.

B. Circular Self-Verification. The most dangerous one, because it looks like diligence: it adds a step, but the same system whose output you're validating executes that step. "Ask Claude to rate its own confidence and send it if the rating is high." An LLM's self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy. Hard rule: a model is never the authoritative source on its own accuracy. Any option whose validation closes inside Claude is false.

C. The Fake Control (instruction-as-control). Confuses asking the model for a behavior with applying a governance control. "Upload the file but instruct Claude not to retain it." The regulated data already crossed the perimeter the moment it was uploaded; the instruction doesn't reverse that or satisfy the policy. This applies equally to variants like "tell Claude not to hallucinate," "ask it to only use real sources," "instruct it not to store the data." Data controls are applied before upload, at the source.

D. The Cosmetic Fix. Fixes the form and leaves the substance untouched. "Reword the summary to sound more formal, then send it." If the stem's problem is factual (a citation, a number, a claim), any option about tone, format, length, or style is a distractor. This archetype hooks the candidate whose communicator instinct confuses presentable with correct.

E. Default Maximalism. "Always use the best / most expensive / most powerful." "Use the most capable, highest-cost model for every reply to maximize quality." Exploits the intuition that more capability never hurts. In this exam it does hurt: it burns cost and latency budget, and contradicts the explicit mandate to "balance quality, efficiency, and cost." Its symmetric twin is blind minimalism ("turn everything off to save money").

F. The Wrong Lever. An action that sounds reasonable but operates on a variable that isn't the one in the trade-off. "Disable all product features to reduce cost." It does reduce something — but not what the stem asked you to optimize, and it degrades work capacity along the way. Detection: ask "does this action touch the variable the stem named?" If not, it's out.

G. The Escape Hatch (abandonment / flight). "Skip the analysis entirely." "Switch to a different AI platform." Solves the problem by eliminating it. In an exam that certifies the ability to apply Claude, abandoning the task or the platform is almost always wrong. The one real exception: when the stem describes a genuinely inappropriate use case (Domain 6: a decision requiring protected professional judgment, data that no anonymization can save, a use prohibited by policy with no compliant path). There, escalating to a human or not using Claude is the correct answer — but you can tell because the stem offers no compliant middle path. If a compliant middle path exists among the options, abandonment is a distractor.

Symmetry note, useful under pressure: exam items tend to be built as one lax extreme (A/E), one paralyzing extreme (G), one sophisticated decoy (B/C/D/F), and the disciplined answer in the middle. Once you identify the two extremes, the correct answer is among the two remaining, and the sophisticated decoy is the one that "does something" without touching the root cause.

3. Verbs and signals that reveal the domain

Items don't announce their domain, but the stem's vocabulary gives it away, and knowing the domain tells you which family of answer to look for. Weights: D2 21%, D4 16%, D6 15%, D1 14%, D3 12%, D5 12%, D7 10%. One in five items is about output evaluation: it's the most profitable domain to master.

Signals in the stemLikely domainShape of the correct answer
"confident", "cites", "specific number/statistic/source", "before sending/sharing", risk audience (legal, compliance, client, executive), "accuracy", "complete", "inconsistent", "biased"2 — Output Evaluation and ValidationVerify against an authoritative external source; involve human review; compare/refine for the audience; choose the right output format (artifact vs. inline vs. structured data)
"high volume", "speed", "cost", "latency", "complex reasoning", "long document", "conversation is getting long", "context", "Haiku / Sonnet / Opus", "Projects / research mode / chat / artifacts"3 — Product and Model SelectionMatch the model or feature profile to the task profile; summarize/persist/restart when context saturates
"sensitive", "regulated", "personal data", "PII", "policy", "privacy", "ethical", "appropriate use", "compliance with organizational standards"6 — Governance, Risk, and Responsible UseApply the control (anonymize, redact, request approval) and proceed; or escalate/decline to use if there's no compliant path
"the output is vague / wrong / too generic", "the prompt isn't working", "results got worse", "diagnose", "improve the workflow's efficiency"7 — Troubleshooting and OptimizationDiagnose the root cause (ambiguous instruction, missing context, absence of success criteria) and fix that cause, iterating on evidence
"write a prompt", "break down", "decompose", "step by step", "the task is complex", named task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)1 — Prompting and Task ExecutionStructure/decompose/iterate; adapt the strategy to the task type
"Project instructions", "knowledge source", "upload documents", "connector", "Google Drive", "Gmail", "system-level instructions", "the knowledge is outdated"5 — Configuration and Knowledge ManagementConfigure/update instructions and knowledge sources in the right place and keep them current
"stakeholders", "existing process", "requirements", "use case", "pilot", "redesign the workflow", "explain the value/limitations to leadership"4 — Workflow Integration and Solution DesignIntegrate Claude into the real process, communicate value AND limitations honestly, iterate the design

Cross-cutting signal: "most appropriate action" appears in two of the three samples. That wording forces you to choose among several defensible options: don't look for the only acceptable one, look for the best one under the stem's constraint. When two options are defensible, the one that addresses the root cause and explicitly respects the named constraint wins.

4. Elimination technique, step by step

  1. Read the last sentence first. That's where the real task is ("what is the most appropriate action?", "which choice best fits?"). Define what you're choosing before you read the options.
  2. Underline the constraint. Almost every stem contains a clause that fixes the criterion: "…where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning", "Organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data", "Before sending the summary to the compliance team". That clause is the filter. Write it down mentally as a rule.
  3. Name the domain using the table above. That tells you which family of answer to expect.
  4. Kill the extremes. Eliminate the Zero-Effort Shortcut (look for the "since/because" subordinate clause) and the Escape Hatch (abandoning the task or the platform) — unless no compliant middle path exists.
  5. Kill the cosmetics and the wrong lever. Does the option touch the variable named in the constraint? If not, it's out.
  6. From the remaining pair, discard the circular one. If an option closes the validation loop inside Claude (self-confidence, "instruct the model to…"), it's the sophisticated decoy. The other one is correct.
  7. Final check: the chosen option must (a) complete the task, (b) satisfy the constraint, (c) act on the root cause and not the symptom. All three, or go back to step 4.
  8. Multiple-response: the item tells you how many to select. Treat each option as an independent true/false item against the constraint; don't look for "the ones that sound best together," and don't pick two that are the same idea reworded — the exam doesn't reward redundancy, and one of those two is usually the distractor.

5. Typical mental errors for this candidate profile

The MQC is a business professional, not an engineer. The exam is calibrated on their biases, and it exploits them deliberately.

  • Fluency bias. The business candidate evaluates text by its rhetorical quality. The exam punishes this: a well-written summary with a fabricated citation is a failure, and "rewording it in a more formal tone" makes it worse. Fluency ≠ accuracy. This bias is why Domain 2 carries 21% weight.
  • Anthropomorphizing the model. Believing "Claude knows if it got something wrong," that "if I ask it not to make things up, it won't," or that "if I tell it not to keep the data, it won't." Every distractor built on this belief is false. The model is not your auditor or your DPO.
  • The "always the best model" reflex. Confusing prudence with maximalism. In this exam, choosing Opus to draft 500 short support replies is a professional judgment error, not a precaution.
  • Risk aversion that turns into paralysis. Over-indexing on governance to the point of canceling legitimate work. The guide is explicit: anonymizing "allows the analysis to proceed"; abandoning the task is "unnecessary." Governance enables, it doesn't block. Domain 6 items don't reward the most fearful answer.
  • Confusing escalation with evasion. The guide does value "recognize limitations and escalate more complex or technical work to Claude Architects and Developers" — but escalating is correct when the work exceeds the Associate's scope (architecture, API integration, agentic systems) or when it requires protected human judgment, not simply because the task is a lot of work. If the option to escalate exists but a compliant action within the Associate's scope also exists, the action wins.
  • Hunting for the technical trick. This isn't an API exam: there are no parameters, no endpoints, no tokens per second. When an option sounds too technically sophisticated for an operations or marketing role, be suspicious: it's probably outside the credential's declared scope and a distractor by definition.
  • Reading 720/1000 as 72% correct. It isn't: it's a scaled score, adjusted for the form's difficulty. Don't calculate "how many I can afford to miss." And since domain percentages don't determine the result, there's no domain you can write off — but there's also none that fails you on its own. Maximize total correct answers, with focus on Domain 2's 21%.

6. One-line summary

For any item: find the constraint, kill the two extremes, distrust anything that validates Claude with Claude, and choose the action that delivers the work with the control in place.
certs.logisticsHtml:
CCAO-F — Exam Operational Logistics

Everything non-academic about the Claude Certified Associate – Foundations (v1.0, effective July 2026). Source: official exam guide, sections 5 and 10–15. Where the guide doesn't say something, it's explicitly marked here as "not specified" rather than invented.

1. Quick reference

FieldValue
CredentialClaude Certified Associate – Foundations
CodeCCAO-F
Items60
Item formatMultiple-choice and multiple-response; each item states how many answers to select
Time120 minutes
DeliveryProctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy. Delivered by Pearson VUE
Passing score720 on a 100–1,000 scale (scaled, not a percentage)
Fee$99 USD per attempt (checkout applies your partner tier's discount, if any)
Validity12 months from the date the credential is awarded
Result reportPass/fail + scaled score + percentage correct by domain
LanguageThe guide doesn't list languages; the sample items are in English. Prepare to take it in English and confirm availability when scheduling with Pearson VUE

Time budget: 120 min / 60 items = 2 minutes per item. Items are short 2–4 line scenarios with 4 options; a comfortable real-world pace is ~90 seconds per item, leaving ~20–25 minutes of buffer to review flagged items.

2. Step-by-step registration

Registration lives in the Anthropic Partner Academy; scheduling and delivery happen through Pearson VUE. These are two separate accounts.

  1. Go to your exam's certification page in the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the details.
  2. Download the Exam Guide and read the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy before registering. (By registering, you're assumed to have accepted them.)
  3. Register and complete checkout. The fee shown already reflects the discount applicable to your partner tier. If you're expecting a discount and it doesn't show up, resolve it before paying.
  4. Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account. This is the most common friction point: the credential is purchased on one side and scheduled on the other.
  5. Log in to Pearson VUE and schedule your session. Choose an available date and modality: online proctoring or Pearson test center.
  6. Verify the name. The name on your registration must match your official ID exactly. If it doesn't match, fix it before scheduling by writing to certifications-support@anthropic.com. A name mismatch on exam day locks you out and forfeits your fee.

If you need accommodations

  • Available to candidates with disabilities or documented needs, per applicable law.
  • Must be requested and approved by Pearson VUE BEFORE scheduling.
  • Don't schedule your appointment until your request is approved. Scheduling first and asking later breaks the flow.
  • Request them at pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations.

3. Online proctored vs. test center — how to choose

The guide doesn't favor one modality; both are subject to the same conduct rules and the same security standard. Practical criteria:

Choose online proctored if: you can guarantee 2+ uninterrupted hours, a closed room nobody will enter, a desk you can fully clear, a stable connection, and a working webcam. Advantage: zero commute, more time slots. Risks of online: anyone entering the frame, any noise suggesting communication, sustained off-screen glances, or a network drop can lead to an incident or session termination. You absorb all the risk of the environment.

Choose test center if: your home/office can't guarantee isolation, your network is unstable, or you'd rather the environment's infrastructure and compliance be the center's problem. Advantage: an already-certified environment. Cost: travel, more rigid scheduling, and the late-arrival window applies (arriving outside it = no-show).

Operational recommendation for online: run the Pearson VUE system test/check on the same machine, same network, and same room you'll test in — not a different one. Close anything that could fire notifications. Physically disconnect the secondary monitor (turning it off isn't enough).

4. Exam-day rules

ID (mandatory). Official government-issued photo ID, current (not expired). The name must match your registration exactly. No valid ID, no exam, no refund.

Before starting you must accept the confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement (NDA — see §7). If you don't accept it, the session ends and there is no refund.

During the exam you MUST:

  • Stay visible to the proctor and the webcam for the entire session (if testing online).
  • Keep your workspace clear: no notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, or materials.
  • Not communicate with any other person during the exam.
  • Not capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce exam content in any form.

PROHIBITED items (explicit list from the guide):

  • Mobile phones
  • Smartwatches
  • Headphones
  • Study materials
  • Any recording device

Permitted items: only whatever Pearson VUE specifies — for example, scratch paper provided by the proctor, if applicable. Don't assume you'll have paper: confirm in your modality's Pearson VUE instructions. Don't bring your own paper or your own calculator.

Consequences of misconduct. Cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in: invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban from future exams. All three, not just one.

5. Cancellation, rescheduling, and no-shows

  • You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment.
  • Any change within the 24 hours prior means forfeiting the exam fee.
  • No-show: not showing up to a scheduled appointment, or arriving after the allowed late-arrival window, means forfeiting the fee and having to register again (paying again).

Practical rule: if 30 hours out from your appointment you have any doubt about being able to show up — travel, illness, network, caregiving — reschedule then, not later. The 24-hour window is hard and non-negotiable.

6. Retake policy

Failed attemptMandatory wait before the next one
After the 1st14 days
After the 2nd30 days
After the 3rd90 days
  • Maximum 4 attempts of the same exam within a rolling 12-month period.
  • Limits apply per exam: failing CCAO-F doesn't stop you from registering for a different exam in the program.
  • The fee applies on every attempt. Four attempts = four payments.

Strategic reading: with a 14-day wait after the first failure, the per-domain score report (percentage correct for each of the 7 domains) is your only diagnostic. Use it to direct your studying before the retake, starting with Domain 2 (21% of the exam).

7. NDA and confidentiality

  • Before the exam begins you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement.
  • By accepting it, you acknowledge that all exam content — questions, answer choices, and scenarios — is Anthropic's confidential and proprietary property, and you agree not to disclose, reproduce, or distribute any part of it.
  • If you don't accept the agreement, the session ends and no refund is issued.

Practical, non-negotiable implication: don't reproduce real exam items anywhere — not in notes, not in a chat, not in forums, not in a "brain dump" for colleagues. Disclosing content is the explicit cause for result invalidation, credential revocation, and a future ban. Legitimate study materials (including this one) are built from the public exam guide and the sample questions the guide itself publishes, never from the live item bank.

8. How the result is reported and scored

  • Criterion-referenced evaluation: you're measured against a fixed standard, not against other candidates. There's no curve.
  • The standard was set with a formal standard-setting study: subject matter experts (SMEs) judged the expected performance level of the minimally qualified candidate.
  • Result = pass/fail + scaled score from 100 to 1,000, with a cut score of 720.
  • 720 is NOT 72% correct. It's a scaled score: the scale adjusts for the difficulty of the exam form you got, so the number of correct answers required varies between forms. Don't plan around "how many I can afford to miss."
  • The score report also shows percentage correct by domain. Those per-section percentages are informational and are NOT used to determine pass/fail, which depends solely on the total scaled score.
  • Consequence: there are no minimum per-domain cut scores (you don't fail by "bombing" one domain), but you also can't ignore Domain 2, which accounts for 21% of the items.

9. Appeals and complaints

  • You can appeal a decision within 14 days of the date you're notified.
  • For a complaint about your result, the deadline is 14 days from your exam date.
  • Appeals are submitted to Pearson VUE support (pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html) and are reviewed under the program's appeals policy.
  • NOT appealable: the outcome of the standard-setting study (i.e., the 720 cut score) or the content of individual items.

Translation: you can appeal a process problem (an incident during the session, an administrative error, how your result was handled). You cannot appeal "that question was wrong" or "the cut score is too high."

10. Recertification and maintenance

  • The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded. It's deliberately time-limited because the underlying technology evolves fast and the program wants holders to keep their knowledge current.
  • On-time renewal: you review what's changed since you certified and complete a free, NOT proctored assessment in the Anthropic Partner Academy. The guide states it explicitly: "There is no fee for on-time renewal" — on-time renewal is FREE.
  • If your credential lapses: you must retake the full exam and pay the full fee ($99 USD) to regain certified status. No grace window is described in the guide.
  • Exception: if the exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam to recertify, instead of the renewal assessment.
  • Holders remain subject to the conduct rules in Section 12 (§4 of this document) for as long as they hold the credential.

Concrete action: set a reminder at 10 months from the award date. The difference between renewing on time and letting it lapse is $0 vs. $99 + 120 proctored minutes.

11. Support — who to contact

IssueContact
Correcting the name on your registrationcertifications-support@anthropic.com — before scheduling
Everything else: registration, scheduling, accommodations, results, appealsPearson VUE support — pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html
Accommodations (request)pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations

Privacy. Personal data collected during registration and testing is handled per Anthropic's privacy policy, Pearson VUE's privacy policy, and applicable data protection law.

12. 24-hours-before checklist

  • Official photo ID, current, name identical to your registration — physically located.
  • Modality confirmed; if test center, route and arrival time calculated with margin (the late-arrival window is real).
  • If online: Pearson VUE system test run on the real machine, network, and room.
  • Room reserved for 2.5 h; nobody enters. Door closed.
  • Desk cleared: no notes, books, phone, smartwatch, headphones, study materials, recording devices.
  • Secondary monitor physically disconnected.
  • System and app notifications silenced; nothing will pop up during the exam window.
  • Confirmed with Pearson VUE whether scratch paper will be allowed — don't assume yes.
  • Mental pacing budget: ~90 s per item, flag doubts, leave 20 min for review.
  • No pending cancellation: within 24 h, any change costs the full fee.

questions.stem: An associate asks Claude to summarize a new regulation, and Claude produces a confident summary citing a specific subsection number. Before sending the summary to the compliance team, what is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Send it as-is, since Claude expressed high confidence.
Verify the cited subsection against the official regulation text before sharing.
Ask Claude to rate its own confidence and send it if the rating is high.
Reword the summary to sound more formal, then send it.

questions.explanationEs: This item measures the 'Apply fact-checking and validation techniques' objective from Domain 2, and the trigger is planted in two words of the prompt: 'confident' and 'specific subsection number.' A citation number is exactly the kind of detail a language model can fabricate with a plausible appearance: it's a hallucination in believable form. B is correct because it's the only option that checks the factual claim against the authoritative source (the official regulation text) before it goes out to a compliance audience, where the cost of an error is regulatory, not cosmetic. A fails by confusing tone with evidence: the confidence the model expresses does not correlate with accuracy, and 'it's internal' or 'it sounded sure' never substitutes for verification. C is the most dangerous distractor because it looks diligent — it introduces an 'extra step' — but that step is circular: you're asking the very system that might hallucinate to grade itself, and self-reported confidence is not a reliable signal of accuracy. D addresses the form (formal register) and not the substance (does the subsection exist and say that?); reformatting a false claim only makes it more convincing. Mental rule: when the prompt shows a verifiable fact and a high-risk audience, the answer is to verify against the external source — not to polish it or ask the model.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 1: B. Language models can fabricate specific-looking details such as citation numbers, a hallucination. Validating factual claims, especially citations bound for a compliance audience, against an authoritative source is the diligence step required. Self-reported confidence (A, C) is not a reliable accuracy signal, and reformatting (D) does not address correctness.
questions.trap: A = 'Confidence as evidence' (confuses the model's confident tone with accuracy; a Zero-Effort Shortcut). C = 'Circular Self-Verification' (looks like diligence because it adds a step, but the verifier is the same potentially hallucinating system — the most tempting archetype). D = 'Cosmetic Fix instead of substance' (fixes style/format and leaves the factual error untouched). All three share the same flaw: none of them touches an authoritative external source.

questions.stem: An associate needs to generate a high volume of short customer-reply drafts where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning. Which choice best fits the task?

options.text: Use the most capable, highest-cost model for every reply to maximize quality.
Use a faster, lower-cost model suited to straightforward, high-volume tasks.
Disable all product features to reduce cost.
Switch to a different AI platform.

questions.explanationEs: This item measures 'Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)' from Domain 3. The prompt already states the decision criterion explicitly: 'speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning' and 'high volume' of 'short' replies. That defines the task profile that corresponds to the family's fast, economical model — Haiku, in the taxonomy the guide lists (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) — leaving the most capable model for complex reasoning. B is correct because it's the only option that matches the model's profile to the task's profile: that matching IS the objective being evaluated. A fails because it maximizes a dimension (quality) that the prompt explicitly downgraded, and it burns cost and latency budget on trivial drafts; it's the mistake of the candidate who believes 'the best model' is always the safe answer. C is an operational non sequitur: turning off features isn't the relevant cost lever here, and it also degrades the ability to do the work without resolving the stated trade-off. D is scope flight (an escape hatch): abandoning the platform doesn't answer the design question, and on a Claude exam it is never the behavior being evaluated. Mental rule: when the prompt hands you the priority (speed/cost vs. depth of reasoning), the correct answer is the one that respects that priority to the letter — not the one that optimizes the dimension the prompt discarded.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 2: B. Aligning model selection with task requirements means matching a faster, lower-cost model to straightforward, high-volume work, reserving the most capable model for complex reasoning. Always using the top model (A) wastes the cost and latency budget; disabling features (C) or switching platforms (D) does not address the trade-off.
questions.trap: A = 'Default Maximalism' (always the best model; ignores the stated cost/latency constraint). C = 'Wrong Lever' (an action that sounds like savings but attacks a variable that isn't the one in the trade-off). D = 'Escape Hatch / abandoning the platform' (doesn't solve the problem, evades it; on these exams, 'switch platforms' or 'don't do the task' is almost never correct).

questions.stem: A project manager wants to upload a spreadsheet containing customer names and account numbers so Claude can analyze trends. Organizational policy restricts sharing regulated personal data. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Upload the file as-is, since the analysis is internal.
Remove or anonymize the personal identifiers before uploading, consistent with policy.
Upload the file but instruct Claude not to retain it.
Skip the analysis entirely.

questions.explanationEs: This item measures 'Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations' from Domain 6. The prompt plants two facts that fix the answer: there is regulated personal data (names and account numbers), and an organizational policy restricts sharing it. The correct answer must satisfy the policy WITHOUT destroying the business value, and anonymizing/removing the identifiers achieves exactly that: the trend analysis doesn't need to know the customer's name, only the pattern. That's why B is correct: it's a real technical control (redaction/anonymization at the source) applied before the upload. A fails because 'it's internal' is not an exception the policy recognizes; the candidate who picks it is substituting the control with a convenience rationalization. C is the sophisticated distractor: it sounds like mitigation, but an instruction in the prompt is a behavioral request to the model, not a policy control or a guarantee of data handling — the regulated data already left your perimeter the moment it was uploaded. D overcorrects: it satisfies the policy at the cost of canceling legitimate work that could actually have been done safely; the exam penalizes both excess risk and paralysis. This domain's mental rule: the correct answer almost always enables the task under control — it neither blocks it nor runs it blindly.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 3: B. Applying data-sensitivity and privacy safeguards means redacting or anonymizing regulated identifiers before use, so the analysis can proceed without exposing protected data. Uploading as-is (A) violates policy; instructing the model not to retain data (C) does not satisfy the policy control; abandoning the task (D) is unnecessary when anonymization enables it.
questions.trap: A = 'Convenience rationalization' (invents an exception to the policy — 'it's internal,' 'no one will see it'). C = 'Fake Control / instruction-as-control' (confuses asking the model to do something with applying a governance control; the sensitive data has already been exposed). D = 'Overcorrection / paralysis' (abandoning the task when a conforming path existed; the symmetric opposite of A, and the exam rejects both extremes).

questions.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
questions.scenario: Vague prompt about a product
questions.stem: An associate types 'write something about our new product' and gets a generic paragraph. What most reliably improves the result?

options.text: Add the missing context and constraints — audience, purpose, key facts, length, and tone — so the prompt actually specifies the task.
Send the exact same prompt again and hope the next draft is better.
Ask Claude to make the paragraph sound more exciting.
Switch to a different AI tool.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks.' A generic output is almost always a symptom of a generic prompt: with no audience, purpose, facts, or constraints, the model fills in with whatever is most probable. A attacks the root cause by supplying the missing context. On the exam, the correct D1 answer is the one that structures the request — not the one that retries blindly or dresses up the tone.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut / not real iteration: repeating the same prompt doesn't change the input, so it doesn't systematically change the output.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: 'more exciting' touches the tone, not the lack of context; a vague, enthusiastic paragraph is still vague.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: switching tools doesn't address the problem (a poor prompt); the exam does not reward fleeing.

questions.trap: B dresses up mere retrying as iteration; iterating means changing the prompt, not repeating it.

questions.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
questions.scenario: Competitive analysis in a single prompt
questions.stem: An associate needs a full competitive analysis — gather competitors, compare features, summarize, and recommend. A single prompt asking for 'a competitive analysis' returns shallow results. The best next step is to:

options.text: Accept the shallow output; the task is simply too big for the tool.
Repeat the same prompt with a more forceful, demanding tone.
Decompose the task into steps — list competitors, compare them on defined criteria, summarize, then recommend — and prompt each step in sequence.
Ask for the analysis as a table so it looks more thorough.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests.' A compound request — gather, compare, summarize, recommend — collapsed into a single instruction produces shallowness. C decomposes it into chained steps, each with a clear objective, which is exactly the technique this domain evaluates. Structuring the task is the lever; tone and format are not.

distractorsEs.A: Escape Hatch / shortcut: giving up ignores that the task is actually manageable if structured; the exam penalizes paralysis.
distractorsEs.B: Cosmetic Fix / Wrong Lever: a more demanding tone doesn't change the structure of the request; the model doesn't respond to pressure, but to specification.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: a table organizes what little there is; it doesn't generate the depth that was missing.

questions.trap: D tempts with 'it looks complete,' but it's dressing up shallowness instead of decomposing the task.

questions.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
questions.scenario: Emails that are too formal
questions.stem: A drafting prompt keeps producing emails that are too formal for a casual audience. The most effective iteration is to:

options.text: Send the prompt several more times until one draft happens to land in the right tone.
Revise the prompt to specify the register, with a short example ('friendly, first-name, one short paragraph'), and regenerate.
Rewrite every email by hand from scratch each time.
Ask Claude to rate the tone of its own drafts and trust that rating.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Iterate prompts to improve output quality.' Iterating is not retrying: it's changing the input based on what was observed. B fixes the cause (the register was never specified) by adding a concrete description and an example of the tone wanted. An example is worth more than an adjective: it gives the model an imitable target.

distractorsEs.A: Non-iteration: repeating the same prompt leaves the input untouched; any improvement would be by chance, not by design.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch: doing everything by hand abandons the leverage of the tool; it isn't 'iterating the prompt.'
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-assessment of its own tone is not a reliable signal and doesn't fix the prompt.

questions.trap: A confuses retrying with iterating; without changing the prompt, there is no iteration.

questions.objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
questions.scenario: Brainstorming that returns a single idea
questions.stem: For a brainstorming task the associate wants many diverse options, but the prompt 'give me the best idea' returns a single safe one. The best adjustment is to:

options.text: Accept the single idea, since Claude presumably picked the best one.
Reformat the idea into bullet points.
Ask Claude how confident it is in the idea and proceed if it is confident.
Adapt the prompt to the task type: ask for a broad set of varied options across different angles first, then narrow down.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Adapt prompting strategies based on task type.' Brainstorming calls for breadth and divergence; asking for 'the best idea' imposes premature convergence and kills the purpose. D adapts the strategy to the task type: variety first, then selection. Recognizing what type of task it is — analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming — and prompting accordingly is exactly what this objective evaluates.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut / anthropomorphization: assuming the model 'picked the best one' hands off the judgment that belongs to the associate and derails the divergent phase.
distractorsEs.B: Cosmetic Fix: bullet points change the format, not the quantity or diversity of ideas.
