distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification: self-reported confidence says nothing about whether alternatives are missing.

questions.trap: A/B/C address everything except what the task calls for: divergence. The strategy must follow the task type.

questions.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
questions.scenario: Consistent data extraction
questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to extract fields from many emails into a consistent structure. Which technique most improves consistency?

options.text: Tell Claude to 'be consistent' and leave the format unspecified.
Give a clear output specification plus one worked example of the exact structure wanted (a few-shot example).
Ask for the output in a more elaborate visual format.
Paste the emails with no instructions and fix the output by hand afterward.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks.' Consistency is achieved by giving an explicit target: an output specification plus a concrete example the model can imitate (few-shot). B does that. 'Be consistent' is an adjective with no referent; the model needs to see the structure, not just be told its name.

distractorsEs.A: Wrong Lever: asking for consistency without defining it gives no imitable pattern; it's an empty instruction.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: a more elaborate format doesn't guarantee the fields come out the same every time.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch / shortcut: with no instructions the output will be inconsistent, and the work shifts entirely to manual correction.

questions.trap: A sounds reasonable ('be consistent'), but it's an instruction without a specification; the example is what anchors it.

questions.objective: Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests
questions.scenario: A 60-page report in a single prompt
questions.stem: Asked in one prompt to 'analyze this 60-page report and give recommendations,' Claude returns output that skips several sections. A better approach is to:

options.text: Break the work down: summarize each section first, synthesize the findings, then derive recommendations from the synthesis.
Resend the identical one-shot prompt.
Ask Claude to confirm it read the whole document, then trust it.
Request the recommendations as slides.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply task decomposition techniques to structure complex requests.' A long document collapsed into a single request invites skips and omissions. A decomposes it: per-section summary → synthesis → recommendations, chaining verifiable steps. Decomposition is the technique; trusting a single massive pass is this domain's trap.

distractorsEs.B: Non-iteration: the same one-shot prompt reproduces the same skip.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification / anthropomorphization: asking it whether it 'read everything' is not a verification; it can affirm that and still have omitted something.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: turning it into slides changes the wrapper, not the coverage of the analysis.

questions.trap: C exploits the belief that the model 'knows' whether it complied; its claim is not evidence of coverage.

questions.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
questions.scenario: An unsatisfying summary without knowing why
questions.stem: The associate is unhappy with a summary but can't articulate why. The most productive iteration is to:

options.text: Just ask Claude to make it 'better'.
Switch to a different tool.
Define explicit success criteria — what it must include, length, and audience — and regenerate against them.
Make the summary bold and add section headers.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Iterate prompts to improve output quality.' Effective iteration starts by naming the standard: without success criteria, 'better' is undefinable and the model has no target. C turns a vague dissatisfaction into concrete requirements to regenerate and evaluate against. Iterating means closing the gap between criterion and result, not vaguely asking for 'more quality.'

distractorsEs.A: Wrong Lever: 'better' with no criterion gives no direction; the model can't optimize toward an undefined target.
distractorsEs.B: Escape Hatch: switching tools evades the work of specifying what is wanted.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: bold text and headers change the appearance, not whether the content fulfills the purpose.

questions.trap: A looks like iterating, but without explicit criteria it's just a wish; define the standard first.

questions.objective: Adapt prompting strategies based on task type (analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming)
questions.scenario: A decision between two vendors
questions.stem: For an analytical decision between two vendors, the associate wants a rigorous comparison rather than a snap verdict. The best prompting strategy is to:

options.text: Ask 'which vendor is best?' and take the first answer.
Ask Claude to compare the vendors against defined criteria and show its reasoning before giving a recommendation.
Ask for the answer in a larger font so it reads as authoritative.
Use the most expensive model to guarantee the right choice.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Adapt prompting strategies based on task type.' An analytical task calls for explicit criteria and visible reasoning, not an instant verdict that hides how it was reached. B adapts the strategy to the analytical type: comparing against criteria and showing the reasoning before recommending, which also makes the conclusion auditable.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: the quick verdict skips the analysis the task requires; you can't validate reasoning you never see.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: font size doesn't add rigor; it confuses the appearance of authority with analysis.
distractorsEs.D: Maximalism / Wrong Lever: model choice (D3) is not the lever here; the problem is the prompting strategy, not capability.

questions.trap: D mixes domains: it swaps models to 'make sure' when what's missing is analytical structure in the prompt.

questions.objective: Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks
questions.scenario: Choosing the best business prompt
questions.stem: Which of these is the most effective business prompt for drafting a client proposal?

options.text: 'Write a proposal.'
'Write the best possible proposal.'
'Write a proposal and make it look professional.'
'Draft a one-page proposal for [client], offering [service], emphasizing [benefit], in a formal tone, ending with a clear next step.'

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective prompts for business and technical tasks.' An effective prompt carries the context the model can't guess: recipient, offering, emphasis, tone, length, and the expected outcome. D makes them explicit; the other three delegate those decisions to the model, which is why they yield something generic. Actionable specificity is the hallmark of a good business prompt.

distractorsEs.A: Vague: with no context, it produces a generic template.
distractorsEs.B: Empty maximalism: 'the best possible' is not a specification; it doesn't say for whom or with what emphasis.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: 'make it look professional' asks for appearance; it doesn't define content or recipient.

questions.trap: B sounds ambitious but specifies nothing; 'best' is not context.

questions.objective: Iterate prompts to improve output quality
questions.scenario: Partially correct multi-step research
questions.stem: A multi-step research prompt returns some accurate parts and some off-target parts. The most effective response is to:

options.text: Isolate the step that went wrong, refine that step's prompt with the missing context or constraints, and re-run just that part.
Discard everything and start over with the same original prompt.
Keep all of the output and change nothing, since parts of it are correct.
Ask Claude to grade its own research and accept whatever grade it gives.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Iterate prompts to improve output quality.' Precise iteration locates the failure and acts on it, instead of discarding what's good or keeping what's bad. A isolates the off-target step, re-specifies it, and reruns just that part: maximum signal, minimum waste. Iterating well is surgical, not all-or-nothing.

distractorsEs.B: Non-iteration: starting over with the same prompt reproduces the same error and discards what did work.
distractorsEs.C: Shortcut: keeping everything without correcting it leaves the wrong parts inside the deliverable.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-assessment neither identifies nor fixes the failed step.

questions.trap: B and C are the two extremes (discard everything / touch nothing); correct iteration is surgical, targeting the step that failed.

questions.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
questions.scenario: Market memo for leadership
questions.stem: Claude drafts a market-sizing memo for the leadership team and states that 'the segment grew 47% year over year,' a figure that appears in none of the source documents the associate provided. What is the most appropriate action before circulating the memo?

options.text: Circulate it as-is, since such a specific percentage signals Claude did the analysis rigorously.
Trace the 47% figure back to a source document or dataset and confirm it, or remove it if it cannot be supported.
Ask Claude whether it is sure about the 47% figure and circulate the memo if it confirms.
Reformat the memo into the leadership template and circulate it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply fact-checking and validation techniques.' The trigger is a specific numeric figure that appears in none of the sources: exactly the shape of a plausible hallucination. The exam's central rule requires delivering work with the control in place, and the only real control is checking the figure against an authoritative source before it goes out to a high-stakes audience (leadership). B does that, and also allows for removing the figure if it can't be supported. The specificity of a number is not evidence of its accuracy — it is, in fact, the cue to verify.

distractorsEs.A: Zero-Effort Shortcut: the clause 'since…' sells you specificity as if it were rigor. It confuses apparent precision with truthfulness.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification: you're asking the very system that may have invented the figure to grade itself. A model is never an authoritative source on its own accuracy.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: it fixes the form (template) and leaves the substance untouched (is the 47% real?). Reformatting a false figure only makes it more convincing.

questions.trap: The decoy is C (it looks diligent because it adds a step, but the verifier is the potentially hallucinating system).

questions.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
questions.scenario: Risks in a vendor contract
questions.stem: An associate asked Claude to 'list the risks' in a vendor contract and received four risks that are each individually correct. The associate happens to know the contract also contains a termination-penalty clause that Claude did not mention. What does this most directly reveal about evaluating the output?

options.text: The output is complete, because every risk it does list is accurate.
Ask Claude to rate how complete its own list is, and trust the list if the rating is high.
Reformat the four risks into a table, which will make any gaps obvious.
Accuracy of the listed items does not guarantee completeness; the output must be checked against the source for material omissions.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Evaluate outputs for accuracy AND completeness,' and the exam deliberately separates the two dimensions. Every item can be correct and something material can still be missing — here, a termination-penalty clause — that changes the business decision. D names exactly that distinction: accuracy of what's listed does not imply exhaustiveness; you must check against the source to catch omissions. Completing the task with the control in place means auditing the output against the original document, not against its own appearance of orderliness.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut / Rationalization: confuses 'what's there is correct' with 'everything is there.' Partial accuracy doesn't cover a material omission.
distractorsEs.B: Circular Self-Verification: an LLM's self-assessment of its own completeness is not a reliable signal; you're asking the very model that already omitted the clause.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix / Wrong Lever: a table organizes what's already there, but it can't reveal what was never listed; it doesn't touch the cause (the omission).

questions.trap: A and C exploit fluency bias: a tidy, correct-looking output 'feels' complete.

questions.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
questions.scenario: Competitive brief with an attributed quote
questions.stem: Claude produces a competitive brief that attributes a direct quote to a named competitor's CEO. The associate cannot find that quote in the provided sources or anywhere in the public record. The most likely explanation is that the quote is:

options.text: a hallucination — a fabricated but plausible-looking detail — that must not be used without verification against a real source.
accurate, because Claude only quotes people when it has an underlying source.
close enough, since it is a paraphrase and attribution accuracy does not really matter.
verifiable simply by asking Claude to provide the link it used for the quote.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases.' A direct quote attributed to a real person, absent from every source, is the textbook case of a hallucination: plausible form, fabricated content. A names it and sets the correct behavior (don't use it without verifying against a real source). The mental error this item penalizes is anthropomorphizing the model — believing it 'only quotes when it has a source'; the model generates plausible-sounding text, it does not guarantee provenance.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut + anthropomorphization: assumes a guarantee of provenance the model doesn't offer. Trust in the model's behavior substitutes for verification.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix / Rationalization: lowers the standard ('paraphrase') to avoid verifying; a false attribution is still false even if you call it a paraphrase.
distractorsEs.D: Fake Control: asking the model for its own 'source' closes the validation loop inside Claude; it can fabricate the link too.

questions.trap: D is the sophisticated one: it sounds like verification, but it asks for proof from the very system that invented the quote.

questions.objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
questions.scenario: Response to a billing dispute
questions.stem: Claude drafts replies to a customer's billing dispute that will be sent under the company's name and could carry contractual consequences. Which factor most strongly indicates that human review is required before anything is sent?

options.text: The drafts read fluently and sound professional.
The associate is busy and review would take extra time.
The output will be sent externally under the company's name and may have contractual consequences.
Claude rated its own drafts as high quality.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Determine when human review or additional verification is required.' The trigger for human review is the risk and destination of the output, not convenience or tone. C names the two signals that raise the risk: external communication under the brand and contractual consequences. When the cost of an error is legal or affects a relationship with a named third party, the output goes through a human before being sent. The exam rewards calibrating review to the case's actual risk.

distractorsEs.A: Fluency bias: rhetorical quality doesn't reduce factual/legal risk; polished text can still be wrong.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: the associate's availability doesn't change the output's risk level; time is not the criterion.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-assessment does not substitute for human review on a communication with contractual consequences.

questions.trap: A confuses 'it reads well' with 'it's safe to send': the trigger for review is risk, not style.

questions.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
questions.scenario: Résumé ranking
questions.stem: Using historical examples the associate provided, Claude ranks job candidates and consistently places graduates of one type of university at the top, mirroring a pattern in that example data. Evaluating this output, the associate should:

options.text: Accept the ranking, since it is internally consistent and therefore objective.
Recognize a likely bias inherited from the example data and add human review or adjust the criteria before using the ranking.
Ask Claude to confirm it was not biased and proceed if it says so.
Reformat the ranking into a scored table before circulating it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases.' A consistent pattern that reproduces the bias in the example data is bias, not objectivity: consistency is not proof of impartiality. B identifies it as inherited bias and applies the correct control — human review / adjusting the criteria — before using the ranking, which also impacts people. The exam wants you to recognize that the model amplifies the patterns you feed it, not that it corrects them on its own.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: elevates 'consistent' to 'objective.' A bias applied evenly is still a bias.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification: asking the model whether it was biased is not a bias audit; it closes the validation loop inside the very system being evaluated.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: a scored table dresses up the presentation of the bias; it neither detects nor corrects it.

questions.trap: A sells consistency as objectivity; it's this domain's rationalization archetype.

questions.objective: Organize and curate information and select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data)
questions.scenario: Reusable project charter
questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to produce a project charter the team will open and edit repeatedly over several weeks. Which output choice best fits that need?

options.text: Have Claude produce the charter as an artifact — a standalone document that can be viewed and iteratively edited over time.
Have Claude paste the full charter inline in the chat again every time it changes.
Ask Claude to output the charter as raw JSON so it looks structured.
Switch to a separate document tool and stop using Claude for it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'select appropriate output formats (artifacts, inline, structured data).' The profile of the task — a document that gets opened and edited iteratively over weeks — is exactly what artifacts exist for: substantial, reusable content that lives as an editable document, separate from the chat flow. A matches format to need. The format-selection rule of this domain: choose the container based on how the content will be consumed and maintained, not by which one looks the most 'technical.'

distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever / inefficiency: re-pasting the charter inline every time it changes is exactly what an artifact avoids; it doesn't fit iterative editing.
distractorsEs.C: Wrong format: raw JSON is for structured data consumed by a system, not for a document humans edit.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: abandoning Claude doesn't answer the format question; the exam does not reward fleeing.

questions.trap: C tempts with 'it looks structured,' but it confuses structured data (JSON) with a human document (artifact).

questions.objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
questions.scenario: Technical analysis for an executive
questions.stem: Claude produced a technically accurate analysis dense with engineering jargon. The associate must present it to a non-technical executive audience. The most appropriate next step is to:

options.text: Send it unchanged, because the content is accurate.
Make the fonts and formatting look more executive, then send it.
Ask Claude whether executives will understand it and send it if Claude says yes.
Edit and adapt the output for the audience — plain language, decisions and implications first — while preserving the accurate substance.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience.' Accuracy and audience fit are different things: a correct analysis full of jargon fails its purpose if the executive can't act on it. D preserves the exact substance and adapts the register — plain language, decisions and implications up front. Curating the output for its recipient is part of the Associate's job, not an optional extra.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: 'it's accurate, so it works' ignores that the audience can't use it. Accuracy without audience fit doesn't fulfill the objective.
distractorsEs.B: Cosmetic Fix: typography and formatting don't translate the jargon; the problem is the language, not the appearance.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification: it delegates the audience judgment to the model instead of adapting the output; it's not a real validation.

questions.trap: A and B bait the communicator who confuses 'presentable' or 'accurate' with 'right for this audience.'

questions.objective: Apply fact-checking and validation techniques
questions.scenario: Financial summary for the CFO
questions.stem: Select the TWO techniques that meaningfully raise confidence that a Claude-generated financial summary is accurate before it goes to the CFO.

options.text: Reconcile the summary's figures against the underlying source spreadsheet.
Ask Claude to state how confident it is in the figures and rely on that.
Have a second qualified person independently verify the key numbers.
Rewrite the summary in a more authoritative, formal tone.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply fact-checking and validation techniques' in multiple-response format: treat each option as an independent true/false against the constraint (meaningfully raising real confidence in accuracy). A (reconcile against the source) and C (independent human verification) are real controls external to the model. B closes the validation loop inside Claude; D is cosmetic. Multiple-response technique note: A and C are not the same idea restated — one is against the source, the other is a second pair of eyes — which is why both count; the exam does not reward picking two redundant options.

distractorsEs.B: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-reported confidence is not a signal of accuracy; it is not a control.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: a more authoritative tone doesn't touch whether the numbers are correct; it dresses up the risk.

questions.trap: B is the decoy: it looks like 'a validation step,' but it validates Claude with Claude.

questions.objective: Evaluate Claude-generated outputs for accuracy and completeness
questions.scenario: Summary of a 40-page policy
questions.stem: Asked to summarize a 40-page policy, Claude returns a crisp one-paragraph summary the associate will use to make a compliance decision. Before relying on it, the associate's first evaluation question should be:

options.text: 'Does it read clearly and professionally?'
'Can Claude make it even shorter?'
'Does it omit any material provision that would change the compliance decision?'
'Is Claude confident it captured everything important?'

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Evaluate outputs for accuracy and completeness.' When compressing 40 pages into one paragraph, the dominant risk is omitting something material, not the wording. C points to the right dimension: is there a missing clause that would change the compliance decision? Evaluating for a risk-bearing decision requires looking at completeness against the purpose, not readability. The right question defines what to check against before trusting a summary.

distractorsEs.A: Fluency bias: clarity says nothing about what's missing; a readable summary can omit the critical part.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: shortening it further worsens the risk of omission instead of reducing it.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's 'confidence' about its own completeness is not evidence; you must check against the source.

questions.trap: A exploits the business instinct to judge by writing quality; the exam penalizes this within Domain 2's 21% weight.

questions.objective: Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases in responses
questions.scenario: Report with a contradictory figure
questions.stem: A Claude-generated report states in its executive summary that revenue rose, while a table later in the same report shows revenue falling. This is best described as:

options.text: An acceptable difference in emphasis between sections.
An internal inconsistency the associate must reconcile against the source data before using the report.
A formatting problem that is solved by aligning the table with the summary.
Something to settle by asking Claude which of the two statements it prefers.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify hallucinations, inconsistencies, and biases.' A report that contradicts itself — up in the summary, down in the table — exhibits an internal inconsistency: a hard signal that at least one statement is wrong. B applies the correct control: reconcile against the source data before using the report. The inconsistency isn't resolved by picking a version at random or dressing up the formatting; it's resolved by going back to the source.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: 'a difference in emphasis' normalizes a factual contradiction that needs investigating.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: 'aligning the table' assumes which figure is correct without verifying it; it touches the form, not the truth.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's 'preference' doesn't determine which figure is correct; you have to go to the data.

questions.trap: C tempts because it sounds like a quick fix, but it decides the truth by formatting convenience instead of by the source.

questions.objective: Determine when human review or additional verification is required
questions.scenario: Interpretation of a tax regulation
questions.stem: Claude's draft interpretation of a tax regulation will directly determine how the company files, and there is no in-scope way for the associate to independently confirm the interpretation. The most appropriate action is to:

options.text: File based on the draft, since the reasoning is detailed and well structured.
Ask Claude to double-check its own interpretation and file if it holds.
Reformat the draft as a formal internal memo and file on that basis.
Route the interpretation to a qualified human (e.g., tax or legal) for review before acting.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Determine when human review or additional verification is required.' This is the case where escalating to a human IS the correct move: high consequence (how the company files), protected professional judgment, and no path within the Associate's scope to confirm it. The decoder flags this: when no conforming intermediate path exists within scope, qualified human review wins. D routes it to tax/legal before acting. This isn't evasion — it's recognizing the limit of one's credential.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut + fluency bias: 'detailed reasoning' is not the same as a correct legal interpretation; filing on that basis transfers a real risk.
distractorsEs.B: Circular Self-Verification: asking the model to double-check itself doesn't provide an independent verification on a tax matter.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: turning it into a formal memo changes the wrapper, not the validity of the interpretation.

questions.trap: The exam distinguishes escalating (correct here, with no conforming path in scope) from fleeing; A and B avoid that recognition.

questions.objective: Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience
questions.scenario: Choosing among three drafts
questions.stem: An associate generated three different Claude drafts of a customer email and must choose one to send. The best basis for the choice is:

options.text: Compare the drafts against the goal and the audience, select or merge the one that best fits, then verify any factual claims.
Pick whichever draft is longest and most detailed.
Pick whichever draft Claude says is the best of the three.
Pick the one with the most polished-looking formatting.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Edit, adapt, refine, and compare outputs for the intended audience.' Comparing outputs is an act of judgment against two explicit references — the goal and the audience — not against surface-level metrics. A does exactly that, allows merging the best of each draft, and closes by verifying the facts before sending. Choosing by length, by the model's opinion, or by appearance replaces the judgment of fit with a proxy that doesn't correlate with quality for that recipient.

distractorsEs.B: Default Maximalism: 'longer/more detailed' is not 'better for this audience'; it's often worse.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-assessment is not the criterion; fit is judged by the associate against the goal.
distractorsEs.D: Cosmetic Fix: polished formatting doesn't say whether the message fits the goal and the recipient.

questions.trap: B/C/D replace the fit criterion with superficial proxies (length, the model's opinion, appearance).

questions.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
questions.scenario: Complex, high-stakes legal analysis
questions.stem: An associate must work through a complex, ambiguous legal-strategy question that demands deep reasoning and the highest quality. Which choice best fits?

options.text: Use the fastest, lowest-cost model to save budget.
Disable product features to reduce cost.
Use the most capable model, suited to complex, high-stakes reasoning, reserving faster models for simpler work.
Switch to a different AI platform.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality).' This mirrors official sample 2: when the prompt prioritizes depth of reasoning and quality over speed/cost, the correct match is the most capable model (the Opus profile), reserving the fast ones for simple work. The rule is the same in both directions: match the model's profile to the task's profile.

distractorsEs.A: Blind minimalism: the cheapest model sacrifices exactly the dimension (deep reasoning) that the prompt prioritized.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: turning off features isn't the variable in this trade-off, and it degrades the ability to do the work.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: abandoning the platform doesn't answer the model-selection question.

questions.trap: A is maximalism's twin: here the error is economizing on a task that demands capability.

questions.objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
questions.scenario: Recurring questions about the same documents
questions.stem: A team repeatedly asks Claude questions that all depend on the same set of internal documents and guidelines. Which product feature best fits?

options.text: Paste the documents into every new chat before asking.
Set up a Claude Project with those documents as knowledge and shared instructions, so every conversation in it starts with that context.
Use the most expensive model so it remembers the documents.
Start a fresh chat each time and re-explain the background from scratch.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Select appropriate Claude product features.' The pattern — shared, stable context reused across many conversations — is exactly what Projects exist for: instructions and knowledge sources that persist and are shared. B matches feature to need. The right feature solves the structural problem; the model tier or re-pasting does not.

distractorsEs.A: Wrong Lever / inefficiency: re-pasting the documents into every chat is the manual work a Project eliminates.
distractorsEs.C: Maximalism / layer confusion: the model's price tier doesn't give it memory of the document; the knowledge container is the feature, not the tier.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut / inefficiency: re-explaining from scratch every time wastes effort and is prone to inconsistencies.

questions.trap: C confuses 'more capable model' with 'remembers my documents'; persistence comes from the Project, not the tier.

questions.objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
questions.scenario: A conversation that has grown too long
questions.stem: A working conversation has grown very long, and Claude's replies are starting to lose track of details established earlier. The most appropriate action is to:

options.text: Summarize the key decisions and context, then start a fresh conversation (or persist them in a Project), instead of continuing to append.
Keep going in the same chat and hope it holds together.
Ask Claude why it forgot and rely on its explanation.
Switch to a more expensive model to fix the memory.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations.' In a very long conversation, context gets saturated and early details lose weight. The correct behavior is to actively manage the context: summarize the essentials and start fresh, or persist it in a Project. A does exactly that. Recognizing when to summarize/restart/persist is what this objective evaluates.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut: continuing to pile onto the same chat worsens the context loss instead of resolving it.
distractorsEs.C: Circular Self-Verification / anthropomorphization: asking the model to explain 'why it forgot' doesn't restore the context and isn't a management action.
distractorsEs.D: Maximalism / Wrong Lever: a more expensive model isn't the lever for a context problem; you need to manage the context, not raise the tier.

questions.trap: D sells 'more model' as the cure for a problem that is about context management, not capability.

questions.objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
questions.scenario: An editable, reusable document
questions.stem: The associate wants Claude to produce a document they can view, iterate on, and reuse as a standalone piece separate from the chat flow. Which feature fits?

options.text: Research mode.
A brand-new chat for every edit.
The highest-cost model.
An artifact — a standalone, iteratively editable document.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Select appropriate Claude product features.' A substantial document that gets viewed, edited, and reused as a piece independent of the chat is the canonical case for an artifact. D matches feature to need. Choosing the feature based on how the output will be consumed — not on which one sounds more powerful — is the objective.

distractorsEs.A: Wrong feature: research is for investigating/synthesizing sources, not for hosting an editable document.
distractorsEs.B: Inefficiency: a new chat per edit fragments the work; the artifact keeps the document alive.
distractorsEs.C: Layer confusion: the model's tier is not an output-format feature.

questions.trap: A and C tempt with features/layers that don't address a 'reusable editable document.'

questions.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
questions.scenario: Classifying thousands of simple tickets
questions.stem: An associate must classify thousands of short support tickets into categories — a simple, repetitive, high-volume task. The best model choice is:

options.text: The most capable, highest-cost model on every ticket, to maximize quality.
A faster, lower-cost model suited to straightforward, high-volume work.
Do all of it manually instead.
Whichever model Claude says is best for itself.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Align model selection with task requirements.' Simple, repetitive, high-volume work is the profile for the fast, economical model (the Haiku profile); the top-tier model is reserved for complex reasoning. B matches profile to profile. Reserving expensive capability for what actually needs it is professional judgment, not a lack of ambition.

distractorsEs.A: Default Maximalism: the top-tier model on every ticket burns cost and latency with no real gain on a trivial task.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch: giving up on automation wastes the lever in exactly the case where it pays off most.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's 'recommendation' about itself is not the criterion; the task's profile is.

questions.trap: A is the reflex of 'always the best model'; at high, simple volume, that's poor cost judgment.

questions.objective: Differentiate between Claude model types (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus)
questions.scenario: How to think about the model family
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects how to think about the Claude model family (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) when choosing for a task?

options.text: Always pick the top model; more capability is never a downside.
Always pick the smallest model; it is the cheapest.
Match the model to the task — lighter, faster models for simple high-volume work; the most capable for complex reasoning — balancing cost, speed, and quality.
The choice of model does not meaningfully affect cost or speed.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Differentiate between Claude model types.' The family is organized around a deliberate trade-off: the lighter models favor speed and cost; the most capable one favors deep reasoning. C captures that profile-matching, which is the correct way to decide. There is no model that's 'always right'; there is a right model for each task profile.

distractorsEs.A: Maximalism: ignores cost and latency; more capability does have a price.
distractorsEs.B: Minimalism: sacrifices quality in cases where reasoning is actually needed.
distractorsEs.D: False: the tier directly affects cost and speed; denying that contradicts the basis of the decision.

questions.trap: A and B are the two symmetric extremes; the answer is profile-matching, not a fixed rule.

questions.objective: Select appropriate Claude product features (Projects, research mode, chat, artifacts)
questions.scenario: Researching and synthesizing many sources
questions.stem: An associate needs Claude to investigate a topic across many sources and produce a synthesized, cited overview. Which capability is the best fit?

options.text: Use the research capability designed to gather information across multiple sources and synthesize it.
Ask a single one-line question in a normal chat and accept the first reply.
Open an artifact and write a one-paragraph note without gathering any sources.
Switch to a different platform for the research.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Select appropriate Claude product features.' The need — combing through many sources and synthesizing them with citations — corresponds to the research capability, not a quick chat reply or a document with no sources. A matches the feature to the depth of the work. The feature is chosen based on the nature of the task, not on speed or habit.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut: a single chat reply doesn't gather or synthesize multiple sources with the rigor requested.
distractorsEs.C: Wrong feature: an artifact is a document container; it doesn't perform multi-source research.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: switching platforms evades the feature choice within Claude.

questions.trap: C tempts because 'artifact' sounds like a deliverable, but the task is to research, not just to host text.

questions.objective: Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations (when to restart, summarize, or persist)
questions.scenario: A monthly report with the same context
questions.stem: An associate will produce a recurring monthly report that always needs the same background context. The best way to manage that context over time is to:

options.text: Re-paste the full background into a new chat every month.
Keep one endless chat running forever so nothing is lost.
Assume Claude will remember the background on its own between months.
Persist the background in a Project (instructions plus knowledge) so each month's conversation starts with it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Understand and manage context limitations and memory considerations.' A stable context that gets reused periodically should be persisted somewhere it lives durably and consistently: a Project. D does that, and every run starts from the same baseline, with no rework or drift. Persisting is the right decision when the context is recurring and stable.

distractorsEs.A: Inefficiency: re-pasting every month is repeated manual work prone to divergent versions.
distractorsEs.B: Context bloat: an endless chat accumulates noise and eventually saturates the useful context.
distractorsEs.C: Anthropomorphization: don't assume magical persistence across sessions; persistence is configured.

questions.trap: B sounds like 'don't lose anything,' but an endless chat saturates the context instead of preserving it.

questions.objective: Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality)
questions.scenario: High quality and speed on a limited budget
questions.stem: A task needs fairly high quality AND fast turnaround at moderate volume, on a limited budget. The most appropriate approach is to:

options.text: Default to the top model regardless of budget.
Choose the mid-tier model that balances quality, speed, and cost, and reserve the top model only for the hardest sub-tasks.
Choose the cheapest model and accept low quality.
Abandon the task as impossible under the constraints.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Align model selection with task requirements (cost, speed, quality).' When the prompt asks for several dimensions at once under a tight budget, the answer is balance: the mid-tier model (the Sonnet profile) covers reasonable quality and speed at contained cost, with the top tier reserved for the hardest sub-cases. B respects all three constraints instead of sacrificing one.

distractorsEs.A: Maximalism: ignores the stated limited budget; it optimizes quality at the expense of the other two constraints.
distractorsEs.C: Minimalism: sacrifices the quality the prompt actually required.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: the task is viable with a balanced model; abandoning it is an overreaction.

questions.trap: A and C fall to the extremes of the trade-off; with three constraints at once, the mid-tier balance wins.

questions.objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
questions.scenario: Presenting a workflow to leadership
questions.stem: An associate is presenting a new Claude-based workflow to leadership. Which framing is most appropriate?

options.text: Emphasize only the benefits, to secure buy-in quickly.
Emphasize only the risks, to look appropriately cautious.
Present the concrete value and the honest limitations (outputs need review, some tasks stay human) so stakeholders can decide realistically.
Let Claude write the pitch and present it without checking it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders.' The guide is explicit about communicating value AND limitations honestly. C does both, which is what enables an informed decision and sustains the associate's credibility. Selling only benefits or only risks are the two extremes the exam penalizes.

distractorsEs.A: Overselling: hiding limitations gets fragile buy-in and erodes trust once the limits show up.
distractorsEs.B: Symmetric paralysis: exaggerating the risk blocks real value; the equally biased opposite of A.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut / Circular: presenting the model's own pitch without checking it hands the judgment over to Claude and risks overclaiming.

questions.trap: A and B are the extremes (only benefits / only risks); honest communication puts both on the table.

questions.objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
questions.scenario: Introducing Claude into a process that already works
questions.stem: A team has a working manual process for triaging requests. The best way to introduce Claude is to:

options.text: Replace the entire process overnight with an untested Claude workflow.
Integrate Claude at a specific high-friction step, pilot it, measure the result, and expand if it helps.
Abandon the idea, since the current process already works.
Ask Claude whether it should replace the team.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them.' Integrating well means augmenting the real process incrementally and measurably: pick a friction point, pilot it, measure, and scale. B is that disciplined middle-ground action. Neither wholesale replacement without evidence nor abandonment counts as integration.

distractorsEs.A: Maximalism / risk: replacing everything at once without piloting bets the process on an unproven solution.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch / paralysis: 'it already works' avoids exploring a bounded, low-risk improvement.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense / Circular: the redesign decision isn't dictated by the model about itself.

questions.trap: A and C are the extremes (replace everything / touch nothing); integrating means piloting one step and measuring.

questions.objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
questions.scenario: Before building a workflow
questions.stem: Before building a Claude workflow, the most useful first step is to:

options.text: Analyze the actual requirements and use case — the problem, the inputs and outputs, and what success looks like — to decide where Claude fits.
Pick the most expensive model and start building immediately.
Automate the first task that comes to mind.
Buy more Claude seats for the team.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases.' Solution design begins with understanding the problem: requirements, inputs/outputs, and the success criterion. A does that analysis, which determines where (and whether) Claude adds value. Jumping to building or buying before analyzing is solving without defining the problem.

distractorsEs.B: Maximalism / premature: picking a model and building before analyzing puts the tool before the problem.
distractorsEs.C: Shortcut: automating 'the first thing that comes to mind' ignores whether it's the use case that actually matters.
distractorsEs.D: Wrong Lever: more licenses isn't a design step; it doesn't answer what problem is being solved.

questions.trap: B and C jump to the solution; the first step is analyzing the requirement and the use case.

questions.objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
questions.scenario: A slow monthly reporting process
questions.stem: An associate wants to use Claude to improve a slow monthly reporting process. The most appropriate use is to:

options.text: Ask Claude to approve the current process as-is.
Use Claude to replace the finance team.
Have Claude rate the process from 1 to 10.
Use Claude to map the current steps, identify bottlenecks, and propose optimizations the team can test.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization.' Optimizing a process means mapping it, finding bottlenecks, and proposing verifiable improvements. D uses Claude for that analytical work with the team validating. Approving it, replacing people, or giving it a score from 1 to 10 optimizes nothing.

distractorsEs.A: Nonsense: 'approving' the process generates no improvement; it isn't the use case being asked for.
distractorsEs.B: Overreach: replacing the team is not process optimization, and it exceeds the role.
distractorsEs.C: Superficial: a numeric rating doesn't identify bottlenecks or propose changes.

questions.trap: C looks like 'analysis,' but a score with no diagnosis doesn't optimize the process.

questions.objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
questions.scenario: A first solution draft with gaps
questions.stem: A first draft of a Claude-assisted solution has gaps. The best approach to the solution design is to:

options.text: Ship the first draft; iterating just wastes time.
Treat the design as iterative — pilot it, gather feedback, and refine across cycles.
Escalate the whole thing to engineering immediately.
Ask Claude whether the design is perfect and ship if it says yes.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration.' Solution design is iterative by nature: pilot it, gather feedback, and refine. B is that cycle. Neither shipping the first draft with gaps, nor escalating prematurely, nor trusting the model's self-assessment counts as iterative design.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: shipping with known gaps transfers the defect to the end user.
distractorsEs.C: Escape / premature: escalating everything before iterating skips the refinement work that belongs to the role.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: 'perfection' according to the model is not a design criterion.

questions.trap: A and C are extremes (ship now / escalate now); correct design iterates with feedback.

questions.objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
questions.scenario: Sending output directly to the customer with no review?
questions.stem: A stakeholder asks whether the Claude workflow can be trusted to send outputs directly to customers with no human check. The most appropriate answer is:

options.text: 'Yes — it's AI, so it's reliable enough to send unchecked.'
'No — AI can never be used for any customer communication at all.'
'It can draft and accelerate the work, but customer-facing outputs should be reviewed; here is where human checkpoints belong.'
'Let me ask Claude how reliable it thinks it is and go with that.'

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders.' The honest answer acknowledges the value (it speeds up the work) and the limit (what goes to the customer gets reviewed), and places the human checkpoint. C does that. Overclaiming reliability or banning all use are the extremes; neither communicates with precision.

distractorsEs.A: Overclaim: 'it's AI, it's reliable' promises something the guide contradicts; risky outputs get verified.
distractorsEs.B: Over-restriction: banning all use ignores the real value and is just as imprecise as A.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: delegating the reliability judgment to the model itself is not communicating honestly.

questions.trap: A and B are the extremes; correct communication situates value and limit with the human checkpoint.

questions.objective: Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them
questions.scenario: Redesign the workflow after a successful pilot?
questions.stem: After a successful pilot, a team sees a chance to redesign a workflow around Claude rather than just bolt it on. The right basis for that decision is:

options.text: Evidence from the pilot showing where redesign adds measurable value, weighed against the cost of change.
Redesign everything now, because the pilot worked once.
Never change the workflow, since change is risky.
Do whatever Claude suggests, without questioning it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Integrate Claude into existing workflows to augment or redesign them.' Redesigning is a value-and-cost decision: it's justified by pilot evidence of where it adds value, weighed against the cost of change. A makes that judgment call. Generalizing from a single pilot or refusing to change are the extremes, and following the model's suggestion without questioning it cedes the judgment.

distractorsEs.B: Maximalism: extrapolating from a single pilot to redesigning everything ignores the cost and risk of broad change.
distractorsEs.C: Paralysis: rejecting all change wastes the value the pilot already demonstrated.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's suggestion does not substitute for the team's value/cost analysis.

questions.trap: B and C are the extremes (redesign everything / nothing); the correct basis is pilot evidence vs. cost.

questions.objective: Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases
questions.scenario: Unreviewable hiring decisions?
questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude to make final, unreviewable hiring decisions. Analyzing the use case, the appropriate conclusion is:

options.text: Proceed — automating the decision saves the most time.
Use the most capable model so the decisions are safe to automate.
Reformat the decision as a formal report and proceed.
This is a poor fit for autonomous decisions; use Claude to support the analysis while a human makes the final call.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply Claude to analyze requirements and use cases.' Analyzing the use case includes recognizing when it's NOT appropriate: a final hiring decision requires human judgment and should not be autonomous. D uses Claude as analytical support and leaves the decision with a human. Good use-case analysis distinguishes 'supporting' from 'deciding.'

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: automating for time savings ignores that the case requires protected human judgment.
distractorsEs.B: Maximalism / Wrong Lever: raising the tier doesn't make an inappropriate use case appropriate.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: turning it into a report doesn't change the fact that the final decision shouldn't be autonomous.

questions.trap: B/C 'improve' the execution of a use case that shouldn't have been automated in the first place; the correct analysis is to reject the autonomy.

questions.objective: Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization
questions.scenario: Planning a product launch
questions.stem: For planning a product launch, the highest-value way to use Claude is to:

options.text: Ask it to guarantee that the launch will succeed.
Use it to draft the plan, surface risks and dependencies, and iterate — with the team validating the decisions.
Have it make every launch decision autonomously.
Ask it how confident it is that the launch will work and act on that.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Leverage Claude for research, planning, and process optimization.' The value lies in accelerating and enriching the planning — draft, risks, dependencies, iteration — while the team validates. B captures that use. Asking for guarantees, delegating all decisions, or being guided by self-reported 'confidence' is not responsible planning.

distractorsEs.A: Nonsense / overclaim: no model guarantees future outcomes; it isn't a valid use.
distractorsEs.C: Overreach: autonomous launch decisions take the team out of the judgment loop.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's confidence doesn't predict success and isn't a basis for a decision.

questions.trap: A and C are extremes (magic guarantee / total autonomy); the value lies in assisting while the team validates.

questions.objective: Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders
questions.scenario: Convincing a skeptical executive
questions.stem: Communicating the value of a Claude workflow to a skeptical executive is most credible when the associate:

options.text: Promises it will eliminate all manual work.
Focuses on how advanced and cutting-edge the technology is.
Ties it to concrete outcomes (time saved, quality, cost) and is candid about where humans stay in the loop.
Repeats what Claude said about its own capabilities.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Communicate Claude's value and limitations to stakeholders.' Facing skepticism, credibility comes from concrete results and honesty about the limits (where the human stays in the loop). C does both. Promising to eliminate all the work, selling 'how advanced it is,' or quoting the model itself are not arguments of verifiable value.

distractorsEs.A: Overclaim: promising to eliminate all manual work invites disappointment and destroys credibility.
distractorsEs.B: Hype: 'how advanced it is' is not business value; the executive is asking about outcomes.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: repeating what the model says about itself is not evidence.

questions.trap: A/B/D sell a promise or hype; credibility is concrete results plus honest limits.

questions.objective: Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration
questions.scenario: Internal tool that fails on edge cases
questions.stem: A Claude-assisted internal tool works for common cases but fails on edge cases. The best next step in solution development is to:

options.text: Identify the failing edge cases, refine the approach for them, and re-test — iterating toward robustness.
Declare it done, since the common cases work.
Scrap the tool and go fully manual.
Ask Claude to certify the tool as complete.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Use Claude to support solution design, development, and iteration.' Developing a robust solution is a cycle: locate the failing cases, adjust, and retest. A does that evidence-driven iteration work. Declaring it done with known failures or scrapping it are the extremes, and the model's own 'certification' validates nothing.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut: 'the common cases work' leaves the edge cases broken in production.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch: scrapping the tool wastes the value it already delivers on the common cases.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's self-certification is not proof of completeness.

questions.trap: B and C are extremes (done already / scrap everything); correct development iterates on the cases that fail.

questions.objective: Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources
questions.scenario: Consistent tone and documents in a Project
questions.stem: A team wants every conversation in a Project to follow the same tone and reference the same policy documents. The right configuration is to:

options.text: Remind Claude of the tone and attach the documents again in each individual message.
Set the Project's instructions (tone and rules) and add the policy documents as its knowledge sources.
Use a more expensive model so it behaves consistently.
Start a separate new Project for each conversation.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Configure Claude Projects with instructions and knowledge sources.' Consistency of tone and sources is achieved by configuring the Project once: shared instructions + documents as knowledge. B does that and it applies to all of its conversations. Repeating it in every message or raising the tier is not configuration, and multiplying Projects breaks the very thing that was meant to be shared.

distractorsEs.A: Inefficiency / inconsistency: reminding the tone and attaching docs per message is fragile and prone to being forgotten.
distractorsEs.C: Wrong Lever: the model's tier doesn't enforce tone or sources; that's Project configuration.
distractorsEs.D: Counterproductive: a Project per conversation eliminates the shared context that was being sought.

questions.trap: C confuses model capability with configuration; consistency is configured, not purchased.

questions.objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
questions.scenario: Outdated pricing sheet in the Project
questions.stem: A Project's knowledge still contains last week's pricing sheet; the prices changed but the old file is still uploaded, and Claude keeps citing the old prices. The fix is to:

options.text: Tell Claude in each chat to 'use the new prices' instead.
Switch to a different model.
Update the knowledge source — replace the outdated pricing sheet with the current one.
Ask Claude why it used the old prices.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions.' If the source is stale, the answer will be stale: the durable fix is to update the knowledge (replace the sheet). C does that at the source. Instructing it in every chat is a patch that leaves the outdated file in place; the tier or asking 'why' doesn't correct the data.

distractorsEs.A: Instruction-as-control: 'use the new ones' in every chat doesn't update the source; the old data is still there, ready to resurface.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: the model isn't the cause; the outdated source is.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: asking why it cited the old data doesn't replace the outdated file.

questions.trap: A looks like it solves it, but it's a per-conversation patch; the stale source is still alive.

questions.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
questions.scenario: System-level instruction for support
questions.stem: Which is the most effective system-level instruction for a customer-support Project?

options.text: A clear, specific instruction: the role, the tone, what to do when unsure (e.g., escalate to a human), and what never to promise.
'Be helpful.'
A very long instruction that repeats 'be accurate' dozens of times.
No instruction at all, so each user can steer it themselves.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective system-level instructions.' An effective instruction is specific and actionable: role, tone, what to do when unsure, and what never to promise. A defines them. 'Be helpful' is vague, repeating 'be accurate' is noise with no behavior attached, and giving no instruction leaves the behavior to each user's whim.

distractorsEs.B: Vague: 'be helpful' fixes no behavior, no boundaries, and no handling of uncertainty.
distractorsEs.C: Noise: repeating an adjective doesn't create a rule; specificity, not insistence, guides the model.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut: with no instruction there's no consistency; every conversation starts from zero.

questions.trap: C simulates rigor through repetition; a good instruction is specific, not insistent.

questions.objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
questions.scenario: Documents that live in Google Drive
questions.stem: An associate wants Claude to answer questions using the team's documents that live in Google Drive. The appropriate approach is to:

options.text: Manually copy every document into the chat before each question.
Email all the documents to Claude.
Use the most capable model so it 'knows' the team's Drive.
Connect the relevant knowledge source or connector (e.g., Google Drive) so Claude can draw on those documents.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail).' For Claude to use documents that live in Drive, that source/connector gets connected; that way it accesses the relevant documents with no manual re-pasting. D is the correct route. Copying everything, 'emailing it,' or raising the tier don't connect the source.

distractorsEs.A: Inefficiency: copying each document for every question is the work a connector eliminates.
distractorsEs.B: Nonsense: 'emailing' the model is not how knowledge sources get connected.
distractorsEs.C: Anthropomorphization / Wrong Lever: a more expensive model doesn't 'know' your Drive; the connection is what grants access.

questions.trap: C confuses capability with access; the connector, not the tier, is what brings in the documents.

questions.objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
questions.scenario: Instructions out of date six months later
questions.stem: Six months after a Project was set up, its instructions no longer match how the team actually works. The appropriate action is to:

options.text: Leave it — it was configured correctly when it was created.
Review and update the Project's instructions and knowledge to reflect the current process.
Delete the Project and stop using Projects altogether.
Ask Claude to rewrite its own instructions autonomously without review.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions.' Configurations are not 'set and forget': when the process changes, they get reviewed and updated. B keeps the Project current with the actual work. Leaving it stale or deleting it are the extremes, and letting the model rewrite itself with no review loses human control.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: 'it was set up right once' ignores that the process evolved and the config fell out of date.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch: deleting the Project throws away the value over a mismatch that updating would fix.
distractorsEs.D: Overreach: autonomous rewriting with no human review risks faulty instructions with no control.

questions.trap: A and C are extremes (don't touch it / delete it); maintaining means reviewing and updating the configuration.

questions.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
questions.scenario: Where to put a rule that always applies
questions.stem: An instruction that should apply to every conversation in a Project is best placed:

options.text: In the Project's shared instructions, so it applies consistently to all of its conversations.
Typed again by the user at the start of each individual chat.
In a separate side document that nobody actually reads.
Nowhere formal — rely on each user to remember it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective system-level instructions.' A universal rule should live where it applies to everything consistently: the Project's shared instructions. A does that. Rewriting it in every chat, hiding it in an external doc, or relying on people's memory all but guarantee inconsistency.

distractorsEs.B: Inefficiency / inconsistency: rewriting the rule per chat depends on nobody forgetting it or varying it.
distractorsEs.C: Ineffective: an instruction the model never receives does not govern its behavior.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut: human memory is not a configuration mechanism.

questions.trap: B/C/D place the rule somewhere that does NOT govern the model; the Project's instructions do.

questions.objective: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (e.g., Google Drive, Gmail)
questions.scenario: A noisy knowledge base
questions.stem: A Project's knowledge base has grown to include many outdated and irrelevant files, and the answers are getting noisier. The best action is to:

options.text: Upload even more files so everything is covered.
Switch to a bigger model to cut through the noise.
Curate the knowledge — remove outdated and irrelevant sources so the relevant ones drive the answers.
Tell Claude in the prompt to ignore the bad files.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors.' Managing knowledge includes curating it: removing the outdated and irrelevant so the good sources dominate. C attacks the cause of the noise. Adding more files makes it worse, raising the tier doesn't clean the source, and 'ignore them' is an instruction that doesn't purge the knowledge base.

distractorsEs.A: Maximalism: more files increase the noise, they don't reduce it.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: the model isn't the cause of the noise; the uncurated knowledge base is.
distractorsEs.D: Instruction-as-control: asking it to ignore the bad ones doesn't remove them or guarantee it won't use them.

questions.trap: A makes the real problem worse (source noise) by assuming 'coverage' equals quality.

questions.objective: Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions
questions.scenario: The Project makes an improper promise
questions.stem: A support Project keeps making a promise it shouldn't ('we always refund within 24 hours'). The durable fix is to:

options.text: Correct it by hand in each conversation where it comes up.
Switch to a different model.
Ask Claude once to stop saying it.
Update the Project's instructions to explicitly forbid that promise and state the correct policy.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Inform, maintain, and update Claude configurations, knowledge sources, and instructions.' An improper, recurring behavior is corrected in the configuration: update the Project's instructions to forbid the promise and state the correct policy. D is the durable fix. Correcting it per chat or asking once are transient patches; the model isn't the cause.

distractorsEs.A: Patch: correcting it per conversation doesn't prevent it from resurfacing in the next one.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: switching models doesn't change a missing instruction.
distractorsEs.C: Transient: asking it 'once' doesn't persist as a Project rule.

questions.trap: A and C treat the symptom per conversation; the durable fix lives in the Project's instructions.

questions.objective: Create effective system-level instructions
questions.scenario: The most reliable system-level instruction
questions.stem: Which system-level instruction will most reliably shape Claude's behavior in a benefits-advisor Project?

options.text: 'Do a good job and be helpful.'
'You are a benefits advisor. Answer only from the uploaded policy documents; if the answer is not in them, say so and route the person to HR. Never speculate about an individual's eligibility.'
'Be smart, careful, thorough, precise, and accurate.'
Leave the instruction blank to keep Claude flexible.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Create effective system-level instructions.' The most reliable instruction is specific and bounded: it defines the role, the source of truth (only the documents), what to do when there's no answer (route to HR), and an explicit limit (don't speculate about eligibility). B sets all of them. Loose adjectives or a blank field leave the behavior ungoverned.

distractorsEs.A: Vague: 'do a good job' defines no source, no boundaries, and no handling of uncertainty.
distractorsEs.C: Adjective pile-up: five qualities with no concrete behavior don't guide real decisions.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut: with no instruction there are no guardrails; 'flexibility' here just means a lack of control.

questions.trap: A and C sound good but fix no behavior; the reliable instruction is specific, with a source and boundaries.

questions.objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations
questions.scenario: Regulated medical record
questions.stem: An associate wants to paste a customer's full medical record into Claude to draft a summary. The record contains regulated health data and policy restricts sharing it. The most appropriate action is to:

options.text: Paste it as-is, since drafting a summary is a legitimate business need.
Remove or de-identify the regulated health data first, consistent with policy, then draft the summary from the de-identified version.
Paste it but instruct Claude not to store the record.
Skip the summary entirely.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations.' Just like official sample 3: the correct answer satisfies the policy WITHOUT abandoning the task. De-identifying the regulated data before using Claude is a real control applied at the source, and the summary can be drafted from the anonymized version. Governance enables the work under control — it neither blocks it nor runs it blindly.

distractorsEs.A: Convenience rationalization: 'it's a legitimate need' is not an exception to the policy on regulated health data.
distractorsEs.C: Fake Control: 'don't store it' is a request to the model, not a data control; the regulated data already crossed the perimeter the moment it was pasted in.
distractorsEs.D: Overcorrection: canceling the summary when a conforming path exists (de-identify) is unnecessary paralysis.

questions.trap: C looks like mitigation, but it confuses instructing the model with applying a control; the data has already been exposed.

questions.objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
questions.scenario: Deciding layoffs autonomously
questions.stem: A manager asks Claude to autonomously decide which employees to lay off, with no human review. Under responsible-use principles, this is:

options.text: Fine, since removing humans removes bias.
Fine, as long as the most capable model is used.
Fine, as long as it is formatted as an official memo.
An inappropriate use case for autonomous decision-making; such decisions require human judgment and accountability.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases.' High-impact decisions about people require human judgment and accountability; automating them with no review is an inappropriate use. D recognizes that. Responsible use distinguishes supporting the analysis from making the decision, and here the decision must not be delegated.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: automating doesn't 'remove bias'; it can amplify the bias already in the data, and it removes human accountability.
distractorsEs.B: Maximalism / Wrong Lever: the model's tier doesn't make an inherently non-autonomous use case appropriate.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: the memo format doesn't change the inappropriate nature of an autonomous decision of this kind.

questions.trap: A/B/C 'enable' an inappropriate use by changing details; the answer is recognizing that it should not be automated.

questions.objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
questions.scenario: Policy that bans certain data from external AI
questions.stem: The organization's AI policy prohibits using external AI tools for a certain class of confidential data. An associate finds Claude would be very useful for exactly that data. The right action is to:

options.text: Follow the policy — do not use Claude for that data — and raise the use case through proper channels if a policy change is warranted.
Use it anyway; the policy is probably outdated.
Use it quietly and not mention it to anyone.
Ask Claude whether the policy really applies and act on its answer.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards.' Usefulness doesn't invalidate the policy; you comply with it, and if there's a case for changing it, you raise it through the proper channels. A respects governance and leaves room for legitimate improvement. Skirting or hiding the use violates the standard, and the policy is not the model's to interpret.

distractorsEs.B: Rationalization: 'it's probably outdated' doesn't authorize violating it; that's decided by the process, not the associate.
distractorsEs.C: Concealment: using it and staying quiet compounds the violation with a lack of transparency.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: whether a policy applies is determined by the organization, not the model.

questions.trap: B and C turn convenience into permission; the policy gets followed and, if warranted, changed through the proper channel.

questions.objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
questions.scenario: Publishing AI content as if it were human-written
questions.stem: An associate uses Claude to generate content that will be published as if solely written by a named human expert, with no disclosure. The core ethical concern is:

options.text: There is none, since a human edits it eventually.
Only the cost of the model used.
Misrepresenting AI-generated content as solely human-authored can mislead the audience; transparency and the organization's disclosure norms should guide it.
That a cheaper model wasn't used for the job.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Understand the ethical implications of AI usage.' Presenting AI-generated content as entirely human-authored can mislead the audience; the ethics here revolve around transparency and the organization's disclosure norms. C names that. The others reduce a problem of honesty to one of cost or editing.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: 'a human edits it' doesn't resolve the misrepresentation of authorship to the audience.
distractorsEs.B: Irrelevant: the model's cost doesn't touch the ethical question of representation.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant: which model was used doesn't change the disclosure problem.

questions.trap: A/B/D deflect to cost or editing; the ethical axis is transparency about authorship.

questions.objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations
questions.scenario: Analysis permitted on anonymized data
questions.stem: An associate can complete an analysis if customer identifiers are anonymized first, and policy explicitly allows the analysis on de-identified data. The responsible action is to:

options.text: Cancel the analysis to be safe.
Anonymize the identifiers and proceed with the analysis on the de-identified data.
Proceed with the raw data, since anonymizing is extra work.
Ask Claude to anonymize the data 'in its own memory' and keep going.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations.' When a conforming path exists — anonymize and analyze the de-identified data — the responsible behavior is to take it: it satisfies the policy and preserves the value. B does that. Canceling is paralysis, using the raw data violates the policy, and having 'the model anonymize it in its own memory' is not a real control.

distractorsEs.A: Overcorrection: canceling when the policy permits de-identified analysis wastes legitimate work.
distractorsEs.C: Violation: using raw data for convenience ignores the control the policy requires.
distractorsEs.D: Fake Control: asking the model to 'anonymize it in its memory' doesn't de-identify the source or satisfy the policy.

questions.trap: A and C are the extremes (paralysis / violation); with a conforming path available, you anonymize and proceed.

questions.objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
questions.scenario: Which is an appropriate use?
questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate use of Claude for an associate?

options.text: Drafting and analyzing internal documents that the associate then reviews and takes ownership of.
Making final, binding legal determinations with no human review.
Storing regulated data that policy does not allow it to hold.
Publishing unverified claims under the company's name.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases.' Appropriate use keeps Claude as support with an accountable human: drafting and analyzing internal documents that the associate reviews and takes ownership of. A fits. The other three are classic inappropriate cases: a binding decision with no review, storing prohibited data, and publishing without verification.

distractorsEs.B: Inappropriate: a binding legal determination with no human review exceeds responsible use.
distractorsEs.C: Inappropriate: retaining regulated data the policy prohibits is a direct violation.
distractorsEs.D: Inappropriate: publishing unverified claims under the brand transfers factual and reputational risk.

questions.trap: B/C/D are this domain's anti-patterns; appropriate use keeps the human in charge and verifies.

questions.objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
