questions.scenario: New use on sensitive data, not yet reviewed
questions.stem: A new use of Claude will touch sensitive data and hasn't been reviewed against governance standards yet. Before rolling it out, the associate should:

options.text: Roll it out and seek approval later if someone complains.
Roll it out quietly to avoid delay.
Get the use reviewed and approved against the organization's governance standards first.
Ask Claude to approve the use.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards.' A use that touches sensitive data gets reviewed and approved against the governance standards BEFORE it's rolled out. C follows the process. Deploying first (openly or quietly) inverts the order of the control, and approval isn't the model's to give.

distractorsEs.A: Violation: 'approval afterward' exposes sensitive data without the required prior control.
distractorsEs.B: Concealment: deploying quietly deliberately evades governance review.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense / Circular: governance approval is an organizational process, not an output from the model.

questions.trap: A and B put deployment before the control; governance reviews and approves first.

questions.objective: Understand the ethical implications of AI usage
questions.scenario: Possible bias against a protected group
questions.stem: An associate notices Claude's outputs for a decision task may disadvantage a protected group. Responsibly, the associate should:

options.text: Ignore it if the outputs are otherwise useful.
Use a bigger model and assume the bias is fixed.
Reformat the outputs to look neutral.
Flag the potential bias, add human oversight, and avoid using the output where it could cause unfair harm.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Understand the ethical implications of AI usage.' Potential harm to a protected group calls for responsible action: flag it, add human oversight, and avoid using the output where it could cause unfair harm. D does that. Ignoring it, raising the tier, or dressing up the format doesn't address the ethical risk.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: usefulness doesn't justify ignoring potential harm to a protected group.
distractorsEs.B: Maximalism / Wrong Lever: switching models doesn't guarantee the bias disappears; assuming so is negligent.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix: 'looking neutral' hides the problem instead of mitigating it.

questions.trap: A/B/C evade the risk; the responsible behavior flags it, supervises it, and limits its use.

questions.objective: Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations
questions.scenario: No conforming path available
questions.stem: An associate is asked to use Claude on data that no anonymization can safely de-identify, for a purpose the policy prohibits, with no conforming alternative available. The correct action is to:

options.text: Find a clever workaround to use it anyway.
Do not use Claude for this — escalate or decline — since there is no policy-conforming path.
Use it but instruct Claude to 'be careful' with the data.
Use the cheapest model to limit the exposure.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Apply data sensitivity, regulatory, and privacy considerations.' This is the case — flagged in the decoder — where declining/escalating IS the correct move: no anonymization can save the data, and there's no conforming path for the purpose. B doesn't use Claude and escalates. Here there is no conforming middle-ground action, so 'not using it' stops being an escape hatch and becomes the responsible choice.

distractorsEs.A: Violation: a 'workaround' to skirt a policy on data that cannot be protected is exactly what's prohibited.
distractorsEs.C: Fake Control: 'be careful' is not a control; the irreducible data remains exposed.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense / Wrong Lever: a cheaper model doesn't reduce the problem that the use is non-conforming.

questions.trap: The exam distinguishes this exception: with no conforming middle-ground path, declining/escalating is correct — not an escape hatch.

questions.objective: Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases
questions.scenario: High-impact recommendation affecting customers
questions.stem: For a high-stakes recommendation that affects customers, the appropriate governance posture is to:

options.text: Use Claude to support the analysis, keep a human accountable for the final decision, and document the basis.
Fully automate the decision to remove human error.
Refuse to use Claude for anything customer-related at all.
Let Claude make the decision and be responsible for it.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify appropriate and inappropriate use cases.' In high-impact decisions, the correct posture uses Claude as support, keeps a human accountable, and documents the basis for the decision. A balances value and control. Fully automating it or banning all use are the extremes, and 'let Claude be accountable' is not a valid governance posture.

distractorsEs.B: Over-automation: removing the human from a high-impact decision eliminates accountability, not error.
distractorsEs.C: Over-restriction: banning all use wastes legitimate analytical support under human control.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense: a model cannot assume accountability; accountability is human.

questions.trap: B and D delegate the decision/accountability to the model; governance keeps a human in charge.

questions.objective: Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards
questions.scenario: Deadline pressure vs. the conforming path
questions.stem: An associate is under deadline pressure, and the compliant path (getting the data approved) is slower than the non-compliant shortcut. The right choice is to:

options.text: Take the faster non-compliant path, just this once.
Skip the task entirely to avoid the dilemma.
Follow the compliant path even under deadline, and flag the timeline risk to the manager.
Ask Claude to speed up the compliance process.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Follow organizational AI policies and governance standards.' Time pressure doesn't create an exception to the policy; the correct behavior is to comply and surface the timeline risk to the person accountable. C does that. The non-conforming shortcut violates the standard, skipping the task is paralysis, and the model doesn't speed up a governance process.

distractorsEs.A: Rationalization: 'just this once' normalizes the violation; the deadline doesn't authorize non-compliance.
distractorsEs.B: Paralysis: abandoning the task is an overreaction when a conforming path exists, even if it's slower.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense: asking the model to 'speed up compliance' doesn't change the process or the obligation.

questions.trap: A and B are the extremes (violate / abandon); complying and communicating the timeline risk is correct.

questions.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
questions.scenario: Consistently vague output
questions.stem: Claude's output is consistently vague. Before doing anything else, the associate should:

options.text: Blame the model and switch to a different tool.
Add emphasis words like 'very detailed' and 'high quality' to the prompt.
Diagnose the cause — usually a prompt missing context, specifics, or success criteria — and fix that cause.
Ask Claude why its answers are vague and rely on the reason it gives.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs.' Troubleshooting starts with diagnosing the cause: vague output almost always comes from a prompt lacking context, specificity, or success criteria. C fixes that cause. Blaming the model, piling on adjectives, or asking it 'why' diagnoses nothing.

distractorsEs.A: Escape Hatch: switching tools avoids the diagnosis; the problem is usually in the prompt.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: emphatic adjectives ('very detailed') don't supply the missing context.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the 'reason' the model gives is not a reliable diagnosis of its own output.

questions.trap: B disguises noise as improvement; diagnosing the cause (lack of context) is the first step.

questions.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
questions.scenario: A change improved some cases and worsened others
questions.stem: After changing a prompt, results improved for some cases but got worse for others. The right adjustment is to:

options.text: Look at which cases changed and why, and refine the prompt based on that evidence rather than guessing.
Revert the change and never modify the prompt again.
Keep the change regardless, because it is the newer version.
Ask Claude to pick whichever version it prefers.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Adjust approach based on feedback and results.' Adjusting well means being guided by evidence: looking at which cases changed and why, and refining based on that data instead of guessing. A does that. Reverting forever or keeping it because it's 'the new version' are reactions with no evidence, and the model's preference is not the criterion.

distractorsEs.B: Paralysis: swearing never to touch the prompt again gives up on evidence-driven improvement.
distractorsEs.C: Recency bias: 'it's newer' doesn't mean better; it ignores that it made several cases worse.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's 'preference' doesn't evaluate performance case by case.

questions.trap: B and C are extremes with no data; the correct adjustment uses the evidence of which cases changed.

questions.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
questions.scenario: The report omits a required section
questions.stem: Claude keeps omitting a required section from a report. The most likely fixable cause is:

options.text: The model is fundamentally incapable of the task.
The prompt never stated that the section is required; adding that explicit instruction fixes it.
The output font is wrong.
A more expensive model is required.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs.' A systematic omission usually has a simple, fixable cause: the prompt never explicitly asked for that section. B diagnoses and fixes the cause. Declaring the model incapable, blaming the formatting, or raising the tier skip the real diagnosis.

distractorsEs.A: Escape / defeatist: assuming incapacity ignores that the prompt never specified the requirement.
distractorsEs.C: Cosmetic Fix / absurd: the font doesn't explain a missing section.
distractorsEs.D: Maximalism: a more expensive model doesn't add an instruction that was never given.

questions.trap: A and D attribute to capability what is actually a missing instruction; diagnose the prompt first.

questions.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
questions.scenario: Three manual prompts every day
questions.stem: An associate runs the same three prompts by hand every single day. To optimize the workflow, the best step is to:

options.text: Just try to do the same manual steps faster.
Switch to a more expensive model.
Add more manual checkpoints for safety.
Standardize the recurring context (e.g., in a Project) and streamline the repeated steps so they aren't rebuilt from scratch each day.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness.' Optimizing a repetitive workflow means eliminating rework: standardizing the recurring context (a Project) and streamlining the steps that repeat. D attacks the structural inefficiency. Going 'faster by hand,' raising the tier, or adding manual checkpoints don't reduce the rework.

distractorsEs.A: No leverage: rushing by hand doesn't change the fact that the workflow gets rebuilt from scratch every day.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: the model's tier isn't the source of the repetitive inefficiency.
distractorsEs.C: Anti-optimization: more manual steps increase the cost of the workflow; they don't optimize it.

questions.trap: A/B/C don't touch the cause (daily rework); standardizing the context does.

questions.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
questions.scenario: Classifier that fails on ambiguous cases
questions.stem: A classification prompt mislabels the ambiguous cases. The most effective fix is to:

options.text: Add clear category definitions and a few labeled examples of the ambiguous cases to the prompt.
Tell the model 'don't make mistakes.'
Switch to a different platform.
Ask the model to grade its own labels.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs.' Errors on ambiguous cases are fixed by giving the model clear criteria and labeled examples of those edge cases. A resolves the cause (unspecified ambiguity). 'Don't make mistakes' is an empty order, switching platforms evades the issue, and self-grading doesn't fix anything.

distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: 'don't make mistakes' gives no criteria for disambiguating the hard cases.
distractorsEs.C: Escape Hatch: switching platforms doesn't supply the missing definitions.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: having the model grade its own labels doesn't fix the ambiguity in the criteria.

questions.trap: B sounds like a solution but specifies nothing; labeled examples are what disambiguates.

questions.objective: Adjust approach based on feedback and results
questions.scenario: Users report unhelpful answers
questions.stem: Users report that a Claude assistant's answers are unhelpful. The best way to improve it over time is to:

options.text: Ignore the feedback, since users are just picky.
Rebuild the whole assistant from scratch after each complaint.
Collect the feedback, find patterns in the failures, and adjust the prompt and instructions to address those patterns.
Ask Claude whether the users are right.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Adjust approach based on feedback and results.' Continuous improvement relies on feedback: collecting it, finding patterns in the failures, and adjusting the prompt/instructions to address them. C is that cycle. Ignoring the feedback or rebuilding everything after each complaint are the extremes, and asking the model whether the user is right doesn't close the loop.

distractorsEs.A: Dismissal: discarding the feedback throws away the signal that enables improvement.
distractorsEs.B: Overreaction: rebuilding everything for every complaint is inefficient and loses what was actually working.
distractorsEs.D: Circular Self-Verification: the model's opinion about the user is not an analysis of the failures.

questions.trap: A and B are extremes (ignore it / rebuild everything); the correct adjustment finds patterns in the feedback.

questions.objective: Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness
questions.scenario: Top-tier model and a huge prompt for a simple task
questions.stem: A workflow uses the top model and a very long prompt for a simple, high-volume task, and it is slow and costly. Optimizing it means:

options.text: Adding even more instructions to the prompt, just to be safe.
Right-sizing it: a lighter model and a leaner prompt matched to the simple task, verifying that quality still holds.
Running the whole thing twice for reliability.
Leaving it as-is, since it does produce correct output.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Optimize workflows for efficiency and effectiveness.' Optimizing means matching resources to the task's profile: for simple, high-volume work, a lighter model and a leaner prompt reduce cost and latency, while verifying that quality holds up. B does that. Adding more instructions, running it twice, or leaving it alone either worsen or ignore the inefficiency.

distractorsEs.A: Bloat: more instructions lengthen the prompt and needlessly worsen cost/latency.
distractorsEs.C: Waste: duplicating the run doubles the cost on a task that doesn't require it.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut: 'it works' ignores that it's slow and expensive for how simple the task is.

questions.trap: A and C 'sound' like robustness, but they raise the cost; optimizing means right-sizing with a quality check.

questions.objective: Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs
questions.scenario: Got worse after adding several instructions
questions.stem: A prompt that used to work now gives worse results after the associate added several new instructions at once. The first diagnostic step is to:

options.text: Escalate the problem to engineering.
Switch to a different model.
Add still more instructions to compensate.
Isolate the change — remove or revise the newly added instructions to find which one degraded the output.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Identify, diagnose, and resolve issues with underperforming prompts or poor outputs.' When something gets worse after a change, the diagnosis isolates that change: remove or revise the newly added instructions to see which one degraded the result. D does that. Escalating, switching models, or adding more instructions all act before identifying the cause.

distractorsEs.A: Premature: escalating without isolating the change skips the diagnosis the associate can do.
distractorsEs.B: Wrong Lever: the model didn't change; the new instructions did.
distractorsEs.C: Bloat: adding more instructions to an already-degraded prompt tends to make it worse and hides the cause.

questions.trap: A/B/C act without diagnosing; isolating the recent change reveals which instruction broke the output.

certs.name: Claude Certified Developer – Foundations
certs.fee: $125 USD per attempt (the fee shown at checkout reflects the discount that applies to your partner tier; the fee is charged on EVERY attempt)
certs.delivery: Proctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy — delivered by Pearson VUE. When scheduling, you choose between online proctoring or a Pearson VUE test center.
certs.prerequisites: There are no mandatory prerequisites or required courses to sit the exam. The recommended experience (1–5 years in software engineering, ≥6 months of practice with Claude or comparable LLMs, proficiency in Python and/or TypeScript, fluency with REST APIs and CLI tools, understanding of LLM fundamentals, agents, context management, and MCP) is recommended, NOT required. The credential is awarded solely based on exam performance.
certs.languages: The v1.0 exam guide does not state a list of available languages. The exam is administered in English (all items, options, and sample scenarios in the guide are in English). Check language availability when scheduling with Pearson VUE.
certs.audience: Technical professionals who build, integrate, and deploy production AI solutions with LLMs, particularly on Anthropic's Claude platform: AI/ML engineers, technical leads, and senior software engineers who operate at the intersection of business requirements and technical implementation. They typically have one to five years of software engineering experience and at least six months of hands-on experience with Claude or comparable LLM-based systems. They are proficient in Python and/or TypeScript, fluent with REST APIs and command-line (CLI) tools, and understand LLM fundamentals, agents, context management, and MCP (Model Context Protocol).
certs.mqc: The Minimally Qualified Candidate (MQC) is a hands-on profile who builds, integrates, and ships Claude-powered applications, agents, and workflows to production. Their role is to bridge Claude's capabilities with production-ready applications, translating technical requirements into working systems. They have solid foundational knowledge and applied software development skills: they know how to build agents and workflows with the Claude Agent SDK and agentic frameworks, integrate Claude via the API and client SDKs, operate Claude Code for codebase modernization, write effective prompts and apply context engineering, design and run evals, and build custom tools and MCP servers. They understand the tradeoffs of model selection (cost, latency, capability) and tool type (built-in, custom, Skills, MCPs), and know how to apply the right pattern to meet a technical requirement. They are not expected to be experts in distributed systems architecture or model research: they are expected to have implementation competence at the foundations level.
certs.notFor: This certification is NOT aimed at non-technical users or casual users of Claude-based applications, nor at people without hands-on software development experience. It also explicitly excludes roles limited to writing prompts or isolated tasks with no broader responsibility for application development (that is, a pure 'prompt engineer' with no ownership of the application is not the target audience).

domains.title: Agents and Workflows
objectives: Agent Architecture (4.5%) — Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.

Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%) — Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions.

Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%) — Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 14.7%

This domain is the third-heaviest on the exam (≈8 of the 53 items) and measures one single thing with three faces: do you know how to pick the cheapest architecture that solves the problem, and do you know how to build it with the right mechanism? It doesn't measure whether you know the word "agent." It measures whether you can tell when a predefined code path (workflow) is enough and when the model needs to decide its own process at runtime (agent) — and, once that's decided, whether you know what the Claude Agent SDK gives you, what a custom loop over the Messages API gives you, and what an Anthropic-managed deployment gives you.

The business decision behind this is about cost and reliability. Anthropic's official numbers are blunt: an agent consumes roughly 4× more tokens than a chat, and a multi-agent system ~15× more than a chat. The same engineering documentation insists on the cross-cutting rule: "find the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed". A candidate who answers "multi-agent system with subagents" to a problem with three fixed steps is burning 15× the budget to buy non-determinism. That's why the exam systematically rewards picking the right architectural level and punishes over-engineering: every item in this domain is, at bottom, a tradeoff between autonomy (flexibility, the ability to handle the unpredictable) and control (determinism, cost, debuggability, security).

Official Objectives

Agent Architecture (4.5%) — "Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution."

In practice: you'll be given a scenario and have to decide workflow or agent, and, if there's a hierarchy, who the manager/supervisor is and what the system gains by isolating work in subagents.

Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%) — "Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions."

In practice: choosing between Client SDK (custom loop) / Claude Agent SDK / Managed Agents, and knowing that deterministic actions (blocking, auditing, transforming) are implemented with hooks, not with instructions in the prompt.

Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%) — "Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks."

In practice: recognizing the pattern by its signature (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer), managing memory and the context window in long runs, and placing abstraction frameworks as an optional layer over the primitives, not as a substitute for understanding them.

Key Concepts

1. Workflow vs Agent — the definition that decides half a dozen items

Anthropic's official definitions (Building effective agents) are literal and must be memorized:

  • Workflows: "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths".
  • Agents: "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks".

The decision criterion is who writes the execution graph. If you, in code, know the steps ahead of time — extract → validate → summarize → save — it's a workflow, even if you use five calls to Claude, three tools, and two different models. The number of LLMs doesn't turn it into an agent. It's only an agent if the model decides at runtime what to do next, how many steps to take, and which tools to invoke, with feedback from the environment at each step.

The nuance that separates those who really know it: an agent is justified when the number of steps is impossible to predict and you can't hardcode a fixed path. In exchange you pay in latency, tokens, non-determinism, and a failure surface that's harder to debug. Anthropic also recommends transparency (explicitly showing the agent's planning steps) and taking care of the ACI (agent-computer interface): documenting and testing tools with the same rigor you'd use to design an API for humans.

The basic building block behind all of this is the augmented LLM: a model with retrieval, tools, and memory, that generates its own queries, chooses tools, and decides what to retain. Many applications perform better by optimizing a single well-built call (retrieval + examples) than by setting up an agentic system. This is a legitimately correct answer on the exam.

2. The Five Workflow Patterns + the Autonomous Agent

PatternSignature that gives it away in the promptWhat it is
Prompt chaining"the task cleanly decomposes into fixed subtasks"Sequential steps; each LLM processes the previous one's output, with programmatic gates between steps. Trades latency for accuracy.
Routing"distinct categories of input", "easy vs. complex queries"Classify the input and send it to a specialized flow. Lets you route the trivial to a cheap model (Haiku 4.5) and the hard cases to Opus 4.8.
Parallelization"independent subtasks", "multiple perspectives", "several reviews"Two variants: sectioning (independent subtasks in parallel) and voting (the same task run several times for confidence/diversity). Classic guardrail: one instance answers and another filters.
Orchestrator-workers"the subtasks depend on the input", "we don't know in advance how many parts there are"A central LLM dynamically decomposes the task and delegates to workers, then synthesizes.
Evaluator-optimizer"clear evaluation criteria", "iterative refinement produces measurable improvement"One LLM generates, another evaluates and gives feedback in a loop.
Autonomous agent"impossible to predict the number of steps", "no fixed path"LLM using tools in a loop with feedback from the environment. Requires a clear toolset, sandbox, guardrails, and ground truth.

The fine-grained discriminator the exam loves: parallelization vs orchestrator-workers. In parallelization the subtasks are predefined by you; in orchestrator-workers they're determined by the orchestrator at runtime based on the specific input. If the prompt says "the number and type of subtasks depends on the document that comes in," it's orchestrator-workers. If it says "we always analyze the same three dimensions," it's parallelization.

3. The Tool-Use Loop: the One You Write vs. the One Written for You

There are two levels of abstraction, and the exam distinguishes between them.

(a) Client SDK — you implement the loop. With the Messages API, Claude never executes anything: it emits a tool_use block and returns stop_reason: "tool_use". You execute it and return tool_result. The loop is yours:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

tools = [{
    "name": "get_inventory",
    "description": "Look up current stock for a SKU in the warehouse system. "
                   "Returns quantity on hand and reserved units. Use this before "
                   "confirming any order to the customer.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"sku": {"type": "string", "description": "SKU code, e.g. 'AX-1042'"}},
        "required": ["sku"],
    },
}]

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Do we have 12 units of AX-1042 available?"}]

while True:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools,
        messages=messages,
    )

    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break  # end_turn, max_tokens, refusal...

    tool_results = []
    for block in response.content:
        if block.type == "tool_use":
            try:
                result = run_tool(block.name, block.input)   # tu código
                tool_results.append({
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id,
                    "content": result,
                })
            except Exception as e:
                tool_results.append({
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id,
                    "content": f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}. Retry with a valid SKU.",
                    "is_error": True,   # el error viaja DENTRO de la conversación
                })

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})  # TODOS en un solo mensaje user

Three hard rules the exam turns into distractors: all tool_result blocks go in a single user message; they go first in the content array (text before them → 400); and a tool failure is not an HTTP exception, it's a tool_result with is_error: true inside a 200 response.

(b) Claude Agent SDK — the loop is already written. The Agent SDK (pip install claude-agent-sdk, Python ≥3.10; npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk) packages the same agentic loop, the built-in tools, and the context management that power Claude Code. The documented cycle: receive prompt → evaluate → execute tools → repeat until Claude responds with no tool calls → emit ResultMessage. Each full cycle is a turn.

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage

async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Find and fix the bug causing test failures in the auth module",
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash", "Glob", "Grep"],
            setting_sources=["project"],   # carga CLAUDE.md, skills y hooks del cwd
            max_turns=30,                  # evita un runaway
            effort="high",
        ),
    ):
        if isinstance(message, ResultMessage):
            if message.subtype == "success":
                print(f"Done: {message.result}")
            elif message.subtype == "error_max_turns":
                print(f"Turn limit. Resume {message.session_id} to continue.")

asyncio.run(main())

Exam-relevant details: max_turns counts only turns that use a tool, and by default there is no limit (same for max_budget_usd). The result field only exists when subtype == "success"; on error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, or error_during_execution it's absent, though total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns, and session_id do still arrive. A single-shot query() call emits the error result and then raises an exception; a streaming-input session stays alive.

4. Manager/Supervisor Hierarchies and Subagents

A subagent is an agent with isolated context that the main agent delegates to. Its value isn't "more intelligence" — it's context hygiene. The subagent does the dirty work (reading 30 files, crawling a website, running tests), and only its final message goes back to the parent, typically a distilled summary of 1,000–2,000 tokens. The parent never sees the 200k intermediate tokens.

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    # 'Agent' DEBE estar en allowed_tools o Claude no delegará (pedirá permiso o denegará)
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],
    agents={
        "security-reviewer": AgentDefinition(
            description=(
                "Expert security review specialist. Use PROACTIVELY when auth, "
                "crypto, or input-handling code changes."   # esto decide la delegación
            ),
            prompt="You are a security review specialist. Report findings as a list...",
            tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],   # read-only: radio de acción acotado
            model="sonnet",                    # override barato para el worker
        ),
    },
)

What a subagent inherits: its own system prompt (AgentDefinition.prompt), the Agent tool's prompt, the project's CLAUDE.md (if settingSources loads it), and the tool definitions. What it does NOT inherit: the parent's history, its tool results, its system prompt. "The only channel from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string." If the subagent needs a file path, a stack trace, or a prior decision, you have to put it in that prompt.

Two naming and configuration traps: (1) the subagent tool is called Agent, not Task (renamed in Claude Code v2.1.63), but Task still shows up in the system:init tool list and in permission_denials[].tool_name — check both names when writing matchers; (2) it's the description, not the prompt, that Claude reads to decide when to delegate: an excellent prompt with a vague description produces a subagent that never gets invoked.

On the manager/supervisor hierarchy: Anthropic's production pattern (its multi-agent research system) is orchestrator-worker: "a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel". A lead running Opus 4 with Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed the single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2% in their internal research eval. To delegate well, each subagent needs a clear objective, output format, guidance on tools/sources, and task boundaries, and you have to scale effort to complexity (simple query = 1 agent with 3–10 tool calls; complex research = 10+ subagents). The documented failure modes: spawning too many subagents for trivial queries, continuing to search when there's already enough, and subagents duplicating work because of vague instructions. Multi-agent is a bad idea when every agent needs the same shared context or there are heavy dependencies between subtasks.

6. Hooks: Deterministic Actions (the Muscle of This Domain)

A hook is your own code that runs at points in the agent's lifecycle. It's the mechanism you use to turn a policy ("don't touch .env") into an enforceable control. It's not persuading the model — it's an if in your process.

async def protect_env_files(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    file_path = input_data["tool_input"].get("file_path", "")
    if file_path.split("/")[-1] == ".env":
        return {
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": input_data["hook_event_name"],
                "permissionDecision": "deny",
                "permissionDecisionReason": "Cannot modify .env files",
            }
        }
    return {}   # {} = permitir sin cambios

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="Write|Edit", hooks=[protect_env_files])]}
)

Facts the exam uses: hooks run in your process, not inside the context window → they don't consume context; but they may not fire if the agent hits max_turns (the session ends first). Decision precedence is deny > defer > ask > allow: if any hook returns deny, the operation is blocked. Hooks that match run in parallel, and the order in which they finish is not deterministic. Matchers are unanchored regex except when they're exact names: mcp__memory matches no tool at all — you need mcp__memory__.*. And updatedInput (to rewrite a tool's input) requires permissionDecision: 'allow' or 'ask', and must go inside hookSpecificOutput.

Available events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, PreCompact, PermissionRequest, Notification, among others. Watch out: SessionStart/SessionEnd do not exist as callbacks in the Python SDK (only as shell hooks via settings).

7. Memory and Context-Window Management in Long Runs

The context window does not reset between turns: it accumulates the system prompt, tool definitions, history, inputs, and tool outputs. Anthropic puts it this way: "Context must be treated as a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns" — the phenomenon is called context rot.

Tools of the trade:

  • Automatic compaction: when the context nears the limit, the SDK summarizes the older history and emits a system message with subtype: "compact_boundary". It's customized with instructions in CLAUDE.md, with the PreCompact hook (receives trigger: manual | auto), or by forcing /compact. Official design advice: "start by maximizing recall … then iterate to improve precision".
  • The #1 trap of long-running agents: compaction replaces old messages with a summary, so the initial prompt's instructions can get lost. Persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md, which gets re-injected on every request, not in the first user message.
  • Tool output pruning: the output of a tool that returns 40k tokens of HTML stays in the context forever. Return only high-signal information.
  • Just-in-time retrieval: store lightweight identifiers (file paths, queries, links) and load the data at runtime, instead of preloading everything.
  • Structured note-taking / agentic memory: writing notes that persist outside the context window (memory tool, files).
  • Subagent isolation: the cleanest way to keep 200k tokens of exploration from polluting the main thread.
  • Sessions: continue (resumes the most recent session for the cwd, no need to handle IDs), resume=<session_id> (a specific session), fork_session=True + resume (a new session with a copy of the history; the original stays intact). Trap: resume with a different cwd returns a new, empty session, because the JSONL path is derived from the encoded cwd. And fork branches the conversation, not the filesystem: any files the fork edits are real.
  • Being selective with tools: every definition takes up context on every request. With many MCP servers, the schemas add up.

8. Agentic Abstraction Frameworks (Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI)

The guide names them explicitly as examples of agentic abstraction frameworks. What the exam expects you to know is their role, not their API:

  • LangGraph models the flow as a stateful graph: nodes (steps/LLM/tools), edges (transitions, conditionals), and a shared state. It fits explicit workflows, controlled cycles, checkpoints, and human-in-the-loop.
  • PydanticAI brings typing and validation to the agent↔application contract: inputs and outputs validated with Pydantic models, injected dependencies, verified structured outputs.
  • Strands (AWS) is a model-driven SDK that exposes the agentic loop with tools and sessions across several providers.

The stance the exam rewards is Anthropic's own documented position: frameworks "simplify implementation but create layers of abstraction that obscure the underlying prompts and responses and make debugging harder". Recommendation: start by using the primitive APIs directly; if you do adopt a framework, understand the code underneath it. In an exam item, "adopt LangGraph" is never the correct answer by itself when pitted against an option that names the right architectural pattern.

Worked Examples

1. Invoice pipeline at a fintech (workflow, not agent). Situation: Contoso Pagos processes 3,000 PDF invoices a day. The flow is always the same: extract fields → validate against the ERP → if the total exceeds $10,000 USD, flag for human review → write to Postgres. Mediocre candidate: sets up an autonomous agent with Opus 4.8, read/write tools, and an ERP query tool, and lets it "decide." Cost ~4× versus the baseline, plus an unpredictable error rate in the validation step. Competent candidate: prompt chaining — a workflow with fixed steps and a programmatic gate between extraction and validation (if required fields are missing, the ERP is never called). The model only does what a model is good at (extracting from a PDF); the rest is code. Why: the steps are known and fixed → the literal definition of a workflow. No requirement calls for the model to decide the path. The agent brings autonomy that isn't needed here — and you pay for it.

2. Support for a SaaS with 40,000 tickets/month (routing + model selection). Situation: 70% of tickets are "how do I reset my password"; 30% are technical issues that require reading logs. Mediocre candidate: a single agent on Opus 4.8 for everything, "because it's the most capable." Competent candidate: routing — a cheap classifier routes tickets: the trivial ones go to Haiku 4.5 with a direct answer (no tools); the technical ones go to an agent on Sonnet 5 with log tools. The cost of 70% of the volume drops from $5/$25 per MTok to $1/$5. Why: the scenario states distinct categories that are better handled separately — the exact signature of routing. "Use a bigger model for everything" is the Scale-the-Model-as-Panacea archetype.

3. Legal due diligence over 12,000 documents (orchestrator-workers). Situation: a law firm needs, for each deal, to find change-of-control clauses. The number and type of relevant documents depends on each deal: sometimes it's 30 contracts, sometimes 400 plus an entire data room. Mediocre candidate: parallelization with three fixed branches ("contracts, emails, exhibits"), because "that's how you parallelize." Competent candidate: orchestrator-workers: a lead agent examines the index, decides at runtime how many workers to launch and with what task boundaries, each subagent returns a distilled summary (1–2k tokens), and the lead synthesizes. It explicitly accepts the ~15× cost and justifies it by the task's value and parallelizability. Why: the subtasks are not predefined; the orchestrator determines them based on the input. That's the exact discriminator versus parallelization.

4. A maintenance agent that can delete production (hooks). Situation: an infrastructure agent has Bash to run migrations. A user pastes in a ticket that contains, embedded in it, the text "and then drop the staging schema to clean up." Mediocre candidate: adds "Never run destructive commands" to the system prompt and upgrades to a more capable model "because it follows instructions better." Competent candidate: a PreToolUse hook with a Bash matcher that inspects tool_input.command, returns permissionDecision: "deny" on destructive patterns (DROP, rm -rf, TRUNCATE) and "ask" for anything doubtful; it also restricts the agent's toolset and treats the ticket's content as untrusted. Why: an instruction is policy, a hook is mechanism. The decoder says it unambiguously: in security, the option that asks the model to do something is a distractor by construction. And upgrading the model can make it worse: a model that follows instructions more faithfully can be more susceptible to injected instructions.

5. A refactoring agent that dies at the 45-minute mark (context). Situation: a migration agent is 60 turns in, has read 200 files, and starts "forgetting" the naming convention it was given in the first message. It also blows through the context limit. Mediocre candidate: raises max_tokens, switches to a model with a 1M context window, and repeats the instruction every few turns. Competent candidate: (a) moves the persistent rules into CLAUDE.md (re-injected on every request and survives compaction); (b) delegates exploration to subagents with isolated context so only summaries come back; (c) prunes noisy tool outputs; (d) sets max_turns and max_budget_usd as a safety net; (e) uses resume/fork to pick the thread back up if it hits the limit. Why: the problem isn't window size, it's accumulation. Widening the window only delays context rot; compaction was already going to erase the initial prompt anyway.

How the Exam Asks This

Verbs and superlatives in the prompt. You'll see "Which approach best fits…", "Which architecture should the team choose…", "What is the most appropriate pattern…", "Which mechanism ensures…". The superlative is a signal that more than one option is technically true: you're looking for the best one, not the only one.

Signals that point to this domain in the first 10 seconds: "workflow versus agent", "supervisor", "manager hierarchy", "multi-step", "the number of steps cannot be predicted", "subagent", "tool-use loop", "deterministic action before the tool runs", "self-hosted vs. hosted agent".

Typical D1 distractors, with their decoder name:

  • Scale-the-Model-as-Panacea: "use Opus 4.8 instead of Sonnet 5 to make the agent more reliable." If the problem is architectural (wrong workflow choice, contaminated context, missing guardrail), switching models doesn't touch it.
  • Control by Good Manners: "add to the system prompt that it shouldn't run destructive commands." Correct mechanism: a PreToolUse hook with deny.
  • The Plausible Micro-optimization: "reduce the agent's max_tokens to cut cost." It's true that it lowers cost, and it's insufficient (and risks truncation). If the scenario says the cost spiked because of multi-agent use, the lever is the architecture (was multi-agent even needed?), not a parameter.
  • The Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: "use subagents, since they inherit the main agent's history and so don't repeat work." The subordinate clause is false: the subagent sees nothing from the parent except the Agent tool's prompt. Read every since/because/which as a factual claim to verify.
  • Optimizing the Wrong Variable: the scenario says "the task can take hours and there's no latency pressure," and the option proposes aggressively parallelizing with 10 subagents "to finish sooner" — spending 15× the tokens to buy slack you were already given for free.
  • Over-engineering as the Answer: "adopt an agentic framework (LangGraph) to orchestrate the three steps." Three fixed steps = a workflow implemented in code. The official rule is start with the simplest thing.

The structural pattern of the correct answer: it names the right layer (workflow vs agent; hook vs instruction; subagent vs single context) and it's usually the most complete option — the one that mentions separation of concerns (e.g., "a lead agent that decomposes at runtime and subagents with isolated context that return summaries"). Use this only to break a tie between two finalists.

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling anything that makes several LLM calls an "agent." Fix: if the path lives in your code, it's a workflow, even if it uses five models. Agent = the LLM dynamically directs its own process.
  2. Defaulting to multi-agent. Fix: ~15× the tokens of a chat. Only justified for a task that's high-value and parallelizable. It's a bad idea if every agent needs the same context or there are strong dependencies between subtasks.
  3. Confusing parallelization with orchestrator-workers. Fix: predefined by you = parallelization; determined by the orchestrator at runtime = orchestrator-workers.
  4. Believing the subagent inherits the parent's context. Fix: it inherits no history, no tool results, and no system prompt from the parent. "The only channel from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string."
  5. Writing an AgentDefinition with a brilliant prompt and a vague description. Fix: it's the description that Claude uses to decide when to delegate. With a poor description, the subagent never gets invoked.
  6. Forgetting Agent in allowed_tools. Fix: without it, Claude doesn't delegate (it asks for permission, or denies in dontAsk mode). It's the #1 cause of "Claude is ignoring my subagent."
  7. Writing a hook with a Task (or mcp__memory) matcher. Fix: the subagent tool has been called Agent since v2.1.63 (though Task persists in system:init and in permission_denials); and matchers are unanchored regex: use mcp__memory__.*.
  8. Putting persistent rules in the first user message. Fix: compaction erases them. They belong in CLAUDE.md, which gets re-injected on every request.
  9. Reading message.result without checking subtype. Fix: result only exists when subtype == "success". On error_max_turns it's absent.
  10. Assuming max_turns counts messages or tokens, and that there's a default limit. Fix: it counts only turns that use a tool, and by default there is no limit (same for max_budget_usd). An agent with no limits is an agent that can drain your account.
  11. Trusting that a hook always runs. Fix: if the agent hits max_turns, the session ends and hooks may not fire. A guardrail can't rely solely on the hook if the failure mode is early termination.
  12. Returning tool_result blocks in separate user messages (in a custom loop). Fix: they all go in a single user message, and before any text block. Splitting them up "teaches" Claude to stop parallelizing.
  13. Believing resume picks the session back up even if you change directories. Fix: the JSONL path is derived from the encoded cwd; with a different cwd you get a new, empty session.
  14. Thinking the Agent SDK's default systemPrompt is the same as Claude Code's. Fix: the default is minimal (it covers tool calling, but omits the coding guidelines and project context). claude -p does use the full prompt. To replicate it: systemPrompt: { type: "preset", preset: "claude_code", append: "..." }.
  15. Substituting a framework for actual design. Fix: frameworks hide prompts and responses and complicate debugging. Start with the primitives; adopt abstraction once the value is measurable.

Checklist

If you can't check off all of them, you don't yet own this domain.

  • I can recite the official definitions of workflow and agent and apply the "who decides the path?" criterion to a new scenario.
  • I can name the five patterns (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) and state in one sentence when to choose each one.
  • I can distinguish parallelization from orchestrator-workers based on whether the subtasks are predefined or decided at runtime.
  • I know how to write my own tool-use loop over the Messages API (while stop_reason == "tool_use"), with all tool_result blocks in a single user message and errors as is_error: true.
  • I can justify when to use Client SDK vs Claude Agent SDK vs Managed Agents in terms of where the loop runs and where the state lives.
  • I know what a subagent inherits and what it does not inherit, and why the only parent→subagent channel is the Agent tool's prompt.
  • I know that Agent must be in allowed_tools and that the description is what triggers delegation.
  • I can explain why a hook is a control and a line in the system prompt is not, and I know the deny > defer > ask > allow precedence.
  • I know that hooks don't consume context but may not fire when the run hits max_turns.
  • I know how compaction can erase instructions from the initial prompt and why persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md.
  • I can list at least four context-management techniques: subagents, tool-output pruning, just-in-time retrieval, structured note-taking, compaction.
  • I know that max_turns counts only turns that use a tool, and that by default there is no limit (neither on turns nor on budget).
  • I can estimate the relative cost: agent ≈ 4× a chat; multi-agent ≈ 15×; and I know when that is not justified.
  • I know what Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI are, and why the official docs recommend starting with the primitives before adopting a framework.
  • When facing an item, I identify the distractor archetype first (scaling the model, control by good manners, micro-optimization, falsehood in the subordinate clause) before choosing an answer.
