domains.title: Claude Code
objectives: Claude Code Operation (3.1%) — Claude Code core components (Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory), features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode), the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration.
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 3.1%

This is the smallest domain on the exam, tied with Debugging: 3.1% of 53 items is one or two items. It has a single skill (Claude Code Operation), and its syllabus fits in one sentence: know which Claude Code mechanism solves which problem, where its configuration lives, and who wins when two configurations collide. You won't be asked to recite flags: you'll be asked to choose between putting a convention in CLAUDE.md, a rule with paths, a skill, a subagent, a hook, or a deny rule — and that choice is a decision about operational architecture, not syntax.

The real weight is deceptively higher than 3.1%. CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model pinning, and plugin dependencies all reappear in D2 · Configuration Management (4.1%); hooks reappear in D7 · Claude Hooks (1.0%) as the executable part of almost every security answer; CLAUDE.md and subagents reappear in D6 · Context Engineering (3.8%) as levers against context bloat; and interpreting instructions across interfaces (Claude Code vs Desktop vs claude.ai vs API) lives in D2 · Claude Application Design (8.6%). A candidate who has mastered Claude Code scores points across four domains. The business decision it represents: Claude Code is the MQC's codebase-modernization tool, and a codebase-modernization operation without deterministic enforcement (hooks, deny rules, managed settings) is an operation that hands a probabilistic model the power to break production.

Official Objectives

Claude Code Operation (3.1%) — "Claude Code core components (Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory), features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode), the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration."

This is the domain's only task statement. Broken down into what you'll actually be asked:

  • Core components: Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory

    In practice: given a problem ("Claude keeps forgetting the convention", "I paste the same playbook every week", "search logs are flooding the conversation", "this must NEVER happen"), pick the right mechanism and know that Commands ≡ Skills (they merged) and that Agent Memory ≠ CLAUDE.md.

  • Session management

    In practice: telling apart /clear vs /compact vs /rewind vs --continue vs --resume, and knowing that sessions resolve per directory: resuming from a different cwd does not return your history.

  • Built-in and custom slash commands

    In practice: recognizing which built-in command solves the task (/init, /context, /permissions, /agents, /mcp, /memory, /plan) and knowing that a custom command is declared with a file, and that its name comes from the path, not from the name frontmatter.

  • Headless mode and streaming mode

    In practice: setting up Claude Code in CI (claude -p) in a reproducible way (--bare), with bounded permissions and parseable output (--output-format json + --json-schema → structured_output; stream-json for live tokens).

  • Auto-mode

    In practice: placing auto in the permission-modes table (everything runs, with a background safety classifier) against default/plan/acceptEdits/dontAsk/bypassPermissions, and knowing when NOT to use it.

  • CLAUDE.md hierarchy

    In practice: the 4 locations, the load order, that they concatenate (rather than overwrite each other), that @ imports do not save context, and that CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement.

  • Repository initialization

    In practice: /init generates the project's CLAUDE.md; what should and should NOT go in it (<200 lines, conventions, no secrets, no long procedures → those go into skills).

  • settings.json configuration

    In practice: locations, precedence (managed beats even CLI flags), and the permission-evaluation order deny → ask → allow, where specificity does not change that order.

Key Concepts

1. The Axis That Organizes the Whole Domain: Context vs. Enforcement

Claude Code is extended through seven mechanisms. They differ in when they load into context, who invokes them, and — the decisive factor for the exam — whether they suggest or whether they enforce.

MechanismWhen does it load?Who invokes it?Nature
CLAUDE.mdEvery session, in fullNobody: it's always thereContext (suggests)
.claude/rules/ with pathsWhen Claude touches files that matchNobody: it fires on its ownContext (suggests)
Agent Memory (auto memory)MEMORY.md at startup (capped); topic files, on demandClaude writes itContext (suggests)
Skills (= custom commands)Only the description; the body when invokedYou (/skill) or ClaudeContext (suggests)
Subagents (Agents)Their own isolated contextClaude or youIsolated context
HooksDon't consume context: run outside the loopThe lifecycleEnforcement (enforces)
settings.json (permissions)Doesn't enter contextThe client, not the modelEnforcement (enforces)

The line from the official docs that sums up the domain, and that the exam turns into an item: "An instruction like 'never edit .env' in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee. A PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement." Golden rule: settings for technical enforcement, CLAUDE.md for behavioral guidance.

And the escalation trigger, also official: Claude gets a convention wrong twice → CLAUDE.md. You write the same prompt over and over → skill. A side task is flooding the conversation → subagent. You want something to always happen without asking → hook. A second repo needs the same setup → plugin.

2. The CLAUDE.md Hierarchy

Four locations, listed in load order, from broadest to most specific scope (the project instruction enters context AFTER the user's):

  1. Managed policy (organization-wide, cannot be excluded): macOS /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md · Linux/WSL /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md · Windows C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md.
  2. User instructions: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — all of your projects, just you.
  3. Project instructions: ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md — shared through version control.
  4. Local instructions: ./CLAUDE.local.md — personal, goes into .gitignore. It is not deprecated.

Mechanics that separate those who really know it:

  • Claude walks up the directory tree from the cwd; every file it finds gets concatenated, not overwritten. Within a directory, CLAUDE.local.md gets appended after CLAUDE.md.
  • CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the cwd do not load at startup: they come in on demand, when Claude reads files from that subdirectory.
  • It's delivered as a user message AFTER the system prompt. That's why there's no guarantee of strict compliance: it's context, not configuration.
  • After /compact, the project root's CLAUDE.md gets re-injected (Claude rereads it from disk). Nested ones do not. Practical corollary for long-running agents: persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md, not the initial prompt, because compaction replaces old messages with a summary.
  • Target size: under 200 lines. Block HTML comments (<!-- ... -->) are stripped before injection (they don't cost tokens).
  • Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, not AGENTS.md. To reuse AGENTS.md: import it.
@AGENTS.md

# Convenciones del repo
- Usa pnpm, nunca npm.
- Los tests corren con `pnpm test -- --run`.
- Nunca edites archivos bajo `db/migrations/` sin pedir confirmación.

Ver @docs/git-instructions.md para el flujo de ramas.

@path imports do NOT save context: imported files load anyway at startup. Paths are relative to the importing file, not to the cwd. Maximum depth: 4 hops. The parser ignores code spans: `@README` inside backticks is literal text; @README outside backticks imports the file.

3. Rules (.claude/rules/) — the Mechanism That Actually Saves Context

.md files discovered recursively. Without paths frontmatter, they load at startup with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md. With paths (globs), they enter context only when Claude reads a file that matches.

---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---

# API Development Rules
- Todo endpoint valida su input antes de tocar la base de datos.
- Usa el formato estándar de error `{ code, message, requestId }`.
- Documenta con comentarios OpenAPI.

User rules (~/.claude/rules/) load before project ones, so project rules take priority.

4. Agent Memory (Auto Memory) — It's Not CLAUDE.md

CLAUDE.mdAgent Memory
Who writes itYouClaude
Where it lives~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ./CLAUDE.md…~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/
How much loadsFull, regardless of lengthFirst 200 lines of MEMORY.md, or 25 KB, whichever comes first
Topic files—Don't load at startup; read on demand
Turning it offDelete itautoMemoryEnabled: false or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1

On by default since Claude Code v2.1.59. The 200-line / 25 KB cap applies only to MEMORY.md.

5. Skills and Commands: They're the Same Thing

"Custom commands have been merged into skills. A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and work the same way."

.claude/commands/*.md still works; skills are the recommended path. If they collide by name, the skill wins.

The command's name does NOT come from the name field — it comes from its location: the directory name in skills/, the file name in commands/. name is the display label. The one exception: a SKILL.md at the root of a plugin, where the frontmatter does take charge.

Skill precedence: enterprise > personal > project. (Yes: personal beats project, the opposite of what almost everyone assumes.)

---
name: pr-summary
description: Summarize changes in a pull request
context: fork          # corre en un subagente con contexto aislado
agent: Explore
allowed-tools: Bash(gh *)   # PRE-APRUEBA, no restringe
---

## Pull request context
- PR diff: !`gh pr diff`
- Changed files: !`gh pr diff --name-only`

## Your task
Summarize this pull request...

Exam nuances:

  • Every !`command` executes before Claude sees anything, and its output replaces the placeholder. It's preprocessing, not a tool call. The substitution runs exactly once: the output isn't re-scanned for more placeholders.
  • allowed-tools pre-approves (it avoids the permission prompt); it does not restrict. To remove tools, use disallowed-tools.
  • disable-model-invocation: true → only you invoke it (Claude doesn't decide to deploy on its own) and its description doesn't enter context (zero cost until you use it). user-invocable: false → only Claude can, hidden from the / menu.
  • Substitutions: $ARGUMENTS, $ARGUMENTS[N] (0-based), $0 (first argument), ${CLAUDE_SESSION_ID}, ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}.
  • Lifecycle: once invoked, the rendered SKILL.md enters as a message and stays for the rest of the session; Claude Code does not reread it on later turns.

6. Agents (Subagents)

Built-in: Explore (read-only), Plan (read-only, used in plan mode), general-purpose.

Explore and Plan skip your CLAUDE.md and the parent's git status so that investigation stays fast and cheap. All other subagents (built-in and custom) load them.

Subagent precedence: managed > --agents (flag) > project > user > plugin. Compare it to skills' precedence: for subagents, project beats user; for skills, personal beats project. That inversion is classic exam-item material.

---
name: code-improver
description: Scans files and suggests improvements. Use after writing or modifying code.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob     # allowlist; si se omite, HEREDA TODAS
model: sonnet               # default real: `inherit`
---

You are a code improvement specialist...

The markdown body is the subagent's system prompt: it does not receive Claude Code's full system prompt. model defaults to inherit (the main conversation's model), not sonnet.

7. Session Management

ActionWhat it does
/clearA new conversation with empty context. It doesn't summarize: it discards.
/compactSummarizes the history to free up context. Re-injects the root CLAUDE.md.
/rewindRolls the conversation and/or the code back to an earlier point.
/resumeResumes a conversation by ID or name.
/contextShows current context usage (where the budget is going).
--continueResumes the most recent session for the current directory (no need to handle IDs).
--resume <id>Resumes a specific session by ID.
forkA new session with a copy of the history; the original stays intact.

Operational trap: sessions are stored at ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl, where <encoded-cwd> is the absolute cwd with every non-alphanumeric character replaced by -. Session-ID lookup is scoped to the project directory: if you run --resume from a different cwd, you get a new session, not your history. A session persists the conversation, not the filesystem.

8. settings.json: Locations, Precedence, and Permissions

Locations: ~/.claude/settings.json (user) · .claude/settings.json (project, goes into git) · .claude/settings.local.json (local, gitignored) · managed (/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json).

Precedence, highest to lowest:

  1. Managed — cannot be overridden, not even with CLI arguments
  2. Command-line arguments
  3. Local (.claude/settings.local.json)
  4. Project (.claude/settings.json)
  5. User (~/.claude/settings.json)

Exception: permission rules merge across scopes instead of overriding each other.

Permission evaluation: deny → ask → allow. The first match in that order decides, and specificity does NOT change the order: a broad deny like Bash(aws *) blocks even what a more specific allow (Bash(aws s3 ls)) would permit. A deny rule admits no allowlist exceptions.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run lint)", "Bash(npm run test *)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(npm run build)"],
    "deny":  ["Bash(curl *)", "Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Read(./secrets/**)"],
    "additionalDirectories": ["/var/log"],
    "defaultMode": "plan"
  }
}

High-yield exam nuances:

  • Bare name vs. specifier in deny: Bash (bare) removes the tool from Claude's context entirely — it never sees it. Bash(rm *) leaves the tool available and blocks only what matches.
  • Read/Edit patterns follow the gitignore spec: //path = absolute from the filesystem root; ~/path = home; /path = relative to the settings source (not the root!); path = relative to the current directory. In other words, Read(/Users/alice/secrets) is not an absolute path.
  • The space before * matters: Bash(ls *) does not match lsof; Bash(ls*) does. And the rules are aware of shell operators: Bash(safe-cmd *) does not authorize safe-cmd && rm -rf . — each subcommand is matched separately.
  • Wrappers get stripped before matching: timeout, time, nice, nohup, stdbuf. npx, docker exec, devbox run are not on that list → a Bash(devbox run *) rule implicitly authorizes devbox run rm -rf ..
  • Protected paths: writes to .git, .claude (except .claude/worktrees), .vscode, .idea, and files like .mcp.json, .zshrc, .npmrc… are never auto-approved except under bypassPermissions. permissions.allow does not pre-approve them: the safety check runs before the allow rules are evaluated.
  • Hooks vs. permissions: a hook's decision cannot bypass a deny (it still blocks). But a hook with exit 2 does stop the call before the allow rules are evaluated.

9. Permission Modes (Including Auto-Mode) and Plan Mode

ModeWhat runs without askingWhen
default (labeled "Manual")Reads onlySensitive work
acceptEditsReads + edits + FS commands (mkdir, mv, cp…) in the working dirIterating on code you're reviewing
planReads onlyExploring before changing anything
autoEverything, with a background safety classifierLong-running tasks
dontAskOnly pre-approved tools; auto-denies the restCI / closed scripts
bypassPermissionsEverythingOnly isolated containers/VMs

Plan mode: Claude reads files and runs read-only shell commands and writes a plan, but does not edit source code; permission prompts still apply. You enter it with Shift+Tab, /plan, or claude --permission-mode plan. Approving the plan exits plan mode.

Auto-mode, two facts almost nobody knows: on entry, broad allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution get discarded (Bash(*), wildcard interpreters, Agent rules), and they're restored on exit. And inside -p, if the classifier blocks repeatedly, the session aborts — there's no human to ask.

10. Headless Mode and Streaming Mode (claude -p)

# CI reproducible: --bare ignora hooks/skills/plugins/MCP/CLAUDE.md locales
claude --bare -p "Summarize this file" --allowedTools "Read"

# Salida estructurada validada por schema → campo `structured_output`
claude -p "Extract the main function names from auth.py" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"functions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["functions"]}' \
  | jq '.structured_output'

# Streaming mode: tokens en vivo (requiere --verbose Y --include-partial-messages)
claude -p "Explain recursion" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages

# Encadenar sesiones (mismo directorio, o el ID no se encuentra)
session_id=$(claude -p "Start a review" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
claude -p "Continue that review" --resume "$session_id"
  • --output-format: text (default) | json | stream-json (NDJSON, one event per line).
  • --bare skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md. It's the answer to "the pipeline produces different results depending on the machine." The docs recommend it for CI/SDK and announce it will become -p's default. In bare mode, auth has to come from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or from an apiKeyHelper passed via --settings.
  • Without --bare, claude -p loads the same configuration as an interactive session — including a hook a teammate happens to have in their ~/.claude.
  • The --output-format json payload carries result, session_id, total_cost_usd, and a per-model cost breakdown → it's the official way to track cost per invocation in scripts.
  • User-invocable skills and commands do work in -p: you include /skill-name in the prompt string. Commands that only run in a terminal (e.g. /login) don't.
  • Piped stdin is capped at 10 MB.

11. Repository Initialization and Built-in Commands

/init initializes the project by generating a CLAUDE.md. What should go in it: stable, short conventions (package manager, test command, structure, prohibitions). What should not: secrets, long multi-step procedures (→ skill), rules that only apply to one folder (→ .claude/rules/ with paths), security guarantees (→ hook or deny).

Built-in commands worth having mapped out: /init, /clear, /compact, /context, /memory, /agents, /skills, /mcp, /permissions, /hooks, /plugin, /model, /effort, /plan, /rewind, /resume, /rename, /export, /usage (alias /cost), /review, /security-review, /config, /add-dir.

12. MCP Inside Claude Code (the Minimum This Domain Touches)

Scopes: local (default, this project only, stored in ~/.claude.json — not in .claude/settings.local.json), project (.mcp.json at the root, goes into git), user (all of your projects). Precedence: local > project > user > plugin > claude.ai connectors. Servers from .mcp.json require explicit approval for security.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "api-server": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "${API_BASE_URL:-https://api.example.com}/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${API_KEY}" }
    }
  }
}

An entry with url but no type is a configuration error: Claude Code reads it as stdio and skips it.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — "Claude Keeps Touching .env in the Payments Repo"

Situation. A 6-person team on a billing service. Twice this week, Claude edited .env.staging during refactors. The tech lead asks to "make sure it never happens again."

Mediocre candidate. Adds to CLAUDE.md: "NEVER edit .env files. This is critical!!!" In all caps, with three exclamation points.

Competent candidate. Two layers, both enforceable:

{ "permissions": { "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.*)", "Edit(./.env*)"] } }

and, if they also want to audit the attempts, a PreToolUse hook with an Edit|Write matcher that returns permissionDecision: "deny" (exit 0 + JSON) or that exits with exit 2.

Why. CLAUDE.md is delivered as a user message after the system prompt: it's a request, not a guarantee. Deny rules are evaluated by the client, not the model, and they're evaluated first (deny → ask → allow), from any scope and in every permission mode. This is the decoder's Control by Good Manners archetype, wearing Claude Code's clothes.

Example 2 — The CI Pipeline That "Works on My Machine"

Situation. A GitHub Actions job runs claude -p "review the diff and output findings" and fails intermittently: sometimes it takes 4 minutes, sometimes it tries to call a Notion MCP server nobody configured on the runner, and sometimes the output isn't parseable.

Mediocre candidate. Raises the job's timeout and wraps json.loads() in a try/except.

Competent candidate.

claude --bare -p "Review the staged diff" \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Bash(git diff *)" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"findings":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}},"required":["findings"]}' \
  | jq '.structured_output.findings'

Why. The root cause isn't the timeout: it's that -p without --bare loads the same configuration as an interactive session (hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md from both the working dir and ~/.claude). --bare removes that source of non-determinism; dontAsk denies anything not pre-approved instead of hanging while it waits for a human who doesn't exist; --json-schema returns validated structured_output instead of text you have to guess how to parse.

Example 3 — The 900-Line CLAUDE.md

Situation. A monorepo with web (Next.js), API (Go), and infra (Terraform). CLAUDE.md grew to 900 lines: React conventions, API rules, Terraform policies, the deployment runbook, and a migrations guide. Every session starts with the context already half full.

Mediocre candidate. Splits the file into five and imports them with @docs/react.md, @docs/api.md… "so it doesn't load everything."

Competent candidate.

  • Short, global conventions (10–20 lines) → stay in CLAUDE.md.
  • React / API / Terraform rules → .claude/rules/react.md with paths: ["apps/web/**/*.tsx"], .claude/rules/api.md with paths: ["services/api/**/*.go"], etc.
  • The deployment runbook → skill .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md with disable-model-invocation: true.
  • The migrations guide → a skill Claude can invoke (user-invocable: false).

Why. @ imports do not save context: imported files load anyway at startup. What saves context is loading on demand: paths in rules (loads in only when Claude touches those files) and skills (only the description is ever in context; the body loads on invocation). And disable-model-invocation: true additionally pulls the description out of context: zero cost until you actually trigger the deploy.

Example 4 — The Skill That Doesn't Show Up Under the Expected Name

Situation. A dev creates .claude/skills/deploy-staging/SKILL.md with name: deploy in the frontmatter. The / menu shows /deploy-staging, not /deploy. Meanwhile, a teammate reports that their personal /review "stomps on" the project's /review, and that the project's reviewer subagent does win over their personal one.

Mediocre candidate. Concludes there's a bug and starts randomly renaming files.

Competent candidate. Knows three things: (1) the command's name comes from the directory, not the name frontmatter (which is just a display label); (2) skills: enterprise > personal > project — the personal skill does beat the project's; (3) subagents: managed > --agents > project > user > plugin — there, the project does beat the user's. The two precedence orders are inverted relative to each other, and that's not a bug: it's the design.

Example 5 — The Script That "Loses" the Session

Situation. A release script captures the session_id from a claude -p launched from /repo, and then, from /repo/packages/api, runs claude -p "continue" --resume "$session_id". Claude responds as if it knows nothing about the prior context.

Mediocre candidate. Blames compaction and raises --max-turns.

Competent candidate. Runs both commands from the same directory. Sessions live at ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<session-id>.jsonl, and ID lookup is scoped to the project directory: if the cwd doesn't match, resume gives you back a new session, not an error. A silent failure is worse than an exception — that's exactly why it's exam material.

How the Exam Asks This

Item format. A short scenario with a role ("a team", "a developer", "an org security lead") + a stated constraint + Which approach best fits? / Which configuration ensures…? / What is the most reliable way to…?. The superlatives are a warning that more than one option will be technically true.

Signals that trigger this domain (from the decoder): CLAUDE.md, settings.json, slash command, headless mode, repository initialization, session, subagent, hook, permission mode. Watch out: if the item's axis is versioning / model pinning / plugin dependencies, the item belongs to D2 · Configuration Management, even if it mentions settings.json. If the axis is preventing a destructive action, it's D7 · Claude Hooks. The correct answer is usually the same; the domain it counts against is not.

The four item molds that repeat most often:

  1. "Guarantee vs. request". "A team wants to ensure Claude never runs terraform apply in the repo. Which approach is most reliable?" → the deny rule / PreToolUse hook wins; "add an instruction to CLAUDE.md" loses (Control by Good Manners).
  2. "CI reproducibility". "A CI job produces different results on different machines." → --bare (+ dontAsk + allowlist) wins; "increase the timeout" (Plausible Micro-optimization) and "switch to a larger model" (Scale-the-Model-as-Panacea) lose.
  3. "Context that keeps inflating". "The project's CLAUDE.md has grown to hundreds of lines and every session starts with a large context." → moving to .claude/rules/ with paths, or to skills, wins; "split it into @ imports" loses — and watch out, that distractor comes with the Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: "…since imported files are only loaded when needed". That's false. They load at startup.
  4. "Precedence". "A managed settings file sets permissions.deny. A developer passes an allow flag on the command line. What happens?" → managed wins, even over CLI flags. Sibling variant: specific allow vs. broad deny → the deny wins (specificity doesn't change the deny → ask → allow order).

Distractors specific to this domain, on top of the decoder's general ones:

  • The precedence inversion. The item tells you "project" or "personal" and the correct option depends on the mechanism. Skills: personal > project. Subagents: project > user. MCP: local > project > user.
  • The capability attributed to the wrong mechanism. "Use allowed-tools in the skill to restrict which tools Claude can use." False: allowed-tools pre-approves; the one that restricts is disallowed-tools (or tools on a subagent, or a deny rule).
  • Plan mode turned absolute. "Plan mode prevents Claude from running any command." False: plan mode allows reads and read-only shell commands; what it doesn't allow is editing source code. (Degrading Absolutism archetype.)
  • False interchangeables. /clear ≠ /compact. A hook with exit 2 ≠ a hook that returns decision JSON. CLAUDE.md ≠ Agent Memory. Custom command ≠ a mechanism distinct from a skill.

Time strategy. 1–2 items. Don't invest weeks: memorize the three precedence tables, the deny → ask → allow order, the permission-modes table, and the five headless flags (-p, --bare, --output-format, --json-schema, --permission-mode). That covers practically everything this domain can ask you — and it scores you points in D2, D6, and D7 along the way.

Common Mistakes

  1. "Custom slash commands are a mechanism distinct from skills." ❌ They merged. .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both produce /deploy. If they collide, the skill wins.
  2. "The name frontmatter defines the command's name." ❌ It comes from the directory name (or the file name, in commands/). name is a display label. The one exception: SKILL.md at the root of a plugin.
  3. "Project always beats user." ❌ Skills: enterprise > personal > project. Subagents: managed > --agents > project > user > plugin. MCP: local > project > user. They're inverted relative to each other.
  4. "Putting the rule in CLAUDE.md guarantees the behavior." ❌ It's delivered as a user message after the system prompt: it's context, not enforced configuration. To actually guarantee it: a PreToolUse hook or permissions.deny.
  5. "Splitting CLAUDE.md into @ imports saves context." ❌ Imported files load anyway at startup. What saves context is .claude/rules/ with paths, or moving the content into skills.
  6. "allowed-tools in a skill restricts Claude's tools." ❌ It pre-approves (avoids the prompt). It removes nothing from the pool. To restrict: disallowed-tools.
  7. "A more specific allow beats a broader deny." ❌ The order deny → ask → allow is fixed; specificity doesn't change it. Bash(aws *) in deny blocks Bash(aws s3 ls) even if it's in allow.
  8. "Read(/Users/alice/secrets) is an absolute path." ❌ A single slash anchors at the settings source. Absolute requires a double slash: //Users/alice/secrets.
  9. "Bash(ls*) and Bash(ls *) are equivalent." ❌ The space enforces a word boundary: Bash(ls *) does not match lsof; Bash(ls*) does. And no Bash(x *) rule authorizes x && some-other-command.
  10. "claude -p in CI only uses what I pass via flags." ❌ Without --bare it loads hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, auto memory, and CLAUDE.md just like an interactive session.
  11. "Exit 2 in a hook and returning JSON are interchangeable." ❌ With exit 2, stdout and all JSON are ignored. Decision JSON is only processed on exit 0.
  12. "Auto memory and CLAUDE.md are the same thing." ❌ You write CLAUDE.md and it loads in full; Claude writes auto memory, and only the first 200 lines / 25 KB of MEMORY.md load.
  13. "Subagents always inherit CLAUDE.md." ❌ Explore and Plan skip it (and the git status too). The rest load it.
  14. "A subagent's default model is Sonnet." ❌ The default is inherit: the main conversation's model.
  15. "Managed settings can be overridden with a CLI flag." ❌ Managed is priority 1, above CLI arguments.
  16. "permissions.allow can pre-approve writes to .git or .claude." ❌ They're protected paths: the check runs before the allow rules. Only bypassPermissions allows them.

Checklist

If you can't check a box, you don't yet own this domain.

  1. I can list the 4 CLAUDE.md locations in load order and explain that they concatenate, not overwrite.
  2. I can explain why CLAUDE.md does not guarantee a behavior, and name the two mechanisms that do guarantee it (PreToolUse hook, permissions.deny).
  3. I know that @ imports do not save context, and I can name the two mechanisms that do (.claude/rules/ with paths; skills).
  4. I can distinguish Agent Memory from CLAUDE.md by author, location, and how much loads (200 lines / 25 KB of MEMORY.md).
  5. I know that custom commands and skills merged, and that the command's name comes from the directory, not the name frontmatter.
  6. I can recite the three precedence orders: skills (enterprise > personal > project), subagents (managed > --agents > project > user > plugin), MCP (local > project > user).
  7. I know the difference between allowed-tools (pre-approves) and disallowed-tools / tools (restrict).
  8. I know which built-in subagents exist and which ones skip CLAUDE.md (Explore and Plan).
  9. I can explain settings.json precedence and that managed beats even CLI flags.
  10. I can apply the deny → ask → allow order and explain why specificity doesn't change it.
  11. I know the permission-syntax traps: // for absolute paths, the space before *, the wrappers that do get stripped (timeout, nice…), and the ones that don't (npx, docker exec, devbox run).
  12. I can pick the right permission mode for a given case (closed CI → dontAsk; exploring → plan; long supervised task → auto; isolated container → bypassPermissions).
  13. I know how to set up a reproducible claude -p in CI: --bare + --permission-mode dontAsk + --allowedTools + --output-format json --json-schema, and read structured_output.
  14. I know how to turn on streaming mode (--output-format stream-json + --verbose + --include-partial-messages) and why it needs all three flags.
  15. I can distinguish /clear, /compact, /rewind, --continue, and --resume, and explain why a --resume from a different cwd returns a new session.
  16. I know what should go in the CLAUDE.md that /init generates (<200 lines of conventions) and what should migrate to rules, skills, hooks, or deny rules.

A `/name` defined by a file; **merged with skills**; its name comes from the path, not the frontmatter.
A skill Claude Code ships with out of the box (`/code-review`, `/debug`, `/run`…).
An agent with **its own context window** that returns only its result to the parent.
Memory **Claude writes** to `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`; only 200 lines / 25 KB of `MEMORY.md` load.
A handler that runs on a lifecycle event; **deterministic enforcement**, outside the context window.
An `allow`/`ask`/`deny` entry in `settings.json`, evaluated by the **client** in that order.
The baseline for what runs without asking: `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`.
Reads + read-only shell commands only; produces an approvable plan without editing code.
Everything runs without asking, with a background **safety classifier**; in `-p` it aborts if it blocks repeatedly.
`claude -p`: one prompt, no TUI; the basis for scripts and CI.
Skips auto-discovery of hooks/skills/plugins/MCP/memory/CLAUDE.md → **CI reproducibility**.
`--output-format stream-json` (+ `--verbose` + `--include-partial-messages`): live NDJSON events.
`--json-schema` with `--output-format json` → a validated result in the `structured_output` field.
Conversation history persisted at `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<id>.jsonl`; scoped to the directory.
Summarizes the history to free up context; re-injects the project root's CLAUDE.md.
Generates the project's `CLAUDE.md` with the detected conventions.
Paths (`.git`, `.claude`, `.mcp.json`…) that **never** auto-approve for writes, not even with `allow`.
Organization-wide policy; **priority 1**, not overridable even by CLI flags.
A project's `allow` rules apply only after accepting the trust dialog; `deny`/`ask` don't depend on it.
A package bundling skills + hooks + subagents + MCP servers to reuse the setup in another repo.

checklist: I can list the **4 `CLAUDE.md` locations** in load order and explain that they **concatenate**, not overwrite.
I can explain why `CLAUDE.md` **does not guarantee** a behavior, and name the two mechanisms that **do** guarantee it (`PreToolUse` hook, `permissions.deny`).
I know that **`@` imports do not save context**, and I can name the two mechanisms that do (`.claude/rules/` with `paths`; skills).
I can distinguish **Agent Memory** from `CLAUDE.md` by author, location, and how much loads (200 lines / 25 KB of `MEMORY.md`).
I know that **custom commands and skills merged**, and that the command's name comes from the **directory**, not the `name` frontmatter.
I can recite the **three precedence orders**: skills (enterprise > personal > project), subagents (managed > `--agents` > project > user > plugin), MCP (local > project > user).
I know the difference between **`allowed-tools`** (pre-approves) and **`disallowed-tools`** / `tools` (restrict).
I know which built-in subagents exist and **which ones skip `CLAUDE.md`** (`Explore` and `Plan`).
I can explain `settings.json` precedence and that **managed beats even CLI flags**.
I can apply the **`deny → ask → allow`** order and explain why **specificity doesn't change it**.

I know the permission-syntax traps: `//` for absolute paths, the **space before `*`**, the wrappers that do get stripped (`timeout`, `nice`…), and the ones that don't (`npx`, `docker exec`, `devbox run`).
I can pick the right **permission mode** for a given case (closed CI → `dontAsk`; exploring → `plan`; long supervised task → `auto`; isolated container → `bypassPermissions`).
I know how to set up a reproducible `claude -p` in CI: `--bare` + `--permission-mode dontAsk` + `--allowedTools` + `--output-format json --json-schema`, and read `structured_output`.
I know how to turn on **streaming mode** (`--output-format stream-json` + `--verbose` + `--include-partial-messages`) and why it needs all three flags.
I can distinguish `/clear`, `/compact`, `/rewind`, `--continue`, and `--resume`, and explain why a `--resume` from a different `cwd` returns a **new session**.
I know what should go in the `CLAUDE.md` that `/init` generates (<200 lines of conventions) and what should migrate to rules, skills, hooks, or deny rules.

domains.title: Eval, Testing, and Debugging
objectives: Debugging and Error Handling (2.6%) — Debugging and error handling techniques for Claude applications, including error type identification, recovery strategy selection, trace analysis to identify failure modes, and problem origin isolation between the integration layer and model output.
domains.html:
Why it's worth 2.6%

It's the smallest domain on the exam — approximately 1 to 2 items out of 53 — and its only stated objective is Debugging and Error Handling. You won't be asked about eval metrics or test suite design: the guide reduces this domain to one very concrete, very operational competency — the one that separates someone who "got the demo working" from someone who maintains a Claude system in production: when something fails, do you know what failed, where it failed, and what to do about it?

The engineering decision this domain measures is cause attribution. A Claude-based system has at least three planes where it can break: the transport layer (HTTP, network, credentials, rate limits), the protocol contract (the shape of messages, content blocks, tool_result, stop_reason), and the model's output (hallucination, invalid format, wrong tool choice, a confidently wrong response). Each plane has its own set of symptoms, its own diagnostic instruments, and its own recovery strategy — and applying the wrong plane's strategy doesn't just fail to fix anything: it burns money (every retry is a new, billable generation), increases latency, and masks the real bug. The exam will put you in a production scenario with an ambiguous symptom and ask you to isolate the origin before acting. That's the whole domain.

Low weight, high failure cost: the concepts in this domain (stop_reason, HTTP codes, is_error, backoff, request_id) reappear inside items from other domains — especially D2 (Claude API Mechanics, 6.8%) and D8 (Tool Implementation, 4.4%). Studying D4 pays off well above its nominal 2.6%.

Official Objectives

  • Debugging and Error Handling (2.6%) — "Debugging and error handling techniques for Claude applications, including error type identification, recovery strategy selection, trace analysis to identify failure modes, and problem origin isolation between the integration layer and model output."

Broken down into the four verbatim competencies the guide names, and what you'll be asked about each:

  • error type identification → Given a symptom or an error payload, name exactly what class of failure it is: HTTP 4xx vs 5xx, rate_limit_error (429) vs overloaded_error (529), an API error vs a stop_reason (which arrives with HTTP 200), a tool error (is_error inside tool_result) vs an SDK exception.

  • recovery strategy selection → Choose the correct action for that type: retry with exponential backoff, respect retry-after, do not retry and fix the request instead, fall back to another model, continue a truncated response, return an error tool_result so the model self-corrects, or switch mechanisms entirely (structured outputs instead of retrying prompts).

  • trace analysis to identify failure modes → Read raw transcripts, spans, and operational metrics (number of tool calls, tokens, runtime, tool errors) to recognize the pattern of failure, not the isolated incident: redundant tool calls, repeated parameter errors, loops that never terminate, context drift.

  • problem origin isolation between the integration layer and model output → The heart of the domain: deciding whether the fault lies in your code (a malformed schema, tool_result in the wrong order, a badly reconstructed history, a fragile parser) or in the model (it hallucinated, ignored an instruction, picked the wrong tool). And knowing which discriminating test to run to find out.

Key Concepts

1. The three failure planes — the domain's mental map

Before any technique, internalize this separation. Almost every D4 item is solved by saying which plane the symptom lives on.

PlaneEvidenceWho produces itTypical recovery
Transport / HTTP4xx/5xx status, error.type, request_idNetwork, your credential, Anthropic's infrastructureRetry (if transient) or fix the request (if not)
Protocol / contractHTTP 200 + stop_reason, shape of content, is_errorYour code assembling the conversation wrong, or the agentic loopContinue, resend, fix block ordering
Model outputHTTP 200 + semantically bad contentThe modelStructured outputs, grounding, citations, judge, fallback

The nuance that separates the ones who know: planes 2 and 3 both arrive with HTTP 200. A system that only looks at response.status_code is blind to two-thirds of its failures.

2. Error type identification: the HTTP code table

Claude API errors. All return JSON with type, error.type, error.message, and request_id.

HTTPerror.typeCauseRetryable?
400invalid_request_errorMalformed request format or contentNo — fix the body
401authentication_errorMalformed, revoked, or expired API keyNo — fix the credential
402billing_errorBilling issueNo
403permission_errorThe key has no permission on the resourceNo
404not_found_errorResource doesn't existNo
409conflict_errorConflict with resource stateYes (SDKs retry it)
413request_too_largeExceeds the byte maximum (32 MB on Messages)No — reduce the payload
429rate_limit_errorYour organization exceeded its limitYes — respect retry-after
500api_errorInternal Anthropic errorYes — backoff
504timeout_errorTimeout while processing the requestYes
529overloaded_errorThe API is overloaded globallyYes — backoff

429 vs 529 is an exam distinction. 429 = you exceeded your quota (RPM / ITPM / OTPM). 529 = the API is saturated for everyone. Both get retried, but the underlying corrective action differs: 429 → smooth out your traffic (rate limits use a token bucket, not a fixed window: a burst of 60 requests in the same second can produce 429 even if your per-minute average is within the 60 RPM limit); 529 → back off and wait. A sharp usage spike can also trigger 429 via acceleration limits → you need to ramp up traffic gradually.

In the SDKs, each code maps to a typed exception. Catch from most specific to most generic, and never string-match the error message:

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

try:
    message = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello, Claude"}],
    )
except anthropic.APIConnectionError as e:
    # No hubo respuesta HTTP: red, DNS, TLS. Reintentable.
    print("The server could not be reached:", e.__cause__)
except anthropic.RateLimitError as e:
    # 429: respeta retry-after, no martillees.
    print("Rate limited. retry-after:", e.response.headers.get("retry-after"))
except anthropic.BadRequestError as e:
    # 400: NO reintentar. Es un bug tuyo. Guarda el request_id para soporte.
    print("Bad request:", e.status_code, e.request_id)
except anthropic.APIStatusError as e:
    print("Other non-2xx:", e.status_code, e.response)

Exception mapping (identical in Python and TypeScript): 400 BadRequestError · 401 AuthenticationError · 403 PermissionDeniedError · 404 NotFoundError · 409 ConflictError · 422 UnprocessableEntityError · 429 RateLimitError · ≥500 InternalServerError · no HTTP response APIConnectionError.

3. stop_reason is NOT an error (stop reasons are HTTP 200)

The official quote is explicit: "Distinguish stop_reason from errors — Stop reasons are successful responses (HTTP 200), errors are failures (4xx/5xx)." Confusing them is the classic error in this domain.

stop_reasonMeaningRecovery strategy
end_turnFinished naturallyUse the response
max_tokensTruncated by the max_tokens limitRaise max_tokens or continue the response
stop_sequenceOne of your stop_sequence values was emittedRead the stop_sequence field
tool_useClaude called a client-side toolExecute it and return tool_result
pause_turnThe server tools loop hit its iteration limit (default 10 per request)Resend the assistant content as-is to continue
refusalClaude declined (safety)Read stop_details; optionally retry with a fallback model
model_context_window_exceededThe context window ran out before max_tokens didTreat as truncated; trim context

Three exam-level nuances:

  • refusal arrives as HTTP 200, not as an error. In Claude Fable 5 the safety classifiers return the refusal inside a normal 200 response. If your error handler doesn't look at stop_reason, a refusal slips through as a "valid response" and breaks the parser downstream.
  • pause_turn ≠ tool_use. pause_turn comes from the server-side loop (web search, web fetch) and is resolved by resending the response. tool_use is a client-side tool and is resolved by sending tool_result. A client-side tool_use never produces pause_turn. Confusing the two is a classic distractor.
  • max_tokens doesn't "resume": it cuts. It can truncate mid-word. For brevity, ask for a limit in paragraphs or sentences, not words (the model counts tokens, not words).

4. Errors inside the stream (post-200 SSE errors)

With "stream": true the response is delivered as Server-Sent Events. A stream can fail after the connection has already returned HTTP 200:

event: error
data: {"type": "error", "error": {"type": "overloaded_error", "message": "Overloaded"}}

Your standard status-code handling doesn't catch this. You have to handle the error event explicitly inside the event loop, and also handle unknown event types gracefully (Anthropic may add new event types; your code must not break).

Two other stream facts that produce "phantom" bugs:

  • The usage on message_delta is cumulative, not incremental. Summing it per event inflates the total and wrecks your cost telemetry.
  • input_json_delta delivers partial JSON as a string. The final tool_use.input is always an object: it can only be parsed once you receive content_block_stop. Parsing the deltas on the fly blows up.

Recovering from cut-off streams: capture the partial output and continue. In Claude 4.6 and later, the continuation goes in a user message (e.g. "Your previous response was interrupted and ended with [previous_response]. Continue from where you left off."), not as an assistant prefill. tool_use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered: you can only resume from the last text block.

5. Tool errors: is_error, not exceptions

When a client-side tool fails, the error travels inside the conversation as structured data, not as an HTTP exception:

{
  "role": "user",
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "tool_result",
      "tool_use_id": "toolu_01A09q90qw90lq917835lq9",
      "content": "ConnectionError: the weather service API is not available (HTTP 500). Retry after 60 seconds.",
      "is_error": true
    }
  ]
}

Points the exam exploits:

  • A tool_result with is_error: true is still a 200 response from the Claude API. The 500 is from the weather service, not from Anthropic.
  • Error messages should be instructive, not generic: "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds." > "failed". Faced with an invalid call or missing parameters, Claude retries 2–3 times with corrections before giving up — a good error message turns a failure into a self-correction.
  • Hard formatting rules: tool_result blocks go immediately after the message with tool_use, all together in a single user message, matched by tool_use_id, and first in the content array. Putting text before a tool_result gives 400. Sending each tool_result in its own separate user message "teaches" Claude to stop parallelizing — it's the #1 cause of "my agent stopped making parallel calls," and it's an integration bug, not a model one.
  • If you decide not to execute a call (because an earlier one failed), you still must return its tool_result with is_error: true. A tool_use without its matching tool_result produces the error "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after."
  • Server tools handle their own errors transparently: you don't construct is_error for them.
  • Documented gotcha: empty responses with stop_reason: "end_turn" (2–3 tokens, no content), typically after a tool_result. Causes: adding text blocks immediately after the tool results, or resending Claude's full response without adding anything new.

6. Recovery strategy selection: retries, backoff, and the hidden cost

The official SDKs already retry transient failures (connection errors, 408, 409, 429, and ≥500) with exponential backoff, 2 times by default, honoring the retry-after header.

from anthropic import Anthropic

# Global (default es 2):
client = Anthropic(max_retries=3, timeout=30.0)  # timeout en SEGUNDOS en Python

# Por request:
client.with_options(max_retries=5).messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}],
)
// TypeScript: timeout en MILISEGUNDOS
const client = new Anthropic({ maxRetries: 3, timeout: 30 * 1000 });

Four facts that get tested:

  1. retry-after rules. "Earlier retries will fail." Retrying earlier than what the header says accomplishes nothing: it fails again.
  2. Timeout: seconds in Python, milliseconds in TypeScript. And requests that time out also get retried, so real wall-clock time can be timeout × (max_retries + 1). A "conservative" but miscalculated timeout multiplies perceived latency by 3.
  3. There is no documented Idempotency-Key on the Messages API. The API is stateless and doesn't create persistent resources: every retry produces a new, billable generation. Deduplication is your responsibility (hash the request, save the request_id, use custom_id in Batches). Any option claiming "the Messages API supports idempotency keys" is false.
  4. Don't retry what isn't transient. 400/401/402/403/404/413 are bugs on your end: retrying in a loop just burns quota and hides the defect.

For requests that might run past ~10 minutes, the fix isn't "raise the timeout": it's streaming or the Message Batches API.

7. Debugging the Message Batches API

A batch has request_counts with exactly five counters: processing, succeeded, errored, canceled, expired. Each individual result carries a result.type with those same states. Critical rules:

  • params validation is asynchronous: validation errors show up when the entire batch finishes, not when you create it. Official practice: do a dry run of the request against the Messages API before sending 10,000 into the batch.
  • Result order does NOT match input order. Always match by custom_id (regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$, unique within the batch).
  • errored, canceled, and expired are not billed.
for result in client.messages.batches.results(batch_id):
    match result.result.type:
        case "succeeded":
            store(result.custom_id, result.result.message)
        case "errored":
            if result.result.error.error.type == "invalid_request_error":
                # BUG DE INTEGRACIÓN: hay que ARREGLAR el body. Reenviar igual = fallar igual.
                quarantine(result.custom_id)
            else:
                # Error de servidor: reintentable tal cual.
                retry_queue.append(result.custom_id)
        case "expired":
            # El batch alcanzó las 24 h. Reenviar en otro batch.
            retry_queue.append(result.custom_id)
        case "canceled":
            pass

This block is literally the domain's competency in miniature: the same symptom ("it failed") branches into three different recovery strategies depending on the error type.

8. Problem origin isolation: integration vs. model

The domain's canonical question. A discriminating procedure that works:

  1. Was there an HTTP 200? No → transport plane. Debate over.
  2. Is stop_reason end_turn? No → protocol plane (max_tokens, pause_turn, refusal, model_context_window_exceeded each have specific recoveries, and none of them is "retry unchanged").
  3. Deterministic replay. Save the exact request body and the request_id. Resend the same body. If the failure reproduces always and identically with a 4xx → it's your request. If it produces different outputs each time → it's model variation (LLMs are non-deterministic by design).
  4. Context isolation test. Reduce the request to the minimum that reproduces the failure. If removing your reconstructed history makes the failure disappear, the bug is in how you rebuild the conversation (modified thinking blocks → 400; out-of-order tool_result → 400; prefill on modern models → 400; temperature on Opus 4.7+ → 400).
  5. If everything arrives as 200 and well-formed, and the output is still wrong → it's model output. And in that case the fix is not to retry: it's to change the mechanism (structured outputs, grounding, judge, fallback).

Signs the bug is yours (integration layer), not the model's:

  • 400 reproducible 100% of the time with the same body.
  • Claude "stopped parallelizing" → you're sending each tool_result in a separate message.
  • Empty responses with end_turn after a tool_result → you're adding text after the tool results.
  • message.content[0].text blows up → content is an array of blocks (thinking, tool_use, text); you have to filter by type.
  • Reported cost is inflated → you're summing the cumulative usage from every message_delta.
  • In Claude Code, a tool_result that "goes missing" → tool responses are capped at 25,000 tokens by default.

Signs it's the model:

  • Same request, different outputs.
  • Invented facts about provided documents.
  • Systematically wrong tool choice given ambiguous descriptions.
  • A confident, false response (confidently wrong).

9. Model failure modes and their mechanical recovery

Failure modeIncorrect recovery (what the mediocre candidate does)Correct recovery
Invalid JSON / schema violationAdd "respond ONLY with valid JSON" to the prompt + retryStructured outputs: output_config.format with type: "json_schema", and/or strict tool use (strict: true). It's constrained decoding: "Always valid: No more JSON.parse() errors... No retries needed for schema violations."
Hallucination about documentsUpgrade the modelExplicitly allow "I don't know"; for long documents (>20k tokens) require literal quote extraction before the task; demand a supporting citation per claim and drop the claim if none is found; best-of-N (run N times and compare: inconsistencies expose hallucination)
Truncated response (max_tokens)Retry the same requestRaise max_tokens or continue the response. (max_tokens does not affect the OTPM rate limit: raising it carries no quota penalty)
refusalTreat it as an HTTP error and retry in a loopRead stop_details, and retry on a fallback model if applicable
Tool loop that never endsKill the processRead the transcript: redundant tool calls ⇒ check pagination parameters; repeated parameter errors ⇒ improve the tool descriptions

Important note against over-generalizing: these techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely." Any exam option promising total elimination is a distractor.

10. Trace analysis: what to look at and with what

Operational metrics for an agent (not optional telemetry — part of the diagnosis): high-level accuracy, runtime per tool call and per task, total number of tool calls, total token consumption, and tool errors. The analysis is done by reading raw transcripts — and an official observation worth treating as a principle: "what agents omit in their feedback and responses can often be more important than what they include."

Structured traces. Claude Code and the Agent SDK export metrics and traces via OpenTelemetry. Span hierarchy:

claude_code.interaction            (root: un prompt de usuario)
├── claude_code.llm_request
├── claude_code.hook
└── claude_code.tool
    ├── claude_code.tool.blocked_on_user
    └── claude_code.tool.execution

Subagents nest under the parent's claude_code.tool span. llm_request, tool.execution, and hook mark OTel status ERROR when they log a failure — that's exactly what you look for to locate the failure plane without reading conversation content. Useful metrics: claude_code.cost.usage (USD) and claude_code.token.usage (tokens).

Agent SDK result states. The ResultMessage carries a subtype: success, error_max_turns, error_max_budget_usd, error_during_execution, error_max_structured_output_retries. The result field only exists on success; on the others, total_cost_usd, usage, num_turns, and session_id are still present. And a single-shot query() call emits the error result and then raises an exception — you need to wrap it in a try. Another gotcha: hooks may not fire if the agent hits max_turns, because the session ends first.

request_id is your forensic anchor. It comes in the request-id header of every response and in the body of every error; the SDKs expose it as message._request_id. Logging it on every call is what turns an unreproducible incident into an actionable ticket.

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}],
)
log.info("claude_call", extra={
    "request_id": message._request_id,     # req_018EeWyXxfu5pfWkrYcMdjWG
    "stop_reason": message.stop_reason,    # NO es un error: audítalo igual
    "input_tokens": message.usage.input_tokens,
    "output_tokens": message.usage.output_tokens,
})

11. Production practices for failures you can no longer reproduce

  • Stateful error handling: resume from a checkpoint, don't restart the agent from scratch (losing 40 tool calls to a transient 529 is a design failure, not an API one).
  • Full production tracing to diagnose failure patterns, not isolated incidents.
  • Rainbow deployments: shift traffic gradually between versions so you don't break agents mid-flight.
  • High-level observability (decision patterns) without inspecting conversation content — you can diagnose without violating privacy.
  • Exploratory human testing: "People testing agents find edge cases that evals miss." Humans to discover failure modes; code and LLM-as-judge to score at scale.

Worked Examples

Scenario 1 — The overnight batch with 812 failures

Context: Nadia processes 12,000 invoices per night with the Message Batches API. In the morning: succeeded: 11,188, errored: 640, expired: 172. The logs just say "failed".

  • Mediocre candidate: resends the entire batch. Result: pays again for the 11,188 that had already succeeded, and the 640 fail exactly the same way again.
  • Competent candidate: iterates the results and branches by result.type and error.type. The errored ones with invalid_request_error are integration bugs (probably a malformed params field in a subset of invoices): they get quarantined and the body gets fixed; resending them unchanged is a guaranteed repeat failure. The errored ones with api_error are transient: requeue as-is. The expired ones are requests that never reached the model (the batch hit the 24-hour mark): resend them in a new batch. And since errored/expired/canceled aren't billed, the incident's cost is only the legitimate retries.
  • Why: the domain doesn't reward "retrying," it rewards selecting the recovery strategy based on the error type. And matching by custom_id is mandatory: output order doesn't match input order.

Scenario 2 — The chat that "cuts off without an error"

Context: Marco's team has a streaming assistant. 0.4% of sessions show a half-finished response and the user sees a truncated message. The error dashboards are green: zero 4xx, zero 5xx.

  • Mediocre candidate: blames the client's network, raises the proxy timeout, and adds a generic retry. The symptom persists.
  • Competent candidate: knows that a stream can fail after the HTTP 200: an overloaded_error arrives as event: error inside the SSE stream, and status-code handling doesn't see it. Adds explicit handling of the error event in the loop, logs the request_id, and on the client resumes using the documented technique (Claude 4.6+: the continuation goes in a user message with the partial content received). Along the way, discovers that the cost counter was inflated because it summed the usage from every message_delta, which is cumulative.
  • Why: the green dashboard was a structural lie. The failure lived on a plane the instrument didn't measure. That's problem origin isolation.

Scenario 3 — "The model doesn't respect JSON"

Context: An internal API asks Claude to extract 9 fields from contracts. 3% of responses break JSON.parse(). The lead proposes: (a) add to the system prompt "IMPORTANT: respond ONLY with valid JSON, no markdown fences", (b) retry up to 3 times, (c) upgrade from Haiku to Opus.

  • Mediocre candidate: implements all three. The 3% drops to 0.8%, cost goes up 4×, p95 latency triples from the retries, and the bug is still alive in production.
  • Competent candidate: recognizes this as a model output failure with an already-built mechanical solution: structured outputs (output_config.format with type: "json_schema") and/or strict tool use (strict: true). It's constrained decoding: the output cannot violate the schema. Zero retries for schema violations, zero ad-hoc defensive parsers. Keeps Haiku 4.5 and cost goes down.
  • Why: this item is the exam's favorite trap: distractor (a) is Control via Good Manners (asking the model instead of enforcing it with a mechanism), (b) is Plausible Micro-optimization (retries work… sometimes, and they cost), and (c) is Scale-the-Model-as-Panacea. The correct answer changes the layer, not the prompt. Note: prefill (putting a { in an assistant message) is not an alternative: it's forbidden on modern models (Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6/4.7/4.8) → 400.

Scenario 4 — The agent that stopped parallelizing and started spinning

Context: Lucía's support agent used to call 3 tools in parallel. After a refactor, it makes the same 3 calls one by one, takes 3× longer, and sometimes returns an empty turn with stop_reason: "end_turn".

  • Mediocre candidate: tweaks the prompt ("call tools in parallel when possible"), raises max_tokens, tries a different model.
  • Competent candidate: reads the raw transcript and sees that the refactor started sending each tool_result in its own user message. That "teaches" Claude to stop parallelizing, and adding text right after the tool results produces exactly the empty response with end_turn. Fix: a single user message with all the tool_result blocks, matched by tool_use_id, first in the content array, and text after (or no text at all). Zero prompt changes, zero model change.
  • Why: the symptom looked like "the model is misbehaving" and it was 100% integration layer. Isolating the origin before touching the prompt is the whole competency.

Scenario 5 — 429s the day after launch

Context: A job migrates 200k records. It worked fine in staging at 40 RPM. In production it launches with 900 concurrent requests and gets a flood of 429s despite being "well under" the per-minute tier quota.

  • Mediocre candidate: wraps everything in a while True: retry with no backoff (hammers the API), or asks to upgrade the tier.
  • Competent candidate: identifies the token bucket: capacity refills continuously, it doesn't reset on fixed intervals, so a burst can fail even if the average is within the limit — and a sharp traffic jump also triggers acceleration limits. Implements a gradual ramp-up, respects the retry-after header (retrying earlier just fails), lets the SDK do its exponential backoff (2 retries by default), and — since the job isn't urgent — moves it to the Message Batches API, which also costs half as much. Also notes that prompt caching improves effective throughput because cache_read_input_tokens don't count toward ITPM on most models.
  • Why: 429 doesn't mean "I need more quota," it means "my traffic shape is wrong." And the correct fix is sometimes to switch APIs, not tune a parameter.

How the Exam Asks This

Verbs and signals in the stem. D4 items almost always use: "identify the most likely cause", "isolate whether the problem originates in…", "which recovery strategy is most appropriate", "which error should NOT be retried", "what does this stop_reason indicate", "a developer sees X in the logs". Context signals: "429", "timeout", "retry", "the response is truncated", "intermittent", "the model returns JSON that sometimes fails to parse", "the logs show no errors but…".

The item's structural bias. As with the rest of the exam, the winning option is the one that installs a mechanism where the problem demands one — not the one that asks the model nicely, and not the one that upgrades the tier. Applied to D4, that becomes three rules:

  1. If the scenario describes a 200 with bad content, the answer is almost never "retry." It's changing the layer: structured outputs, grounding with citations, fallback, or fixing the message contract.
  2. If the scenario describes a 4xx, the answer is almost never "retry." It's fixing the request.
  3. If the scenario describes a 429/529/5xx/timeout, the answer is retry — but with exponential backoff and respecting retry-after, not in a closed loop.

Distractors you'll see, with their decoder name:

  • The Irrelevant Knob: "Increase temperature to make outputs more varied and avoid the parse error" — temperature governs sampling, not JSON validity (and it's also unsupported on Opus 4.7+/4.8: sending it gives 400).
  • Control via Good Manners: "Add an instruction to the system prompt telling Claude to always return valid JSON". A prompt describes; it doesn't guarantee. Structured outputs guarantees.
  • Scale-the-Model-as-Panacea: "Switch to Opus so it follows the schema better." Raises cost, doesn't close the failure class.
  • Degrading Absolutism: "Retry all failed requests with exponential backoff" / "Always retry on any 4xx". A 400 or a 401 retried 5 times is still a 400 or a 401. Watch for all / always / any / regardless.
  • Plausible Micro-optimization: "Increase the client timeout" for a stream that dies from a post-200 overloaded_error. It's not false that timeouts exist; it's insufficient, because the failure wasn't a timeout.
  • The Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: "Retry the request with an Idempotency-Key header, since the Messages API deduplicates identical requests". The subordinate clause is false: there is no documented idempotency key. Read every since / because / which clause as a factual claim you must verify.
  • Deliberate plane confusion: one option treats refusal or max_tokens as if they were HTTP errors; another treats a tool_result with is_error: true as if it were an Anthropic API failure. Both are false by construction: they're 200s.

"Select TWO" items. These show up in D4 when asked for "two signals that indicate the problem is in the integration layer" or "two errors that should not be retried." Count how many answers the item asks for: marking only one when it asks for two = a failed item.

Common Mistakes

  1. Treating stop_reason as an error. refusal, max_tokens, pause_turn, and model_context_window_exceeded all arrive with HTTP 200. → Audit stop_reason on every response, not just the status code.
  2. Retrying a 400/401/403/404/413. These aren't transient. → Fix the request or the credential. Retrying just burns quota and hides the bug.
  3. Confusing 429 with 529. 429 = your organization exceeded its limit; 529 = the API is overloaded globally. → Both get retried, but only 429 requires you to smooth out your traffic (ramp-up, token bucket).
  4. Retrying earlier than retry-after says. "Earlier retries will fail." → Respect the header; the SDKs already do this for you.
  5. Confusing pause_turn with tool_use. pause_turn = iteration limit of the server tools loop (default 10 per request) → the response gets resent. tool_use = a client-side tool → answer with tool_result. A client-side tool_use never produces pause_turn.
  6. Assuming a tool error is an HTTP error. Tool failures travel as a tool_result with is_error: true inside a 200 response. → Don't catch them in your except APIStatusError.
  7. Sending each tool_result in a separate user message. Breaks parallelism and is the #1 cause of "Claude stopped parallelizing." → All tool_result blocks in one user message, first in the content array. Text before a tool_result = 400.
  8. Believing the 4xx/5xx dashboard covers streaming. An overloaded_error can arrive as event: error after the 200. → Handle the error event inside the SSE loop.
  9. Summing the usage from every message_delta. It's cumulative, not incremental. → Your cost metric is inflated; use the last value, not the sum.
  10. Parsing input_json_delta on the fly. These are fragments of partial JSON as a string. → Accumulate and parse only once content_block_stop arrives.
  11. Fixing invalid JSON with prompting and retries. The documented mechanism exists: structured outputs (output_config.format) and strict tool use (strict: true). → "No retries needed for schema violations." And don't use prefill: it gives 400 on modern models.
  12. Assuming the Messages API deduplicates retries. There is no Idempotency-Key. Every retry is a new, billable generation. → Deduplicate yourself (request hash, request_id, custom_id in Batches).
  13. Resending the whole batch when part of it failed. → Branch by result.type; match by custom_id (output order doesn't match input order); errored/canceled/expired aren't billed.
  14. Expecting the Batches API to validate at batch creation. params validation is asynchronous: errors appear when the batch finishes. → Do a dry run of the request shape against the Messages API first.
  15. Reading message.content[0].text directly. content is an array of blocks (thinking, tool_use, text, …). → Filter by type before reading.
  16. Modifying thinking blocks when reconstructing history. Editing, reordering, or filtering them returns 400. → Resend them exactly as they arrived.
  17. Raising the timeout as a universal fix. Requests that time out also get retried (2 times by default): wall-clock time can be timeout × (max_retries + 1). And in Python the timeout is in seconds, in TypeScript in milliseconds. → For long requests: streaming or Batches, not heroic timeouts.
  18. Diagnosing an agent without operational metrics. Total tool calls, tokens, runtime, and tool errors are part of the diagnosis, not optional telemetry: redundant tool calls ⇒ check pagination; repeated parameter errors ⇒ improve the tool descriptions.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossMeaning
stop_reasonStop reasonField on a 200 response saying why Claude stopped generating; never an error.
end_turnEnd of turnClaude finished naturally: the response is usable as-is.
max_tokens (as stop_reason)Truncated by limitGeneration was cut off at the limit; raise the limit or continue the response.
pause_turnTurn pausedThe server tools loop hit its iteration limit (default 10): resend the response to continue.
refusalRefusalClaude declined for safety reasons; arrives as HTTP 200 with stop_details, not as an error.
model_context_window_exceededContext window exhaustedThe context window filled up before max_tokens did: treat as a truncated response.
rate_limit_error (429)Rate limit errorYour organization exceeded its quota (RPM/ITPM/OTPM); retry while respecting retry-after.
overloaded_error (529)Overload errorThe Anthropic API is saturated globally; retry with exponential backoff.
invalid_request_error (400)Invalid requestYour body is malformed or violates a rule; not retried, it's fixed.
request_too_large (413)Request too largeYou exceeded the byte maximum (32 MB on Messages); reduce the payload.
retry-afterWait headerSeconds you must wait before retrying; retrying earlier fails.
Exponential backoffExponential backoffGrowing waits between retries; the SDKs do this 2 times by default.
Token bucketToken bucketRate-limiting algorithm with continuous refill: a burst can fail even if the average is within the limit.
request_idRequest IDUnique identifier in the request-id header of every response; your forensic anchor for support and correlation.

tool_resultTool resultBlock in a user message that returns the output (or error) of a tool_use, matched by tool_use_id.
Structured outputsStructured outputsConstrained decoding (output_config.format / strict: true) that guarantees schema conformance: no retries for violations.
Post-200 stream errorPost-200 stream errorevent: error arriving via SSE after an HTTP 200; invisible to status-code handling.
Trace / spanTrace / spanStructured execution record (OTel: claude_code.interaction → llm_request / tool / hook) used to locate the failure plane.
Failure modeFailure modeA recurring error pattern (tool loop, hallucination, format drift), not an isolated incident.
End-state evaluationEnd-state evaluationJudging the agent's final result, not turn by turn, because multiple valid paths exist.
Held-out test setHeld-out test setCases you don't use to iterate, so you don't overfit to your own suite.
Stateful error handlingStateful error handlingResuming from a checkpoint instead of restarting the whole agent.

Checklist

If you can't check every one of these, you don't have D4 mastered.

  1. I can name the three failure planes (transport / protocol / model output) and say what evidence characterizes each one.
  2. I can recite which HTTP codes are not retried (400, 401, 402, 403, 404, 413) and which are (408, 409, 429, ≥500, connection errors).
  3. I can explain the difference between 429 (rate_limit_error) and 529 (overloaded_error) and what different corrective action each implies.
  4. I know that stop_reason values arrive with HTTP 200, and I can give the correct recovery for max_tokens, pause_turn, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded.
  5. I can explain why a client-side tool_use never produces pause_turn, and what to do with each.
  6. I know that a tool error is communicated via is_error: true inside a tool_result — and that this is still a 200 response.
  7. I can state the tool_result formatting rules (one per tool_use, all in one user message, first in content) and explain why violating them breaks parallelism or causes 400.
  8. I know a stream can fail after an HTTP 200 with an event: error, and I know how to handle it.
  9. I know that the usage on message_delta is cumulative and that input_json_delta is partial JSON in a string.
  10. I can choose between retrying, continuing, falling back to another model, or switching mechanisms (structured outputs) depending on the failure type — and justify why retrying is the wrong answer for a 200 with bad content.
  11. I know there is no idempotency key on the Messages API and that every retry is a new, billable generation.
  12. I can triage batch results by result.type (succeeded / errored / canceled / expired), match by custom_id, and distinguish an invalid_request_error (fix it) from a server error (retry it).
  13. I know that batch validation is asynchronous and that the correct practice is a dry run against the Messages API before sending thousands of requests.
  14. I can describe an origin isolation procedure: replaying the exact body, reducing to a minimal reproduction, and the signals that expose an integration bug vs. a model one.
  15. I can name the operational metrics for an agent needed for diagnosis (tool calls, tokens, runtime, tool errors) and what conclusion to draw from each (redundant ⇒ pagination; parameter errors ⇒ tool descriptions).
  16. I know where request_id lives, why I log it on every call, and what the OpenTelemetry span hierarchy gives me (claude_code.interaction → llm_request / tool / hook).
