  • "context drift" · "bloat" · "long-running agent" · "tool output is huge" · "compaction" · "subagent" → D6 · Context Engineering (pruning tool outputs, compaction, isolation via subagents).
  • "the model returns JSON that sometimes fails to parse" · "validate" · "confidently wrong" → D6 · Output Handling (structured output, validation, defensive parsing, skepticism toward output that sounds confident of itself).
  • "Opus vs. Sonnet vs. Haiku" · "quality/latency/cost" · "extended thinking" · "effort level" · "prompt caching" → D5 · Model Selection / Cost and Token Management.
  • "CLAUDE.md" · "settings.json" · "slash command" · "headless mode" · "repository initialization" → D3 · Claude Code (3.1%) or D2 · Configuration Management (4.1%) if the axis is versioning/pinning.
  • "workflow versus agent" · "supervisor" · "manager hierarchy" · "multi-step" → D1 · Agent Architecture. Rule from the guide: if the steps are known and fixed → workflow; if the path is decided at runtime → agent.
  • "API key" · "secret" · "rotate" · "who can approve" → D7 · Identity, Secrets, and Key Management.

Weight ⇒ study priority. D2 (33.1%) + D5 (16.8%) + D1 (14.7%) = 64.6% of the exam. If your time is limited, that's where your passing score lives. D3 (3.1%) and D4 (2.6%) together are ~3 items: don't ignore them, but don't spend weeks on them either.

4. Elimination Technique, Step by Step

  1. Read the last sentence of the prompt first. It contains the actual question ("Which mitigation is most effective?", "Which approach best fits?"). Superlatives —best, most effective, most appropriate— warn you that more than one option will be technically true; you're looking for the best one, not the only one.
  2. Extract the stated constraints (2–3 maximum) and mentally write them down as a list: primary cost · tolerated latency · high volume. This list is your decision criterion.
  3. Count how many answers the item asks for. The guide states that every item indicates how many to select. If it says "Select TWO," a single correct answer = a failed item, with no partial credit guaranteed.
  4. Sweep for absolutes. regardless / always / never / any / all → flag those options as suspicious before you even reason through them.
  5. Verify every since/because/which subordinate clause as an independent factual claim. A false reason kills the option.
  6. Apply the mechanism test: can this option physically do what it promises? A prompt doesn't invoke APIs. A request doesn't block an action. temperature doesn't govern obedience.
  7. Apply the variable test: does it attack the scenario's primary constraint, or a secondary one?
  8. Between the two finalists, the one that is complete wins (it names the separation of responsibilities, the deterministic control, or the reusability) over the one that is partial.
  9. Flag it and move on. 53 items / 120 min = ~2 min 15 s per item. You have slack, but not enough to get stuck: flag the doubtful ones, finish the pass, and come back once you know where the clock stands.

5. Typical Mental Errors for This Candidate Profile

The MQC is an engineer with 1–5 years of experience and ≥6 months working with LLMs. Their failure patterns are characteristic:

  • Production-engineer bias: "more power = better." Picks Opus, picks extended thinking, picks the big model. The exam punishes this: Domain 5 exists to measure whether you know how to downgrade models when the task allows it.
  • Confusing policy with control. Comes from writing prompts all day: believes a well-worded instruction is a defense. Against an active adversary, it isn't. (Sample 2 is exactly this trap.)
  • Solving with context what should be solved with tools. "I'll just paste the data into the prompt." Works in the demo, dies in production: stale data, bloat, linear cost per request.
  • Ignoring the word "reusable." Jumps straight to "custom tool" without noticing that the scenario asked for sharing across apps and independent maintenance → MCP.
  • Optimizing latency by reflex. The engineer is trained to treat "fast" as good. When the scenario gives you latency for free ("overnight"), spending that slack is the mistake.
  • Reading 720/1000 as "72% correct." It's a scaled score, not a percentage. Don't plan your prep around that arithmetic; and remember that the per-domain percentages on the score report are informational and do not determine pass/fail — there's no minimum per section you have to clear.
  • Studying the syllabus instead of the items. The item bank is written against skills using application verbs ("selecting," "applying," "weighing tradeoffs"), not recall verbs. Almost every item is a scenario with a decision. Preparing by memorizing definitions leaves you defenseless against the Plausible Micro-optimization.
  • Discarding an option for being long. In this exam, the complete option is usually the correct one; elegant brevity is usually the false shortcut.
certs.logisticsHtml:
CCDV-F Exam Logistics

Claude Certified Developer – Foundations · Exam Guide v1.0 · Effective July 2026 Everything operational: registration, scheduling, exam day, policies, and recovery. Source: official exam guide (sections 5, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15).

1. Quick Facts (memorize this)

FieldValue
CredentialClaude Certified Developer – Foundations
Exam codeCCDV-F
Number of items53
Item formatMultiple-choice and multiple-response. Each item indicates how many answers to select.
Time limit120 minutes (~2 min 15 s per item)
DeliveryProctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy
ProviderPearson VUE
Passing score720 on a 100–1,000 scale (scaled, NOT a percentage)
Fee$125 USD (minus your partner tier discount, if applicable) — per attempt
Validity12 months from the date the credential is awarded
Score reportPass/fail + scaled score (100–1,000) + percentage correct per domain
PrerequisitesNone mandatory. Recommended experience is not a requirement.

2. Step-by-Step Registration

Registration happens in the Anthropic Partner Academy; scheduling happens in Pearson VUE. These are two chained systems: you cannot schedule without having paid in the Academy.

  1. Go to the certification page for your exam in the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
  2. Download the Exam Guide and review the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy BEFORE registering. (This isn't a decorative formality: by paying, you accept those policies, including the ones on refunds and conduct.)
  3. Register and complete checkout. The fee you see at checkout already reflects the discount corresponding to your partner tier. If you expect a discount and it doesn't show up, resolve it before paying.
  4. Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account, then log in to schedule your session.
  5. Choose a date and format: online proctoring or a Pearson VUE test center.
  6. Verify your name. The name on your registration must match exactly the name on your official ID. If it doesn't match, correct it before scheduling by writing to certifications-support@anthropic.com.

Accommodations — watch the order

Reasonable accommodations are available for candidates with disabilities or documented needs, in accordance with applicable law. They must be requested and APPROVED by Pearson VUE BEFORE scheduling. Do not schedule your appointment until your request is approved — if you schedule first, you complicate the process for yourself. Request them at: pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations

3. Online Proctored vs. Test Center

The guide allows both ("online proctored and/or test center, per program policy"). Choose deliberately:

Online proctored — you take the exam from your home/office.

  • You must stay within the proctor's and webcam's field of view for the ENTIRE session.
  • Your workspace must be clear: no notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, or other materials.
  • Real risks: long check-in, network failures, interruptions from other people in the room, noise.
  • Practical recommendation: a closed room with a door, a clean desk, no second monitor connected, a wired connection if possible, and block off 45 minutes beforehand for check-in.

Pearson VUE test center — you take the exam at a physical location.

  • Eliminates the risk of your own setup (network, camera, lighting, interruptions).
  • Subject to the late-arrival window: arriving late = no-show (see §6).
  • Recommendation: if your connection or home environment isn't reliable, the test center is the safe option.

The same conduct rules apply in both formats. The format doesn't change the exam.

4. Exam Day: Identification and Conduct Rules

Identification (non-negotiable)

  • Official government-issued photo ID that is NOT expired.
  • The name on the ID must match your registration name EXACTLY. If it doesn't match, you cannot test. Correct it beforehand: certifications-support@anthropic.com.

During the exam you MUST:

  • Remain visible to the proctor and webcam for the entire session (if online).
  • Keep your workspace clear of notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, and any other material.
  • Refrain from communicating with any other person.
  • Not capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce exam content in any form.

PROHIBITED items

Mobile phones · smart watches · headphones/earbuds · study materials · any recording device.

Permitted items

These are defined by Pearson VUE. If any are allowed (for example, scratch paper provided by the proctor), the proctor will tell you. Don't assume you can use something: ask, or don't bring it.

Consequences of misconduct

Cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in: invalidation of your result, revocation of the credential, and being barred from taking future exams. Credential holders remain subject to these rules after certifying.

5. NDA / Confidentiality

Before the exam begins you must accept a non-disclosure agreement (NDA). By accepting it you acknowledge that all exam content — questions, answer options, and scenarios — is Anthropic's confidential, proprietary property, and you agree not to disclose, reproduce, or distribute any part of it.

If you do NOT accept the agreement, the session ends and there is NO refund. The NDA clock runs within your 120-minute check-in/exam session per Pearson VUE's implementation: read it beforehand, in the guide — not on exam day.

6. Cancellation, Rescheduling, No-Shows, and Late Arrival

  • You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment.
  • Changes made within the 24 hours prior: you LOSE the exam fee.
  • No-show (not showing up) or arriving after the permitted late-arrival window: you lose the fee and must register again (and pay again).

Practical rule: if you're unsure you'll be able to attend, reschedule with >24 h of margin. Rescheduling is free outside the window; inside it, it costs $125 USD.

7. Retake Policy

If you don't pass, you can retake the exam after a mandatory waiting period that grows with each failure:

Failed attemptWait before next attempt
1st14 days
2nd30 days
3rd90 days
  • Maximum 4 attempts at the same exam within a rolling 12-month period.
  • Limits apply per exam: failing CCDV-F does not prevent you from registering for a different exam in the program.
  • The fee is paid on EVERY attempt. Four attempts = four fees.

Arithmetic worth keeping in mind: 14 + 30 + 90 = 134 days of cumulative waiting if you fail three times. Plan your first attempt for when you're genuinely ready — not as a "cheap diagnostic."

8. Scoring and Reading the Score Report

  • Criterion-referenced assessment: you're measured against a fixed standard, not against other candidates. There's no curve.
  • The standard was set through a formal standard-setting study with subject matter experts (SMEs) who judged the expected performance of a minimally qualified candidate.
  • Result: pass/fail + scaled score 100–1,000, cut score of 720.
  • 720 does NOT mean 72% correct. It's a scaled score. Don't plan around that arithmetic.
  • The score report also shows the % correct per domain. Those percentages are informational (they help you understand your performance) and are NOT used to determine pass/fail — the verdict depends solely on your total scaled score. There is no minimum per domain.

9. Appeals and Complaints

  • Deadline: 14 days from the date you're notified of the decision; or, if your concern is about your result, 14 days from your exam date.
  • Where: submit to Pearson VUE support → pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html
  • They are reviewed under the program's appeals policy.
  • NOT appealable: the outcome of the standard-setting study (i.e., the 720 cut score) or the content of individual items. Appealing "that question was wrong" doesn't fly.

10. Recertification and Maintaining the Credential

  • Validity: 12 months from the date it's awarded. It's deliberately time-limited because the underlying technology evolves fast.
  • On-time renewal: you review what has changed since you certified and complete a FREE, non-proctored assessment in the Anthropic Partner Academy. → On-time renewal has NO cost. The guide states this explicitly: "There is no fee for on-time renewal."
  • If the credential lapses: you must retake the FULL exam, paying the full fee, to regain certified status. No grace period is stated in the guide.
  • Exception: if the exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam to recertify, instead of the renewal assessment.
  • Holders remain subject to the conduct rules (Section 12 of the guide) for as long as they hold the credential.

Practical action: set a calendar reminder for 10 months after your certification date. Renewing for free without a proctor costs an afternoon; letting it lapse costs $125 USD and 120 minutes under a webcam.

11. Support — Who to Contact for Each Issue

IssueContact
Correct your registration namecertifications-support@anthropic.com (do this before scheduling)
Registration, scheduling, accommodations, results, and everything elsePearson VUE: pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html
Request accommodationspearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations

12. Privacy

Personal data collected during registration and exam administration is handled in accordance with Anthropic's privacy policy, Pearson VUE's privacy policy, and applicable data protection legislation.

13. Operational Checklist (72 h before → exam day)

72 h before

  • Registration name matches your current official ID exactly.
  • If you need accommodations and they aren't approved yet: you're not ready to schedule — resolve it first.
  • You confirmed the format (online vs. center) and the address/link.
  • Last window to cancel/reschedule without losing the $125 USD: 24 h before.

24 h before

  • Final decision: attend or reschedule. After this point, canceling = losing the fee.
  • (Online) You ran the Pearson VUE system check; webcam, microphone, and network tested.
  • (Online) You prepared a closed room, clear desk, second monitor disconnected.

Exam day

  • Valid official photo ID in hand.
  • Phone, smart watch, headphones/earbuds, and study materials out of the room.
  • Arrive/connect with margin: arriving late = no-show = losing the fee.
  • Read and accept the NDA (declining it ends the session with no refund).
  • Mental budget: 53 items / 120 min ≈ 2 min 15 s per item. Flag the doubtful ones and move on.

questions.stem: A developer must process 10,000 documents overnight to produce a non-urgent analytics report. Cost is the primary concern, and results are not needed until the following morning. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Send every request synchronously through the Messages API in parallel to finish as quickly as possible.
Use the Message Batches API, which processes large asynchronous workloads within a 24-hour window at reduced cost.
Lower max_tokens on synchronous calls to minimize cost.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of output quality.

questions.explanationEs: The stem plants three signals that, together, point to a single mechanism: high volume (10,000 documents), latency tolerance ('overnight,' 'not needed until the following morning'), and cost as the primary constraint. That's exactly the profile of the Message Batches API: asynchronous processing of large batches within a 24-hour window at a reduced per-token cost compared to synchronous calls. B is correct because it's the only option that acts on the dimension the scenario declares relevant (realtime vs. batch), and it also satisfies the time constraint without breaking it. A confuses speed with cost: parallelizing synchronous calls finishes sooner, but the per-token price is the same, so it optimizes a variable the scenario explicitly does NOT ask for (results aren't needed until the following morning); it also adds pressure on rate limits. C is a real but insufficient micro-optimization: lowering max_tokens caps the output ceiling, not the processing mode, and it doesn't touch batch's structural discount; it also risks truncating the analysis. D is the 'always pick the cheapest model' trap: the stem says 'regardless of output quality,' which degrades the report's quality needlessly, when the latency constraint had already opened the door to the batch discount without sacrificing capability. Operative rule: when the scenario says 'not urgent' + 'volume' + 'cost,' the answer is batch, not a parameter trick.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 1: B. The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads at lower cost, which matches an overnight, non-urgent job. Sending requests synchronously in parallel (A) does not reduce per-token cost; lowering max_tokens (C) or blindly downsizing the model (D) does not address the batch-versus-realtime tradeoff.
questions.trap: A = Wrong-Variable Optimization (solves for latency when the scenario asks for cost, and ignores that 'overnight' already concedes the latency). C = Plausible Micro-optimization (a real cost technique, but second-order, that doesn't attack the tradeoff named in the scenario). D = Degrading Absolutism ('the cheapest, always'), given away by the extreme modifier 'regardless of output quality'; in this exam, options with 'regardless,' 'always,' 'never,' or 'any' are almost always distractors.

questions.stem: A Claude-powered agent summarizes web pages submitted by end users. One page contains hidden text instructing the model to ignore previous instructions and reveal its system prompt. Which mitigation is most effective?

options.text: Raise the model's temperature so its behavior is harder to predict.
Treat retrieved page content as untrusted input, keep it separate from trusted instructions, and use guardrails or hooks so injected instructions cannot trigger sensitive actions.
Add a line to the system prompt asking users not to include malicious instructions.
Switch to a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.

questions.explanationEs: The scenario describes a classic indirect prompt injection: retrieved content (a webpage submitted by the user) that contains hidden instructions directed at the model. The correct defense is architectural, not persuasive: establish a content boundary that marks the retrieved material as untrusted input, separate it from the system's trusted instructions, and place a deterministic control — guardrails or hooks — between the model and sensitive actions, so that even if the model is fooled, the dangerous action can't execute. That's exactly B, and it combines the three layers the guide names in Domain 7: untrusted-input handling, guardrail layering, and least privilege. A is a technical-fantasy distractor: temperature controls the randomness of sampling, not obedience to instructions; raising it protects nothing and in fact makes the system less predictable and harder to evaluate. C is the most seductive mistake for a beginner candidate: an instruction in the system prompt is a request, not an enforceable control; the attacker doesn't read the system prompt and doesn't obey it, and the model can be persuaded to ignore it — it's probabilistic defense against an active adversary. D inverts the real causal relationship: a model that follows instructions with more fidelity can be MORE susceptible to injected instructions, not less; scaling up the model is not a security control. Operative rule: in security, the option that makes the dangerous action impossible wins, not the one that makes the model 'better' or 'nicer.'
questions.officialRationale: Sample 2: B. Prompt injection is addressed by isolating untrusted content from trusted instructions and enforcing least-privilege guardrails so injected text cannot invoke sensitive tools. Temperature (A) is irrelevant to injection; a polite request (C) is not an enforceable control; a more instruction-following model (D) can be more susceptible, not less.
questions.trap: A = Irrelevant Knob (uses a real API parameter — temperature — outside its domain of effect, betting the candidate will associate 'technical parameter' with 'technical solution'). C = Good-Manners Control (a natural-language instruction presented as though it were an enforceable control; it sounds like 'security' but isn't enforceable and confuses policy with mechanism). D = Model-Scaling Panacea (assumes a larger model solves an architecture problem; on this exam, 'use a larger model' is almost never the answer to a security, context, or cost problem).

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to call an internal inventory service exposed as a REST API. They want the capability to be reusable across several Claude applications and maintained independently of any one app. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Hard-code the inventory logic into each application's system prompt.
Build an MCP server that exposes the inventory operations as tools so multiple Claude applications can connect to it.
Paste the current inventory data into the context window on every request.
Rely on a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API.

questions.explanationEs: This item evaluates Agentic Customization: the tradeoff among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs. The two phrases that decide the answer are 'reusable across several Claude applications' and 'maintained independently of any one app.' That pair of requirements — sharing the capability across multiple applications and decoupling its life cycle from any single one of them — is the functional definition of an MCP server: it exposes operations as tools over a standard protocol, and any Claude client connects to it. B is correct. A fails both requirements at once: putting the logic in the system prompt doesn't give the model executable access to the service (a prompt describes, it doesn't invoke), and it duplicates the logic in every app, multiplying maintenance instead of centralizing it. C confuses data with capability: pasting the inventory into the context delivers a snapshot that's stale from the instant it's sent, allows no live queries or writes, and burns tokens on every request (context bloat, exactly what Domain 6 teaches you to avoid). D is a false claim disguised as a shortcut: built-in tools are platform-provided capabilities with a defined scope; they don't automatically reach arbitrary internal REST APIs behind the team's firewall. Operative rule: if the stem says 'reusable across several apps' and 'maintained independently,' the answer is MCP; if it said 'a single app, a single integration,' a custom tool would suffice.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 3: B. An MCP server exposes reusable tools that multiple Claude applications can share and that can be maintained independently. Hard-coding logic into prompts (A) is neither reusable nor maintainable; pasting data (C) gives no live access and wastes context; built-in tools (D) do not automatically reach arbitrary internal APIs.
questions.trap: A = Prompt-as-Implementation (puts executable logic into text; ignores that a prompt doesn't invoke systems). C = Data-Instead-of-Capability (solves with context what actually requires a tool; produces stale data and bloat — a very common variant on this exam). D = Factual-Falsehood-Wrapped-in-Justification (the clause 'since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API' is the error; the 'since/because' clause is where this exam hides the lie — always read it as a claim you must verify, not as backup).

questions.objective: Agent Architecture (4.5%) — Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.
questions.scenario: Fixed expense-reimbursement pipeline
questions.stem: A finance team processes expense reports through the same four steps every time: extract fields from the receipt, validate them against the policy table, route anything above $500 to a human approver, and write the result to the ledger. The steps are always the same and are already known in code. Which architecture best fits this task?

options.text: Implement the four steps as a code-orchestrated workflow — extract, validate, and a programmatic gate that routes anything above the threshold to a human approver before writing to the ledger.
Deploy a fully autonomous agent with a broad toolset that decides its own sequence of actions for every receipt, regardless of how consistent the pipeline has been so far.
Use the Claude Agent SDK's autonomous loop with a generous max_turns budget so the model can adapt its own path in case a receipt doesn't fit the usual shape.
Keep a single Claude call per receipt and add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to always follow the four steps in order.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Architecture' — the workflow vs. agent decision criterion. Anthropic's official definition is literal: a workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; an agent exists when the model dynamically decides its own process. Here the four steps are known and fixed in advance, so the correct architecture is a workflow with a programmatic gate (prompt chaining), not an agent. Having several calls to Claude doesn't make it an agent: what decides is who writes the execution graph. General rule: if you can enumerate the steps in code, pay the cheap, deterministic route; reserve agent autonomy for when the path is genuinely unpredictable.

distractorsEs.B: Degrading Absolutism: the modifier 'regardless of how consistent the pipeline has been' gives away the trap — it buys autonomy (and often several times the token cost) for a task the scenario itself defines as predictable. Unrequested autonomy is expense, not merit.
distractorsEs.C: Wrong-Variable Optimization: the scenario already conceded that the path is fixed and known; paying for runtime adaptability (Agent SDK + a high max_turns) solves for flexibility nobody needed.
distractorsEs.D: Good-Manners Control: replaces the programmatic gate with a natural-language instruction ('always follow the four steps in order'). A request is not a control — nothing stops the model from skipping the order under context pressure.

questions.trap: The decoy is D: it sounds disciplined ('follow the steps in order'), but it asks for obedience instead of enforcing it with code — the Good-Manners Control trap.

questions.objective: Agent Architecture (4.5%) — Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.
questions.scenario: Security audit with unknown scope
questions.stem: Before a release, a security team runs an automated scan of a large codebase. The scan flags anywhere from 3 to 40 suspicious modules depending on what patterns it finds, and each flagged module needs a different depth of review depending on what is actually inside it. Which approach best coordinates the review work?

options.text: Three fixed, parallel Claude calls — one for 'authentication code,' one for 'network code,' one for 'dependency manifests' — run every time, regardless of what the scan actually flagged.
Paste the full source of every flagged module into a single Claude conversation's context and ask it to review everything in one response.
A lead agent that inspects the scan results at runtime, decides how many specialized subagents to delegate to and what each should focus on, then synthesizes their summarized findings.
Skip delegation and rely on a model with a larger context window to read every file in the repository in a single pass.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Architecture,' specifically the domain's finest discriminator: parallelization vs. orchestrator-workers. In parallelization the subtasks are predefined by you; in orchestrator-workers the orchestrator determines them at runtime based on the concrete input. Here the number and type of suspicious modules varies from 3 to 40 and depends on the scan — exactly the signature of orchestrator-workers. C names the correct manager/supervisor hierarchy: a lead agent that decides how many subagents to launch and with what focus, and synthesizes distilled summaries instead of loading every finding in full. General rule: if the branches of work are fixed, parallelize; if they depend on the input, delegate at runtime.

distractorsEs.A: Degrading Absolutism: 'regardless of what the scan actually flagged' forces three fixed branches (parallelization) onto a task whose number and type of subtasks varies — exactly the discriminator the exam rewards you for spotting.
distractorsEs.B: Data-Instead-of-Capability: puts the full source of every module into context instead of delegating the review; it produces context bloat and doesn't scale past a handful of modules.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: replaces architectural delegation with 'a model with a larger window.' A larger window postpones the problem — it doesn't replace the need to decompose the work at runtime.

questions.trap: The decoy is A: it looks like 'reasonable parallelization,' but it fixes in advance branches that the scenario says vary — exactly the error that separates parallelization from orchestrator-workers.

questions.objective: Agent Architecture (4.5%) — Principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, including the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent, the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies, and the role of subagents in improving task execution.
questions.scenario: Delegating to a subagent midway through a migration
questions.stem: A lead agent is 40 tool calls into a large codebase migration. It has just decided which replacement library to use and has a specific error trace it needs investigated in an unfamiliar module, and wants to delegate that investigation to a subagent while it continues the migration. What must the lead agent do to make sure the subagent can act on that context?

options.text: Nothing — since subagents automatically inherit the parent's message history and tool results, the context is already available to it.
Explicitly include the file path, the error trace, and the library decision in the prompt text passed to the subagent, since that prompt is the only channel from parent to subagent.
Increase the subagent's max_turns so it has enough turns to rediscover the same context independently.
Give the subagent a larger-context-window model so it can hold more information once it starts working.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'the role of subagents in improving task execution.' A subagent runs with isolated context: it inherits neither the parent's message history, nor its tool results, nor its system prompt. The only parent→subagent channel is the prompt text passed to it through the Agent tool. B applies this correctly: if the lead already knows the path, the trace, and the library decision, it has to write them explicitly into that prompt, or the subagent starts blind. That isolation is precisely what makes the subagent valuable — it keeps exploration from polluting the main thread — but it demands discipline when delegating: nothing transfers for free.

distractorsEs.A: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the clause 'since subagents automatically inherit the parent's message history' is factually false. Context isolation is the defining characteristic of the subagent, not an accidental limitation.
distractorsEs.C: Irrelevant Knob: max_turns governs the tool-turn budget, not context transfer. More turns doesn't give the subagent any data the parent hasn't explicitly passed to it.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: a model with a larger window doesn't solve a channel problem — the subagent still receives nothing that isn't in the delegation prompt, no matter how much window it has available.

questions.trap: The decoy is A: it assumes 'subagent' implies automatic context continuity, when the property that defines it is exactly the opposite — isolation.

questions.objective: Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%) — Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions.
questions.scenario: Custom loop on top of the Messages API
questions.stem: A developer is implementing a custom tool-use loop directly against the Messages API (not the Claude Agent SDK). A get_inventory tool call fails because the requested SKU does not exist in the warehouse system. Which approach correctly continues the loop?

options.text: Terminate the loop and surface an HTTP-level error to the caller, since a failed tool call means the whole request is broken.
Add an instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to double-check SKUs before calling the tool, so failures become rare.
Switch to a larger, more capable model so it is less likely to request an invalid SKU.
Return a tool_result block with the matching tool_use_id, is_error: true, and a message describing the problem, inside the next user message, and let Claude continue the loop.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Construction with Claude,' specifically how to write a custom loop on top of the Messages API. The model emits a tool_use block and stops with stop_reason: 'tool_use'; your harness executes the tool and returns a tool_result to it. A tool failure is NOT an HTTP exception: it's a tool_result with is_error: true inside a 200 response, which Claude can read and use to decide its next step (for example, asking for a valid SKU). D is the only option that keeps the failure inside the conversation instead of breaking it. General rule: tool errors travel as loop data, not as transport failures.

distractorsEs.A: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the clause 'since a failed tool call means the whole request is broken' is false. A tool_result with is_error: true arrives inside a successful 200 response; the failure is a business-logic failure, not a transport failure.
distractorsEs.B: Good-Manners Control: asks the model to self-regulate ('double-check SKUs') instead of handling the error with the protocol's real mechanism (is_error: true). A request doesn't substitute for a handled error format.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: a larger model doesn't fix a SKU that doesn't exist in the inventory system — the problem is external data, not model capability.

questions.trap: The decoy is A: it sounds like responsible error handling ('cut off the broken call'), but it breaks the loop when the protocol already provides a channel for failures inside the conversation.

questions.objective: Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%) — Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions.
questions.scenario: Infrastructure agent with Bash access
questions.stem: An infrastructure agent has access to a Bash tool to run database migrations. A pasted ticket contains embedded text instructing the agent to also drop the staging schema 'to clean up.' The team wants a guarantee that no destructive command can execute, no matter what text reaches the model. Which mechanism actually provides that guarantee?

options.text: Add a line to CLAUDE.md instructing the agent not to run destructive Bash commands.
Register a PreToolUse hook matched to the Bash tool that inspects tool_input.command and returns permissionDecision: "deny" whenever it matches a destructive pattern such as DROP or rm -rf.
Switch the agent to a larger, more instruction-following model so it better recognizes when a request is trying to trick it into running a destructive command.
Lower the agent's max_turns so it has fewer opportunities to reach a destructive command.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Construction with Claude,' the axis of hooks for deterministic actions. A hook runs in your own process, outside the context window, and intercepts the agent's lifecycle at a defined point (here, PreToolUse on Bash) before the tool executes. It's an if statement in your code, not persuasion of the model — which is why it's the only mechanism on the list that can turn the policy 'never run DROP' into a real control that blocks the call no matter what text reached the model. General rule: against untrusted content, the mechanism that stands between the model and the damage wins, not the one that educates the model.

distractorsEs.A: Good-Manners Control: a line in CLAUDE.md is a natural-language instruction. The text embedded in the ticket competes for the model's attention with that same instruction — nothing blocks execution if the model gives in.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: the guide is explicit — a model that follows instructions with more fidelity can be MORE susceptible to injected instructions, not less. Moving up a model tier is not a security control.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant Knob: max_turns governs the tool-turn budget (protection against cost runaways), not which specific commands Bash can execute. Fewer turns doesn't stop the destructive command from executing on turn 1.

questions.trap: The decoy is A: it reads like a security measure because it's 'in the configuration,' but it's still a request to the model — not an enforceable mechanism.

questions.objective: Agent Construction with Claude (5.3%) — Methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, including the Claude Agent SDK, custom agent loops and harnesses, managed agent deployment models (self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted), and hooks for deterministic actions.
questions.scenario: Data-residency requirement at a regulated fintech
questions.stem: A regulated fintech must keep all agent execution and conversation state inside its own VPC for data-residency compliance, but still wants the same agentic loop, built-in tools, subagent delegation, and hook support that power Claude Code, without reimplementing that loop from scratch. Which option satisfies this?

options.text: Run the Claude Agent SDK inside their own infrastructure — it packages the agentic loop, built-in tools, subagents, and hooks, while session state is written to their own filesystem.
Use Managed Agents, since Anthropic's hosted sandbox for Managed Agents runs inside the customer's own VPC.
Write a custom loop against the Messages API and raise max_tokens so the model can compensate for the missing built-in tools, subagents, and hooks in a single call.
Keep calling the plain Messages API and paste the CLAUDE.md rules and the hook-enforcement logic into the system prompt on every request instead of registering real hooks.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Construction with Claude,' the self-hosted vs. Anthropic-hosted axis. The Claude Agent SDK runs in your own process and infrastructure, with session state persisted to your filesystem, and it packages the same loop, built-in tools, subagents, and hooks that power Claude Code — exactly what the data-residency requirement asks for, without reimplementing the loop. Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to operate the sandbox for you, but it runs hosted by Anthropic, not inside your VPC. General rule: 'the same loop, without reimplementing it, inside my own infrastructure' is the operative definition of self-hosted via the Agent SDK.

distractorsEs.B: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the clause 'since Anthropic's hosted sandbox... runs inside the customer's own VPC' is false. Managed Agents is precisely the Anthropic-hosted option: the sandbox and the event log are hosted by Anthropic, not the customer.
distractorsEs.C: Irrelevant Knob: max_tokens caps the length of a response — it doesn't give the model built-in tools, subagents, or hooks that don't exist in a homegrown loop. Raising it doesn't compensate for a missing capability.
distractorsEs.D: Good-Manners Control: pasting the hooks' logic as text into the prompt swaps an enforceable mechanism (deterministic deny before the tool runs) for a request the model can ignore under context pressure.

questions.trap: The decoy is B: it names the right product for 'without operating your own infrastructure,' but it inverts the central fact — Managed Agents is hosted by Anthropic, not self-hosted.

questions.objective: Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%) — Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.
questions.scenario: Refactoring agent that forgets the initial convention
questions.stem: A refactoring agent is 60 turns into a large migration. The naming convention it must follow was given only in the very first user message. After context compaction runs, the agent starts violating that convention, and the conversation is again approaching the context limit. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Increase max_tokens so each response can be longer, giving the agent more room to restate the convention itself before every edit.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the same conversation can keep growing without hitting the limit as soon.
Move the naming convention into CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request and survives compaction, instead of relying on the first user message.
Every few turns, ask Claude to re-read the full conversation history from the beginning to refresh its memory of the original convention.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Patterns and Frameworks,' specifically context-window management. Compaction summarizes older history as the context nears its limit — and that summary can lose instructions that only ever lived in the first user message. C attacks the real cause: persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md, which gets re-injected on every request and survives compaction, not in a message that compaction can summarize or discard. The problem isn't window size but accumulation (context rot); widening the window or lengthening responses only delays the symptom. General rule: an instruction that must survive the whole session → persistent configuration, not a message in the history.

distractorsEs.A: Irrelevant Knob: max_tokens limits how much the model can write in a single response; it doesn't affect whether an instruction from the first message survives compaction, nor how much context accumulates.
distractorsEs.B: Model-Scaling Panacea: this is exactly the mediocre-candidate move the domain itself describes — a larger window delays context rot, it doesn't resolve it, because compaction was still about to erase the initial prompt anyway.
distractorsEs.D: Plausible Micro-optimization: rereading the entire history every few turns is a real but second-order technique — expensive in tokens, and nothing guarantees the original instruction is still in a history that compaction has already summarized.

questions.trap: The decoy is B: 'more context window' sounds like the obvious fix for a context problem, but the domain flags this as long-running agents' number-one mistake — confusing size with accumulation.

questions.objective: Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%) — Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.
questions.scenario: The temptation to adopt a framework for three fixed steps
questions.stem: A team has exactly three fixed steps to run in sequence every time: translate the document, check it against a terminology glossary, and format the final output. One engineer proposes adopting LangGraph 'to make the pipeline more agentic and easier to extend later.' Which response best follows Anthropic's own guidance on agentic frameworks?

options.text: Adopt LangGraph immediately, since any multi-step Claude pipeline requires a graph framework to run correctly.
Skip any framework or workflow code, and instead write one long system prompt listing all three steps and asking Claude to perform them in order within a single call.
Adopt LangGraph and use a large, high-capability model at every node so the graph framework's abstraction layer does not slow down reasoning.
Implement the three steps directly in code as a simple sequential workflow with a programmatic gate between steps, and skip adopting a graph framework for now.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Patterns and Frameworks,' the role of agentic abstraction frameworks (Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI). Anthropic's guidance is explicit: these frameworks simplify implementation but create layers that obscure the underlying prompts and responses and make debugging harder; the recommendation is to start with the primitives and adopt abstraction only when its value is measurable. With three fixed, known steps, the literal definition of a workflow already applies without needing a stateful graph. D names the correct layer: simple sequential code with a programmatic gate. General rule: 'adopt a framework' never wins on its own against the option that solves the real architectural tradeoff with the simplest tool.

distractorsEs.A: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the clause 'since any multi-step Claude pipeline requires a graph framework' is false — a fixed-step workflow is implemented in plain code without any graph framework.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-Implementation: compresses three steps with an intermediate check into a single prompt. A prompt describes a sequence; it doesn't impose an enforceable gate between 'check glossary' and 'format,' so a failed step doesn't block the next one.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: raises model capability to compensate for the debugging cost the framework itself introduces, instead of asking whether the framework was needed for three fixed steps at all.

questions.trap: The decoy is C: it looks like the 'serious' solution (framework + large model), but it stacks two layers of cost onto a task Anthropic's own guidance would solve with simple code.

questions.objective: Agent Patterns and Frameworks (4.9%) — Common agent design patterns (tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, context-window management) and agentic abstraction frameworks (e.g., Strands, LangGraph, PydanticAI) for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.
questions.scenario: Tool-use loop mechanics
questions.stem: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe how tool use works when a developer implements a custom agent loop directly on the Messages API.

options.text: When Claude decides to use a tool, it emits a tool_use content block and stops with stop_reason: "tool_use" — Claude itself never executes the tool.
Claude directly invokes the function in the developer's backend the moment it decides a tool is needed, since it has direct network access to any tool registered in the tools array.
The developer's harness is responsible for actually running the requested tool and sending the result back as a tool_result block so the loop can continue.
Raising the model's temperature makes tool selection more accurate, since a less predictable model considers more possible tools before choosing.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Agent Patterns and Frameworks,' the central pattern of every agent: the tool-use loop. Claude never executes anything — it only emits a tool_use block and stops with stop_reason: 'tool_use'; it's the developer's harness that actually runs the tool and returns a tool_result so the loop can continue. A and C describe the two halves of the same mechanism (emitting vs. executing), which is why both count as independent answers, not redundant ones. Note on multiple-response technique: each option is evaluated true/false against the real mechanism, not as a block. General rule: in any agent architecture, the boundary between 'deciding' (the model) and 'executing' (your code) is absolute.

distractorsEs.B: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the clause 'since it has direct network access to any tool registered' is false. Claude has no network access to anything; it only emits a structured request that your harness decides whether to execute.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant Knob: temperature governs token sampling (how deterministic the output is), not the accuracy of which tool gets picked or how many are considered — the same misattributed parameter that shows up in the exam's official security sample.

questions.trap: The decoy is B: it sounds like a plausible technical description of tool use, but it inverts the real mechanism — the model requests, the harness executes, never the reverse.

questions.objective: Claude API behavior and mechanics (messages, tools, streaming, caching, batch API, realtime vs batch)
questions.scenario: 50,000 records, result by tomorrow, cost is primary
questions.stem: A pipeline must classify 50,000 stored records where the results are not needed until the next business day and minimizing cost is the primary concern. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Fire 50,000 parallel realtime requests to finish as fast as possible.
Use the Message Batches API to submit them asynchronously at roughly half the cost.
Lower max_tokens on each request to cut cost.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of output quality.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude API Mechanics' (the realtime vs. batch tradeoff). The scenario states high volume, latency tolerance ('by tomorrow'), and cost as the primary variable: exactly the profile of the Message Batches API, which processes asynchronously at ~50% of the cost. B attacks the primary variable while accepting the latency that was already conceded.

distractorsEs.A: Wrong-Variable Optimization: spends effort finishing fast when the scenario already gave away the latency requirement; it also doesn't reduce cost.
distractorsEs.C: Plausible Micro-optimization: lowering max_tokens reduces some cost but isn't the lever for volume, and it risks truncating outputs.
distractorsEs.D: Degrading Absolutism: 'regardless of output quality' gives away the extreme; it sacrifices accuracy that was never conceded.

questions.trap: C isn't false, it's insufficient: it doesn't attack the primary variable (cost at volume) the way batch does.

questions.objective: Claude API behavior and mechanics (messages, tools, streaming, caching, batch API, realtime vs batch)
questions.scenario: Same large context on every request
questions.stem: An application sends the same large 30-page policy as context on every request, and both cost and latency are high. The most effective optimization is to:

options.text: Replace the policy with a short summary and hope it is enough.
Raise the temperature so responses vary more.
Use prompt caching so the stable policy prefix is cached and reused across requests.
Switch to Opus to make the requests faster.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude API Mechanics / caching.' A large, stable prefix resent on every call is the canonical case for prompt caching: the prefix (system/context) gets cached, and subsequent calls read it more cheaply and faster. C attacks cost and latency without losing the policy's content.

distractorsEs.A: Plausible Micro-optimization: summarizing reduces tokens but loses policy information; it attacks the symptom with loss.
distractorsEs.B: Irrelevant Knob: temperature governs sampling, not the cost or latency of the repeated prefix.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: Opus isn't 'faster'; it's more capable and more expensive/slower. It doesn't solve the resending of context.

questions.trap: D confuses 'more capable' with 'faster'; the problem is the repeated context, which caching solves.

questions.objective: Claude API behavior and mechanics (messages, tools, streaming, caching, batch API, realtime vs batch)
questions.scenario: A chat UI that feels slow
questions.stem: A chat UI feels unresponsive because users wait for the entire answer before seeing anything. The right fix is to:

options.text: Stream the response so tokens render incrementally, improving time-to-first-token.
Reduce max_tokens so answers are shorter.
Switch to a larger model to speed it up.
Increase the temperature.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude API Mechanics / streaming.' The complaint is about perceived latency: the user sees nothing until the very end. Streaming (SSE) delivers tokens incrementally and improves time-to-first-token, which is exactly the problem. A attacks the cause (a blocking response), not the length or the model.

distractorsEs.B: Plausible Micro-optimization: shortening the response changes the content, not how/when it appears; it doesn't fix the perception of blocking.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: a larger model isn't faster, and it doesn't change the fact that the response still arrives all at once at the end.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant Knob: temperature doesn't affect the UI's responsiveness.

questions.trap: The axis is perceived latency (time-to-first-token); only streaming attacks it.

questions.objective: Claude API behavior and mechanics (messages, tools, streaming, caching, batch API, realtime vs batch)
questions.scenario: Real-time interactive assistant
questions.stem: A customer-facing assistant must answer interactively within seconds. A teammate proposes the Batch API to cut cost. The correct call is:

options.text: Use the Batch API anyway, since it is cheaper.
Use the Batch API and tell users to wait for the results.
Raise the temperature to make it respond faster.
Use realtime (standard) requests, because the interaction requires low latency; the Batch API is asynchronous and unsuitable here.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude API Mechanics' (when NOT to use batch). The scenario states a hard low-latency constraint (interactive, seconds). The Batch API is asynchronous and delivers results on a deferred basis: incompatible with that requirement. D respects the primary constraint; cost savings are secondary and can't violate the stated latency requirement.

distractorsEs.A: Wrong-Variable Optimization: optimizes cost while sacrificing the latency the scenario set as a requirement.
distractorsEs.B: Mechanism failure: 'have them wait' breaks the interactive requirement; batch cannot be realtime.
distractorsEs.C: Irrelevant Knob: temperature doesn't change delivery latency, nor does it turn batch into realtime.

questions.trap: A/B sound like savings, but batch is asynchronous; when the requirement is realtime, cost doesn't get to call the shots.

questions.objective: Core software engineering principles (REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, refactoring)
questions.scenario: Hundreds of independent, I/O-bound calls
questions.stem: A service makes hundreds of independent Claude API calls per job and is I/O-bound. To improve throughput without changing the results, the appropriate engineering technique is to:

options.text: Switch to a larger, more capable model.
Use asynchronous/concurrent requests to overlap the I/O-bound calls.
Concatenate all the data into one giant prompt to make a single call.
Remove version control to reduce overhead.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Software Engineering Foundations' (async). An I/O-bound job with many independent calls gains throughput by overlapping the network wait through concurrency/asynchrony. B is the correct technique and doesn't alter the results. The bottleneck is I/O, not model capability or prompt structure.

distractorsEs.A: Model-Scaling Panacea: the model isn't the bottleneck; the problem is I/O, not capability.
distractorsEs.C: Data-Instead-of-Capability: a giant prompt lumps independent tasks together, risks bloat, and changes the result.
distractorsEs.D: Absolutism/nonsense: removing version control doesn't improve throughput and it degrades the engineering.

questions.trap: The scenario says 'I/O-bound': the lever is concurrency, not the model or the prompt.

questions.objective: Core software engineering principles (REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, refactoring)
questions.scenario: Building a robust client against the REST API
questions.stem: The Claude API is a REST API that returns JSON. When integrating it into a production client, the robust approach is to:

options.text: Assume responses always parse correctly and skip error handling.
Ask the model to 'always return valid JSON' and skip validation.
Parse JSON defensively, check HTTP status codes, and handle errors and retries.
Use a larger model so errors never occur.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Software Engineering Foundations' (REST/JSON, error handling). A production client doesn't assume the happy path: it validates the JSON, inspects status codes, and handles errors/retries. C is the robust practice. Network and formatting errors are part of a REST API's contract, not an anomaly.

distractorsEs.A: Degrading Absolutism: 'always parse / skip error handling' is the fragile optimism that breaks in production.
distractorsEs.B: Good-Manners Control: asking the model for 'always valid JSON' isn't a guarantee; without validation, a failure slips through unchecked.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: a larger model doesn't eliminate 429s, timeouts, or malformed JSON; the problem is one of integration.

questions.trap: B trusts the model's good will instead of validating; the control is defensive, and it lives in the client.

questions.objective: Core software engineering principles (REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, refactoring)
questions.scenario: Claude in a production codebase
questions.stem: When integrating Claude into a production codebase, which practice best supports long-term maintainability?

options.text: Keep prompts only in a chat window, outside the repository.
Skip code review on the integration to move faster.
Raise temperature to give the integration more flexibility.
Commit prompts and integration code to version control and review changes like any other code.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Software Engineering Foundations' (version control, code review, SDLC). Prompts and integration glue code are software artifacts: they get versioned and reviewed like any other code, which gives traceability and reversibility. D is the maintainability practice; leaving them out of the repo or unreviewed introduces silent risk.

distractorsEs.A: Anti-practice: prompts outside version control have no history and no review; they get lost and drift apart.
distractorsEs.B: Absolutism/risk: skipping code review for speed sacrifices quality and error detection.
distractorsEs.C: Irrelevant Knob: temperature has nothing to do with maintainability or the SDLC.

questions.trap: A/B opt for fragile speed; maintainability comes from versioning and reviewing like code.

questions.objective: Core software engineering principles (REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, refactoring)
questions.scenario: A 2,000-line monolithic script
questions.stem: A monolithic 2,000-line prompt-and-glue script has become unmaintainable. The sound engineering response is to:

options.text: Refactor it into modular, testable components with clear boundaries.
Leave it as-is, since it currently works.
Feed the entire script to a larger model on each run to compensate.
Delete the version history to reduce clutter.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Software Engineering Foundations' (refactoring). An unmaintainable monolith is addressed with a refactor: modularize into testable components with clear responsibilities. A is the engineering answer. Neither leaving it alone, nor delegating to a larger model, nor deleting history resolves the structural debt.

distractorsEs.B: Shortcut: 'it works' ignores the growing cost of maintaining a fragile monolith.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea/irrelevant: the model doesn't refactor your architecture; the problem is structural.
distractorsEs.D: Nonsense/risk: deleting the history destroys traceability without touching maintainability at all.

questions.trap: C brings in the model where the problem is one of code structure, not capability.

questions.objective: Design considerations for Claude applications (instruction interpretation across interfaces, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugin management)
questions.scenario: Different behavior across interfaces
questions.stem: The same assistant behaves differently through the API, Claude Desktop, and claude.ai. The most likely cause is that:

options.text: The model itself is broken.
Instructions and system context are configured differently across those interfaces; align the instruction placement per interface.
Temperature differs and temperature governs how obediently instructions are followed.
A larger model is needed to behave consistently.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Application Design' (instruction interpretation across interfaces). Different surfaces (API, Desktop, claude.ai) place and apply instructions differently; aligning where and how instructions are placed explains and fixes the divergence. B attacks the real design cause.

distractorsEs.A: Defeatist: 'the model is broken' avoids the analysis; the cause is per-interface configuration.
distractorsEs.C: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause/Irrelevant Knob: the clause 'temperature governs obedience' is false; temperature governs sampling.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: a larger model doesn't unify different configurations across interfaces.

questions.trap: C names a real parameter and attributes a false effect to it (obedience); always verify what the knob actually does.

questions.objective: Design considerations for Claude applications (instruction interpretation across interfaces, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugin management)
questions.scenario: Untrusted content alongside instructions
questions.stem: An app concatenates untrusted user content directly into the same block as its trusted system instructions. The core design flaw is that:

options.text: The model is too small to handle the input.
max_tokens is set too low for the combined text.
There is no content boundary between trusted instructions and untrusted input, enabling injection; separate and clearly mark them.
The temperature is too high.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Application Design' (content boundaries). Mixing untrusted input with trusted instructions in the same block erases the content boundary and enables prompt injection. C names the flaw and the fix: separate and clearly mark the untrusted content. It's a boundary-design problem, not one of size or parameters.

distractorsEs.A: Model-Scaling Panacea: model size doesn't create the missing content boundary.
distractorsEs.B: Micro-optimization/Knob: max_tokens has no relation to separating trusted from untrusted content.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant Knob: temperature doesn't defend against the mixing of untrusted content.

questions.trap: A/B/D go after parameters; the flaw is one of design (content boundary), and only C touches it.

questions.objective: Design considerations for Claude applications (instruction interpretation across interfaces, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugin management)
questions.scenario: Output consumed by downstream code
questions.stem: An integration needs Claude's output to be reliably consumed by downstream code. The best design is to:

options.text: Accept free-form prose and extract fields with regex later.
Ask the model to 'always output valid JSON' and trust it without checking.
Raise the temperature so the output has more variety.
Define a clear output schema and validate the response against it, parsing defensively.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Application Design' (schema design / structured output). For reliable consumption by code, you design an output schema and validate the response against it, with defensive parsing. D is the robust pattern. Trusting free-form prose or the model's 'good will' produces intermittent parsing failures.

distractorsEs.A: Fragile/Micro-optimization: regex over free-form prose is brittle and breaks with formatting variations.
distractorsEs.B: Good-Manners Control: 'always valid JSON' without validation isn't a guarantee; the failure slips through unchecked.
distractorsEs.C: Irrelevant Knob: more variety (temperature) worsens the structural consistency you need.

questions.trap: B substitutes a mechanism (schema + validation) with a request to the model; never trust without validating.

questions.objective: Design considerations for Claude applications (instruction interpretation across interfaces, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugin management)
questions.scenario: A long session contaminated by stale turns
questions.stem: A long-lived assistant session accumulates unrelated prior turns that confuse new requests. Good design calls for:

options.text: Session hygiene: scope, reset, or summarize context so stale turns don't contaminate new tasks.
Always keep the entire session history forever.
A larger model so it can remember everything better.
A higher temperature to shake off the old context.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Application Design' (session hygiene). Old, irrelevant turns contaminate new tasks; the correct design scopes, resets, or summarizes context so stale material doesn't interfere. A is session hygiene. Accumulating everything or upgrading the model makes the bloat worse instead of solving it.

distractorsEs.B: Degrading Absolutism: 'keep entire session forever' is the extreme that causes the problem (bloat/drift).
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: more capability doesn't clean up contaminated context; it drags it along all the same.
distractorsEs.D: Irrelevant Knob: temperature doesn't remove old turns from the context.

questions.trap: B is the 'never delete anything' extreme; session hygiene is exactly the opposite.

questions.objective: Design considerations for Claude applications (instruction interpretation across interfaces, content boundaries, schema design, session hygiene, plugin management)
questions.scenario: Several plugins with different versions
questions.stem: An application depends on several plugins/integrations with differing versions. Sound design manages this by:

options.text: Automatically installing the latest of everything, always.
Tracking plugin dependencies and their versions explicitly.
Ignoring versions entirely to keep things simple.
Switching to a larger model to absorb incompatibilities.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Application Design' (plugin management). Dependencies with mismatched versions are managed by making them explicit and controlled, like any software dependency. B gives reproducibility and avoids breakage from silent changes. Auto-updating everything or ignoring versions invites incompatibilities.

distractorsEs.A: Degrading Absolutism: 'always the latest' introduces untested changes and breaks compatibility.
distractorsEs.C: Fragile: ignoring versions guarantees failures that are hard to diagnose.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: the model doesn't resolve plugin dependency conflicts.

questions.trap: A and C are the extremes (everything new / no control at all); explicit version management is the middle path.

questions.objective: Configuration management for Claude components (CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning, plugin dependencies)
questions.scenario: A subtle break after a model update
questions.stem: A production app breaks subtly after an automatic model update changed behavior. To prevent this, the team should:

options.text: Always auto-upgrade to the newest model as soon as it ships, regardless of testing.
Raise the temperature to absorb behavior changes.
Pin a specific model version so behavior is stable, and test before upgrading.
Remove the model from the app to avoid updates.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Configuration Management' (model version pinning). Behavior changes between versions break apps that don't pin a version. Pinning a version stabilizes behavior and allows testing before upgrading. C is the config-management practice; auto-upgrading without testing is exactly what caused the break.

distractorsEs.A: Degrading Absolutism: 'always auto-upgrade regardless of testing' is the extreme that caused the problem.
distractorsEs.B: Irrelevant Knob: temperature doesn't stabilize a model version change.
distractorsEs.D: Escape Hatch: removing the model eliminates the feature instead of managing the version.

questions.trap: A is the reflex of 'always the newest'; the control is pinning a version and testing before upgrading.

questions.objective: Configuration management for Claude components (CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning, plugin dependencies)
questions.scenario: A bad prompt edit with no rollback
questions.stem: Prompts evolve over time, and a bad edit degraded quality with no way to roll back. The fix is to:

options.text: Keep only the latest prompt in a shared document.
Ask the model to remember the previous prompt.
Switch to a different model.
Version prompts like code so changes are tracked and reversible.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Configuration Management' (prompt versioning). A prompt with no history can't be reverted when an edit makes it worse. Versioning prompts like code gives traceability and rollback. D resolves the cause; keeping only the latest version or asking the model to 'remember' doesn't provide reversibility.

distractorsEs.A: Anti-practice: 'only the latest' has no history; there's nothing to revert to.
distractorsEs.B: Good-Manners Control/anthropomorphizing: the model is not your prompt version-control system.
distractorsEs.C: Model-Scaling Panacea: switching models doesn't recover the prompt's previous version.

questions.trap: B treats the model as a repository; prompt versioning is a mechanism, not a request.

questions.objective: Configuration management for Claude components (CLAUDE.md, settings.json, model version pinning, prompt versioning, plugin dependencies)
questions.scenario: Consistent Claude Code configuration in the repo
questions.stem: A team wants consistent, versioned configuration for how Claude Code behaves across a repository. The right place for it is:

options.text: Committed CLAUDE.md and settings.json in the repository, under version control.
Each developer's individual memory of the rules.
A temporary chat message at the start of each session.
A larger model that infers the team's conventions.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Configuration Management' (CLAUDE.md, settings.json). Consistent, versioned Claude Code configuration lives in committed files — CLAUDE.md and settings.json — under version control, so the whole repo shares and tracks the rules. A is the right place; each person's own memory or an ephemeral message don't provide consistency.

distractorsEs.B: Inconsistent: each developer's own 'memory' is neither shared nor versioned configuration.
distractorsEs.C: Ephemeral: a chat message doesn't persist or get versioned in the repo.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: the model doesn't substitute for explicit, versioned configuration.

questions.trap: B/C place the config somewhere it neither persists nor gets shared; the repo's files do both.

questions.objective: Functional and infrastructure requirements based on business requirements and solution architecture
questions.scenario: Before architecting the integration
questions.stem: Before architecting a Claude integration, the most important first step is to:

options.text: Pick the biggest model and start coding immediately.
Translate the business requirements into functional and infrastructure requirements that guide the solution architecture.
Maximize token usage on every call to ensure quality.
Skip requirements gathering to save time.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Understanding Requirements.' Solution architecture starts by translating business needs into functional and infrastructure requirements, which then drive the technical decisions. B does that analysis. Picking a model and coding, or maximizing token usage, puts the implementation before the problem.

distractorsEs.A: Model-Scaling Panacea/premature: picking the biggest model and coding skips defining the problem.
distractorsEs.C: Micro-optimization/irrelevant: 'more tokens' isn't a requirement; it doesn't define the solution.
distractorsEs.D: Shortcut: skipping requirements gathering guarantees building the wrong solution.

questions.trap: A puts the tool before the requirement; business needs get translated first.

questions.objective: Systems life cycle management (develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems)
questions.scenario: After deployment
questions.stem: After deploying a Claude application to production, ongoing responsibility across the systems life cycle includes:

options.text: Considering the system finished at launch.
Never changing anything again to avoid risk.
Operating and maintaining it — monitoring, updating, and managing changes over time.
Switching to a larger model periodically for no particular reason.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Systems Life Cycle.' A system doesn't end at launch: the life cycle includes operating and maintaining it — monitoring, updating, and managing changes — on an ongoing basis. C captures that. 'Done at launch' or 'never change anything' ignore the operation and maintenance phases.

distractorsEs.A: Shortcut: treating launch as the end ignores operation and maintenance.
distractorsEs.B: Degrading Absolutism: 'never change anything' freezes the system and blocks necessary maintenance.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: switching models 'just because' is not life-cycle management.

questions.trap: A and B are the extremes (finished / frozen); the life cycle is about operating and maintaining.

questions.objective: Claude Code Operation (3.1%) — Claude Code core components (Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory), features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode), the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration.
questions.scenario: A CLAUDE.md that bloats in a monorepo
questions.stem: A monorepo's root CLAUDE.md has grown to hundreds of lines, mixing short global conventions with framework-specific rules for the web app, the API, and the infrastructure code. Every session now starts with a large chunk of context that is mostly irrelevant to the file the developer is actually touching. What is the most effective way to reduce this without losing the framework-specific guidance?

options.text: Move the framework-specific guidance into .claude/rules/ files scoped with paths globs, so each set of rules only enters context when Claude actually touches a matching file — keeping only short, global conventions in CLAUDE.md.
Split CLAUDE.md into separate files and pull them back in with @ imports, since imported files are only loaded into context when Claude actually needs them.
Leave CLAUDE.md as a single file, but add an instruction asking Claude to only pay attention to the section relevant to the current task.
Switch the team to a model with a larger context window so the full CLAUDE.md fits more comfortably in every session.

questions.explanationEs: Tests 'Claude Code Operation' on the context axis: Rules versus CLAUDE.md and imports. The scenario states the classic bloat problem — framework-specific content that always gets loaded, even though it's rarely relevant to the file actually being touched. A is the correct architectural answer: .claude/rules/ with path globs loads on demand, only when Claude touches a file matching the glob, leaving CLAUDE.md with just the short, global conventions. B is the domain's finest trap: its @ imports SOUND like lazy loading because of the 'since…' clause, but it's false — imported files load in full, all the same, at session start. Checking that clause as a factual claim is what separates the correct option from the most dangerous distractor.

distractorsEs.B: Falsehood in the Subordinate Clause: the reason the option gives — 'since imported files are only loaded when needed' — is factually false. @ imports load in full at session start, exactly as if they were pasted into the file; they don't save a single token of context.
distractorsEs.C: Good-Manners Control: asking Claude to 'only pay attention' to one section is a natural-language request about a file that has already loaded in full regardless; it doesn't reduce the context consumed, it just hopes for good behavior.
distractorsEs.D: Model-Scaling Panacea: a larger context tolerates more bloat, but it doesn't fix the fact that most of that content is irrelevant noise for the current task; the cause (content loaded without need) remains untouched.

questions.trap: The trap is B: it looks like the 'clean' solution because it organizes the file into smaller pieces, and its own justification sounds technical and reasonable — but that justification is the lie you have to catch.

questions.objective: Claude Code Operation (3.1%) — Claude Code core components (Rules, Skills, Commands, Agents, Agent Memory), features (session management, built-in and custom slash commands, headless mode, streaming mode, auto-mode), the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, repository initialization, and settings.json configuration.
questions.scenario: Guaranteeing that terraform apply gets blocked
questions.stem: A security lead wants to guarantee that Claude Code can never run terraform apply inside the infrastructure repository — not just discouraged from it, but technically blocked before the command executes, in every session and every permission mode. Which configuration actually guarantees this?

options.text: Add a bolded instruction to the project's CLAUDE.md: 'NEVER run terraform apply. This is critical.'
Raise the model's temperature so risky commands become statistically less likely to be chosen.
Switch the team to a larger, more capable model that makes fewer risky suggestions.
