They know how to configure Claude Code for a team: CLAUDE.md hierarchy, .claude/rules/ with globs, skills with frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools), and MCP servers in .mcp.json with environment variable expansion. They design MCP tool interfaces with descriptions that differentiate similar tools and return structured errors (errorCategory, isRetryable) instead of generic failures. They enforce structured output with tool_use + JSON Schema, know tool_choice (auto/any/forced), and know when a retry will NOT help. And, above all, they apply tradeoff judgment: choosing the intervention proportionate to the problem (programmatic enforcement when compliance must be deterministic; prompt/few-shot when the root cause is a fuzzy decision boundary) instead of the most sophisticated solution.
certs.notFor: This isn't for someone who has only used Claude as a casual chat or copilot without building on the API. It isn't for anyone looking for ML/training content: fine-tuning, RLHF, Constitutional AI, embeddings, vector databases, and the model's internal architecture are explicitly out of scope. It's also not for DevOps/infra: hosting and deployment of MCP servers, AWS/GCP/Azure configurations, rate limits, pricing, OAuth, and API key rotation are out. And it isn't for anyone looking for vision, computer use, or streaming: all out of scope.

domains.title: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
objectives: Task Statement 1.1: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution
Knowledge of: The agentic loop lifecycle: sending requests to Claude, inspecting stop_reason ("tool_use" vs "end_turn"), executing requested tools, and returning results for the next iteration
Knowledge of: How tool results are appended to conversation history so the model can reason about the next action
Knowledge of: The distinction between model-driven decision-making (Claude reasons about which tool to call next based on context) and pre-configured decision trees or tool sequences
Skills in: Implementing agentic loop control flow that continues when stop_reason is "tool_use" and terminates when stop_reason is "end_turn"
Skills in: Adding tool results to conversation context between iterations so the model can incorporate new information into its reasoning

Skills in: Avoiding anti-patterns such as parsing natural language signals to determine loop termination, setting arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism, or checking for assistant text content as a completion indicator
Task Statement 1.2: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns
Knowledge of: Hub-and-spoke architecture where a coordinator agent manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing
Knowledge of: How subagents operate with isolated context—they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history automatically
Knowledge of: The role of the coordinator in task decomposition, delegation, result aggregation, and deciding which subagents to invoke based on query complexity
Knowledge of: Risks of overly narrow task decomposition by the coordinator, leading to incomplete coverage of broad research topics
Skills in: Designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline
Skills in: Partitioning research scope across subagents to minimize duplication (e.g., assigning distinct subtopics or source types to each agent)

Skills in: Implementing iterative refinement loops where the coordinator evaluates synthesis output for gaps, re-delegates to search and analysis subagents with targeted queries, and re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient
Skills in: Routing all subagent communication through the coordinator for observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow
Task Statement 1.3: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning
Knowledge of: The Task tool as the mechanism for spawning subagents, and the requirement that allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke subagents
Knowledge of: That subagent context must be explicitly provided in the prompt—subagents do not automatically inherit parent context or share memory between invocations
Knowledge of: The AgentDefinition configuration including descriptions, system prompts, and tool restrictions for each subagent type
Knowledge of: Fork-based session management for exploring divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline
Skills in: Including complete findings from prior agents directly in the subagent's prompt (e.g., passing web search results and document analysis outputs to the synthesis subagent)
Skills in: Using structured data formats to separate content from metadata (source URLs, document names, page numbers) when passing context between agents to preserve attribution
Skills in: Spawning parallel subagents by emitting multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response rather than across separate turns
Skills in: Designing coordinator prompts that specify research goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedural instructions, to enable subagent adaptability
Task Statement 1.4: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns
Knowledge of: The difference between programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) and prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering
Knowledge of: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate
Knowledge of: Structured handoff protocols for mid-process escalation that include customer details, root cause analysis, and recommended actions

Skills in: Implementing programmatic prerequisites that block downstream tool calls until prerequisite steps have completed (e.g., blocking process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID)
Skills in: Decomposing multi-concern customer requests into distinct items, then investigating each in parallel using shared context before synthesizing a unified resolution
Skills in: Compiling structured handoff summaries (customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action) when escalating to human agents who lack access to the conversation transcript
Task Statement 1.5: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization
Knowledge of: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them
Knowledge of: Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules (e.g., blocking refunds above a threshold)
Knowledge of: The distinction between using hooks for deterministic guarantees versus relying on prompt instructions for probabilistic compliance
Skills in: Implementing PostToolUse hooks to normalize heterogeneous data formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) from different MCP tools before the agent processes them
Skills in: Implementing tool call interception hooks that block policy-violating actions (e.g., refunds exceeding $500) and redirect to alternative workflows (e.g., human escalation)
Skills in: Choosing hooks over prompt-based enforcement when business rules require guaranteed compliance
Task Statement 1.6: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows
Knowledge of: When to use fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) versus dynamic adaptive decomposition based on intermediate findings
Knowledge of: Prompt chaining patterns that break reviews into sequential steps (e.g., analyze each file individually, then run a cross-file integration pass)
Knowledge of: The value of adaptive investigation plans that generate subtasks based on what is discovered at each step
Skills in: Selecting task decomposition patterns appropriate to the workflow: prompt chaining for predictable multi-aspect reviews, dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation tasks
Skills in: Splitting large code reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution

Skills in: Decomposing open-ended tasks (e.g., "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase") by first mapping structure, identifying high-impact areas, then creating a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
Task Statement 1.7: Manage session state, resumption, and forking
Knowledge of: Named session resumption using --resume <session-name> to continue a specific prior conversation
Knowledge of: fork_session for creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches
Knowledge of: The importance of informing the agent about changes to previously analyzed files when resuming sessions after code modifications
Knowledge of: Why starting a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results
Skills in: Using --resume with session names to continue named investigation sessions across work sessions
Skills in: Using fork_session to create parallel exploration branches (e.g., comparing two testing strategies or refactoring approaches from a shared codebase analysis)
Skills in: Choosing between session resumption (when prior context is mostly valid) and starting fresh with injected summaries (when prior tool results are stale)
Skills in: Informing a resumed session about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis rather than requiring full re-exploration
domains.html:
Why it's worth 27%

It's the largest domain in the CCAR-F because it's the one that decides whether an agentic system reaches production or stays a demo. Everything else on the exam — tools, MCP, prompts, context — exists to serve the loop: if the loop is closed incorrectly, if the coordinator distributes work poorly, or if a business rule involving money gets "guaranteed" with a sentence in the system prompt, the system fails in expensive, intermittent ways. Anthropic isn't testing whether you can write a while loop; it's testing whether you know where each guarantee lives: what gets delegated to the model's judgment and what gets locked down in code.

The business decision this domain represents is exactly that: autonomy or determinism? The model contributes adaptability (deciding which tool to call, when to stop, how to decompose an open-ended problem); code contributes guarantees (this operation doesn't run unless identity verification has passed). The competent architect doesn't pick a side: they know that verifying identity before a refund is a hook, and that calibrating when to escalate is a prompt with explicit criteria and few-shot examples. The candidate who confuses the two axes fails the exam's most expensive questions, because the distractors are designed exactly around that confusion.

Official objectives

Task Statement 1.1: Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution In practice: implementing the flow control that continues while stop_reason == "tool_use" and ends at "end_turn", reinjecting tool_result blocks into the history; and recognizing termination anti-patterns (parsing natural language, using an iteration cap as the primary mechanism, detecting assistant text as "it's done now").

Task Statement 1.2: Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns In practice: designing hub-and-spoke (everything passes through the coordinator), decomposing the task to cover the full problem space, partitioning scope across subagents without duplication, and iterating (the coordinator evaluates the synthesis, detects gaps, re-delegates, and re-synthesizes).

Task Statement 1.3: Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning In practice: using the Task tool (requires "Task" in allowedTools), passing context explicitly in the subagent's prompt — it inherits nothing — configuring AgentDefinition (description, system prompt, tool restriction), and parallelizing by emitting several Task calls in a single response.

Task Statement 1.4: Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns In practice: programmatically blocking process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID, decomposing multi-topic requests and investigating each one in parallel, and compiling structured handoffs (customer ID, root cause, amount, recommended action) for the human who doesn't see the transcript.

Task Statement 1.5: Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization In practice: PostToolUse to normalize heterogeneous formats (Unix timestamps vs. ISO 8601 vs. numeric codes) before the model sees them; intercepting outgoing tool calls to block policy violations (refunds > $500) and redirect to escalation; and choosing a hook over a prompt when compliance must be guaranteed.

Task Statement 1.6: Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows In practice: choosing prompt chaining (fixed pipeline) for predictable multi-aspect reviews and dynamic decomposition for open-ended research; splitting a large code review into a per-file pass plus a cross-file integration pass to avoid attention dilution.

Task Statement 1.7: Manage session state, resumption, and forking In practice: --resume <session-name> to pick up a named investigation, fork_session to branch from a shared baseline, and identifying when starting fresh with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results.

Key concepts

1. The agentic loop and the stop_reason contract

The loop is a state contract, not a heuristic. Each iteration: you send messages + tools → you receive a Message with stop_reason → the value of stop_reason decides whether there's another round.

  • "tool_use" → Claude requested one or more tools. You execute them, return tool_result blocks, and call again.
  • "end_turn" → Claude finished on its own. You exit the loop and present the response.

Other values that exist in the Messages API and are worth recognizing even though the guide focuses on the two above: max_tokens (truncated response), stop_sequence, refusal, pause_turn (server-tool loop), and model_context_window_exceeded. Official rule: a stop_reason is not an error — it arrives in an HTTP 200; errors are 4xx/5xx.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5"

TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "get_customer",
        "description": (
            "Verify a customer's identity and retrieve their account record. "
            "Input: email OR phone OR customer_id. Returns a verified customer_id, "
            "account status and entitlements. Call this BEFORE any order or refund "
            "operation. Do NOT use it to look up orders — use lookup_order for that."
        ),
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "email": {"type": "string"},
                "phone": {"type": "string"},
                "customer_id": {"type": "string"},
            },
        },
    },
    # lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human ...
]

def run_agent(user_message: str, max_iterations: int = 25) -> str:
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": user_message}]

    for _ in range(max_iterations):          # circuit breaker, NO el criterio de parada
        response = client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL,
            max_tokens=2048,
            system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,
            tools=TOOLS,
            messages=messages,
        )

        # 1) El turno del assistant SIEMPRE entra al historial, tal cual llegó
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})

        # 2) El contrato: solo continúa si stop_reason == "tool_use"
        if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
            return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")

        # 3) Ejecutar TODAS las tools pedidas y devolver los resultados
        #    en UN SOLO mensaje user (si van en mensajes separados, se degrada
        #    el uso de tools en paralelo)
        tool_results = []
        for block in response.content:
            if block.type != "tool_use":
                continue
            try:
                content = execute_tool(block.name, block.input)
                tool_results.append({
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id,
                    "content": content,
                })
            except ToolFailure as exc:
                tool_results.append({
                    "type": "tool_result",
                    "tool_use_id": block.id,
                    "content": str(exc),
                    "is_error": True,      # el error viaja DENTRO de la conversación
                })

        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})

    raise RuntimeError("Iteration cap hit — investigar, no es una salida normal")

Three nuances that separate those who know from those who guess:

  • max_iterations is a circuit breaker, not the stopping mechanism. The guide explicitly flags "setting arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism" as an anti-pattern. The cap exists so a bug doesn't burn through budget; if the loop ends because of the cap, that's an incident, not a normal termination. (In the Agent SDK the equivalent is max_turns, which counts only turns that use a tool and has no limit by default.)
  • tool_result blocks must go back into the history, not into a log. The model reasons about the next step based on the accumulated history. If you "summarize" the tool's result in natural language instead of returning the tool_result block with its tool_use_id, you break the correlation and lose hard information.
  • Tool errors are data, not exceptions. is_error: true inside the tool_result lets the model decide (retry, switch tools, explain to the user). A raise in your code kicks it out of the loop and wastes its recovery capacity.

Termination anti-patterns the exam uses as distractors: parsing the model's output for phrases like "I'm finished" or "done"; checking whether the content includes text (Claude can emit text and a tool_use in the same turn); using the iteration count as the primary criterion.

2. Model-driven decisions vs. a preconfigured decision tree

A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths. An agent is a system where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and its use of tools. The exam makes you choose: when the number of steps is impossible to predict and there's no fixed path, the model-driven loop wins; when the sequence is fixed, a pipeline (prompt chaining) is cheaper, more testable, and faster to debug. A "routing classifier" that preselects tools by keyword is a decision tree in disguise: it resolves which tools are available, not in what order they get called, and that nuance is literally the trap in an official question.

3. Hub-and-spoke: coordinator and subagents

The canonical architecture of Scenario 3 (Multi-Agent Research System): a coordinator decomposes, delegates, aggregates, and decides; subagents execute. All communication between subagents passes through the coordinator — not for theoretical observability, but because it's the only point where you can centralize error handling, information-flow control, and traceability.

Properties the exam assumes you already know:

  • The subagent does NOT inherit the parent's context. It sees neither the history, nor the tool results, nor the coordinator's system prompt. The only parent→subagent channel is the prompt string of the Task tool. Whatever it needs (prior findings, URLs, decisions) has to be written there, explicitly.
  • The coordinator needs "Task" in allowedTools. Without it, it can't spawn anything — it's cause #1 of "Claude ignores my subagent."
  • Parallelism = multiple Task calls in ONE single response from the coordinator, not across successive turns. If the coordinator emits a Task, waits for the result, then emits another, you've serialized the pipeline and lost the advantage.
  • The subagent returns a distilled summary (typically ~1,000–2,000 tokens), not its transcript. That's the whole point: isolating verbose context.
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    # "Task" habilita el spawn de subagentes desde el coordinador
    allowed_tools=["Task", "Read", "Grep", "Glob"],
    agents={
        "web-researcher": AgentDefinition(
            description=(
                "Searches the public web for primary sources on a subtopic. "
                "Use when the coordinator needs external evidence with URLs."
            ),
            prompt=(
                "You are a web research specialist. For every finding return a JSON "
                "object: {claim, evidence_excerpt, source_url, publication_date}. "
                "Never merge two sources into one claim."
            ),
            tools=["WebSearch", "WebFetch"],   # scope acotado al rol
            model="sonnet",
        ),
        "doc-analyst": AgentDefinition(
            description="Analyzes local PDFs/papers and extracts claims with page numbers.",
            prompt="You are a document analyst. Return {claim, excerpt, doc_name, page}.",
            tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],
        ),
        "synthesizer": AgentDefinition(
            description="Merges findings from other agents into a cited report.",
            prompt=(
                "You are a synthesis specialist. You receive findings as structured JSON. "
                "Preserve every claim→source mapping. Annotate conflicting values with "
                "both sources instead of picking one."
            ),
            tools=["verify_fact"],  # cross-role tool acotada, para el caso frecuente
        ),
    },
)

Version nuance (this separates the architect from the memorizer): the exam guide v1.0 names the spawn tool as Task, and that's the correct answer on the exam. In the real SDK the tool was renamed to Agent (Claude Code v2.1.63), although Task still appears in the system:init tool list and in permission_denials. In production, if your hook matches on Task and doesn't fire, this is why. On the exam, answer Task.

4. Decomposition: coverage, not just granularity

The risk the guide explicitly flags is decomposition that's too narrow: the coordinator splits "AI's impact on creative industries" into three visual-arts subtasks, each subagent flawlessly executes its assignment, and the final report ignores music, writing, and film. Every component passed its unit test; the system failed. Diagnosis: when every subagent finishes successfully and the overall result is incomplete, the failure is in the assignment, not the execution.

Design countermeasures:

  • The coordinator's prompt should specify goals and quality criteria ("cover every material branch of the domain; enumerate the branches before assigning"), not a step-by-step procedural recipe. Procedural instructions kill the subagent's adaptability.
  • Partition the scope explicitly (distinct subtopics, or distinct source types per agent) to minimize duplication.
  • Iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates the synthesis looking for gaps → re-delegates to search/analysis with targeted queries → re-invokes synthesis. This repeats until coverage is sufficient. It's the evaluator-optimizer pattern applied to coverage.
  • Dynamic subagent selection: the coordinator decides who to invoke based on query complexity, instead of always running the full pipeline. Scaling effort to complexity is explicit Anthropic doctrine (multi-agent systems consume on the order of 15× the tokens of a chat: over-invocation has a cost).

5. Programmatic enforcement vs. prompt-based guidance — the domain's master axis

When compliance must be deterministic, a prompt won't do. An instruction in the system prompt has a non-zero failure rate. With money, identity, or regulatory compliance on the line, "almost always" is an incident waiting for a date.

Guarantee mechanisms, in order of use:

  1. Prerequisite gate / interception hook (PreToolUse): blocks the tool call before it executes.
  2. Forced tool_choice ({"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}) to guarantee that a specific tool gets called first.
  3. Server-side MCP validation: the tool rejects the input if the prerequisite is missing.
from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher

VERIFIED = {"customer_id": None}   # estado del proceso, fuera del modelo

async def enforce_refund_policy(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    tool = input_data["tool_name"]
    args = input_data["tool_input"]

    # Gate 1 — orden obligatorio: nada de órdenes/reembolsos sin identidad verificada
    if tool in ("lookup_order", "process_refund") and not VERIFIED["customer_id"]:
        return {
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
                "permissionDecision": "deny",
                "permissionDecisionReason": (
                    "Identity not verified. Call get_customer first and obtain a "
                    "verified customer_id before any order or refund operation."
                ),
            }
        }

    # Gate 2 — política de negocio: reembolsos > $500 no los ejecuta el agente
    if tool == "process_refund" and args.get("amount", 0) > 500:
        return {
            "hookSpecificOutput": {
                "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
                "permissionDecision": "deny",
                "permissionDecisionReason": (
                    "Refunds above $500 require human approval. Call escalate_to_human "
                    "with a structured handoff summary instead."
                ),
            }
        }

    return {}   # {} = permitir sin cambios


options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    hooks={"PreToolUse": [HookMatcher(matcher="lookup_order|process_refund",
                                      hooks=[enforce_refund_policy])]}
)

Details the exam may touch on: permissionDecisionReason goes back to the model — that's why the denial message must tell it what to do instead (redirect to escalation), not just "denied." And the precedence order among hook decisions is deny > defer > ask > allow: a single deny is enough to block.

The mirror side: PostToolUse for normalization. Different MCP servers return dates as Unix timestamps, as ISO 8601, and statuses as numeric codes. Normalizing that before the model reads it eliminates an entire class of reasoning errors (and avoids spending tokens teaching it to convert formats in the prompt).

from datetime import datetime, timezone

STATUS = {1: "pending", 2: "shipped", 3: "delivered", 4: "returned"}

async def normalize_order_data(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    if input_data["tool_name"] != "lookup_order":
        return {}

    out = dict(input_data["tool_response"])

    if isinstance(out.get("created_at"), (int, float)):        # Unix → ISO 8601
        out["created_at"] = datetime.fromtimestamp(
            out["created_at"], tz=timezone.utc
        ).isoformat()

    if isinstance(out.get("status"), int):                     # código → etiqueta
        out["status"] = STATUS.get(out["status"], "unknown")

    # Además: recortar el payload a los campos relevantes (los 40+ campos del
    # lookup contaminan el contexto sin aportar nada al razonamiento)
    keep = {"order_id", "created_at", "status", "total", "items"}
    out = {k: v for k, v in out.items() if k in keep}

    return {"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
                                   "updatedToolOutput": out}}

Architectural bonus almost nobody mentions: hooks run in your process, not inside the context window. They consume no tokens. Moving determinism and data cleanup into hooks is free in context and costly only in code.

6. Prompt chaining vs. dynamic decomposition

  • Prompt chaining (fixed pipeline): the task splits cleanly into subtasks known in advance. Guide example: reviewing a PR by analyzing each file individually and then a cross-file integration pass. You trade latency for accuracy.
  • Dynamic decomposition (orchestrator-workers): subtasks are not predefined; the orchestrator determines them at runtime based on what it discovers along the way. Guide example: "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase" → map the structure → identify high-impact areas → a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies surface.

The exam signal for choosing chaining: contradictory or superficial feedback in a review spanning many files. That's attention dilution, and it isn't fixed with a larger context window (the model already had the 14 files). It's fixed by specializing passes.

7. Structured handoff in escalation

The human you escalate to doesn't see the transcript. A valid handoff is an object, not a sentence: verified customer ID, root-cause analysis, refund amount, recommended action, and what's already been tried. It's the same philosophy as the structured error propagation in Domain 5: the recipient needs data to decide, not a label ("complex case") that forces them to reconstruct the case from scratch.

8. Sessions: resume, fork, and "starting fresh with a summary"

  • --resume <session-name>: continues a specific, already-named conversation. Use it when the prior context is still mostly valid.
  • fork_session: creates an independent branch from a shared baseline; the original session stays intact and the fork gets its own session ID. Canonical case: analyze the codebase once and from that same baseline explore two testing strategies or two refactors in parallel, without cross-contamination.
  • Starting a new session with an injected structured summary: when the prior tool results are stale (the code changed under the agent's feet). Resuming while dragging along reads of files that no longer exist that way is worse than starting clean: the model reasons about a world that's no longer there.
  • If you resume after modifying files, tell the agent exactly which files changed so it re-analyzes in a targeted way, instead of forcing a full re-exploration.
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage

# 1) Baseline compartido: una sola exploración cara del codebase
async for msg in query(prompt="Map the payment module and its test coverage",
                       options=ClaudeAgentOptions(allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"])):
    if isinstance(msg, ResultMessage):
        baseline = msg.session_id

# 2) Rama A y rama B desde el MISMO baseline — fork_session siempre acompaña a resume
branch_a = ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline, fork_session=True)   # estrategia: unit tests
branch_b = ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=baseline, fork_session=True)   # estrategia: integration tests

Real-world trap (the guide doesn't ask about this, but it explains production failures): resume derives the history path from cwd; if you resume from a different directory, you get a new, empty session instead of the expected history.

Worked examples

Example 1 — The agent skips verification in 12% of cases

Situation. Scenario 1 (Customer Support). Telemetry: in 12% of tickets the agent skips get_customer and calls lookup_order using only the name the customer gave. Consequence: misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds.

Mediocre candidate. Reinforces the system prompt: "verification with get_customer is MANDATORY before any order operation." Or adds few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first. Sounds responsible, and the 12% drops… to 4%.

Competent candidate. Puts in a programmatic prerequisite gate: a PreToolUse hook denies lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID, and the denial reason tells the model what to do instead.

Why. There's money and there's identity involved. The requirement is deterministic compliance, and a prompt instruction has a non-zero failure rate by construction. Going from 12% to 4% isn't a solution: it's the same bug, just harder to reproduce. A "routing classifier" that enables subsets of tools doesn't work either: it controls availability, not order.

Example 2 — The research report covers only visual arts

Situation. Scenario 3. Topic: "AI's impact on creative industries." All three subagents report success. The final report ignores music, writing, and film. The coordinator's logs show its decomposition: "AI in digital art creation," "AI in graphic design," "AI in photography."

Mediocre candidate. Blames the one below: "the synthesis agent doesn't detect coverage gaps," "the web search agent's queries are too narrow," "the document analysis agent filters too aggressively." All three fix a component that did its job well within the scope it was assigned.

Competent candidate. The failure is one layer up: task decomposition that's too narrow in the coordinator. The fix: a coordinator prompt that requires enumerating the domain's material branches before assigning, explicit scope partitioning by subtopic, and a refinement loop where the coordinator evaluates the synthesis against the list of branches and re-delegates over the gaps.

Why. The evidence is right there in the log: the assignment was already skewed from the start. When every subagent finishes successfully and the aggregate fails, look at whoever divided up the work.

Example 3 — Latency from synthesis with verification (85/15)

Situation. The synthesis agent needs to verify claims while combining findings. Right now it returns control to the coordinator, which invokes the web search agent and re-invokes synthesis: 2-3 round trips per task, +40% latency. The evaluation says: 85% are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics); 15% require deep research.

Mediocre candidate. Gives the synthesis agent access to all the web search tools "so it can manage on its own." Or batches all the verifications and sends them at the end of the pass.

Competent candidate. A scoped cross-role tool: verify_fact for the frequent case (85%), and the complex 15% is still delegated to the web search agent through the coordinator.

Why. The 85/15 distribution is the design instruction. Over-provisioning the synthesis agent with the entire search toolkit degrades its tool selection and breaks the separation of responsibilities (agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them). Batching at the end creates blocking dependencies: later synthesis steps depend on facts verified earlier.

Example 4 — A $1,200 refund on an angry customer's ticket

Situation. Policy: the agent can authorize refunds up to $500. A customer claims $1,200 for a damaged order, with photos. The agent, pressured by the tone, calls process_refund(amount=1200).

Mediocre candidate. Adds to the prompt "NEVER refund more than $500" in all caps with three exclamation points.

Competent candidate. A tool-call interception hook that blocks any process_refund with amount > 500 and returns a reason that redirects to the alternative workflow: calling escalate_to_human with a structured handoff (verified customer ID, root cause "product damaged in transit, photographic evidence attached," requested amount $1,200, recommended action "approve full refund, open a claim with the carrier").

Why. It's a business rule with a financial consequence: it demands a guarantee, not persuasion. And escalation isn't "passing the buck": the human doesn't see the transcript, so the value lives in the structured handoff.

Example 5 — Resuming after the code changed, or starting fresh

Situation. Yesterday a session named perf-investigation mapped the checkout module: 30 files read, three bottlenecks identified. Today, another dev refactored checkout/pricing.py and checkout/cart.py.

Mediocre candidate. --resume perf-investigation and carries on as if nothing happened. The agent reasons over file reads that no longer reflect what's on disk and "remembers" classes that no longer exist.

Competent candidate. Evaluates staleness. If most of the analysis is still valid: resume and explicitly report which files changed, forcing a targeted re-analysis of just those two. If the refactor touched the heart of what was analyzed: a new session with an injected structured summary (the three bottlenecks, the decisions made, the open questions), which is more reliable than dragging along stale tool results.

Why. The session persists the conversation, not the filesystem. A resume doesn't re-read anything on its own: it reinjects what was read back then. The criterion is the validity of the prior context, not convenience.

How the exam asks about this

Verbs and signals that trigger this domain: stop_reason, "loop", "iteration", "coordinator", "subagent", "Task tool", allowedTools, "decomposed the topic into…", "hook", PostToolUse, "prerequisite", "programmatic", "deterministic", --resume, fork_session, "parallel subagents".

Item patterns, with their logic:

  1. Failure metric + operation with an irreversible consequence → enforcement. "In 12% of cases the agent skips…", "occasionally leading to incorrect refunds." Any option that starts with "Enhance the system prompt…" or "Add few-shot examples…" is dead on arrival. Look for a hook, prerequisite gate, or forced tool_choice.
  2. Fuzzy decision boundary → prompt. The same scenario, the symmetric question: the agent escalates poorly, resolves poorly, chooses badly among plausible alternatives. Here the correct answer is explicit criteria + few-shot, and the distractor is infrastructure (a trained classifier, a routing layer). This pair of axes is the whole exam: two questions on the same scenario with correct answers pointing in opposite directions.
  3. "Each subagent completes successfully" + incomplete overall result → go up a layer. The distractors blame the executor (synthesis, search, doc analysis). The answer points at whoever did the assigning. Lethal variant: fabricated evidence — an option invents an "overly restrictive relevance criterion" that the prompt never mentioned.
  4. A percentage split in the prompt (85/15, 60/40) → least-privilege design. The distribution tells you what to optimize and what to leave alone. "Give it all the tools" is always wrong.
  5. Invented feature. Flags and objects that don't exist, written with credible syntax. Scan for 3 seconds before reasoning. This domain's real surface: stop_reason (tool_use / end_turn), tool_result + is_error, tool_choice (auto / any / forced), the Task tool, allowedTools, AgentDefinition, PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks, --resume, fork_session, /compact. Whatever isn't on this list, be suspicious of it.
  6. Half-right. An option starts well (retry with backoff inside the subagent — correct) and ends badly (returning a generic "search unavailable" — destroys the context the coordinator needed). In this exam, the final clause rules. Read the whole option before falling in love with the first line.
  7. Confusing context capacity with attention quality. "Switch to a model with a bigger window so the 14 files fit." They already fit. The cure for dilution is splitting into passes, not enlarging the window.

The decoder's golden rule applied to D1: the correct option is usually an almost-literal paraphrase of a "Skills in:" bullet from the corresponding task statement. If an option sounds copied from the guide, it probably is.

Common mistakes

  1. Ending the loop by parsing text. Looking for "done," "I'm finished," or checking whether there are text blocks. → The only criterion is stop_reason. Claude can emit text and tool_use in the same turn.
  2. Using the iteration cap as the stopping criterion. → It's a circuit breaker. If the loop exits because of the cap, there's a bug, not a happy ending.
  3. Not returning tool_result blocks to the history (logging them, or summarizing them in prose). → The model reasons over the history; the tool_result block with its tool_use_id is the vehicle. Without it, there's no correlation.
  4. Returning multiple tool_result blocks in separate user messages. → All of a turn's results go in a single user message; separating them degrades parallel tool use.
  5. Throwing an exception when a tool fails. → The error goes inside the tool_result with is_error: true. That way the model can recover; an exception kicks it out of the loop.
  6. Assuming the subagent inherits the coordinator's context. → It inherits nothing: no history, no tool results, no system prompt. The only channel is the Task tool's prompt. It's the #1 real-world implementation error, and the guide repeats it three times.
  7. Forgetting "Task" in allowedTools. → Without it, the coordinator can't spawn subagents. Symptom: "Claude ignores my subagent."
  8. Spawning subagents across successive turns thinking it's parallelism. → Parallelism = multiple Task calls in one single response from the coordinator.
  9. Shielding business rules with the system prompt. → Money, identity, mandatory ordering, and policy compliance demand a hook / gate / forced tool_choice. The prompt has a non-zero failure rate.
  10. Using hooks where the problem is one of judgment. The mirror of the previous error: putting in a hook to "escalate complex cases" doesn't work, because "complex" isn't a computable condition. That's where explicit criteria + few-shot belong.
  11. Writing procedural coordinator prompts ("step 1: search; step 2: analyze; step 3: synthesize"). → Specify goals and quality criteria; procedural detail kills the subagent's adaptability.
  12. Blaming the component that executed well. → If every subagent fulfilled its assignment and the aggregate fails, the failure is in the decomposition/assignment.
  13. Resuming sessions with stale tool results. → If the code changed, either explicitly report the modified files or start fresh with an injected structured summary. Dragging along stale reads is worse than starting clean.
  14. Believing fork_session forks the filesystem. → It forks the conversation. The files are shared and real; if the branch writes, it writes for real.

Checklist

  • I can write from memory an agentic loop that continues on stop_reason == "tool_use" and ends on "end_turn", returning all tool_result blocks in a single user message.
  • I know why an iteration cap is a circuit breaker and not a termination criterion, and I can name the other two stopping anti-patterns.
  • I know how to propagate a tool failure as is_error: true inside the tool_result instead of throwing an exception, and can explain what the model gains from that.
  • I can explain why a subagent sees nothing from the coordinator and what literally has to go into the Task tool's prompt.
  • I know the coordinator needs "Task" in allowedTools and can diagnose the symptom when it's missing.
  • I know how to parallelize subagents (multiple Task calls in one response) and can explain why doing it across successive turns isn't parallelism.
  • I distinguish AgentDefinition.description (decides when it gets delegated to) from prompt (decides how the subagent works).
  • Faced with a coverage failure where every subagent is green, I know to point at the coordinator's decomposition as the root cause, not the executor.
  • I can decide in 10 seconds whether a problem demands a deterministic guarantee (hook, gate, forced tool_choice) or judgment calibration (explicit criteria + few-shot), and justify it.
  • I know how to implement a PreToolUse that blocks a policy violation and redirects to the alternative workflow, with a reason the model can act on.
  • I know how to implement a PostToolUse that normalizes heterogeneous formats and trims verbose payloads before they enter context.
  • I know how to choose between prompt chaining (fixed steps) and dynamic decomposition (open-ended research), and can explain why a 14-file review gets split into a per-file pass plus an integration pass.
  • I know why a larger context window doesn't fix attention dilution.
  • I know when to use --resume, when to use fork_session, and when to open a new session with an injected structured summary.
  • I know how to compile a structured escalation handoff for a human who has no access to the transcript.

The block that returns a tool's output to the history, correlated by `tool_use_id`; supports `is_error: true`.
Claude reasons at runtime about which tool to call, as opposed to a decision tree fixed in code.

All communication between subagents passes through the coordinator, never subagent to subagent.
The subagent-spawning mechanism; the coordinator needs `"Task"` in `allowedTools` to use it.
A subagent's configuration: `description` (decides when it gets delegated to), `prompt` (its system prompt), and tool restriction.
The subagent doesn't see the parent's history; it only receives what's written into the `Task` tool's prompt.
How the coordinator splits the problem; if the split is narrow, the result's coverage will be incomplete.
A pipeline of fixed steps known in advance; trades latency for accuracy.
The orchestrator generates subtasks at runtime based on what it discovers.
When processing many files at once, depth degrades and contradictory findings appear.

domains.html:
Why it's worth 18%

This domain measures one thing, with many faces: the quality of the interface between the model and your backend. An agent doesn't fail because Claude "doesn't understand"; it fails because you gave it two tools with six-word descriptions and expect it to guess which one to use, because your MCP server returns "Operation failed" for a timeout and for a policy violation alike, or because the synthesis subagent has access to all 18 tools in the system and decides to run web searches. The exam treats tool design as API design: a contract with a name, a description, an input/output contract, error semantics, and scope. The difference from a traditional API is who the client is: the client is an LLM, and its only documentation is what you wrote in description.

The business decision it represents is one of reliability and cost. Incorrect tool selection produces misidentified accounts and erroneous refunds (Scenario 1), incomplete reports (Scenario 3), and latency round-trips nobody budgeted for (Scenario 3, Q9). Bad error semantics produces wasted retries on non-retryable errors and suppresses the information the coordinator needed to recover. And MCP is the layer that decides whether your team integrates Jira once or five times. At 18% of the exam — roughly 11 items out of 60 — the domain is also embedded across four of the six scenarios (1, 3, 4, and, via .mcp.json, 2). It isn't the heaviest domain, but it is the most cross-cutting: almost any D1 item about subagents touches tool distribution, and almost any D5 item about error propagation touches the shape of the error your tool returns.

Official objectives

Task Statement 2.1: Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries

  • Knowledge of: Tool descriptions as the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection; minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection among similar tools
  • Knowledge of: The importance of including input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundary explanations in tool descriptions
  • Knowledge of: How ambiguous or overlapping tool descriptions cause misrouting (e.g., analyze_content vs analyze_document with near-identical descriptions)
  • Knowledge of: The impact of system prompt wording on tool selection: keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations

→ In practice: you'll be given a log where the agent called the wrong tool, plus options proposing few-shot, a router, consolidating tools, or rewriting the descriptions. If the prompt says the descriptions are minimal or nearly identical, the description is the answer. And you'll be asked to recognize that a system prompt with keywords ("analyze the documents…") can hijack selection toward a similarly-named tool.

Key concepts

1. The tool description is the selection mechanism (tool description as selection surface)

When you send tools in a request, the API builds a system prompt with the definitions in JSON Schema. That's all the model knows about your backend. It doesn't see your code, doesn't see your database, doesn't know that lookup_order hits a different microservice than get_customer. It reads name, description, and input_schema, and decides.

Hence the operating rule the exam rewards again and again: if two tools get confused, the root cause is the description, and the cheapest, highest-leverage fix is rewriting it (official Q2). Anthropic's documentation recommends extremely detailed descriptions — at least 3–4 sentences per tool — covering: what it does, what inputs it accepts and in what format, what it returns, and when to use it versus the similar alternative.

Minimal description (the one that causes the exam's bug):

{ "name": "get_customer",  "description": "Retrieves customer information" }
{ "name": "lookup_order",  "description": "Retrieves order details" }

Description with explicit boundaries (the fix):

{
  "name": "lookup_order",
  "description": "Look up a single order by its order number. Use this whenever the user references an order, purchase, shipment, delivery, or return of a specific item — e.g. 'where is order #12345', 'my package never arrived', 'I want to return the jacket I bought'. Input: order_id, format ORD-XXXXXXXX or a bare 8-digit number (both accepted). Returns: order status, line items, dates, shipping carrier and tracking, refund eligibility. Does NOT return customer profile, billing address, or loyalty tier — for those use get_customer. If the user gives a name or email instead of an order number, call get_customer first to obtain the verified customer_id, then list their orders.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "order_id": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Order number, e.g. 'ORD-48210937' or '48210937'."
      }
    },
    "required": ["order_id"]
  }
}

The nuance that separates those who know: the description doesn't just say what the tool does; it says what it does NOT do and who to delegate to in that case. That "boundary" block is exactly what the guide calls boundary explanations.

Two sibling techniques the guide names explicitly:

  • Renaming to eliminate overlap. analyze_content and analyze_document with near-identical descriptions always get misrouted. The cure isn't a few-shot: it's renaming analyze_content → extract_web_results with a web-specific description. The name is the first semantic signal the model reads (use namespacing: github_list_prs, slack_send_message).
  • Splitting a generic tool into purpose-specific tools. An analyze_document(document, instruction) that does everything forces the model to encode intent in a free-form string. Splitting it into extract_data_points, summarize_content, and verify_claim_against_source gives three defined input/output contracts and eliminates decision ambiguity.

The system prompt can hijack selection. Objective 2.1 says it plainly: keyword-sensitive instructions create unwanted associations. If your system prompt says "always analyze the retrieved documents carefully," don't be surprised when the model calls analyze_document on web search results. Facing a misrouting, two surfaces get reviewed: the descriptions and the system prompt's wording.

2. Structured errors: isError + metadata (structured tool errors)

A tool error is not an HTTP exception. It's data that travels inside the conversation. In the Messages API the tool_result block carries is_error: true; in the MCP spec, the result of tools/call carries isError: true (camelCase — MCP speaks JSON-RPC 2.0). In both cases the request is still a 200: the failure is interpreted by the model, not your try/except. Hard MCP rule: tool execution failures are reported with isError: true in the result, not as a JSON-RPC protocol error; the model never sees a protocol error.

And here's the heart of objective 2.2: a uniform error ("Operation failed") destroys the agent's ability to recover because it collapses four distinct semantics into one:

CategoryExampleisRetryableWhat the agent should do
Transienttimeout, 503, rate limittrueRetry (locally, with backoff)
Validationorder_id with an invalid formatfalse (but correctable)Fix the input and retry with a different value
Businessrefund outside the 30-day windowfalseDo not retry. Explain to the customer in plain language, offer an alternative, or escalate
Permissionthe agent lacks scope for process_refundfalseEscalate to a human / request authorization

MCP server returning a structured error (TypeScript, official MCP SDK):

import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/mcp.js";
import { z } from "zod";

const server = new McpServer({ name: "billing", version: "1.0.0" });

server.registerTool(
  "process_refund",
  {
    title: "Process refund",
    description:
      "Issue a refund against a verified order. Requires a customer_id already verified via get_customer. " +
      "Input: customer_id, order_id, amount_cents (integer), reason. Returns: refund_id and settlement date. " +
      "Refunds are only permitted within 30 days of delivery; outside that window this tool returns a business " +
      "error and the case must be escalated. Do NOT use this tool to quote or estimate a refund — use quote_refund.",
    inputSchema: {
      customer_id: z.string(),
      order_id: z.string(),
      amount_cents: z.number().int().positive(),
      reason: z.string(),
    },
  },
  async ({ customer_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason }) => {
    try {
      const order = await billing.getOrder(order_id);

      if (daysSince(order.deliveredAt) > 30) {
        return {
          isError: true,                       // el modelo VE esto
          content: [{
            type: "text",
            text: JSON.stringify({
              errorCategory: "business",
              isRetryable: false,              // no gastes reintentos
              code: "REFUND_WINDOW_EXPIRED",
              message:
                "Order was delivered 47 days ago; the refund window is 30 days.",
              customerExplanation:
                "This order is outside our 30-day refund window, but a store credit " +
                "or a warranty replacement may still apply.",
              suggestedAction: "offer_store_credit | escalate_to_human",
            }),
          }],
        };
      }

      const refund = await billing.refund({ customer_id, order_id, amount_cents, reason });
      return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(refund) }] };

    } catch (e) {
      if (e instanceof TimeoutError) {
        return {
          isError: true,
          content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify({
            errorCategory: "transient",
            isRetryable: true,
            retryAfterSeconds: 5,
            message: "Billing service timed out after 10s.",
            attempted: { order_id, amount_cents },
          })}],
        };
      }
      throw e;
    }
  }
);

Three architect-level nuances:

  • customerExplanation isn't decoration. Objective 2.2 explicitly asks for "customer-friendly explanations for business rule violations so the agent can communicate appropriately." Without it, the agent improvises — or worse, retries.
  • Local recovery before propagating. A subagent should absorb transients itself (retry) and propagate to the coordinator only what it can't resolve, accompanied by what it tried and what partial results it has. Propagating everything upward saturates the coordinator; suppressing everything downward blinds it. (Crosses with D5.3.)
  • Empty result ≠ error. search_documents("quantum llamas") returning [] is a success: the query ran and there were no matches. Marking that as an error triggers useless retries; marking a timeout as an empty result makes the system report "no information exists" about a topic that does exist. This pair is an exam question waiting to happen.

3. Tool distribution and tool_choice (tool scoping / least privilege)

The guide's numeric rule: 18 tools on an agent instead of the 4–5 its role needs degrades selection reliability — every extra tool adds decision complexity — and agents with tools outside their specialty also misuse them (the classic case: the synthesis agent attempting web searches). The correct design is a tool set per role:

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Task"],   # el coordinador necesita "Task" para spawnear
    agents={
        "web-search": AgentDefinition(
            description="Searches the public web for sources on an assigned subtopic. Use for open-web discovery.",
            prompt="You research one assigned subtopic. Return findings as structured claim/evidence/source_url/published_at records.",
            tools=["WebSearch", "WebFetch"],          # 2 tools, no más
        ),
        "doc-analysis": AgentDefinition(
            description="Analyzes provided documents (PDF/markdown) and extracts data points with page-level attribution.",
            prompt="Analyze only the documents given in your prompt. Never search the web.",
            tools=["Read", "Grep", "extract_data_points"],
        ),
        "synthesis": AgentDefinition(
            description="Merges findings from other agents into a cited report. Does not gather new sources.",
            prompt="Combine the findings included in your prompt. Preserve every claim→source mapping.",
            tools=["verify_fact"],                    # scoped cross-role tool: cubre el 85% de fact-checks
        ),
    },
)

That verify_fact is the official answer to Q9: when 85% of verifications are simple fact-checks and 15% require deep research, the traffic distribution IS the design instruction. Neither deny the synthesis agent everything (round-trips and +40% latency), nor give it all the web tools (over-provisioning that violates separation of responsibilities). You give it a scoped tool for the common case, and the complex 15% still goes through the coordinator.

Sibling technique: replacing generic tools with restricted alternatives. fetch_url(url) lets the agent fetch anything from the internet; load_document(document_url) validates that the URL is a document from the allowed corpus. Less surface, less error, less prompt injection.

tool_choice — the guide names three values (the API also supports none, the default when there are no tools):

ValueSemanticsWhen the exam asks for it
{"type": "auto"}Claude decides whether to call a tool or respond with text. Default when you send tools.Conversation and general-purpose agents
{"type": "any"}Claude must call some tool, chooses whichGuaranteeing structured output when there are multiple extraction schemas and you don't know the document type
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}Claude must call that toolForcing a step to run first (e.g., extract_metadata before the enrichment tools), then continuing in later turns
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    tools=[EXTRACT_METADATA_TOOL, ENRICH_TOOL],
    tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"},  # este turno: metadata sí o sí
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": document_text}],
)
metadata = next(b.input for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use")
# El enriquecimiento se procesa en el SIGUIENTE turno, con tool_choice="auto".

Nuances the mediocre candidate doesn't know:

  • With any or tool, the API does a prefill of the assistant's turn: the model will not emit natural-language text before the tool_use, even if you ask it to.
  • any and tool are not compatible with extended thinking (they return an error). With thinking, only auto / none.
  • Forcing a tool doesn't chain steps: it forces that turn. The sequence gets built across successive turns (that's why the objective says "then processing subsequent steps in follow-up turns").
  • tool_choice: "any" guarantees that it calls a tool, not that the content is correct. The schema eliminates syntax errors, not semantic ones (that's D4).

4. MCP: what it is and what the exam asks about it (Model Context Protocol)

MCP is an open standard (Anthropic, Nov. 2024) for connecting AI apps to external systems: it replaces N×M integrations with a single protocol. Host / client / server architecture over JSON-RPC 2.0, with stdio (local) and Streamable HTTP (remote) transports. Official analogy: "a USB-C port for AI applications." A server exposes three primitives:

PrimitiveWhat it isMethodsWhen the exam picks it
ToolsExecutable functions — the agent does somethingtools/list, tools/callActions and parameterized queries
ResourcesData sources that provide contextresources/list, resources/readContent catalogs: issue summaries, doc hierarchy, DB schema
PromptsReusable templatesprompts/list, prompts/getStandardized workflows the user can invoke

The tools/resources pair is objective 2.4's discriminator. If the agent makes 12 exploratory tool calls just to discover what exists (what issues are there? what tables does the DB have? what docs?), the answer isn't "more tools": it's exposing a resource with the catalog, so the agent sees the inventory without spending calls. Tools = action; resources = visibility.

5. Configuring MCP servers: where it lives and how secrets get in

The guide sets two scopes:

  • Project-level → .mcp.json at the repo root. Goes into version control. It's the mechanism for shared team tooling: everyone who clones the repo gets the server.
  • User-level → ~/.claude.json. Lives in the user's home directory, doesn't travel via git. It's for personal/experimental servers.
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "github": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.githubcorp.internal/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "jira": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@acme/jira-mcp-server"],
      "env": {
        "JIRA_BASE_URL": "${JIRA_BASE_URL:-https://acme.atlassian.net}",
        "JIRA_API_TOKEN": "${JIRA_API_TOKEN}"
      }
    }
  }
}

Environment variable expansion: ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}. That's the canonical mechanism for credentials: the committed file contains the variable's name, never the secret. If a required variable doesn't exist and has no default, the config fails to parse (a loud failure, not a silent one — that's a good thing).

Other facts the exam uses as distractors:

  • All configured servers are discovered on connection and their tools become available simultaneously. There's no "activate the server on the fly": a project server and a personal one coexist in the same session.
  • MCP tool names: mcp__<server>__<tool> (relevant when writing hook matchers or permission allowlists).
  • Don't build what already exists. For standard integrations (Jira, GitHub, Postgres, Slack), the guide says: use the existing community MCP server; reserve custom servers for workflows specific to your team. An item offering "write your own Jira MCP server" is almost always the over-engineering distractor.
  • Poor descriptions on MCP tools make the agent prefer the built-ins. If your search_codebase MCP (which indexes semantically) has a one-line description, Claude will use Grep because it knows what Grep does. The fix: enrich the MCP description explaining capabilities and outputs — the same principle from 2.1, applied to competing with native tools.

6. Built-in tools: Grep, Glob, Read, Write, Edit, Bash

The mental contract the exam expects, unambiguously:

NeedToolReason
Search content (function name, error message, import)GrepSearches inside files
Search paths/names (**/*.test.tsx, every .tf)GlobPattern matching over paths
Read a whole file / write it wholeRead / WriteWhole-file operations
Targeted modification anchored to unique textEditRequires the anchor text to be unique
Edit fails because the anchor text appears multiple timesRead + WriteReliable fallback documented in the guide
Run commands, tests, buildsBash—

And the exploration pattern the guide turns into a skill: understanding a codebase incrementally. Grep to locate entry points → Read to follow imports and trace the flow → repeat. Never "read all the files first" (exhausts context and produces the degradation from D5.4). To trace a function's usage across wrapper modules: first identify all the exported names, then search for each name across the codebase — because the re-export changes the name, and a single Grep for the original name finds nothing.

Worked examples

Example 1 — Misrouting between get_customer and lookup_order (Scenario 1)

Situation. In production, when a user types "check my order #12345," the agent calls get_customer 30% of the time. Both tools have one-line descriptions ("Retrieves customer information" / "Retrieves order details") and both accept similar-looking identifier strings.

Mediocre candidate. Adds 5–8 few-shot examples to the system prompt showing "order → lookup_order." Or builds a routing layer that parses the input and preselects the tool by keyword and identifier pattern.

Competent candidate. Rewrites both descriptions with input format, query examples, edge cases, and explicit boundaries ("does NOT return order data — for that use lookup_order"). Then measures. If the misrouting persists after that, then review the system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions, and only after that consider few-shot.

Why. Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism: the root cause is stated literally ("minimal descriptions"). Few-shot adds tokens to every request without touching the cause. The router bypasses the model's natural-language understanding and has to be maintained forever. The exam calls this a low-effort, high-leverage fix.

Example 2 — The out-of-window refund (Scenario 1)

Situation. process_refund returns {"error": "Operation failed"} for everything: payment service timeouts, malformed order_id, and refunds outside the 30-day window. Metric: the agent retries every failure 3 times (policy failures included) and then tells the customer "there was a technical error, try again later" when the truth is their purchase is 47 days old.

Mediocre candidate. Adds to the system prompt: "if a refund fails, do not retry more than once and explain the error to the customer."

Competent candidate. Restructures the error payload: errorCategory: "business", isRetryable: false, code: "REFUND_WINDOW_EXPIRED", a customerExplanation in customer-facing language, and suggestedAction. Transients do carry isRetryable: true with retryAfterSeconds. The agent now retries only what's retryable and correctly communicates what's policy.

Why. A prompt can't infer the category of an error that arrives without one — you're asking the model to guess a distinction your server knows and didn't communicate. The information has to exist in the data before any instruction can use it. Also, customerExplanation is exactly what 2.2 asks for.

Example 3 — The synthesis agent that runs web searches (Scenario 3)

Situation. The multi-agent research system has 18 tools registered globally and every subagent inherits them. The synthesis agent, which should be combining findings, starts firing off web_search on its own: it duplicates the search agent's work, pulls in unverified sources, and adds 40% latency.

Mediocre candidate. Adds to the synthesis agent's prompt: "You must not perform web searches."

Competent candidate. Restricts tools in each subagent's AgentDefinition to its role (search: 2 tools; doc-analysis: 3; synthesis: 1). Gives synthesis just one scoped cross-role tool, verify_fact, because measurement shows 85% of its verification needs are simple fact-checks. The complex 15% is still delegated through the coordinator.

Why. It's this domain's guarantee vs. judgment axis: removing the tool is deterministic; asking it not to use it is probabilistic. And the scoped verify_fact is the answer provided — neither over-provisioning (official option C of Q9) nor round-trips for everything.

Example 4 — 12 tool calls to discover which issues exist (Scenario 4)

Situation. Your project-management MCP server exposes get_issue(id), search_issues(query), and list_projects(). Agents spend 10–15 calls per session just discovering which issues are open and in which projects, before doing anything useful. Context runs out mid-task.

Mediocre candidate. Adds a list_all_issues() tool that returns everything, or raises the result limit on search_issues.

Competent candidate. Exposes an MCP resource with the catalog: issues://open/summary with a compact index (id, title, project, status, assignee, last update). The agent reads the catalog once and then calls get_issue only on the relevant ids.

Why. Objective 2.4, verbatim: "Exposing content catalogs as MCP resources to give agents visibility into available data without requiring exploratory tool calls." Tools = action; resources = visibility. Adding a tool that dumps everything has the same context cost as the 12 calls, just packed into one.

Example 5 — The new team member doesn't have the Jira server (Scenario 2/4)

Situation. You configured the Jira MCP server and it works. A coworker clones the repo and Claude Code sees no Jira tools at all. On top of that, your config has the token hardcoded and someone proposes committing it "so it works for everyone."

Mediocre candidate. Sends a Slack message with the JSON so everyone pastes it into their own ~/.claude.json. Or commits the file with the token.

Competent candidate. Moves the definition to .mcp.json at the repo root (project scope, versioned) and replaces the secret with ${JIRA_API_TOKEN} via environment variable expansion. Each dev exports their own token; nobody commits a secret. Personal experimental servers stay in ~/.claude.json. And for Jira, uses the existing community MCP server instead of writing one.

Why. It's the decoder's scope flip: ~/ doesn't travel via git. The requirement "make it work for the whole team on clone" fixes the scope at project level, exactly like .claude/commands/ in D3.

How the exam asks about this

Domain 2's signal verbs and phrases. "Tool selection reliability," "misroutes / calls X instead of Y," "minimal descriptions," "near-identical descriptions," "structured error," "retry," "the coordinator receives," "each subagent has access to N tools," "guarantee the model calls a tool," "available to every developer when they clone," "without committing secrets," "exploratory tool calls," "search the codebase for."

Pattern A — the tool-selection bug. Prompt: logs show misrouting + a hint about the descriptions. Typical distractors: few-shot (correct as a technique, applied to the wrong cause), a keyword routing layer (over-engineering), consolidating both tools into one generic lookup_entity (a valid architectural decision, but disproportionate as a "first step"). Answer: rewrite descriptions with input format, examples, edge cases, and boundaries.

Pattern B — error semantics. Prompt: a tool fails; you have to decide what it returns. Distractors: retry with backoff that ends up returning a generic message ("half-right practice": the final clause kills the option); catching the error and returning an empty result marked as success (suppresses the signal); propagating the exception and terminating the workflow. Answer: structured error context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives).

Pattern C — tool distribution. Prompt: a specialized agent misuses a tool outside its role, or has 18 tools. Distractors: "give it access to every tool so it doesn't have to round-trip" (over-provisioning), "have it batch the verifications and send them at the end" (creates blocking dependencies), "speculatively cache whatever it might need" (predicting the unpredictable). Answer: a tool set scoped by role + one scoped cross-role tool if the data justifies the frequent case.

Pattern D — MCP configuration. Prompt: "shared with the team when they clone" vs. "personal experiment"; or "without committing the token." Distractors: invented features (an mcp-config.yaml, a settings.mcp with an array of servers), inverted scope (~/.claude.json for the shared case). Answer: project-scoped .mcp.json + ${VAR}; personal → ~/.claude.json.

Pattern E — built-in tools. Prompt: "find all the callers of processPayment" (→ Grep), "find all the test files" (→ Glob with **/*.test.tsx), "Edit fails because the text appears 4 times" (→ Read + Write). Recurring distractor: using Bash with raw grep/find, or "read all 40 files and then decide."

Tying back to the decoder. The three distractor archetypes that hit hardest in D2 are: over-engineering (router, custom server, classifier), half-right practice (starts with the correct retry and ends up returning a generic message), and fabricated feature (config files that don't exist). And the master axis applies here just the same: if the requirement is guarantee (a subagent can't perform web searches, a tool must run first), the answer is structural — restricted tools, forced tool_choice. If it's judgment (which of two similar tools to use), the answer is informational — better descriptions.

Practice items (prompt stated in English, like the real exam):

Q. Your MCP server's search_documents tool returns {"results": []} both when the backend times out and when the query legitimately matches no documents. The research coordinator reports "no information available" on topics that are well covered in the corpus. What change most directly fixes this? A. Return isError: true with errorCategory: "transient", isRetryable: true and the attempted query on access failures, while keeping the empty array (no isError) for successful queries with zero matches. Explanation: objective 2.2 requires distinguishing an access failure from a valid empty result. Collapsing them makes an infrastructure failure get reported as a truth about the world. Any option that "always retries when the list comes back empty" is incorrect: it would retry legitimately empty queries forever.

Q. A document-processing agent must always run extract_metadata before any enrichment tool. Which configuration guarantees this on the first turn? A. tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on that request, then continue with tool_choice: "auto" in follow-up turns. Explanation: "any" guarantees it calls some tool, not that tool. Forcing the tool applies to the current turn; the rest of the sequence is handled in later turns. And with a forced tool the model doesn't emit text beforehand (prefill).

Common mistakes

  1. Believing few-shot fixes misrouting caused by minimal descriptions. Few-shot is powerful and is still the wrong answer here: it doesn't touch the root cause and adds tokens to every request. Fix: descriptions first (3–4 sentences, inputs, examples, edge cases, boundaries); few-shot is for genuine ambiguity, not for an informational void.
  2. Writing descriptions that say what the tool does but not what it does NOT do. Without the boundary clause ("for customer profile data use get_customer"), two adjacent tools keep competing. Fix: always include "when to use the other one."
  3. Returning uniform errors ("Operation failed"). Collapses transient / validation / business / permission into a single semantic and the agent can't decide. Fix: errorCategory + isRetryable + a readable description (+ a customer-facing explanation for business errors).
  4. Retrying business errors. A refund outside the window doesn't improve on the third attempt. Fix: explicit isRetryable: false, plus a suggested alternative action.
  5. Marking a timeout as a successful empty result (or, the reverse, marking a legitimate [] as an error). Fix: an empty result is success; an access failure is isError with a category. They're distinct states and the coordinator acts differently on each.
  6. Propagating every error to the coordinator. The subagent should recover locally from transients and propagate only what it can't resolve — along with what it attempted and any partial results. Fix: local recovery + structured propagation.
  7. Trusting the prompt to stop a subagent from using a tool. "Don't perform web searches" has a non-zero failure rate. Fix: don't give it the tool (restrict tools in the AgentDefinition). Enforcement > instruction.
  8. Over-provisioning "just in case." Giving the agent 18 tools because "it might need them sometime" degrades selection among the 4 it actually uses. Fix: least privilege, and a scoped cross-role tool only when the data shows a frequent need.
  9. Confusing tool_choice: "any" with forcing a specific tool. any = some; {"type":"tool","name":"..."} = that one. And neither one chains steps: both apply to the current turn.
  10. Believing forced tool + extended thinking works. any and tool aren't compatible with extended thinking (error). Only auto/none.
  11. Putting the shared MCP server in ~/.claude.json. It doesn't travel via git; the coworker who clones doesn't have it. Fix: .mcp.json at the repo root (project scope).
  12. Committing the token in .mcp.json. Fix: ${GITHUB_TOKEN} / ${VAR:-default} — environment variable expansion; the versioned file never contains the secret.
  13. Building a custom MCP server for a standard integration (Jira, GitHub, Postgres). Fix: use the community server; reserve custom builds for workflows specific to your team.
  14. Assuming the agent will prefer your powerful MCP tool over Grep. With a poor description, it won't: Grep has known semantics. Fix: describe the MCP tool's capabilities and outputs in detail.
  15. Solving "I want to see what's available" with more tools instead of a resource. Fix: a content catalog as an MCP resource; tools for acting.
  16. Using Glob to search content or Grep to search file names. Grep = inside the file; Glob = the path. And when Edit can't find a unique anchor: Read + Write, not blindly retrying Edit with more context.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat it means

input_schemainput parameter specJSON Schema with the parameters the tool accepts (type, properties, required, enum).

Misroutingwrong-tool callThe model calls the wrong tool because two descriptions overlap or are minimal.
Tool splittingone generic tool → several specific onesSplitting a generic tool into several with a defined purpose and contract (analyze_document → extract_data_points + summarize_content + verify_claim_against_source).
isError / is_errorfailure flagA marker on the tool result telling the model the execution failed; in MCP it's isError, in the Messages API is_error. The request is still a 200.

Scoped tool accessrole-limited toolsetEach agent gets only the tools for its role (4–5, not 18).
