Checklist

If you can't check one of these, you don't have a handle on D2.

  1. I can explain why a tool's description — not the system prompt or few-shot — is the primary selection mechanism, and write a 3–4 sentence description with inputs, examples, edge cases, and boundaries.
  2. I know how to diagnose a misrouting: I review descriptions and the system prompt's keyword-sensitive wording before touching anything else.
  3. I know when to rename a tool to eliminate overlap and when to split a generic one into purpose-specific tools, and I can give the canonical example of each.
  4. I can write an MCP error payload with isError: true + errorCategory + isRetryable + a readable description + a customer explanation, and say what the agent will do with each category.
  5. I distinguish, without hesitation, an access failure (timeout → isError, retryable) from a valid empty result ([] → success), and I know what each confusion breaks.
  6. I know when a subagent should recover locally and when to propagate to the coordinator, and what that propagation must include (failure type, what it tried, partials, alternatives).
  7. I can justify with numbers why 18 tools degrade selection compared to 4–5, and I know how to restrict tools per AgentDefinition.
  8. I know when to grant a scoped cross-role tool (the 85/15 from Q9) instead of denying everything or granting full access.
  9. I distinguish tool_choice: "auto" vs. "any" vs. {"type":"tool","name":...}, and I know forcing a tool applies to that turn, not to the sequence.
  10. I know forcing a tool does a prefill (no text beforehand) and that any/tool aren't compatible with extended thinking.
  11. I know where a shared MCP server goes (.mcp.json, versioned) and a personal one (~/.claude.json), and why the latter never reaches my coworker on clone.
  12. I know how to put credentials in .mcp.json with ${VAR} without committing the secret.
  13. I distinguish MCP tools (action) from MCP resources (catalog/context) and I know a catalog exposed as a resource eliminates exploratory tool calls.
  14. I know when to use a community MCP server instead of writing my own, and why a poor MCP description makes the agent prefer Grep.
  15. I choose without thinking between Grep (content), Glob (paths), Read/Write (whole file), Edit (unique anchor), and Read+Write (fallback when the anchor isn't unique), and I explore a codebase incrementally, never reading it whole.

domains.html:
Why it's worth 20%

This domain measures a concrete transition: turning Claude Code from a personal tool into team infrastructure. A lone developer can live with instructions in their home directory, commands only they have, and decisions made on the fly. A team of twenty can't. Once configuration has to travel via git, apply conditionally based on which file gets touched, and run without a human inside a CI pipeline, every decision has measurable consequences: conventions that don't get applied, context wasted on irrelevant rules, jobs that hang waiting for input, duplicate comments on every PR.

The exam treats it that way. The guide's 29 task statements distribute 20% of the blueprint — roughly 12 items out of 60 — and two of the bank's six scenarios (Scenario 2, Code Generation with Claude Code, and Scenario 5, Claude Code for CI) have this domain as primary, plus a third (Scenario 4, Developer Productivity) where it shows up secondarily. Statistically, it's the domain most likely to appear twice on your exam form.

The engineering decision it represents is the most-cited in the domain and also the most misunderstood: is this context, or is it applied configuration? A CLAUDE.md suggests — it's delivered to the model as text and the model decides what to do with it. A permission rule or a hook enforces — the client evaluates it, not the model, and it has no failure rate. The rest of the domain (where the file lives, when it loads, who sees it) are corollaries of that distinction. The candidate who internalizes it also gets half of Domain 1 right, because it's the same axis: deterministic guarantee vs. probabilistic guidance.

Official objectives

The guide's six task statements, verbatim in English, with what they'll actually ask you to do:

  • Task Statement 3.1: Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization → You'll diagnose why an instruction doesn't reach a coworker (it's in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which doesn't travel via git), and decide when to split a monolithic CLAUDE.md into @imports or into .claude/rules/ files. The diagnostic command is /memory.

  • Task Statement 3.2: Create and configure custom slash commands and skills → You'll choose between .claude/commands/ (project, versioned) and ~/.claude/commands/ (personal), and configure skill frontmatter: context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint. And decide skill (on demand) vs. CLAUDE.md (always loaded).

  • Task Statement 3.3: Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading → You'll write rules in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter paths: using globs, and justify why a glob (**/*.test.tsx) beats a per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md when the affected files are scattered across the repo.

  • Task Statement 3.4: Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution → You'll be given a task and will decide: plan mode (large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, multi-file) or direct execution (a single-file bug with a clear stack trace). And you'll use the Explore subagent to isolate verbose discovery.

  • Task Statement 3.5: Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement → You'll correct Claude with concrete input/output examples instead of prose, with tests written before the implementation, with the interview pattern, and you'll decide whether problems go in a single message (they interact) or in separate iterations (they're independent).

  • Task Statement 3.6: Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines → You'll run Claude Code without a human (-p / --print), get parseable output (--output-format json + --json-schema), feed project context via CLAUDE.md, and recognize why an independent instance reviews code better than the session that generated it.

Key concepts

1. The domain's law: context suggests, configuration enforces

The whole of Domain 3 sorts into two columns. On the left, the mechanisms that inject text into the model: CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/, skills, the body of a slash command. They're context. The model reads them and decides. They always have a non-zero failure rate. On the right, the mechanisms the client evaluates before the model acts: permission rules (allow / ask / deny), lifecycle hooks, permission modes. They're enforcement. They don't depend on the model's judgment.

The official documentation states it unambiguously: "An instruction like 'never edit .env' in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee. A PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement." And the operating rule: settings for technical enforcement, CLAUDE.md for behavioral guidance.

Why the distinction exists: CLAUDE.md isn't part of the system prompt. It's delivered as a user message after the system prompt. In other words, it's just one more instruction in the conversation, subject to the model weighing it against everything else. Writing "ALWAYS run the tests before committing" in all caps doesn't change its nature.

The nuance that separates those who know: on the exam, when the prompt includes a measured failure rate ("in 12% of cases the agent skips…"), a money/identity requirement, or the word guaranteed / must never, the correct answer is never "improve the prompt/CLAUDE.md." It's a hook, a programmatic gate, or a permission rule. When the prompt describes a fuzzy decision boundary (inconsistency, variable format, choosing among plausible alternatives), the correct answer really is context: explicit criteria, examples, rules.

2. The CLAUDE.md hierarchy

The guide defines three levels, and the exam asks about them:

LevelPathWho sees itTravels via git?
User~/.claude/CLAUDE.mdOnly you, across all your projectsNo
Project./CLAUDE.md (root) or ./.claude/CLAUDE.mdThe whole team that clones the repoYes
DirectoryCLAUDE.md in a subdirectoryIncluded on demand, when Claude reads files from that subdirectoryYes

Facts verified in the official documentation that the exam can use as distractors:

  • Files found get concatenated, not overwritten. Claude walks up the directory tree from the cwd and accumulates. There's no "the project CLAUDE.md overrides the user CLAUDE.md."
  • CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories below the cwd don't load at startup: they come in when Claude touches files from there. That's why they're a poor mechanism for conventions that apply to scattered files (see §4).
  • There are two more levels the guide doesn't list but the docs do: managed policy (organization level, non-excludable) and local (./CLAUDE.local.md, personal and gitignored).
  • Target size: under 200 lines per file.
  • After /compact, the project root's CLAUDE.md gets reinjected; nested ones don't.

The exam's canonical scenario: a new team member doesn't get the conventions. Diagnosis: they're in user-level configuration, which by definition isn't shared via version control. Fix: move them to project-level. Verification: the /memory command lists which memory files are loaded in the session and is the official tool for diagnosing inconsistent behavior across sessions or people.

3. @import — modularity, not context savings

Syntax: @path/to/file. Paths relative to the file containing the import (not to the cwd), or absolute. Maximum depth: 4 hops.

# CLAUDE.md  (raíz del monorepo)

Monorepo de pagos. Node 22, pnpm, TypeScript estricto.

@docs/standards/testing.md
@docs/standards/api-conventions.md

Ver @README para el overview y @package.json para los scripts disponibles.

Intended use per the guide (Task 3.1): each package's maintainer selectively includes the standards files relevant to their domain, instead of dragging around one giant CLAUDE.md with everything for everyone.

The nuance that separates: @import organizes, it doesn't save context. Imported files still load at session startup, adding their tokens. If the stated problem is "the CLAUDE.md consumes too much context / loads irrelevant rules," the solution is NOT splitting it into imports: it's .claude/rules/ with paths: (conditional loading) or moving it to a skill (on-demand loading). Confusing "modular" with "cheap" is an exam error waiting to be served.

A parser detail worth knowing: imports inside code spans or code blocks are ignored (`@README` inside backticks is literal text).

4. .claude/rules/ — the only path-conditional loading mechanism

.md files inside .claude/rules/, with optional YAML frontmatter. With paths: (globs) → the rule enters context only when Claude works with files that match. Without paths: → it loads at startup, with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md (in other words, it works as a way to split the CLAUDE.md by topic: testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md).

---
paths:
  - "**/*.test.tsx"
  - "**/*.test.ts"
---

# Convenciones de tests

- React Testing Library, nunca Enzyme.
- Un `describe` por componente exportado; nombres de test en inglés, forma "should …".
- Prohibido `waitFor` con timeout literal: usa `findBy*`.
- Mocks de red con MSW; nunca `jest.mock('axios')`.
---
paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
---

# Terraform

- Todo módulo nuevo declara `required_version` y `required_providers`.
- Nada de `count`; usa `for_each` con claves estables.
- Los secretos vienen de SSM Parameter Store, jamás en `.tfvars`.

Why it exists: two problems at once. (1) Context savings: a repo with rules for React, API, database, and Terraform shouldn't load all four to edit a test. (2) Automatic, deterministic application by file type, not by location.

The nuance that separates — and it's literally an official question (Q6): test files live next to the code they test (Button.test.tsx beside Button.tsx), scattered across the whole repo. A per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md is tied to the directory: you'd have to replicate it across dozens of folders and keep them in sync. A **/*.test.tsx glob captures all of them, wherever they live, with a single file. A convention that crosses directories ⇒ a glob in .claude/rules/. A convention specific to one area of the code ⇒ can live in that subdirectory's CLAUDE.md.

And the other distractor on that same question: putting the conventions into skills. It fails for a precise reason: skills get invoked (by you, or by the model's decision), they don't activate by path match. If the requirement says "Claude should automatically apply the correct conventions," any mechanism that depends on someone deciding to invoke it is disqualified.

5. Slash commands and skills: scope, frontmatter, and isolation

Scope (the domain's cheapest question):

LocationScopeAvailable on cloning the repo?
.claude/commands/review.mdProjectYes — versioned in git
~/.claude/commands/review.mdPersonalNo — lives in the user's home directory
.claude/skills/review/SKILL.mdProjectYes
~/.claude/skills/review/SKILL.mdPersonalNo

Mnemonic rule: the tilde (~/) never travels via git. If the prompt says "available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository," the answer is the repo path. And .claude/config.json with a commands array doesn't exist — it's an invented feature from an official distractor.

A fact from the current documentation worth knowing for the real world (and one that doesn't contradict the guide): custom commands merged with skills. .claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both produce /deploy and work the same way; if they collide, the skill wins. The command's name comes from the directory name (or the file in commands/), not from the frontmatter's name field.

Frontmatter the guide names explicitly:

---
name: analyze-codebase
description: Mapea la estructura del módulo indicado y devuelve un resumen de dependencias.
argument-hint: [module-path]
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---

Analiza el módulo `$ARGUMENTS`.

1. Localiza los entry points con Grep.
2. Sigue los imports con Read para trazar el flujo.
3. Devuelve SOLO: (a) diagrama de dependencias en texto, (b) 5 riesgos, (c) archivos clave.
No incluyas el volcado de los archivos leídos.
  • context: fork — the skill runs in a subagent with isolated context. Its intermediate work (reads, greps, probing) doesn't contaminate the main conversation; only the result comes back. It's the mechanism for skills that produce verbose output (codebase analysis) or exploratory, disposable context (brainstorming alternatives).
  • allowed-tools — the guide describes it as "restrict tool access during skill execution (e.g., limiting to file write operations to prevent destructive actions)." Answer with that reading on the exam. (Production warning: Claude Code's current documentation clarifies that allowed-tools pre-approves tools — it skips the permission prompt — and that the one that removes tools from the pool is disallowed-tools. On an exam item, the guide's wording rules; in your real repo, check which of the two keys you actually need.)
  • argument-hint — an autocomplete hint that tells the developer what parameter is missing when they invoke the skill without arguments.

Skill vs. CLAUDE.md (Task 3.2, final bullet): CLAUDE.md = universal standards, always loaded, a permanent context cost. Skill = task-specific workflow, on demand, near-zero cost until invoked (only its description lives in context). If you find yourself pasting the same five-step playbook into the chat for the third time, that's a skill, not one more section of the CLAUDE.md.

Personalizing without breaking the team: the guide says to create personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with a different name. Overwriting the project skill's name with your personal version is exactly how invisible bugs get generated ("works on my machine").

6. Plan mode vs. direct execution

Plan mode is a read-only permission mode over your source code: Claude reads files, runs read-only shell commands, explores dependencies, and presents an approvable plan — but doesn't edit. You enter it with Shift+Tab (cycling default → acceptEdits → plan), by prefixing a prompt with /plan, or by starting with claude --permission-mode plan. Approving the plan exits the mode and executes.

The guide's criteria, no frills:

Choose plan mode when…Choose direct execution when…
Large-scale changes (restructuring a monolith into microservices)A simple, well-scoped change
There are multiple valid approaches and one must be chosenThe approach is obvious and singular
There are architectural decisions (service boundaries, dependencies)There's no design decision to make
Multi-file modifications (a library migration touching 45+ files)A single file, clear scope
Approaches with different infrastructure requirementsA bug with a clear stack trace; adding a date validation

The nuance that separates — the official distractor (Q5-D) is "start in direct execution and switch to plan mode if unexpected complexity appears." It sounds like agile pragmatism. It fails because the complexity is already declared in the prompt: it isn't something that might emerge. When the requirement says "dozens of files," "service boundaries," "module dependencies," the decision is already made. The other distractor (Q5-C, "direct execution with exhaustive upfront instructions") assumes you already know the correct structure without having explored the code: it's planning without data.

Combined pattern (the guide explicitly calls for it): plan mode for the investigation, direct execution for the implementation. You plan the migration, approve the plan, and execute from there.

The Explore subagent: read-only, with its own context window. Used for phases of verbose discovery ("find all the test files," "trace the dependencies of the refund flow") in multi-phase tasks, so hundreds of lines of greps and reads stay in the subagent and only the summary returns to the main conversation. It's the direct countermeasure against context-window exhaustion during long explorations. (Verified detail: Explore and Plan skip your CLAUDE.md files to keep exploration fast; other subagents do load them.)

7. Iterative refinement: how you correct Claude

Four techniques, each with its trigger. The exam gives you the symptom and expects you to pick the technique.

  1. Concrete input/output examples (2-3). Trigger: "the prose description is interpreted inconsistently." When explaining the transformation in words produces different results each time, a couple of literal input/expected-output examples solve what three paragraphs of prose don't. It's also the cure for poorly handled edge cases: give the test case with the exact input (e.g., the null value in the migration script) and the expected output.
  2. Test-driven iteration. Trigger: "the expected behavior is verifiable." You write the suite first — expected behavior, edge cases, performance requirements — the implementation comes after, and you iterate by sharing the test failures. The test is the objective criterion that replaces "no, not like that."
  3. Interview pattern. Trigger: a domain unfamiliar to you. You ask Claude to ask you questions before implementing, so considerations you didn't anticipate surface (cache invalidation strategy, failure modes, concurrency). It reverses the direction of information flow: instead of you specifying poorly, it interviews you.
  4. One message vs. successive iterations. Trigger: do the problems interact? If the fixes affect each other (changing the data model and the error handling and the function signature), they all go in a single detailed message — fixing them one at a time makes each fix break the previous one. If they're independent (a typo, a missing import, a badly formatted log), sequential iteration.

8. Claude Code in CI/CD

The flag that decides an entire official question (Q10): -p / --print. Without it, claude "…" on a runner sits waiting for interactive input and the job hangs indefinitely. With -p, Claude processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits. That question's distractors are invented features (CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true, --batch) or Unix patches (< /dev/null) that don't address the CLI's real syntax.

Structured output for posting PR comments:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

SCHEMA='{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "findings": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "file":     { "type": "string" },
          "line":     { "type": "integer" },
          "severity": { "type": "string", "enum": ["critical", "major", "minor"] },
          "issue":    { "type": "string" },
          "suggested_fix": { "type": "string" },
          "detected_pattern": { "type": "string" }
        },
        "required": ["file", "line", "severity", "issue", "suggested_fix"]
      }
    }
  },
  "required": ["findings"]
}'

git diff "origin/${BASE_SHA}...HEAD" > /tmp/pr.diff

claude -p "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against the review criteria in CLAUDE.md.
Report ONLY bugs and security issues. Skip style and local convention nits.
Previously reported findings (do NOT repeat them if still open, do NOT re-report if fixed):
$(cat /tmp/prior-findings.json)" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$SCHEMA" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" \
  > /tmp/review.json

jq -c '.structured_output.findings' /tmp/review.json > /tmp/prior-findings.json

jq -c '.structured_output.findings[] | {path: .file, line: .line,
        body: ("**[" + .severity + "]** " + .issue + "\n\n" + .suggested_fix)}' \
  /tmp/review.json \
| while read -r comment; do
    gh api "repos/${GH_REPO}/pulls/${PR_NUMBER}/comments" \
      --method POST --input - <<< "$(jq --arg sha "$HEAD_SHA" '. + {commit_id: $sha, side: "RIGHT"}' <<< "$comment")"
  done

Points the exam might touch on in that block:

  • --output-format accepts text (default), json, and stream-json. With --json-schema (which requires --output-format json), the validated output lands in the payload's structured_output field. That's what makes the result machine-parseable and allows posting inline comments without parsing prose with regex.
  • CLAUDE.md is the project-context mechanism in CI. The guide is explicit: testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria get documented in CLAUDE.md so the instance invoked from the pipeline has them. A CI prompt shouldn't carry 300 lines of embedded conventions.
  • Duplicate comments on re-runs: when the review gets run again after new commits, you have to include the prior findings in the context and instruct Claude to report only what's new or still unresolved. Without that, every push re-comments the same things and the team stops reading the comments.
  • Test generation: pass the existing test files in context so it doesn't propose already-covered scenarios, and document in CLAUDE.md what counts as a valuable test for the team (reduces the flood of trivial tests like getter returns the getter's value).
  • Verified useful flags: --max-turns N (print mode only), --allowedTools (same syntax as permission rules), --resume <session-id> for chaining, and --bare — skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and local CLAUDE.md files: it's what's recommended for reproducibility in CI (without it, -p loads the same configuration as an interactive session).

Session context isolation (the conceptual core of 3.6, and also the basis of Task 4.6): the same session that generated the code is worse at reviewing it than an independent instance. Reason: it retains the generation's reasoning context and is less inclined to question its own decisions — it already "knows" why it wrote what it wrote. A second instance, without that prior reasoning, finds more subtle problems than any instruction along the lines of "now review yourself" or turning on more extended thinking. In CI that translates to: the generation job and the review job are separate invocations, not two turns of the same session.

9. The surface that actually exists (a defense against invented features)

This domain's most profitable distractor archetype is the plausible-sounding flag/file that doesn't exist. Memorize the real surface and every factual item resolves by elimination in three seconds:

Exists: -p / --print · --output-format json|text|stream-json · --json-schema · --allowedTools · --max-turns · --bare · --permission-mode · --resume · fork_session · /memory · /compact · /plan · CLAUDE.md · CLAUDE.local.md · .claude/CLAUDE.md · .claude/rules/*.md (frontmatter paths:) · .claude/commands/*.md · .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (frontmatter context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint) · .claude/settings.json · .mcp.json · ~/.claude.json · the Explore subagent.

Doesn't exist (all have appeared as an official distractor or are obvious variants): CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true · --batch · .claude/config.json with a commands array · --headless · claude review --ci.

Worked examples

Example 1 — The convention that doesn't arrive

Situation. A 9-person team on a Next.js monorepo. In your home directory's CLAUDE.md you've had it documented for months: "use pnpm, never npm" and "every new component ships with co-located tests." They hire Priya. In her first week, Claude Code generates components for her without tests and suggests npm install. You can't reproduce the bug: on your machine it works perfectly.

Mediocre candidate. Writes a Slack message: "remember to tell Claude to use pnpm." Or worse: turns up the volume — rewrites the instruction in ALL CAPS with three exclamation points, still in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.

Competent candidate. Recognizes the bug's signature: works for me, not for the new hire ⇒ it's a configuration scope problem, not a wording one. The instructions live in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user-level), which doesn't travel via version control. Moves them into the project root's CLAUDE.md, commits it, and asks Priya to run /memory to verify which memory files her session loads.

Why. The symptom "behavior differs between people on the same repo" has only one structural cause: something one person has loaded and the other doesn't. /memory is the diagnostic tool the guide names for exactly this.

Example 2 — Conventions that cross directories (official question Q6)

Situation. A codebase with three distinct convention areas: React components (functional + hooks), API handlers (async/await with their own error handling), data models (repository pattern). Tests are co-located (Button.test.tsx beside Button.tsx), scattered across the whole tree, and all must follow the same conventions regardless of where they are.

Mediocre candidate. Consolidates everything into the root CLAUDE.md with four sections and headers, trusting Claude to infer which one applies. Or puts a CLAUDE.md in every subdirectory.

Competent candidate. Four files in .claude/rules/, each with its own glob:

.claude/rules/react.md      →  paths: ["src/components/**/*.tsx"]
.claude/rules/api.md        →  paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]
.claude/rules/models.md     →  paths: ["src/models/**/*.ts"]
.claude/rules/testing.md    →  paths: ["**/*.test.tsx", "**/*.test.ts"]

Why. Two cumulative reasons. (1) Deterministic activation: glob matching is automatic; inference over a monolithic CLAUDE.md's headers isn't (official item option B: "relying on Claude to infer which section applies" — the word infer is what kills it). (2) Location independence: a per-directory CLAUDE.md is tied to the directory, and the tests are scattered across dozens of folders. A single **/*.test.tsx glob covers them all. Bonus: the React rules don't enter context when you're editing Terraform.

And skills (item option C) fail for a different reason: they require invocation. The requirement says automatically.

Example 3 — A library migration across 45 files

Situation. You need to migrate from moment to date-fns across 45 files in a billing service. There are two possible approaches: a compatibility wrapper (fast, technical debt) or a site-by-site rewrite (slow, clean). On top of that, three files deliberately rely on moment's mutability, and they need to be found.

Mediocre candidate. Runs claude "migrate moment to date-fns across the whole repo" in direct execution and approves edits as they come out. By file 20 they discover the mutability pattern, realize the first 20 came out wrong, and redo them. Alternatively: writes a 400-line prompt explaining exactly how each file should end up, without having read the code.

Competent candidate.

  1. Plan mode (Shift+Tab or /plan): Claude reads, maps the 45 usages, identifies the three mutability cases, and compares the two approaches with their tradeoffs. Doesn't touch a line of code.
  2. The verbose discovery phase (locating every usage, tracing imports) is delegated to the Explore subagent, so hundreds of lines of grep and reads don't eat into the main conversation's context window — only the inventory comes back.
  3. Approves the plan and moves to direct execution to implement, with the approach already decided.

Why. It checks all four of the guide's plan-mode boxes: large scale, multi-file, multiple valid approaches, a decision with architectural consequences. And it exemplifies the combined pattern the guide explicitly calls for: plan the migration, then execute the plan. Starting direct and "switching to plan mode if complexity appears" is wrong because the complexity is declared right in the prompt — it isn't hypothetical.

Contrast, same repo, a different task: "the /invoices endpoint blows up with TypeError: cannot read property 'toISOString' of null at line 88 when due_date is null." Clear stack trace, one file, one validation conditional. Direct execution. Entering plan mode here is useless ceremony.

Example 4 — The CI review that hangs, duplicates, and distrusts

Situation. A GitHub Actions pipeline with three accumulated problems: (a) the job claude "Analyze this PR for security issues" hangs and gets killed by the timeout at 60 min; (b) once fixed, the output is prose and the regex-based parser script fails on 1 in 4 PRs; (c) when it finally posts comments, every push re-comments the same 12 findings and the team already ignores them.

Mediocre candidate. (a) Redirects stdin from /dev/null and raises the timeout. (b) Writes a more robust prose parser with more regex. (c) Adds an instruction to the prompt: "don't repeat previous comments" — without giving it access to what those were.

Competent candidate.

  • (a) claude -p. It's the documented non-interactive mode flag. < /dev/null is a shell patch that doesn't address the CLI's syntax, and CLAUDE_HEADLESS / --batch don't exist.
  • (b) --output-format json + --json-schema with a findings schema (file, line, severity, issue, suggested_fix). The validated output comes out in structured_output and gets posted as inline comments without regex. Zero JSON syntax errors by construction.
  • (c) Includes the prior findings in the context of the re-run and instructs: report only findings that are new or still unresolved. The instruction without the data is an order the model can't fulfill: it has no way of knowing what was commented before.

Why. Each fix attacks the layer where the failure lives: execution mode (CLI), data contract (schema), and context (prior findings). And none of the three is "improve the prompt," which is the reflexive answer from the candidate who doesn't read the symptom.

Example 5 — The skill that floods the conversation

Situation. The team has an /analyze-module skill that maps a module's structure: reads 30-40 files, runs greps, follows imports. It works, but after invoking it the main conversation gets so full of file dumps that Claude starts giving inconsistent answers about the work they were doing before. On top of that, a coworker invoked it without arguments and the skill analyzed the entire repo.

Mediocre candidate. Tells the team "only invoke /analyze-module at the start of the session" and adds to SKILL.md the instruction "be concise, don't dump files." And for the missing argument, adds a line of prose: "remember to pass the module."

Competent candidate. Three frontmatter changes:

---
name: analyze-module
description: Mapea estructura y dependencias de un módulo. Devuelve resumen, no volcados.
argument-hint: [module-path]
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
  • context: fork → the skill runs in an isolated subagent; the 40 reads stay there and only the summary returns to the main conversation. Attacks the cause (context contamination), not the symptom.
  • argument-hint: [module-path] → when someone invokes it without arguments, it's shown the missing parameter.
  • allowed-tools: Read, Grep, Glob → the skill is for analysis; it doesn't need to write or execute arbitrary commands (per the guide's reading: it scopes tool access during the skill's execution).

Why. "Ask it to be concise" is context: probabilistic. context: fork is architecture: the isolation doesn't depend on the model obeying. It's the same law from §1, applied to skills.

How the exam asks about this

The prompt's verbs and what they trigger:

Phrase in the promptWhat it's askingWhere to look
"available to every developer when they clone or pull"ScopeA path inside the repo (.claude/…), never ~/
"spread throughout the codebase" / "regardless of location"Conditional loadingGlobs in .claude/rules/, never a per-directory CLAUDE.md
"automatically applies"Deterministic activationRule out anything requiring invocation (skills) or inference
"dozens of files" / "service boundaries" / "multiple valid approaches"Declared complexityPlan mode
"clear stack trace" / "a single validation check"Bounded scopeDirect execution
"the job hangs" / "waiting for interactive input"Non-interactive mode-p / --print
"post as inline PR comments" / "machine-parseable"Output contract--output-format json + --json-schema
"duplicate comments on every push"Cross-run contextInclude prior findings + instruct "only new or unresolved"
"inconsistent behavior across sessions"Memory diagnosis/memory
"prose description is interpreted inconsistently"Refinement2-3 concrete input/output examples
"the same session that generated the code"Session isolationAn independent review instance

Distractors that sound good and fail (mapped to the decoder):

  1. Fabricated feature. CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true, --batch, .claude/config.json with a commands array. Written with credible syntax. It's this domain's gift: if you know the real surface (§9), you eliminate 1-2 options before even reasoning.
  2. Scope flip. Offering you ~/.claude/commands/ when the requirement says "the whole team on cloning the repo." The tilde never travels via git.
  3. Prompt-as-guarantee. "Add to CLAUDE.md that it should ALWAYS do X." When the prompt demands deterministic behavior, CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee.
  4. Right technique, wrong axis. "Switch to a model with a bigger context window" to fix an inconsistent review across 14 files (Q12-C). The model already had the 14 files: the problem is attention dilution, not capacity. The cure is specializing passes (per-file + one integration pass), not enlarging the window. Context ≠ attention.
  5. Over-engineering. Building a router, a classifier, or a parser when the cheap fix (a description, a flag, a glob) solves the root cause. If the prompt says "most effective first step," the expensive option is disqualified by definition.
  6. Half-right practice. Options that start well and ruin it with the final clause. Read every option to the final period before picking it.
  7. Externalizing the problem. "Have developers split PRs into chunks of 3-4 files" (Q12-B): shifts the burden onto the human without fixing the system.

Scenario pattern. This domain's items fall on Scenario 2 (Code Generation with Claude Code) and Scenario 5 (Claude Code for CI). In Scenario 5 you'll see overlap with Domain 4: the Message Batches API question (synchronous for the blocking pre-merge check, batch for the overnight report) lives there even though it's D4. Don't confuse the axis: "blocking / developers wait" → synchronous API; "overnight / next morning / weekly" → batch.

Common mistakes

  1. Believing @import saves context. It doesn't: imported files still load at startup. → To save context: .claude/rules/ with paths: (conditional) or a skill (on demand).
  2. Putting the team's conventions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. It doesn't travel via git; the rest of the team doesn't have them. → Project-level (CLAUDE.md at the root or .claude/CLAUDE.md), committed.
  3. A per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md for conventions that cross directories. CLAUDE.md files are tied to the directory and only load when Claude touches files from there. → Globs in .claude/rules/ (**/*.test.tsx).
  4. Using skills for conventions that must apply "automatically." Skills get invoked; they don't activate by path match. → .claude/rules/ with paths:.
  5. Assuming CLAUDE.md guarantees behavior. It's delivered as a user message after the system prompt: it's context, not applied configuration. → For guarantees: a PreToolUse hook, a deny rule, a programmatic gate.
  6. Starting in direct execution "and switching to plan mode if it gets complicated." If the complexity is already declared in the requirement (multiple files, architecture decisions, alternative approaches), the decision is already made. → Plan mode from the start.
  7. Using plan mode for everything. A single-file bug with a clear stack trace doesn't need a planning phase. Plan mode has a cost (time, tokens, an approval turn). → Direct execution when the scope is clear.
  8. Running claude "…" without -p in CI. The job hangs waiting for input. → claude -p "…". And for reproducibility, consider --bare.
  9. Parsing prose with regex in the pipeline. Fragile by construction. → --output-format json + --json-schema; read structured_output.
  10. Instructing "don't repeat previous comments" without passing it the previous comments. It's an order that's impossible to fulfill. → Include the prior findings in the re-run's context.
  11. Asking the session that generated the code to review itself. It retains the generation's reasoning and doesn't question its own decisions. → An independent review instance, without that prior context.
  12. Fixing interacting problems one at a time. Each fix breaks the previous one. → All in one detailed message when they interact; sequential only when they're independent.
  13. Describing in prose a transformation that comes out inconsistent. Three more paragraphs of prose won't fix it. → 2-3 concrete input/output examples.
  14. Generating tests without giving it the existing tests or quality criteria. Result: duplicates and trivial tests. → Pass the existing suite in context and document in CLAUDE.md what counts as a valuable test and what fixtures exist.

Checklist

If you can't check one of these, you don't have a handle on this domain.

  • I can explain, without hesitation, why an instruction in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md doesn't reach a teammate, and what the command is to diagnose it.
  • I know that CLAUDE.md files at different levels get concatenated (not overwritten) and that subdirectory ones don't load at startup.
  • I can explain why @import modularizes but doesn't save context, and what the two mechanisms are that do save it.
  • I know how to write a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter paths: and globs, and can explain when it loads.
  • I can justify in one sentence why a glob (**/*.test.tsx) beats a per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md when the affected files are scattered across the repo.
  • I know why a skill doesn't work for conventions that must apply "automatically" based on path.
  • I know where to create a slash command so the whole team has it on cloning the repo, and where to put one that's just mine.
  • I can explain what context: fork does and what concrete problem it solves (contaminating the main conversation with verbose output).
  • I know what allowed-tools and argument-hint are for in a skill's frontmatter.
  • I can decide between skill (on demand, specific workflow) and CLAUDE.md (always loaded, universal standards) without hesitating.
  • I can list the guide's four plan mode criteria and give an example task that corresponds to direct execution.
  • I know what the Explore subagent is and why it's used during phases of verbose discovery.
  • I know why the CI job hangs without -p, and I can name two "flags" that don't exist and appear as distractors.
  • I can write the CI invocation that produces parseable findings (--output-format json + --json-schema → structured_output) and explain how to avoid duplicate comments on the re-run.
  • I can explain why an independent instance reviews code better than the session that generated it, and why enlarging the context window doesn't fix attention dilution.
  • I know when to give all the problems in a single message (they interact) and when to iterate sequentially (independent).

domains.title: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
objectives: Task Statement 4.1: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
Knowledge of: The importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions (e.g., "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior" vs "check that comments are accurate")
Knowledge of: How general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria
Knowledge of: The impact of false positive rates on developer trust: high false positive categories undermine confidence in accurate categories
Skills in: Writing specific review criteria that define which issues to report (bugs, security) versus skip (minor style, local patterns) rather than relying on confidence-based filtering
Skills in: Temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while improving prompts for those categories
Skills in: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification
Task Statement 4.2: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
Knowledge of: Few-shot examples as the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results
Knowledge of: The role of few-shot examples in demonstrating ambiguous-case handling (e.g., tool selection for ambiguous requests, branch-level test coverage gaps)
Knowledge of: How few-shot examples enable the model to generalize judgment to novel patterns rather than matching only pre-specified cases
Knowledge of: The effectiveness of few-shot examples for reducing hallucination in extraction tasks (e.g., handling informal measurements, varied document structures)
Skills in: Creating 2-4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios that show reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives
Skills in: Including few-shot examples that demonstrate specific desired output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) to achieve consistency
Skills in: Providing few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable code patterns from genuine issues to reduce false positives while enabling generalization
Skills in: Using few-shot examples to demonstrate correct handling of varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies, methodology sections vs embedded details)
Skills in: Adding few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats to address empty/null extraction of required fields
Task Statement 4.3: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
Knowledge of: Tool use (tool_use) with JSON schemas as the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output, eliminating JSON syntax errors

Knowledge of: The distinction between tool_choice: "auto" (model may return text instead of calling a tool), "any" (model must call a tool but can choose which), and forced tool selection (model must call a specific named tool)
Knowledge of: That strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors (e.g., line items that don't sum to total, values in wrong fields)
Knowledge of: Schema design considerations: required vs optional fields, enum fields with "other" + detail string patterns for extensible categories
Skills in: Defining extraction tools with JSON schemas as input parameters and extracting structured data from the tool_use response
Skills in: Setting tool_choice: "any" to guarantee structured output when multiple extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown
Skills in: Forcing a specific tool with tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} to ensure a particular extraction runs before enrichment steps
Skills in: Designing schema fields as optional (nullable) when source documents may not contain the information, preventing the model from fabricating values to satisfy required fields
Skills in: Adding enum values like "unclear" for ambiguous cases and "other" + detail fields for extensible categorization
Skills in: Including format normalization rules in prompts alongside strict output schemas to handle inconsistent source formatting
Task Statement 4.4: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
Knowledge of: Retry-with-error-feedback: appending specific validation errors to the prompt on retry to guide the model toward correction
Knowledge of: The limits of retry: retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source document (vs format or structural errors)
Knowledge of: Feedback loop design: tracking which code constructs trigger findings (detected_pattern field) to enable systematic analysis of dismissal patterns
Knowledge of: The difference between semantic validation errors (values don't sum, wrong field placement) and schema syntax errors (eliminated by tool use)
Skills in: Implementing follow-up requests that include the original document, the failed extraction, and specific validation errors for model self-correction

Skills in: Identifying when retries will be ineffective (e.g., information exists only in an external document not provided) versus when they will succeed (format mismatches, structural output errors)
Skills in: Adding detected_pattern fields to structured findings to enable analysis of false positive patterns when developers dismiss findings
Skills in: Designing self-correction validation flows: extracting "calculated_total" alongside "stated_total" to flag discrepancies, adding "conflict_detected" booleans for inconsistent source data
Task Statement 4.5: Design efficient batch processing strategies
Knowledge of: The Message Batches API: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing window, no guaranteed latency SLA

Knowledge of: Batch processing is appropriate for non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation) and inappropriate for blocking workflows (pre-merge checks)
Knowledge of: The batch API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request (cannot execute tools mid-request and return results)
Knowledge of: custom_id fields for correlating batch request/response pairs
Skills in: Matching API approach to workflow latency requirements: synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks, batch API for overnight/weekly analysis
Skills in: Calculating batch submission frequency based on SLA constraints (e.g., 4-hour windows to guarantee 30-hour SLA with 24-hour batch processing)
Skills in: Handling batch failures: resubmitting only failed documents (identified by custom_id) with appropriate modifications (e.g., chunking documents that exceeded context limits)
Skills in: Using prompt refinement on a sample set before batch-processing large volumes to maximize first-pass success rates and reduce iterative resubmission costs
Task Statement 4.6: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
Knowledge of: Self-review limitations: a model retains reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions in the same session
Knowledge of: Independent review instances (without prior reasoning context) are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking
Knowledge of: Multi-pass review: splitting large reviews into per-file local analysis passes plus cross-file integration passes to avoid attention dilution and contradictory findings
Skills in: Using a second independent Claude instance to review generated code without the generator's reasoning context
Skills in: Splitting large multi-file reviews into focused per-file passes for local issues plus separate integration passes for cross-file data flow analysis
Skills in: Running verification passes where the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding to enable calibrated review routing
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 20%

This domain measures exactly one competency: turning a model's probabilistic output into a contract a downstream system can consume without human supervision. It isn't "write good prompts." It's deciding where to put the guarantee. The schema guarantees syntax; the prompt calibrates judgment; validation catches the semantic errors; batching decides what it costs; multi-pass decides whether the result can be trusted. An architect who confuses these layers ships pipelines that work in the demo and bleed in production: extractions that fabricate values to satisfy required fields, code reviews with a 40% false-positive rate that the team stops reading, infinite retries over information that was never in the document.

The two scenarios where this domain calls the shots — Structured Data Extraction and Claude Code for CI — share the same business decision: how much human review can I remove without breaking trust? That's the question the exam is really testing. Every D4 item is a variant of it: cutting false positives (developer trust), guaranteeing schema (downstream-system trust), separating generation from review (trust in self-evaluation), choosing batch vs. synchronous (trust in the SLA). The 20% weight reflects that this is where agentic engineering touches money: cost per token, reviewer hours, and product credibility.

Official Objectives

Task Statement 4.1: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives

In practice: you'll be given an automated review with too many false positives, and you'll have to choose between specific categorical criteria (correct) and vague confidence filters (incorrect).
