scenarios.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.summary: Sistema de extracción de datos estructurados desde documentos no estructurados, validando salida con JSON Schema y manteniendo alta exactitud. Debe manejar edge cases con elegancia e integrarse con sistemas downstream.

certs.retakePolicy: If you fail, you can retake the exam after a mandatory waiting period, and the wait grows with each failed attempt: 14 days after the first failure, 30 days after the second, and 90 days after the third. Maximum 4 attempts per exam within a rolling 12-month window. The limit is per exam: failing CCAR-F does not stop you from registering for a different exam in the program. The $125 USD fee is paid on EVERY attempt.
certs.recertification: The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded. To renew on time, you review what changed since you certified and complete a NON-proctored assessment on the Anthropic Partner Academy. The guide is explicit: on-time renewal is FREE — there's no fee for renewing on schedule. If you let the credential expire, you lose that route: you have to retake the full exam and pay the full fee. Additionally, if the exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam instead of the renewal assessment. Holders remain subject to the Section 13 conduct rules.
examDayRules: Present valid, government-issued photo ID. The name on the ID must match the registration name EXACTLY (name correction: certifications-support@anthropic.com, before scheduling).
If testing online: stay in view of the proctor and the webcam for the entire session.
Keep your workspace clear: no notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, or other materials.
Do not communicate with any other person during the exam.
Do not capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce exam content in any form.
Prohibited items: mobile phones, smart watches, headphones, study materials, and any recording device.
Permitted items (if any), such as scratch sheets provided by the proctor, are defined by Pearson VUE.
Accept the confidentiality/NDA agreement before starting. If you don't accept it, the session ends and there is NO refund.
Consequences of misconduct: invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban from future exams.
certs.scoring: Criterion-referenced evaluation: you're compared against a fixed performance standard, NOT against other candidates — there's no curve and no pass quota. The score is reported on a scale of 100 to 1,000, and the cut score is 720. NOTE: 720/1000 is a SCALED score, not a percentage — it does NOT mean 'getting 72% of items right.' Scaling exists to equate exam forms with slightly different difficulty, so the number of correct answers needed varies by form. The passing standard was set through a formal standard-setting study in which trained SMEs judged the expected performance of a minimally qualified candidate. The score report includes pass/fail, the scaled score, and the percentage correct by domain; those per-domain percentages are diagnostic and informational and are NOT used to determine the outcome, which depends solely on the total scaled score.
howToPrepare: Build an agent with the Claude Agent SDK: implement a complete agentic loop with tool calling, error handling, and session management. Practice spawning subagents and passing context between them.

Configure Claude Code for a real project: set up CLAUDE.md with a configuration hierarchy, create path-specific rules in .claude/rules/, build your own skills with frontmatter options (context: fork, allowed-tools), and integrate at least one MCP server.

Design and test MCP tools: write descriptions that clearly differentiate similar tools. Implement structured error responses with error categories and retryable flags. Test tool-selection reliability with ambiguous requests.

Build a structured data extraction pipeline: use tool_use with JSON Schemas, implement validation-retry loops, design schemas with optional/nullable fields, and practice batch processing with the Message Batches API.

Practice prompt engineering techniques: write few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios. Define explicit review criteria to reduce false positives. Design multi-pass review architectures for large code reviews.

Study context-management patterns: practice extracting structured facts from verbose tool outputs, implementing scratchpad files for long sessions, and designing subagent delegation to handle context limits.

Review escalation and human-in-the-loop patterns: understand when to escalate (policy gaps, customer request, inability to make progress) vs. resolve autonomously. Practice designing human review workflows with confidence-based routing.
preparationExercises: Exercise 1: Build a Multi-Tool Agent with Escalation Logic — 3-4 tools MCP bien diferenciadas (dos con funcionalidad similar a propósito), agentic loop que inspecciona stop_reason, errores estructurados (errorCategory/isRetryable), hook programático que bloquea operaciones sobre un umbral y redirige a escalación, y prueba con mensajes multi-concern. Refuerza dominios 1, 2 y 5.

Exercise 2: Configure Claude Code for a Team Development Workflow — CLAUDE.md a nivel proyecto, .claude/rules/ con globs en frontmatter YAML, skill project-scoped con context: fork y allowed-tools, servidor MCP en .mcp.json con expansión de variables + servidor personal en ~/.claude.json, y prueba de plan mode vs ejecución directa en tareas de distinta complejidad. Refuerza dominios 3 y 2.

Exercise 3: Build a Structured Data Extraction Pipeline — tool de extracción con JSON Schema (campos requeridos/opcionales, enum con 'other' + detalle, nullables), loop validación-retry con el error específico, few-shot para formatos variados, estrategia de batch con 100 documentos y manejo de fallos por custom_id, y ruteo a revisión humana por confidence a nivel campo. Refuerza dominios 4 y 5.

Exercise 4: Design and Debug a Multi-Agent Research Pipeline — coordinador con 'Task' en allowedTools y contexto pasado explícitamente, subagentes en paralelo (múltiples Task calls en UNA respuesta), salida estructurada que separa contenido de metadatos (claim, excerpt, fuente, fecha), propagación de errores con contexto estructurado ante timeout, y manejo de datos en conflicto preservando ambos valores con atribución. Refuerza dominios 1, 2 y 5.
registrationSteps: Go to the certification page on the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
Download the Exam Guide and read the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy BEFORE registering.
Register and complete checkout. The fee shown reflects any discount applicable to your partner tier (list price is $125 USD).
Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account, then log in to schedule your exam session.
Choose an available date and select online proctoring or a Pearson test center. The exam is delivered by Pearson VUE.
You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment. Changes within the 24 hours prior: you lose the exam fee.

If you need accommodations (accessibility), request them and wait for Pearson VUE's approval BEFORE scheduling (pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations). Do not schedule until your request is approved.
outOfScope: Fine-tuning de modelos Claude o entrenamiento de modelos propios
Autenticación, facturación o gestión de cuenta de la Claude API
Implementación detallada de lenguajes o frameworks concretos (más allá de lo necesario para configurar tools y schemas)
Despliegue u hosting de servidores MCP (infraestructura, redes, orquestación de contenedores)
Arquitectura interna de Claude, proceso de entrenamiento o pesos del modelo
Constitutional AI, RLHF o metodologías de safety training
Modelos de embeddings o detalles de implementación de vector databases
Computer use (automatización de navegador, interacción con escritorio)
Implementación de streaming API o server-sent events
Rate limiting, cuotas o cálculos de pricing de la API
OAuth, rotación de API keys o detalles de protocolos de autenticación
Configuraciones específicas de cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure)
Benchmarking de performance o métricas de comparación entre modelos
Detalles de implementación de prompt caching (más allá de saber que existe)
Algoritmos de conteo de tokens o especificidades de tokenización

support.appeals: Puedes apelar una decisión dentro de los 14 días de la notificación, o —si es sobre tu resultado— dentro de los 14 días de la fecha del examen. La apelación se envía a soporte de Pearson VUE. NO son apelables: el resultado del standard-setting ni el contenido de los ítems individuales.

certs.decoderHtml:
CCAR-F Exam Decoder

Analysis of how the items on the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations exam are constructed, derived from the 12 official sample questions in the v1.0 guide and the language of the domain objectives. This isn't theory — it's reverse engineering of the exam.

1. The core answer rule

The correct option is almost always the PROPORTIONATE intervention that attacks the ROOT CAUSE at the correct LAYER.

This exam doesn't reward sophistication. It rewards architect's judgment. Across the 12 official samples, the correct answer is never the most technologically advanced option. It's the one that:

  1. Attacks the stated root cause, not the symptom. If the stem says "both tools have minimal descriptions" (Q2), the answer is to fix the descriptions — not add few-shot examples, not build a router.
  2. Is proportional to the problem. The exam uses the words "first step" or "most effective" to force cost/benefit judgment. A trained ML classifier (Q3-C) solves the problem, but it's disproportionate when the prompt hasn't even been optimized yet.
  3. Operates at the layer where the failure lives. If the coordinator decomposed the task poorly (Q7), don't fix the synthesis agent. Go up a layer.

On top of that base rule sits the exam's master axis, and mastering it is worth more than memorizing half the guide:

Does the problem demand deterministic GUARANTEE or judgment CALIBRATION?

  • Guarantee (money, identity, mandatory operation ordering, policy compliance) → programmatic enforcement: hooks, prerequisite gates, forced tool_choice. Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate, and that's unacceptable. → Q1: answer A (programmatic prerequisite).
  • Judgment (fuzzy decision boundary, inconsistent formatting, selection among plausible alternatives) → prompt, explicit criteria, few-shot. → Q3: answer A (escalation criteria + few-shot).

Q1 and Q3 share the same scenario (Customer Support), have nearly symmetrical options, and their correct answers point in opposite directions. That pair is the entire exam in two questions. If you don't distinguish the axis, you miss both or get them right by luck.

2. The seven distractor archetypes

Every distractor on this exam has a role. Name it, and it dies.

1. Prompt-as-guarantee. Offers a system prompt or few-shot where deterministic compliance is required. Q1-B: "Enhance the system prompt to state that customer verification is mandatory". Sounds responsible. It's still probabilistic. Kill test: is there money or irreversible harm on the line? Then a prompt isn't enough.

2. Over-engineering / ML escape. Heavy infrastructure (routing classifier, trained model, parsing layer) for a problem that a better description would fix. Q2-C (keyword-based routing layer), Q3-C (classifier trained on historical tickets). Kill test: has the cheap option already been tried? If not, the expensive answer is wrong by definition.

3. Fabricated feature. A file, flag, or environment variable that DOES NOT EXIST, written with credible-looking syntax. Q10-B (CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true), Q10-D (--batch), Q4-D (.claude/config.json with a commands array). This archetype is a free gift if you know the real surface: -p/--print, --output-format json, --json-schema, --resume, fork_session, /memory, /compact, .claude/commands/, .claude/rules/, .claude/skills/, .mcp.json, ~/.claude.json. Anything not on that list, suspect it.

4. Scope flip. Swaps user-level and project-level. Q4-B: ~/.claude/commands/ when the requirement is "available to everyone when they clone the repo". Kill test: does this travel through git? User-level (~/) never travels.

5. Right technique, wrong axis. A real, correct technique applied to the wrong dimension of the problem. Q1-D: the routing classifier controls WHICH tools are available, when the problem is the ORDER in which they're called. Q12-C: a larger context window solves whether the files FIT, not whether they get quality attention. Q3-D: measures sentiment when the real variable is complexity.

6. Half-right practice. Starts well and ruins the ending. Q8-B: retry with exponential backoff inside the subagent (correct, the guide calls for it) that ends up returning a generic "search unavailable" (destroying the context the coordinator needs). On this exam, the bad half wins. Read the full option before falling for its first clause.

7. Downstream patch / blame the executor. Blames the component that did its job correctly within its assigned scope. Q7-A/C/D: the synthesis agent, the web search agent, and the document analysis agent all did their jobs well; the coordinator assigned the work badly. Variant: fabricated evidence — Q7-D invents a "restrictive relevance criterion" that the stem never mentions.

Minor but lethal archetypes: consensus voting (Q12-D: requiring a finding to appear in 2 of 3 runs suppresses intermittent bugs — raises precision, destroys recall), speculative caching (Q9-D: predicting the unpredictable), over-provisioning (Q9-C: give it every tool and let it figure things out — violates least privilege and degrades selection), externalize the problem (Q12-B: make developers split their PRs — doesn't fix the system).

3. Verbs and signals: which domain is being tested

The stem tells you the domain if you know how to read the signal. Operational map:

Signals in the stemDomainWhat to look for in the options
stop_reason, "loop", "iteration", coordinator/subagent, Task tool, allowedTools, "decomposed the topic into", hooks, PostToolUse, "prerequisite", --resume, fork_sessionD1 – Agentic Architecture (27%)Enforcement vs. prompt? Does the decomposition cover the full space? Does the coordinator route everything?
Tool names (get_customer, lookup_order), "descriptions", "misroutes", isError, errorCategory, isRetryable, tool_choice, .mcp.json, MCP resources, Grep/Glob/Read/Write/EditD2 – Tool Design & MCP (18%)Is the description the cause? Is the error structured? Is the tool set scoped to the role?
CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/, .claude/commands/, .claude/skills/, SKILL.md, context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint, plan mode, -p, --output-format json, CI/CD, PR commentsD3 – Claude Code Config (20%)Project or user scope? Glob or directory? Plan mode or direct execution?
"false positives", "criteria", few-shot, JSON Schema, tool_use, nullable/optional, enum + "other", validation-retry, Message Batches API, custom_id, "self-review", multi-passD4 – Prompt Eng. & Structured Output (20%)Explicit criteria > vague instruction? Latency-tolerant = batch? Per-file pass + integration pass?
"lost in the middle", summarization, "case facts", trimming tool outputs, escalation, "customer demands a human", policy gap, error propagation, scratchpad, /compact, confidence calibration, stratified sampling, claim-source mappingD5 – Context & Reliability (15%)Is the hard data preserved? Does it escalate for the right reason? Does the error travel with context?

Action signals — which word triggers which answer:

  • "most effective first step" → the cheap option that attacks the root cause. Rule out refactors and ML.
  • "deterministic" / "guaranteed" / "must never" / money / identity → hook, gate, forced tool_choice.
  • "inconsistent" / "contradictory" / "varies between runs" → few-shot or explicit criteria (judgment), or multi-pass (if it's diluted attention).
  • "blocking" / "developers wait" → synchronous API. "overnight" / "next morning" / "weekly" → Message Batches API.
  • "spread throughout the codebase" → globs in .claude/rules/, NEVER per-directory CLAUDE.md.
  • "available to every developer when they clone" → project scope (.claude/… in the repo).
  • "root cause" → go up a layer: suspect the component that ASSIGNED the work, not the one that EXECUTED it.
  • "each subagent completes successfully" but the overall result fails → the failure is in the assignment/decomposition.

4. Elimination technique, step by step

Apply it in this order. It's faster than reasoning out the correct answer from scratch.

  1. Kill the invented features. Three-second sweep: does any option mention a flag, file, or variable that doesn't exist? Out. (Eliminates 1-2 options on factual items.)
  2. Identify the axis: guarantee or judgment. Is there money, identity, mandatory ordering, a policy that MUST be honored? → look for programmatic enforcement and rule out every prompt-side option. Is it a fuzzy boundary, inconsistent formatting, or ambiguous selection? → look for prompt/criteria/few-shot and rule out heavy infrastructure.
  3. Locate the layer of the failure. Which component caused the problem according to the EVIDENCE in the stem (logs, metrics, symptom description)? Any option that fixes a different component is out, no matter how sensible it sounds.
  4. Apply the proportionality filter. Among the survivors, if the stem asks for "first step" or "most effective", eliminate the one that requires more infrastructure, labeled data, or changes to the team's human behavior.
  5. Read every option TO THE END. The half-right archetype (Q8-B) survives on you falling for the first clause. The final clause is what decides.
  6. Check it against the guide's objective. The correct option is usually a near-literal paraphrase of a "Skills in:" bullet from the corresponding task statement. If an option sounds like it was copied straight from the guide, it probably was.
  7. Multiple-response: the item ALWAYS tells you how many to select. Count them. Don't go by a gut feeling of "looks like two".

5. How to read a long scenario without getting lost

The exam presents 4 scenarios drawn at random from a bank of 6, and each scenario frames a group of questions. The scenarios are:

  1. Customer Support Resolution Agent (D1, D2, D5) — tools get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human. Goal: 80% first-contact resolution.
  2. Code Generation with Claude Code (D3, D5) — slash commands, CLAUDE.md, plan mode vs. direct execution.
  3. Multi-Agent Research System (D1, D2, D5) — coordinator + subagents for search, analysis, synthesis, reporting.
  4. Developer Productivity with Claude (D2, D3, D1) — built-in tools + MCP over unfamiliar codebases.
  5. Claude Code for CI (D3, D4) — automated code review, test generation, PR feedback.
  6. Structured Data Extraction (D4, D5) — JSON Schema, validation, edge cases.

Reading method (two passes, not one):

Pass 1 — the scenario, once, to build the map. Mentally extract four things and nothing more: (a) what tools/components exist and what they're called; (b) what the stated METRIC or goal is (80% resolution, minimizing false positives, high accuracy); (c) what hard constraints exist (money, blocking latency, shared team); (d) which domains it lists as primary. That map serves you for EVERY question in the scenario. Don't re-read the full scenario between questions.

Pass 2 — the question, which is where the answer lives. Here's the key that separates the candidates who pass: the scenario gives you context; the EVIDENCE is in the question's stem. Every official question carries a hard data point that decides the answer:

  • "in 12% of cases, your agent skips get_customer" (Q1) → there's a failure rate → you need a guarantee.
  • "Both tools have minimal descriptions" (Q2) → root cause served on a platter.
  • "you see it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: digital art, graphic design, photography" (Q7) → the log points at the culprit.
  • "85% are simple fact-checks while 15% require deeper investigation" (Q9) → the distribution IS the design instruction.
  • "a blocking pre-merge check" vs "generated overnight" (Q11) → the latency classification is handed to you.
  • "contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere" (Q12) → the unmistakable signature of attention dilution.

Operating rule: underline the number, the log, or the literal quote. If the stem gives you a percentage, a log line, or a literal description of a configuration, THAT is the discriminator. Everything else in the scenario is set dressing. When you're torn between two options, go back to the hard data point and ask: which of the two explains or fixes EXACTLY this data point?

Scenario trap: scenarios are written so you'll carry one question's answer over into the next. Q1 and Q3 share a scenario, and the correct answer switches axis (enforcement → prompt). There is no thematic consistency between answers within a scenario. Resolve every item against its own evidence.

6. Typical thinking errors for this candidate profile

The CCAR-F candidate is a senior engineer. Their mistakes are senior-engineer mistakes:

  • Reflexive over-engineering. The experienced architect sees a problem and designs a system. The exam punishes this systematically: routing layers (Q2-C), trained classifiers (Q3-C), hybrid architectures with fallback (Q11-D). Antidote: always ask yourself "has the cheap option already been tried?" The guide explicitly values the "low-effort, high-leverage fix".
  • Confusing context capacity with attention quality. "A bigger context window fixes the inconsistent review" (Q12-C) is the most human error on the exam. No. The model already had all 14 files and still diluted its attention. Antidote: context ≠ attention. The cure for dilution is specializing passes, not enlarging the window.
  • Trusting the model's self-reported confidence. Q3-B. Engineers love numeric thresholds. The guide explicitly states that self-reported confidence is an unreliable proxy for complexity — and in Q3 the evidence itself proves it: the agent is already confidently wrong. Important nuance: the guide DOES accept field-level confidence scores in extraction (D5.5), but calibrated against a labeled validation set. Raw confidence = trap; calibrated confidence = legitimate tool. Tell them apart.
  • Treating a good pattern as a universal answer. Retry with backoff is good practice… and Q8-B is still wrong. Few-shot is extremely powerful… and Q2-A is still wrong. Antidote: the right technique applied to the wrong cause is still a wrong answer.
  • Fallback optimism. "Batch it, and if it's slow, fall back to real-time" (Q11-D) sounds like resilience. It's two code paths, two possible costs, and new failure modes, all to avoid accepting the simple solution. Antidote: on this exam, complexity has to be EARNED. If the simple answer meets the requirements, the complex one is the distractor.
  • Suppressing signal to gain precision. Q12-D (2-of-3 consensus) and "only report high-confidence findings" (D4.1) are the same temptation: filtering to cut false positives. The guide is blunt about this: vague instructions like "be conservative" do NOT improve precision; what improves it is specific categorical criteria. And filtering by consensus suppresses real, intermittent bugs.
  • Forgetting that subagents don't inherit context. This is the #1 real-implementation error, and the guide repeats it three times (D1.2, D1.3, D5.1): the subagent does NOT inherit the coordinator's history. Everything it needs goes EXPLICITLY in its prompt, and the coordinator needs "Task" in allowedTools to spawn it. Parallelism = multiple Task calls in ONE response, not across successive turns.
  • Escalating for the wrong reasons. Escalating "complex cases" is not a valid criterion. The three legitimate triggers are: the customer asks for a human, there's a policy gap/exception, or the agent can't make progress. Complexity alone isn't enough; customer sentiment never is.

7. 20-second checklist per item

  1. Are there invented features? → eliminate them.
  2. Guarantee or judgment? → pick the axis.
  3. Where's the hard evidence (number, log, quote)? → that's the discriminator.
  4. Which layer failed according to that evidence? → rule out fixes at other layers.
  5. Is any option over-engineering before the cheap option is exhausted? → out.
  6. Did I read the last clause of every option? (half-right)
  7. Does the survivor paraphrase a "Skills in:" bullet from the guide? → that's the one.
certs.logisticsHtml:
CCAR-F — Exam Logistics

Everything operational about the Claude Certified Architect – Foundations (code CCAR-F), per the official exam guide v1.0 (effective July 2026). Data verbatim from the guide — nothing invented.

Quick facts

ItemValue
CredentialClaude Certified Architect – Foundations
CodeCCAR-F
Items60
Item formatMultiple-choice and multiple-response. Every item states how many answers to select.
Structure4 scenarios, drawn at random from a bank of 6
Time120 minutes
DeliveryProctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy. Delivered by Pearson VUE.
Passing score720 on a 100–1,000 scale (scaled, NOT a percentage)
Fee$125 USD (per attempt; checkout may apply a discount depending on your partner tier)
Validity12 months from the date the credential is awarded
Result reportPass/fail + scaled score + % correct by domain (informational, doesn't decide the outcome)
LanguageThe guide doesn't specify. All official material and sample items are in English: assume English.
Formal prerequisitesNone. Expected profile: 6+ months building with the Claude API, Agent SDK, Claude Code, and MCP.

Pace: 120 min / 60 items = 2 minutes per item. But scenarios are read once and serve several questions. Budget ~3-4 min to read each new scenario and ~90 seconds per item within a scenario you've already read. Leave a 10-minute buffer for flagging and review.

1. Step-by-step registration

Registration is hybrid: you pay through the Anthropic Partner Academy, you schedule through Pearson VUE.

  1. Go to the certification page on the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
  2. Download the Exam Guide and read the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy BEFORE registering. (This isn't decorative bureaucracy — that's where the conduct rules and the NDA live, which you can't later reject without losing your money.)
  3. Register and complete checkout. The fee you see reflects any discount applicable to your partner tier — list price is $125 USD.
  4. Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account. Then log in there to schedule.
  5. Choose a date and select online proctoring or a Pearson test center.
  6. If you need accommodations, do NOT schedule yet → see section 3.

Critical order: checkout on the Academy first, then account creation and scheduling on Pearson VUE. And if you're going to request accommodations, that process goes BEFORE scheduling.

2. Online proctoring vs. test center

The guide allows both ("online proctored and/or test center, per program policy"). The choice is yours when scheduling.

Online (OnVUE / remote proctoring)

  • Advantage: no commute, more time-slot options.
  • Requires: a completely clear workspace, a working webcam, and staying in view of the proctor and the webcam for the ENTIRE session.
  • Real risk: any network, camera, or environment problem is your problem. Run the Pearson VUE system check ahead of time, not on the same day.
  • Remote check-in includes a camera scan of the room and ID verification.

Pearson VUE test center

  • Advantage: controlled environment, guaranteed hardware, zero risk of your router deciding to give up mid-exam.
  • Requires: arriving with margin. Arriving late outside the allowed window = you lose the fee and have to re-register.

Operational recommendation: if your network or your space isn't 100% reliable, or if remote scrutiny makes you nervous, go to the test center. A no-show or an ejection because a third party walked into your room costs $125 and a retake.

3. Accommodations (accessibility)

  • Available to candidates with documented disabilities or needs, per applicable law.
  • Must be requested and approved by Pearson VUE BEFORE scheduling the exam.
  • Do NOT schedule your appointment until your request is approved.
  • Request them at: pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations

4. Exam-day rules

The exam is administered in a standardized, secure, proctored environment. The same rules apply online and in-center.

You must:

  • Present valid, government-issued photo ID.
  • The name on your ID must match the registration name EXACTLY. If it doesn't match, fix it BEFORE scheduling by emailing certifications-support@anthropic.com.
  • If testing online: stay in view of the proctor and the webcam for the entire session.
  • Keep your workspace clear: no notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, or other materials.
  • Not communicate with any other person during the exam.
  • Not capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce exam content in any form.

Prohibited (per the guide's list):

  • Mobile phones
  • Smart watches
  • Headphones
  • Study materials
  • Any recording device

Permitted: only what Pearson VUE specifies — for example, scratch sheets provided by the proctor, if applicable. Don't assume you'll get scratch paper — confirm it with Pearson VUE for your delivery mode.

Consequences of misconduct: cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban from future exams. This isn't a rhetorical threat — the credential exists because it's protected.

5. NDA / Confidentiality

Before the exam starts you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement.

By accepting it you acknowledge that all exam content — questions, answer options, and scenarios — is Anthropic's confidential, exclusive property, and that you will not disclose, reproduce, or distribute any portion of it.

If you do NOT accept the agreement, the exam session ENDS and NO refund is issued. The NDA is not negotiable and cannot be "skipped." Read it beforehand (it's in the Terms & Conditions you download in step 2 of registration), not at minute zero with the clock already running.

Practical consequence: don't share items, don't post "what I got on my exam," don't do braindumps. That revokes credentials.

6. Cancellation, rescheduling, and no-shows

  • You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment.
  • Changes within the 24 hours prior: you LOSE the exam fee.
  • No-show (you don't show up) or late arrival outside the allowed window: you lose the fee and must re-register (and pay again).

The 24-hour rule is the only deadline worth memorizing. If you have any doubt about whether you'll be able to show up, reschedule with 25+ hours of margin: rescheduling is free, not showing up costs $125.

7. Retake policy

Failed attemptMandatory wait before the next attempt
1st14 days
2nd30 days
3rd90 days
  • Maximum 4 attempts per exam within a rolling 12-month window.
  • The fee applies to EVERY attempt. Failing costs $125 each time.
  • Limits are per exam: not passing CCAR-F does not stop you from registering for a different exam in the program.

Strategic reading: with 4 attempts/12 months and growing wait times, a third failure sidelines you for 90 days. It's worth investing two extra weeks of prep rather than burning an attempt.

8. How scoring works (and what 720 does NOT mean)

  • Criterion-referenced evaluation: you're measured against a fixed performance standard, not against other candidates. There's no curve, no pass quota.
  • The passing standard was established through a formal standard-setting study: trained subject matter experts (SMEs) judged the expected performance level of a minimally qualified candidate.
  • The score is reported on a 100–1,000 scale. The cut score is 720.

⚠️ 720/1000 is a SCALED score, not a percentage. It does NOT mean "getting 72% of items right." Scaling exists precisely to equate scores across different exam forms that may have slightly different difficulty. The number of correct answers needed to reach 720 varies depending on which form you get. Don't do math like "I can afford to miss 16 questions" — that's not how it works.

Result report:

  • Pass/fail + scaled score (100–1,000).
  • The score report also shows the percentage correct by domain.
  • Those per-domain percentages are diagnostic and informational: they are NOT used to determine the outcome. Pass/fail depends solely on the total scaled score. In other words: you don't have to "pass every domain," you have to clear 720 overall.

Domain weights (use these to allocate your study time):

#DomainWeight
1Agentic Architecture & Orchestration27%
2Tool Design & MCP Integration18%
3Claude Code Configuration & Workflows20%
4Prompt Engineering & Structured Output20%
5Context Management & Reliability15%

9. Appeals and complaints

  • You can appeal a decision within 14 days of the date you're notified.
  • For a concern about your result: within 14 days of your exam date.
  • Appeals go to Pearson VUE support (pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html).
  • Appeals are reviewed under the program's appeals policy.

NOT appealable: the standard-setting result (i.e., the 720 cut score) and the content of individual items. You can appeal process irregularities; you cannot appeal "that question was wrong."

10. Recertification and credential maintenance

  • The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded.
  • The guide explains why: the underlying technology evolves quickly, so the credential is time-limited to keep holders' knowledge current.

On-time renewal (the good path):

  • You review what changed since you certified.
  • You complete a non-proctored assessment on the Anthropic Partner Academy.
  • It's FREE. The guide is explicit: there is no fee for on-time renewal ("There is no fee for on-time renewal").

If you let the credential expire (the expensive path):

  • You must retake the FULL exam and pay the FULL fee to regain certified status.
  • You lose the free, non-proctored route. Pay attention to this: the difference between renewing on time and letting it lapse is $0 vs. $125 + a 120-minute proctored exam.

Exception: if the exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam to recertify, instead of the renewal assessment.

Also: holders remain subject to the conduct rules (Section 13 of the guide) for as long as they hold the credential.

Concrete action: set a calendar reminder for 10 months after earning the credential. That's your margin to do the free renewal without rushing.

11. Support — who to contact for what

Privacy: personal data collected during registration and testing is handled under Anthropic's privacy policy, Pearson VUE's privacy policy, and applicable data protection law.

12. Operational checklist

Weeks before

  • Download the Exam Guide and read the Terms & Conditions + Exam Policy.
  • Verify your registration name matches your valid official ID EXACTLY.
  • If you need accommodations: request them and wait for approval before scheduling.
  • Check out through the Anthropic Partner Academy (check whether a partner-tier discount applies).
  • Create your Pearson VUE account and schedule (online or center).

Days before

  • If online: run the Pearson VUE system check (webcam, network, permissions). Don't leave it for exam day.
  • Prepare your space: clear desk, no notes, no second monitor, no phone, no smart watch.
  • Give a heads-up to anyone you live with: no one can enter the room during the session.
  • Confirm with Pearson VUE whether you'll have scratch paper allowed in your delivery mode.

Exam day

  • Valid, official photo ID on hand.
  • Arrive/connect with margin (late arrival = lost fee).
  • Accept the NDA (rejecting it ends the session with no refund).
  • Pace: ~3-4 min per new scenario, ~90 s per item, 10 min final buffer.
  • Every item tells you how many answers to select: count them before marking.

Afterward

  • Save the score report (it gives you % by domain — your study map if you need to retake).
  • If you're appealing: you have 14 days from notification (or from the exam date, if it's about the result).
  • If you passed: set a reminder at 10 months for the free, non-proctored renewal.

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.stem: Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your agent skips get_customer entirely and calls lookup_order using only the customer's stated name, occasionally leading to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would most effectively address this reliability issue?

options.text: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund calls until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
Enhance the system prompt to state that customer verification via get_customer is mandatory before any order operations.
Add few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first, even when customers volunteer order details.
Implement a routing classifier that analyzes each request and enables only the subset of tools appropriate for that request type.

questions.explanationEs: The stem's decisive signal is twofold: there's a mandatory tool ORDER (verify identity before touching money) and the failure's consequences are financial. That pair — mandatory order + irreversible consequence — is Task Statement 1.4's signature: when deterministic compliance is required, prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate, and the observed 12% is exactly that rate showing up. A installs a programmatic prerequisite (hook/gate) that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID: that drives the failure rate to zero by construction, not by probability. B is the most attractive trap because it sounds like 'the proportionate solution': rewrite the system prompt. But a more emphatic prompt is still probabilistic compliance — it might drop the 12% to maybe 3%, and 3% of refunds going to the wrong account is still unacceptable. C has the same underlying flaw as B (few-shot is guidance, not guarantee) and also pays token overhead on every turn. D is a wrong-category distractor: a routing classifier controls WHICH tools are available, not WHAT ORDER they're called in; it could leave lookup_order enabled and the agent would still call it without verifying first. Portable rule: if the stem says 'X must happen before Y' and Y moves money or data, the answer is programmatic enforcement, never prompt.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. When a specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic (like verifying customer identity before processing refunds), programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees that prompt-based approaches cannot. Options B and C rely on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when errors have financial consequences. Option D addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering, which is not the actual problem.
questions.trap: B = 'Prompt-as-guarantee' (confuses probabilistic guidance with a deterministic guarantee). C = 'Few-shot reflex' (same flaw as B, dressed up as an advanced technique). D = 'Right technique, wrong axis' (solves tool availability when the problem is order/sequence).

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.stem: Production logs show the agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders (e.g., "check my order #12345"), instead of calling lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions ("Retrieves customer information" / "Retrieves order details") and accept similar identifier formats. What's the most effective first step to improve tool selection reliability?

options.text: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct tool selection patterns, with 5-8 examples showing order-related queries routing to lookup_order.
Expand each tool's description to include input formats it handles, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools.
Implement a routing layer that parses user input before each turn and pre-selects the appropriate tool based on detected keywords and identifier patterns.
Consolidate both tools into a single lookup_entity tool that accepts any identifier and internally determines which backend to query.

questions.explanationEs: The stem hands you the root cause literally: 'Both tools have minimal descriptions.' Tool descriptions are THE primary mechanism the LLM uses to select a tool; if they're anemic, the model has nothing to differentiate with. B attacks that exact cause and adds precisely what the guide asks for in Task Statement 2.1: input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries ('use this one and not that one when...'). The stem also asks for a 'first step,' and B is the lowest-effort, highest-leverage fix. A (few-shot) is tempting because it also improves selection, but it compensates for the symptom without fixing the broken description, and it pays token overhead on every request, forever — it's patching over the hole. C builds a keyword routing layer: over-engineering that also wastes what the LLM already does well (natural-language understanding) and breaks on any phrasing that doesn't match the anticipated keywords. D (consolidating into lookup_entity) isn't absurd — the guide does acknowledge merging/splitting tools as a valid architectural decision — but it's disproportionate as a 'first step,' and it erases the semantic boundary instead of clarifying it. Note that this item is the exact mirror of the previous one: here the correct answer is the cheap, prompt-side one, there it was hard enforcement. What marks the difference is whether the failure is one of JUDGMENT (poor description) or of GUARANTEE (money at stake).
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: B. Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection. When descriptions are minimal, models lack the context to differentiate between similar tools. Option B directly addresses this root cause with a low-effort, high-leverage fix. Few-shot examples (A) add token overhead without fixing the underlying issue. A routing layer (C) is over-engineered and bypasses the LLM's natural language understanding. Consolidating tools (D) is a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a "first step" warrants when the immediate problem is inadequate descriptions.
questions.trap: A = 'Few-shot reflex' (correct technique applied to the symptom, not the cause; adds permanent overhead). C = 'Over-engineering' (deterministic infrastructure replacing the LLM's native capability). D = 'Disproportionate refactor' (an architecturally defensible option, but ruled out by the keyword 'first step').

questions.scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent
questions.stem: Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?

options.text: Add explicit escalation criteria to your system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1-10) before each response and automatically route requests to humans when confidence falls below a threshold.
Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation before the main agent begins processing.
Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration levels and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold.

questions.explanationEs: The failure pattern is inverted: it escalates what's easy and keeps what's hard. That isn't a lack of capability, it's a fuzzy DECISION BOUNDARY — the agent doesn't know what counts as 'escalatable.' The cure is making the criterion explicit: A adds escalation criteria to the system prompt with few-shot showing the judgment call on ambiguous cases, which is literally what Task Statement 5.2 asks for. B self-destructs against the stem's own evidence: the agent is already incorrectly confident on the hard cases (that's why it attempts them), so routing by its self-reported confidence amplifies the existing error; the guide explicitly says self-reported confidence is an unreliable proxy for complexity. C trains an ML classifier: it requires labeled data and infrastructure and prompt optimization hasn't even been tried — disproportionate, and it also moves the decision outside the agent instead of teaching it the criterion. D is the cleanest distractor to catch: customer sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity; a customer furious about a standard damage replacement (an easy case) would get escalated, worsening exactly the metric you want to raise. Watch the contrast against Question 1: here deterministic guarantee is NOT what's asked for (no money is going out unverified), calibrating judgment is — and for judgment, prompt + few-shot is the right tool.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries. This is the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure. Option B fails because LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated—the agent is already incorrectly confident on hard cases. Option C is over-engineered, requiring labeled data and ML infrastructure when prompt optimization hasn't been tried. Option D solves a different problem entirely; sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity, which is the actual issue.
questions.trap: B = 'Self-reported confidence' (a proxy the guide explicitly flags as unreliable; also contradicted by the stem's own evidence). C = 'ML infrastructure escape' (an expensive solution before exhausting the cheap one). D = 'Wrong signal' (measures sentiment when the real variable is complexity; solves a problem nobody raised).

questions.scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.stem: You want to create a custom /review slash command that runs your team's standard code review checklist. This command should be available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where should you create this command file?

options.text: In the .claude/commands/ directory in the project repository
In ~/.claude/commands/ in each developer's home directory
In the CLAUDE.md file at the project root
In a .claude/config.json file with a commands array

questions.explanationEs: A pure knowledge item on scoping (Task Statement 3.2), with no tradeoff to reason through: you just have to know the hierarchy. The operative requirement is 'available to every dev upon cloning or pulling' → that means version-controlled in the repo → project scope → .claude/commands/. B is the inverted-scope trap: ~/.claude/ is user-level, lives on each person's own machine, and does NOT travel through git; it would work for you alone and fail exactly the stated requirement. C confuses artifacts: CLAUDE.md provides context and instructions that are always loaded, it doesn't define invokable commands; the skills/commands distinction (on-demand invocation) vs. CLAUDE.md (always-loaded standards) is an explicit guide objective. D is a fabricated distractor: .claude/config.json with a 'commands' array doesn't exist in Claude Code — the exam uses this archetype frequently (see also --batch and CLAUDE_HEADLESS in Q10). If an option mentions a file, flag, or variable you've never seen in the documentation, be suspicious: it's probably invented.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Project-scoped custom slash commands should be stored in the .claude/commands/ directory within the repository. These commands are version-controlled and automatically available to all developers when they clone or pull the repo. Option B (~/.claude/commands/) is for personal commands that aren't shared via version control. Option C (CLAUDE.md) is for project instructions and context, not command definitions. Option D describes a configuration mechanism that doesn't exist in Claude Code.
questions.trap: B = 'Scope flip' (user-level when project-level is asked for; the 'shared via git' requirement kills it). C = 'Wrong artifact' (mixes up CLAUDE.md context with command definitions). D = 'Fabricated feature' (a nonexistent configuration mechanism that sounds plausible).

questions.scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.stem: You've been assigned to restructure the team's monolithic application into microservices. This will involve changes across dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Enter plan mode to explore the codebase, understand dependencies, and design an implementation approach before making changes.
Start with direct execution and make changes incrementally, letting the implementation reveal the natural service boundaries.
Use direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions detailing exactly how each service should be structured.
Begin in direct execution mode and only switch to plan mode if you encounter unexpected complexity during implementation.

questions.explanationEs: The stem triggers all three criteria the guide lists for plan mode (Task Statement 3.4): large-scale changes ('dozens of files'), multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions ('service boundaries and module dependencies'). With all three present, A is automatic: plan mode lets you explore the codebase and design BEFORE committing to changes, avoiding expensive rework. B ('let the implementation reveal the boundaries') sounds like pragmatic agilism, but in microservices, badly cut dependencies get discovered late and the rework is very expensive — that's exactly the failure plan mode exists to prevent. C is subtle and worth understanding: it proposes direct execution but with exhaustive instructions, meaning it assumes you ALREADY know the correct structure without having explored the code. Its flaw isn't a lack of detail, it's the false premise. D is the 'best of both worlds' trap: start direct and switch to plan mode if unexpected complexity shows up. It fails because the complexity is NOT unexpected — it's stated in the requirements. Learn this pair of signals: 'multi-file + architectural decisions + several valid paths' → plan mode. 'One file + a clear stack trace + obvious scope' → direct execution.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions—exactly what monolith-to-microservices restructuring requires. It enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes. Option B risks costly rework when dependencies are discovered late. Option C assumes you already know the right structure without exploring the code. Option D ignores that the complexity is already stated in the requirements, not something that might emerge later.
questions.trap: B = 'Emergent design' (lets the code reveal what should have been designed; ignores the cost of rework). C = 'False premise' (direct execution assuming knowledge you don't have yet). D = 'Deferred plan mode' (conditions the switch on complexity 'emerging' that the stem already stated).

questions.scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code
questions.stem: Your codebase has distinct areas with different coding conventions: React components use functional style with hooks, API handlers use async/await with specific error handling, and database models follow a repository pattern. Test files are spread throughout the codebase alongside the code they test (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx), and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. What's the most maintainable way to ensure Claude automatically applies the correct conventions when generating code?

options.text: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns to conditionally apply conventions based on file paths
Consolidate all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md file under headers for each area, relying on Claude to infer which section applies
Create skills in .claude/skills/ for each code type that include the relevant conventions in their SKILL.md files
Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each subdirectory containing that area's specific conventions

questions.explanationEs: Two constraints in the stem eliminate 75% of the options if you read them carefully. First: the tests are SCATTERED across the whole codebase, next to the code they test — they don't live in one directory. Second: the application must be AUTOMATIC. A satisfies both: .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter and globs (**/*.test.tsx) activates by PATH PATTERN, not by directory, and loads only when editing files that match — precisely the use case the guide describes in Task Statement 3.3 (the advantage of glob rules over per-directory CLAUDE.md when conventions cut across directories). D is the mirror trap: a per-subdirectory CLAUDE.md is a real, correct mechanism... for conventions confined to one directory. With tests scattered around, you'd have to duplicate the same CLAUDE.md across dozens of folders and keep them in sync — unmaintainable, which is exactly the adjective the stem uses ('most maintainable'). B puts everything in the root CLAUDE.md and trusts Claude to INFER which section applies: inference ≠ explicit matching, and it also always loads all the irrelevant context (token cost). C uses skills, which are invoked ON DEMAND: they depend on someone calling them or on Claude deciding to load them — that contradicts the 'automatically' requirement. Rule: scattered by file type → globs in .claude/rules/. Convention confined to one directory → directory CLAUDE.md.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Option A is correct because .claude/rules/ with glob patterns (e.g., **/*.test.tsx) allows conventions to be automatically applied based on file paths regardless of directory location, essential for test files spread throughout the codebase. Option B relies on inference rather than explicit matching, making it unreliable. Option C requires manual skill invocation or relies on Claude choosing to load them, contradicting the need for deterministic "automatic" application based on file paths. Option D can't easily handle files spread across many directories since CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound.
questions.trap: B = 'Inference over matching' (trusts the model to guess the applicable section; always loads irrelevant context). C = 'On-demand vs automatic' (skills require invocation; the stem demands automation). D = 'Right mechanism, wrong topology' (a per-directory CLAUDE.md is valid, but it's directory-bound and the tests are scattered).

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.stem: After running the system on the topic "impact of AI on creative industries," you observe that each subagent completes successfully: the web search agent finds relevant articles, the document analysis agent summarizes papers correctly, and the synthesis agent produces coherent output. However, the final reports cover only visual arts, completely missing music, writing, and film production. When you examine the coordinator's logs, you see it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: "AI in digital art creation," "AI in graphic design," and "AI in photography." What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The synthesis agent lacks instructions for identifying coverage gaps in the findings it receives from other agents.
The coordinator agent's task decomposition is too narrow, resulting in subagent assignments that don't cover all relevant domains of the topic.
The web search agent's queries are not comprehensive enough and need to be expanded to cover more creative industry sectors.
The document analysis agent is filtering out sources related to non-visual creative industries due to overly restrictive relevance criteria.

questions.explanationEs: This item trains a diagnostic skill the exam rewards heavily: locating the failure at the correct LAYER. The stem hands you the evidence: the coordinator's logs show it decomposed 'creative industries' into three subtasks, all visual (digital art, graphic design, photography). Music, writing, and film were never assigned to anyone. Hence B: the coordinator's decomposition is too narrow — the risk Task Statement 1.2 literally names ('risks of overly narrow task decomposition by the coordinator, leading to incomplete coverage of broad research topics'). A, C, and D share the same logical error: they blame downstream agents that the stem itself declares are working correctly WITHIN their assigned scope. The synthesis agent (A) can't synthesize findings about music that nobody searched for; detecting gaps would be a patch, not the cause. The web search agent (C) executed the queries it was given well — the problem is what it was asked to search for, not how it searched. The document analysis agent (D) invents a restrictive filter for which there's no evidence in the stem at all (a fabricated-fact distractor). Heuristic: when every component 'completes successfully' but the overall output is incomplete, the failure is in the ASSIGNMENT, not the execution. Go up a layer.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: B. The coordinator's logs reveal the root cause directly: it decomposed "creative industries" into only visual arts subtasks (digital art, graphic design, photography), completely omitting music, writing, and film. The subagents executed their assigned tasks correctly—the problem is what they were assigned. Options A, C, and D incorrectly blame downstream agents that are working correctly within their assigned scope.
questions.trap: A = 'Downstream patch' (asks the last agent to detect what was never collected). C = 'Blame the executor' (blames whoever executed a poorly formulated assignment well). D = 'Fabricated evidence' (invents a filtering criterion the stem never mentions).

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.stem: The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator agent. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?

options.text: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
Implement automatic retry logic with exponential backoff within the subagent, returning a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted.
Catch the timeout within the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
Propagate the timeout exception directly to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.

questions.explanationEs: The question is about error PROPAGATION, not about retries, and that's where the trap lives. A returns structured context — failure type, attempted query, partial results, possible alternatives — which is exactly what Task Statement 5.3 demands so the coordinator can decide with information: retry with a modified query, switch approaches, or proceed with partial results and note the coverage gap. B is the quality distractor: retry with exponential backoff inside the subagent is a GOOD practice (the guide does ask for local recovery on transient failures) — but B ruins it by ending up returning a generic 'search unavailable' status, which hides all the valuable context from the coordinator. It's half right, and in this domain the bad half rules. C is an explicit guide anti-pattern: marking a failure as success (an empty result set 'successful') erases the signal, prevents any recovery, and contaminates the final report with invisible gaps. Watch the distinction the guide underlines: a VALID empty result (successful query, zero matches) is legitimate information; a timeout disguised as an empty result is a lie to the coordinator. D is the other named anti-pattern: killing the entire workflow over a single failure, when recovery strategies were available. Rule: never collapse an error into a boolean or a generic string — the coordinator can only be intelligent if you give it something to work with.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Structured error context gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions—whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative approach, or proceed with partial results. Option B's generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator, preventing informed decisions. Option C suppresses the error by marking failure as success, which prevents any recovery and risks incomplete research outputs. Option D terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily when recovery strategies could succeed.
questions.trap: B = 'Half-right practice' (correct local retry, ruined by a generic final status that destroys the context). C = 'Silent suppression' (explicit anti-pattern: failure reported as success). D = 'Fail-the-world' (explicit anti-pattern: one local failure ends the entire workflow).

questions.scenario: Multi-Agent Research System
questions.stem: During testing, you observe that the synthesis agent frequently needs to verify specific claims while combining findings. Currently, when verification is needed, the synthesis agent returns control to the coordinator, which invokes the web search agent, then re-invokes synthesis with results. This adds 2-3 round trips per task and increases latency by 40%. Your evaluation shows that 85% of these verifications are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) while 15% require deeper investigation. What's the most effective approach to reduce overhead while maintaining system reliability?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications continue delegating to the web search agent through the coordinator.
Have the synthesis agent accumulate all verification needs and return them as a batch to the coordinator at the end of its pass, which then sends them all to the web search agent at once.
Give the synthesis agent access to all web search tools so it can handle any verification need directly without round-trips through the coordinator.
Have the web search agent proactively cache extra context around each source during initial research, anticipating what the synthesis agent might need to verify.

questions.explanationEs: The stem's 85/15 isn't decoration: it's the design instruction. It tells you to optimize the common case without breaking the exceptional one. A does exactly that — a SCOPED cross-role tool (verify_fact) for the 85% of simple fact-checks, while the complex 15% still routes through the coordinator. It's the pattern Task Statement 2.3 names: 'providing scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs while routing complex cases through the coordinator,' i.e., least privilege with one measured exception. C is the greedy trap: 'give it ALL the web search tools and let it sort itself out.' It violates separation of concerns, over-provisions the agent, and triggers the failure the guide warns about — agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them (a synthesis agent doing web searches) — on top of degrading tool selection by inflating the set. B (accumulating verifications and sending them as a batch at the end) looks efficient but creates blocking dependencies: synthesis steps usually depend on facts verified BEFORE, not after; you can't write the paragraph while waiting to confirm the data point holding it up. D bets on speculative caching: the web search agent can't reliably predict what the synthesis agent will want to verify, so it either over-caches (bloated context) or misses the hit exactly when it matters. Portable rule: 'expand tool access' is almost never the answer; 'expand it in a scoped way for the frequent case' almost always is.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Option A applies the principle of least privilege by giving the synthesis agent only what it needs for the 85% common case (simple fact verification) while preserving the existing coordination pattern for complex cases. Option B's batching approach creates blocking dependencies since synthesis steps may depend on earlier verified facts. Option C over-provisions the synthesis agent, violating separation of concerns. Option D relies on speculative caching that cannot reliably predict what the synthesis agent will need to verify.
questions.trap: C = 'Over-provisioning' (grant every tool; violates least privilege and degrades selection). B = 'Batch-blocks-pipeline' (apparent efficiency that introduces blocking dependencies). D = 'Speculative caching' (optimization based on predicting the unpredictable).

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.stem: Your pipeline script runs claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" but the job hangs indefinitely. Logs indicate Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. What's the correct approach to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline?

options.text: Add the -p flag: claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"
Set the environment variable CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true before running the command
Redirect stdin from /dev/null: claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null
Add the --batch flag: claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"

questions.explanationEs: Pure factual CLI knowledge, no tradeoff to weigh (Task Statement 3.6): -p (or --print) is the documented flag for non-interactive mode — it processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits without waiting for input. That's exactly what a CI pipeline requires. B and D are FABRICATED features: neither the CLAUDE_HEADLESS environment variable nor the --batch flag exist in Claude Code. This archetype recurs across the exam (see also .claude/config.json in Q4) and is the easiest to neutralize if you know the CLI's real surface: -p/--print, --output-format json, --json-schema, --resume. Any flag outside that list deserves immediate suspicion. C deserves separate attention because it's the experienced engineer's trap: redirecting stdin from /dev/null is a legitimate Unix workaround in other contexts, and it might even accidentally avoid the hang — but it isn't the correct way to invoke Claude Code in non-interactive mode, it doesn't guarantee the behavior (process and exit), and it doesn't give you the structured output the pipeline needs. It's 'plausible by analogy with another tool,' which is exactly the bias this distractor exploits. Close the loop with what comes next in CI: -p to avoid hanging, --output-format json + --json-schema to post findings as inline PR comments.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. The -p (or --print) flag is the documented way to run Claude Code in non-interactive mode. It processes the prompt, outputs the result to stdout, and exits without waiting for user input—exactly what CI/CD pipelines require. The other options reference non-existent features (CLAUDE_HEADLESS environment variable, --batch flag) or use Unix workarounds that don't properly address Claude Code's command syntax.
questions.trap: B = 'Fabricated env var' (CLAUDE_HEADLESS doesn't exist). D = 'Fabricated flag' (--batch doesn't exist; it also cross-contaminates with the Message Batches API concept, which is a different thing). C = 'Unix workaround by analogy' (a real technique from another context that isn't the correct way to invoke this tool).

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.stem: Your team wants to reduce API costs for automated analysis. Currently, real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a technical debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?

options.text: Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks.
Switch both workflows to batch processing with status polling to check for completion.
Keep real-time calls for both workflows to avoid batch result ordering issues.
Switch both to batch processing with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long.

questions.explanationEs: There's exactly one variable that decides this: LATENCY TOLERANCE. The Message Batches API gives 50% savings but with a processing window of up to 24 hours and NO guaranteed latency SLA (Task Statement 4.5). The stem hands you the classification for free: the pre-merge check is BLOCKING (devs waiting to merge) and the technical debt report is overnight (tolerant). Hence A: batch only for the report, synchronous for the blocking gate — each API matched to its use case. B is the 'in practice it's usually fast' fallacy: polling doesn't turn an SLA-less service into one with an SLA; a batch that takes 6 hours leaves the team unable to merge. C rests on a FALSE premise (result-ordering problems): the guide is clear that request/response pairs are correlated via custom_id, so ordering isn't a real problem — and along the way C throws away the legitimate 50% savings on the overnight workflow. D is the unnecessary-complexity trap: batch with a real-time fallback on timeout means maintaining TWO code paths, potentially paying for both calls, and adding new failure modes, all to avoid accepting the simple, correct solution, which is A. Also remember, for other items: the batch API does NOT support multi-turn tool calling within a single request.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. The Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings but has processing times up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. This makes it unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks where developers wait for results, but ideal for overnight batch jobs like technical debt reports. Option B is wrong because relying on "often faster" completion isn't acceptable for blocking workflows. Option C reflects a misconception—batch results can be correlated using custom_id fields. Option D adds unnecessary complexity when the simpler solution is matching each API to its appropriate use case.
questions.trap: B = 'Polling ≠ SLA' (assumes 'usually fast' is acceptable in a blocking flow). C = 'False premise' (invents an ordering problem custom_id already solves, and gives up the legitimate savings). D = 'Unnecessary complexity' (hybrid fallback architecture where the simple answer was already optimal).

questions.scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
questions.stem: A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?

options.text: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.
Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files before the automated review runs.
Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window to give all 14 files adequate attention in one pass.
Run three independent review passes on the full PR and only flag issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.

questions.explanationEs: This is a textbook symptom: uneven depth across files, obvious bugs missed, and CONTRADICTORY feedback (the same pattern flagged in one file and approved in another in the same PR). That's attention dilution, not a lack of context. A attacks the root cause with the pattern the guide prescribes in Task Statements 4.6 and 1.6: a local per-file pass (consistent depth) plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow. C is the most common confusion and the item's most dangerous distractor: a bigger context window solves the files FITTING, not them receiving quality attention — the model already had all of them in context and still diluted. Amount of context ≠ quality of attention. B externalizes the problem onto the developers (make them split their PRs) without fixing anything in the system: if a legitimately large PR arrives tomorrow, the review fails again. D is actively harmful and worth reasoning through: requiring a finding to appear in 2 of 3 runs SUPPRESSES real bugs that get caught intermittently — precisely the subtle ones that matter most. It raises precision at the cost of recall, exactly where you can't afford to. Compare it to A's multi-pass: A doesn't vote, A specializes each pass.
questions.officialRationale: Correct Answer: A. Splitting reviews into focused passes directly addresses the root cause: attention dilution when processing many files at once. File-by-file analysis ensures consistent depth, while a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues. Option B shifts burden to developers without improving the system. Option C misunderstands that larger context windows don't solve attention quality issues. Option D would actually suppress detection of real bugs by requiring consensus on issues that may only be caught intermittently.
questions.trap: C = 'Bigger context fallacy' (confuses context capacity with attention quality). B = 'Externalize the problem' (shifts the burden onto the human without improving the system). D = 'Consensus voting' (majority filter that suppresses intermittent findings — sacrifices recall on the subtle bugs).

questions.objective: Terminate the agentic loop using stop_reason, not text-content heuristics
questions.scenario: Agentic loop that sometimes terminates before executing a tool it already requested.
questions.stem: A team's custom agent loop checks 'if len(response.content_text) > 0: return response_text' to decide when to stop, ignoring the API's stop_reason field entirely. In some tickets the loop exits early even though Claude also emitted a tool_use block in the same turn, leaving a requested lookup_order call unexecuted. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Replace the text-length check with an explicit check on stop_reason, continuing the loop only when stop_reason equals tool_use and exiting only when stop_reason equals end_turn.
Keep the text check, but only trigger it after the response contains at least two paragraphs, to reduce false positives.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to prefix any incomplete answer with 'STILL WORKING', and check for that string before treating the text as final.
Cap the loop at a fixed maximum of 5 iterations so it can never run past the point where Claude would normally have produced a final answer.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.1: the only valid termination criterion is the response's stop_reason field — tool_use continues the loop, executing tools and reinjecting results; end_turn ends it. The guide explicitly names checking for text content as an anti-pattern, because Claude can emit text and a tool_use block in the same turn: stopping there abandons a pending tool call. A is the only option that anchors the decision to the API's real state contract instead of a heuristic over the content.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — widening the text-length threshold is still anchored in analyzing content, not the real state contract; Claude can emit text and a tool_use in the same turn, so no length threshold distinguishes a final turn from an intermediate one.
distractorsEs.C: Prompt-as-guarantee — asking the model to self-tag with a magic string delegates the stopping criterion to a probabilistic text convention, exactly the anti-pattern the guide names: parsing natural-language signals to decide termination.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — an iteration cap is a legitimate circuit breaker, but it is not the primary stopping mechanism; using it as the normal termination criterion is the second anti-pattern the guide explicitly names.

questions.trap: C is tempting because it looks like it fixes the root error with an explicit convention, but it is still the model self-reporting in natural language, not the stop_reason contract.

questions.objective: Correctly handle tool failures and multi-tool turns within the agentic loop's tool_result contract
questions.scenario: Production bug: tool failures crash the conversation, and results from a single turn get split across separate messages.
questions.stem: A team is debugging their agentic loop implementation. Two problems keep surfacing: (1) when a tool call fails, an uncaught exception crashes the whole conversation, and (2) when Claude requests two tools in the same turn, the code sometimes sends each tool's result back in its own separate user message across two API calls. Select the TWO changes that correctly fix these problems according to the tool_result contract.

options.text: Wrap tool execution in a try/except; on failure, append a tool_result block with the original tool_use_id, is_error set to true, and a description of the failure, then let the loop continue so Claude can react to it.
On failure, log the exception to an external system and let the Python exception propagate normally, since that is the documented way tool errors reach the Messages API.
When multiple tools were requested in one turn, execute all of them and return all of their tool_result blocks together inside a single user message, each correlated to its tool_use_id.
When multiple tools were requested in one turn, send each tool_result in its own separate user message immediately after that specific tool finishes, to reduce perceived latency.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.1 and two of the domain's most commonly repeated errors: tool failures must travel as data inside the tool_result (is_error true, same tool_use_id), never as an exception that interrupts the loop; and when a turn requests multiple tools, ALL the corresponding tool_result blocks go in a single user message, correlated by their tool_use_id — splitting them into separate messages degrades parallel tool use. A and C are exactly those two rules of the contract. B invents an exception-propagation convention that doesn't exist, and D applies a reasonable-sounding latency intuition to the wrong axis of the problem.

distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature — there is no documented convention of letting the exception propagate as an official path to the Messages API; the guide is emphatic about the opposite: a tool error travels as data inside the tool_result with is_error true, never as an exception that knocks the model out of the loop.
