distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — splitting results across separate messages looks like a reasonable latency optimization, but the guide explicitly warns that doing so degrades parallel tool use; all of a turn's results must go in a single user message.

questions.trap: D is the subtlest trap: it sounds like a reasonable performance optimization, but the contract requires grouping all of a turn's tool_result blocks into a single message.

questions.objective: Recognize that subagents do not inherit coordinator context and require explicit prompt passing
questions.scenario: Research coordinator delegates synthesis without passing along the findings it already collected.
questions.stem: A coordinator in a multi-agent research system has already collected findings from a web-researcher subagent (with URLs and excerpts) and a doc-analyst subagent (with page numbers). It now spawns a synthesizer subagent with the prompt: 'Synthesize the research findings we've gathered into a cited report.' The synthesizer's report comes back with no citations and generic claims. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The synthesizer subagent's model is too small to perform synthesis reliably; it should be swapped for a larger model.

The coordinator's prompt to the synthesizer never included the actual findings — subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history, so anything they need must be written explicitly into the Task prompt.
The synthesizer needs its own WebSearch and Read tools so it can re-fetch the sources itself instead of relying on the coordinator's summary.
The coordinator should lower its temperature setting so subsequent delegations are more deterministic and consistent.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.3 and the domain's #1 implementation error, repeated three times in the guide: the subagent inherits NOTHING from the coordinator — no history, no tool results, no system prompt. The only parent-subagent channel is the Task tool's prompt string; if the findings with URLs and excerpts aren't written there explicitly, the synthesizer simply doesn't have them. B names the exact cause. Switching models, adding tools, or adjusting temperature don't fix the real absence: context that was never transmitted.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — switching models is a real lever in other scenarios, but here the subagent never received the findings at all; no model size can cite data that isn't in its prompt.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — giving the synthesizer its own search tools so it can rediscover what the coordinator already found duplicates work and violates role-scoped boundaries; the problem isn't a lack of tools, it's a lack of explicit context in the Task tool's prompt.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — temperature governs sampling randomness, not what information the subagent receives; lowering it doesn't make findings appear that were never written into the delegation prompt.

questions.trap: C is the subtlest trap: it looks like a reasonable 'give it more capability' fix, but the subagent could already cite perfectly well if the coordinator had passed it the findings — the failure isn't about tooling.

questions.objective: Achieve true subagent parallelism via multiple Task calls in a single coordinator response
questions.scenario: Three search subagents that should run in parallel, but get spawned one after another.
questions.stem: A developer wants a research coordinator to run three search subagents in parallel to cut latency. Their implementation has the coordinator emit one Task call, wait for that subagent's full result, then emit the next Task call, and so on for all three. Total latency is roughly the sum of all three subagent runtimes. What must change to achieve true parallelism?

options.text: Switch the three subagents to a faster model so each individual run completes quicker, keeping the sequential structure.
Merge the three subagents into a single subagent responsible for all three subtopics, removing the need for multiple Task calls.
Have the coordinator emit all three Task calls together within a single response, rather than waiting for one subagent's result before spawning the next.
Increase allowedTools so the coordinator can call Task, WebSearch, and Read directly, bypassing subagent spawning for the search step.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.3: real parallelism means multiple Task calls emitted in ONE single coordinator response, not in successive turns where each result is awaited before spawning the next. If the coordinator serializes — emits one Task, waits, emits another — it has lost the parallelism advantage regardless of each subagent's individual speed. C is the only change that attacks the problem's real structure; the other options optimize or redesign around a symptom without touching the cause.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — a faster model reduces each individual run's time, but as long as the structure stays one Task per turn, total latency still adds up the three runs in series; it doesn't attack the underlying problem.
distractorsEs.B: Downstream patch / blame the executor — merging the three subagents into one dodges the parallelism problem instead of solving it, and sacrifices the per-subtopic specialization that the hub-and-spoke design itself is meant to preserve.
distractorsEs.D: Scope flip — giving the coordinator search tools directly inverts the hub-and-spoke architecture the scenario already adopted; the problem isn't that the coordinator needs to search itself, it's that it's serializing Task calls that should go together.

questions.trap: A tempts because 'faster' sounds like it attacks latency, but one Task per turn is still serial no matter how fast each individual subagent runs.

questions.objective: Diagnose missing Task in allowedTools as the cause of a coordinator that never spawns subagents
questions.scenario: Coordinator configured with a subagent that never actually gets invoked.
questions.stem: A coordinator agent is configured with an AgentDefinition for a web-researcher subagent and a prompt instructing it to delegate web research tasks. In practice, the coordinator never spawns the subagent — it always attempts the research itself using its own tools, or produces a text response saying it cannot search the web. What is the most likely configuration problem?

options.text: The web-researcher subagent's description field is too long, confusing the coordinator about when to delegate.
The coordinator needs a lower temperature so it more reliably follows its delegation instructions.
The AgentDefinition is missing a model field, so the subagent silently fails to initialize.
The coordinator's allowedTools list does not include Task, so it has no mechanism available to spawn any subagent at all.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.3: without Task in allowedTools, the coordinator has no mechanism at all to spawn subagents, no matter how well-configured the AgentDefinition is. The guide flags this as the number-one real-world cause of 'Claude ignores my subagent.' D is the only option that points to a real, documented requirement; the others invent requirements or apply levers that don't touch the spawn tool's availability.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — a poorly written description can indeed make the coordinator choose badly AMONG several available subagents, but the described symptom is that it never delegates at all; that points to the spawn mechanism not even being enabled, not to a suboptimal description.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — temperature affects sampling randomness, not whether a tool is available to the model; no temperature adjustment makes an invocation mechanism appear that isn't in allowedTools.
distractorsEs.C: Fabricated feature — AgentDefinition doesn't require a model field to function, nor does the guide document a silent failed initialization from its absence; it's a credible-sounding explanation built around a requirement that doesn't exist.

questions.trap: C sounds plausible because 'a missing config field' is a real bug pattern, but the guide doesn't document that requirement or that failure mode — the real cause is simpler: Task is missing from allowedTools.

questions.objective: Diagnose a coverage failure at the coordinator's decomposition layer, not the executor layer
questions.scenario: Report on global AI regulation that ends up covering only the European Union.
questions.stem: A coordinator is asked to research 'global AI regulation trends.' Its logs show it decomposed the task into two subtasks: 'EU AI Act provisions' and 'EU AI Act enforcement timeline.' Both subagents report success with well-cited findings. The final report is technically accurate but says nothing about the US, China, or any other jurisdiction. Where does the fix belong?

options.text: In the web-researcher subagent, by adding stricter relevance filtering so it stops returning tangential EU sources.
In the synthesizer subagent, by instructing it to flag when a report seems narrower than the original topic.
In the coordinator's decomposition step — it should enumerate the material jurisdictions or branches of the topic before assigning subtasks, and partition scope explicitly across them.
In the document analyst subagent, by giving it a broader set of source URLs to pull from.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.2 and the domain's canonical example: when every subagent finishes successfully and the overall result is incomplete, the failure is in the assignment, not the execution. Here the coordinator split 'global AI regulation' into two subtasks that only cover the EU, leaving out the United States, China, and everywhere else. The fix lives in the coordinator: enumerate the topic's material branches before assigning, and partition scope explicitly across them. Blaming any of the three executing subagents is the exam's most repeated distractor archetype.

distractorsEs.A: Downstream patch / blame the executor — the web-researcher executed its assignment well within the scope it was given (EU AI Act); tightening its relevance filter doesn't make the United States or China appear, since they were never part of its task.
distractorsEs.B: Downstream patch / blame the executor — asking the synthesizer to detect that the report 'seems narrow' delegates a coverage diagnosis to an agent that only sees what the other two handed it; it can't flag gaps about jurisdictions that never reached its prompt.
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch / blame the executor — the document analyst also worked correctly within its assignment; giving it more URLs doesn't fix the fact that the original decomposition never included other jurisdictions as a subtopic.

questions.trap: B is the most elegant variant of this trap: it sounds like a reasonable self-check mechanism, but it asks the wrong agent — the one with the least visibility into the original scope — to detect a gap that only the coordinator can see.

questions.objective: Design an iterative refinement loop for coverage gaps the coordinator did not anticipate
questions.scenario: After fixing a narrow decomposition, a standing mechanism against future gaps is still missing.
questions.stem: After correcting a coordinator's initial decomposition to cover all material branches of a topic, the team wants a standing mechanism that catches coverage gaps the coordinator didn't anticipate up front, without a human re-reviewing every report. Which pattern best fits this need?

options.text: A fixed five-step pipeline that always runs search, then analysis, then synthesis, then formatting, then citation-checking, regardless of the topic.

An iterative refinement loop: the coordinator evaluates the synthesized output against the enumerated branches, identifies gaps, re-delegates to search or analysis subagents with targeted queries for just those gaps, and re-invokes synthesis.
A rule that any subtopic with fewer than three sources automatically triggers a full restart of the entire research pipeline from scratch.
A voting mechanism where three independent coordinators each produce a full report, and only claims present in at least two of the three reports are kept.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.2: the pattern the guide prescribes for coverage is the iterative refinement loop — evaluator-optimizer applied to coverage: the coordinator evaluates the synthesis against the enumerated branches, detects gaps, re-delegates with targeted queries to search or analysis, and re-synthesizes, repeating until coverage is sufficient. B is that exact pattern. A fixed pipeline doesn't adapt to unanticipated gaps, a full restart is disproportionate, and consensus voting trades recall for precision.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — a fixed five-step pipeline is prompt chaining, useful when the sequence is predictable; but the problem here is detecting coverage gaps that weren't anticipated up front, something a rigid sequence neither evaluates nor corrects at runtime.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — a full pipeline restart for any subtopic with few sources is disproportionate: it burns all the already-valid work to fix one isolated gap, instead of re-delegating with a query targeted only at what's missing.
distractorsEs.D: Consensus voting — requiring a finding to appear in at least 2 of 3 runs suppresses real signal: legitimate but less-documented topics get discarded for not repeating across independent runs, instead of being fixed with a targeted re-delegation.

questions.trap: D sounds like a reasonable quality mechanism, but consensus across independent runs punishes exactly the findings that are real but infrequent — it doesn't detect coverage gaps.

questions.objective: Replace repeated prompt-side enforcement with a programmatic prerequisite gate for identity-order compliance
questions.scenario: Cancellation agent that skips ownership verification in 9% of cases.
questions.stem: Telemetry shows that in 9% of subscription-cancellation tickets, the agent calls cancel_subscription directly using only the account email the customer typed in chat, without first calling verify_account_owner to confirm they control that account. This has caused a handful of cancellations by people impersonating the account holder. The team's first fix was adding 'You MUST call verify_account_owner before any cancellation' to the system prompt in bold, which reduced the rate to 3%. What should the team do next?

options.text: Add a few-shot example showing the agent correctly calling verify_account_owner before cancel_subscription, to reinforce the bolded instruction further.
Reduce the bold instruction to a shorter, punchier phrase, on the theory that the original wording was too long for the model to fully attend to.
Build a machine-learning classifier trained on past tickets to predict which cancellation requests are likely impersonation attempts, and route flagged ones to a human.

Add a programmatic prerequisite gate (e.g., a PreToolUse hook) that blocks cancel_subscription until verify_account_owner has returned a verified account ID, with a denial reason telling the model what to do instead.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.4/1.5, the domain's master axis: identity verification before an irreversible operation is deterministic compliance, and a prompt instruction — no matter how emphatic or reinforced — has a non-zero failure rate by construction. Dropping from 9% to 3% isn't a fix, it's the same bug made harder to reproduce. D is the correct intervention: a programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks cancel_subscription until verify_account_owner returns a verified ID, with a denial reason that tells the model what to do instead.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee — few-shot is a real judgment-calibration technique, but the problem here isn't a fuzzy boundary: it's a mandatory-order requirement with identity at stake. Lowering the rate with more prompt is still the same bug, just harder to reproduce — it isn't guaranteed compliance.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee — shortening or rewording the instruction still bets compliance on the model obeying a prompt sentence; no wording has a zero failure rate by construction, no matter how direct it is.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — training an impersonation classifier is heavy, labeled-data infrastructure for a problem a programmatic prerequisite gate already solves deterministically without training anything.

questions.trap: A is the most tempting trap because the guide does value few-shot in general — but here the axis is guarantee, not judgment: identity plus an irreversible operation demands enforcement in code, not a more persuasive demonstration in the prompt.

questions.objective: Distinguish a fuzzy escalation-judgment problem from a deterministic-compliance problem in the same agent
questions.scenario: The same cancellation agent, now with a judgment problem, not a compliance problem.
questions.stem: The same subscription-cancellation agent now has a separate, unrelated issue: when a customer asks to cancel but also mentions they were double-charged last month, the agent sometimes resolves the cancellation and drops the billing complaint, and sometimes escalates the whole ticket to a human even though the cancellation itself is routine. There is no money-safety violation here — just inconsistent judgment about when the situation needs a human. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt (e.g., cancel routine requests immediately; escalate only when the billing discrepancy itself needs investigation) with a few-shot example showing both paths handled in the same ticket.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks cancel_subscription whenever the word 'charged' appears anywhere in the conversation, forcing escalation.
Build a sentiment-analysis classifier that scores customer frustration and escalates whenever the score crosses a fixed threshold.
Add a PostToolUse hook that automatically appends a billing-complaint flag to every cancellation record, regardless of what the agent decided.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.4/5.2 and the domain's master axis on its judgment side: there's no irreversible operation to shield here, there's a fuzzy decision boundary about when a multi-topic ticket needs human intervention. The guide says this is solved with explicit criteria and few-shot, not infrastructure. A specifies the criterion (resolve the routine part, escalate only the part that needs it) and exemplifies it. A keyword hook is brittle and over-blocks; sentiment and automatic tagging don't touch the decision criterion.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — a programmatic hook is the right tool for deterministic guarantee, but there's no binary business rule to enforce here: it's a fuzzy decision boundary about WHEN to escalate. Blocking on a word's presence is also brittle and will block legitimate cancellations that mention 'charged' with no real dispute.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis — the guide is explicit: customer sentiment is an unreliable proxy for a case's real complexity. A sentiment classifier can't distinguish a genuine billing dispute from a customer merely annoyed by the process.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering / ML escape — a hook that indiscriminately tags everything doesn't help the agent decide, in the moment, whether to resolve, escalate, or both; it adds infrastructure without touching the missing decision criterion.

questions.trap: B is the symmetric trap of this question pair: here there IS money mentioned (a charge), but the real problem is a judgment boundary about escalation scope, not a binary compliance rule — same agent, opposite axis from the cancellation question.

questions.objective: Use PostToolUse hooks to normalize heterogeneous tool data before it reaches the model
questions.scenario: Two MCP servers return dates and statuses in different formats to the same agent.
questions.stem: A support agent pulls order data from two different MCP servers: one returns created_at as a Unix timestamp and status as a numeric code (1, 2, 3, 4); the other returns created_at as an ISO 8601 string and status as a text label. The agent occasionally reasons incorrectly about order age and status because it has to guess the meaning of raw numeric codes inline. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing the numeric-to-label status mapping and explaining how to convert Unix timestamps, so the model can do the conversion itself each time.
Implement a PostToolUse hook that normalizes both formats — converting Unix timestamps to ISO 8601 and numeric status codes to text labels — before the tool_result reaches the model's context.
Switch to a single MCP server for all order data so format inconsistency can never arise again.
Instruct the agent, via few-shot examples, to always double-check its date and status interpretation before using it in reasoning.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.5: normalizing heterogeneous formats — Unix timestamp vs ISO 8601, numeric codes vs labels — before the model reads them eliminates an entire class of reasoning errors. A PostToolUse hook does exactly that, and runs in the developer's process, not inside the context window: it's free in tokens. B is the only option that moves the conversion to the right place; the others leave the conversion burden on the model or dodge the real problem without solving it.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee — teaching the model to convert formats on every call spends tokens on a mechanical, deterministic task, and still depends on the model executing that conversion correctly every time; the guide flags this as work that belongs to a hook, not an instruction.
distractorsEs.C: Scope flip — consolidating into a single MCP server isn't the option that attacks the problem: the point isn't how many servers exist, it's that the heterogeneous data that ALREADY arrives must be normalized before it enters the model's context.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice — asking the model to double-check before reasoning acknowledges the problem, but leaves the actual conversion in the model's own hands on every turn, instead of eliminating it at the root before the data reaches its context.

questions.trap: A seems reasonable because documenting the mapping is better than not documenting it, but it still spends tokens and reasoning capacity on a purely mechanical task that a hook solves for free, outside the context window.

questions.objective: Compile a structured handoff for human escalation instead of a generic summary
questions.scenario: Escalation of a disputed refund that reaches the human as a generic label.
questions.stem: A support agent escalates a disputed refund to a human agent using escalate_to_human(reason='complex case, needs review'). The human, who has no access to the conversation transcript, has to re-read the entire order history and ask the customer to repeat their story before they can act. What should the escalation payload contain instead?

options.text: Only the customer's most recent message verbatim, since that captures their current state of mind most accurately for the human agent.
A numeric complexity score from 1-10 computed by the agent, so the human can prioritize this ticket in their queue relative to others.
A shortened version of the reason string, e.g., 'refund dispute, has photos', kept under 10 words so the human can scan it quickly.
A structured object with the verified customer ID, a root-cause summary (damaged in transit, photo evidence attached), the disputed amount, what was already attempted, and a recommended action.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.4: the human being escalated to doesn't see the transcript, so the real value is in the structured handoff — an object with verified customer ID, root cause, amount, what was already attempted, and a recommended action — not a phrase or label that forces them to reconstruct the case. D is that complete object. A message fragment, a made-up score, or a short label each fail to give the human what they need to decide without re-investigating from scratch.

distractorsEs.A: Half-right practice — the customer's last message is real, relevant information, but on its own it doesn't reconstruct the case: the human is still missing the verified ID, the root cause, the amount, and what was already attempted. A transcript fragment is not a structured handoff.
distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature — a numeric complexity score self-generated by the agent isn't a mechanism the guide describes for escalation; moreover the guide is explicit that model-self-reported confidence or complexity is an unreliable proxy, not a figure the human should take as objective prioritization.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch / blame the executor — shortening the reason to a generic label shifts the work of reconstructing the case onto the human, who doesn't have the transcript; a short, readable label still forces them to investigate from scratch instead of deciding with data.

questions.trap: C is this pattern's most common trap: it looks actionable because it's short and readable, but it's still a label, not the data the human needs to decide without reconstructing the case.

questions.objective: Distinguish a keyword-based routing classifier (controls tool availability) from control over call order
questions.scenario: Keyword-based triage layer that claims to solve a call-order problem.
questions.stem: A team builds a 'triage layer' in front of their support agent: a keyword classifier reads the incoming message and pre-selects which subset of tools (e.g., only lookup_order and process_refund, or only get_customer) gets passed into the Claude API call for that turn. They claim this solves their problem of the agent sometimes calling process_refund before get_customer has verified the customer's identity. Does it?

options.text: Yes, because restricting the available tool set per message is functionally equivalent to enforcing call order.
Yes, but only for messages where the classifier has high confidence in its keyword match.

No — the classifier controls which tools are available for a given message, not the order in which an available tool set gets called; get_customer and process_refund can still both be exposed together and called in the wrong order within the same turn.
No, because keyword classifiers are inherently less accurate than the underlying Claude model at every task, including tool selection.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the concept of model-driven decision-making vs. a preconfigured decision tree in its most deceptive form: a keyword routing classifier is a decision tree in disguise that solves WHICH tools are available, not WHAT ORDER they're called in. If get_customer and process_refund both end up exposed in the same turn — quite likely if the message mentions both topics — nothing stops Claude from calling them in the wrong order. C names exactly that nuance; the mandatory-order problem demands a prerequisite gate, not a keyword triage layer.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — a keyword router is a real technique for scoping which tools the model sees, but that solves availability, not sequence; if both relevant tools end up exposed in the same turn, nothing stops them from being called in the wrong order.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — conditioning the mitigation on the classifier's confidence still doesn't touch the problem's real axis: even at high confidence, restricting availability doesn't impose sequence among the tools that do end up exposed together.
distractorsEs.D: Fabricated feature — the guide doesn't claim keyword classifiers are inherently less accurate at everything; they're a legitimate technique for other problems. The real reason this doesn't solve THIS problem is architectural (availability vs. order), not general accuracy.

questions.trap: A is this concept's central trap: a real technique (keyword routing) gets confused with sequence control, when in reality it only controls which tools are available.

questions.objective: Distinguish AgentDefinition.description from prompt, and prefer goal-based coordinator prompts over procedural ones
questions.scenario: AgentDefinition with an empty description and an overly prescriptive coordinator prompt.
questions.stem: A team configures a doc-analyst subagent's AgentDefinition. They write a detailed, step-by-step procedural prompt for the coordinator itself: 'Step 1: call web-researcher. Step 2: call doc-analyst. Step 3: call synthesizer. Never deviate from this order.' Separately, the doc-analyst's own description field just says 'A subagent.' The coordinator now invokes doc-analyst on every query, even ones with no documents involved, and struggles to adapt when a query needs two rounds of search before synthesis makes sense. What are the two configuration problems here?

options.text: The vague description field gives the coordinator no basis for deciding WHEN to delegate to doc-analyst, and the rigid step-by-step coordinator prompt removes the adaptability needed to decide how many rounds or in what order subagents should run for a given query.
The doc-analyst's prompt field, its own system prompt, is missing, and the coordinator needs a larger context window to hold all three subagents' instructions at once.
The AgentDefinition needs a tools field restricting doc-analyst to Read, Grep, and Glob, and the coordinator prompt needs to be even more detailed, spelling out every possible query type in advance.
The coordinator should be merged with all three subagents into a single agent to eliminate the need for delegation decisions entirely.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.3: an AgentDefinition's description field is what the coordinator uses to decide WHEN to delegate — empty or generic, it gives no such basis and the subagent gets invoked indiscriminately. Separately, the guide is explicit that the coordinator's prompt should specify goals and quality criteria, not a step-by-step recipe: procedural instructions kill the adaptability needed to vary how many rounds or in what order to act depending on the query. A names both problems correctly; the other options invent an undescribed problem, worsen the error, or are disproportionate.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — a missing subagent prompt would indeed be a real problem, but the stem doesn't describe that (it says description is empty, not prompt); and a larger context window doesn't fix instructions being rigid and procedural.
distractorsEs.C: Half-right practice — scoping doc-analyst's tools down to Read, Grep, and Glob is a step in the right direction, but capping it off by asking for an EVEN MORE detailed, procedural coordinator prompt worsens exactly the problem described: step-by-step instructions kill the adaptability the coordinator needs.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering / ML escape — merging all four agents into one eliminates the hub-and-spoke architecture entirely instead of fixing its two broken configurations; it's a disproportionate response that throws out the whole design.

questions.trap: C is the subtlest trap: the first half is a legitimate, reasonable fix, but the second half asks for MORE procedural prescription, exactly the opposite of what the guide recommends for coordinator prompts.

questions.objective: Choose dynamic decomposition over prompt chaining when steps cannot be predicted in advance
questions.scenario: Adding test coverage to a legacy codebase with no structure known up front.
questions.stem: A team wants Claude to 'add comprehensive test coverage to a legacy codebase' with no existing test infrastructure and unknown module boundaries. They are deciding between a fixed 4-stage pipeline (always: scan all files, then generate unit tests, then generate integration tests, then run coverage report) and a plan where Claude first maps the codebase structure, identifies high-impact untested areas, and builds a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered along the way. Which approach fits this task, and why?

options.text: The fixed 4-stage pipeline, because a predictable sequence of stages is always cheaper and more testable than letting the model decide its own steps.
The fixed 4-stage pipeline, because test generation is a well-known task type regardless of codebase structure, so the steps can be defined in advance.
Neither — the task should be split by file count into N parallel subagents, each handling an equal slice of the codebase's files, decided before any exploration happens.

The adaptive plan, because the codebase structure and dependency graph are unknown up front; the number and nature of steps can't be predicted, so the model needs to discover structure first and let each finding shape the next step.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.6: the guide uses exactly this example — full test coverage on a legacy codebase — as the canonical case of dynamic decomposition: map structure, identify high-impact areas, and a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies surface, because the number and nature of the steps can't be predicted up front. D captures that pattern. A fixed pipeline trades latency for accuracy ONLY when the sequence is already known; here it isn't, and partitioning by files before exploring ignores the real dependency structure.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — prompt chaining IS cheaper and more testable when the sequence is known up front, but that advantage doesn't apply here: the codebase's structure and dependencies are exactly what isn't known until you explore.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — test generation being a well-known task type doesn't mean its steps are predictable in this specific codebase; the guide distinguishes the task type from whether its decomposition is predictable, and here it isn't until the structure gets mapped.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — partitioning by file count before exploring ignores that high-impact areas and dependencies are exactly what needs discovering first; a mechanical pre-exploration partition can split tightly coupled modules across different subagents.

questions.trap: B is the most reasonable-looking trap: 'test coverage' sounds like a routine, well-understood task, but the guide distinguishes the TYPE of task from whether ITS STEPS are predictable in this specific case — here they aren't, until you explore.

questions.objective: Apply hub-and-spoke and proportional design when distributing a high-frequency cross-role tool
questions.scenario: Synthesizer that pays 2-3 round trips for every factual verification, no matter how simple.
questions.stem: In a multi-agent research system, the synthesizer subagent frequently needs to verify small factual claims (dates, names, statistics) while merging findings from other subagents. Today, every verification, however simple, requires the synthesizer to hand control back to the coordinator, which invokes the web-researcher subagent, then re-invokes the synthesizer: 2-3 round trips per verification. Telemetry shows 90% of these are simple fact-checks and 10% require deeper multi-source investigation. Select the TWO design choices consistent with the guide's hub-and-spoke and proportionality principles.

options.text: Give the synthesizer full access to the web-researcher's entire toolkit (web search, page fetching, source ranking) so it can handle every verification itself without round trips.
Give the synthesizer a single scoped cross-role tool (e.g., verify_fact) for the frequent, simple case, so the 90% doesn't pay the round-trip cost.
Pre-fetch and cache likely verification queries in advance based on the research topic, before the synthesizer even requests them, to eliminate round trips entirely.
Keep the 10% of complex, multi-source verifications routed through the coordinator to the web-researcher subagent, preserving centralized error handling and observability for the harder cases.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Tasks 1.2/1.3 with the guide's 85/15 pattern, here 90/10: the distribution IS the design instruction. B solves the frequent case with a scoped cross-role tool (verify_fact), avoiding the round-trip cost for the simple 90%. D preserves hub-and-spoke for the complex 10%, which still needs the coordinator's centralized error handling and observability. Over-provisioning with the full toolkit (A) breaks least privilege by role, and speculatively pre-caching (C) tries to guess facts that depend on findings not yet produced.

distractorsEs.A: Over-provisioning — giving the synthesizer the full search toolkit violates the role-scoped tools design; the guide warns that agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them, and it degrades the synthesizer's own tool selection for its main job.
distractorsEs.C: Speculative caching — pre-caching likely verifications before they're requested tries to predict the unpredictable; the real set of facts to verify depends on what each research run finds, and can't be reliably anticipated in advance.

questions.trap: A is the most common trap here: give it every tool and let it sort itself out looks like it fixes the bottleneck at the root, but the guide is explicit that over-provisioning degrades tool selection and breaks separation of concerns.

questions.objective: Apply facts about resume, fork_session, and stale-context tradeoffs correctly
questions.scenario: Named session with refactored files on one side, and two strategies to compare on the other.
questions.stem: A team used a named session perf-investigation to map a codebase's payment module (30 files read, three bottlenecks identified). Overnight, another developer refactored two of those files. Separately, the team also wants to explore two different refactor strategies starting from that same completed analysis, without either exploration contaminating the other. Select the TWO statements below that are accurate.

options.text: Running --resume perf-investigation from a different working directory than the original session will still reliably reattach to the same conversation history, since session state is keyed only by session name.

fork_session creates an independent branch of the conversation from a shared baseline — the original session stays intact — but it does not fork the filesystem; both branches read and write the same real files on disk.

If the refactor touched the core of what was previously analyzed, starting a brand-new session with a structured summary injected (the three bottlenecks, decisions made, open questions) is more reliable than resuming and reasoning over now-stale file reads.

Because sessions persist the full filesystem state at the time of each tool call, resuming perf-investigation automatically re-reads any files that changed since the last session, with no further action needed.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 1.7 in its exact nuances: fork_session branches the conversation from a shared baseline without touching the filesystem — the files are shared and real (B); and when the refactor touched the heart of what was analyzed, starting fresh with an injected structured summary is more reliable than carrying stale tool results forward (C). A inverts a real production trap: resume depends on cwd and fails silently from a different directory. D invents that sessions persist the filesystem; they only persist the conversation, and no resume re-reads files on its own.

distractorsEs.A: Fabricated feature — the guide flags exactly the opposite as a real production trap: resume derives the history path from cwd; resuming from a different directory produces a new, EMPTY session, not a reliable reconnection to the expected history.
distractorsEs.D: Fabricated feature — the session persists the conversation, not the filesystem; a resume doesn't re-read anything on its own. If the code changed out from under the agent, you have to explicitly tell it which files changed or start fresh — it never happens automatically.

questions.trap: A is the most dangerous trap of this pair because it's a silent production failure: there's no error, just a new, empty session that appears to have worked until the agent starts hallucinating context it never had.

questions.objective: Diagnose tool misrouting caused by minimal descriptions and apply the highest-leverage fix
questions.scenario: Support agent confuses tools due to minimal descriptions
questions.stem: In production, when a user writes "check my order #48213", the agent calls `get_customer` instead of `lookup_order` in 30% of cases. Both tools currently have one-line descriptions: `get_customer` -> "Retrieves customer information" and `lookup_order` -> "Retrieves order details." What is the most effective first step to fix this?

options.text: Rewrite both tool descriptions to include input formats, example queries, edge cases, and explicit boundary statements about when to use each tool instead of the other.
Add 5-8 few-shot examples to the system prompt showing "order number -> lookup_order" mappings.
Build a keyword-based routing layer that pre-selects the tool before the model sees the request.
Merge both tools into a single generic `lookup_entity` tool that accepts either an order number or a customer identifier.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.1: the tool description is the primary selection mechanism the model reads, not the system prompt or history. When two tools share minimal one-line descriptions, the root cause is informational: missing input format, missing example queries, and above all, an explicit boundary stating what each tool does NOT do and which one to defer to. Rewriting with those four elements is the cheap, highest-leverage intervention the guide calls a 'low-effort, high-leverage fix.' The other options are real techniques applied before exhausting this one, or disproportionate for a first step.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis: few-shot is a real, valuable technique in the domain (D4), but applied here to the wrong cause — the missing information in the description itself, not a genuine judgment ambiguity — it still doesn't touch the root of the problem.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering: a keyword router bypasses the model's natural-language understanding and has to be maintained forever — heavy infrastructure for a problem that's fixed with a better description.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering / disproportionate decision: consolidating into a generic tool is a valid architectural decision in other contexts, but as a 'first step' it's the expensive answer without having exhausted the cheap one.

questions.trap: B is the main decoy: it looks diligent and is a real technique from the guide, but applied to the wrong cause — the minimal descriptions, not genuine ambiguity.

questions.objective: Eliminate functional overlap between near-identical tools through renaming and description rewrites
questions.scenario: Overlap between analyze_content and analyze_document
questions.stem: Your research agent has two tools with nearly identical descriptions: `analyze_content` ("Analyzes content and returns insights") is meant only for text scraped from web search results, while `analyze_document` ("Analyzes content and returns insights") is meant only for user-uploaded PDFs. The agent frequently calls the wrong one. Which change most directly eliminates the functional overlap?

options.text: Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the model to "always analyze the retrieved documents carefully," so it remembers to inspect the content before responding.
Rename `analyze_content` to `extract_web_results` and rewrite its description to be specific to web-search output; keep `analyze_document` unchanged for uploaded files.
Build a classifier that inspects the input string and pre-selects the correct tool before the model sees the request.
Merge both tools into a single `analyze(content, instruction)` tool where a free-text `instruction` parameter tells the model what kind of analysis to perform.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.1, the renaming-to-eliminate-overlap technique. Two tools with near-identical descriptions get confused because the name is the first semantic signal the model reads, even before the body of the description. Renaming `analyze_content` to `extract_web_results` and writing a description specific to its input source eliminates the ambiguity at the root, without touching `analyze_document`. The guide names this technique alongside its sibling, splitting generic tools into purpose-built tools — both act on the tool's contract, not on instructions the model has to interpret on every request.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee: adds prompt wording where objective 2.1 calls for a structural intervention (rename + rewrite); and this exact phrase — 'analyze the retrieved documents carefully' — is itself the example of keyword-sensitive wording that objective 2.1 warns can hijack selection toward `analyze_document`.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering: an external classifier bypasses the model's natural-language selection and requires its own upkeep, for a problem that's solved by renaming and describing better.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis: consolidating generic tools is valid when two tools ARE redundant, but here they aren't — they serve different input sources (web vs. uploaded document); merging them reverses the 2.1 skill that calls for splitting generic tools into purpose-built ones, not the other way around.

questions.trap: A is the most dangerous: it sounds like it 'reinforces' correct selection, but the guide explicitly flags it as the mechanism that hijacks routing.

questions.objective: Recognize keyword-sensitive system prompt wording as a secondary cause of tool misrouting
questions.scenario: Persistent misrouting after rewriting descriptions
questions.stem: You already rewrote `get_customer` and `lookup_order` with detailed input formats, examples, and explicit boundary clauses, but misrouting still occurs in 8% of cases. You inspect the system prompt and find the line: "Always look up customer records first before addressing any request." What is the most likely cause of the remaining misrouting, and the appropriate fix?

options.text: Ask customers to explicitly type the word "order" or "account" in their first message, so the agent has a clearer keyword to route on.
Add a `.claude/routing-rules.yaml` file that maps request keywords to tool names, bypassing the model's own tool selection for these two tools.
The system prompt instruction is keyword-sensitive and biases tool selection toward `get_customer` regardless of the request; revise the wording to remove the blanket preference.
Replace both tools with a single routing layer that inspects the request text before either tool is exposed to the model.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.1 in its second layer: when descriptions are ALREADY rewritten with explicit boundaries and misrouting persists, objective 2.1 says plainly that you need to check the system prompt's wording for keyword-sensitive instructions. The line 'Always look up customer records first' biases selection toward `get_customer` regardless of the request's actual content — it's the hijacking mechanism the guide warns about. The fix is surgical: adjust that phrase, not rewrite again descriptions the stem already declares corrected, nor build new infrastructure for a problem whose hard evidence already points to its cause.

distractorsEs.A: Externalize the problem: shifting the disambiguation burden onto the customer doesn't fix the system — objective 2.1 places responsibility on the description and the prompt, not on how the user phrases their message.
distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature + over-engineering: there is no `.claude/routing-rules.yaml` mechanism that maps keywords to tools outside the model's selection; inventing that layer is undocumented infrastructure for a problem that already has an identified cause in the stem.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: a router bypasses the model's natural-language understanding and requires its own upkeep — the stem's textual clue (the system prompt line) points to a much cheaper cause to fix.

questions.trap: B is the most technical-looking decoy: it uses credible Claude Code syntax (`.claude/*.yaml`) for a mechanism that doesn't exist — the 'fabricated feature' pattern the exam uses as a gift for anyone who knows the real surface.

questions.objective: Replace uniform error responses with structured error metadata distinguishing failure categories
questions.scenario: process_refund returns a generic error for everything
questions.stem: Your MCP `process_refund` tool currently returns `{"error": "Operation failed"}` for every failure mode: payment-service timeouts, malformed order IDs, and refunds requested outside the 30-day policy window. The agent retries all three the same way and eventually tells customers "there was a technical error, try again later" -even when the real reason is a policy violation. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Wrap the tool call in a longer exponential-backoff retry loop before giving up and returning the generic error.
Add a PostToolUse hook that inspects the generic error string and guesses whether it was transient, validation, or business by pattern-matching keywords in the message text.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent not to retry more than once and to explain refund errors to the customer.
Return structured error metadata that includes `errorCategory` (transient/validation/business), `isRetryable`, and a customer-facing explanation for policy violations.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.2: a uniform error collapses transient, validation, and business failures into a single semantics and stops the agent from deciding an appropriate recovery strategy. The structural fix is to return `errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, and, for business errors like an expired refund window, a customer-facing `customerExplanation` — exactly what objective 2.2 asks for. No layer outside the tool can invent that category: not a longer retry, not a hook guessing from free text, not a prompt instruction. The information has to be born structured in the data the tool returns, not reconstructed afterward.

distractorsEs.A: Half-right practice: retrying with backoff is correct for what's transient, but applied indiscriminately to all three failure types (including the policy violation) wastes attempts on an error that will never improve.
distractorsEs.B: Downstream patch: trying to guess the category by pattern-matching over a generic string fixes the symptom one layer up instead of fixing the source — the MCP server itself knows the real category and should declare it, not leave it for something else to infer.
distractorsEs.C: Prompt-as-guarantee: you're asking the model to infer a distinction (technical vs. policy) that the data it receives doesn't contain. No prompt instruction can invent a category the server never communicated.

questions.trap: B looks the most sophisticated: it adds a processing layer and sounds like serious engineering, but it still lacks the real information — it only guesses over free text instead of receiving the structured data objective 2.2 asks the tool to return.

questions.objective: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results in structured tool responses
questions.scenario: search_tickets doesn't distinguish a downed backend from zero results
questions.stem: Your MCP `search_tickets` tool returns `{"tickets": []}` both when the ticketing backend is unreachable and when the customer genuinely has no open tickets. A downstream agent now reports "no tickets found" to customers during a backend outage, when in fact tickets exist but could not be retrieved. What change most directly fixes this?

options.text: On backend unavailability, return `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "transient"` and `isRetryable: true`; keep the plain empty array (no `isError`) only for genuinely zero-match queries.
Increase the timeout so the backend has more time to respond before the tool gives up.
Have the agent always tell customers "please check back later" whenever `search_tickets` returns zero results, regardless of the cause.
Cache the last successful result and return it whenever the backend is unreachable, so the tool never appears to fail.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.2 in its most-cited distinction: access failure vs. valid empty result. A downed backend and a query with no matches produce the same `[]`, but they mean opposite things — one is a failure that can be fixed by retrying, the other is a success that must never be retried. The fix flags unavailability with `isError: true`, `errorCategory: 'transient'`, and `isRetryable: true`, and reserves the unflagged empty array for genuinely zero-match queries. Any alternative that tweaks an adjacent parameter, compensates in the agent, or substitutes stale data leaves the confusion between 'I found nothing' and 'I couldn't search' untouched.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis: a longer timeout is a real technique (latency tolerance) but attacks the wrong dimension — the empty result will still fail to distinguish 'I found nothing' from 'I couldn't search' the moment the new limit also runs out.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch: compensating in the agent with a generic message for any empty result fixes a layer above the cause, and it also breaks the legitimate zero-results case, which is a genuine success and shouldn't trigger that message.
distractorsEs.D: Speculative caching: serving the last successful result as if it were current substitutes unverified data instead of communicating the failure — it hides the problem and can show stale information as if it were fresh.

questions.trap: C looks like a reasonable product-level fix, but it inverts the problem: now the LEGITIMATE empty result also triggers the failure message, when that case is actually a success.

questions.objective: Apply local error recovery within subagents before propagating irresolvable failures to the coordinator
questions.scenario: Intermittent timeout in the web-search subagent
questions.stem: A web-search subagent in a multi-agent research system occasionally hits a provider timeout. Per the coordinator-subagent error-handling guidance, what should the subagent do?

options.text: Add a `retryPolicy: "coordinator-managed"` field to the subagent's `AgentDefinition` so the coordinator transparently retries any failed tool call on the subagent's behalf.
Retry the transient timeout locally with backoff; only if it cannot resolve the failure, propagate to the coordinator along with what was attempted and any partial results already gathered.
Silently merge whatever partial results exist into the final report without flagging that the query failed partway through.
Report the failure as caused by the coordinator's original query being too broad, and terminate the subtask without attempting a local retry.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.2 in its local-recovery clause: a subagent should absorb what's transient itself (retry with backoff) and propagate to the coordinator only what it can't resolve, along with what it attempted and what partial results it obtained. A timeout from an external provider is the textbook example of a transient error — it doesn't warrant escalating, reassigning blame, or aborting the whole workflow. The correct option implements exactly that sequence: local recovery first, structured propagation after, only if necessary. Suppressing the failure flag or blaming the coordinator's decomposition without evidence each break a different part of that contract.

distractorsEs.A: Fabricated feature: there is no `retryPolicy: "coordinator-managed"` field in `AgentDefinition` — the guide documents LOCAL recovery within the subagent itself, not reassigning retry responsibility to the coordinator via a nonexistent field.
distractorsEs.C: Half-right practice: preserving partial results is the correct half (objective 2.2 explicitly asks for it), but omitting the failure flag is the half that ruins the result — the coordinator can no longer distinguish complete coverage from incomplete coverage.
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch / blame the executor: blaming the coordinator's decomposition is correct in other scenarios, but here the stem itself says the failure is a provider timeout — a transient, local problem the subagent should have tried to resolve before escalating or reassigning blame.

questions.trap: C is the subtlest: preserving partial results sounds responsible, and it is indeed half of the correct answer — but without the failure flag, the coordinator can't know that coverage was left incomplete.

questions.objective: Restrict subagent tool sets to role-relevant tools to prevent cross-specialization misuse
questions.scenario: 18 inherited tools degrade selection in the synthesis agent
questions.stem: A multi-agent research system registers 18 tools globally, and every subagent -search, document-analysis, and synthesis- inherits access to all 18. Tool-selection reliability has degraded, and the synthesis agent has started issuing its own web searches, duplicating the search agent's work. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a line to the synthesis agent's prompt stating "You must not perform web searches."
Give every subagent access to all 18 tools, but add a coordinator-level policy that reviews and rejects inappropriate tool calls after the fact.
Restrict each subagent's `tools` list in its `AgentDefinition` to only what its role needs (e.g., search: 2 tools, doc-analysis: 3, synthesis: none or a narrowly scoped fact-check tool).
Reduce the global tool count from 18 to 10 so that even with full access, each agent has fewer options to choose from.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.3: giving access to too many tools — or to tools outside an agent's role — degrades selection reliability and produces misuse, like the synthesis agent firing off its own web searches. The exam's master axis applies here without detours: removing the tool from the `AgentDefinition` is a deterministic guarantee; asking the agent to 'not use it' is an instruction with a non-zero failure rate. Restricting each subagent's `tools` to what its role needs — 2-3 tools, not 18 — is the only intervention that doesn't depend on the model obeying. The alternatives grant full access with reactive controls, or touch the wrong dimension of the problem.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking the subagent to 'not do' something has a non-zero failure rate. Removing the tool is deterministic; instructing it not to use it is probabilistic — the exam's master axis applied to tool distribution.
distractorsEs.B: Over-provisioning: granting full access to all 18 tools 'with a later review' is still granting total access just in case — the late review doesn't undo the fact that the duplicate call and the latency already happened before the control stepped in.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis: reducing the global catalog is a real lever, but it operates on the wrong dimension — the problem isn't how many tools EXIST in total, it's how many each individual agent sees OUTSIDE its role.

questions.trap: A is the 'reasonable' answer from a rushed engineer: instructing instead of restricting. The exam systematically punishes it in this domain.

questions.objective: Provide a scoped cross-role tool for high-frequency needs while routing complex cases through the coordinator
questions.scenario: 90% simple verifications, 10% complex in the synthesis agent
questions.stem: Production measurements show that 90% of the synthesis agent's verification needs are simple checks of a single statistic against its already-cited source, while the remaining 10% require re-opening and re-reading the full source document. Which tool-distribution design best fits this data?

options.text: Give the synthesis agent full access to the document-analysis agent's entire toolset, so it never needs to round-trip through the coordinator.
Have the synthesis agent accumulate all its verification needs and submit them as a single batch to the coordinator only after drafting the full report, rather than checking incrementally.
Have the synthesis agent pre-fetch and cache every statistic it might conceivably need to verify before synthesis even begins.

Give the synthesis agent a narrowly scoped `verify_stat` tool that checks a figure against its cited source, and route the remaining complex cases through the coordinator to the document-analysis agent.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.3 in its finest nuance: when the data shows most of an agent's needs are simple and only a minority requires deep investigation, the traffic distribution IS the design instruction. Neither denying it any verification tool (forces blocking dependencies on the frequent case), nor giving it another role's full toolset (over-provisioning that violates least privilege), solves the problem proportionately. A scoped `verify_stat` covers the simple 90% locally, and the complex 10% still routes through the coordinator to the specialized agent — the cross-role tool pattern objective 2.3 describes.

distractorsEs.A: Over-provisioning: giving the synthesis agent another role's full toolset 'to avoid round-trips' violates least privilege and degrades its own tool selection — the 90/10 doesn't justify full access, it justifies one scoped tool.
distractorsEs.B: Creates blocking dependencies: accumulating all verifications for the end turns each one into a step that blocks closing out the report — the typical tool-distribution distractor the decoder names, disguised as 'batch efficiency.'
distractorsEs.C: Speculative caching: precomputing and storing every possible statistic before knowing which ones will be needed is predicting the unpredictable — it doesn't scale and doesn't cover the 10% that requires re-reading the full source anyway.

questions.trap: B is the decoy dressed up as engineering discipline ('batch processing is more efficient'), but here batching saves nothing — it only postpones and blocks verifications that could have been resolved on the spot with a scoped tool.

questions.objective: Distinguish tool_choice forced selection from "any" and understand that forcing applies to a single turn
questions.scenario: extract_metadata must run first, guaranteed
questions.stem: A document-processing agent must run `extract_metadata` before any enrichment tool, guaranteed on the very first turn. Select the TWO statements that are correct about achieving this with `tool_choice`.

options.text: Setting `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on the first request guarantees that specific tool is called on that turn.
Setting `tool_choice: "any"` on the first request also guarantees `extract_metadata` specifically, since it is the only metadata tool defined.
After the forced turn, the enrichment tools should be processed in a follow-up turn with `tool_choice` set back to `"auto"`, since forcing a tool applies only to that turn, not to the whole sequence.
The same forced-tool configuration can be reused for the enrichment step within a single combined request, since forcing a tool chains automatically through subsequent tool calls.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.3 on `tool_choice`: forcing a specific tool guarantees THAT tool gets called on the current turn, not just any tool. `'any'` only guarantees that SOME tool among those available gets called; with more than one tool registered (metadata and enrichment coexist), it doesn't pin down which one. And neither mode chains future steps: forcing applies to the current turn, and the enrichment sequence gets processed in later turns with `tool_choice: 'auto'`. A and C describe both correct ends of this mechanism; they aren't the same idea repeated, but two independent facts that together complete the procedure.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis: `any` is a real mechanism that guarantees SOME tool gets called, but assuming it pins down that tool's IDENTITY is the wrong dimension — only `{"type":"tool","name":...}` fixes the exact tool when there's more than one candidate.
distractorsEs.D: Fabricated feature: there is no `tool_choice` mode that automatically chains multiple calls across turns — the guide is explicit that forcing a tool applies only to the current turn; the sequence is built across successive turns.

questions.trap: B is the most dangerous decoy because 'any' and 'forcing a specific tool' feel interchangeable when there's only one candidate tool in the reader's head — but the API's semantics are different, and the exam tests it literally.

questions.objective: Configure shared MCP servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with environment variable expansion for credentials
questions.scenario: Teammate has no GitHub tools after cloning the repo
questions.stem: You configured a GitHub MCP server that works on your machine, with the API token hardcoded directly in the config file. A teammate clones the repository and Claude Code shows no GitHub tools at all. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Move the server definition to `~/.claude/settings.json` under a `sharedServers` key, since user-level config is easier to edit than project files.
Move the server definition into a project-scoped `.mcp.json` at the repo root, and replace the hardcoded token with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` so each developer supplies their own via environment variable.
Leave the server in `~/.claude.json` as it already is, and tell the teammate to run `claude mcp sync` after cloning to pull your personal configuration.
Commit the current config as-is to `.mcp.json` so it works immediately for everyone who clones, and rotate the token later if needed.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.4: the scope distinction between `.mcp.json` (project, version-controlled, shared with the team) and `~/.claude.json` (user, doesn't travel through git). A server that 'works on my machine' but doesn't show up after cloning almost always lives in the wrong file. The fix moves the definition to `.mcp.json` at the repo root AND replaces the hardcoded token with `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` — environment variable expansion, the canonical mechanism so the version-controlled file never contains the secret. Getting only the scope right without removing the secret, or keeping the file at user scope while inventing a sync mechanism, both leave the real problem unsolved.

distractorsEs.A: Scope flip + fabricated feature: there is no `sharedServers` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, and even if there were, the user file by definition doesn't travel through version control — it inverts which scope is the shared one.
distractorsEs.C: Fabricated feature: there is no `claude mcp sync` command that imports another developer's personal configuration; moreover, keeping the server in `~/.claude.json` is precisely the scope error that stops the teammate from seeing it after cloning.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice: it gets the right file (`.mcp.json`, project scope) but commits the opposite error — committing the secret in plain text instead of using environment variable expansion; the good half doesn't save the half that exposes the token.

questions.trap: D is the most dangerous: it looks like it solves the whole problem ('works for everyone after cloning') because it gets the scope right, but it does so by exposing the token — the final clause ('rotate later') is the clue that it's already too late.

questions.objective: Expose content catalogs as MCP resources to reduce exploratory tool calls
questions.scenario: 10-15 exploratory calls just to discover issues
questions.stem: Agents using your project-management MCP server spend 10-15 tool calls per session just discovering which issues exist and in which projects, before doing anything useful -often exhausting context mid-task. Select the TWO statements that correctly describe the fix and its rationale.

options.text: Add a new `list_all_issues()` tool that returns every issue across every project in a single call.
Expose an MCP resource (e.g., `issues://open/summary`) with a compact catalog -id, title, project, status, assignee, last update- so the agent can see the inventory without exploratory tool calls.
Raise the result limit on `search_issues` so a single call returns more issues per page.
MCP resources exist specifically to give agents visibility into available data without requiring exploratory tool calls, which is a different purpose than tools, which perform actions.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.4 on the tools-vs-resources discriminator: when an agent spends 10-15 exploratory calls just to discover what exists, the answer isn't a tool that dumps everything at once, but an MCP resource that exposes a compact catalog for the agent to read at a glance. Tools are for ACTION; resources are for VISIBILITY/context — objective 2.4 names it literally. B and D attack the same axis from two different angles: the concrete implementation (exposing the resource) and the general principle (resources reduce exploratory tool calls); they aren't the same idea repeated.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: a tool that returns everything is still an ACTION tool applied to a VISIBILITY need — objective 2.4 distinguishes those two axes (tools=action, resources=catalog) and this option stays on the wrong axis, with the same context cost as the 10-15 calls, just concentrated into one.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: raising the pagination limit still treats discovery as a series of action tool calls; it doesn't solve the agent needing to see the inventory BEFORE deciding what to request.

questions.trap: A is the strongest decoy: 'a tool that brings everything' sounds like the obvious solution, but objective 2.4 is explicit that the right mechanism for content catalogs is a resource, not more tools.

questions.objective: Select Grep for content search and apply the Read+Write fallback when Edit's anchor text is non-unique
questions.scenario: Exploring a legacy codebase: callers, and an edit with a repeated anchor
questions.stem: While exploring an unfamiliar codebase, you need to (1) find every caller of `processPayment` across the repo, and (2) apply a small edit to a config file, but `Edit` reports the anchor text is not unique because it appears four times. What is the correct tool choice for each step?

options.text: Use `Grep` to find `processPayment` by content across files; when `Edit` fails on the non-unique anchor, fall back to `Read` the full file followed by `Write` with the corrected content.
Use `Glob` to find `processPayment` by content across files; when `Edit` fails, retry `Edit` repeatedly with slightly longer anchor strings until one happens to match.
Use `Bash` with a raw `grep`/`sed` pipeline for both steps, since it avoids the built-in tools' limitations entirely.
Read every file in the repository first, then visually scan for `processPayment`, then use `Edit` repeatedly until the anchor happens to match.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task Statement 2.5: the mental contract of built-in tools the guide expects without ambiguity. Grep searches file CONTENT; Glob matches PATHS/names, not content, so it can't locate `processPayment` inside the code. When `Edit` fails because the anchor text appears multiple times, the documented fallback is `Read` the full file followed by `Write` with the corrected content — not blindly retrying `Edit` with more context. Raw Bash commands and 'read the whole repo first' are the two recurring distractors the decoder itself names for this question pattern: they bypass the already-provided tool contract with no real advantage.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis (twice over): Glob is real but matches PATHS/names, not content — it can't find `processPayment` inside a file; and blindly retrying `Edit` ignores the documented fallback (Read + Write), trying its luck instead of fixing the cause (non-unique anchor).
distractorsEs.C: Recurring distractor the decoder names for this pattern: using Bash with raw `grep`/`sed` bypasses the already-provided tool contract (Grep/Edit) with no real advantage, and loses its error handling and predictability.
distractorsEs.D: Recurring distractor the decoder names / exploration anti-pattern: 'read the whole repo first, then decide' exhausts context unnecessarily; the guide asks for building understanding incrementally (Grep to locate, Read to follow the flow), never reading everything up front.

questions.trap: B is the most tempting for anyone who confuses 'searching code' with 'searching files': Glob sounds plausible because it's also a search tool, but it operates on paths, not content.

questions.objective: Diagnose CLAUDE.md hierarchy scoping issues
questions.scenario: CLAUDE.md configuration that doesn't reach a new team member
questions.stem: A nine-person team's tech lead has kept "always use pnpm, never npm" and "every new component ships with co-located tests" in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` for months. A new engineer clones the repository and Claude Code generates components without tests and suggests `npm install`. The lead cannot reproduce the problem on their own machine. What is the most appropriate fix?

options.text: Move the conventions from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the project's `CLAUDE.md` (or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`) and commit it, since user-level configuration is never distributed through version control.
Have the new engineer manually copy the tech lead's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` file into their own home directory.
Have the new engineer run `/compact` at the start of the session to load the missing conventions.
Rewrite the instruction in CLAUDE.md using stronger imperative language (all caps, "ALWAYS") so Claude Code treats it as a hard rule instead of a suggestion.

questions.explanationEs: Tests diagnosing and fixing a CLAUDE.md hierarchy problem (Task 3.1). The symptom — works for the lead, not for the new hire, same repo — has exactly one possible structural cause: something loaded for one and not the other. The conventions live in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, user-level configuration that by definition never travels through version control. The real fix moves them into the project's CLAUDE.md and commits it, so anyone who clones the repo receives them automatically. It's the domain's canonical scenario: 'works for me, not for the new hire' is always a scope problem, never a wording problem.

distractorsEs.B: Downstream patch: manually copying the file fixes the symptom for THIS person, at THIS moment, but doesn't fix the system — the next hire who joins will have the same problem, and the lead's file and the copy will drift out of sync the moment either one changes something. It isn't a structural fix.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: `/compact` is a real command, but it compresses a long session's history and re-injects the project's root CLAUDE.md after compacting; it doesn't sync configuration across different home directories, nor does it fix a file that was never loaded.
distractorsEs.D: Prompt-as-guarantee: turning up the instruction's volume doesn't change its delivery layer — it's still in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, still doesn't travel through git, still doesn't reach the new hire. It confuses rhetorical emphasis with configuration scope.

questions.trap: C is the most believable because `/compact` is indeed a real Claude Code command — but it attacks a different problem (long-session context), not the cross-machine scope issue.

questions.objective: Distinguish context-saving mechanisms from @import modularization
questions.scenario: Monolithic CLAUDE.md that loads irrelevant context
questions.stem: A monorepo's root `CLAUDE.md` has grown to include React conventions, API conventions, database conventions, and Terraform conventions in one file. The team reports that every session — even one that only touches a Terraform module — loads all of it, wasting context. Select the TWO changes that would actually reduce the context loaded into an unrelated session.

options.text: Split the file into four `@import`-ed files (`@docs/react.md`, `@docs/api.md`, ...) referenced from the root `CLAUDE.md`.
Move each topic into its own file under `.claude/rules/` with a `paths:` frontmatter glob scoped to that topic's files.
Keep everything in the root `CLAUDE.md` but add clearer markdown section headings so Claude can skip irrelevant ones.
Move the Terraform-specific workflow into a skill that is invoked on demand rather than loaded automatically.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the distinction between modularizing and saving context (Task 3.1). The chapter is explicit: `@import` organizes but doesn't save context — imported files load just the same when the session starts. The two mechanisms that actually reduce loaded tokens are `.claude/rules/` with `paths:` (enters context only when Claude touches files matching the glob) and a skill (lives in context only as its `description` until invoked on demand). Reorganizing with headings doesn't save anything either: the whole file still loads in full either way, only its internal readability changes, not its cost.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: splitting into `@import` is a real guide technique for modularity, but it attacks the wrong axis — it organizes, it doesn't reduce loaded tokens. Confusing 'modular' with 'cheap' is, per the chapter, an exam error served up on a plate.
distractorsEs.C: Half-right practice: clear headings help human readability, but the clause that matters — reducing loaded context — isn't satisfied: the full file still loads the same either way, with or without headings, and it depends on Claude inferring which section applies.

questions.trap: A is the most dangerous: it looks like the textbook answer (modularize with imports), but the chapter is explicit that `@import` doesn't save a single token — it only organizes.

questions.objective: Use /memory to diagnose inconsistent behavior across sessions
questions.scenario: Inconsistent behavior across developers
questions.stem: Two developers working from the same commit of the same repository report that Claude Code behaves inconsistently — one gets certain conventions applied automatically, the other does not. Before changing any configuration, what is the most appropriate first step to diagnose the discrepancy?

options.text: Have both developers run `/compact` to force a fresh reload of all configuration files.
Have both developers paste their `CLAUDE.md` file contents into the chat and compare them manually line by line.
Have both developers run `/memory` to compare which memory files are actually loaded in each of their sessions.
Reinstall Claude Code for the developer who is missing the conventions.

questions.explanationEs: Tests using `/memory` as a diagnostic tool (Task 3.1). Faced with a 'same repo, different behavior' symptom, the cause is always that something is loaded for one and not the other — and the only reliable way to know is to ask the session itself what it has loaded. `/memory` lists exactly that: the memory files active in the current session.
