It's the tool the material explicitly names for diagnosing inconsistent behavior across sessions or people, before touching any configuration.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: `/compact` is a real command, but it compresses a long session's history to free up context — it isn't a diagnostic tool for which memory files are loaded.
distractorsEs.B: Downstream patch: attacks the symptom with manual work instead of using the tool Claude Code itself exposes for this. It also compares what each person BELIEVES they have, not what's actually loaded in the session — which is exactly what might be failing.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: reinstalling is a disproportionate intervention for a configuration-scope problem; the exam rules out expensive options when it asks for the first diagnostic step, not the repair step.

questions.trap: B looks diligent ('compare the files'), but it compares what's declared, not what's loaded; `/memory` is the only reliable source of what's actually in the session.

questions.objective: Scope custom slash commands for team-wide availability
questions.scenario: Team command available upon cloning the repo
questions.stem: A team wants a custom `/review` slash command to be available to every developer automatically the moment they clone or pull the repository — no manual setup step required. Where should the command be created?

options.text: `~/.claude/commands/review.md`
`.claude/config.json`, adding `"review"` to a top-level `commands` array
`.claude/commands/review.md`
A team wiki page documenting the `/review` prompt for developers to paste manually

questions.explanationEs: Tests the correct scope for shared slash commands (Task 3.2) — 'the domain's cheapest question' according to the material itself. The 'available upon cloning or pulling' requirement demands a path inside the repo, version-controlled by git: `.claude/commands/review.md`. The chapter's mnemonic rule is blunt: the tilde (`~/`) never travels through git. A command in `~/.claude/commands/` works just as well for whoever created it, but doesn't exist for anyone else who clones the repo. Any location outside the repo, or any mechanism that depends on a human manually copying something, fails to satisfy 'automatically upon cloning.'

distractorsEs.A: Scope flip: inverts user-level and project-level. Everything living under `~/` is personal and never travels through version control; the requirement asks for exactly the opposite.
distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature: `.claude/config.json` with a `commands` array doesn't exist in Claude Code's real surface — it's an invented feature with credible-looking syntax, explicitly named as the domain's typical distractor.
distractorsEs.D: Externalize the problem: shifts the responsibility of 'having the command' onto the human developer (copy-pasting from a wiki) instead of solving it in the system's own version-controlled configuration.

questions.trap: A is the domain's cheapest and most repeated trap: the tilde never travels through git, no matter how reasonable 'put it in my personal config' sounds.

questions.objective: Configure skill frontmatter to prevent context pollution and missing arguments
questions.scenario: Skill that floods the main conversation
questions.stem: A team's `/analyze-module` skill reads 30-40 files and runs greps to map a module's structure. After it runs, the main conversation is so full of file dumps that Claude starts giving inconsistent answers about the earlier task. Separately, a developer invoked the skill without specifying which module, and it analyzed the entire repository by mistake. Select the TWO frontmatter changes to `SKILL.md` that directly address these two problems.

options.text: `context: fork` — runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent so its intermediate reads and greps never enter the main conversation, only the final summary does.
`description: "Be concise. Do not dump files."` — instructs the skill to summarize its own output instead of pasting file contents.
`argument-hint: [module-path]` — prompts the developer for the missing parameter when the skill is invoked without arguments.
`name: analyze-module-v2` — renames the skill so it no longer collides with any similarly named command.

questions.explanationEs: Tests skill frontmatter configuration (Task 3.2), lifted straight from the chapter's worked example. `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent: the 30-40 reads stay there, and only the summary comes back to the main conversation — it attacks the cause of the pollution, not the symptom. `argument-hint: [module-path]` solves the second problem: it tells the developer the missing parameter when invoking without arguments. The example team also scopes `allowed-tools` down to `Read, Grep, Glob`, but that limits permissions, it doesn't solve either problem stated here.

distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking the skill, in its own description, to 'be concise' is a prose instruction — probabilistic. It isolates nothing structurally — the same failure can repeat the next time someone invokes it on a bigger module. `context: fork` is architecture; this is a plea.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis: renaming can avoid name collisions with another command, but it doesn't solve either of the two stated problems (context pollution, missing argument). It's a real solution to a problem the stem never raised.

questions.trap: B is the most natural decoy: 'add an instruction asking it to be brief' sounds like a direct fix, but it's exactly the difference between context (suggests) and architecture (guarantees) that organizes the whole domain.

questions.objective: Recognize session context isolation benefits for code review
questions.scenario: CI pipeline that reviews its own code
questions.stem: A CI pipeline uses the same Claude Code session that just generated a feature to also review it, appending "now review your own code for bugs" as a final instruction in that same session. Code review quality is noticeably worse than reviews done by a fresh instance on identical diffs. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The session has run out of available context window, causing the review to be truncated.
Self-review requires extended thinking to be enabled, and it was not turned on for this run.
The instruction to "review your own code" was not emphatic enough; more forceful wording would have produced a properly critical review.
The reviewing instance retains the reasoning context from generation and is less likely to question decisions it already committed to.

questions.explanationEs: Tests session context isolation (Task 3.6, crossing into 4.6). The material explains it without hedging: the same session that generated the code retains the generation reasoning and is less likely to question its own decisions — it already 'knows' why it wrote what it wrote. An independent instance, without that prior reasoning, catches more subtle problems than any self-review instruction or more extended thinking. In CI, that requires the generation job and the review job to be separate invocations, not two turns of the same session.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: context exhaustion is a real problem in long sessions, but the stem doesn't report token limits or truncation — it reports the SAME session reviewing its own work. It attacks a cause the stem never put on the table.
distractorsEs.B: Over-engineering: reaches for a heavier lever (extended thinking) when the chapter is explicit that turning on more extended thinking does NOT substitute for an instance without the generation's prior reasoning. The problem is independence, not depth of reasoning.
distractorsEs.C: Prompt-as-guarantee: assumes more emphatic wording turns a structural limitation (retaining its own reasoning) into different behavior. The chapter explicitly rules this out: no self-review instruction substitutes for an independent instance.

questions.trap: C is the whole domain's reflex trap: when something doesn't work, turn up the prompt's tone. Here the failure isn't wording, it's session architecture.

questions.objective: Choose path-specific rules over subdirectory CLAUDE.md for cross-cutting conventions
questions.scenario: Test conventions scattered across the repo
questions.stem: A codebase has three distinct convention areas (React components, API handlers, data models) plus a fourth requirement: every test file, co-located next to the code it tests and scattered across dozens of directories, must follow the same testing conventions regardless of where it lives. What is the most effective way to guarantee the testing conventions apply automatically to every test file?

options.text: Create a `CLAUDE.md` file in every directory that contains test files, each with the same testing conventions copy-pasted in.
Create one file in `.claude/rules/` with a `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx", "**/*.test.ts"]` frontmatter glob.
Create a `testing-conventions` skill that developers invoke before writing any test.
Add a "Testing" section to the root `CLAUDE.md` and rely on Claude to infer that it applies when it is working on a test file.

questions.explanationEs: Tests exactly the pattern of the domain's official Q6 item (Task 3.3). Two cumulative reasons favor the glob: activation determinism (the `paths:` match is automatic; inferring sections of a monolithic CLAUDE.md is not) and location independence (a per-directory `CLAUDE.md` is tied to the folder, and the tests are scattered across dozens of them). A single `**/*.test.tsx` glob covers all of them, wherever they live, without duplicating anything and without depending on anyone invoking anything.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: a per-directory CLAUDE.md is a real mechanism, but it's tied to LOCATION, not to file TYPE. With tests scattered across dozens of folders, you'd have to replicate it everywhere and keep them in sync.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch: a skill doesn't activate by path match, it gets invoked — by the developer or by the model's own decision. The stem asks for the convention to apply automatically regardless of where the files are; any mechanism that depends on invocation is ruled out.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice: consolidating into the root CLAUDE.md sounds tidy, but the clause that kills it is 'relying on Claude to infer' — glob matching is deterministic, inferring sections of a monolithic file is not.

questions.trap: A is the most expensive: it looks like 'the right way to organize it by area,' but it demands manual upkeep multiplied by every folder that has tests.

questions.objective: Select plan mode for multi-file changes with multiple valid approaches
questions.scenario: Library migration across 45 files
questions.stem: A billing service needs to migrate from `moment` to `date-fns` across 45 files. Two valid approaches exist — a compatibility wrapper (fast, adds technical debt) or a full rewrite (slower, cleaner) — and an unknown number of files rely on `moment`'s mutability in ways not yet identified. What is the most effective way to start this task?

options.text: Start in direct execution mode, approving edits as they come, and switch to plan mode only if unexpected complexity appears.
Enter plan mode so Claude can map all 45 usages, identify the mutability edge cases, and compare the two approaches before any code changes.
Write an exhaustive prompt specifying exactly how each of the 45 files should end up, then run it in direct execution.
Skip planning and mapping; ask Claude to pick whichever approach it thinks is best and execute immediately.

questions.explanationEs: Tests selecting plan mode (Task 3.4) against the official distractor the chapter names (Q5-D). The stem checks all four plan-mode boxes: large scale, multi-file, multiple valid approaches, and a decision with architectural consequences. Plan mode lets Claude map all 45 usages and find the mutability edge cases BEFORE touching code, comparing tradeoffs with no rewrite cost. The combined pattern the material asks for: plan the migration, approve the plan, and only then move to direct execution to implement.

distractorsEs.A: Half-right practice, named by the chapter as the official distractor: it sounds like agile pragmatism, but it fails because the complexity is ALREADY stated in the stem (45 files, two valid approaches, mutability) — it isn't something that 'might' emerge later.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering without data: assumes the correct structure of the 45 files is already known without having explored them. It's extremely high-effort planning without the discovery phase that makes it trustworthy — the chapter itself describes this as 'planning without data.'
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch: delegates the architectural decision (wrapper vs. rewrite) to the model without a human comparing tradeoffs, and with no discovery phase to find the mutability edge cases before they break something.

questions.trap: A is the distractor with the most traction among senior engineers: 'start simple, add complexity if needed' is good general heuristics, but the exam punishes it when the complexity is already stated in the stem itself.

questions.objective: Use the Explore subagent to isolate verbose discovery output
questions.scenario: Verbose multi-file discovery phase
questions.stem: Before making any changes, a multi-phase task requires locating every test file in a large codebase and tracing all dependencies of the refund flow — work that will involve hundreds of grep and read operations. What is the most effective way to perform this discovery phase without exhausting the main conversation's context window?

options.text: Run all the greps and reads directly in the main conversation, then manually summarize the findings before continuing.
Increase the model's context window setting so the main conversation can absorb the additional output.
Run `/compact` immediately before starting the discovery phase to make room for the upcoming output.
Delegate the discovery work to the Explore subagent, which operates read-only in its own context window and returns only a summary.

questions.explanationEs: Tests use of the Explore subagent (Task 3.4). It's read-only, with its own context window, built exactly for verbose discovery phases in multi-phase tasks: the hundreds of lines of grep and read output stay in the subagent, and only the inventory comes back to the main conversation. It's the direct countermeasure against context exhaustion in long explorations — the alternative that preserves the main conversation's capacity to keep reasoning about the rest of the task.

distractorsEs.A: Downstream patch: does the verbose work in the wrong place and then tries to clean up manually afterward — it doesn't prevent the pollution, it only remedies it late, once the damage to the context has already happened.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis: enlarging the context window solves the output FITTING, not the main conversation staying clean and focused. It's the same capacity-vs-attention confusion the chapter flags as the domain's typical error.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: `/compact` is a real tool for long sessions, but it compresses what's ALREADY in context — it doesn't stop hundreds of lines of discovery output from entering the main conversation in the first place.

questions.trap: B is tempting because it is a real lever in the domain (context window), but it solves the wrong dimension: token quantity, not isolating the main conversation.

questions.objective: Apply concrete input/output examples for inconsistent transformations
questions.scenario: Date transformation interpreted inconsistently
questions.stem: A developer describes in prose how a migration script should transform date fields, including how `null` values should be handled. Across several attempts, Claude produces a differently-shaped transformation each time, and consistently mishandles the `null` case. What is the most effective way to fix this?

options.text: Write a longer, more detailed paragraph explaining the transformation rules one more time, with additional emphasis on precision.
Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples, including one with the exact `null` input and its expected output.
Ask Claude to first explain its understanding of the transformation back in its own words before implementing.
Break the task into smaller sequential messages, fixing one transformation rule per message.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the correct iterative-refinement technique (Task 3.5) for the stated trigger: 'the prose description is interpreted inconsistently.' When explaining the transformation in words produces different results every time, two or three literal input/output examples fix what more prose doesn't. It's also the specific cure for the edge case: giving the test case with the exact `null` input and its expected output eliminates the ambiguity no general description manages to close.

distractorsEs.A: Half-right practice: starts from the right premise (the transformation needs to be communicated better) but repeats the same medium that already proved ambiguous. Three more paragraphs don't fix what three paragraphs didn't fix before.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: the interview pattern is designed for unfamiliar domains where considerations the developer didn't anticipate need to surface — not for an already-known transformation that's simply being described poorly. It doesn't attack the stated inconsistency.
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch: treats the transformation rules as if they were independent and could be fixed one at a time, when the stated symptom is that the whole transformation — including the `null` edge case — comes out different every time.

questions.trap: A is the careful engineer's reflex: write better. But the chapter is explicit: once prose has already proven to produce inconsistent results, more prose isn't the cure.

questions.objective: Decide between a single message and sequential iteration for interacting fixes
questions.scenario: Three interacting code-review findings
questions.stem: A code review surfaces three findings that all touch the same code path: the data model needs a new field, error handling must change to account for it, and a public function's signature must be updated to accept the new field. Each change affects how the other two should be implemented. What is the most effective way to communicate these three fixes to Claude?

options.text: Report all three findings together in a single detailed message, since fixing them affects one another.
Report them one at a time across three separate messages, verifying each fix before moving to the next.
Report only the data model change first, and let Claude discover the other two issues on its own while implementing it.
Open three separate sessions, one per finding, so each fix can be reviewed independently.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the domain's refinement criterion (Task 3.5): do the problems interact? When fixes affect each other — here, the data model, error handling, and function signature are coupled — they all go in one detailed message. Fixing them one at a time makes each fix break or contradict the previous one, because each correction changes the ground the next one applies to. Sequential iteration is reserved for independent problems: a typo, a missing import, a badly formatted log.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis: iterating one at a time is a real, valid technique, but the material reserves it for independent problems. Here the three findings interact: fixing the data model first and error handling afterward will likely make the second fix break or contradict the first.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch: delegates to the model the task of discovering on its own problems the developer ALREADY identified and described. Omitting known information isn't refinement, it's an incomplete specification.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: splitting into three isolated sessions is the worst possible option for changes that interact — each session loses the context of the other two, guaranteeing the three fixes end up inconsistent with each other.

questions.trap: B is the natural instinct to 'go step by step,' but it's exactly what the chapter warns against: fixing interacting problems one at a time makes each fix break the previous one.

questions.objective: Run Claude Code non-interactively in CI with -p
questions.scenario: CI job that hangs waiting for input
questions.stem: A GitHub Actions job runs `claude "Analyze this PR for security issues"` and hangs until the 60-minute timeout kills it. What change to the command most directly fixes this?

options.text: Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag: `claude -p "Analyze this PR for security issues"`.
Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` before the command runs.
Add the `--batch` flag to run the command in batch mode.
Redirect standard input from `/dev/null`: `claude "Analyze this PR for security issues" < /dev/null`.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the flag that decides a full official domain question (Task 3.6). Without `-p`/`--print`, `claude "…"` on a runner sits waiting for interactive input and the job hangs indefinitely. With `-p`, Claude processes the prompt, writes the result to stdout, and exits — it's the documented non-interactive mode, built exactly for automated pipelines. No invented environment variable and no shell patch attacks the real cause: the process keeps waiting for interactive mode by default until told otherwise with the right flag.

distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true` doesn't exist in the CLI's real surface. It's credible-looking syntax — it looks like a reasonable environment variable — but the chapter explicitly names it as the domain's typical distractor.
distractorsEs.C: Fabricated feature: `--batch` doesn't exist as a Claude Code flag either. There's a separate Message Batches API (from another domain), which makes this distractor more believable, but it isn't a Claude Code CLI flag.
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch / Unix workaround: redirecting stdin from `/dev/null` is a generic shell patch that doesn't address the CLI's real syntax. Claude Code keeps waiting for interactive mode by default; the underlying problem goes untouched.

questions.trap: D is the most plausible for someone with shell-scripting experience, but the chapter is emphatic: no Unix workaround attacks the CLI's real syntax. The documented flag is `-p`.

questions.objective: Enforce machine-parseable structured output in CI with --json-schema
questions.scenario: PR comments parsed with brittle regex
questions.stem: A CI script parses Claude Code's free-text output with regular expressions to post inline PR comments, and fails on roughly 1 out of every 4 runs because the prose format varies. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Write a more sophisticated regex parser with additional fallback patterns to catch more prose formats.
Add explicit formatting instructions to the prompt asking Claude to always use the exact same three-line structure.
Run `claude -p` with `--output-format json` and a `--json-schema` describing the findings structure, then read the validated result from the `structured_output` field.
Ask Claude to output the findings as a Markdown table instead of prose paragraphs.

questions.explanationEs: Tests the structured-output contract in CI (Task 3.6). `--output-format json` together with `--json-schema` (which it requires) validates the output against a JSON Schema and deposits it in the payload's `structured_output` field — that's what makes the result machine-parseable by construction, with no JSON syntax errors and with no reliance on Claude 'remembering' a format. It lets you post inline comments by reading fields (`file`, `line`, `severity`, `issue`) instead of parsing prose with regular expressions that are brittle against any wording variation.

distractorsEs.A: Downstream patch: investing in a more robust prose parser still treats unguaranteed free text as if it were a data contract. It's brittle by construction — any future variation in Claude's wording breaks it again.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking in the prompt that it 'always' use a fixed structure is still a prose instruction with a non-zero failure rate. It's exactly the same problem that caused the original failure, just worded in more detail.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice: a Markdown table is more readable for a human, but it's still free text that has to be parsed with heuristics — it's not a data contract validated by the tool.

questions.trap: B is the whole exam's reflex trap: when something fails, improve the prompt. But the stem asks for a guaranteed machine-parseable output, and only a tool-validated schema eliminates syntax errors by construction.

questions.objective: Place explicit categorical review criteria in the system prompt, not vague instructions
questions.scenario: PR-review bot with criteria that get reworded on every call.
questions.stem: A team's CI review bot calls Claude once per pull request. Each call's user message repeats a paragraph asking Claude to 'be thorough but conservative, and only flag things you're confident about.' Findings remain inconsistent across similar PRs and false positives stay high. What change most directly fixes this?

options.text: Move a fixed set of categorical criteria — which issue types to report (e.g., bugs, security) and which to skip (e.g., minor style, local patterns) — into the system prompt, and keep only the diff itself in the user turn.
Keep the same per-call instruction but increase the confidence threshold implied by the wording, e.g. 'only report findings you are extremely confident about.'
Replace the paragraph with a call to a fine-tuned classifier that scores each finding's likely false-positive probability before posting.
Leave the instruction in the user message but repeat it twice for emphasis on every call.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.1 and the prompt-placement axis: durable review rules (what to report, what to skip) should live in the system prompt, where they apply to every call without depending on anyone remembering them; the specific diff goes in the user turn. The guide is explicit that vague instructions like 'be conservative' or 'only high confidence' do NOT improve precision, no matter how much they're repeated or emphasized — what moves the decision boundary is categorical criteria fixed once. A solves both problems: it moves the criterion to the right place and makes it explicit, not an adjective.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — pushing the model harder toward 'high confidence' doesn't move the boundary of what gets reported; the guide says 'be conservative' / 'only high confidence' doesn't improve precision no matter how much the wording is intensified. It's still an adjective, not a categorical criterion.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — building and maintaining a trained classifier is heavy infrastructure for a problem an explicit prompt criterion already solves; the guide penalizes jumping to ML before exhausting the cheap solution.
distractorsEs.D: Scope flip — the criterion should live in the system prompt (it applies to every PR, fixed once); leaving it in the user turn and just repeating it inverts the right place for a durable rule. Repeating doesn't fix the vagueness, nor does it stop some developer from assembling the user prompt without including it.

questions.trap: B tempts because 'extremely high confidence' sounds like raising the bar, but it's still the same adjective with no verifiable criterion behind it.

questions.objective: Define severity levels using concrete code examples per level
questions.scenario: Severity classification inconsistent across runs of the same review bot.
questions.stem: A code-review prompt defines severity levels only as 'critical, major, minor' without further explanation. Two runs on the same diff classify the same finding differently — once as 'major,' once as 'critical.' What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Add a fourth severity level, 'urgent,' so the model has a more precise top category.
Instruct the model to 'be consistent about severity across runs.'
Lower the temperature parameter used for the review calls so the model's judgment becomes more deterministic.

Define each severity level with a concrete code example showing what qualifies at that level (e.g., a snippet that skips error handling on a payment call = critical; a snippet with a missing null check on a rarely-hit branch = major).

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.1: severity defined only with adjectives ('critical,' 'major,' 'minor') anchors nothing — the model reclassifies the same finding differently between runs because there's no concrete boundary between levels. Option D fixes that boundary with real code examples per level, exactly what the guide asks for to achieve consistent classification. Neither an extra category, nor a plea for consistency, nor a sampling parameter touches the cause: the absence of a concrete anchor per level. Only the code example fixes the problem at the root.

distractorsEs.A: Over-engineering / ML escape — adding a new category with no concrete examples is added complexity before exhausting the cheap solution: anchoring each EXISTING level with a code example. It doesn't attack the cause, it just makes the problem bigger.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee — asking the model to 'be consistent' chases a deterministic result via a plea in the prompt, not via the mechanism that actually anchors judgment: concrete code examples per level.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis — temperature governs sampling variability, not instruction adherence or the classification boundary. Lowering it doesn't anchor what code counts as 'critical' vs. 'major.'

questions.trap: C is the most technical of the three: it sounds like 'less randomness = more consistency,' but temperature doesn't touch the classification criterion itself.

questions.objective: Use 2-4 targeted few-shot examples that show reasoning, not just format
questions.scenario: Tool selector with ambiguous cases the prose prompt fails to cover.
questions.stem: A tool-selection prompt has detailed prose instructions describing when to call search_web versus search_internal_docs, but the model still misroutes ambiguous requests (e.g., 'what's our policy on X' when both an internal doc and a public web page could apply). The team wants to fix this with few-shot examples. Which approach best matches how few-shot should be used here?

options.text: Add 8-10 examples covering as many request phrasings as possible, so the model has broad pattern coverage.
Add one example per tool showing its correct output format, since format consistency is the main issue.
Add 2-4 examples of ambiguous requests, each showing which tool was chosen AND a short explanation of why that tool won over the plausible alternative.
Remove the prose instructions entirely and let the few-shot examples serve as the sole specification.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.2: despite detailed prose instructions, tool routing is still inconsistent on ambiguous cases — the classic signal that few-shot is needed, not more prose. The guide asks for 2-4 targeted examples that show not just which tool was chosen, but why it was preferred over the plausible alternative: that teaches the decision boundary and lets the model generalize to new patterns. C does exactly that. A battery of examples, one format-focused example per tool, or dropping the prose entirely each fail on a different axis of the same routing problem.

distractorsEs.A: Over-engineering / ML escape — a battery of 8-10 examples is more prompt infrastructure than needed; the guide asks for 2-4 targeted examples. More examples isn't 'safer': it raises tokens and the risk that the model memorizes patterns instead of generalizing the criterion.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — one example per tool that only shows the output format teaches form, not the decision boundary; the described symptom is misrouting, not inconsistent formatting. Correct few-shot has to show the reasoning behind the choice.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice — recognizing that examples are missing is on the right track, but it caps it off by removing the prose instructions; few-shot complements the specification, it doesn't fully replace it, and it leaves the model without coverage for cases no example touched.

questions.trap: B confuses the symptom: the problem is routing, not formatting; a pretty-output example doesn't teach when to choose each tool.

questions.objective: Use few-shot examples to handle varied document structures in extraction
questions.scenario: Research-data extraction with very different citation structures across documents.
questions.stem: An extraction pipeline pulls citation data from research papers. Papers that use inline citations extract correctly, but papers with a separate bibliography section frequently return null for fields that are clearly present, just in a different structural location. The schema and field descriptions are already precise. What should be added?

options.text: A stricter JSON schema with additional required fields to force the model to look harder.
A post-processing script that searches the raw document text for a bibliography section using regex, independent of the model's extraction.
A longer field description that repeats, in different words, that citations 'may appear anywhere in the document.'
2-4 few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both inline-citation documents and bibliography-style documents, including a case where the citation is deliberately in the less common location.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.2 in extraction: the schema and descriptions are already precise, but the model fails against a document structure it never saw exemplified. The guide is explicit that few-shot reduces hallucination in extraction precisely by showing correct handling of varied structures. D adds 2-4 targeted examples, including the less common location's case, which teaches the model to recognize the new structural pattern. A stricter schema, a parallel regex, or a longer description don't teach the model to recognize a structure it has never seen exemplified.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — a stricter schema hardens the output's syntax, it doesn't help the model recognize an unexemplified document structure; in fact, more required fields without more examples pushes toward more fabrication, not less.
distractorsEs.B: Over-engineering / ML escape — building a parallel regex extractor is additional, brittle infrastructure that doesn't generalize to unforeseen bibliography formats, for a problem 2-4 targeted examples already solve within the prompt itself.
distractorsEs.C: Half-right practice — reinforcing the field description goes in the right direction, but it stays at repeated prose; detailed prose instructions, on their own, produce inconsistent results against varied structures — the concrete example is missing.

questions.trap: C is the most tempting: it looks like 'giving more context,' but it's repeated prose, not the concrete example the guide asks for with varied structures.

questions.objective: Select tool_choice: any when document type is unknown across multiple schemas
questions.scenario: Ingestion pipeline receiving invoices, purchase orders, and credit notes mixed and unclassified.
questions.stem: An ingestion pipeline receives a mixed stream of documents — invoices, purchase orders, and credit notes — with no upstream classification of which is which. Three separate extraction tools exist (extract_invoice, extract_purchase_order, extract_credit_note), each with its own schema. The pipeline must always get back structured tool_use output, never a plain-text reply. Which tool_choice configuration fits this case?

options.text: {'type': 'any'}, so the model must call one of the three tools but is free to choose which one based on the document's content.
{'type': 'auto'}, so the model can decide whether the document matches any of the known types.
{'type': 'tool', 'name': 'extract_invoice'}, since invoices are the most common document type in the stream.
Send three separate requests, one per forced tool, and keep whichever response has the fewest null fields.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.3: the pipeline doesn't know in advance which document type is arriving, but it demands guaranteed structured output — never plain text. tool_choice: 'any' forces the model to call one of the three tools, leaving the choice of which one to the model itself based on content, which is exactly the unknown-document-type situation the guide describes for this value. 'auto' leaves the door open to a conversational reply, forcing extract_invoice assumes the type before reading the document, and tripling the calls is more cost and an unreliable heuristic for solving something 'any' already solves in a single call.

distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee — 'auto' allows the model to respond with plain text instead of calling a tool; for a pipeline that always demands structured output, leaving that door open bets the guarantee on the model's goodwill, not on a mechanism that enforces it.
distractorsEs.C: Scope flip — forcing a specific tool inverts the decision's correct scope: the document type is exactly what's unknown per request, so the schema choice should live in the model via 'any,' not get fixed in advance by aggregate frequency.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering / ML escape — tripling the calls and deciding by a 'fewest nulls' heuristic is more cost, more latency, and an unreliable heuristic, when 'any' already solves the problem in a single call by letting the model recognize the document.

questions.trap: C tempts because 'invoices are the majority,' but the question is about each individual document, not the stream's aggregate distribution.

questions.objective: Design nullable schema fields to prevent fabricated required values
questions.scenario: 18% of purchase-order numbers fabricated in an invoice pipeline.
questions.stem: An invoice-extraction schema marks purchase_order_number as a required string. An audit finds that in 18% of invoices, the extracted PO number does not exist anywhere in the source document — the model composed it from the invoice number. It turns out several vendors simply never print a PO number on their invoices. The prompt already says 'do not invent values; leave the field blank if you cannot find it.' What is the root-cause fix?

options.text: Strengthen the instruction further: 'Under no circumstances should you fabricate a purchase_order_number.'

Change purchase_order_number to type ['string', 'null'] and remove it from required, adding a description that null means 'not present in the document,' then add a few-shot example from a PO-less vendor showing the correct null output.
Add a post-hoc validation step that flags any PO number matching the invoice number as suspicious and deletes it.
Switch to a larger, more capable model, since a stronger model should be less likely to fabricate values.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.3, the canonical example of schema-driven fabrication: purchase_order_number is required and non-nullable, so constrained decoding forces a string to be produced even when the document has no PO — no prose instruction beats that hard constraint. B attacks the root cause: it makes the field nullable, documents that null means absence, and adds a few-shot example from a PO-less vendor showing the correct output. Reinforcing the instruction, patching after the fact with a matching heuristic, or switching models don't touch the schema constraint that produces the fabrication in the first place.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee — a prose instruction, however emphatic, competes against a hard schema constraint (required non-nullable forces constrained decoding to produce a string). The root cause lives in the schema, not in the instruction's text.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch / blame the executor — patches the symptom after the fabrication already happened, instead of fixing the required non-nullable field that produces it; the matching heuristic will also generate false positives and negatives.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — switching models is a real lever in other contexts, but as long as the field stays required non-nullable, any model under constrained decoding must produce a string. The failure's axis is the schema's design.

questions.trap: A is the most common trap: a stronger prose instruction against a schema constraint. The guide is emphatic — the schema always wins.

questions.objective: Distinguish schema syntax guarantees from semantic validation needs
questions.scenario: Invoices that validate against the schema but whose amounts don't add up.
questions.stem: An extraction pipeline uses tool_use with a strict JSON schema. Every response now parses cleanly and matches the schema's types and required fields. Despite this, a sample audit finds that in some extractions, line_items do not sum to stated_total, and in others a due date was placed in the issue_date field. Select the TWO actions that would actually catch problems like these.

options.text: Instruct the model in the prompt to 'always double-check your math before responding,' and continue trusting the parsed output as-is.
Trust the tool_use output as final once it parses and matches the schema, since strict schemas guarantee correctness.
Run an external validation step (e.g., Pydantic or business-rule checks) after parsing, independent of the model, before the extraction is used downstream.
Add self-verification fields to the schema (e.g., calculated_total alongside stated_total, a conflict_detected boolean) and validate them against each other outside the model.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.3 and 4.4 at their central knot: tool_use with a strict schema eliminates malformed JSON and missing fields, but the guide is emphatic that it never guarantees line items add up or that a value sits in the right field — that's semantics, not syntax. C and D are real controls external to the model: an external validation step and self-verification fields the pipeline itself can compare. Trusting that the schema already guarantees everything, or asking the model to 'double-check itself' in the prompt, are both ways of believing confident-but-wrong output without actually verifying it.

distractorsEs.A: Prompt-as-guarantee — asking in the prompt for the model to 'double-check itself before responding' and then still trusting the output as-is is a prompt plea over a problem that demands external, independent verification, not one more round of the model convincing itself.
distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — tool_use with a strict schema is the correct technique for eliminating syntax errors. Treating it as if it also guaranteed semantic correctness applies that real guarantee to the wrong axis: syntax isn't semantics.

questions.trap: B is the domain's central trap: the strict schema does eliminate malformed JSON, but nothing in constrained decoding verifies the numbers add up.

questions.objective: Implement retry follow-ups with document, failed extraction, and specific errors
questions.scenario: Retry after a validation failure on an insurance policy.
questions.stem: A validation step rejects an extraction because issue_date is not in ISO 8601 format. The pipeline needs to retry. Which follow-up request is most likely to produce a correct result on the next attempt?

options.text: Resend the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error (e.g., 'issue_date value 15/03/2024 is not ISO 8601; expected YYYY-MM-DD'), asking the model to correct only the flagged field.
Resend the original document along with a message stating only that 'the previous extraction failed validation.'
Resend only the word 'retry' as the new user message, relying on the model to remember the prior context.
Increase max_retries to 5 and resend the identical original request each time without modification.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.4: retry-with-feedback demands three ingredients — the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error — so the model knows exactly what to fix. A includes all three and also scopes the correction to the flagged field. Resending the document without saying why it failed, sending only the word 'retry,' or simply raising the retry count without changing the content each repeat the same roll without giving the model new information to correct with — each one is missing a different ingredient from the same recipe the guide specifies for an effective retry.

distractorsEs.B: Half-right practice — resends the document, which goes in the right direction, but omits the data that actually guides the correction: the specific validation error. Saying 'it failed' without saying why repeats the same failure with high probability.
distractorsEs.C: Half-right practice — retrying is the correct technique for a formatting error, but capping it off with a content-free message leaves the model without the information it needs to correct; it's missing document + failed extraction + concrete error.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — raising the retry count is a real lever for other problems, but here, without error feedback, every retry repeats the same roll — it doesn't change the odds of success because it adds no new information.

questions.trap: B is the subtlest trap: it looks like a retry 'with context' because it resends the document, but it's missing the ingredient that actually fixes things — the specific error.

questions.objective: Recognize when retries cannot succeed because information is absent from source
questions.scenario: 9% of policy effective dates fail validation despite retries.
questions.stem: A field policy_effective_date fails validation in 9% of extracted policies. The pipeline retries up to 3 times with error feedback on each failure. The 9% failure rate does not improve, and token costs have risen. Manual inspection shows that for these specific documents, the effective date is only present in a separate attachment that the pipeline never sends to the model. What should the team do?

options.text: Increase max_retries to 5 and add one more few-shot example to the prompt.

Make the field nullable, have the model return null with a reason code (e.g., source_missing), route these cases to human review, and separately fix the ingestion process to include the missing attachment.
Rewrite the validation error message to be more detailed, assuming the model isn't understanding the current one.
Switch the retry strategy to exponential backoff to give the model more 'thinking time' between attempts.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.4 at its most important boundary: retry fixes formatting or structural errors, never the absence of information in what was sent to the model. Here the data lives in an attachment the pipeline never sends — no retry, extra example, more detailed error message, or backoff strategy can make it appear. B is the only option that correctly classifies the failure: nullable + reason code + human review, and underneath, fixes the ingestion to include the missing attachment. Three of the four options insist on variants of the same mechanism against a problem retry can't solve.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — more retries and one more example are levers that work against formatting or structural errors; here the data simply isn't in what's sent to the model. No retry makes an absent piece of data appear, it just raises the cost.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis — a more detailed error message helps when the model misunderstands the problem; here the model understands perfectly well what's being asked, but the data doesn't exist in the document it received. Detailing the error further doesn't create missing information.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis — exponential backoff is a real technique, useful against transient errors (rate limits, timeouts), not against the absence of information in the source document. No waiting pattern makes a piece of data appear that was never sent.

questions.trap: A is the predictable decoy: 'more attempts' sounds like reasonable persistence, but the guide is explicit — retry has zero chance of success against the absence of information.

questions.objective: Apply Message Batches API facts correctly
questions.scenario: Team evaluating moving an overnight workload to the Message Batches API.
questions.stem: A team is evaluating the Message Batches API for a nightly document-processing job. Select the TWO statements below that are accurate.

options.text: Because batch requests are cheaper, they are also always faster in practice than the synchronous API, so latency-sensitive workflows can safely use batch too.
Batch requests support full multi-turn tool calling within a single request, including executing a tool mid-request and returning its result to the model before it finishes.
custom_id correlates each request in a batch with its corresponding response; the order of returned results is not guaranteed to match submission order.
The Batches API offers roughly 50% cost savings compared to the standard synchronous API, with a processing window of up to 24 hours and no guaranteed latency SLA.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.5, the Message Batches API's core facts: 50% savings versus the standard API, a window of up to 24 hours, no guaranteed latency SLA — and custom_id correlates each request with its response because the order of returned results isn't guaranteed. C and D are both verifiable facts from the guide. Being cheaper doesn't imply it's always faster in practice, and the batch API explicitly doesn't support multi-turn tool calling within a single request — attributing that capability to it invents a function that doesn't exist.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — batch USUALLY finishing before 24 hours isn't the same as having a latency guarantee; you can't design a blocking workflow around 'usually fast.' Cheap-and-fast-in-practice isn't the same as cheap-and-guaranteed.
distractorsEs.B: Fabricated feature — the Batches API doesn't support multi-turn tool calling within a single request; you can't execute a tool mid-request and return its result within that same call. Attributing that capability to it invents a function the guide rules out.

questions.trap: A is the business trap: it costs less, so it 'must be better at everything.' Cost savings don't buy a latency SLA.

questions.objective: Calculate batch submission frequency to satisfy an SLA constraint
questions.scenario: 6,000 contracts with a 30-hour SLA commitment from arrival.
questions.stem: A contract-processing pipeline must guarantee that each contract is fully processed within 30 hours of arrival. The team wants to use the Message Batches API (up to a 24-hour processing window) instead of the synchronous API, to control cost. Which submission strategy keeps the pipeline within the SLA in the worst case?

options.text: Submit a new batch every 4 hours; worst case, a contract waits up to 4 hours in queue plus up to 24 hours to process, totaling 28 hours — within the 30-hour SLA.
Submit one batch per day at midnight; worst case, a contract arriving just after submission waits up to 24 hours in queue plus up to 24 hours to process.
Use the synchronous API for all contracts to eliminate queueing risk entirely, accepting the higher per-document cost as the cost of certainty.
Submit batches every 4 hours, but automatically fall back to the synchronous API for any contract that hasn't returned within 20 hours.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.5, the SLA-calculation pattern the guide asks you to master: with 4-hour submission windows, the worst case is 4h in queue plus 24h max processing = 28h, within the 30h commitment with a 2h margin. A is the only cadence that satisfies it. Daily submission leaves up to 48h in the worst case, paying for everything synchronously is disproportionate when batch at the right cadence already gets there, and adding a synchronous fallback at 20h throws in two code paths and two costs for a problem simple arithmetic already solves.

distractorsEs.B: Right technique, wrong axis — batch is still the right API for this latency-tolerant workload, but submission frequency is the axis that fails: daily submission leaves up to 24h in queue plus 24h processing, up to 48h in the worst case — that breaks a 30h SLA.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering / ML escape — paying the full synchronous price for 6,000 contracts eliminates queueing risk, but it's disproportionate: the 4-hour window arithmetic already meets the SLA with margin, without doubling the cost.
distractorsEs.D: Half-right practice — starts off right with correct 4h windows, but caps it off by adding a synchronous fallback path at 20h; that introduces two code paths, two costs, and new failure modes for a problem the 4h cadence already solves on its own.

questions.trap: D is the most elegant decoy: the 4h window is already correct, but the 'just in case' fallback is the complexity the exam punishes when the simple answer already gets there.

questions.objective: Use an independent review instance instead of self-review
questions.scenario: The same thread that generated the code reviews itself and approves it.
questions.stem: In the same session, Claude generates a payment-reconciliation module and is then asked, 'now review your own implementation for bugs.' It reports no issues. A production incident later reveals an off-by-one error in the period-boundary logic. What is the most effective structural fix for future reviews?

options.text: In the same session, ask Claude to enable extended thinking before reviewing its own code, so it reasons more carefully.
Spawn a second, independent Claude instance that receives only the diff and the review criteria — without the generator's reasoning context — to perform the review.
In the same session, instruct Claude more forcefully: 'Be extremely critical and skeptical of your own work.'
Ask a different developer on the team to manually re-read the generated module before merging.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.6: the model that generated the code retains its reasoning context and has already convinced itself its decision was good — asking it to 'review itself' in the same session doesn't erase that bias, no matter how much effort or insistence is added. B is the structural intervention the guide prescribes: a second, independent instance, without that reasoning context, that receives only the diff and the review criteria. Extended thinking and a more emphatic instruction attack effort, not bias; asking a human to manually reread everything doesn't scale and dodges the solution the Agent SDK itself already allows.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — extended thinking is a real reasoning lever, but self-review's bias isn't about how much effort the model applies, it's about it retaining the generation's reasoning context. More 'thinking' in the same biased session doesn't eliminate the bias.
distractorsEs.C: Prompt-as-guarantee — asking the model to be 'extremely critical of itself' is a prompt plea over a structural problem; the model that generated the code has already convinced itself its decision was good, and no attitude instruction erases that retained context.
distractorsEs.D: Externalize the problem — moving the review to a human who rereads manually doesn't fix the automated pipeline and doesn't scale; it shifts the system's cost onto the developer's time instead of using the independent instance the Agent SDK itself lets you spawn.

questions.trap: C is the classic trap: it sounds like 'more pressure' in the instruction compensates for the bias, but the bias lives in the retained context, not in the model's effort.

questions.objective: Split large reviews into per-file and cross-file integration passes
questions.scenario: 14-file PR with contradictory feedback between identical files.
questions.stem: A single review pass over a 14-file pull request produces contradictory feedback: a pattern is flagged as a problem in one file and approved as acceptable in another, seemingly identical, file elsewhere in the same PR. All 14 files fit comfortably within the model's context window. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Switch to a model with an even larger context window so it can hold more of the PR's surrounding code at once.
Require that any finding appear consistently in at least 2 of 3 independent review passes before it is reported.
Split the review into a local per-file pass for bugs and correctness, plus a separate cross-file integration pass for data flow and consistency between files.
Ask developers to submit smaller PRs of no more than 5 files going forward.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Task 4.6: the 14 files already fit within the context window, so the symptom — a pattern flagged as a problem in one file and approved in an identical other — is attention dilution, not a lack of capacity. C is the cure the guide prescribes: separate a local per-file pass from a cross-file integration pass. A bigger window doesn't change how attention gets spread across many files in a single pass; requiring consensus across runs suppresses real, intermittent signal; and asking the team to shrink their PRs shifts the system's cost onto the human instead of fixing the review pipeline.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis — the 14 files already fit within the context window; the problem isn't capacity, it's the quality of attention spread across many files in a single pass. A bigger window doesn't fix attention dilution.
distractorsEs.B: Consensus voting — requiring consensus across 2 of 3 runs raises apparent precision by suppressing signal: findings that are real but intermittent, exactly the described symptom, get discarded for not repeating, instead of fixing the cause, which is attention dilution.
distractorsEs.D: Externalize the problem — asking the team to split their PRs shifts the review system's cost onto the human workflow; it doesn't fix the review pipeline itself, whereas multi-pass does attack the cause without changing anyone else's behavior.

questions.trap: A is the exam's most human mental error: confusing the files FITTING with them receiving even, quality attention.

questions.objective: Preserve critical case facts outside summarized conversation history
questions.scenario: Refund lost in the rolling summary
questions.stem: A customer support agent's conversation reaches turn 48 under a design that re-summarizes the rolling history every 15 turns. Session logs show that at turn 30 the summary compressed three concrete facts ($247.50 refund amount, order A-88231, and a stated 5-business-day expectation) into: 'Customer has multiple issues including a damaged order and a billing problem.' At turn 48 the agent calls process_refund with an empty amount field. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Switch the agent to a model with a larger context window so the full 48-turn history never needs to be summarized.
Instruct the summarization prompt to 'preserve all important numeric details and customer commitments' whenever it condenses the history.

Extract transactional facts (order ID, amount, status, dates, stated customer expectations) into a persistent case-facts block that is re-injected verbatim in every request, outside the summarized history.
Train a lightweight classifier to predict which conversation turns are likely to contain critical data, and exclude only those turns from summarization.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.1 on extracting transactional facts into a 'case facts' layer. The root cause isn't how much gets summarized or how often, but WHERE the data lives: as long as the amount, the order, and the customer's stated expectation depend on the summarizer, the loss rate is never zero. C pulls those hard facts out of the summarizable history and re-injects them verbatim on every request — a structured block the LLM can't compress by its own decision. It's the structural cure, not a good-behavior instruction or a bigger window.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: a bigger window solves the history FITTING, not the summarizer deciding well what to keep. The data already fit within 48 turns; the problem is attention and design, not capacity.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking the summarizer to 'preserve important details' still delegates to the LLM the decision of what's critical — the same component that already failed. Probabilistic where a guarantee is needed.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: building and maintaining a trained classifier is heavy infrastructure for a problem that's solved with a structured data layer outside the summarizer — the low-effort fix wasn't even tried.

questions.trap: The decoy is B: it sounds responsible ('preserve what's important'), but it still follows the rules of a probabilistic component for data that must survive, always.

questions.objective: Trim verbose tool outputs before they accumulate in context
questions.scenario: lookup_order tool with 40+ irrelevant fields
questions.stem: A support agent's lookup_order tool returns more than 40 fields per call (warehouse metadata, internal IDs, logistics timestamps), even though only 5 fields (order_id, total_usd, delivered_at, status, return_window_days) are ever relevant to a conversation. Every tool_result is retained and re-sent on each subsequent turn. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Project the tool_result to only the relevant fields (e.g., in a PostToolUse hook) before it enters the conversation context, so the trimmed version — not the raw 40+ fields — is what accumulates turn over turn.
Instruct the agent in the system prompt to 'only pay attention to order_id, total_usd, delivered_at, status, and return_window_days when reading tool results.'
Have the response-generation step ignore irrelevant fields when composing its reply to the customer, while still storing the full 40+ fields in history.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the extra fields don't crowd out the relevant ones.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.1 on trimming tool outputs. Every junk field from a 40+-field lookup_order gets resent on every subsequent turn and also pushes the relevant content toward the middle of the window. The cure is to trim BEFORE the result enters context — the PostToolUse hook is the natural point, exactly as the guide describes it. A attacks the root cause at the right layer: the construction of the tool_result, not its later consumption or the window's capacity.

distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking the agent to 'ignore' fields that are already in the history doesn't remove them from it — they keep consuming tokens and getting resent every turn. A probabilistic instruction over a structural accumulation problem.
distractorsEs.C: Downstream patch: fixes the component that READS the tool_result (response generation) instead of the one that PRODUCES it. The 40+ fields keep piling up in the history; it only hides the symptom in the final output.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis: a bigger window lets the 40+ fields FIT better, but it doesn't reduce the tax paid on every turn, nor does it fix the relevant content staying buried under irrelevant metadata.

questions.trap: C tempts because it 'works' in the response visible to the customer, but the raw history keeps growing turn over turn — the fix is cosmetic, not structural.

questions.objective: Mitigate the lost-in-the-middle effect in aggregated synthesis input
questions.scenario: Multi-source synthesis over 12 documents
questions.stem: A synthesis agent receives an aggregated input combining excerpts from 12 source documents. Reviewers notice the synthesis reliably reflects findings from the first two and last two sources, but frequently omits or garbles findings from sources 5 through 9. What is the most effective way to restructure the aggregated input to mitigate this?

options.text: Move the synthesis step to a model with a larger context window so all 12 sources fit without truncation.
Build a custom retrieval-ranking model that reorders the 12 sources by predicted relevance before every synthesis call.
Set a context_priority field on the tool_result blocks for sources 5 through 9 to mark them as high-importance for the model.

Place a summary of key findings at the beginning of the aggregated input, and organize the detailed source excerpts with explicit section headers (e.g., '## Source 6 — Report X') so each finding is independently recoverable regardless of its position.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.1 on the 'lost in the middle' effect: models reliably process the beginning and end of a long input, and omit the middle more often — it isn't anecdotal, it's a documented position effect. D attacks exactly that: it moves the key-findings summary to the front (where attention is more reliable) and turns each source into a block anchored by an explicit header, recoverable even in the middle of the aggregated document. None of the other options restructure WHERE the information lives within the input.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: the 12 documents already fit within the window — the symptom isn't about capacity, it's about attention quality by position. Enlarging the window doesn't change how well the middle of a long input gets read.
distractorsEs.B: Over-engineering: a trained ranking model is heavy infrastructure for a problem that's solved by reordering and heading the text — the low-effort fix (headers + summary up front) wasn't even tried.
distractorsEs.C: Fabricated feature: there is no context_priority parameter on tool_result blocks that flags importance for the model. It's an invented feature with credible-looking syntax.

questions.trap: C is the most dangerous: it sounds like a real, specific API, but it's a field that doesn't exist — sweep for invented features first.

questions.objective: Honor explicit customer escalation requests without delay
questions.scenario: Customer asks to speak with a human
questions.stem: Mid-conversation, a customer tells the support agent: 'I don't want to keep doing this back and forth — please connect me with a human agent right now.' The underlying issue appears straightforward and within the agent's resolution authority. What should the agent do?

options.text: Run one lookup_order call to confirm the issue is real, then escalate to a human with the findings attached.
Escalate to a human immediately, honoring the explicit request without first attempting further investigation or resolution.
Continue monitoring the customer's sentiment, and escalate only once negative sentiment crosses a defined threshold, regardless of what the customer explicitly asked for.
Deploy a classifier trained on historical tickets to predict escalation likelihood, and route based on the classifier's prediction rather than the customer's stated request.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.2: a customer who explicitly asks for a human gets escalated IMMEDIATELY, with no prior investigation — investigating first ignores a preference already stated, even when the case looks simple to resolve. B honors the request as-is. This is different from a frustrated customer who hasn't explicitly asked, where it's fine to acknowledge the frustration and offer to resolve first, escalating only if the customer insists. Here the request is already unambiguous: any intermediate step, however well-intentioned, postpones what the customer already asked for clearly.

distractorsEs.A: Half-right practice: the first clause sounds diligent (verify before escalating), but the explicit request no longer requires prior investigation — the extra step delays exactly what the guide asks to be done immediately.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: sentiment is a real signal, but it doesn't correlate with case complexity, nor does it substitute for a request the customer already explicitly made — it measures the wrong variable.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: a classifier trained on historical tickets is heavy infrastructure that, on top of that, ignores the strongest possible signal — the customer's literal request — in favor of a statistical prediction.

questions.trap: A is the finest decoy: it looks like the responsible candidate who 'confirms first,' but the guide is explicit that an explicit request is honored without investigating beforehand.

questions.objective: Escalate when policy is silent on a customer's request
questions.scenario: Matching a competitor's price, a policy gap
questions.stem: A customer asks a support agent to match a lower price found at a competing retailer. The agent's policy documentation defines rules only for price adjustments on purchases made on the company's own site; it says nothing about matching a competitor's price. What should the agent do?

options.text: Have the agent self-rate its confidence that price-matching is reasonable in this case, and proceed automatically whenever that self-reported score is high.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to 'use good judgment and be helpful when the policy doesn't explicitly cover a customer's request.'
Escalate to a human, since the policy is silent on this specific request and the agent has no authority to invent a policy exception.
Train a classifier on past policy-gap tickets to predict whether similar requests were eventually approved, and auto-apply its prediction.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.2: a policy gap (the policy doesn't cover the case) is one of the three legitimate escalation triggers, alongside the customer's explicit request and the inability to proceed. C recognizes this: the agent has no authority to invent a policy exception, no matter how reasonable the request looks. The solution isn't for the agent to decide better — it's for the case to leave its decision scope entirely.

distractorsEs.A: Raw self-reported confidence — the trap decoder.md names among the typical mental errors ('trusting the model's self-reported confidence'): a score uncalibrated against a labeled validation set is the model's opinion about itself, not authorization to decide something outside its scope.
distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: 'use good judgment' is a probabilistic instruction for a decision the agent, by design, has no authority to make. A policy gap doesn't get closed with a sentence in the prompt.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: a classifier trained on historical cases is heavy infrastructure before even applying the simple, cheap rule — escalate when the policy is silent.

questions.trap: B is the elegant decoy: it sounds like empowering the agent with judgment, but a policy gap demands escalation, not 'using judgment.'

questions.objective: Return structured error context instead of a generic failure status
questions.scenario: Web-search subagent timeout
questions.stem: In a multi-agent research system, the web-search subagent times out after 30 seconds while querying a niche subtopic. Which subagent behavior gives the coordinator what it needs to recover intelligently?

options.text: Retry the query twice with exponential backoff inside the subagent; if retries are exhausted, return a structured result including failure_type, the exact query attempted, any partial results already retrieved, and suggested alternative approaches.
Retry the query twice with exponential backoff inside the subagent, and if both retries also time out, return a generic status: search_unavailable.
Catch the timeout exception and return an empty results list marked as a successful query, so the coordinator does not need special-case handling for failures.

Upon timeout, spin up three alternative search strategies in parallel (different query phrasing, a different search API, and a cached snapshot lookup), and return whichever finishes first without reporting that the original query ever timed out.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.3: the subagent should locally recover what's transient (retry with backoff, the practice the guide asks for) and, if it can't resolve it, propagate a STRUCTURED error — failure type, what was attempted, partials, alternatives — not a generic status. A is the only one that preserves that full context. Every tool_use needs its tool_result, even an error one, so the coordinator can decide with real information instead of guessing. The local retry is necessary but not sufficient: what travels after it decides the quality of the recovery.

distractorsEs.B: Half-right practice: the retry with backoff is exactly what the guide asks for — but the final clause destroys the value. A generic search_unavailable status blinds the coordinator: it doesn't know what was attempted, it doesn't have the partials, it doesn't have alternatives. In this domain, the bad half rules.
distractorsEs.C: Silent suppression — the family d5.md calls 'silent suppression / consensus,' a cousin of the 'consensus voting' decoder.md names (Q12-D): turning an access failure into an empty result marked as success buys apparent cleanliness by destroying real signal.
distractorsEs.D: Over-engineering: deploying three parallel search strategies is heavy infrastructure, and it also still hides the original failure from the coordinator — it solves the symptom without reporting the cause.

questions.trap: B is this domain's favorite decoy: the first clause is a real good practice, and that's exactly why it's easy to fall for it without reading to the end.

questions.objective: Distinguish access failures from valid empty results
questions.scenario: Empty result vs. access failure
questions.stem: A coordinator receives two results from its search subagent, from two different queries. Result 1: status ok, results: [] — the query executed successfully and simply found no matching documents. Result 2: status failure, failure_type timeout — the query never completed. Select the TWO statements that correctly describe how the coordinator should treat these results.

options.text: Both results should be treated identically, since neither one gave the coordinator any usable data.
Result 1 is valid information — the search worked and found nothing; retrying the identical query is unlikely to change the outcome.
Result 1 should be retried automatically, since an empty results list is itself suspicious and likely indicates the subagent is malfunctioning.
Result 2 represents an absence of information, not evidence of absence — a retry, a reformulated query, or an alternative source is appropriate here.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.3, the task statement's most testable distinction: status ok, results: [] is a search that WORKED and found no matches — valid information, don't retry the same query. status failure, failure_type timeout means we DON'T KNOW if there are results — that's where retrying or reformulating fits. B and D name exactly that distinction. Collapsing both cases into 'empty' is the classic multi-agent reliability bug: the final report might say 'we found no evidence' when the truth is 'we couldn't look.'

distractorsEs.A: Silent suppression — the same 'silent suppression / consensus' family decoder.md names via consensus voting: treating both results the same erases the distinction between 'there's no data' and 'we couldn't look,' compressing real signal into a single category.
distractorsEs.C: Right technique, wrong axis: retry is a real, correct technique — but applied to the wrong case. Retrying a query that already executed successfully and found no matches will return the same thing; retry belongs to the access failure, not to the valid empty result.

questions.trap: C is the finest decoy: 'retry just in case' sounds prudent, but retrying a VALID empty result wastes budget without changing the outcome — retry is for the absence of information, not for information about absence.

questions.objective: Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration
questions.scenario: Legacy codebase exploration, hour 3
questions.stem: Three hours into a code-exploration session on a large legacy codebase, the agent identified two specific classes (OrderValidator, PaymentGateway) as the core of the checkout flow during the first hour. Now, asked to describe the checkout flow again, the agent responds: 'Typically in this kind of e-commerce system, checkout validates the cart and then calls the payment provider,' naming neither class, and contradicting what it said earlier about validation order. What does this response indicate, and what is the most effective fix?

options.text: Set a --context-retention high flag on the session to prevent the agent from forgetting earlier findings.

The specific findings have fallen out of the context window and the agent is substituting generic domain knowledge; the fix is to persist key findings to a scratchpad file and delegate further verbose exploration to subagents with isolated context.
Add an instruction to the system prompt telling the agent to 'always remember and cite the specific classes discovered earlier in the session.'
Re-read OrderValidator and PaymentGateway in full within the current conversation to refresh the agent's understanding.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.4: 'typical patterns' instead of naming the concrete class is the clinical signature of context degradation — the specific finding is no longer in the window and the model substitutes generic knowledge for it, even contradicting what it said earlier. B applies the correct cure: persist findings outside the window (scratchpad) and isolate future verbose exploration in subagents with isolated context. No other option gets state OUT of the already-degraded window; some even degrade it further.

distractorsEs.A: Fabricated feature: there is no --context-retention flag in the real session-configuration surface. Credible-looking syntax, invented functionality.
distractorsEs.C: Prompt-as-guarantee: asking the model to 'always remember and cite' doesn't change the fact that the specific data has already fallen out of the window — a probabilistic instruction over a problem of capacity already consumed.
distractorsEs.D: Right technique, wrong axis: re-reading the files is a generally valid technique, but doing it in the SAME already-degraded conversation adds more verbose tokens to the problem instead of isolating it — the read should go to a subagent or a scratchpad, not the main window.

questions.trap: D is the most tempting: 're-read the code' sounds like rigorous verification, but it makes exactly the problem that caused the degradation worse.

questions.objective: Design human review workflows and confidence calibration
questions.scenario: 96% aggregate accuracy in extraction
questions.stem: A structured-extraction pipeline processes three document types: digital invoices (70% of volume), scanned purchase orders (22%), and hand-annotated lab reports (8%). The pipeline reports 96% overall extraction accuracy. Leadership proposes removing human review from all high-confidence extractions to reduce reviewer headcount.
