What should happen before that change is made?

options.text: Lower the model's sampling temperature to 0 for all extractions, and treat that as sufficient grounds to remove human review.
Have the model self-report a confidence rating from 1 to 10 for each document, and automate any document whose self-reported score is 8 or above.
Train a machine-learning model on the reviewer override history to predict, per document, whether a human should double-check it.

Measure accuracy separately by document type and by field, calibrate the confidence threshold against a labeled validation set per segment, and automate only the segments that validate — keeping human review on the rest.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.5: a 96% aggregate can hide a minority segment (the lab reports, 8% of volume) with a much higher error rate, in exactly the highest-risk segment. D demands segmenting by document type and by field, and calibrating the confidence threshold against a labeled validation set — without that, no confidence score authorizes automating. Only after validating per segment does human review get reduced, and only in the segments that support it.

distractorsEs.A: Right technique, wrong axis: temperature controls the model's sampling randomness, not the reliability or accuracy of an extraction. Lowering it to 0 makes outputs more deterministic, but it doesn't validate whether they're correct — a real lever applied to the wrong axis.
distractorsEs.B: Raw self-reported confidence — the same decoy decoder.md explicitly names: a 1-10 score uncalibrated against a labeled validation set is a numeric hallucination, not a real accuracy measurement.
distractorsEs.C: Over-engineering: training an ML model on override history is heavy infrastructure that skips the cheap, necessary step — segmenting and calibrating — before building anything more sophisticated.

questions.trap: A is the technical decoy: temperature sounds like a reliability parameter because it 'reduces randomness,' but it's purely about sampling — it doesn't measure or improve accuracy.

questions.objective: Preserve information provenance and handle uncertainty in multi-source synthesis
questions.scenario: Two conflicting cloud-adoption figures
questions.stem: A synthesis agent receives two conflicting statistics from its document-analysis subagent: 'cloud migration adoption reached 42%' (from a Q1-2025 vendor telemetry report) and 'cloud migration adoption reached 58%' (from a Q4-2025 self-reported industry survey). The synthesis agent selects 58%, the more recent figure, and omits 42% from the final report entirely. A reader later asks where the 58% figure came from and cannot reconstruct it. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Change the upstream document-analysis agent's output contract to a structured claim-source mapping (claim, source name, URL, published_at, data_collected_at, methodology) for every finding, and have the synthesis agent preserve and annotate both conflicting values — including their collection dates — instead of silently selecting one.
Add an instruction to the synthesis agent's prompt: 'Always cite your sources when reporting statistics.'
Have the synthesis agent compute an average of the two figures (50%) and report that single blended number as the adoption rate.
Since the contradiction surfaced in the final report, revise the synthesis agent's citation logic; the upstream document-analysis agent's output does not need to change.

questions.explanationEs: Tests Skill 5.6: attribution gets lost at the SUMMARY/analysis step, not at synthesis — by the time synthesis acts, if the upstream output contract didn't preserve source and date, there's nothing left to cite. A changes the contract of the agent that PRODUCES the findings, demands collection dates (which reveal that 42% and 58% might be a time trend, not a contradiction), and leaves both values annotated for the coordinator to reconcile. Picking one value, even 'the most recent one,' is information loss disguised as coherence.

distractorsEs.B: Prompt-as-guarantee: 'always cite your sources' is a probabilistic instruction on an agent that no longer has the source — synthesis can't cite an attribution the previous step didn't hand it in structured form.
distractorsEs.C: Silent suppression — a variant of the 'silent suppression / consensus' family (consensus voting in decoder.md): averaging 42% and 58% invents a third number no source reported, merging two distinct measurements into a false figure.
distractorsEs.D: Downstream patch: blames the component that worked correctly within what it received (synthesis) and absolves the one that actually lost the attribution (document analysis). You need to go up a layer, not patch the one below.

questions.trap: B is this domain's classic decoy: asking for 'cite your sources' in the synthesis prompt doesn't fix data that was already lost upstream.

certs.name: Claude Certified Architect – Professional
certs.fee: $175 USD (per attempt; the price shown at checkout reflects whatever discount applies to your partner tier)
certs.delivery: Proctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy — delivered by Pearson VUE. The candidate chooses, when scheduling, between online proctoring or a Pearson test center.
certs.prerequisites: There are no mandatory prerequisites or required courses to sit the exam. The recommended experience (a software engineering background; 3+ years in systems architecture or platform engineering; 6+ months of hands-on experience with Claude or other production LLM-based systems; having delivered end-to-end systems from discovery through operationalization) is recommended, NOT required. The credential is awarded solely on exam performance.
certs.languages: The exam guide v1.0 does not publish a list of available languages. The exam is administered in English: the official sample items in Section 8 are in English, and no localization is mentioned. Prepare to read technical stems in English under time pressure.
certs.audience: Mid-to-senior technical professionals who design, build, and ship production-grade AI solutions with LLMs, Claude in particular: solution architects, AI/ML engineers, technical leads, and senior software engineers operating at the intersection of business requirements and technical implementation. They translate business problems into scalable AI solutions: model selection, prompt engineering, tool and agent orchestration, context management, and ensuring safety, compliance, and governance. They typically participate in stakeholder engagement, advise clients or internal teams, and lead architectural decisions — including security, legal, and executive-level discussions — across industries such as financial services, healthcare, retail, technology, education, and government.
certs.mqc: The Minimally Qualified Candidate (MQC) is an experienced practitioner who pairs an engineering mindset with real-world experience deploying AI solutions. They design, implement, and govern AI solutions with Claude within production environments, translating business requirements into scalable, secure, and reliable architectures. They demonstrate the ability to design end-to-end AI systems: prompt and context engineering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), API integration, orchestration, and evaluation frameworks. They understand the trade-offs between cost, latency, performance, safety, and maintainability, and know how to justify a decision — not just make one. In terms of recommended experience: a solid foundation in good software engineering practices (modular design, separation of concerns, scalability), 3+ years in systems architecture or platform engineering, 6+ months of hands-on experience with Claude or comparable LLMs in production, and having delivered complete systems from discovery through operationalization.
certs.notFor: This is not aimed at entry-level developers, casual users of Claude-based applications, or people without experience designing end-to-end AI systems. It also excludes purely non-technical roles, or roles limited to isolated tasks like writing prompts without broader system-design responsibility. If your work with Claude begins and ends at writing prompts or using an app someone else built, this exam will punish you: it measures architectural decisions, not chat skills.

domains.title: Solution Design & Architecture
objectives: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops)
Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM)
Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies
Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving
Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs)
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 17%

This domain measures a single skill, and it isn't technical in the narrow sense: the ability to choose the simplest architecture that satisfies the business requirement, and to justify why you didn't choose the most impressive one. The other domains ask you how something is done (how to cache, how to index, how to evaluate). This one asks you what to build and why, given a business problem with cost, latency, risk, and SLA constraints. It's the domain where the exam most brutally punishes the senior architect's professional bias: reflexive over-engineering.

Anthropic has an explicit, published editorial stance on this — "find the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed" — and the exam applies it as a scoring criterion. A multi-agent system consumes roughly 15× the tokens of a chat (single-thread agents, ~4×); an autonomous agentic system introduces a state space you can't test exhaustively; a poorly designed feedback loop leaves you blind in production. At 17% of the blueprint — the second-highest weight after Integration — and ~11 of the 63 items, this domain decides whether you pass or fail more than any other except Integration. And its decision rule is the same as the decoder's: the option that resolves the root cause with the least structural complexity the prompt allows wins, not the one that stacks the most capabilities.

The other half of the domain is bidirectional translation: from business problem to architecture, and from architecture to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLA). An architect who designs an elegant pipeline but can't say which of the five pillars it moves, or by what metric, isn't an architect — they're an implementer with vocabulary. The exam distinguishes between the two with surgical precision.

Official Objectives

Verbatim from the exam guide (Section 6, Domain 1), with the operational translation of what you'll actually be asked.

  • Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions In practice: you're given a business situation with quantified pain ("the legal team reviews 400 contracts/month at 45 min each") and you have to identify which part of the process is automatable with an LLM, which part needs a human, and which part an LLM should NOT touch. The distractors propose automating the wrong part.

  • Design end-to-end architectures (input → processing → output → feedback loops) In practice: you're given an incomplete architecture and you have to spot the missing link. In the vast majority of cases the missing link is the feedback loop: no logging, no eval in production, no human correction channel, no way to know if the system degraded.

  • Select appropriate architectural patterns (workflow, agentic, augmented LLM) In practice: given a problem, choose between an augmented call (retrieval + tools), a workflow with predefined code paths, or an agent that decides its own process. The correct answer is almost never "agent" unless the prompt states that the number of steps cannot be predicted.

  • Design multi-agent systems and orchestration strategies In practice: when to justify orchestrator-workers, how to delegate (the subagent contract), and — critically — when NOT to use multi-agent: when subtasks depend on each other or all agents need the same shared context.

  • Apply decomposition techniques for complex problem solving In practice: break a complex task into verifiable steps, put programmatic gates between steps, isolate context in subagents, and decide the cutoff point between what the model does and what your deterministic code does.

  • Align solutions to business value pillars (efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs) In practice: justify the architectural decision to a stakeholder with the right metric. If the pillar is latency SLA, the answer can't be "the Batch API is 50% cheaper." If the pillar is cost on an overnight job, the answer can't be "let's use the most capable model just in case."

Key Concepts

1. The Base Building Block: Augmented LLM

The augmented LLM is the atomic unit of every Claude architecture: a model with access to retrieval, tools, and memory, where the model itself generates its own search queries, selects which tools to use, and decides what information to retain. It isn't "a chatbot" — it's a component with state, the capacity to act, and the capacity to query.

The nuance that separates the ones who know: most production problems are solved by optimizing a single augmented call, not by standing up an agentic system. Before introducing a second LLM into the design, the mandatory question is: have I already squeezed retrieval, examples, and a well-written tool definition? If the answer is no, any multi-step architecture is optimizing prematurely.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

# Augmented LLM: una sola llamada, con retrieval declarado como tool
# y el modelo decidiendo cuándo consultarla.
TOOLS = [
    {
        "name": "search_policy_corpus",
        "description": (
            "Search the internal underwriting policy corpus. Returns the top-k policy "
            "clauses relevant to a natural-language query, each with its clause id, "
            "effective date and full text. Use this whenever a question depends on "
            "current company policy rather than general knowledge. Prefer one precise "
            "query over several broad ones."
        ),
        "input_schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "query": {"type": "string", "description": "Natural-language search query."},
                "top_k": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 10, "default": 5},
            },
            "required": ["query"],
        },
    }
]

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=4096,
    system=[
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "You are an underwriting assistant. Cite the clause id for every claim you make.",
            "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},  # prefijo estable → cacheable
        }
    ],
    tools=TOOLS,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Does policy allow coverage for a 2019 flood claim in zone AE?"}],
)

print(resp.stop_reason)  # 'tool_use' → ejecuta la tool y devuelve tool_result

Detail the exam rewards: sending tools automatically adds a tool-use system prompt that consumes tokens (e.g., Sonnet 5: 354 tokens with tool_choice: auto; Opus 4.8: 290). Every tool you add to the design has a fixed cost per request, not just the cost of using it.

2. Workflow vs. Agent — The Distinction That Decides the Most Items

Anthropic's official definition, and you need to know it verbatim:

Workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are systems where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

The operative criterion: who decides the next step, your code or the model? If the next step is written in an if in your Python, it's a workflow — even if you use five different LLMs. If the model decides at runtime how many iterations to run and which tool to call, it's an agent.

Exam corollary: a pipeline of 6 Claude calls in a fixed sequence is not agentic. A candidate who calls that an "agent" has already lost the item.

When to use an agent (and only then): when it's difficult or impossible to predict the number of steps required and you can't hardcode a fixed path. Autonomous agents additionally require: a clear, well-documented toolset, sandbox testing, guardrails, and ground-truth feedback from the environment at every step. Coding agents work well precisely because automated tests give them that ground truth; an agent without an objective truth signal is a generator of unwarranted confidence.

3. The Five Workflow Patterns (Name Them and Tell Them Apart)

PatternWhat it doesCondition for useTrade-off
Prompt chainingOne LLM's output feeds the next, with programmatic gates between stepsThe task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasksTrades latency for accuracy
RoutingClassifies the input and sends it to a specialized flowDistinct categories exist that are better handled separatelyLets you send the easy stuff to a cheap model (Haiku)
ParallelizationSectioning: independent subtasks in parallel. Voting: the same task run multiple timesSubtasks are predefined and independent, or you need confidence/diversityMore tokens in exchange for speed or confidence
Orchestrator-workersA central LLM decomposes at runtime and delegates to workers, then synthesizesSubtasks can't be predefined: they depend on the inputMaximum flexibility, maximum token cost
Evaluator-optimizerOne LLM generates, another evaluates and gives feedback, in a loopThere are clear evaluation criteria and iteration measurably improves the resultLatency and cost per iteration

Exam confusion #1 in this domain: parallelization vs. orchestrator-workers. The difference isn't "how many agents" or "whether they run in parallel." It's who defines the subtasks: in parallelization they're predefined in your code; in orchestrator-workers they're determined by the orchestrator at runtime based on the specific input. If the prompt says "the system always analyzes the same 4 aspects of the contract," that's parallelization by sectioning. If it says "the number and type of aspects depends on the type of contract that comes in," that's orchestrator-workers.

Confusion #2: evaluator-optimizer isn't "evals." Evals are Domain 4 (measuring the system offline). Evaluator-optimizer is a runtime pattern: the critic runs on every request, not in CI.

4. Routing: The Most Underrated Pattern, and the One That Saves the Most Money

Routing is the pattern with the best value-to-complexity ratio because it simultaneously attacks cost and latency without breaking accuracy: you send the 80% of trivial traffic to Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 per MTok) and reserve Opus 4.8 ($5/$25) or Fable 5 ($10/$50) for the 20% that needs it.

import anthropic, json

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

ROUTE_SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "route": {"type": "string", "enum": ["faq", "account_action", "complex_dispute"]},
        "confidence": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 1},
    },
    "required": ["route", "confidence"],
}

def classify(ticket: str) -> dict:
    # Clasificador barato y rápido. Structured outputs, NO prefill (400 en modelos modernos).
    r = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5",
        max_tokens=256,
        system="Classify the support ticket. Output JSON only.",
        output_config={"format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": ROUTE_SCHEMA}},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket}],
    )
    return json.loads(next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text"))

HANDLERS = {
    "faq":             ("claude-haiku-4-5", 1024),
    "account_action":  ("claude-sonnet-5",  4096),
    "complex_dispute": ("claude-opus-4-8",  8192),
}

def handle(ticket: str) -> str:
    decision = classify(ticket)
    # Gate programático: baja confianza NO va al modelo grande — va al humano.
    if decision["confidence"] < 0.7:
        return escalate_to_human(ticket, reason="low_router_confidence")
    model, max_tokens = HANDLERS[decision["route"]]
    r = client.messages.create(
        model=model,
        max_tokens=max_tokens,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket}],
    )
    return next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")

The nuance that separates: the low-confidence gate doesn't escalate to the bigger model, it escalates to the human. An unsure router isn't fixed by more intelligence; the bigger model will inherit the same input ambiguity. This is Domain 1's version of the axiom "the model is not a security boundary."

5. Multi-Agent: The Pattern the Exam Wants You to Know How to Reject

Architecture documented by Anthropic (the research system): a lead agent coordinates and delegates to specialized subagents that operate in parallel, then synthesizes. Published data you need to have memorized:

  • Agents consume ~4× the tokens of a chat. Multi-agent systems, ~15×.
  • In Anthropic's internal research eval, a lead Claude Opus 4 with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%. In other words: multi-agent does work — when the task admits real parallelization and has high value.
  • A subagent returns to the coordinator a distilled summary of typically 1,000–2,000 tokens, not its full transcript. That's the mechanism by which multi-agent saves context even while spending tokens.

Delegation contract (memorize it — it's the answer to "how to delegate well"): every subagent needs (1) an objective, (2) an output format, (3) guidance on which tools and sources to use, (4) clear task boundaries. And you have to scale effort to complexity: simple query = 1 agent with 3–10 tool calls; complex research = 10+ subagents.

Documented failure modes (potential distractors): spawning too many subagents for simple queries; continuing to search when enough has already been found; subagents duplicating work due to vague instructions; overly verbose search queries.

When NOT to use multi-agent — the part the exam actually tests: when all agents need to share the same context, or when subtasks have strong dependencies on each other. Multi-agent only pays for its cost when the branches are genuinely independent.

import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition, ResultMessage

async def main():
    async for message in query(
        prompt=(
            "Assess vendor Acme Corp for onboarding. Cover: (1) security posture, "
            "(2) financial stability, (3) contractual red flags. Synthesize a single "
            "go/no-go recommendation with the evidence for each dimension."
        ),
        options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
            # 'Agent' DEBE estar en allowed_tools o Claude no delega.
            allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "WebSearch", "Agent"],
            agents={
                "security-reviewer": AgentDefinition(
                    description="Reviews vendor security posture. Use for SOC2, pentest reports, CVEs.",
                    prompt=(
                        "Objective: assess the vendor's security posture.\n"
                        "Output format: markdown table | finding | severity | evidence path |\n"
                        "Tools/sources: Read and Grep over ./vendor_docs; WebSearch for public CVEs.\n"
                        "Boundaries: do NOT assess pricing or contract terms."
                    ),
                    tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "WebSearch"],  # read-only
                    model="sonnet",   # worker barato; el lead es el modelo caro
                ),
                "finance-reviewer": AgentDefinition(
                    description="Reviews vendor financial stability from filings and reports.",
                    prompt=(
                        "Objective: assess financial stability (runway, revenue trend, concentration).\n"
                        "Output format: 5 bullets max, each with a figure and its source.\n"
                        "Tools/sources: Read over ./vendor_docs/financials.\n"
                        "Boundaries: do NOT assess security or legal terms."
                    ),
                    tools=["Read", "Grep"],
                    model="sonnet",
                ),
            },
            max_turns=40,          # cortafuegos: cuenta SOLO turns con tool use
            max_budget_usd=5.00,   # cortafuegos económico
        ),
    ):
        if isinstance(message, ResultMessage) and message.subtype == "success":
            print(message.result, message.total_cost_usd)

asyncio.run(main())

Three details that are exam items waiting to happen:

  1. Agent must be in allowed_tools. Without that, Claude doesn't delegate (it asks for permission or denies). It's cause #1 of "my subagent never gets invoked."
  2. The subagent sees NOTHING from the parent. It inherits no history, no tool results, no parent system prompt. The only channel from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string. If the subagent needs a file path or a prior finding, you put it there explicitly.
  3. description, not prompt, is what decides automatic delegation. An excellent prompt with a vague description = a subagent that never gets used.
  4. max_turns only counts turns with tool use, and by default there is no limit; same for max_budget_usd. A production design without both firewalls is a design with an open cost hole.

To coordinate dozens or hundreds of agents, conversational orchestration stops scaling: the official docs recommend moving orchestration to a script outside the context (the Workflow tool, TypeScript SDK ≥ v0.3.149).

6. Decomposition: Cutting Along Verification Seams

Decomposing isn't "splitting into pieces." It's splitting where you can verify. Practical rules the exam rewards:

  • Programmatic gates between steps. In prompt chaining, deterministic code that validates the output (schema, range, presence of a field, length) sits between step N and N+1. If the gate fails, you don't advance: you retry or escalate. A chain without gates is just one long call with more latency.
  • Isolate context in subagents. A subtask that produces a lot of noise (reading 40 files, exploring a repo) pollutes the main thread's context. A subagent returns only the distillation.
  • The boundary between model and deterministic code. Anything that can be decided with a reliable if, gets decided with an if. LLMs are for the ambiguous, not for what you already know how to compute.
  • Poka-yoke in tool design: make the interface error impossible. The documented canonical case: requiring absolute paths instead of relative ones eliminated an entire class of model errors on SWE-bench. Applied to the exam: if two tools can be confused, the fix is redesigning the interface, not writing a stricter prompt.
  • ACI (agent-computer interface). Anthropic asks you to invest in the agent-computer interface as much as you'd invest in HCI for humans: extremely clear tool descriptions (3-4 sentences minimum per tool), no functional overlap, no decision ambiguity, and real testing of how the model uses them.

7. Context Engineering in Architecture (It's Not a Prompting Topic)

Context is a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns — the phenomenon is called context rot. This is an architectural constraint, not a prompting tip: it determines whether your design needs subagents, compaction, or just-in-time retrieval.

  • Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, saved queries, links) and load the data at runtime, instead of pre-loading the entire corpus. This is Domain 1's counterpart to Domain 3's objective "progressive discovery vs. monolithic context."
  • Structured note-taking / agentic memory: persist notes outside the context window.
  • Compaction: when context approaches the limit, the system summarizes the old history. Documented trap that's critical for design: "compaction replaces old messages with a summary, so specific instructions from the start of the conversation may not be preserved." Persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md (re-injected on every request), not in the thread's first message. A long-running agent whose business rules live in the initial prompt will lose them.
  • Windows: Fable 5, Opus 4.8, and Sonnet 5 have 1M tokens by default, no beta header, at standard pricing. Haiku 4.5 is the exception: 200k. Fitting doesn't mean it's a good idea: 1M of dirty context performs worse than 50k of clean context.

8. The Feedback Loop: The Link the Exam Wants Missing

"input → processing → output → feedback loops" is written literally in the objective. An end-to-end design without a feedback loop is incomplete by definition, and the items exploit that. The four feedback channels a production architecture must have:

  1. Ground truth from the environment — the agent observes the real outcome of its action (tests that pass, the record that got created, the API that returned 200). Without this, an autonomous agent doesn't converge.
  2. Continuous evaluation — an eval set that runs against real or sampled traffic, not just in CI. Metrics before intuition.
  3. Human-in-the-loop — human review on irreversible or high-blast-radius actions, and as a source of labels for improvement.
  4. Observability and telemetry — usage (including cache_read_input_tokens and output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens), stop_reason, p50/p95 latency, request-id for tracing. Without this you can't diagnose anything in Domain 4.
# Esqueleto del loop de feedback: telemetría por request, no "logging genérico".
resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=2048, messages=msgs)

telemetry = {
    "request_id": resp._request_id,          # trazabilidad con soporte
    "stop_reason": resp.stop_reason,         # 'refusal' y 'max_tokens' son HTTP 200, no errores
    "input_tokens": resp.usage.input_tokens,
    "cache_read": resp.usage.cache_read_input_tokens,   # ¿el cache está pegando?
    "cache_write": resp.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens,
    "output_tokens": resp.usage.output_tokens,
    "thinking_tokens": resp.usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens,
}
emit(telemetry)

if resp.stop_reason == "refusal":
    route_to_fallback(msgs)      # rechazo por safety classifier: 200 con stop_reason='refusal'
elif resp.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    handle_truncation(resp)      # respuesta TRUNCADA, no completa

9. Business Value Pillars and SLAs: Translating to Business Language

The five pillars from the objective — efficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, performance SLAs — aren't decoration: they're the axis by which the item decides which optimization is correct.

PillarWhat it measuresTypical architectural lever
EfficiencyLess human work per unit of outputAutomate the repetitive step; HITL only on exceptions
TransformationDoing what was previously impossible, not the same thing fasterNew capabilities: analyzing 100% of calls instead of a 2% sample
ProductivityMore output per personClaude Code / assisted tooling (Domain 7)
Cost$ per unit of workRouting to a cheaper model, prompt caching (read = 0.1× of input), Batch API (−50%)
Performance SLAsp50/p95 latency, throughput, availabilityStreaming (TTFT), caching (reduces time-to-first-token), a faster model, NEVER Batch

The trade-off that generates the most items: Batch API vs. interactive SLA. The Batch API gives a 50% discount on input and output, most batches finish in under 1 hour, but the window is up to 24 hours and batches expire if they don't complete within 24h. It's the correct answer for evals, bulk enrichment, offline classification, asynchronous moderation. It's always the wrong answer when the prompt mentions a waiting user or an SLA measured in seconds. A candidate who proposes Batch for an interactive flow confuses "cheaper" with "better": they broke the requirement (decoder archetype D5).

Symmetrically: prompt caching attacks cost and latency at once (write 1.25× with a 5-min TTL, 2× with a 1-hour TTL; read 0.1×), without sacrificing context. That's why it's the answer when both metrics are asked for — it's the official sample 2 from the exam guide itself.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Northwind Insurance: Claims Triage (Routing, Not Agent)

Situation. Northwind receives 12,000 First Notice of Loss (FNOL) claims per day. 68% are low-complexity (simple collision, complete documentation). 22% require checking the policy. 10% are complex multi-party disputes. The team wants to cut the average triage time from 6 minutes to under 30 seconds, with a p95 SLA of 4 seconds response time. Budget: cost per claim cannot exceed $0.02.

Mediocre candidate. Designs an agentic system with orchestrator-workers: a lead agent that decomposes each claim, subagents for policy, customer history, fraud, and quoting, all on Opus 4.8. Argues that "this way the system adapts to any claim."

Competent candidate. Designs routing: a Haiku 4.5 classifier (~200 input tokens, structured output) that assigns one of three routes. Route 1 (68%) → Haiku 4.5 with the direct-resolution template. Route 2 (22%) → Sonnet 5 with policy retrieval. Route 3 (10%) → Sonnet 5 with more tools + mandatory human-in-the-loop before any payment decision. The system prompt and templates carry cache_control (stable prefix → read at 0.1×). Router confidence < 0.7 → human escalation, not model escalation.

Why. The categories are known in advance and distinct → that's the literal definition of routing, not orchestrator-workers (where the orchestrator decides subtasks at runtime). The 4 s p95 SLA kills any design that chains 5 sequential calls or uses the multi-agent pattern (15× tokens, coordination latency). And having the cheapest model handle the 68% of trivial traffic is what makes the $0.02 ceiling viable.

Example 2 — Halcyon Legal: Due Diligence on 3,400 Contracts (Orchestrator-Workers, Justified)

Situation. A law firm must run due diligence on 3,400 contracts from an acquisition. Each contract can have between 0 and 15 problematic clauses, of different types depending on whether it's an MSA, an NDA, an employment contract, or a lease. The team has 3 weeks. There's no per-document latency SLA: the deliverable is a report.

Mediocre candidate. Proposes a fixed 6-step prompt chain, identical for all 3,400 contracts, run synchronously. Or proposes turning an autonomous agent loose on the whole corpus.

Competent candidate. Two separate decisions:

  1. Pattern: orchestrator-workers per document, because the number and type of subtasks depends on the type of contract that arrives — exactly the criterion that distinguishes orchestrator-workers from parallelization. The orchestrator classifies the contract, decides which reviews apply, delegates to workers (change-of-control clause, indemnification, non-compete, termination), and synthesizes. Workers on Sonnet 5, lead on Opus 4.8.
  2. Execution: Message Batches API (−50% on input and output) because there's no real-time requirement and volume is high. Prompt caching on the review guide (a stable document) — batch and caching stack.

Why. This is the case where the multi-agent cost is justified: genuinely independent subtasks (one clause doesn't depend on another), high value per document, and real parallelization. And the absence of a latency SLA turns the Batch API into free money. The mediocre candidate's mistake isn't using chaining — it's using it when the prompt explicitly says the subtask composition varies by input.

Example 3 — Meridian Bank: Reconciliation Agent (The Agent That Shouldn't Exist)

Situation. A bank wants an agent to reconcile transactions between the banking core and the accounting ledger. The process is documented: 4 steps, always the same order, with deterministic matching rules (amount, date ±2 days, reference). Exceptions (~3%) require judgment.

Mediocre candidate. Builds an autonomous agent with access to both databases and a write tool on the ledger, arguing that "the agent learns the rules."

Competent candidate. 97% of the process carries no LLM at all: it's deterministic matching in SQL. The LLM only enters for the 3% of exceptions, as an augmented LLM with read-only tools, returning a reconciliation proposal that a human approves. Writing to the ledger is done by your code after approval, never by the model.

Why. Three principles at once. (a) Fixed, known steps = not an agent, and here not even an LLM: using an LLM for deterministic rules replaces precision with probability. (b) Least privilege: if the agent doesn't need to write, don't give it the write tool — remove the capability, don't monitor it. (c) HITL on the irreversible: a wrong ledger entry is expensive to reverse; the gate goes before the write, not in a log afterward. This scenario is the exam guide's official sample 1, transplanted into Domain 1.

Example 4 — Corvus Retail: Enriching 2.1M SKUs (the Pillar Decides the Architecture)

Situation. A retailer with 2.1M SKUs needs to generate descriptions, structured attributes, and SEO tags. The CFO wants minimum cost. The CTO wants them in the catalog "as soon as possible." Product wants an editor to be able to correct output and have the system learn.

Mediocre candidate. Chooses Opus 4.8 in synchronous mode with 2.1M calls in parallel "to finish fast," and discovers halfway through the 429s from rate limiting and a six-figure bill.

Competent candidate. Separates the pillars and negotiates them explicitly:

  • Cost trumps "as soon as possible," because there's no user waiting → Batch API (−50%), in batches of up to 100,000 requests / 256 MB, with a custom_id per SKU to correlate results (they arrive in any order).
  • Model: Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5) for the bulk, with a sample evaluated against Sonnet 5 to verify quality is sufficient. Choose the model by measured fit, not prestige.
  • Prompt caching on the style guide and attribute schema (stable prefix, read 0.1×) — stacks with the batch discount.
  • Feedback loop: every editor correction is saved as an (input, corrected output) pair and feeds the eval set and the few-shot examples.

Why. The item doesn't reward "knowing the Batch API exists": it rewards noticing that no SLA pillar is at stake, and therefore that optimizing latency would be spending money on a metric nobody cares about. And watch the fine print: the tokenizer of the newer models (Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, Fable 5) produces ~30% more tokens for the same text, so comparing cost by list price alone underestimates the real spend — you have to measure with count_tokens.

Example 5 — Vertex Health: Clinical Assistant Under a Retention Constraint

Situation. A clinical decision-support system. It requires long-horizon reasoning over extensive medical histories. The compliance team requires zero data retention (ZDR).

Mediocre candidate. Chooses Claude Fable 5 because it's the most capable model for long-horizon reasoning.

Competent candidate. Rules out Fable 5 from the start: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 require 30-day data retention and are NOT available under ZDR — an organization on ZDR gets a 400 on every request to Fable 5. The viable solution is Opus 4.8 (1M context, explicit thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}, effort: "xhigh" if the task justifies it) with mandatory HITL: the clinician decides, the model suggests and cites.

Why. The compliance constraint doesn't get traded against capability. The candidate who picks the best model without checking the prompt's regulatory constraint falls into archetype D5: they optimized a metric by breaking a requirement. And there's a cross-cutting design lesson here: governance constraints get resolved at the selection stage, not patched in afterward.

How the Exam Asks This

The verbs. This domain's blueprint uses translate, design, select, apply, align. None of them is list or define. Translated into real stems, expect: "Which architecture best satisfies…", "Which pattern should the architect select…", "The team wants X while maintaining Y. What should be done first?", "Which change most directly aligns the solution with the stated business value?". Note the superlative: best, most directly, first. It's a ranking exam, not true/false — more than one option can be technically defensible.

The canonical mold of a Domain 1 item. A business scenario with figures + an explicit constraint (SLA, budget, compliance, volume) + four architectures. One is too simple and breaks a requirement. One is correct. Two are over-engineering that sounds like senior experience: multi-agent where routing would have sufficed, an autonomous agent where the process is fixed, orchestrator-workers where the subtasks are known.

Distractors specific to this domain (mapped to the decoder):

  • D3 — The Model as Universal Solution, architecture edition. "Use a larger model so the agent handles all case types." Scaling the model never substitutes for choosing the right pattern. If the problem is that categories are distinct, the answer is routing, not Opus.
  • D4 — The Self-Incriminating Absolute. "Always use an agentic architecture for complex workflows," "Multi-agent systems are the standard for enterprise scale." In a blueprint that says trade-offs four times, any option that denies the trade-off is false.
  • D5 — The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. The most frequent form in Domain 1: proposing Batch API when there's an interactive SLA ("50% cheaper"), or removing the human verification step to lower latency on an irreversible action.
  • D6 — The Relabel With No Effect. "Split the single prompt into a five-step chain" when the five steps have no gates and change nothing: same tokens, more latency, zero accuracy gained. Simulate the option: which number moves?
  • D2 — The Cautious Mitigation That Doesn't Remove the Privilege. In architecture this shows up as "add an approval log for the agent's write actions" instead of "the agent proposes, your code writes." Legitimate exception: if the prompt says the business needs that write capability, then HITL goes from distractor to correct answer. The prompt decides.

The option that sounds good and fails. This domain's star: "Design a multi-agent system with an orchestrator and specialized subagents." It's the option a senior architect would write on a whiteboard and a panel would applaud. It fails when (a) subtasks are predefined → it was parallelization; (b) subtasks depend on each other or share context → multi-agent is counterproductive; (c) there's a latency SLA; (d) volume is high and margins are thin → 15× tokens. It only wins when the prompt makes clear the task composition isn't predictable from the input.

Lexical signal → pattern: "categories", "types of request", "route" → routing. "The same four checks every time" → parallelization (sectioning). "Depends on what kind of document arrives" → orchestrator-workers. "Clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement" → evaluator-optimizer. "Cannot predict how many steps" → autonomous agent. "One well-crafted call with retrieval" → augmented LLM.

Common Mistakes

  1. Calling a fixed-step pipeline an "agent." If the steps are in your code, it's a workflow, even if you use six LLMs. Correction: the criterion is who decides the next step, not how many models are involved.

  2. Confusing parallelization with orchestrator-workers. Correction: in parallelization, subtasks are predefined; in orchestrator-workers, the orchestrator determines them at runtime based on the input. That's the only boundary.

  3. Defaulting to multi-agent in "enterprise" scenarios. Correction: multi-agent costs ~15× the tokens of a chat and only pays off with independent subtasks and high value. If the subtasks share context or depend on each other, it's the wrong architecture.

  4. Recommending the Batch API in a flow with a waiting user. Correction: Batch = −50% but with a window of up to 24h (most finish in <1h, and it expires if it doesn't complete within 24h). It's for evals, backfills, bulk enrichment, asynchronous moderation. Never for an interactive SLA.

  5. Designing the architecture without a feedback loop. Correction: the official objective literally says "input → processing → output → feedback loops." A design without telemetry (usage, stop_reason, p95 latency), without evals in production, and without a human correction channel is incomplete by definition, not "phase 2."

  6. Putting persistent business rules in a long-running agent's first message. Correction: compaction replaces old messages with a summary and those instructions get lost. Persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md, which is re-injected on every request.

  7. Escalating to the big model when the router has low confidence. Correction: the ambiguity is in the input, not in the model's intelligence. Low confidence → human, not → Opus.

  8. Forgetting that the subagent doesn't inherit context from the parent. Correction: the only channel is the Agent tool's prompt string. File paths, prior findings, output format, and task boundaries go there, explicitly. And description — not prompt — is what makes Claude delegate.

  9. Designing an agentic system without cost/turn firewalls. Correction: max_turns (counts only turns with tool use) and max_budget_usd are unlimited by default in the Agent SDK. A production agent without both is an incident waiting its turn.

  10. Putting an LLM where deterministic code would have sufficed. Correction: if the rule can be written with a reliable if, write it with an if. The LLM is for the ambiguous. Replacing deterministic precision with probability is a downgrade, not a modernization.

  11. Choosing the model by prestige instead of by fit and constraint. Correction: Fable 5 is the most capable generally-available model, but it requires 30-day retention and doesn't work under ZDR (400 on every request). Haiku 4.5 is 200k/64k, not 1M. The prompt's constraint outranks the benchmark.

  12. Comparing costs by list price alone. Correction: the tokenizer of Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. You have to re-measure with count_tokens, not extrapolate from $/MTok.

  13. Treating the number of tools as free. Correction: every tool occupies context on every request, and tools adds a tool-use system prompt (290–675 tokens depending on model and tool_choice). More tools = more context, more decision ambiguity, more attack surface. Consolidate > accumulate.

  14. Presenting the architecture without naming the value pillar. Correction: every decision must be tied to efficiency / transformation / productivity / cost / performance SLA with a metric. "It's more scalable" is not a justification; "it lowers the cost per claim from $0.11 to $0.018 while keeping p95 < 4s" is.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat It Means
Augmented LLMBase building blockA model with retrieval, tools, and memory that generates its own queries and decides what to use.
WorkflowPredefined code pathA system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths — your code decides the next step.
AgentSelf-directing systemA system where the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool use; used when you can't predict the number of steps.
Prompt chainingFixed sequential stepsDecomposing into fixed sequential steps with programmatic gates between them; trades latency for accuracy.
RoutingClassify-and-dispatchClassifying the input and sending it to the specialized flow (and model); the cheapest path to attacking both cost and latency.
Parallelization (sectioning / voting)Predefined parallel subtasksPredefined subtasks run in parallel, or the same task run N times to gain confidence.
Orchestrator-workersRuntime decompositionA central LLM decomposes at runtime based on the input, delegates, and synthesizes.
Evaluator-optimizerGenerate-critique loopA runtime loop: one generates, another critiques, the result gets refined; requires clear evaluation criteria.
Multi-agent systemLead + parallel subagentsA lead agent plus specialized subagents in parallel; ~15× the tokens of a chat.
SubagentIsolated-context workerAn isolated context that returns only a distilled summary (~1,000–2,000 tokens) to the parent.
DecompositionSplitting at verification seamsBreaking the problem apart along verification seams, not into arbitrary chunks.
Feedback loopFourth architecture legThe fourth leg of the architecture: ground truth, evals, HITL, and observability.
Human-in-the-loop (HITL)Human gateA human gate before irreversible or high-blast-radius actions.
Business value pillarsThe five value axesEfficiency, transformation, productivity, cost, and performance SLA.
Performance SLAMeasurable commitmentA measurable commitment (p50/p95 latency, throughput, availability) that no cost optimization may break.
Context rotDiminishing returnsContext is a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns: more tokens ≠ a better answer.
Just-in-time retrievalLoad-on-demandKeeping lightweight identifiers and loading data at runtime, instead of preloading everything.
CompactionAuto-summarizationAutomatic summarization of old history as the context limit approaches; can erase initial instructions.
ACI (agent-computer interface)Tool-interface qualityThe quality of tool descriptions and schemas; designed and tested the way a human UI is.
Poka-yokeError-proofingDesigning the tool so the error is impossible (e.g., requiring absolute paths).
Blast radiusDamage scopeHow much damage a system action can do if it goes wrong; determines where HITL goes.

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you don't yet command the domain.

  1. I can give the official definition of workflow vs. agent and correctly classify a pipeline of 6 LLM calls in a fixed sequence.
  2. I can name the five workflow patterns, state each one's condition for use, and the trade-off it introduces.
  3. I can articulate in one sentence the difference between parallelization and orchestrator-workers without using the word "parallel."
  4. I can state the three conditions that justify an autonomous agent (unpredictable steps, clear toolset + sandbox + guardrails, ground-truth feedback) and reject it when one is missing.
  5. I can cite the relative cost of a multi-agent system (~15× a chat; agents ~4×) and name two scenarios where multi-agent is the wrong architecture.
  6. I can recite a subagent's delegation contract: objective, output format, tools/sources guidance, task boundaries.
  7. I know a subagent inherits nothing from the parent except the Agent tool's prompt, and that Agent must be in allowed_tools for delegation to happen.
  8. I can sketch an end-to-end architecture including the feedback loop with its four channels (ground truth, evals, HITL, observability).
  9. I can decide Batch API vs. synchronous from the prompt, and I know Batch gives −50% with a window of up to 24h (most finish <1h) and that it expires if it doesn't complete.
  10. I know when prompt caching is the correct answer to an item asking to lower cost and latency without sacrificing context (write 1.25×/2×, read 0.1×).
  11. I can choose a model by fit + constraint, not prestige: I know Haiku 4.5 is 200k/64k, that Fable 5 doesn't operate under ZDR, and that the new tokenizer produces ~30% more tokens.
  12. I can identify the cutoff point between LLM and deterministic code, and defend it to a stakeholder who wants "AI in the whole process."
  13. I can map any architectural decision to one of the five value pillars with a concrete metric and a figure.
  14. I know where to put the human-in-the-loop (before the irreversible) and why a log after the fact is not a substitute.
  15. I know why a long-running agent's persistent rules can't live in the thread's first message (compaction) and where they should live instead.
