domains.title: Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engineering
objectives: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
Optimize context windows and manage token usage
Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 13%

This domain measures a single thing with five faces: whether you know how to decide what goes into the context window, how it gets in, and which model processes it — and whether you can defend that decision with numbers. It doesn't measure whether you remember that few-shot exists. It measures whether, faced with a system that sends 8,000 static tokens on every request, you choose reordering + caching instead of truncating the policy or downgrading the model. The official sample from Section 8 assigned to this domain (Sample 2) is exactly that: two conflicting metrics (latency and cost), an untouchable requirement (the policy document), and four options, three of which optimize by breaking something.

The business decision this represents is the system's unit-cost and latency structure. In a real deployment, the difference between a cached prefix and an uncached one is an order of magnitude on the bill (cache read = 0.1x of base input) and up to an 85% latency reduction on long prompts. The difference between Opus 4.8 and Haiku 4.5 on a classification task is 5x on input and 5x on output — with the same quality if the task is simple. The architect who doesn't master this domain builds systems that work in the demo and bleed money in production. The exam knows this, which is why almost every item here is of the type "which optimization attacks both metrics without sacrificing a requirement?"

It's worth 13% (about 8 of the 63 items) — less than Integration (19%) or Solution Design (17%) — but its content bleeds into the other domains: diagnosing a prompt failure lives in Domain 4, the system-prompt guardrail lives in Domain 5, the progressive-vs-monolithic context strategy lives in Domain 3. Studying this domain poorly costs you points in three others.

Official Objectives

Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs

You're given a case with constraints (volume, latency, budget, data residency, ZDR, required quality) and you have to choose a model. The trap is always the extreme: "the cheapest one regardless of fit" or "the most capable one just in case." The correct answer names the trade-off.

Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails

You're asked to structure the prompt: role in the system parameter (not a role: "system" message), positively-framed instructions, XML tags to separate instructions/data/examples, explicit permission to say "I don't know," and structured output guaranteed by schema — not by pleading.

Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)

You're given a symptom (inconsistent format, poor reasoning, hallucination) and you have to choose the technique that attacks that symptom. 3–5 diverse examples for format; thinking/CoT for multi-step reasoning; citation grounding for hallucination over documents.

Optimize context windows and manage token usage

You're given a system that's running out of context or spending too much. You have to know what counts against the window (everything: system, tools, history, thinking, output), how to measure it before spending (count_tokens), and what to do when it overflows (compaction, just-in-time retrieval, subagents) — without cutting what the business needs.

Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)

The most technically dense objective in the domain. Prompt caching (where the breakpoint goes, how much writing vs. reading costs, what invalidates it), modular prompts, and Skills as on-demand loading (only the description sits in context until it's invoked).

Key Concepts

1. Model Selection — the Capability ↔ Latency ↔ Cost Axis

The family current as of July 2026 has four flagship models in the public API. Memorize the table, but above all memorize where the pattern breaks:

Claude Fable 5Claude Opus 4.8Claude Sonnet 5Claude Haiku 4.5
API IDclaude-fable-5claude-opus-4-8claude-sonnet-5claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
Official positioning"Next-generation intelligence for long-running agents""For complex agentic coding and enterprise work""The best combination of speed and intelligence""The fastest model with near-frontier intelligence"
Price (in/out per MTok)$10 / $50$5 / $25$3 / $15 (intro $2 / $10 through 31-Aug-2026)$1 / $5
Context window1M1M1M200k
Max output (Messages API)128k128k128k64k
ThinkingAdaptive, always onAdaptive (off unless requested)Adaptive on by defaultManual only (budget_tokens)
effortYes (up to xhigh)Yes (up to xhigh)Yes (up to xhigh)Does not support effort
Comparative latencySlowerModerateFastFastest

Facts that separate the ones who know from the ones who guess:

  • There is no "Claude 5" as a model. Generation 5 consists of Fable 5, Mythos 5, and Sonnet 5. Any exam option that says claude-5 is noise.
  • The 1M window is the default: no beta header, standard pricing. A 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token price as a 9k one. The old scheme ("1M context beta + premium rate") no longer applies. Haiku 4.5 is the exception: 200k / 64k.
  • New tokenizer (~30% more tokens for the same text) in Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, Fable 5, and Mythos 5. Comparing costs by $/MTok alone underestimates the real spend: you have to re-measure with count_tokens.
  • Fable 5 and Mythos 5 require 30-day data retention and are NOT available under zero data retention (ZDR). An organization on ZDR gets a 400 on every request to Fable 5. If the scenario says "financial services client with mandatory ZDR," Fable 5 is dead even though it's the most capable model.
  • Fable 5 carries safety classifiers that can decline requests. A refusal is HTTP 200 with stop_reason: "refusal", not an exception. Code that reads response.content[0].text without checking stop_reason breaks in production.
  • Non-default temperature, top_p, and top_k return 400 on Fable 5, Mythos 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7 — always, whether thinking is on or off. Style is steered with prompting, not sampling. (Exam corollary: the option "lower the temperature to reduce hallucinations" is doubly false at the high end.)
  • Model IDs without a date are still pinned snapshots, not evergreen pointers.

Programmatic discovery (the docs recommend this over hardcoding tables):

m = client.models.retrieve("claude-opus-4-8")
m.max_input_tokens   # ventana de contexto — OJO: no existe el campo `context_window`
m.max_tokens         # máximo de output
m.capabilities       # p. ej. m.capabilities["effort"]["max"]["supported"]

2. Thinking and effort — Reasoning Control

This is where candidates who learned Claude in 2025 stumble.

  • budget_tokens is dead at the high end. thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N} returns 400 on Fable 5, Mythos 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7. It survives, deprecated, on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6, and is the only path on Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 4.5 / Opus 4.5.
  • The replacement is output_config.effort — a GA parameter, no beta header, inside output_config, not at the root. Levels: max, xhigh, high (default), medium, low. effort: "high" ≡ omitting it.
  • effort is not a token budget: "Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget." The hard limit is max_tokens (which covers thinking + text). If you see stop_reason: "max_tokens", raise max_tokens or lower effort.
  • effort affects all tokens: text, tool calls, and thinking. It works with thinking off. Lower effort → fewer tool calls, more consolidated, less preamble.
  • Omitting thinking doesn't mean the same thing across models: Opus 4.8/4.7 run without thinking if you don't request it; Sonnet 5 runs with adaptive on by default; Fable 5 always thinks and rejects {type: "disabled"}.
  • thinking.display's default is "omitted" on Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and Opus 4.7: the thinking block arrives empty. It's billed the same. Omitting it reduces latency, not cost. The breakdown lives in usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens.
# Opus 4.8: hay que ENCENDER el thinking explícitamente
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=64000,                      # límite duro: thinking + texto
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},         # {"type": "enabled", ...} → 400
    output_config={"effort": "xhigh"},     # recomendación oficial para coding/agentic
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Refactor the payment reconciliation module."}],
)
print(response.usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens)  # tokens de razonamiento facturados

3. System Prompts, Templates, and Guardrails

  • The role goes in the top-level system parameter, not in a role: "system" message inside messages. It's the classic structural difference from the OpenAI API, and it's item material.
  • Positively-framed instructions. Instead of "Do not use markdown," "Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs." Say what to do, not what not to do.
  • Adding motivation improves compliance. Instead of NEVER use ellipses, "Your response will be read aloud by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses since the TTS engine will not know how to pronounce them." The docs close the loop: "Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation."
  • Don't shout. On newer models, CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when... triggers overtriggering. The docs recommend lowering the tone: "Use this tool when..."
  • XML tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs (<instructions>, <context>, <documents>, <example>). Consistent names, nested when there's a hierarchy. They also work to mark the output format.
  • The hard guardrail does NOT get written in prose: it gets written in the schema. Assistant prefill (sending a partial assistant message for Claude to continue) is dead: it returns 400 as of Claude 4.6. The official replacement is Structured Outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) or strict tool use (strict: true), both via constrained decoding, with no retries.
from pydantic import BaseModel

class TicketTriage(BaseModel):
    category: str
    severity: str
    requires_human_review: bool

response = client.messages.parse(          # helper del SDK: parse(), no create()
    model="claude-sonnet-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a support triage assistant for a fintech platform.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket_text}],
    output_format=TicketTriage,            # escribe output_config.format por debajo
)
triage = response.parsed_output

Nuances the exam might probe: Structured Outputs does not support recursive schemas, minimum/maximum, minLength/maxLength, additionalProperties != false, external $refs, or regex with lookahead/backreferences (minItems only accepts 0 or 1). And a refusal or a max_tokens cutoff can produce output that doesn't comply with the schema: the schema constrains decoding, it doesn't eliminate the terminal states.

To force tool use: tool_choice ∈ auto (default with tools), any, tool (requires name), none. Recommended combo: tool_choice: {"type":"any"} + strict: true. Critical restriction: with extended thinking, any and tool are not supported — only auto and none.

Anti-hallucination (content guardrail):

  1. Explicit permission to say "I don't know": "If you're unsure ... say 'I don't have enough information to confidently assess this.'" The docs call it the technique that "can drastically reduce false information."
  2. Citation grounding for documents >20k tokens: request verbatim extraction before the task (<quotes> → <info>), and prohibit claims without a citation.
  3. Best-of-N verification when there's no ground truth: run N times and compare; inconsistency is a signal of hallucination.

The docs add a disclaimer the exam can use as an absolute-statement distractor: these techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely." No option that promises total elimination is correct.

4. Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought

  • Zero-shot with a clear, specific instruction is the starting point. Official golden rule: "Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they'd be confused, Claude will be too."
  • Few-shot / multishot: the most reliable lever for format, tone, and structure. Recommended number: 3–5 examples. They must be relevant, diverse (covering edge cases; low-diversity examples teach unwanted patterns) and structured in <example> tags inside <examples>. "More examples is always better" is false.
  • Manual chain-of-thought (CoT) is today a fallback, for when thinking is turned off: <thinking> … <answer>. With thinking active, the docs prefer general instructions ("think thoroughly") over hand-written step-by-step plans. Gotcha: with extended thinking disabled, Opus 4.5 is especially sensitive to the word "think" — use "consider," "evaluate," "reason through" instead.
  • Self-check: "Before you finish, verify your answer against [test criteria]." Cheap and effective, especially for code and math.
  • Few-shot examples work with thinking: putting <thinking> inside the examples teaches the reasoning pattern the model will generalize.

5. Context Window Optimization and Token Usage

Everything counts against the window: system prompt, tool definitions, full history, tool results, images, documents, and the generated output including thinking tokens. With prompt caching, input is split into input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens, and all three count.

  • Overflow: if the input alone already exceeds the window → 400 invalid_request_error ("prompt is too long"). On 4.5+ models, if input + max_tokens exceeds the window, the request is accepted, and if generation hits the limit, it stops with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded". These are two distinct failures and the exam may ask you to distinguish them.
  • Measure before spending: POST /v1/messages/count_tokens (client.messages.count_tokens) returns {"input_tokens": N}. It's the right tool for model-routing decisions and for verifying the new tokenizer's impact.
  • Context rot: context is "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns." Filling 900k tokens because they fit isn't context engineering — it's the opposite. A large, noisy context degrades quality and cost.
  • Long context (>20k tokens): documents on top, query at the end. "Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30% in tests, especially with complex, multi-document inputs." Structure with <documents> / <document index="n"> / <source> / <document_content>.
  • Levers for reducing context without losing information: just-in-time retrieval (keep lightweight identifiers — paths, queries, links — and load at runtime), subagents (isolated context that returns a distilled summary of ~1,000–2,000 tokens), compaction / context editing (beta), and being selective with tool definitions (each one occupies context on every request).
  • The compaction trap: it replaces old messages with a summary, so instructions from the initial prompt can get lost. Persistent rules go in a mechanism that gets re-injected on every request (CLAUDE.md in Claude Code), not in the thread's first message.

6. Prompt Reuse: Caching, Modular Prompts, and Skills

Prompt caching is the domain's canonical answer (and the answer to the official Sample 2).

  • Syntax: "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"} on the last stable block of the prefix. TTL "5m" (default) or "1h".
  • Maximum of 4 explicit breakpoints. The prefix's hierarchical order is tools → system → messages.
  • Pricing (multipliers over base input): write 5m = 1.25x, write 1h = 2x, read = 0.1x. It pays for itself after one read with a 5m TTL; after two with a 1h TTL.
  • Minimum cacheable tokens: 512 (Fable 5 / Mythos 5), 1,024 (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6/4.5), 2,048 (Opus 4.7), 4,096 (Opus 4.6, Opus 4.5, Haiku 4.5). Below the minimum, it doesn't cache and no error is returned. You detect it because cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are both 0.
  • Verification: cache_creation_input_tokens = write (miss); cache_read_input_tokens = read (hit). And input_tokens is NOT the total: it's only the tokens after the last breakpoint. Total = cache_read + cache_creation + input_tokens.
  • Cascading invalidation tools → system → messages: changing a tool definition invalidates everything; changing tool_choice, adding/removing images, or changing thinking parameters invalidates only messages. Switching between thinking modes (adaptive ↔ enabled/disabled) breaks messages breakpoints but not system/tools ones.
  • Classic causes of a 0% hit rate: a breakpoint placed on variable content (timestamp, the user's question); JSON serialization that randomizes key order; a breakpoint more than 20 blocks (the lookback window) from the last cache write; concurrent requests fired before the first response starts.
  • The cache can't be cleared manually — it only expires via TTL. And it doesn't change the output: "The response you receive is identical to what you would get if prompt caching were not used."
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {"type": "text",
         "text": "You are a compliance assistant for ACME Bank."},
        {"type": "text",
         "text": POLICY_DOCUMENT,                       # ~8.000 tokens ESTÁTICOS
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},       # breakpoint en el último bloque estable
    ],
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": user_question}      # lo VARIABLE va después del prefijo
    ],
)
u = response.usage
assert u.cache_read_input_tokens > 0 or u.cache_creation_input_tokens > 0  # si ambos = 0, no cacheó

Modular prompts: split the prompt into blocks by volatility (constitution/role → policies → tools → examples → session context → user turn), ordered from most stable to most volatile. That's not aesthetics — it's what makes the prefix cacheable. A "modular" prompt that interleaves the user's name near the top is a non-cacheable prompt.

Skills (the open Agent Skills standard): knowledge and workflows on demand. The architectural key is progressive disclosure: only the skill's description lives permanently in context; the SKILL.md body enters the conversation when invoked. Compared to stuffing it all into the system prompt, a skill costs ~0 tokens until it's used.

  • description + when_to_use get truncated to 1,536 characters in the skills listing: the description is the selection mechanism, so it has to be precise and short.
  • disable-model-invocation: true → only the user can invoke it, and the description drops out of context (0 cost until invoked).
  • allowed-tools pre-approves, it doesn't restrict. To remove tools from the pool, use disallowed-tools.
  • Once invoked, the rendered SKILL.md stays in the conversation for the rest of the session (it isn't re-read). It's on-demand loading, not ephemeral loading.

Batch API as a reuse lever: 50% discount on input and output, for non-urgent workloads (mass evals, moderation, enrichment). It stacks with prompt caching (50% × 0.1x on reads). Official tip: inside a batch, use a 1h TTL, because a batch can take longer than 5 minutes.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — "Meridian Health": The Prefix Nobody Caches

Meridian Health runs a clinical coding assistant. Every request sends: (a) a 1,200-token system prompt, (b) the 22,000-token ICD coding guide, (c) the 6 tool definitions (2,800 tokens), (d) the patient's clinical note (~900 tokens). Volume: 40,000 requests/day on Opus 4.8. Current p95 latency: 9.4s.

Mediocre candidate: proposes moving the ICD guide to a vector store with RAG "to avoid sending 22k tokens." Sounds sophisticated. Introduces a new component, the risk of incomplete retrieval in a regulated domain, and a new source of confidently-wrong errors.

Competent candidate: the 26,000 tokens of (a)+(b)+(c) are identical on every request. Orders tools → system → messages, puts cache_control on the last static block (the ICD guide), and keeps the clinical note out of the prefix. Result: one 1.25x write, reads at 0.1x (26,000 × $0.50/MTok = $0.013 vs. $0.13 without caching), and a sharp drop in TTFT. Adds an observability alert: if cache_read_input_tokens drops to 0, something broke the prefix.

Why: the untouchable requirement is that the full guide be available (a regulated clinical domain). RAG sacrifices completeness to save tokens; caching sacrifices nothing. Preventive on cost, zero impact on quality.

Example 2 — "Volta Retail": The Big Model Nobody Needed

Volta classifies 2.4 million reviews per month into 12 categories + sentiment. They run Opus 4.8 with a 700-token prompt. Monthly input bill: growing. The VP of Engineering asks to "lower cost without losing accuracy."

Mediocre candidate: lowers effort to low on Opus 4.8 and declares victory. Saves reasoning tokens on a task that doesn't need reasoning — but keeps paying $5/$25 per MTok for a classifier.

Competent candidate: (1) builds a labeled eval set, (2) measures Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5) with strict tool use / enum against the same set, (3) sends the volume through the Batch API (−50%) because classification isn't interactive. If Haiku matches within the accepted margin, cost drops ~5x from the model and another 50% from batching. If it doesn't match, escalate to Sonnet 5 before Opus.

Why: the correct trade-off is measured, not guessed. And watch the detail: Haiku 4.5 doesn't support effort or adaptive thinking, and its cacheable minimum is 4,096 tokens — a 700-token prompt won't cache even if you mark it (no error). Whoever doesn't know this "turns on caching," sees no savings, and doesn't understand why.

Example 3 — "Nordwind Legal": The ZDR Client That Wants the Best Model

Nordwind requires zero data retention by contract with its clients. The team wants the most capable model for a long-horizon document review agent, and someone proposes Claude Fable 5.

Mediocre candidate: chooses Fable 5 because it's the most capable for long-horizon agents. Technically true. Operationally impossible.

Competent candidate: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are Covered Models: they require 30-day retention and aren't available under ZDR — an org on ZDR gets a 400 on every request. The viable option is Opus 4.8 (1M context, explicit adaptive thinking, effort: xhigh), documenting the capability trade-off against the compliance requirement. If the client also requires U.S. residency, inference_geo: "us" applies a 1.1x multiplier across all token categories: that belongs in the cost model, not a footnote.

Why: compliance doesn't get traded for capability. This item is answered with a binary fact, not an aesthetic judgment.

Example 4 — "Kestrel Ops": The JSON Output That Breaks Once in a Thousand

Kestrel's pipeline extracts 14 fields from invoices and inserts them into Postgres. The prompt ends with "Respond ONLY with valid JSON. Do not include any preamble," and the team prefills {" in the assistant turn. It fails ~0.1% of the time, and now, after migrating models, it fails 100% with a 400.

Mediocre candidate: adds a retry with a JSON-repair regex and bumps the model up to Opus for "better instruction following."

Competent candidate: identifies the exact cause — prefilling the final assistant turn returns 400 as of Claude 4.6 — and migrates to Structured Outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) or strict tool use. The guarantee shifts from "the model obeyed" to constrained decoding, with no retries. Adds handling for the two states that can still break the schema: stop_reason: "refusal" and a max_tokens cutoff.

Why: the structural fix eliminates the entire class of failure; the regex retry just watches for it. Preventive > compensatory. And "bigger model" is never a format guarantee.

Example 5 — "Atlas Support": The System Prompt That Ballooned to 40k Tokens

Atlas's support agent accumulated 18 months of rules in its system prompt: 40,000 tokens of policy across 9 products. Every conversation pays for those 40k, even though 92% of tickets touch only one product. Startup latency is bad, and the model starts "forgetting" instructions near the end.

Mediocre candidate: asks for a model with more context. It already has 1M. The problem isn't capacity, it's signal-to-noise (context rot).

Competent candidate: decomposes the monolith. The stable core (role, tone, escalation, security) stays in system and gets cached. The 9 product policies become Skills (on-demand loading: only the description lives in context; the body enters if the ticket requires it) or just-in-time retrieval with lightweight identifiers. Per-ticket context drops from 40k to ~6k, the stable prefix becomes cacheable, and the signal goes up.

Why: this is the "progressive discovery vs. monolithic context" objective seen from the prompting angle. The correct answer is not "more window": it's loading only what the task needs, when it needs it.

How the Exam Asks This

The verb gives away the level. This domain's stems use superlatives: "Which optimization most directly addresses both?", "Which change best reduces cost without…", "Which model is the most appropriate…". Never "which one is valid?" That means several options will be technically defensible and only one is optimal. Don't look for the true one: rank the true ones.

The five disguises you already know (from the decoder), applied to this domain:

  • D4 · The Self-Incriminating Absolute. "Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit," "always use the largest model," "never use few-shot." In a blueprint that says "trade-offs" four times, the option that denies the trade-off is false. Immediate discard.
  • D5 · The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. "Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens." Lowers cost and latency by destroying the policy that governs behavior. For every option, ask: what do I lose? If you lose something the prompt presented as a requirement, it's out.
  • D6 · The Relabel With No Effect. "Move the policy document into a few-shot example block." Impeccable blueprint vocabulary. Zero tokens saved, zero cacheable prefix, zero ms. Simulate the option numerically: if no number moves, the option does nothing.
  • D3 · The Model as Universal Solution. "Use a larger model that follows instructions more reliably" for a formatting, retrieval, or authorization problem. Model size is never a control for format, security, or architecture.
  • D8 · The Irrelevant Knob. "Lower the temperature," "reduce max_tokens," "increase the context window" with an invented causal chain. Demand a narrated event → mechanism → symptom chain in one sentence. Lethal bonus: on Fable 5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 4.8/4.7, touching temperature returns 400.

Lexical signals that flag this domain in 5 seconds: "same system prompt on every request," "static policy document," "8,000-token prefix," "token usage," "context window," "few-shot," "chain-of-thought," "prompt caching," "Skills," "modular prompts," "trade-offs between models," "latency and cost are both concerns."

The exam's favorite pattern: two goals, one answer. "Latency and cost are both concerns." Count the goals before choosing. The correct answer covers both without collateral damage; the distractors optimize one by breaking the other (truncating), or neither (relocating).

Model-selection items: always carry a hidden constraint — ZDR, data residency, interactive latency, volume, a >200k window, or an audit requirement. That constraint, not raw power, decides. Underline it before looking at the options.

Common Mistakes

  1. Putting cache_control on variable content (the user's question, a timestamp) → the prefix hash never matches → 0% hit rate, and you're paying 1.25x to write a cache that's never read. Correction: the breakpoint goes on the last stable block; the variable part goes after.
  2. Believing input_tokens is the total input. It's only what comes after the last breakpoint. Correction: total = cache_read + cache_creation + input_tokens.
  3. Marking cache_control on a prompt below the model's minimum (e.g., 700 tokens on Haiku 4.5, whose minimum is 4,096) → doesn't cache and returns no error. Correction: verify that cache_creation_input_tokens or cache_read_input_tokens is > 0.
  4. Using budget_tokens on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5 → 400. Correction: thinking: {type: "adaptive"} + output_config.effort.
  5. Believing effort is a token budget. It's a behavioral signal. Correction: the hard limit is max_tokens; if you get stop_reason: "max_tokens", raise max_tokens or lower effort.
  6. Believing display: "omitted" saves money. It saves latency; thinking is billed in full. Correction: to save on reasoning cost, lower effort or switch models.
  7. Assuming that omitting thinking disables reasoning across all models. On Sonnet 5, adaptive is on by default; on Fable 5 it can't be turned off; on Opus 4.8 it is off. Correction: check the default per model.
  8. Prefilling the assistant turn to force JSON → 400 as of Claude 4.6. Correction: Structured Outputs (output_config.format) or strict: true on the tool.
  9. Sending the role as a {"role": "system", ...} message inside messages. Correction: the top-level system parameter (which also accepts an array of blocks, a necessary condition for caching it).
  10. Putting the query on top and the documents below. Correction: documents on top, query at the end — up to +30% quality on multi-document inputs.
  11. Stuffing in 15 few-shot examples "just in case." Correction: 3–5, prioritizing diversity over quantity; homogeneous examples teach unwanted patterns.
  12. Lowering temperature to reduce hallucinations at the high end. Correction: non-default values of temperature/top_p/top_k return 400 on Fable 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, and 4.7; against hallucination, use citation grounding, permission to say "I don't know," and verification.
  13. Changing a tool definition believing it only invalidates the tools cache. The cascade is tools → system → messages: it invalidates everything. Correction: separate volatile tools from the cached prefix, or accept the write.
  14. Choosing Fable 5 in an organization with ZDR. → 400 on every request. Correction: Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Haiku 4.5.
  15. Comparing costs across generations by $/MTok alone. The tokenizer of Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. Correction: re-measure with count_tokens.
  16. Solving a latency/cost problem with prompt engineering. The docs themselves say it: "latency and cost can be sometimes more easily improved by selecting a different model." Correction: identify whether the problem is one of quality (prompt) or economics (model/caching/batch).

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat It Means

Prompt cachingPrefix reuseReuses an already-processed prefix: writing costs 1.25x (5m) or 2x (1h); reading costs 0.1x.
Cache breakpointCache markerThe cache_control mark on the last stable block; maximum 4 per request.
Cache hit / writeRead vs. writecache_read_input_tokens vs. cache_creation_input_tokens in usage.
TTL (time to live)Cache entry lifespanThe duration of the cache entry: "5m" (default, refreshes on use) or "1h" (write at 2x).
Context windowEverything the model seesEverything the model sees in a request: system + tools + history + thinking + output.
Context rotDiminishing returnsContext is a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns: more tokens ≠ a better answer.
Adaptive thinkingModel-decided reasoningthinking: {type: "adaptive"}: the model decides how much to think; replaces budget_tokens.
EffortBehavioral signaloutput_config.effort (low…max, default high): a behavioral signal, not a token budget.

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you don't yet command the domain.

  1. I can name the four current models with their API ID, price, window, max output, and thinking mode — and point out where Haiku 4.5 breaks the pattern.
  2. I know when a non-technical requirement (ZDR, data residency, audit) eliminates the most capable model, and I can justify it with the API's behavior (400 on Fable 5 under ZDR).
  3. I can explain why budget_tokens returns 400 on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5 and write the correct equivalent with thinking: {type:"adaptive"} + output_config.effort.
  4. I know effort is a behavioral signal and that the hard limit is max_tokens, and I know what to do when I see stop_reason: "max_tokens".
  5. I can place a correct cache_control in a real prompt, say what stays inside the prefix and what stays out, and verify in usage that there was a hit.
  6. I can calculate caching's break-even point: 1 read with a 5m TTL (write 1.25x), 2 reads with a 1h TTL (write 2x), read 0.1x.
  7. I can list at least four causes of a 0% cache hit rate (breakpoint on variable content, prompt below the model's minimum, JSON key order, the 20-block lookback, concurrency).
  8. I know the tools → system → messages invalidation cascade and which changes invalidate only messages.
  9. I can choose between few-shot, CoT/thinking, and citation grounding based on the described symptom, not the prompt's vocabulary.
  10. I know assistant prefill is dead (400) and I can migrate to Structured Outputs or strict tool use, including handling refusal and a max_tokens cutoff.
  11. I can explain why documents-on-top + query-at-the-end improves quality by up to 30% on long inputs.
  12. I know what counts against the context window (everything, including thinking) and I distinguish the 400 "prompt is too long" from stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded".
  13. I can argue for progressive context (Skills, just-in-time retrieval, subagents) over monolithic context, using the context-rot argument and not just cost.
  14. I know when the problem is not the prompt: latency and cost get fixed faster by switching models, caching, or batching than by rewriting instructions.
  15. Faced with an item with two goals ("latency and cost"), I verify that my option covers both without sacrificing any stated requirement — and I ruthlessly discard the one that "sounds good" but doesn't move any number.
