Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch)
Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 16%

This domain measures one single thing, said six different ways: whether you can know, with evidence, if your system works — and whether you can improve it without fooling yourself. It's the domain that separates the architect who believes their prompt improved from the one who proved it improved. Anthropic treats building with LLMs as empirical science: you define measurable success criteria BEFORE writing the prompt, you build an eval set that reflects the task's real distribution (edge cases included), you pick the cheapest grading method that does the job, and you iterate. An architect who can't instrument that cycle can't operate the system they designed.

The business decision this represents is twofold. First, the spend decision: latency and price are not secondary metrics — the official documentation lists them as first-class success criteria, alongside task fidelity and privacy preservation. Optimizing tokens, caching, and batching is the mechanism by which a Claude-based solution goes from pilot to production line with margin. Second, the risk decision: when the system fails in production (hallucinations, regression after an index change, a poorly chosen model), this is the domain that says where to look first. The exam reflects this: its only official Domain 4 sample item is not a definitions question — it's a causal diagnosis with control variables already frozen into the stem.

Official Objectives

The six verbatim task statements from the exam guide, with what they'll actually ask you underneath:

• Define evaluation metrics (accuracy, latency, cost, safety, security) Translate a vague goal ("quality responses") into Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and multidimensional criteria, knowing that latency and price are criteria, not side effects.

• Design evaluation datasets and test frameworks using mixed methodologies Build the suite: input prompt + golden answer + grading method; choose between code-based, LLM-based, and human depending on the nature of the criterion; include explicit edge cases; maintain a held-out test set.

• Conduct A/B testing and iterative improvements Compare two prompts/models/configurations without fooling yourself with noise: paired differences over the same questions, error bars, and regression detection when re-running the suite.

• Diagnose system issues (prompt failure, hallucinations, model mismatch) Given a symptom in production, locate the guilty component (prompt / retrieval / model / parser / tools) by reasoning about what changed and what was declared unchanged.

• Optimize token usage, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs Pick the right lever: prompt caching, the Batches API, model routing, effort, streaming, trimming tool definitions — without sacrificing a stated requirement.

• Monitor system performance using logging and observability tools Instrument production: usage per request, the Usage & Cost Admin API, OpenTelemetry (metrics and spans), and detect the failures that don't show up as an HTTP error.

Key Concepts

1. Success criteria — SMART and multidimensional

Official docs require Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant criteria. The canonical example of a bad criterion is "Safe outputs." The good one: "Less than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by our content filter." And the real criterion is almost never just one: "Most use cases will require multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria."

The official categories of criteria you should be able to recite and map to a case: task fidelity, consistency, relevance and coherence, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, price. The nuance that separates those who know: latency and price are on that list. They are not "infra considerations" — they are success criteria that get defined, measured, and gated like any other. An official multidimensional example: F1 ≥ 0.85; 99.5% non-toxic outputs; 90% of errors cause only inconvenience (not a serious error); 95% of responses under 200 ms.

Metrics named in the docs: task-specific (F1, BLEU, perplexity), generic (accuracy, precision, recall), operational (response time in ms, uptime in %). Methods: A/B testing against a baseline, user feedback with implicit measures (task completion rate), edge case analysis (% of edge cases handled without error), Likert scales, and expert rubrics.

2. Anatomy of an eval and its economics

An eval has four parts: (a) the input prompt — usually variables injected into a prompt template; (b) the evaluated model's output; (c) the golden answer — either the mandatory exact match, or an example of a perfect response that serves as a reference for the grader; (d) the score produced by the grading method.

The economic nuance decides the entire design: writing questions and golden answers is a fixed, one-time cost. Grading is a recurring cost every time you re-run the suite. That's why an eval is designed to make grading fast and cheap — not to make the questions pretty.

Three official design principles:

  1. Be task-specific — the eval reflects the task's real distribution, including edge cases: irrelevant or missing input, excessively long input, poor/harmful user input in chat, and ambiguous cases where even humans wouldn't reach consensus.
  2. Automate when possible — structure questions so they can be graded on their own (multiple choice, string match, code-graded, LLM-graded).
  3. Prioritize volume over quality — literally: "More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals." This principle is counterintuitive for a senior architect, which is exactly why it's exam material.

3. The grading hierarchy (the heart of the domain)

The docs rank the methods by "fastest, most reliable, most scalable":

MethodOfficial quoteWhen
Code-based"Fastest and most reliable, extremely scalable, but also lacks nuance for more complex judgements"Categorical or verifiable answer: exact match, string match, ROUGE-L, cosine similarity
LLM-based"Fast and flexible, scalable and suitable for complex judgement. Test to ensure reliability first then scale"Subjective or open-ended judgment: tone, empathy, coverage, presence of PHI
Human"Most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive. Avoid if possible"Discovering unknown edge cases — not for scoring at scale

The expensive mistake: believing humans are the operational gold standard. In the official hierarchy, humans are the last resort for scoring. But watch the complementary nuance, because the exam can attack from the other side: for agents, Anthropic documents that "People testing agents find edge cases that evals miss" — humans discover failure modes (hallucinations, source-selection bias), they don't score 10,000 rows.

Exact match — the cheapest grader there is:

def evaluate_exact_match(model_output: str, correct_answer: str) -> bool:
    return model_output.strip().lower() == correct_answer.lower()

accuracy = sum(
    evaluate_exact_match(output, tweet["sentiment"])
    for output, tweet in zip(outputs, tweets)
) / len(tweets)

Grading cost ≈ 0, deterministic, runs in CI on every commit. It's always the right answer when the task admits a canonical answer. The docs say it plainly: "Often all that lies between you and an automatable eval is clever design... Reformatting questions into multiple choice is a common tactic here."

4. LLM-as-judge: the three requirements the exam asks about literally

  1. Detailed, explicit rubrics. Official example: "The answer should always mention 'Acme Inc.' in the first sentence. If it does not, the answer is automatically graded as 'incorrect.'" A single success criterion may need several rubrics.
  2. Empirical or specific output. The judge emits correct/incorrect or a 1-5 scale. "Purely qualitative evaluations are hard to assess quickly and at scale."
  3. Reasoning first, then discarded. "Ask the LLM to think first before deciding an evaluation score, and then discard the reasoning."

And a fourth, in the comment of the official code: "Generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate than the model used to generate the evaluated output."

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def build_grader_prompt(answer: str, rubric: str) -> str:
    return f"""Grade this answer based on the rubric:
    <rubric>{rubric}</rubric>
    <answer>{answer}</answer>
    Think through your reasoning in <thinking> tags, then output 'correct' or 'incorrect' in <result> tags."""


def grade_completion(output: str, golden_answer: str) -> str:
    grader_response = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-4-8",          # juez ≠ generador
        max_tokens=2048,                  # espacio para el <thinking> que luego se tira
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": build_grader_prompt(output, golden_answer)}],
    ).content[0].text

    return "correct" if "<result>correct</result>" in grader_response.lower() else "incorrect"

The XML tags make parsing deterministic; the <thinking> raises judgment quality and is not saved. Note max_tokens=2048: if you starve the budget, the judge runs out of room to reason and the <result> never arrives.

Other graders from the official catalog, with their associated criterion: cosine similarity with embeddings (consistency under paraphrasing, code-based, spends no Claude tokens), ROUGE-L (relevance/coherence in summarization against a reference summary), LLM Likert 1-5 (tone and style), LLM binary classification (privacy preservation: does it contain PHI?, with a short-circuit to avoid calling the judge if the input never had PHI), LLM ordinal 1-5 (context utilization).

5. The Console's Evaluation tool

Lives in the prompt editor, Evaluate tab. Hard requirement: the prompt must include at least 1-2 dynamic variables with {{variable}} syntax — without them you can't create test sets. Test cases: manual '+ Add Row', 'Generate Test Case' (Claude generates rows; the generation logic is editable), or CSV import. Changing the prompt lets you re-run the entire suite against the new version — that's the basis of regression detection in Console. Features: side-by-side comparison, quality grading on a 5-point scale, prompt versioning.

What doesn't exist (don't invent it in an item): a programmatic "Evals API" product from Anthropic. The Evaluation tool lives in Console.

6. A/B testing done like an engineer, not a pundit — error bars

This is where the mediocre senior architect crashes. Running the suite twice and comparing averages is not an A/B test: it's noise with a table format. The five official recommendations from Anthropic's paper on eval statistics:

  1. Standard error of the mean (SEM) always alongside the score. 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM. Questions are conceived as a sample from a "question universe."
  2. Clustered standard errors if questions are grouped (several questions about the same passage, the same customer, the same document). Hard fact: clustered SEs can be more than 3× the naive SEs. Ignoring this makes you believe your measurement is three times more precise than it actually is.
  3. Within-question variance reduction: with chain-of-thought → resample several answers and average at the question level before the overall score.
  4. Paired-differences analysis: when comparing two models on the same list of questions, use a paired test instead of two independent samples. It eliminates the variance that comes from question difficulty. The correlation between frontier models runs 0.3 to 0.7 — that's free variance reduction you're throwing away if you don't use it.
  5. Power analysis: before running, decide how many questions are needed to detect the difference that matters to you (e.g., 3 percentage points) with the desired power.
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# scores por pregunta (0/1 o 0.0-1.0), MISMAS preguntas para A y B
a = np.array(scores_prompt_v1)
b = np.array(scores_prompt_v2)

diff = b - a                                   # paired differences
mean_diff = diff.mean()
sem = diff.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(diff))    # standard error de la DIFERENCIA
ci95 = (mean_diff - 1.96 * sem, mean_diff + 1.96 * sem)
t_stat, p_value = stats.ttest_rel(b, a)        # test pareado, no ttest_ind

print(f"delta={mean_diff:+.3f}  IC95%={ci95}  p={p_value:.4f}")
# Si el IC95% cruza 0, NO tienes evidencia de mejora. No promuevas el prompt.

Decision rule: if the difference's confidence interval crosses zero, no improvement has been demonstrated. And if the questions come grouped, the correct SEM is the one clustered by the unit of randomization, not this one.

7. Evals for agents and tool-using systems

Different rules, and the exam distinguishes them:

  • Start now, with small n. Anthropic launched its multi-agent system with ~20 representative queries. In early stages, changes have huge effects ("30% → 80% success rate"): a small n is enough to detect large changes. Waiting until you have "eval infrastructure at scale" is a way of never evaluating.
  • End-state evaluation, not turn-by-turn. When the agent can reach the same correct outcome via different paths, evaluate the final state. Scoring every turn penalizes valid routes.
  • Mandatory operational metrics, not optional telemetry: top-level accuracy, runtime for each tool call and for the task, total number of tool calls, total token consumption, tool errors. Diagnosis: redundant tool calls ⇒ review pagination parameters; frequent parameter errors ⇒ improve tool descriptions.
  • Single-call LLM-as-judge with a structured rubric over factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency; emits 0.0–1.0 scores plus a pass/fail grade. It was "most consistent and aligned with human judgements" and scaled to hundreds of outputs.
  • Held-out test set to avoid overfitting to the suite you're iterating on.
  • Realistic, multi-tool eval tasks. Strong task: "Customer ID 9182 reported that they were charged three times for a single purchase attempt. Find all relevant log entries and determine if any other customers were affected by the same issue." Weak task: "Schedule a meeting with jane@acme.corp next week."
  • Verifiers that are not too strict: rejecting valid alternative phrasings turns your eval into a false-negative generator.

Cost context that justifies all of the above: agents consume ~4× more tokens than a chat; multi-agent systems ~15×. An agent eval with no token metrics is an eval that's blind to the budget.

8. Diagnosis: the causal tree

The master principle (and the one that answers the official sample item): the cause lives in the variable that moved; the ones the stem declares unchanged are dead as hypotheses. A symptom → first place to look map:

SymptomFirst suspectWhy
Confident but incorrect after a document refresh, model and latency unchangedRetrieval/indexing: stale chunks, broken re-index, misaligned embeddingsIt's the only component the event touched
Output breaks the downstream parser (invalid JSON, missing fields)Structured outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) and/or strict: true on toolsConstrained decoding: "No more JSON.parse() errors", no retries
Response truncated mid-wordstop_reason: "max_tokens"max_tokens is a hard cutoff, not a summarizer
The agent "gets stuck halfway" with server toolsstop_reason: "pause_turn" — the server-tools loop hit its limit (default 10 iterations per request)The assistant's content is resent as-is to continue
The system "responds fine" but the user gets refusalsstop_reason: "refusal" — arrives as HTTP 200, not as an errorMonitoring based solely on error rate doesn't see it
The model invents facts about provided documentsExplicitly allow "I don't know"; extract literal quotes before the task (documents >20k tokens); verify with citations and retract unsourced claimsOfficial hallucination-reduction techniques
Hallucination with no ground truth to detect itBest-of-N verification: run the same prompt N times; inconsistencies suggest hallucination—

Two technical traps the exam can plant as a "plausible" distractor:

  • "Lower the temperature." In Claude Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, and Sonnet 5, temperature, top_p, and top_k with non-default values return 400. Style is directed through prompting, not sampling. Proposing to touch temperature on those models isn't just causally irrelevant: it's a call that doesn't even execute.
  • "Retry after a refusal." You need to reset the context or fall back to another model; resending the same thing produces another refusal.

And the disclaimer the docs state and an architect must repeat to the stakeholder: anti-hallucination techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely."

9. Cost, latency, and token optimization

The warning first, because it's an expected item: "It's always better to first engineer a prompt that works well without model or prompt constraints, and then try latency reduction strategies afterward. Trying to reduce latency prematurely might prevent you from discovering what top performance looks like." Optimizing before you have quality hides your performance ceiling.

Latency. Official definitions: baseline latency (total time to process the prompt and generate the response) and time to first token (TTFT) (time to the first token, relevant with streaming). Three strategies: (1) the right model — Claude Haiku 4.5 for speed-critical applications; (2) prompt and output length — max_tokens as a hard limit ("blunt" technique: cuts off mid-word), and asking for brevity in paragraphs/sentences, not exact word counts (the model counts tokens, not words); (3) streaming, which improves perceived responsiveness without changing total latency.

Prompt caching — the lever that solves latency and cost at once without sacrificing context:

OperationMultiplier over base input
Cache write 5 min1.25×
Cache write 1 hour2×
Cache read (either TTL)0.1×

Rules the exam attacks: maximum 4 explicit breakpoints; the prefix order is tools → system → messages; cache_control goes on the last STABLE block (never on content that changes per request); if the prefix doesn't reach the model's token minimum (512 on Fable 5; 1,024 on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5; 4,096 on Haiku 4.5), it is not cached and no error is returned. Changing the tool definitions invalidates EVERYTHING (the tools → system → messages cascade).

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[
        {"type": "text", "text": "You are an AI assistant analyzing legal documents."},
        {"type": "text",
         "text": "<policy document, 8,000 tokens>",
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},   # último bloque ESTABLE
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What are the key terms of this agreement?"}],  # variable, fuera del prefijo
)

u = response.usage
# Verificación obligatoria: si AMBOS son 0, no se cacheó nada (probable: bajo el mínimo del modelo)
print(u.cache_creation_input_tokens, u.cache_read_input_tokens, u.input_tokens)
total_input = u.cache_read_input_tokens + u.cache_creation_input_tokens + u.input_tokens

Exam nuance: input_tokens is NOT the total input — it's only the tokens after the last breakpoint. And cache_read_input_tokens doesn't count toward the ITPM limit on most models (documented exception: Claude Haiku 3.5): that's why caching raises effective throughput without touching the rate limit.

Message Batches API — the official route for running large eval suites: 50% discount on input and output, limit of 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch (whichever comes first), most finish in under 1 hour, maximum window 24 h (requests not processed expire and are not charged), results available 29 days from created_at. Results do not come back in order: they're paired by custom_id. Discounts stack with prompt caching (official tip: within a batch use a 1-hour TTL, because a batch can take longer than 5 minutes).

from anthropic.types.message_create_params import MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming
from anthropic.types.messages.batch_create_params import Request

batch = client.messages.batches.create(
    requests=[
        Request(
            custom_id=f"eval-{case['id']}",     # 1-64 chars, único en el batch
            params=MessageCreateParamsNonStreaming(
                model="claude-sonnet-5",
                max_tokens=1024,
                system=[{"type": "text",
                         "text": SYSTEM_PROMPT_AND_RUBRIC,          # prefijo IDÉNTICO en todos
                         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}],
                messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["input"]}],
            ),
        )
        for case in eval_cases
    ]
)
# Polling: la única condición de salida documentada es processing_status == "ended"

Estimate before spending: POST /v1/messages/count_tokens (client.messages.count_tokens(...)) returns {"input_tokens": N} — useful for model routing and rate-limit control before the call. Critical fact for comparing costs across generations: Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 use a new tokenizer that produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. Comparing list $/MTok across generations without re-counting tokens underestimates real spend.

Reasoning control: output_config.effort (low … max; high is the default, and setting it explicitly is equivalent to omitting it). effort is a behavior signal, not a token budget; the hard limit remains max_tokens. thinking.display: "omitted" reduces latency, not cost: the full thinking is billed (visible in usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens).

Agent context: every tool definition costs tokens on every request, and simply sending tools injects an additional system prompt (Opus 4.8: 290 tokens with auto/none, 410 with any/tool). Trimming unused tools is both a cost and an accuracy optimization. In Claude Code, tool responses are capped at 25,000 tokens by default.

10. Observability and logging

Three layers, and the exam asks about the one that isn't obvious:

  1. Per request — the usage object: input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens, output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens, server_tool_use. Log request_id (a header on every response) so you can report incidents.
  2. Aggregate — the Usage & Cost Admin API, which requires an Admin API key (sk-ant-admin01-..., not a regular API key): GET /v1/organizations/usage_report/messages (groupable by model, inference_geo, speed; bucket_width in 1m, 1h, 1d) and GET /v1/organizations/cost_report (daily granularity only, costs in USD as decimal strings). Not available for individual accounts.
  3. Traces — Claude Code and the Agent SDK export via OpenTelemetry. Metrics: claude_code.cost.usage (USD), claude_code.token.usage, claude_code.session.count, claude_code.active_time.total. Span hierarchy: claude_code.interaction (root per prompt) → claude_code.llm_request, claude_code.hook, claude_code.tool → and inside the latter, claude_code.tool.execution. Subagents nest under the parent's tool span. llm_request, tool.execution, and hook mark OTel status ERROR when they record a failure.

The non-obvious, exam-worthy point: there are failures that never show up in your error rate. A stop_reason: "refusal" is an HTTP 200. A max_tokens that truncated the response is an HTTP 200. A pause_turn is an HTTP 200. A 5xx/4xx dashboard will tell you everything is green while the system delivers garbage. stop_reason must be instrumented as a first-class dimension. And in production with agents, Anthropic adds: stateful error handling (resume from checkpoint, don't restart), full production tracing to diagnose failure patterns, rainbow deployments (gradual traffic shift so you don't break agents mid-flight), and high-level observability of decision patterns without inspecting conversation content.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Nordwind Bank: "Sonnet 5 performs the same as Opus 4.8, let's migrate"

Situation. A card-dispute classifier runs on Opus 4.8. The platform team wants to downgrade to Sonnet 5 to cut inference spend (~$18k/month). An engineer runs 40 test cases against both models: Opus scores 36/40 (90%), Sonnet 34/40 (85%). Reports: "5 points lower, within margin, and we save 60%. Let's migrate."

Mediocre candidate. Accepts the result. At most, proposes "run 40 more cases." Presents the comparison to the committee with two percentages and no error bars.

Competent candidate. Rejects the experiment by design, not by result. With n=40, the 5 pp difference is buried in noise: the SEM of a proportion at that n is around 5-6 pp, so the difference's confidence interval crosses zero with room to spare. Does three things: (1) power analysis — decides upfront that the tolerable degradation is 2 pp and calculates how many cases are needed to detect it; (2) paired differences over the same held-out set (both models see the same disputes, variance from case difficulty cancels out; correlation between frontier models is 0.3-0.7, which gives free variance reduction); (3) clustered standard errors, because the disputes come grouped by merchant and several rows share the same merchant — and clustered SEs can be >3× the naive ones. Runs the expanded suite via the Batches API (50% discount) with the system prompt cached at a 1h TTL.

Why. The exam rewards knowing that an experiment without error bars is not evidence. The correct answer isn't "use more data": it's "use the statistical design that eliminates the variance you don't care about and quantifies what's left."

Example 2 — Lexora Legal: confident hallucinations after an embeddings change

Situation. A RAG assistant over 240k contracts starts returning invented clauses in a confident tone. p95 latency identical, model version identical, prompt unchanged for 6 weeks. What did change: 3 days ago they migrated the index's embedding model "to improve recall."

Mediocre candidate. Diagnoses "model hallucination" and attacks the prompt: adds "don't make things up," bumps the model to Fable 5, and proposes lowering temperature.

Competent candidate. Marks the control variables (model, latency, and prompt declared unchanged) and goes to the only one that moved: the index. Concrete, falsifiable hypothesis: query embeddings are generated with the new model but the index still holds vectors from the old model (or was only partially re-indexed) ⇒ retrieval returns irrelevant chunks ⇒ the model generates with poor context and sounds confident because nothing in the context contradicts it. Verifies by measuring retrieval, not generation: retriever recall@k against a set of queries with known ground-truth chunks. As a permanent damage control measure, adds citation grounding (extract literal quotes before answering; if there's no quote, retract the claim) and explicitly allows "I don't have enough information."

Why. It's the shape of the official sample item. And note the mediocre candidate's double failure: temperature isn't just causally irrelevant — on Opus 4.8 / Sonnet 5 / Fable 5 a non-default value returns 400.

Example 3 — Helios Health: the eval suite costs more than production

Situation. A 12,000-test-case suite (clinical extraction) runs 3×/day in CI against Opus 4.8 on the synchronous Messages API, with an identical 9,000-token system prompt + rubric on every request. Grading is done by an LLM judge running on the same Opus 4.8. Eval bill: higher than production's. The CTO asks to "cut the suite to 2,000 cases."

Mediocre candidate. Cuts to 2,000 cases. Lowers cost and destroys the signal: the suite no longer covers the rare edge cases, which are exactly what made it useful.

Competent candidate. Rejects the cut — it violates the volume over quality principle — and attacks cost without touching coverage, stacking four levers: (1) Message Batches API: 50% off input and output, and the nightly suite doesn't need an immediate response; (2) prompt caching with a 1h TTL on the stable 9,000-token prefix (reads at 0.1×; 1h TTL because a batch can take more than 5 minutes), making sure the cache_control block is identical across every request in the batch; (3) move everything that admits a golden answer to code-based — structured field extraction gets graded with exact match at zero cost, leaving only the residual subjective judgment for the LLM judge; (4) for the judge that remains, use a different, cheaper model (Haiku 4.5), after verifying its reliability against a hand-graded sample before scaling it up.

Why. Each lever attacks a different part of the cost (when it runs, what repeats, who scores, with which model). The typical distractor ("cut the dataset") improves the requested metric by destroying a requirement — the D5 pattern from the decoder.

Example 4 — Meridian Retail: the agent that shines in the demo and fails in production

Situation. A customer-service agent with 9 tools (orders, inventory, returns, shipping…). In the team's 12 manual tests it works. In production, 22% of sessions end without resolution, token spend triples the budget, and nobody knows why.

Mediocre candidate. Asks to bump the model to Fable 5 and add more emphatic instructions to the system prompt ("CRITICAL: YOU MUST use the right tool").

Competent candidate. Builds a real agent eval. (1) Realistic, multi-tool tasks, with a verifiable answer, not "look up an order." (2) End-state evaluation: scores whether the order got resolved, not whether the agent followed the path the designer imagined. (3) Instruments the operational metrics: total tool calls, tokens, runtime per tool, and tool errors. The data speaks for itself: 34% of tool calls redundant against search_orders ⇒ pagination parameters are poorly described; spikes in tool errors on create_return ⇒ ambiguous parameter description. (4) Reads raw transcripts — "what agents omit in their feedback and responses can often be more important than what they include." (5) Maintains a held-out set to avoid overfitting while iterating with Claude over the transcripts.

Why. None of the real defects (pagination, tool descriptions, bloated tool responses) get fixed by a bigger model. It's the D3 archetype from the decoder: model capability doesn't substitute for architecture. And the item rewards knowing agents cost ~4× a chat (multi-agent, ~15×): the overspend isn't a bug, it's the price of an unmeasured design.

Example 5 — Aurora Insurance: "the system is green" while users complain

Situation. A claims-assistant dashboard: 0.03% error rate, p95 latency within SLA, 99.98% uptime. And yet, NPS is falling and support tickets say "the assistant cuts off mid-sentence" and "it tells me it can't help me."

Mediocre candidate. Concludes it's "user perception" or blames the UI. Proposes a survey.

Competent candidate. Knows that an LLM system's failures travel inside HTTP 200s. Instruments stop_reason as a first-class dimension and finds two invisible populations: responses with stop_reason: "max_tokens" (truncated mid-word — max_tokens was set low "to control cost") and responses with stop_reason: "refusal" (safety classifiers, which arrive as a successful 200 and, in Batches, even as a succeeded result). Neither shows up on a 4xx/5xx dashboard. Fix: raise max_tokens (doesn't penalize the OTPM rate limit, which is calculated on tokens actually generated) and, on the refusal path, reset context or fall back to another model — don't retry the same thing.

Why. It's the domain's classic observability item: "which monitoring change would first reveal the cause?". The correct option adds a dimension that isn't currently logged; the distractors add more granularity to metrics that are already green.

How the Exam Asks This

The verbs. This domain almost never asks "which is valid?" It asks with superlatives: "What is the most likely first place to investigate?" · "Which optimization most directly addresses both?" · "Which change best improves…?" · "Which metric should be defined first?" · "What is the most reliable way to determine whether the new prompt is an improvement?". The superlative is the signature of a ranking item: more than one option is technically defensible, and only one is optimal. Don't look for the single true answer — rank the true ones.

The three shapes of a Domain 4 item:

  1. Causal diagnosis. The stem hands you control variables ("latency and model version are unchanged", "the prompt has not changed", "only the index was rebuilt"). The rule: the cause lives where the change happened. Underline the unchanged items before looking at the options — it kills one or two distractors for free.
  2. Eval / measurement design. You're given a criterion ("empathetic responses," "no PHI," "faithful summaries") and asked for the grading method. The correct answer is the cheapest method that captures the criterion: code-based if there's a golden answer, LLM-based with a rubric if the judgment is subjective, human almost never for scoring.
  3. Optimization with two objectives. "Latency and cost are both concerns." The correct answer covers both without harming a requirement. Count the objectives before choosing.

The distractors this domain plants, with their decoder name:

  • D8 · The Irrelevant Knob. "The temperature setting is too low." / "Increase top_p." Names a real parameter with an inverted or nonexistent causal relationship. Aggravating factor in 2026: on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 those parameters return 400. Antidote: demand the full causal chain — event → mechanism → symptom. If you can't narrate it in one sentence, it's not the answer.
  • D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem. "The model weights have silently changed" when the stem said model version unchanged. Instant death.
  • D3 · The Model as Universal Solution. "Upgrade to a larger model." If the problem lives in retrieval, in the index, in tool descriptions, or in the parser, scaling the model is the LLM version of "buy more RAM."
  • D5 · The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. "Truncate the policy document." / "Reduce the eval set from 12,000 to 2,000 cases." Improves the requested metric by paying with something the scenario declared necessary. Always ask: what do I lose?
  • D6 · The Relabeling With No Effect. "Move the rubric into a few-shot block." / "Re-run the evaluation to confirm." Impeccable vocabulary, zero numbers moved. Simulate the option: how many tokens, ms, or USD change? If none, it does nothing. Watch out for "run it again": repeating a noisy measurement does not reduce the noise unless you change the statistical design.
  • D1 · The Wrong-Category Control. "Add more human reviewers to grade the outputs." Sounds responsible; contradicts the official hierarchy (human: "avoid if possible") and doesn't scale. Humans discover edge cases, they don't score 10,000 rows.
  • D4 · The Self-Incriminating Absolute. "Always use the same model as judge and generator." / "Human evaluation is always the gold standard." Any absolute in an exam whose blueprint says "trade-offs" four times is false.

Lexical signals that place you in this domain (load the frame in 5 seconds): metrics, eval dataset, golden answer, A/B test, hallucinations, confident but incorrect, regression after X, diagnose, cost-performance, token usage, latency, TTFT, logging, observability, monitoring.

Common Mistakes

  1. Believing "more quality per question" wins. The docs say the opposite: prioritize volume over quality. More questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading > fewer hand-graded questions. Fix: design to automate grading, then scale volume.
  2. Treating human grading as the operational gold standard. The official hierarchy is code-based → LLM-based → human, and it literally says of humans "slow and expensive. Avoid if possible." Fix: human for discovering edge cases; code and LLM for scoring at scale.
  3. LLM-as-judge with no rubric and no output format. A judge that returns prose doesn't scale or audit. Fix: explicit rubric + correct/incorrect or 1-5 output + prior reasoning that gets discarded.
  4. Using the same model as both judge and generator. Fix: "Generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate." And test the judge's reliability before scaling it.
  5. Reporting a score with no error bars. Without SEM you don't know if your +3 pp is signal or noise; with grouped questions, clustered SEs can be >3× the naive ones. Fix: SEM (clustered if applicable), 95% CI, and paired differences to compare two models on the same questions.
  6. Comparing models with two independent samples. Throws away the variance reduction that the 0.3-0.7 correlation between frontier models gives you for free. Fix: paired test over the same list of questions.
  7. Optimizing latency or cost before quality. "Trying to reduce latency prematurely might prevent you from discovering what top performance looks like." Fix: quality ceiling first, then constraints.
  8. Believing max_tokens "summarizes" the output. It's a hard cutoff: truncates mid-word and returns stop_reason: "max_tokens". Fix: for brevity, ask for limits in paragraphs/sentences; max_tokens is a safety cap, and raising it does not penalize the OTPM rate limit.
  9. Putting cache_control on variable content (the user's question, a timestamp). The prefix hash never matches ⇒ 0% hit rate. Fix: the breakpoint goes on the last stable block, verified with cache_read_input_tokens > 0.
  10. Monitoring only the HTTP error rate. refusal, max_tokens, pause_turn, and model_context_window_exceeded travel inside HTTP 200. Fix: instrument stop_reason as a first-class dimension.
  11. Evaluating agents turn-by-turn. Penalizes valid paths different from the one the designer imagined. Fix: end-state evaluation + operational metrics (tool calls, tokens, runtime, tool errors).
  12. Overfitting to the eval suite while iterating (especially if you feed the transcripts to Claude to optimize your tools). Fix: a held-out test set that stays untouched during iteration.
  13. Confusing latency with cost when reading thinking. thinking.display: "omitted" reduces latency, not cost: the full thinking tokens are billed (usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens). Fix: to lower reasoning cost, lower effort or switch models.
  14. Comparing costs across generations by $/MTok alone. Opus 4.7+, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5 use a tokenizer that produces ~30% more tokens for the same text. Fix: re-measure with count_tokens before promising savings.
  15. Blaming the model for invalid JSON. The documented fix is structured outputs (output_config.format with json_schema) and/or strict: true on tools — constrained decoding, no retries. It's not "more prompting."

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you don't yet own the domain.

  • I can turn "we want good answers" into a SMART, multidimensional success criterion, and I know that latency and price are criteria, not side effects.
  • I can name the four parts of an eval (input prompt, output, golden answer, score) and explain why grading is the cost you need to optimize.
  • I can recite the grading hierarchy (code-based → LLM-based → human) and explain why humans are told to "avoid if possible" for scoring but are irreplaceable for discovering edge cases.
  • I can write a correct LLM-as-judge: explicit rubric, empirical output (correct/incorrect or 1-5), prior reasoning that gets discarded, and judge model ≠ generator model.
  • I know how to pick the grader that fits each criterion: exact match, cosine similarity, ROUGE-L, Likert 1-5, binary classification (PHI/toxicity) with a short-circuit.
  • I know that the Console's Evaluation tool requires {{ }} variables and that Anthropic has no programmatic "Evals API."
  • I can design an A/B test that doesn't fool me: paired differences, SEM, clustered SEs when there's grouping, and power analysis before running.
  • Facing a production regression, I know how to underline the stem's control variables and look for the cause in the one variable that moved.
  • I can list the official anti-hallucination techniques (allowing "I don't know," literal quotes for documents >20k, citation verification, best-of-N) and I know they don't eliminate it entirely.
  • I know that refusal, max_tokens, and pause_turn arrive as HTTP 200 and that an error-rate dashboard doesn't see them.
  • I can stack the cost levers correctly: Batches (50%) + prompt caching (0.1× reads, 1h TTL in batches) + code-based grader + cheap judge model, without cutting the dataset.
  • I know where cache_control goes (last stable block), how many breakpoints exist (4), in what order the prefix is built (tools → system → messages), and how to verify the cache worked.
  • I know input_tokens is not the total input, and I know how to compute it: cache_read + cache_creation + input_tokens.
  • I know how to evaluate an agent: end-state instead of turn-by-turn, operational metrics (tool calls, tokens, runtime, tool errors), realistic multi-tool tasks, and a held-out set.
  • I can instrument production across three layers: per-request usage + the Usage & Cost Admin API (Admin key; cost report is daily only) + OpenTelemetry (claude_code.* metrics, interaction → llm_request / tool / hook spans).
