domains.title: Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Management
objectives: Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering
Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs
Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 14%

This is the domain the engineer looks at, thinks "this is politics, not architecture," and decides to skim on the plane. That's why they fail it. The exam doesn't measure it as charisma: it measures it as rigor — structured discovery, explicit articulation of trade-offs, written SLAs, decision records, documented handoff, monitoring and iteration loops. All of that is verifiable, and therefore testable with the same ranking logic as the other six domains. Nobody here asks whether you're likable with the client. They ask whether, faced with a vague request and a hard deadline, you know what gets produced before a single line of code is written; and whether, faced with a committee that demands you sign off on "99% accuracy," you know what can be promised about a non-deterministic system, and what can't.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. With 63 items and 14%, this domain contributes ≈ 9 items: the same weight as Governance (D5) and more than Models and Prompting (13% ≈ 8 items) — the domain that same engineer actually does study. That's twice Developer Productivity (7% ≈ 4 items). For the average candidate, nine items are more points than their entire preparation for this domain is worth, combined. And the exam guide flags it three times, in sections nobody reads carefully:

  • Section 2, among the seven capabilities the credential certifies: "Collaborate with cross-functional stakeholders and communicate architectural decisions effectively".
  • Section 3, on the target audience: "They are often involved in stakeholder engagement, advising clients or internal teams, and leading architectural decisions, including discussions of security, legal, and executive considerations."
  • Section 4, the MQC profile: "Experience delivering end-to-end systems from discovery through deployment and operationalization."

The full lifecycle is inside the definition of the minimally qualified candidate. It's not a soft appendix to the blueprint: it's the frame the other six domains live inside. And Section 7 closes with a verb nobody underlines: "Build and operate at least one end-to-end Claude solution." Building it isn't enough.

The correct answer in Domain 6 is almost always the same sentence: do the diligence, write it down, align explicitly, and only then proceed. The distractors are the four ways of skipping it: the confident shortcut (start building, we'll refine as we go), the false control (a meeting instead of a document; a promise instead of an SLO), the cosmetic fix (better slides, zero measurable criteria), and abandonment (cancel, renegotiate, tell them it can't be done). And the golden rule, the counterpart to D5's ("compliance is never traded for latency"):

Never promise what you can't measure. A number with no eval producing it and no alert watching it isn't a commitment: it's hope dressed up as a contract.

That's where the senior architect crashes — the one who genuinely knows how to cache, index, and sandbox. They sign off on "99% accuracy" in a meeting because the pilot came out at 98.3% with n=60.

Official Objectives

The five task statements from the blueprint, verbatim in English, with what they'll actually ask of you:

• Conduct structured discovery and requirement gathering

Turn a vague request ("we want a chatbot that answers well") into measurable success criteria, a quantified baseline, declared untouchable constraints, and verified availability of ground truth. Discovery doesn't end with a meeting: it ends with a document that lets you write "this is done when ___".

• Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs

Present the decision at the right altitude for each audience, with the trade-off in full — the lever, what it gains, what it costs, and the number — and put it in writing in a decision record with the rejected alternatives and their reasoning. Hiding the trade-off's cost to get the "yes" is the archetypal failure.

• Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)

Distinguish SLI / SLO / SLA; know what is promisable about a non-deterministic system (latency, availability, quality, cost) and what is not (bare "accuracy," "zero hallucinations," the provider's uptime copied straight into your contract); and turn a production signal into a spec change by classifying it before touching anything.

• Document architectures and provide implementation guidance

Produce the package that lets another team operate the system without you: an ADR, a runbook, executable evals, declarative config, versioned prompts and Skills, a dashboard with the agreed-upon SLIs, and guidance on what not to touch and why. The exit criterion isn't "gave the walkthrough": it's that an engineer who wasn't involved can reproduce, operate, and diagnose from the document.

• Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)

Know which mandatory artifact each phase produces and what its exit gate is. A phase whose output is "a meeting" didn't happen. And skipping a phase doesn't eliminate it: it defers it, at a higher cost.

Key Concepts

1. Structured Discovery: From Vague Request to Measurable Criterion

The stakeholder doesn't speak in criteria; they speak in wishes. "Have it answer well." "Make it accurate." None of those phrases can be built, tested, or delivered, because none of them can be falsified. Structured discovery turns the wish into something a test can contradict.

Anthropic treats building with LLMs as empirical science: success criteria get defined before you write the prompt, and they must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant. You need to be able to recite the canonical pair — ❌ "Safe outputs" vs. ✅ "Less than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by our content filter." The difference isn't vocabulary: the second one has a threshold, a denominator, and a measurement instrument.

And the real criterion is almost never a single one: "Most use cases will require multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria." The eight official categories:

task fidelity · consistency · relevance and coherence · tone and style · privacy preservation · context utilization · latency · price

The nuance that separates the ones who know: latency and price are on that list. They're not "infrastructure considerations" you deal with later — they are first-class success criteria defined in discovery, measured in evals, and gated like any other. That fact turns the SLA conversation into an architecture decision, not a political negotiation.

The official example of a multidimensional criterion: F1 ≥ 0.85 · 99.5% of outputs non-toxic · 90% of errors cause only inconvenience (not a severe error) · 95% of responses under 200 ms. Note the third clause: it models the cost of the error, not just its frequency. A system with 92% accuracy where 8% of failures are catastrophic is worse than one with 85% where 15% are mere annoyances. Discovery that doesn't ask about the blast radius didn't produce a criterion: it produced a number.

The discovery instrument — every axis, and the decision it unlocks:

Discovery questionDecision it unlocks
What problem, for whom, how many times a day?Pattern (workflow / agentic / augmented), model, budget (D1)
What's today's baseline, and how is it measured?Every ROI calculation and the acceptance criterion
What does "good" mean, as a number?The entire eval suite (D4)
Can the business produce ground truth for N cases?Whether an acceptance criterion exists — or whether there's no project
What shape does the data have, and what's the query pattern?Retrieval strategy — or none (D3)
What's untouchable? (regulation, residency, retention)Model, platform, eligible features (D5)
What latency is tolerated, and at what percentile?Synchronous vs. Batch, streaming, model size
What action is irreversible?Where the mandatory HITL goes (D5)
Who decides, who signs off, who operates afterward?The handoff package and the communication plan

The exit gate — it's the answer to an entire item:

Discovery ends when you can write "this is done when ___" in a way verifiable by an eval, a command, or a metric, and when the business has demonstrated it can produce ground truth. If you can't write it, that's the task — not building.

Corollary the exam loves: discovery sometimes erases the architecture. If the corpus turns out to be 180,000 tokens, the output isn't "design a better RAG": it's there is no RAG (< 200k tokens ≈ 500 pages → everything goes into the prompt with caching, D3). Discovery done well is the cheapest phase at which to kill a piece of infrastructure nobody needed.

2. The ADR, and How a Trade-off Gets Communicated

An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a short, dated document, immutable once accepted, with five sections: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences, status. It's not an Anthropic product — it's an industry convention, and the exam treats it as the standard vehicle for "communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs." Its reason for existing: the decision outlives the person, the project, and the context window. Six months later, when someone asks "why didn't we use Batch here?", the ADR answers without you.

# ADR-014 — Retrieval del corpus de protocolos clínicos
Estado: Aceptado · 2026-03-11 · Supersede: ADR-009 · Firman: Arquitectura, Clínica, Compliance

## Contexto
380 páginas ≈ 180.000 tokens; 40.000 consultas/mes. Intocables: BAA, org HIPAA-enabled,
PHI nunca en un JSON schema (ADR-007). SLO: completion p95 < 5 s.

## Decisión
Corpus completo en el prompt con `cache_control` (TTL 1 h). **No** se construye RAG.

## Alternativas consideradas
1. RAG con vector store + reranking. **Descartada:** 180k < umbral documentado de 200k tokens.
   Introduciría una tasa de fallo de retrieval que hoy NO existe (recall 100% por construcción),
   +6 semanas y una infraestructura que mantener.
2. Híbrido BM25 + vector sobre chunks. Descartada por lo mismo.

## Consecuencias
(+) Recall 100%; sin índice; implementación en días; cache read = 0.1× del input.
(−) Primer request del ciclo paga cache write 2× (TTL 1 h).
(−) **Disparador de revisión:** corpus > 400.000 tokens **o** requisito de cita por cláusula.

## Verificación
Eval `protocols_v3` (n=200, golden answers firmadas por Clínica); se re-corre en cada release.

Notice what it does that a deck doesn't: it names the rejected alternative and why, quantifies the negative consequence, and leaves a review trigger. An ADR without rejected alternatives isn't an ADR: it's a press release.

The canonical shape for communicating a trade-off has four pieces, none optional:

the lever · what it gains · what it costs · the number

"Prompt caching drops the prefix cost to 0.1× and reduces time-to-first-token, at the cost of 1.25× on the first write (5 min TTL) or 2× (1 h TTL)" is an argument. "It's more scalable" is not. Without a number and without a counterpart, you didn't communicate a trade-off: you communicated a preference.

The altitude principle. For a non-technical audience, you don't translate concepts: you translate consequences. The symmetric error is equally fatal: bringing them the tool's schema (too low) or "everything's going to be fine" (too high, and dishonest on top of it).

AudienceWhat the engineer says → what they need to hear
Executive / sponsor"p95 = 4 s" → "1 in 20 users will wait more than 4 s". "F1 = 0.85" → "out of every 100 cases, ~15 need human correction: the review team is sized for that". They get decision + consequence + number + what you need from them — never the tool's input_schema
Legal / compliance"Residency requirement" → "costs a 1.1× multiplier on every token, and it's non-negotiable". They get the per-feature eligibility matrix and its exceptions: ZDR doesn't cover Batches (29 d) or Covered Models; flagged content may be retained for up to 2 years; PHI never in a JSON schema; HITL + disclosure mandatory in high-risk (D5) — never "the model is safe"
SecurityThe controls and their class (preventive / detective / compensating), least privilege, filesystem and network sandbox — never a system-prompt policy sold as architecture
FinanceCost per unit with stated assumptions (cache hit rate, model mix) and actual spend via the Usage & Cost Admin API — never the total bill without the volume that produced it
Delivery teamADR + runbook + evals + config + dashboard + guidance on what not to touch — never a 40-slide deck
End userScope, limits, escalation path, and AI disclosure when applicable (in consumer chatbots, at the start of the session)

If the executive and the security team leave the room with incompatible versions of the same truth, that is the Domain 6 failure — even if the system works.

3. SLA, SLO, and SLI on a Non-Deterministic System

Vocabulary first, because the distractors live in the confusion:

TermWhat it isExample
SLI (Service Level Indicator)What you measure: an instrumented signalRate of stop_reason: "refusal"; TTFT p95; F1 on the held-out set
SLO (Service Level Objective)The internal target on that SLI, with a window"TTFT p95 < 1.2 s, measured weekly"
SLA (Service Level Agreement)The contractual commitment, with a consequence"TTFT p95 < 2 s; below that, X% credit on the invoice"

Confusing them produces the domain's most expensive mistake: signing an SLA with no SLI behind it. That's not a control — it's a promise disguised as a control (distractor D2, transplanted here).

Latency — promisable, but you have to say which one. There's no such thing as "the latency": there's TTFT (time to first token) and completion, and there are percentiles. An SLO that doesn't say which one, or at what percentile, is not an SLO. Two hard rules: streaming improves TTFT and perceived latency, not total time (promising "2 s" leaning on streaming, when completion takes 9 s, breaks the moment the user needs the last line); and no workload with an interactive SLA goes through Message Batches — a 50% discount, most finish in < 1 h, but the window runs up to 24 h and whatever doesn't complete expires. Proposing Batch with a user waiting is D5 in its purest form.

Availability — the one you sign is yours, not the provider's. This is what sinks the architect with classic-infra experience, who copies the provider's uptime straight into their contract. Your availability depends on what's on your side: rate limits (a 429 is your unavailability, caused by your tier and your traffic pattern — and remember that cache_read_input_tokens don't count toward ITPM in most models, so caching increases your effective throughput without touching the quota); retries with backoff and idempotency; a declared fallback (another model, another region via inference_geo, another platform: Claude API ↔ Bedrock ↔ Vertex); and a declared degraded mode — "it goes down" is not a degraded mode; "shows the data from the source system and offers human escalation" is.

Just like with FedRAMP in D5: the exam guide doesn't publish an Anthropic uptime number. Don't memorize it, don't invent it, and don't copy it into a contract. What's testable is that an availability SLO declares its external dependency and its failure behavior.

Quality — the domain's central trap. An LLM is non-deterministic: the API reference says so with no room for optimistic reading — even with temperature of 0.0, the results will not be fully deterministic — and on the newest models (Opus 4.7+) temperature isn't even adjustable (400). Inevitable consequence:

"Accuracy: 95%" is not an SLA. It's a number with no universe.

The only thing you can sign is a rate measured over a declared evaluation set, with its uncertainty and its re-measurement cadence:

❌ Not signed✅ Signed
"The system is 95% accurate.""≥ 0.92 F1 on the held-out set v2 (n=500), measured weekly, reported with SEM."
"It doesn't hallucinate.""0 claims about nonexistent transactions: each one arrives with the transaction ID (citations), and in the absence of data it answers 'I don't have that data'."
"It's unbiased.""Recommendation rate disaggregated by subgroup within the declared band, with an escalation procedure if the threshold is crossed."
"It responds fast.""TTFT p95 < 1.2 s with streaming; completion p95 < 6 s. No step uses Batch."

The five reasons bare "accuracy" is a trap — any one of these is an item on its own:

  1. No denominator. Over what distribution? The pilot's distribution is not production's: the demo used cherry-picked inputs, production brings the tail.
  2. No error bars. With n=60 you don't have a measurement, you have an anecdote. The evals statistical guidance requires SEM alongside the score (95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM); and with clustered questions (several from the same client or document) clustered standard errors can be more than 3× the naive ones — your measurement is three times less precise than the committee thinks.
  3. No disaggregation. A 92% overall can hide a 61% in one subgroup (D5).
  4. No cost of error. The official criterion models it: "90% of errors only cause inconvenience."
  5. It expires. The index changes, the corpus refreshes, the model gets deprecated, traffic drifts. Every quality SLA carries a measurement date and a re-measurement cadence, or it's a historical number presented as a future promise.

And the sentence you need to be able to say out loud, backed by the docs: anti-hallucination techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely." You never promise zero hallucination. You promise a measured rate + a detection mechanism (citations, "I don't know" permitted) + a human escalation path.

Cost — promised per unit of work. The total bill depends on volume, and volume belongs to the business. You sign cost per ticket / claim / document, with explicit assumptions (cache hit rate, model mix) and with the compliance cost built into the model: inference_geo: "us" applies a 1.1× multiplier across every token category. That 10% gets declared in discovery, not discovered on the first invoice.

The artifact. An SLO is written down (it's not an Anthropic API — it's the specification backing the number you sign):

# slo/asistente-consultas.yaml — el contrato, en un archivo que un pipeline puede leer
- id: latencia_ttft
  sli: p95(time_to_first_token)      # medido en el cliente, no en el servidor
  objetivo: "< 1.2 s"
  ventana: "rolling 7d"

- id: calidad_tarea
  sli: "F1 sobre held-out set v2 (n=500)"
  objetivo: ">= 0.92"
  medicion: "suite de evals en CI; juez != generador; SEM reportado; cadencia semanal"
  al_cruzar_umbral: "bloquea release; abre revisión de spec"

- id: rechazos                        # el SLI que casi nadie instrumenta
  sli: "tasa de stop_reason == 'refusal'"
  objetivo: "< 0.5%"
  nota: "llega como HTTP 200 — INVISIBLE en un dashboard de error rate"

- id: costo_unitario
  sli: "USD por consulta (p50)"
  objetivo: "<= 0.018"
  supuestos: ["cache hit rate >= 0.8", "mezcla 70% Haiku 4.5 / 30% Sonnet 5"]

The rule that closes the section: every number you sign must have an eval producing it and an alert watching it behind it. An SLA without an SLI is a promise, and a promise is not a control.

4. Expectations and Evaluation-Backed Claims

The demo → production gap. The demo was done with inputs you picked yourself; production brings the tail of the distribution: the empty input, the 400-page one, the hostile user, the case where not even two humans would agree. A system that shines in the demo and fails in production didn't change: the input distribution changed.

The three expectations you reset at the start, in writing, or they haunt the whole project:

  1. The system is not deterministic. The same question can produce two different answers, and neither has to be wrong. If the business needs byte-for-byte reproducibility, it doesn't need an LLM: it needs a deterministic rule in code (a D1 decision).
  2. Quality isn't declared: it's measured — against a set the business helps build. Without ground truth there's no acceptance criterion; without an acceptance criterion there's no delivery, there's an argument.
  3. The system degrades on its own. The corpus changes, the model gets deprecated, traffic drifts. Without periodic re-evaluation, the number you signed expires silently.

Evaluation-backed claims: the domain's communication rule. Every capability claim travels with (a) the method, (b) the n, (c) the date, (d) the uncertainty. And with a distinction the exam rewards: verified (and by what method) ≠ believed (and for what reason). Saying "it improved" after running the suite and seeing the number is verified. Saying it because the prompt "looks better" is believed — and presenting it as the former is lying even if you turn out to be right. The evidence hierarchy decides which verb you get to use:

EvidencePermitted verb
Real behavior observed end-to-end in production"It's doing X"
New eval that failed before and passes now"We verified that X"
Existing suite in green"We detected no regression"
The code compiles / the demo went well— (not evidence of quality)
"I reviewed it and it looks good""I believe X"

The human is an instrument of discovery, not of scoring. The grading hierarchy (D4) puts them last for scoring at scale ("slow and expensive. Avoid if possible"), but Anthropic documents the opposite for finding failures: "People testing agents find edge cases that evals miss." The citable case: in its own multi-agent system, Anthropic discovered a source-selection bias (the agent preferred SEO-optimized content over academic sources) through exploratory human testing — the automated suite didn't see it. For Domain 6: exploratory testing is a lifecycle phase, not a luxury, and its output is new cases for the suite, not a score.

5. The Five Phases and the Artifact Each One MUST Produce

The objective literally says "discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration." Five phases, five artifacts, five gates. If you memorize a single thing from this chapter, make it this table:

PhaseMandatory artifactExit gate
DiscoverySuccess criteria document (SMART, multidimensional) + baseline + untouchable constraints + data inventoryYou can write "this is done when ___" and the business can produce ground truth
DesignADR + end-to-end diagram (input → processing → output → feedback loop) + evals plan + risk register (D5)Every decision has a rejected alternative + reason; the feedback loop exists in the diagram
HandoffHandoff package: runbook, implementation guidance, executable evals, declarative config, versioned prompts/Skills, dashboard, on-callAn engineer who wasn't involved can reproduce, operate, and diagnose from the document
MonitoringDashboard with the agreed-upon SLIs + alerts + review cadenceThe dashboard's SLIs are exactly the SLA's, and include the ones that aren't HTTP errors
IterationSpec change record: updated evals + new ADR (or supersede) + change communicationNo improvement ships without running the suite; if the commitment changed, the SLO was renegotiated in writing

Three exam rules about this table:

  1. A phase whose output is "a meeting" didn't happen. The artifact is written and verifiable, or the phase got skipped. That's the edge that cuts through the false control distractor.
  2. Skipping a phase doesn't eliminate it: it defers it. The discovery you didn't do at the start, you'll do in production, with real users, with no acceptance criterion, and with the budget spent.
  3. It's a loop, not a line. Monitoring → Iteration → back to Discovery when a signal reveals a criterion that was never defined. That's the key to a classic item: "the bot is correct but sounds cold" → the tone and style criterion was never defined → it's not a prompt bug: it's a discovery gap.

6. Handoff: Documentation That Executes

Here's what makes this domain specific to this platform and not a generic PMO chapter: in a system built with Claude, a large part of the documentation is the system. The highest-leverage handoff artifact isn't a PDF: it's a file the agent loads and executes.

ArtifactWhy it's the right handoff
CLAUDE.mdPersistent rules; gets re-injected on every request. The only place a rule survives compaction
Agent Skill (SKILL.md)Progressive disclosure: only the name and description live in context until invoked. A runbook for the human and a capability for the agent, in the same file
Eval suiteThe executable specification. Without it the receiving team can't detect regression or re-qualify a new model: you delivered an opinion
Declarative configallowedTools, permissionMode, deny rules, sandbox, hooks: control lives in code, not in the verbal agreement made at handover (D5)
Versioned promptsA prompt with no version has no rollback
ADRsKeeps the receiving team from "improving" the system by undoing a constraint that existed for a reason

The compaction trap, which is exactly a handoff item: compaction replaces old messages with a summary, so instructions placed in the thread's first message may not survive. A long-running agent whose business rules live in the initial turn loses them silently. They belong in CLAUDE.md (which gets re-injected) or in a Skill.

The runbook written as a Skill is the pattern this domain rewards:

---
name: diagnose-inbox-agent
description: Diagnostica al agente resumidor de bandeja cuando "deja de resumir correos".
  Úsalo ante caída del volumen de resúmenes, quejas de operaciones o alerta de refusals.
---
# Runbook — El agente dejó de resumir

## 0. Lo que NO es
No es "el modelo se puso tonto". El dashboard de error rate está en verde **por diseño**:
los cuatro fallos probables llegan como **HTTP 200**.

## 1. Clasifica (en este orden)
1. `stop_reason == "refusal"` → el clasificador de safety declinó. **Resetea el contexto** o
   haz fallback; reenviar el mismo prompt produce más refusals.
2. `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` → la respuesta se **truncó**. No es un rechazo.
3. `tool_result` con `is_error: true` → falló la tool, no el modelo. Revisa el ERP.
4. `stop_reason == "pause_turn"` → el loop de server tools llegó al límite.
   **Reenvía el contenido del assistant tal cual.** No es un error.

## 2. Escalamiento
SLO de rechazos < 0.5% incumplido durante 1 h → on-call de Plataforma + aviso a Operaciones.

Implementation guidance: what the receiving team needs and nobody writes. It's not "how it works" — it's what not to touch and why: what invalidates the cache (changing the tool definitions invalidates the entire prefix — tools → system → messages; the developer who "reorders the tools so they read better" just doubled the bill), where the breakpoint goes (last stable block; four max), how to roll back a prompt, a Skill, and a model version, and how to run the suite and what a failure means (blocks the release; you don't "fix the test").

The model ID is a dependency with an expiration date. Anthropic publishes a model deprecation policy with retirement dates. Don't memorize the notice window, and don't invent it — that's not what gets tested. What is architecture: dated snapshots are stable, while aliases point to the most recent snapshot and can shift under your feet; in production, you pin the snapshot, so a migration is a planned event and not an unexplained regression on the dashboard. And the handoff includes the re-qualification procedure: run the eval suite against the candidate model, compare with paired differences on the same questions (not two independent samples), and apply the ADR's acceptance criterion. Without a suite, migrating models is a leap of faith.

And the rollout. An atomic deploy kills agents mid-flight: a long-running agentic session doesn't survive having its code swapped out from under it. The practices Anthropic documents are rainbow deployments (gradual traffic shift, versions coexisting) and stateful error handling (resuming from a checkpoint, not restarting the whole agent). These get agreed upon with whoever's going to operate the system: they're handoff decisions, not infrastructure ones.

7. Feedback Loops: From Production Signal to Spec Change

"Manage stakeholder feedback loops" doesn't mean "listen to the user." It means classifying the signal before touching anything. A team that turns every complaint into a prompt or model change is doing prompt engineering by rumor — and that behavior is, literally, a distractor.

signal → triage → cause classification → decision → artifact

A complaint isn't a bug until it's classified:

Production signalCorrect classificationWhere it goes
"It cites coverage that no longer exists" after a document refreshRetrieval/indexing bug (D3) — model and latency didn't changeIndex fix + new case in the suite
"It doesn't answer half the time," with the dashboard greenMissing SLI, not a model incident: refusal / max_tokens / is_error arrive as HTTP 200Instrument first, diagnose after
"It's correct but sounds cold"Discovery gap: the tone and style criterion was never definedGo back to discovery — not blindly tuning the prompt
"It went over budget"Optimization (D4): usage, cache hit rate, model mixOptimize and renegotiate the cost SLO if volume changed
"Now we also want it to draft the response"Scope change, not a bugBacklog, with its own discovery
"A lawyer found a case where it invents a clause"New failure mode, found by a humanNew case in the suite + assess whether it changes the quality SLA

The rule the exam rewards and almost nobody applies:

A production fix that doesn't update the eval suite isn't a fix: it's a patch that's going to break again. Every finding ends up as a new case in the evaluation set — and, if it changes the commitment, as a revision of the success criterion and the SLA.

The four sources of signal: ground truth from the environment (the record got created, the API returned 200); continuous evals against real or sampled traffic, not just in CI; human — HITL is control (D5) and a source of labels (D4) at the same time: every reviewer correction is a free (input, correct output) pair; and telemetry (usage, stop_reason, p50/p95, request-id, OTel spans, tool error rate, cache hit rate), plus the Usage & Cost Admin API for finance.

Prefer implicit measures. A survey tells you what people remember; telemetry tells you what they did: task completion rate, draft edit rate (how much does the human rewrite what the model proposed?), human escalation rate, abandonment rate. Draft edit rate is probably the best quality SLI that exists in a human-in-the-loop system — and it's free.

The loop runs on a clock. An SLO with no periodic review expires; a suite that doesn't get re-run doesn't detect regression. And a change in expectation gets communicated before the stakeholder discovers it on their own: the worst way to manage an expectation is for someone else to discover it first.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Meridian Health: "We Want an Assistant That Answers Well"

Situation. Meridian Health already runs a triage assistant on the Claude API (BAA signed, HIPAA-enabled org, 40,000 queries/month). The VP of Clinical Operations requests a second system: "an assistant that answers nurses' questions about protocols. It has to be accurate. I need a demo for the board in three weeks."

Mediocre candidate. Starts building: Opus 4.8 "because it's the best," RAG with a vector store and reranking, a demo with 10 questions he picked himself. The board applauds and the project kicks off with an implicit promise of "95% accuracy" that nobody wrote down and nobody can measure. When a nurse reports a wrong answer, there will be no way to know whether the system is right or wrong: there was never an acceptance criterion.

Competent candidate. Doesn't write a line of code until discovery produces five things: (1) Baseline — today they call the on-call physician, median 7 minutes, and 30% of calls are about 12 protocols; that's the number ROI gets measured against, and nobody had it. (2) Ground truth — can Clinical sign off on correct answers for 200 questions? Yes, in two weeks; if they'd said no, there's no project, there's a demo. (3) A SMART, multidimensional criterion, not "accurate": task fidelity (F1 on the 200-question set), privacy preservation (0 patient identifiers in a JSON schema — D5's constraint, which here is a success criterion, not a footnote), latency (completion p95), and price (USD per query). (4) Untouchable constraints — PHI never in enum, const, pattern, or property names (schemas get cached separately for up to 24 h and don't receive PHI protections); and the nail the VP didn't see coming: clinical advice to a professional is a High-Risk Use Case → HITL + disclosure mandatory, which changes the product (the system suggests and cites; the nurse decides). (5) The done sentence: "Done when it reaches F1 ≥ 0.88 on the clinical set v1 (n=200), with p95 < 5 s, 0 PHI in the schema, and visible disclosure."

And then what the exam wants you to see happens: discovery changed the architecture before it got built. The corpus is 380 pages ≈ 180,000 tokens, below the 200k (~500-page) threshold. There is no RAG: the entire corpus goes into the prompt with cache_control, 100% recall by construction, implemented in days. The vector store, the reranking, and the six weeks disappear. And the hard conversation, which is the one that's actually being tested: "I can't promise you accuracy. I can promise you a measured rate on a set you sign off on, re-measured on every release, and an escalation path for what the system doesn't know. What I do guarantee is that no answer will arrive without its source."

Why. "Start building" is the confident shortcut: it gains three weeks and destroys the acceptance criterion — the D5 archetype, where what gets destroyed is the very possibility of knowing whether the project worked.

Example 2 — Aurora Bank: The Committee That Wants to Sign "99% Accuracy"

Situation. Aurora Bank already runs its treasury agent with HITL on irreversible transfers. Now it wants a customer query assistant. The risk committee wants three numbers written into the contract: "99% accuracy, response under 2 seconds, 99.9% availability."

Mediocre candidate. Signs it. The pilot (n=60) came out at 98.3%, so 99% "looks reachable with a bit of tuning." Copies the 99.9% straight from their cloud provider's contract. And promises the 2 seconds because with streaming the user sees text almost immediately. Signed three things they can't measure, don't control, and aren't true.

Competent candidate. Breaks down the three figures and comes back with a signable commitment, more useful than the one they were asked for:

  • Latency. "Under 2 seconds" isn't an SLO until it says which one and at what percentile. Commits to TTFT p95 < 1.2 s (with streaming) and completion p95 < 6 s — "if your customer needs to read the last line, they're waiting on completion, not the first token" — and declares the negative dependency: no step goes through Message Batches (window of up to 24 h).
  • Availability. "The one I'm signing is our system's, not the model's." Retries with backoff on 429 (the rate limits are ours), a platform fallback (Claude API ↔ Bedrock), and a declared degraded mode: if the model doesn't respond, the assistant shows balance and transactions from the banking core and offers human escalation. It doesn't go down: it degrades. And doesn't copy the provider's uptime: a number you can't verify doesn't get signed.
  • Quality. The 99% doesn't get signed. What gets signed is "≥ 0.92 F1 on the held-out set v2 (n=500), measured weekly, reported with SEM" — plus the criterion the committee actually cares about and that nobody had formulated: "zero claims about nonexistent transactions," which is not accuracy but a safety criterion with its own mechanism (every claim arrives with the transaction ID via citations, and in the absence of data the system says it doesn't have it). Anti-hallucination techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely" → which is why anything irreversible still goes through HITL.
  • The demolition of 98.3%, which is where the item gets won: "n=60, no error bars, and the questions are clustered by client. With clustered standard errors — which can be more than 3× the naive ones — the interval is so wide that 99% and 93% are indistinguishable. It's not that the number is optimistic: it's that it isn't a measurement."
  • Cost. USD per query (p50) with stated assumptions, not the total bill: volume belongs to the business.

Close: every signed number has an eval producing it and an alert watching it — including the one no error-rate dashboard sees: the rate of stop_reason: "refusal", which arrives as HTTP 200.

Why. Signing a number you can't measure or defend is the Domain 6 version of a false control: a promise presented as a control (D2). And "99% accuracy" is also a self-incriminating absolute (D4) about a system the API reference says isn't fully deterministic even at temperature: 0.0. The competent candidate doesn't say "no": they say "here's what I actually can sign."

Example 3 — Northwind Logistics: The Handoff Nobody Can Operate

Situation. The architect delivers the agent that summarizes the operations inbox (least privilege: no send_email; emails only inside JSON-encoded tool_result; screening with Haiku 4.5; red-teamed with deliberate injections). The "handoff" was: a 40-slide deck, a recorded 90-minute session, and the link to the repo. Three weeks later, Operations opens an incident: "the agent stopped summarizing half the emails." Nobody knows if it's a bug, a volume change, or the model. The error-rate dashboard is green. The architect is already on another project.

Mediocre candidate. Schedules another knowledge transfer session, or proposes "documenting it better" — i.e., more slides. Or, the more expensive variant, jumps in to fix it themselves: confirming that the system has no owner and guaranteeing the next incident will be theirs too.

Competent candidate. Names the real problem: the handoff never happened. The exit criterion isn't "gave the walkthrough" — it's "an engineer who wasn't involved reproduces, operates, and diagnoses from the document." The deck is a cosmetic artifact (D6: impeccable vocabulary, zero variables moved). Rebuilds the package:

  1. Runbook as a Skill (SKILL.md): the diagnostic lives where both the human and the agent can use it.
  2. Persistent rules in CLAUDE.md, not in the thread's first message — compaction summarizes old messages and the initial instructions can get lost.
  3. The executable eval suite, including the red-team's injection emails. Without it, nobody can detect regression or re-qualify a new model.
  4. Versioned declarative config (allowedTools, deny rules, filesystem and network sandbox): control is code, not the verbal agreement at handover.
  5. Implementation guidance: what not to touch (reordering the tool definitions invalidates the entire cache), how to roll back, a pinned model ID (dated snapshot, not an alias), and the re-qualification procedure for when it gets deprecated.

And the dashboard with the agreed-upon SLIs — where the cause shows up: there was never a stop_reason SLI. "Stopped summarizing half the emails" isn't a model failure: it's refusal, or max_tokens, or a tool_result with is_error: true — all three arrive as HTTP 200. The error rate was green by design. There wasn't a bug: there was an SLI nobody agreed on, and that's a Domain 6 failure, not a Domain 3 one.

Why. Handoff is measured by the receiving team's capability, not the sender's effort. And the cross-cutting lesson: on this platform, the highest-leverage documentation is the kind the system executes. A PDF nobody reads and an agent nobody can diagnose are the same artifact.

Example 4 — Lex Europa: The Iteration That Would Break the Contract

Situation. The legal RAG (org with ZDR, sensitive workloads on non-Covered, synchronous models). Two signals: the lawyers say long-form analysis "takes too long" and that the system "sometimes gives up." An engineer proposes two improvements: (a) move the heavy analysis to Message Batches (−50% cost) and (b) upgrade to Claude Fable 5, which reasons better on long documents. Product wants to announce "analysis 2× faster" in the firm's newsletter.

Mediocre candidate. Approves both. They're real improvements, and each one breaks a stated constraint: Batches retains results for 29 days — a feature that's not ZDR-eligible, which doesn't fail outright but pulls that data out of the ZDR arrangement promised to the client; and Fable 5 is a Covered Model that requires 30-day retention → in a ZDR org, the API returns 400 invalid_request_error. ZDR and Fable 5 are mutually exclusive. And "2× faster" is a new promise nobody measured, about to go out in writing to clients.

Competent candidate. The signal gets classified before it becomes a change.

  • "Takes too long" → against what SLO? There is no latency SLO for long-form analysis. So the finding isn't a bug: it's a discovery gap. Goes back to discovery and finds out what nobody asked: long-form analysis isn't an interactive flow, it's a deliverable. The axis isn't latency — it's the due date. Half the "urgency" evaporates; the other half turns into an honest SLO ("available before 9:00 AM the next day").
  • "Sometimes gives up" → classify before touching anything. refusal (HTTP 200)? max_tokens (truncated)? pause_turn (the server-tools loop hit its limit and needs a resend)? None of these shows up as an error. The first fix isn't changing models: it's instrumenting.
  • Both "improvements" get checked against the ADR's constraints and rejected in writing, with the reason — that documented rejection stops the same proposal from coming back next quarter with a different engineer. (And the ADR does allow a valid way out: non-sensitive or anonymized workloads can go through Batches in a different organization. The per-feature eligibility matrix lets you say "yes here, no there" instead of just "no.")
  • The announcement. "2× faster" doesn't go out without evidence: method, n, date, and uncertainty, measured on the real flow, not the demo.
  • What does move forward: the findings go in as new cases in the suite, the new SLO gets written, and it's communicated to the client before they discover it themselves.

Why. The feedback loop is about classifying the signal — bug, tech debt, discovery gap, or scope change? — and routing it to the right artifact. Two complaints produced three different responses, and none of them was "change the model," which is exactly what the team was about to do (D3). And the compliance trap is the usual one: each piece is correct and the combination is invalid.

Example 5 — Talenta: The Expectation Sales Already Sold

Situation. Talenta pre-screens résumés with Claude. Sales already signed three clients, promising "a 60% reduction in screening time, automatic decisions, no bias." The architect arrives with the promise already made, the contracts already signed, and a kickoff on Monday.

Mediocre candidate. Two variants, and both lose the item:

  • (a) Builds what was promised. Automatic rejection without review violates the Usage Policy: employment is a High-Risk Use Case, which makes two safeguards mandatory — human-in-the-loop (a qualified professional reviews before dissemination) and disclosure. It's not "debatable": it's policy.
  • (b) Gives up. "It can't be done, the contracts need renegotiating." Abandonment is a distractor in this domain and is almost never the key: the stem leaves a compliant path, and finding it is the job.

Competent candidate. Realigns the expectation in writing, with numbers, without breaking policy and without throwing away the business value. Splits the promise into three:

What was promisedClassificationWhat gets signed
"60% reduction in screening time"Feasible and measurableKept — but as assistance, not as decision: the system ranks, summarizes, and justifies with evidence from the résumé; the recruiter decides. The savings get measured (time per candidate, before vs. after), not assumed
"Automatic decisions"Non-compliantHITL mandatory at the decision point + disclosure. A Usage Policy requirement for employment, not the architect's preference
"No bias"Not promisable as an absoluteEval disaggregated by subgroup, held-out test set, declared threshold, re-measurement cadence, judge ≠ generator, and an escalation procedure if the threshold is crossed. Plus exploratory human testing for the biases the suite doesn't catch

And brings it to the committee in the stakeholder's language: not "this violates policy," but "here's what I can actually sign, here's what it costs, and here's what happens if we don't" — with the business value preserved (the 60% is still achievable with assistance + HITL, and now it's also measurable) alongside the consequence of the non-compliant option (regulatory exposure, access revocation, a product indefensible in front of the client's own compliance team). An ADR gets written declaring the constraint non-negotiable, and the client is notified before their legal team discovers it themselves.

Why. Managing an expectation isn't fulfilling it or denying it: it's correcting it with evidence and offering the compliant path. The two distractors fail on opposite sides — building what was promised breaks an untouchable constraint (D5); abandoning breaks the entire business requirement — and the correct answer does the usual thing: the diligence, in writing, with explicit alignment, and only then proceed. Notice the detail that decides the item: the business number is preserved. What changes isn't the value promise: it's the mechanism.

How the Exam Asks It

The stem's verbs. Conduct structured discovery… · Communicate architectural decisions and trade-offs… · Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment… · Document architectures… · Support lifecycle phases… None of them is "define." And the stem carries the usual superlative — "What should the architect do first?", "Which approach best aligns expectations?", "Which artifact is most important for the handoff?" — so it's a ranking exam: more than one option will be defensible, and only one is optimal.

Lexical signals that shout "Domain 6": stakeholder, discovery, requirements, expectation, SLA, handoff, document the architecture, communicate the trade-off, executive, steering committee, non-technical audience, sign off, acceptance criteria, pilot, rollout, runbook, feedback, iterate, go-live.

The domain's six item molds:

MoldShape of the stemThe correct answer
1. Discovery"A stakeholder asks for X with a vague quality bar and a hard deadline. What does the architect do first?"Extract measurable success criteria, establish a baseline, confirm ground truth availability
2. Trade-off"Must present decision X to a non-technical committee."The decision + the consequence + the number + what you need from the committee
3. SLA"The client demands a contractual guarantee of 99% accuracy."A rate measured over a declared set, with n, cadence, and uncertainty, + the mechanisms (citations, HITL, escalation)
4. Handoff"The system passes to the delivery team. What must the handover include?"Runbook + evals + config + ADR + dashboard, gated on the receiving team reproducing it
5. Feedback loop"Users report X. What should happen with that signal?"Classify it and route it: bug → fix + new case in the suite; missing criterion → back to discovery; scope → backlog
6. Lifecycle phase"The team wants to skip phase Y to hit the deadline."Name the artifact that phase produces and why delivery is impossible without it

The distractors, with the decoder's nomenclature:

  • D5 · The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. The confident shortcut: "skip discovery and start building — we'll refine as we go." Gains time and destroys the acceptance criterion, which was the requirement. Its maximal form is abandonment ("cancel the project / renegotiate the contract"): it doesn't break a requirement — it breaks the project. Antidote: "what requirement does it sacrifice?" And remember: the exam almost never rewards abandoning — the stem leaves a compliant path (Talenta).
  • D2 · The Prudent Mitigation That Eliminates Nothing. Here it disguises itself as a false control: a meeting instead of a document; a promise instead of an SLO; a "let's review it together" instead of a criterion. Antidote: "after applying this option, what stays written down, and who can verify it?" If the answer is "nothing" and another option produces an artifact, the other one wins.
  • D6 · The Relabel With No Effect. The cosmetic fix: "prepare a clearer executive deck", "add a glossary to the docs", "add 'be accurate' to the system prompt". Impeccable vocabulary, zero numbers moved. Antidote: what variable changed — a criterion, an SLI, an artifact, a permission?
  • D4 · The Self-Incriminating Absolute. This one is lethal here, because the domain lives on promises: "guarantee 100% accuracy", "the system will never hallucinate", "zero downtime". About a system the API reference warns isn't fully deterministic even at temperature: 0.0, any absolute is false by construction.
  • D3 · The Model as Universal Solution. "Upgrade to a larger model so the stakeholder's quality concerns go away." The model doesn't substitute for an acceptance criterion, an SLA, or a runbook. Upgrading the model never solves a communication problem.
  • D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem. The stem says "success criteria were signed off last quarter" and an option proposes "define success criteria." Dead on arrival. Underline the control variables (already, signed off, unchanged) before looking at the options.
  • D1 · Wrong-Category Control. A real artifact from the wrong phase: answering with monitoring when the stem asks about discovery; with documentation when it asks about an SLA. Antidote: identify the phase the stem names, and demand the artifact from that phase.
  • D8 · The Irrelevant Knob. "Lower the temperature so the stakeholder gets consistent answers" — and on Opus 4.7+ temperature isn't even adjustable (400).

The option that "sounds good but fails" has an unmistakable signature here: it's a communication action that leaves no artifact ("schedule an alignment session with stakeholders") or a promise with no measurement behind it ("commit to 95% accuracy"). Both are things a reasonable professional would do. Neither is the best when an option exists that produces a measurable criterion, a verifiable document, or an instrumented SLI.

Multiple-response. The key usually combines two artifacts from different phases ("define measurable acceptance criteria with the business" + "document the decision with its rejected alternatives"), while the distractors come in a pair from the same family (two flavors of meeting, two of deck). Count how many they ask for, and cover different phases, not two variants of the same ritual.

Time management. This domain's items are long — business scenarios with three stakeholders and a deadline. Read the last line first: at ~1 min 54 s per item, you can't afford to let the scenario hold you hostage before you know what's actually being asked.

Common Mistakes

  1. Treating discovery as a kickoff meeting. Correction: it ends when you can write "this is done when ___" in a verifiable way and the business has demonstrated it can produce ground truth. A meeting with no artifact is not a phase.

  2. Accepting "have it answer well" or "make it accurate" as a criterion. Correction: the criterion is SMART and multidimensional. The official pair: ❌ "Safe outputs" vs. ✅ "Less than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by our content filter." And the eight categories — task fidelity, consistency, relevance/coherence, tone and style, privacy preservation, context utilization, latency, price — include latency and price as first-class criteria.

  3. Not asking about the baseline, or failing to verify that ground truth exists. Correction: without a baseline there's no ROI and no acceptance criterion ("better than today" requires knowing how much today is). And if the business can't produce correct answers for N cases, you can't build the eval — and without an eval you can't promise anything. That's not an obstacle to the project: it is the project.

  4. Signing an "accuracy" SLA. Correction: it's a number with no universe. What gets signed is a rate measured over a declared set, with n, date, SEM, and re-measurement cadence.

  5. Presenting the pilot measurement as the contract number. Correction: with a small n and no error bars you don't have a measurement. The evals statistical guidance requires SEM; and with clustered questions, clustered standard errors can be >3× the naive ones.

  6. Copying the provider's uptime into your own SLA. Correction: the availability you sign is your system's: rate limits (429), retries, model/region/platform fallback, and a declared degraded mode. And the exam guide doesn't publish an Anthropic uptime number — don't invent one.

  7. Promising a latency without saying which one or at what percentile. Correction: TTFT ≠ completion; p50 ≠ p95. Streaming improves TTFT and perceived latency, not the total. And nothing with an interactive SLA goes through Batch (window of up to 24 h; whatever doesn't complete expires).

  8. Promising "zero hallucinations." Correction: the docs are explicit — the techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely." What gets promised is a measured rate + citations + "I don't know" permitted + a human escalation path.

  9. Confusing SLI, SLO, and SLA. Correction: SLI = what you measure · SLO = the internal target with a window · SLA = the contractual commitment with a consequence. An SLA with no SLI measuring it is a promise disguised as a control.

  10. Communicating half the trade-off — or bringing the technical detail to the executive. Correction: the trade-off goes in full (lever, what it gains, what it costs, the number); hiding the cost to get the "yes" comes back as an incident six months later. And bringing technical detail to the executive, and reassurance with no numbers, are the same mistake: same fact, different resolution, never different facts.

  11. Writing an ADR without the rejected alternatives. Correction: a decision record with no "alternatives considered and why not" is a press release. The rejected alternative prevents the discussion from repeating every quarter and keeps the receiving team from "improving" the system by undoing a constraint that existed for a reason.

  12. Considering the handoff done because you gave the walkthrough. Correction: the exit criterion is "an engineer who wasn't involved reproduces, operates, and diagnoses from the document." A deck is not a runbook.

  13. Putting persistent rules in the thread's first message. Correction: compaction replaces old messages with a summary → the initial instructions can get lost. They belong in CLAUDE.md (re-injected on every request) or in a Skill.

  14. Delivering without the eval suite. Correction: the suite is the executable specification. Without it, the receiving team can't detect regression, can't re-qualify a new model, and can't defend the SLA number.

  15. Assuming the model version is permanent. Correction: Anthropic publishes a deprecation policy; the model ID is a dependency with a lifecycle. In production, you pin the dated snapshot (an alias can shift), with a re-qualification procedure (run the suite against the candidate, compare with paired differences) and an acceptance criterion in the ADR. Don't memorize the notice window; memorize that it expires.

  16. Doing an atomic deploy over long-running agents. Correction: it kills the sessions mid-flight. The documented practices are rainbow deployments (gradual traffic shift) and stateful error handling (resuming from a checkpoint).

  17. Turning every complaint into a prompt or model change. Correction: classify the signal first — bug, tech debt, discovery gap, or scope change? "It's correct but sounds cold" is a criterion (tone and style) that was never defined. And a fix that doesn't update the evals isn't a fix: it's a patch that's going to break again.

  18. Dashboard green, users angry. Correction: the dashboard's SLIs must be exactly the SLA's, and include what isn't an HTTP error: stop_reason: "refusal" (arrives as 200; in Batches, as a succeeded result), max_tokens, pause_turn, and tool_result with is_error: true.

  19. Letting the stakeholder find out before you tell them. Correction: a change in expectation gets communicated proactively, with the evidence and the option. Someone else discovering it first is the worst possible expectation management.

  20. Choosing "cancel / renegotiate the contract" as the answer. Correction: it's almost never the key. The stem usually leaves a compliant path: correct the expectation, offer what's signable, and preserve the business value (Talenta: the 60% is still achievable with assistance + HITL). The architect who only knows how to say "no" isn't more rigorous: they're less useful.

Glossary

Term (EN)GlossWhat it means, in a sentence
DiscoveryStructured requirements phasePhase that turns a vague request into measurable criteria; it ends with a document, not a meeting.
Success criteriaSMART, multidimensional targetsSMART and multidimensional, defined before the prompt. Eight categories — and latency and price are among them.
BaselineToday's quantified performanceToday's performance, quantified. Without it there's no ROI and no acceptance criterion.
Ground truthBusiness-verified correct answersThe correct answers the business must be able to produce. Without it there's no eval, and without an eval there's no promise.
Golden answerSigned-off reference answerThe reference answer for an eval case; signed off with the business unit.
Acceptance criteriaThe "done when" testThe "this is done when ___" sentence, verifiable by an eval, a command, or a metric.
ADR (Architecture Decision Record)Dated decision documentA dated document with context, decision, rejected alternatives, consequences, status. Industry convention, not an Anthropic product.
Trade-offLever + gain + cost + numberCommunicated in full: the lever, what it gains, what it costs, and the number.
AltitudeAudience-matched resolutionSame fact, different resolution depending on the audience — never different facts.
StakeholderDecider, signer, payer, operator, or userWhoever decides, signs off, pays, operates, or uses. Each one gets the same fact at a different resolution.
SLI (Service Level Indicator)The measured signalWhat you measure: TTFT p95, refusal rate, F1 on the held-out set.
SLO (Service Level Objective)Internal target with a windowThe internal target on an SLI, with a time window.
SLA (Service Level Agreement)Contractual commitment with teethThe contractual commitment with a consequence. With no SLI behind it, it's a promise, not a control.
TTFT (time to first token)What streaming improvesWhat streaming improves. It is not total latency: promising one on the strength of the other breaks the SLA.
Percentile (p50 / p95)Which fraction of users, exactly"p95 = 4 s" means 1 in 20 users waits more than 4 s. An SLO with no percentile is not an SLO.
Degraded modeWhat happens when the model doesn't respondWhat the system does when the model doesn't respond. "It goes down" is not a degraded mode.
Non-determinismSame input, possibly different outputEven with temperature of 0.0, the results will not be fully deterministic. This is why bare "accuracy" never gets signed.
Evaluation-backed claimMethod + n + date + uncertaintyEvery capability claim travels with method, n, date, and uncertainty.
Held-out test setThe set you never iterated onThe set that was not used for iterating; without it you overfit the suite and the number lies.
SEM / error barsUncertainty around the score95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM. A score with no error bars is not a measurement.
Clustered standard errorsWider bars for grouped dataWith clustered questions (same client, same document) they can be >3× the naive ones.
HandoffDelivery to the operating teamDelivery to the team that's going to operate the system. Measured by the receiving team's capability, not the sender's effort.
RunbookDiagnostic procedureThe diagnostic procedure. Here it gets written as a Skill, used by both the human and the agent.
Implementation guidanceWhat not to touch, and whyWhat not to touch and why: what invalidates the cache, where the breakpoint goes, how to roll back, what happens when the model gets deprecated.
CLAUDE.md—Persistent rules; re-injected on every request. The only place a rule survives compaction.
Agent Skill (SKILL.md)On-demand capabilityA procedure the agent loads on demand; only the name and description live in context until invoked.
CompactionOld messages get summarizedSummarizes old messages → the first turn's instructions can get lost.
Model deprecationAn expiring dependencyThe model ID is a dependency with an expiration date. Pin the snapshot, not the alias, and keep a re-qualification procedure.
Rainbow deploymentGradual traffic shiftGradual traffic shift between versions; an atomic deploy kills agents mid-flight.
Stateful error handlingResume, don't restartResuming from a checkpoint, not restarting the whole agent.
Feedback loopSignal → triage → artifactSignal → triage → classification → decision → artifact. It's not "listen to the user."
Signal triageClassify before you touch anythingDeciding whether a complaint is a bug, tech debt, discovery gap, or scope change — before touching anything.
DisclosureTelling the user AI is involvedTelling the user AI is involved; mandatory in high-risk cases and, in consumer chatbots, at the start of the session.
Usage & Cost Admin APIGround truth for actual spendThe source of truth for actual spend — the finance stakeholder's feedback loop.

Domain Checklist

If you can't check one of these off, you don't own the domain.

  1. I can turn a vague request ("have it answer well") into a SMART, multidimensional criterion, and recite the official pair ❌ "Safe outputs" / ✅ "Less than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity."
  2. I can name the eight categories of success criteria and explain why latency and price are among them — and what consequence that has for the SLA conversation.
  3. I know what discovery's exit gate is: the verifiable "this is done when ___" sentence, plus confirmation that the business can produce ground truth.
  4. I always ask about the baseline and the blast radius (what action is irreversible?), and I know which architecture decision each answer unlocks.
  5. I know that discovery can erase the architecture (corpus < 200k tokens ≈ 500 pages → there is no RAG), and that this is the cheapest phase at which to discover it.
  6. I can write an ADR with rejected alternatives, their reasoning, the negative consequences, and a review trigger.
  7. I communicate a trade-off with all four pieces: the lever, what it gains, what it costs, the number — and I know that omitting the third one to get the "yes" is the domain's archetypal failure.
  8. I apply the altitude principle: I translate "p95 = 4 s" into "1 in 20 users waits more than 4 seconds." Same fact, different resolution, never different facts.
  9. I distinguish SLI / SLO / SLA without hesitation, and know that an SLA with no SLI measuring it is a promise disguised as a control.
  10. I know exactly what can be promised across the four dimensions (latency, availability, quality, cost) about a non-deterministic system — and what can't.
  11. I can explain the five reasons "95% accuracy" is a trap: no denominator, no error bars, no disaggregation, no cost of error, and it expires.
  12. I know that the availability I sign is my system's (429, retries, fallback, degraded mode) and that I must not invent or copy a provider uptime number.
  13. I never promise "zero hallucinations": I cite that the techniques "significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely" and offer a measured rate + citations + escalation.
  14. I can take apart a pilot measurement (small n, no SEM, clustered questions → clustered SE >3× the naive ones) without sounding obstructionist.
  15. I can recite the five phases with the mandatory artifact and the gate for each one — and I know that a phase whose output is "a meeting" didn't happen.
  16. I know that handoff's exit criterion is that an engineer who wasn't involved can reproduce, operate, and diagnose from the document, and I can enumerate the full package.
  17. I know why persistent rules go in CLAUDE.md or in a Skill and not in the thread's first message (compaction), and why runbook-as-Skill is the highest-leverage handoff artifact.
  18. I treat the model ID as a dependency with a lifecycle: a pinned snapshot (not an alias), re-qualification with the suite (paired differences), an acceptance criterion in the ADR. And I know that an atomic deploy kills agents mid-flight (rainbow deployments + stateful error handling).
  19. I can classify a production signal (bug / tech debt / discovery gap / scope change) before touching anything, and know that every fix ends up as a new case in the suite. And that the dashboard's SLIs must be the SLA's, including refusal (200), max_tokens, pause_turn, tool_result.is_error.
  20. Faced with an item, I can recognize in 20 seconds whether the "reasonable" option is a communication action that leaves no artifact or a promise with no measurement behind it — and I know that the answer is almost never to abandon: the stem leaves a compliant path, and finding it is the job.

domains.title: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement
objectives: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
Support debugging and operational issue resolution
domains.html:
Why It's Worth 7%

I'm going to be honest with you, because a guide that pretends all seven domains deserve equal effort is lying to you.

With 63 items and a 7% weight, this domain contributes roughly 4–5 items. It's the smallest on the exam: half of Governance (14%, ~9 items) and a little over a third of Integration (19%, ~12 items). And because pass/fail depends exclusively on the total scaled score — there's no per-domain minimum — one Domain 7 item is worth exactly the same as one Domain 3 item.

Add the other half of the truth: it's the domain you already know. The MQC has run LLMs in production for 6+ months and opens Claude Code every day. The marginal return per study hour is the lowest of the seven. The correct strategy is explicit: read it once, close the concrete gaps, and put the hours you recover back into Domains 1 and 3.

And now the trap — the reason this chapter exists:

Your day-to-day competence is your liability. You use Claude Code as an individual. The exam asks about it as an organization. You're going to answer from your habits, and your habits belong to one person.

The stem doesn't say "configure your Claude Code". It says "a team of 40 engineers across 12 repositories", "every developer when they clone the repository", "a new hire does not get the conventions", "no engineer can disable the check", "leadership needs to know whether it helped". Each of those phrases kills the answers that work on your laptop. Personal configuration (~/.claude/…) doesn't travel through git. A trick that works for one staff engineer is not a team asset. And "so the team doesn't get blocked" does not authorize opening broad permissions: it authorizes configuring scoped, reviewable enablement.

Those 4–5 items are free points — but only if you make the jump from individual to team/organization. That jump is the whole chapter; you already know the rest.

Boundary notice: this domain borders three neighbors, and the exam doesn't mark the line. Observability at scale is also Domain 3; permissions and sandboxing are also Domain 5; onboarding and handoff are also Domain 6. The label doesn't matter: the same law resolves it.

Official Objectives

The three task statements from the blueprint, verbatim in English, with what they'll actually ask of you:

• Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)

Decide which scope each piece of configuration lives in and defend it: what gets committed to the repo (.claude/settings.json, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json), what is legitimately personal (~/.claude/, .claude/settings.local.json), and what the organization imposes and nobody can disable (managed settings). And configure the environment, not just the client: sandbox, devcontainer with a firewall, CI authentication.

• Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling

Turn a trick that works for one person into a team asset: versioned skills and slash commands, subagents in .claude/agents/, plugins distributed from an internal marketplace, and Claude Code inside the pipeline (-p, --output-format json + --json-schema). And measure whether it actually helped, separating activity metrics from outcome metrics.

• Support debugging and operational issue resolution

Two readings, and the exam uses both. (a) Debugging the tool itself: why your teammate doesn't see your configuration, why the CI job hangs, why the context filled up (/status, /memory, /context, /permissions, /doctor). (b) Using the tool to debug production: reproduce → isolate → fix → verify the mechanism, and leave the runbook as a reusable asset instead of individual heroics.

Key Concepts

1. The Domain's Three Laws

Law 1 — Context suggests, configuration compels. A CLAUDE.md is handed to the model as text: the model decides what to do with it and always has a non-zero failure rate. A permission rule or a hook is evaluated by the client, before the model acts. The docs leave no ambiguity: "An instruction like 'never edit .env' in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a guarantee. A PreToolUse hook that blocks the edit is enforcement."

If the stem carries a measured failure rate, a requirement involving money, identity, or secrets, or the words guaranteed / must never / no engineer can → the answer is never "improve it in the CLAUDE.md." It's a deny rule, a hook, or a managed setting.

Law 2 — The tilde never travels through git. Everything living under ~/ is yours and yours alone. If the requirement says "available to every developer when they clone the repository", the answer is a path inside the repo. It's the cheapest question in the domain and the one most people miss — because their own configuration lives exactly there.

Law 3 — Committed is not the same as enforced. A .claude/settings.json in the repo is shared and reviewable, but a developer overrides it with their own .claude/settings.local.json, with CLI flags, or by editing the file. If the requirement is "no engineer can turn this off", the only level that guarantees it is managed settings. Confusing "it's in git" with "it's mandatory" is what separates Foundations from Professional.

2. The Five Configuration Scopes

Precedence, from highest to lowest. It's the domain's skeleton:

Managed (organization) → CLI arguments → .claude/settings.local.json → .claude/settings.json → ~/.claude/settings.json

ScopePathGit?Overridable?

The table that answers the item. Ask what property the stem requires:

What the stem requiresCorrect scope
"The whole team has it on clone"Project — .claude/settings.json, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json, .claude/rules/, skills/, agents/, commands/
