The nuance that separates the ones who know. There are three questions hidden inside one: does it need to be identical everywhere? → managed. Does it need to be shared and reviewable? → project, in git, where a reviewer sees it in the diff. Is it legitimately personal? → user/local. The architect's mistake is putting everything in managed ("so nobody can break it") and strangling the team — or putting everything in the repo and discovering the security control was optional.

3. Enabling the Team Without Opening the Door

The three lists, inside permissions in any settings.json. deny is evaluated first and wins over allow — and wins even under bypassPermissions. ask forces confirmation even if an allow existed. allow pre-approves: it removes the prompt without widening anything else. Format: Tool(specifier). The six permission modes, exact: default (alias manual), acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions.

// .claude/settings.json — COMMITEADO. Lo ve el equipo, se revisa en el PR.
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(npm run lint)", "Bash(git status)",
              "Read(src/**)", "Edit(src/**)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push:*)"],
    "deny":  ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./secrets/**)", "Bash(terraform apply:*)"],
    "defaultMode": "default",
    "additionalDirectories": ["../shared-types/"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Bash",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/block-prod-deploy.sh" }] }
    ]
  }
}

And the item this domain will almost certainly ask:

The team complains that permission prompts break their flow. Someone proposes bypassPermissions / --dangerously-skip-permissions "so nobody gets blocked."

That's the confident shortcut, and it's wrong. The correct answer doesn't trade security for speed: it reduces prompts AND narrows privilege at the same time, because allow and deny are independent axes. Noisy, frequent, safe commands (tests, lint, git status) go into allow in the committed .claude/settings.json: the prompt disappears and the granted scope stays written, versioned, and reviewable in the PR. The dangerous stuff goes into deny. And if the requirement is "no engineer can reopen the shortcut", it gets locked from the top:

// managed-settings.json — nivel organización, NO sobreescribible
{
  "permissions": {
    "disableBypassPermissionsMode": "disable",
    "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(~/.aws/**)", "Read(~/.ssh/**)"]
  }
}

permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" prevents an engineer from using --dangerously-skip-permissions. It's the only mechanism that satisfies "no engineer can disable it": a paragraph in the CLAUDE.md doesn't satisfy it (Law 1), and neither does a committed .claude/settings.json (Law 3).

Secrets and committable configuration. The project's .mcp.json supports environment variable expansion (${VAR} and ${VAR:-default}) in command, args, env, url, and headers. That's what makes it committable without leaking the token:

// .mcp.json — raíz del repo, COMMITEADO. Cero secretos dentro.
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "internal-observability": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "${OBS_MCP_URL:-https://obs.internal.example.com/mcp}",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${OBS_MCP_TOKEN}" }
    }
  }
}

MCP at scale: claude mcp add --scope local|project|user. local (default) is private to you in that repo; project writes the root .mcp.json — committed, shared; user is yours across all your repos. Testable fact: Claude Code asks for explicit approval before using project-scoped MCP servers, precisely because that file arrives via git and a PR could introduce a malicious server. Reset them with claude mcp reset-project-choices.

The environment gets configured too — the objective says "tools and environments":

  • Sandbox (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2; WSL1 not supported; /sandbox panel). By default no domain is pre-allowed. Official warning: "Effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation." And the fine nuance: allowing a broad domain like github.com creates an exfiltration path, because the proxy decides based on the hostname the client hands it without inspecting TLS → domain fronting. At the organization scale, network.allowManagedDomainsOnly exists. (The full sandbox detail lives in Domain 5.)
  • Reference devcontainer: the anthropics/claude-code repo publishes a .devcontainer with init-firewall.sh, which blocks all egress except the necessary domains. It's the canonical answer to "give the contractors a standardized, isolated environment."

4. Shared Assets — and the Plugin as the Unit of Distribution

Where each file goes, you already know. What changes at the Professional level is scale: it's not where it goes, it's how you roll it out to 200 engineers across 40 repos without it drifting out of sync.

AssetPath (team)When it enters context
MemoryCLAUDE.md / .claude/CLAUDE.mdAlways, at startup. Universal standards
Path-scoped rules.claude/rules/*.md (frontmatter paths: with globs)Only when touching matching files
Skills.claude/skills/<n>/SKILL.md (name, description, allowed-tools, disable-model-invocation)On demand; only its description lives in context
Slash commands.claude/commands/<n>.mdOn invocation
Subagents.claude/agents/<n>.md (name, description, tools, model)On delegation; isolated context
MCP servers.mcp.json (root)On connection
Hookshooks in .claude/settings.jsonOn the event (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, SessionStart…)

Reminders the exam reuses: @import modularizes but does NOT save context (imports still load at startup; max 4 hops). There are only two mechanisms that save context: .claude/rules/ with paths: (conditional) and skills (on demand). And a skill doesn't work for conventions that must apply "automatically" by path: skills get invoked, they don't match globs.

The organizational-scale answer: plugins. A plugin packages skills, subagents, slash commands, MCP servers, and hooks into an installable unit with a manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json), distributed from a marketplace that can be an internal git repo.

Copying .claude/ from repo to repo is guaranteed drift: three months in, there are seven versions of the same skill and nobody knows which one is the good one. A versioned plugin is a single source of truth with updates. But security invariants don't travel in the plugin — a plugin can be uninstalled. They travel in managed settings.

5. The Human-Free Workflow: Headless and CI

An assisted workflow that only exists when a human is typing isn't team enablement: it's a personal skill. The team version runs in the pipeline.

claude -p "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against the review criteria in CLAUDE.md.
Report ONLY bugs and security issues. Skip style nits." \
  --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA" \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" --max-turns 15 --bare \
  > /tmp/review.json

jq -c '.structured_output.findings' /tmp/review.json
  • -p / --print keeps the job from hanging while waiting for interactive input. --headless, --batch, and CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true don't exist: they're distractors for invented features.
  • --output-format json + --json-schema → the validated output lands in structured_output. Parsing prose with regex in a pipeline is fragile by construction.
  • --allowedTools / --disallowedTools — least privilege applies in CI too: a review job doesn't need Write or Bash.
  • --max-turns — a hard cap on cost and time for a job that runs away.
  • --bare — skips auto-discovery of local hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, and CLAUDE.md: reproducibility in CI. Without it, -p loads the same configuration as an interactive session, and the result depends on the machine.
  • Auth in CI: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, Bedrock via OIDC, or workload identity on GCP. For a long-lived token, claude setup-token.
  • Official integrations: the GitHub Action anthropics/claude-code-action (installed with /install-github-app) and documented support for GitLab CI/CD.

And the conceptual rule the exam loves: the same session that generated the code is worse at reviewing it than an independent instance — it retains the reasoning behind the generation and doesn't question its own decisions. In CI: the generation job and the review job are separate invocations, not two turns of the same session. No instruction along the lines of "now review yourself" substitutes for context isolation.

6. Debugging: The Tool Itself, and Production

The third objective has two readings, and the exam uses both.

(a) Debugging the configuration. The classic team symptom is "it works on my machine", and it has exactly one structural cause: someone has something loaded that the other doesn't. There's a command for every question:

SymptomCommandWhat it tells you
"It works for me, not for Priya"/statusWhich settings sources are active — including whether managed settings are in effect
"The convention isn't reaching them"/memoryWhich memory files the session loads
"Why did the context fill up?"/contextWhat occupies the window by category (system prompt, memory, skills, subagents with the source each loaded from, MCP tools, messages)
"Why does/doesn't it ask me about this tool?"/permissionsEvery rule and the file it comes from
"The install looks off"/doctorInstallation health, invalid settings, duplicate subagents
"How much have I spent?"/usageCost and tokens for this session — personal, not team governance

Add --debug, and transcripts at ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl, recoverable with --resume <session-id>.

The nuance that separates: /permissions and /context tell you which file each thing came from. An item whose symptom is inconsistent behavior across developers is never resolved by "improving the prompt": it's resolved by finding the file one person has and the other doesn't.

(b) Debugging production with AI. Here the exam isn't measuring whether you know how to use the tool: it's measuring whether you have engineering discipline and whether you make it repeatable instead of heroic.

The cycle: reproduce (a test that captures the real condition and that you watch fail first — without reproduction there's no diagnosis, just assisted guessing) → isolate (the cause lives where the change happened: this is the rule from official sample 3) → fix → verify. And the domain's point lives in the last step:

A fix without a mechanism isn't a fix: it's a symptom patch. "The tests pass now" is not a causal explanation. If you can't narrate event → mechanism → symptom in one sentence, you don't know why it broke — and therefore you don't know whether it's going to break again. It is.

Evidence hierarchy, from strongest to weakest: real behavior observed end-to-end > a new test you watched fail and then pass > the existing suite in green > compiles / typechecks > "I reread the code carefully", which is not verification.

And the jump from individual to organization, which is what this domain actually scores:

Heroic = a senior, in a terminal, at 3:40 AM, solving it on intuition. It works once and leaves nothing behind. Repeatable = the runbook becomes a committed skill or slash command; the violated invariant becomes a test or a deny rule; and the next on-call — or the pipeline — runs the same play without depending on who happens to be awake.

A postmortem that ends in a paragraph in the CLAUDE.md is context: probabilistic, forgettable, non-executable. One that ends in a hook or a test is configuration: it compels. Law 1, again.

7. Measuring the Workflow: Telemetry and Cost Governance

Telemetry is OFF by default. It's turned on with CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and exported via OpenTelemetry (OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER / OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER: otlp | prometheus | console | none; cadence via OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL, default 60000 ms).

The metrics that exist (exact names — the exam may build a distractor out of a made-up one): claude_code.session.count · claude_code.lines_of_code.count · claude_code.pull_request.count · claude_code.commit.count · claude_code.cost.usage · claude_code.token.usage · claude_code.code_edit_tool.decision · claude_code.active_time.total. Events: claude_code.user_prompt, claude_code.tool_result, claude_code.tool_decision, claude_code.api_request, claude_code.api_error, claude_code.api_refusal.

And the governance fact that's almost certainly an item:

Prompt content is NOT logged by default. Logging it is an explicit opt-in: OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 (and its relatives OTEL_LOG_ASSISTANT_RESPONSES, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT, OTEL_LOG_RAW_API_BODIES).

You can therefore measure the workflow without reading what people write — the same pattern Anthropic documents for its own agentic systems: high-level observability over decision patterns, without inspecting conversation content. Hence the inverse trap: at Lex Europa — an EU law firm whose promise to its client is that no prompt persists at rest, and whose organization runs under ZDR — turning on OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS "to better understand how the team uses the tool" contradicts the retention arrangement they signed, and it was unnecessary: the metric they actually wanted (claude_code.cost.usage per team) doesn't require the content. Turning it on is a compliance decision, not an observability one.

Cost governance. /usage tells you what you spent in this session: it's personal introspection, not governance. If the stem says "leadership needs visibility into spend across the team", /usage is a distractor.

NeedMechanism
Spend and adoption per memberClaude Code Analytics dashboard — claude.ai/analytics/claude-code (Teams/Enterprise) or platform.claude.com/claude-code (API)
Feeding your own dashboard / per-team chargebackClaude Code Analytics API (Admin API key, scope read:analytics)
Metrics in your existing stackOTel: claude_code.cost.usage, claude_code.token.usage
Hard spend ceilingWorkspaces + spend limits (API side)
Per-invocation cap in CI--max-turns

This section's distractor has a recognizable signature: "document a per-developer token budget in the CLAUDE.md." Impeccable vocabulary, zero enforcement, zero number moved: it's the decoder's D6 wearing FinOps clothing. A budget the model merely reads isn't a budget — it lives in the workspace's spend limit.

8. The Honest Limits: Where This Does NOT Help

An architect who only knows how to sell the tool isn't an architect. The exam rewards whoever knows how to name the limit.

  • It doesn't fix a broken spec. With ambiguous acceptance criteria, AI produces confidently wrong code, faster. The bottleneck was the requirement, and it still is.
  • It's not an authorization boundary. Not the model, not the prompt, not the CLAUDE.md (Law 1, and the decoder's D3).
  • It doesn't turn an edit into working software. Diff velocity ≠ delivered-value velocity. If PR review becomes the bottleneck, you moved the problem, you didn't solve it.
  • A bigger model doesn't fix attention dilution. With 14 files competing in a single pass, the context already fit; what gets divided up is attention. The cure is specializing passes, not enlarging the window. Context ≠ attention.
  • It doesn't speed up what's blocked by the organization. If the task is waiting on an approval, an absent owner, or an unstable external dependency, no model moves it.
  • Activity metrics are not value metrics. lines_of_code.count and session.count measure usage: they could go up because the team rewrote the same thing three times. Outcome is measured where it always was — lead time, change failure rate, escaped defects, review latency — and those series already exist in your delivery telemetry. A success criterion is a number, declared beforehand.

Worked Examples

Example 1 — Northwind Logistics: The Configuration That Only Worked on Diego's Machine

Situation. 60 engineers, 12 repos. Diego, a staff engineer, tuned his Claude Code for months: conventions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, a review skill in ~/.claude/skills/, and permissions.allow in ~/.claude/settings.json that remove the prompts for test commands. Leadership wants "everyone to work like Diego"; he zips up his ~/.claude/ and sends it over Slack. Two months later there are seven variants of the same skill, nobody knows which one is the good one, and two new hires still haven't received the conventions. Security additionally requires that no engineer can disable the ban on reading .env.

Mediocre candidate. Uploads the zip to Confluence: "copy these files into your ~/.claude/." Or dumps everything — including the security rule — into the repo's CLAUDE.md, in all caps, and declares it solved.

Competent candidate. Recognizes there are three distinct questions, not one:

  1. Shared and reviewable → into the repo: .claude/settings.json (Diego's test/lint allow entries, now visible in the diff), CLAUDE.md, .claude/rules/ with paths:, .mcp.json with ${VARS}.
  2. Identical across the 12 repos, without copying files → a versioned plugin on an internal marketplace: a single source of truth with updates, instead of seven copies drifting apart.
  3. Nobody can disable it → managed settings: deny on Read(./.env) + disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable". A plugin can be uninstalled; a .claude/settings.json can be overridden with a .local.json. Managed, not those.

Diagnosis for the two engineers without the conventions: /status and /memory.

Why. The symptom "works for one person and not for the team" is always a scope problem, never a wording one. And the Professional-level nuance: committed ≠ enforced. Putting the security rule in the repo makes it visible, not mandatory — and the stem asked for mandatory.

Example 2 — Aurora Bank: "Remove the Permissions, the Team Isn't Moving"

Situation. Aurora Bank enables Claude Code for the platform team. Two weeks in, complaints: permission prompts constantly interrupt (tests, lint, git status). A tech lead proposes "defaultMode": "bypassPermissions" in the repo's .claude/settings.json and running with --dangerously-skip-permissions, "so nobody gets stuck." Audit requires a trail of what the agent can touch, and that the ban on reading credentials not depend on each engineer's goodwill.

Mediocre candidate. Accepts the trade-off ("it's a dev tool, speed matters more"). Or leaves the permissions untouched and adds to the CLAUDE.md: "NEVER read .env files" — and believes that's a control.

Competent candidate. Sees that the stem isn't asking you to choose between speed and security: it wants both, and there's a configuration that delivers both, because allow and deny are independent axes.

  1. The noisy prompts die via allow (Bash(npm run test:*), Bash(npm run lint), Read(src/**)) in the committed .claude/settings.json — and the granted scope stays written, versioned, and reviewed in the PR, which is exactly the trail audit asked for.
  2. The dangerous stuff dies via deny (Read(./.env), Bash(terraform apply:*)), which wins even under bypassPermissions.
  3. The shortcut gets closed with disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable" in managed settings — the only mechanism that satisfies "must not depend on each engineer."
  4. And the money/identity boundary, where the guarantee must be total, goes to a PreToolUse hook: it decides deny in code, not by persuasion.

Why. This is the archetypal item of the domain, and its distractor is the confident shortcut: broad permissions "so the team doesn't get blocked." Sounds like leader pragmatism. It's a decoder D5 — an optimization (friction) that breaks a stated requirement (auditability, non-optionality). And "fix it in the CLAUDE.md" is D6: impeccable vocabulary, zero enforcement. Whoever believes security has to be traded for speed hasn't understood the permission model.

Example 3 — Meridian Health: The 3:40 AM Incident and the Fix Without a Mechanism

Situation. Meridian Health's triage assistant intermittently returns 500s: ~2% of requests, no clear pattern. The on-call engineer opens Claude Code, pastes in the production logs, gets a patch in 20 minutes, the suite passes, merges, and closes the incident at 4:10 AM. Nine days later it happens again. In the postmortem, someone proposes "documenting in the CLAUDE.md that null handling in migrations needs review," and the platform team suggests turning on OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 "to understand how on-call used the tool."

Mediocre candidate. Accepts the patch because "the tests pass," writes the paragraph in the CLAUDE.md, turns on prompt logging, and closes the postmortem. Three decisions, three mistakes.

Competent candidate. Takes them apart one by one:

  1. "It passes now" is not a mechanism. Without a narratable causal chain (event → mechanism → symptom), it's a symptom patch — and an intermittent 2% failure is exactly what a symptom patch doesn't fix. The first step was missing: reproduce, with a test watched fail before fixing anything. "The suite passes" is the third rung of the evidence hierarchy, used here as if it were the first.
  2. The postmortem must end in configuration, not context. A paragraph in the CLAUDE.md is a request to the model: probabilistic, forgettable, and it also doesn't protect against the human who repeats the mistake. The violated invariant gets encoded as a regression test (or a deny rule / hook if the operation is destructive), and the runbook gets committed as a skill — so the next incident takes 20 minutes because the play is written down, not because the senior happened to be awake.
  3. Don't turn on prompt logging. Meridian Health handles PHI under a BAA. Content isn't logged by default; OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 is an opt-in that would pull the production logs — pasted into the chat at 3:40 AM — into the telemetry pipeline, outside the boundary the team designed. And it was unnecessary: the metrics they wanted (cost.usage, token.usage, tool_decision) don't require the content.

Why. The domain is called operational issue resolution, not incident closure. The patch isn't what's scored: what's scored is that the second time costs 20 minutes, not 4 hours, and that the fix has a reason. And, as usual, the item hides a Domain 5 layer: the "operationally useful" option that breaks the compliance posture is a distractor, however reasonable it sounds.

Example 4 — Talenta: The Rollout That Measured What Didn't Matter

Situation. Talenta rolls out Claude Code to 80 engineers. Three months in, the platform team presents to leadership: sessions +5×, accepted lines of code +340%, 94% adoption. Leadership wants to double the investment. Missing from the report: PR review time doubled, the change failure rate went up, and the real bottleneck — ambiguous acceptance criteria that force whole features to be rewritten — hasn't budged.

Mediocre candidate. Presents activity as if it were value and recommends expanding. Or falls into the opposite extreme — "developer productivity can't be measured" — and delivers zero evidence, leaving the decision to anecdote.

Competent candidate. Separates what the report conflated. Activity (session.count, lines_of_code.count, code_edit_tool.decision) tells you how much it was used, not whether it helped: more accepted lines is perfectly compatible with rewriting the same thing three times, or with flooding review with code some other human now has to read. Outcome — lead time, change failure rate, escaped defects, review latency — lives in series that already exist in Talenta's delivery telemetry; the AI tool doesn't produce them, which is why the report never looked at them.

And treats it like an evaluation, not an announcement: a stated hypothesis, a baseline measured beforehand, a comparison period, and — what almost nobody writes — the null-result condition: "if the change failure rate goes up and lead time doesn't go down, the rollout didn't work." Cost is governed with the Analytics dashboard/API and spend limits, not a budget written in a CLAUDE.md that nobody evaluates.

And names the honest limit in front of leadership, which is the part that earns the points: the tool didn't fix the bottleneck, because the bottleneck wasn't writing code. It was the ambiguous requirements. Accelerating code production on top of a broken spec produces wrong code, faster — and the rise in change failure rate is exactly that signature.

Why. "We adopted AI tooling" doesn't move any number the business cares about unless you named the number first. Presenting activity as value is the decoder's D6 in an executive suit. The rule holds exactly as it does in safety: a success criterion is a figure declared up front, not an adoption percentage presented after the fact.

How the Exam Asks It

The verbs. Configure… · Improve… · Support… None of them is "define." And the stem almost always carries a superlative: "which configuration best ensures…", "what should the architect do first…". More than one option will be defensible. Don't look for the one true answer: rank the true ones.

Lexical signals of the domain: Claude Code · team environment · developer workflow · onboarding · debugging · CI/CD pipeline · settings · permissions · every developer · when they clone · new hire · across N repositories · engineering leadership · adoption · spend.

And the signals that decide the answer before you read the options:

Phrase in the stemWhat it's askingThe answer lives in
"available to every developer when they clone"Shared scopePath inside the repo — never ~/
"no engineer can disable" · "security requires"EnforceabilityManaged settings — neither the repo nor the CLAUDE.md is enough
"across 12 repositories" · "without copying files"Distribution at scalePlugin + internal marketplace
"the job hangs" · "waiting for input"Non-interactive mode-p / --print
"machine-parseable" · "post as inline comments"Output contract--output-format json + --json-schema → structured_output
"CI must not depend on local config"Reproducibility--bare
"works on my machine" · "inconsistent across developers"Scope diagnosis/status, /memory, /permissions, /context
"the fix passed the tests but the bug returned"Debugging disciplineCausal mechanism + reproduction watched failing
"leadership wants visibility into spend"GovernanceAnalytics dashboard / API — not /usage
"so the team isn't blocked"⚠️ The confident shortcutScoped allow + deny — never bypassPermissions

The distractors, with the decoder's nomenclature:

  • D1 · Wrong-Category Control. "Add logging for every tool call to audit whether someone reads .env." Logging is post-hoc detection; what was asked was preventing it.
  • D2 · The Mitigation That Doesn't Remove the Privilege. "Put .env in ask so the dev confirms." The capability is still live and depends on a tired human saying no at 3 AM. If another option has deny, deny wins.
  • D3 · The Model as a Security Boundary. "Use a better model, it follows the CLAUDE.md more reliably" / "raise the context window so the 14-file review doesn't degrade." Model capability is never a configuration control; and context ≠ attention.
  • D4 · The Self-Incriminating Absolute. "Always run with bypassPermissions in CI", "never use hooks: they slow the team down."
  • D5 · The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. ⚠️ This domain's signature distractor. "Turn off the permission prompts, so nobody gets blocked." Improves the metric asked for (friction) at the cost of a stated requirement (audit, non-optionality).
  • D6 · The Relabel With No Effect. "Document the convention in Confluence," "add to the CLAUDE.md that tests must ALWAYS run," "write a per-dev token budget in the CLAUDE.md." Zero enforcement, zero number moved.
  • D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem. The stem says "the standards are already committed in the repository's CLAUDE.md" and an option proposes… writing them into the CLAUDE.md. Underline already, only, every, no engineer.
  • D8 · The Irrelevant Knob. --max-turns to improve a review's accuracy: it caps cost, not quality.

The option that "sounds good but fails" in this domain has two signatures, and only two:

(1) It solves for ONE person what the stem asked for a TEAM (~/.claude/…, "have each dev configure it," a wiki). (2) It grants broad permissions "so the team doesn't get blocked" instead of configuring scoped, reviewable enablement (specific allow + deny + managed).

If you recognize those two in 20 seconds, you've got the 4–5 items.

Multiple-response. The item tells you how many to mark. Count. Here the distractor pairs tend to be two flavors of the same wrong scope or two detective controls. The key usually combines different layers: e.g., a deny in managed settings (mandatory) + an asset committed in the repo (shared) — not two variants of the same thing.

Time management. ~1 min 54 s per item. A Domain 7 item is worth the same as a Domain 3 item: at 90 seconds without two finalists, mark it, flag it, and move on. And don't gift it study hours: it's the cheapest to close and the most expensive to over-prepare.

Common Mistakes

  1. Answering as an individual to a team question. This is the error of the domain: faced with every developer / when they clone / new hire / across N repos, every option with ~/ is dead.

  2. Believing "it's committed" = "it's mandatory." A .claude/settings.json gets overridden by .local.json or by CLI flags. For "no engineer can disable it" → managed settings.

  3. Granting broad permissions "so the team doesn't get blocked." Friction is removed with a specific allow; danger with deny (wins even under bypassPermissions); the shortcut is closed with disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable". allow and deny are independent axes.

  4. Putting a security control in the CLAUDE.md. "…is a request, not a guarantee." For a guarantee: a deny rule, a PreToolUse hook, or a managed setting.

  5. Believing @import saves context. Imports load the same way at startup (max 4 hops). Only .claude/rules/ with paths: and skills save context — and a skill doesn't work for automatic path-based conventions: it gets invoked, it doesn't match globs.

  6. Distributing configuration by copying .claude/ from repo to repo. Guaranteed drift → a versioned plugin from an internal marketplace. And security invariants don't go in the plugin (it can be uninstalled): they go in managed settings.

  7. Committing an .mcp.json with the token inside. It supports ${VAR} / ${VAR:-default}: the file gets committed, the secret doesn't. And project-scoped servers require explicit user approval.

  8. Running claude "…" without -p in CI. The job hangs waiting for input. --headless, --batch, and CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true don't exist.

  9. Parsing prose with regex in the pipeline. → --output-format json + --json-schema → structured_output. And --bare for reproducibility.

  10. Asking the session that generated the code to review itself. It retains the reasoning from the generation. In CI: generation job ≠ review job.

  11. Accepting a fix because "the tests pass now." Without a causal chain it's a symptom patch. The omitted step is the first one: reproduce, with a test watched fail beforehand.

  12. Closing a postmortem with a paragraph in the CLAUDE.md. The invariant gets encoded as a regression test, a deny rule, or a hook; the runbook gets committed as a skill.

  13. Turning on prompt logging "to better understand usage." It's opt-in (OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1) — and with PHI or under ZDR it's a compliance decision. The useful metrics (cost.usage, token.usage, tool_decision) don't require the content.

  14. Confusing /usage with cost governance. /usage is your session. The team is governed with the Analytics dashboard / API and the workspace's spend limits.

  15. Presenting activity metrics as value metrics. lines_of_code.count measures usage, not outcome (lead time, change failure rate). A success criterion is a number declared beforehand, including the null-result condition.

  16. Believing a bigger window fixes a degraded 14-file review. The model already had all 14: it's attention dilution, and the cure is specializing passes. Context ≠ attention.

Checklist

If you can't check one off, you don't own the domain. And if you can check them all off, close the chapter and go to Domain 3 — this one has no more points left to give you.

  1. I can recite settings precedence (managed → CLI args → local → project → user) and know, for every piece of configuration, which one it should live in and why.
  2. I know that "committed" is not "mandatory": only managed settings satisfies "no engineer can disable it."
  3. I can write a permissions block with allow/ask/deny, I know that deny wins even under bypassPermissions, and I can name all six permission modes.
  4. I know that "remove the permissions so the team doesn't get blocked" is answered with scoped allow + deny + disableBypassPermissionsMode, and I can explain why allow and deny are independent axes.
  5. I can justify why "never read .env" in the CLAUDE.md is not a control, and name the three things that are.
  6. I can commit an .mcp.json without leaking the token (${VAR}) and know that project-scoped servers require user approval.
  7. I can explain why @import doesn't save context, what the two mechanisms that do are, and why a skill doesn't work for automatic path-based conventions.
  8. I can defend the plugin + internal marketplace approach to bring the same configuration to 12 repos — and know why security invariants don't travel there.
  9. I can write the full CI invocation (-p, --output-format json + --json-schema → structured_output, --allowedTools, --max-turns, --bare) and name two "flags" that don't exist.
  10. I can explain why the review job must be an independent invocation from the generation job.
  11. Faced with "it works for me, not for him," I know what to run (/status, /memory, /permissions, /context, /doctor) and what each one tells me.
  12. I can state the debugging discipline (reproduce → isolate → fix → verify the mechanism) and the evidence hierarchy, and defend why "the tests pass now" is not a fix. And I can turn a heroic debug into a repeatable one: runbook as a committed skill; invariant as a test or deny rule.
  13. I know that telemetry is off by default, I can name the real metrics (cost.usage, token.usage, session.count, lines_of_code.count, code_edit_tool.decision…), and I know that prompt content is NOT logged by default.
  14. I know that /usage is not governance: team spend lives in the Analytics dashboard / API; the hard ceiling lives in the workspace's spend limits.
  15. I separate activity from outcome and can argue to an executive that "accepted lines +340%" doesn't prove value — by declaring the number and the null-result condition up front.
  16. I can name three things AI-assisted tooling does NOT fix: an ambiguous spec, an authorization boundary, and an organizational bottleneck. And I know that context ≠ attention.
  17. I can recognize the distractor's two signatures in 20 seconds: the one that solves for one person what was asked for a team, and the one that opens up permissions instead of scoping them.
  18. I know this domain is worth 4–5 items and that there's no per-domain minimum — so I don't give it a single hour more than it needs.

certs.retakePolicy: If you fail, you can retake the exam after a mandatory waiting period that grows with each failed attempt: 14 days after the first failure, 30 days after the second, and 90 days after the third. Maximum 4 attempts of the same exam within a rolling 12-month window. Limits apply per exam: failing CCAR-P does not stop you from registering for a different exam in the program. The $175 USD fee is paid on EVERY attempt — there is no free retake.
certs.recertification: The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded. The program limits it in time on purpose, because the underlying technology evolves quickly and they want holders to keep their knowledge current. To renew ON TIME: you review what's changed since you certified and complete a FREE, NON-proctored assessment in the Anthropic Partner Academy. The guide states it explicitly: there is no fee for on-time renewal ("There is no fee for on-time renewal"). If you let the credential lapse, you lose that path: you have to retake the FULL exam and pay the FULL fee to recover certified status. In addition, if exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam instead of the renewal assessment. Holders remain subject to the rules of conduct in Section 12 for as long as they hold the credential.
examDayRules: The exam is administered in a standardized, secure, proctored environment, whether online or at a Pearson VUE test center; the same rules apply in both modalities.
If you test online, you must remain visible to the proctor and the webcam for the entire session.
You must keep your workspace free of notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, and any other material.
Communicating with any other person during the exam is prohibited.
Capturing, copying, photographing, or reproducing exam content in any form is prohibited.
Prohibited items: mobile phones, smart watches, headphones, study materials, and any recording device.
Permitted items (if any), such as scratch paper provided by the proctor, are defined by Pearson VUE — don't assume.
You must present an unexpired, government-issued photo ID; the name on the ID must match your registration EXACTLY.
Before starting, you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement (NDA); if you don't accept it, the session ends and there is NO refund.

Consequences of misconduct: cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in invalidation of your result, revocation of your credential, and a ban on future exams.
No-show or arriving late outside the permitted window: you lose the exam fee and must register again.
certs.scoring: The exam is criterion-referenced: you're measured against a fixed performance standard, NOT against other candidates. You're not competing with anyone — you pass by demonstrating the knowledge and skills in the blueprint. The score is reported on a scale from 100 to 1,000, and the cut score is 720. KEY POINT: 720 is a SCALED score, not a percentage. It does NOT mean 72% correct. The scale starts at 100, not 0, and applies equating to compensate for difficulty differences between exam forms; that's why the actual percentage of correct answers needed to reach 720 isn't calculable from the guide and varies by form. The passing standard was set through a formal standard-setting study in which trained subject matter experts judged the expected performance level of a minimally qualified candidate. The score report gives you: pass/fail status, your scaled score (100–1,000), and the percentage of items correct WITHIN each content domain. Those per-domain percentages are diagnostic only — they help you understand your performance and are NOT used to determine pass/fail, which depends exclusively on your total scaled score. Practical corollary: there is no per-domain minimum you must clear; you can do poorly in one domain and still pass if your total scaled score reaches 720.
howToPrepare: There is no mandatory course. Anthropic does not guarantee that any particular resource will get you a pass. Combine hands-on experience with the resources below.
Study the exam blueprint (Section 6) and self-assess against EVERY objective, one by one.
Review Anthropic's official documentation on the Claude API, models, prompt engineering, MCP, and Skills.
Build AND OPERATE at least one end-to-end solution with Claude that includes RAG, evaluation, and observability — building it isn't enough, you have to operate it.
Practice architectural decision-making: model selection, integration protocols, and security trade-offs.
Work through the sample questions in Section 8 to get familiar with the item style.
registrationSteps: Go to your exam's certification page in the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
Download the Exam Guide and review the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy BEFORE registering.
Register for the exam and complete checkout. The fee shown at checkout already reflects whatever discount applies to your partner tier.
Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account, then log in to schedule your exam session.
Choose an available date and select online proctoring or a Pearson test center. The exam is delivered by Pearson VUE.

If you need accommodations (for a documented disability), request them and wait for Pearson VUE's approval BEFORE scheduling — don't schedule until they're approved (pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations).
You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment. Changes within the preceding 24 hours mean forfeiting the exam fee.

certs.decoderHtml:
CCAR-P Exam Decoder

Claude Certified Architect – Professional · v1.0 · effective July 2026 · 63 items · 120 minutes · cut score 720/1000 scaled

This document doesn't teach you Claude. It teaches you how the items on this specific exam are built, derived from the three official samples in Section 8 and the literal language of the blueprint objectives. Read it once you already know the content: it's built to convert knowledge into points.

0. The fact that reframes everything: this is a JUDGMENT exam, not a recall exam

Read the verbs in the blueprint. They don't say "list," "define," "name," "describe." They say:

Evaluate tool/agent configuration… · Analyze authentication and authorization requirements… · Evaluate accuracy-latency trade-offs and justify configuration decisions · Select appropriate architectural patterns · Diagnose system issues · Apply retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern · Evaluate progressive discovery vs. monolithic context strategy

Almost every objective sits at the analyze / evaluate level of Bloom's taxonomy, not remember. The operational consequence is brutal: memorizing the names of Claude features will not pass this exam. The items hand you a scenario with constraints and ask you to pick the correct action given those constraints. None of the three official samples is answered by knowing a definition; all three are answered by reasoning through a trade-off.

Corollary: when you're torn between two options, don't ask "which one is more true?" Ask "which one answers the constraint the stem bothered to write?"

1. The central rule for answering

The winning option attacks the ROOT CAUSE or structurally eliminates the RISK, while respecting every constraint in the stem and without destroying a requirement.

The three official samples are the same rule wearing three different costumes:

SampleCorrectWhy it wins
1 (Integration/least privilege)B — remove the refund and delete toolsEliminates the capability. It doesn't watch it (A, logging), doesn't interpose a human (C, confirmation), doesn't delegate it to the model's good judgment (D, bigger model).
2 (Prompting/caching)C — put the static content first + prompt cachingSolves both requested metrics (latency and cost) without sacrificing required context. The others optimize one thing by breaking another, or optimize nothing at all.
3 (Evaluation/diagnosis)B — the retrieval/indexing stepPoints to the only component the described event touched (document refresh). The rest contradict the variables the stem froze.

Distilled into three axioms you can apply cold:

  1. Preventive > detective > compensating. If one option eliminates the problem and another detects or contains it, the one that eliminates it wins. (Sample 1: B > A > C.)
  2. No optimization counts if it breaks a requirement. Truncating the policy lowers cost… and defeats the entire reason the policy exists. The correct answer is usually the only one that satisfies the objective without paying for it with a requirement. (Sample 2: C vs. A.)
  3. The cause lives where the change happened. In diagnostic items, the stem hands you the control variables ("latency and model version are unchanged"). The correct answer lives in the variable that actually moved. (Sample 3.)

2. Distractor archetypes (named, with evidence)

Every distractor on this exam has a job. Learn to name them and you'll see them coming.

D1 · The Wrong-Category Control

Offers a real, responsible security measure — but from the wrong phase of the lifecycle. It's the most dangerous distractor because it isn't wrong in the abstract, it's only wrong for what's being asked.

  • Evidence: Sample 1, option A ("add logging so misuse can be audited later"). Logging is good practice; it is not least privilege. It's post-hoc detection.
  • Antidote: classify the option — does it prevent, detect, or compensate? If the stem names a preventive principle (least privilege, defense in depth, data minimization), the answer is preventive.

D2 · The Prudent Mitigation That Doesn't Remove the Privilege

Adds friction, gates, confirmations, reviews. Sounds like a responsible architect. Leaves the dangerous capability alive.

  • Evidence: Sample 1, option C (confirmation before refund/delete). The agent can still delete accounts.
  • Antidote: ask "after applying this option, does the dangerous capability still exist in the system?" If the answer is yes, and another option removes it entirely, the other one wins. Watch for the legitimate exception: if the stem states the business needs that capability, human-in-the-loop flips from distractor to correct answer (Domain 5 lists it as an objective). The stem decides.

D3 · The Model as Security Boundary (or as Universal Fix)

"Use a bigger / better model, one that follows instructions more reliably." Confuses a property of the system (authorization, architecture, data) with a property of the model.

  • Evidence: Sample 1, option D ("replace the agent with a larger model").
  • Antidote: model capability is never a security control, nor a substitute for architecture. If the problem is authz, retrieval, indexing, scope, or data, scaling up the model is almost always wrong. This archetype is the LLM version of "buy more RAM."

D4 · The Self-Incriminating Absolute

Contains a word no architect would use: always, never, regardless, the smallest, the cheapest, all cases, simply.

  • Evidence: Sample 2, option B — "switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit." The text confesses that it ignores fit with the task.
  • Antidote: on an exam whose blueprint literally says "trade-offs" four times, any option that denies the existence of a trade-off is false. Flag it and move on.

D5 · The Optimization That Breaks the Requirement

Improves the requested metric, but pays for it with information or functionality the scenario declared necessary.

  • Evidence: Sample 2, option A (truncating the policy document to 1,000 tokens). Lowers cost and latency — and mutilates the policy that governs behavior.
  • Antidote: for every option, ask "what do I lose?" If what you lose is something the stem presented as a requirement ("policy document," "compliance," "audit"), discard it.

D6 · The Relabel With No Effect (null action)

Moves, renames, or relocates something using correct blueprint vocabulary, without changing any of the variables that matter.

  • Evidence: Sample 2, option D ("move the policy document into a few-shot example block"). You're still sending ~8,000 tokens on every request. Zero impact on cost, zero on latency, zero cacheable prefix.
  • Antidote: simulate the option numerically. How many tokens get sent after the change? How many ms? If the numbers don't move, the option does nothing.

D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem

Proposes as the cause something the text itself already declared unchanged.

  • Evidence: Sample 3, option A ("the model weights have silently changed") when the stem says "model version unchanged."
  • Antidote: underline the control variables before you even look at the options. Any option that violates them dies without discussion.

D8 · The Irrelevant Dial

Names a real parameter (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, context window) with a causal relationship to the symptom that's inverted or nonexistent.

  • Evidence: Sample 3, option C ("the temperature setting is too low") — low temperature produces more deterministic outputs, not new, confidently wrong answers; and nobody touched temperature in the incident.
  • Antidote: demand a complete causal chain: event → mechanism → observed symptom. If you can't narrate it in one sentence, it isn't the answer.

3. Stem signals → the domain being tested

Identifying the domain in 5 seconds tells you which mental framework to load and which distractor archetype to expect. The relative weight tells you where to invest study time: Integration 19% > Solution Design 17% > Evaluation 16% > Governance 14% = Stakeholder 14% > Models/Prompting 13% > Developer Productivity 7%.

Lexical signal in the stemDomainFramework to load
"least privilege", "tools the agent can call", "capability bloat", "auth/authz", "MCP vs API/CLI vs agent-to-agent", "chunking", "indexing", "retrieval strategy", "progressive discovery vs monolithic", "observability at scale"3 — Integration (19%)Remove > watch. The right protocol for the data's shape. Retrieval that matches the query pattern.
"translate this business problem", "end-to-end architecture", "workflow vs agentic vs augmented LLM", "multi-agent", "orchestration", "decompose", "SLA", "business value"1 — Solution Design (17%)The simplest pattern that satisfies the requirement. Agentic only if the problem demands it.
"metrics", "eval dataset", "A/B test", "hallucinations", "confident but incorrect", "regression after X", "diagnose", "cost-performance", "logging"4 — Evaluation (16%)Causal diagnosis: what changed? Metrics before intuition.
"guardrails", "GDPR/HIPAA/FedRAMP", "PII", "human-in-the-loop", "bias", "fairness", "transparency", "failure modes", "risk"5 — Governance (14%)Compliance is not negotiable against latency. Preventive control first.
"stakeholder", "discovery", "requirements", "expectation", "handoff", "document the architecture", "communicate the trade-off", "executive"6 — Stakeholder & Lifecycle (14%)Communicate the trade-off honestly, align expectations, don't overpromise.
"system prompt", "few-shot", "chain-of-thought", "context window", "token usage", "prompt caching", "Skills", "modular prompts", "same prompt every request"2 — Models & Prompting (13%)Stable content first + cache. Choose the model by fit, never by size per se.
"Claude Code", "team environment", "developer workflow", "debugging", "onboarding devs"7 — Developer Productivity (7%)Team enablement; the smallest domain — don't gift it extra study time.

The stem's verb = the expected cognitive level. "Which change best reduces risk?", "Which optimization most directly addresses both?", "What is the most likely first place to investigate?" — note the three superlatives. This exam almost never asks "which one is valid?"; it asks "which one is best / first / most direct?" That means more than one option can be technically defensible, and only one is optimal. Don't hunt for the single true answer: rank the true ones and pick the highest-ranked.

4. Elimination technique, step by step

Apply it in this order. With 63 items in 120 minutes, you have ~1 min 54 s per item: the process has to be mechanical.

Step 0 — Read the last line first. The real question sits at the end ("which change best reduces risk?"). Knowing what's being asked before you read the scenario stops the scenario from hijacking you.

Step 1 — Extract the constraints and mark them. Three types:

  • Objective: what has to be achieved (reduce risk / lower cost AND latency / find the cause).
  • Untouchable requirements: what CANNOT be broken (the policy, compliance, business functionality).
  • Control variables: what the stem declares unchanged ("latency and model version are unchanged," "support staff only ever need to read tickets"). These are ammunition. They almost always kill one or two distractors on their own.

Step 2 — Name the domain using the table in Section 3. Load the framework.

Step 3 — Sweep for absolutes. Scan all four options hunting for regardless / always / never / smallest / cheapest / simply. Cross them out (D4). Usually one falls right away.

Step 4 — Sweep for contradiction. Cross out any option that violates a control variable (D7). In Sample 3 this eliminates A immediately.

Step 5 — Destruction test. For every surviving option: what requirement does it sacrifice? If it sacrifices a stated one, it's out (D5).

Step 6 — Null-effect test. For every surviving option: what number moves? (tokens, ms, USD, attack surface, number of tools). If none, it's out (D6).

Step 7 — Category test. Among the survivors, classify each: does it prevent, detect, or compensate? Does it attack the cause or the symptom? The preventive/causal option wins (D1, D2).

Step 8 — Security-boundary test. Does any option delegate to the model (or to its size) something the system should be guaranteeing instead? It's out (D3).

Step 9 — Causal-chain test. If it's a diagnostic item, narrate it in one sentence: event → mechanism → symptom. The option that completes the sentence wins; the ones that don't, don't.

Step 10 — Multiple-response: the item tells you how many to select ("each item states how many responses to select"). Count. Never fail to mark the exact number. And watch out: on multiple-response items, distractors usually come in same-family pairs (two detective controls, two cosmetic optimizations) — if two options are nearly synonymous, chances are neither is in the key, or both are; decide it with the framework, not by resemblance.

Time management. ~2 minutes per item, with no real cushion. Rule: if you haven't narrowed it to two survivors by the 90-second mark, mark your best guess, flag it, and move on. An Integration item (19%) is worth exactly the same as a Developer Productivity item (7%): there's no prize for suffering. Save the last 10 minutes for the flagged ones.

5. Typical mental errors for THIS candidate profile

The MQC is a senior architect with 3+ years in systems and 6+ months of LLMs in production. Their experience is their greatest asset… and the exact source of their failures on this exam.

1. Reflexive over-engineering. The senior architect loves complete solutions: "logging and confirmation and a better model." The exam rewards the minimal intervention that resolves the root cause. Sample 1 proves it: the correct answer is deleting two lines of configuration, not building an audit system. If your instinct says "I'd do all four things," ask yourself which one you'd do first — that's the answer.

2. Confusing model capability with system guarantee. The most expensive bias of the LLM era. "A better model will follow the instructions." No. A model is never an authorization boundary, a compliance control, or a correctness guarantee. If the proposed fix lives inside the model and the problem lives in the system (authz, indexing, scope, data), it's a distractor.

3. Reading "720" as "72%." The score is scaled across a 100–1,000 range with equating. It is not a percentage of correct answers. And the per-domain percentages on the score report are diagnostic: they don't determine pass/fail, which depends exclusively on the total scaled score. Practical consequence: there is no per-domain minimum; don't sacrifice easy items in a large domain by wrestling with a hard one in another.

4. Ignoring the control variables. The candidate in a hurry reads the symptom ("confident but incorrect") and fires off "hallucination! lower the temperature!" without noticing that the stem already froze the model and latency and pointed at a document refresh. The words "unchanged," "only ever," "already," "same" are free ammunition. Underline them.

5. Choosing by vocabulary recognition. Seeing "few-shot" or "chain-of-thought" in an option and feeling like it sounds correct because it's in the blueprint. Sample 2, option D uses impeccable vocabulary and does absolutely nothing. The exam knows you recognize the terms; that's exactly why it puts them in the distractors.

6. Optimizing one metric when two are requested. "Latency and cost are both concerns." Truncating improves both… by destroying the policy. When the stem asks for two objectives, the correct answer covers both, with no collateral damage. Count the objectives before you choose.

7. Hunting for the single true option. This exam builds distractors that are true but suboptimal. Logging is good. Confirming before deleting is good. Neither is the best. If you catch yourself thinking "but A is also correct," you're in a ranking item: go back to the stem's superlative ("best," "most directly," "first") and rank.

8. Treating governance as a negotiable tax. In Domain 5 items, compliance (GDPR/HIPAA/FedRAMP) and safety are not traded away for latency or cost. If an option proposes relaxing a regulatory control to gain performance, it's a distractor — no matter how elegant the trade-off sounds.

9. Under-preparing Domain 6 because it's "soft." Stakeholder communication and lifecycle carries 14% — the same weight as Governance and more than Prompting. The engineering profile tends to dismiss it and study features instead. These items are answered with the same trade-off logic: the correct option communicates the compromise honestly and aligns expectations (SLAs included); the traps are overpromising, hiding uncertainty, or dragging irrelevant technical detail in front of an executive.

6. Pocket card (memorize it)

  • The correct answer eliminates the cause; the distractors watch it, contain it, or delegate it to the model.
  • Variables declared unchanged = free dead distractors.
  • Absolute word (regardless, always, smallest) = instant discard.
  • Optimization that erases required context = discard.
  • Option that doesn't move a single number = discard.
  • Bigger model ≠ security control, ≠ architecture, ≠ correct retrieval.
  • Two metrics requested → the correct answer covers both, with no damage.
  • Superlative in the stem (best / most / first) → it's ranking, not true/false.
  • Multiple-response: the item tells you how many to mark. Count.
  • ~1:54 per item. At 90 s with no two finalists: mark, flag, move on.
certs.logisticsHtml:
CCAR-P Exam Logistics

Claude Certified Architect – Professional · Exam Guide v1.0 · effective July 2026 Everything operational: registration, scheduling, exam day, policies, and what to do when something goes wrong. Source: the official exam guide. Where the guide doesn't specify something, that's stated explicitly.

1. Quick reference

ItemValue
CodeCCAR-P
Items63
FormatMultiple-choice and multiple-response. Each item states how many answers to select.
Time120 minutes (~1 min 54 s per item)
DeliveryProctored: online proctored and/or test center, per program policy. Delivered by Pearson VUE.
Passing score720 on a 100–1,000 scale (scaled, NOT 72% correct)
Fee$175 USD per attempt
Validity12 months from the date the credential is awarded
Score reportPass/fail + scaled score + % correct by domain (diagnostic, doesn't decide pass/fail)
PrerequisitesNone mandatory. Recommended experience is not a requirement.
LanguageThe guide doesn't publish a list of available languages. The official sample items are in English.
Registration name supportcertifications-support@anthropic.com
General supportpearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html

2. Registration, step by step

Registration runs through Anthropic Partner Academy, and scheduling runs through Pearson VUE. They're two separate systems: you pay in Academy first, then schedule in VUE.

  1. Go to the certification page in the Anthropic Partner Academy and review the exam details.
  2. Download the Exam Guide and read the Certification Terms and Conditions and the Certification Exam Policy before registering. This isn't a decorative formality: by sitting the exam, you become subject to both.
  3. Register and complete checkout. The price you see already reflects whatever discount applies to your partner tier — if the number doesn't match the $175 USD list price, that's why.
  4. Follow the confirmation instructions to create your Pearson VUE account. Then log in to VUE.
  5. Schedule your session: pick an available date and modality — online proctoring or Pearson test center.
  6. If you need accommodations, do NOT schedule yet. (See Section 4.)

Before you pay, verify this

  • Your legal name. The name on the registration must match your official ID exactly. If it doesn't, fix it before scheduling by writing to certifications-support@anthropic.com. A mismatch on exam day = access denied and you lose the fee.
  • Your partner tier, if you're expecting a discount.
  • That the date leaves you margin: rescheduling within the previous 24 hours costs the full fee.

3. Online proctoring vs. test center

The guide allows both modalities ("online proctored and/or test center, per program policy"). The rules of conduct are identical in both. The choice is logistical, not about difficulty.

Online proctored (OnVUE) — you sit the exam from home or your office.

  • You must stay visible to the proctor and the webcam for the entire session. Stepping out of frame is an incident.
  • You're responsible for the environment: clear desk, no noise, no interruptions, nobody entering the room.
  • You're responsible for your connection and your equipment. A network drop during a 120-minute exam is your problem.
  • Advantage: zero commute, more scheduling windows.

Pearson test center — you sit the exam at a physical site.

  • Controlled infrastructure: the center provides the equipment, network, and proctoring.
  • Less surface area for technical failure. It's the defensive option if your home isn't a reliable environment (unstable internet, housemates, noise).
  • Extra advantage: you shed the burden of proving your room is clean.

Practical recommendation: if your internet has failed even once in the last 3 months, or you can't guarantee 2.5 hours of total isolation, go to a test center. The cost of a session invalidated by a proctoring incident is the full fee.

If you choose online: run the OnVUE system test / check days in advance, not an hour before. And plan to arrive early for check-in — the process (ID photo, camera room scan, verification) takes time, and the late-arrival window is finite.

4. Accommodations

  • Reasonable accommodations are available for candidates with documented disabilities or needs, in accordance with applicable law.
  • Pearson VUE requests and approves them, not Anthropic.
  • Hard rule: do NOT schedule your appointment until your request is approved. The guide is explicit about this. If you schedule first, the process gets complicated.
  • Request them at: pearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations
  • Operational translation: if you're going to request extended time or another accommodation, start the process weeks before your target date, not days.

5. Cancellation and rescheduling — the 24-hour rule

You can cancel or reschedule up to 24 hours before your appointment. Any change within the preceding 24 hours means forfeiting the exam fee.

And the flip side:

No-show and late arrival. If you don't show up for your scheduled appointment, or you arrive after the permitted late-arrival window, you lose the fee and must register again (another $175 USD).

Practical consequences:

  • Treat the T-24 h marker as a real deadline. If, 25 hours out from your exam, you sense you're not going to make it, reschedule now: it's free. At 23 hours out, it costs $175 USD.
  • Arrive with margin. "Running late" isn't just a test-center thing — online, taking too long at check-in also eats into your window.

6. Identification

  • You need an unexpired, government-issued photo ID.
  • The name on the ID must match the name on your registration EXACTLY. No variations, no abbreviations, no missing surnames.
  • Need to correct the name on your registration? certifications-support@anthropic.com, and do it before scheduling.
  • This is administrative failure #1 in certification programs. Verify it today, not on exam day.

7. Exam-day rules and what's prohibited

The exam is administered in a standardized, secure, proctored environment. These rules protect the integrity of the credential for everyone who holds it.

During the exam you MUST:

  • Stay visible to the proctor and the webcam for the entire session (if testing online).
  • Keep your workspace clear of notes, books, phones, secondary monitors, and any other material.
  • Refrain from communicating with any other person during the exam.
  • Do NOT capture, copy, photograph, or reproduce exam content in any form.

Prohibited items (the guide's explicit list):

  • Mobile phones
  • Smart watches
  • Headphones
  • Study materials
  • Any recording device

Permitted items:

  • Pearson VUE defines these, not you. The guide mentions as an example scratch paper provided by the proctor — "if any." Don't assume you'll have paper, a whiteboard, or a calculator: confirm it in your appointment instructions.

Consequences of misconduct

Cheating, attempting to access prohibited resources, or disclosing exam content can result in:

  • Invalidation of your result
  • Revocation of your credential
  • A ban on future exams

There's no gray zone. A phone on the desk, even powered off, is an incident.

8. NDA (confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement)

  • Before the exam begins you must accept a confidentiality and non-disclosure agreement.
  • By accepting it you acknowledge that all exam content — questions, answer options, and scenarios — is confidential, proprietary property of Anthropic, and you commit to not disclosing, reproducing, or distributing any portion of it.
  • If you do NOT accept the agreement, the session ends and NO refund is issued. You've lost the $175 USD.
  • Real-world scope: you can't post questions on forums, you can't "share what came up" with a colleague, you can't reconstruct items from memory in a blog post. This survives the exam — it stays in force afterward.
  • Credential holders remain subject to the rules of conduct for as long as they hold it.

9. Retake policy

Failed attemptMandatory wait before the next one
After the 1st failure14 days
After the 2nd failure30 days
After the 3rd failure90 days
  • Maximum 4 attempts of the same exam within a rolling 12-month window.
  • Limits apply per exam. Failing CCAR-P does not stop you from registering for a different exam in the program.
  • The fee applies on every attempt. There's no free retake: each attempt is $175 USD.

Strategic read: with growing wait times and payment per attempt, showing up "just to see how it goes" is expensive and blocks your calendar. Use the blueprint's objective list as a self-assessment checklist before you pay.

10. How scoring works (what matters operationally)

  • Criterion-referenced exam: you're measured against a fixed standard, not against other candidates. No curve, no quota.
  • The standard was set through a formal standard-setting study: trained subject matter experts judged the expected performance of a minimally qualified candidate.
  • Scale: 100–1,000. Cut score: 720.
  • 720 is NOT 72% correct. It's a scaled score. The scale starts at 100, and equating is applied to compensate for difficulty differences between exam forms. The actual percentage of correct answers required isn't derivable from the guide.
  • The score report includes the percentage correct by domain. Those percentages are informational/diagnostic: they are NOT used to determine pass/fail. Pass/fail depends exclusively on your total scaled score.
  • Corollary for in-room strategy: there's no per-domain minimum. You can do poorly in one domain and still pass. Don't get stuck on a hard item in one domain "because I have to nail that domain" — that constraint doesn't exist.

11. Appeals and complaints

  • You have 14 days to appeal, counted from:
    • the date you're notified of the decision you're appealing, or
    • your exam date, if your concern is about the result.
  • Where: appeals are filed with Pearson VUE support (pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html).
  • Appeals are reviewed under the program's appeals policy.
  • NOT appealable:
    • the outcome of the standard-setting study (meaning, you can't dispute that the cut score is 720), and
    • the content of individual items (you can't contest a specific question).
  • In practice: appeals exist for process irregularities (a proctoring incident, a technical failure, an administrative error), not for "I think I deserved more points."

12. Recertification and maintaining the credential

  • The credential is valid for 12 months from the date it's awarded. This is deliberately temporary: the underlying technology evolves fast, and the program wants holders to keep their knowledge current.
  • On-time renewal (the cheap path): you review what's changed since you certified and complete a free, NON-proctored assessment in the Anthropic Partner Academy. The guide says it plainly: there's no fee for on-time renewal.
  • If you let it lapse: you lose that path. You must retake the FULL exam and pay the FULL fee ($175 USD) to recover certified status.
  • Exception: if exam content changes significantly, Anthropic may require holders to retake the full exam instead of the renewal assessment.
  • Holders remain subject to the rules of conduct for as long as they hold the credential.

Concrete action: set a calendar reminder for 10 months out from the date you're awarded the credential. Renewing on time is free and non-proctored; letting it lapse costs $175 USD and 120 minutes under a webcam.

13. Support and privacy

I need to…Contact
Correct the name on my registrationcertifications-support@anthropic.com (do it before scheduling)
Registration, scheduling, accommodations, results, appeals — everything elsePearson VUE support: pearsonvue.com/us/en/anthropic.html
Request accommodationspearsonvue.com/us/en/test-takers/accommodations

Privacy. Personal data collected during registration and testing is handled in accordance with Anthropic's privacy policy, Pearson VUE's privacy policy, and applicable data protection law.

14. Operational checklist

Weeks before

  • Registration name = official ID name, exact match.
  • Accommodations requested and approved by Pearson VUE (if applicable) — before scheduling.
  • Terms & Conditions and Certification Exam Policy read.
  • Self-assessment against every objective in the blueprint (all 7 domains).
  • At least one end-to-end solution built AND operated with Claude (RAG + evaluation + observability).

When scheduling

  • Modality chosen deliberately (test center if your environment or internet isn't reliable).
  • Date with margin: you know exactly when your T-24 h mark falls.

If testing online — days before

  • OnVUE system test run and passed.
  • Room identified and clearable: no notes, no books, no second monitor, no phone.
  • Isolation plan for ~2.5 hours (nobody enters, nothing makes noise).

On the day

  • Valid official ID physically in hand.
  • Clear desk: no phone, no smart watch, no headphones, no study materials, no recording devices.
  • Early check-in (the late-arrival window is finite and gets eaten by the verification process).
  • Accept the NDA (if you don't accept it: session terminated, no refund).

In the room

  • ~1 min 54 s per item. At 90 s with no two finalists: mark your best guess, flag it, move on.
  • On multiple-response, the item tells you how many to select. Count.
  • Last ~10 minutes: review flagged items.
  • Remember: there's no per-domain minimum. Only the total scaled score counts.

Afterward

  • Calendar reminder at 10 months → free, non-proctored renewal.
  • If something went wrong in the process: you have 14 days to appeal to Pearson VUE.

questions.stem: A team exposes a customer-support agent that can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds, and delete user accounts. Support staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies. Applying least-privilege principles, which change best reduces risk?

options.text: Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited later.
Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely.
Keep all tools but add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.

questions.explanationEs: The stem names the principle explicitly ("applying least-privilege principles") and describes a case of capability bloat: the agent has four tools but the role only needs two. Least privilege is a PREVENTIVE control: it is exercised by REMOVING the capability, not by watching it. That's why B is the only option that attacks the attack surface itself — without the refund and delete tools in the configuration, the agent cannot execute them, whether via prompt injection, hallucination, or a malicious operator. A (logging) is a DETECTIVE control: you find out about the damage after it happened; it doesn't reduce the privilege, it only audits it. C (confirmation) is a COMPENSATING control that moves the decision to an already-fatigued human, still leaves the capability alive, and is vulnerable to rubber-stamping and to manipulation of the text shown to the approver. D (larger model) confuses MODEL CAPABILITY with AUTHORIZATION SCOPE: no model, however good, is a security boundary — authorization is a property of the system, not of the model's reasoning. Exam takeaway: when the question invokes least privilege, the answer is to remove, not to observe or to ask.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 1: B. Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not require, eliminating the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it. Logging (A) and confirmations (C) are detective/compensating controls, not removal of unnecessary privilege; model size (D) is unrelated to authorization scope.
questions.trap: A = Wrong-Category Control (detective instead of preventive): plausible from a security standpoint, but it answers a different phase of the lifecycle. C = Partial Mitigation That Sounds Prudent: adds friction but does NOT remove the privilege; it exploits the bias that 'more control = better'. D = The-Model-as-Security-Boundary: wrong-domain distractor that swaps an authorization decision for a model-selection decision; it's the 'buy bigger hardware/model' archetype that shows up throughout the exam and is almost never correct.

questions.stem: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost are both concerns. Which optimization most directly addresses both?

options.text: Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit.
Place the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching.
Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.

questions.explanationEs: The stem hands you every signal of the cacheable pattern: large content, STATIC, repeated on every request, followed by a short, VARYING portion. And it asks you to optimize TWO axes at once (latency and cost). Prompt caching works on PREFIXES: the system reuses the identical leading span between calls, so order matters — stable content goes first, dynamic content last. That attacks both time-to-first-token (the prefix isn't reprocessed) and per-request cost (cached tokens are billed at a reduced rate) at once, and it doesn't sacrifice required context. A (truncate) does lower cost and latency, but it DESTROYS information the system needs: the policy is there for a reason, and mutilating it changes behavior — it optimizes one metric by breaking the requirement. B (smaller model "regardless of task fit") carries the trap written into the text itself: 'regardless of whether it fits the task' is an admission that it degrades quality; an architect doesn't switch models blindly. D (moving the policy into a few-shot block) is cosmetic relocation: it changes the LABEL on the content, not its volume or its cacheable position; you're still sending and paying for the same ~8,000 tokens on every request, and using a policy as few-shot examples is a misuse of the technique besides. Exam takeaway: large stable content + variable suffix + cost/latency pressure = order stable content first + prompt caching.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 2: C. Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets repeated prefixes be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. Truncation (A) loses needed policy; downsizing blindly (B) risks quality; relocating to few-shot (D) does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix.
questions.trap: A = Optimization-That-Breaks-the-Requirement: improves the requested metric at the cost of removing necessary context (the classic 'truncate/trim'). B = Self-Incriminating-Absolute: the phrase 'regardless of task fit' is the red flag; any option that says 'always', 'regardless', 'the cheapest' is usually false on a trade-offs exam. D = Relabeling-Without-Effect: moves the content around and sounds technical ('few-shot'), but changes neither metric — a null-action distractor that trades on recognizing a blueprint term.

questions.stem: A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. What is the most likely first place to investigate?

options.text: The model weights have silently changed.
The retrieval/indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
The temperature setting is too low.
The context window has shrunk.

questions.explanationEs: This is a causal-diagnosis item, and the technique is to read the VARIABLES THE STEM FREEZES. You're told latency didn't change and the model version didn't change; the only thing that changed was the document refresh. By causal elimination, the failure has to live in the component that refresh touches: the retrieval/indexing pipeline. Confident-but-wrong is, on top of that, the classic signature of bad context: the model is reasoning correctly over chunks that are wrong, stale, or badly embedded (a broken re-index, embeddings from a different embedding-model version, orphaned chunks, misaligned metadata), which is exactly why it sounds convincing while being wrong. A (the model weights silently changed) directly contradicts the stem, which pins the model version; besides, a versioned model's weights don't change underneath you. C (temperature too low) is incoherent with the symptom: low temperature produces more deterministic outputs, not new hallucinations — and in any case nobody touched temperature in this incident. D (the context window shrank) is a configuration change nobody made, and one that would show up as truncation or errors, not as confident, false answers; a document refresh doesn't trigger it either. Exam takeaway: in troubleshooting, the correct answer is the component the described event actually touched — everything else is a variable the stem already declared stable.
questions.officialRationale: Sample 3: B. Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options would not be triggered specifically by a document refresh.
questions.trap: A = Contradicts-the-Stem: offers a cause the text itself already ruled out ('model version unchanged'); it punishes anyone who skips the control conditions.
