questions.objective: Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment (including SLAs)
questions.scenario: Announcing a fix after running the eval suite
questions.stem: After a prompt change, an engineer reruns the eval suite: a case that used to fail now passes, and the rest of the suite stays green. Which statement is the most accurate way to describe this evidence to stakeholders?

options.text: 'The model itself reports high confidence that the issue is fixed, so the team is confident too.'
'We verified that the fix resolves the previously failing case, and we did not detect a regression elsewhere in the suite.'
'The updated prompt reads more clearly and the demo we ran for leadership went smoothly, so the fix is confirmed.'
'The engineer who wrote the fix reviewed it and believes it looks correct, so it can be announced to stakeholders as verified.'

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Manage stakeholder feedback loops and expectation alignment' on its evaluation-backed-claims rule: the verb you use depends on the real evidence behind it. An eval that used to fail and now passes gets announced as 'we verified that X'; an existing suite staying green gets announced as 'we did not detect a regression.' B uses both verbs exactly where they belong. The model's self-reported confidence is never evidence for a stakeholder — it's exactly the kind of number with no method, no n, and no date that this domain forbids promising.

distractorsEs.A: D2 · Prudent Mitigation That Keeps the Privilege (a false control): the 'confidence' the model reports about itself looks like a check, but it isn't an SLI or an eval — it's a promise disguised as a control, just like an SLA with no SLI behind it.
distractorsEs.C: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect: 'the code reads better' and 'the demo went well' are, literally, the row in the chapter's evidence table marked 'not evidence of quality.' No number moved.
distractorsEs.D: D4 · Self-Incriminating Absolute: the evidence hierarchy only permits saying 'I believe X' when the basis is 'I reviewed it and it looks right.' Announcing it as 'verified' turns a belief into an absolute the evidence doesn't support.

questions.trap: D is the most dangerous because it almost gets it right: there was human review, which is real work. But upgrading it from 'I believe' to 'verified' is lying even if the fix turns out to be correct.

questions.objective: Document architectures and provide implementation guidance
questions.scenario: The handoff that was a 40-slide deck
questions.stem: Three weeks after an agent ships, the receiving operations team cannot diagnose an incident because the only handoff was a 40-slide deck and a recorded 90-minute walkthrough. Which combination of artifacts correctly satisfies the handoff exit gate -- an engineer who did not build the system can reproduce, operate, and diagnose it from the documentation alone?

options.text: A runbook written as a versioned Agent Skill, an executable eval suite, declarative tool and permission configuration, versioned prompts, and the ADRs behind the key decisions.
Access to a larger, more capable Claude model, so the agent needs less operator intervention going forward.
A single additional onboarding meeting where the receiving team can ask the original architect questions directly.
An even more detailed slide deck, plus a second, longer knowledge-transfer recording.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Document architectures and provide implementation guidance.' On a platform built with Claude, much of the highest-leverage documentation is the kind the system executes. A brings the chapter's full package: a runbook written as a Skill (both human and agent use it), an executable eval suite (the specification that catches regression), declarative config (the control lives in code, not in a verbal agreement), versioned prompts (rollback is possible), and the ADRs (so nobody 'improves' the system by undoing a constraint that existed for a reason). The exit criterion is the receiving team's capability, not the sender's effort.

distractorsEs.B: D3 · Model as Universal Solution: a larger model doesn't substitute for a runbook, an eval suite, or declarative configuration. Model capability is never a substitute for operational documentation.
distractorsEs.C: D2 · Prudent Mitigation That Keeps the Privilege (a false control): another meeting still leaves nothing verifiable behind — it's the same pattern that already failed (the 90-minute recorded session) under a different name.
distractorsEs.D: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect (cosmetic fix): more slides and more recording change no operational variable. The deck is exactly the artifact the chapter flags as cosmetic next to an executable runbook.

questions.trap: D is this domain's classic trap: the intuitive reaction to a failed handoff is 'document it better' -- but more of the same cosmetic artifact is still not an operable artifact.

questions.objective: Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration)
questions.scenario: Skipping the monitoring dashboard to hit the launch date
questions.stem: To hit an aggressive launch date, the delivery team proposes shipping without building a monitoring dashboard: 'we'll keep an eye on the error-rate graphs we already have, and set up proper monitoring next quarter.' What is the strongest objection the architect should raise, grounded in the lifecycle framework?

options.text: Approve the plan and move forward -- the team can always add proper monitoring once the initial launch metrics look stable.
Approve the plan as long as the team promises the system will never go down without someone noticing.

Skipping the monitoring phase doesn't eliminate the risk, it postpones it -- and the existing error-rate graphs won't surface the signals that actually matter (for example, refusal, max_tokens, pause_turn, or a tool call returning is_error: true), all of which return HTTP 200 and are invisible on that dashboard.
Object only mildly, since the design and handoff phases matter more for a successful launch than monitoring does.

questions.explanationEs: Measures 'Support lifecycle phases (discovery, design, handoff, monitoring, iteration).' Every phase produces a mandatory artifact and a gate; monitoring is no exception: a dashboard with the agreed-on SLIs, alerts, and a review cadence -- and those SLIs must be exactly the SLA's, including the ones that aren't HTTP errors. C names the two things the chapter demands you see together: 'skipping a phase doesn't eliminate the risk, it postpones it' and the concrete fact that refusal/max_tokens/pause_turn/is_error all arrive as 200, so a generic error-rate dashboard doesn't see them. A phase whose output is 'a meeting' or 'an occasional glance' didn't happen.

distractorsEs.A: D5 · Optimization That Breaks the Requirement (confident shortcut): 'we'll add it later' is the exact shape of the shortcut the chapter describes -- it buys time now and postpones the cost, it doesn't eliminate it.
distractorsEs.B: D4 · Self-Incriminating Absolute: promising the system will 'never' fail without someone noticing is an impossible guarantee over a non-deterministic system, and it doesn't substitute for a dashboard with instrumented SLIs.
distractorsEs.D: D1 · Wrong-Category Control: design and handoff are real phases with real artifacts, but the stem asks specifically about monitoring -- downplaying the phase being skipped is not an objection to skipping it.

questions.trap: A is the most tempting because it sounds pragmatic and common-sense -- but 'we'll add it later' is precisely the pattern the chapter names as postponing the cost, not eliminating it.

questions.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
questions.scenario: Team conventions on repository clone
questions.stem: Orion Freight has 45 engineers working across 18 repositories. A staff engineer, Dana, has spent months tuning a Bash test/lint allowlist and a set of coding conventions, but they currently live in Dana's own `~/.claude/settings.json` and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Engineering leadership wants every engineer — including new hires — to have the same allowlist and conventions automatically active the moment they run `git clone` on any of the 18 repositories, with no manual setup step. There is no requirement yet that the rules be impossible to override. Which change best satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Have Dana export `~/.claude/` as a zip file, post it in the team wiki, and instruct every engineer to copy its contents into their own home directory.
Move the allowlist entries into a `.claude/settings.json` at the root of each repository and the conventions into a `CLAUDE.md` at the root of each repository, then commit both files.
Deploy the allowlist and conventions as organization-wide managed policy settings pushed to every engineer's machine via MDM, independent of which repository is open.
Move the allowlist entries into `.claude/settings.local.json` at the root of each repository, so the rules take effect immediately without going through a pull request review.

questions.explanationEs: The objective measures 'Configure Claude tools and environments for teams,' and the lexical signal is exact: 'when they clone... any of the 18 repositories,' with no mention of making the rules impossible to disable. The chapter's Law 2 is literal: everything living under `~/` belongs to Dana and only Dana — it never travels through git. The only way for the allowlist and conventions to appear automatically on clone is to commit them inside the repo: `.claude/settings.json` (Project scope, shared and reviewable in the PR) and `CLAUDE.md` (project memory, always loaded on startup). B is exactly the 'Project' scope from the precedence table.

distractorsEs.A: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect. Distributing a zip of `~/.claude/` on the wiki 'sounds like' sharing the configuration, but it doesn't change a single file inside the repo: three months in, there are seven drifting copies (the same pattern as Northwind Logistics with Diego), and the new engineer still receives nothing on clone.
distractorsEs.C: D1 · Wrong-Category Control. Managed settings is a real, responsible mechanism — but from the wrong layer: it's deployed via MDM, not via `git clone`, and the stem didn't ask for 'nobody can disable it,' only that everyone has it on clone. It's over-engineering that, on top of that, doesn't solve the literal requirement.
distractorsEs.D: D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem. `.claude/settings.local.json` is auto-gitignored by design — it is precisely the file that does NOT travel with `git clone`. The very advantage the option offers ('without going through a PR') is the proof that it's personal, not shared, and it contradicts the stem's central requirement.

questions.trap: D is the most dangerous option: it uses '.claude/' and 'settings' vocabulary that sounds like the correct answer, but `.local.json` itself is structurally incapable of traveling through `git clone`.

questions.objective: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (e.g., Claude Code)
questions.scenario: The bypassPermissions shortcut under audit
questions.stem: Vantage Diagnostics rolls out Claude Code to its 30-engineer platform team. Within two weeks, engineers are complaining that permission prompts for routine commands (`npm run test`, `npm run lint`, `git status`) interrupt their flow constantly. A tech lead proposes setting `"defaultMode": "bypassPermissions"` in the repository's `.claude/settings.json` so nobody gets blocked. Separately, the compliance team requires (1) a reviewable record of exactly what the agent is allowed to touch, and (2) a guarantee that no individual engineer can turn off the prohibition on reading credential files, regardless of local settings or CLI flags. Which configuration change satisfies both compliance requirements while also removing the noisy prompts?

options.text: Move `Read(./.env)` out of an implicit block and into `permissions.ask` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, so an engineer is prompted to confirm before Claude reads it.
Set `"defaultMode": "bypassPermissions"` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, as the tech lead proposed.
Leave the existing prompts untouched and add a line to `CLAUDE.md` stating: 'NEVER read `.env` files under any circumstances.'

Add the noisy, safe commands (`Bash(npm run test:*)`, `Bash(npm run lint)`, `Bash(git status)`) to `permissions.allow` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`, add `Read(./.env)` to `permissions.deny`, and set `disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"` in the organization's managed settings.

questions.explanationEs: This is the domain's archetypal item: the stem doesn't ask you to choose between speed and auditability, it asks for both — and `allow`/`deny` are independent axes (Law 3). The noisy, safe commands go into `allow` in the committed `.claude/settings.json`: the prompt disappears and the scope stays written and reviewable in the PR, which is exactly the 'reviewable record' compliance asked for. `Read(./.env)` goes into `deny`, which wins even under `bypassPermissions`. And the requirement 'no engineer can disable it, regardless of local flags' is only satisfied by `disableBypassPermissionsMode: "disable"` in managed settings — the only level that neither a `.local.json` nor a CLI flag can override.

distractorsEs.A: D2 · Prudent Mitigation That Keeps the Privilege. Putting `.env` in `ask` leaves the capability to read it alive: it still depends on a tired engineer saying no. The stem asks for a guarantee, and `ask` is never a guarantee.
distractorsEs.B: D5 · Optimization That Breaks the Requirement — this domain's signature distractor. `bypassPermissions` does remove the prompts (it improves the requested metric), but it pays for that with the auditability requirement and the non-optionality requirement: nothing stops any engineer from re-enabling it. It sounds like tech-lead pragmatism; it breaks exactly what compliance asked for.
distractorsEs.C: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect. A line in CLAUDE.md is a text request to the model ('a request, not a guarantee' — Law 1), with a non-zero failure rate. It isn't a control, and it doesn't even reduce the prompts that were bothering the team.

questions.trap: B is the confident shortcut: it looks like it resolves the team's complaint (zero prompts), but it's precisely the option compliance came to prohibit. Recognizing it in 20 seconds is this domain's core skill.

questions.objective: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
questions.scenario: An automated review job in CI
questions.stem: A platform team wants to add an automated diff-review job to its CI pipeline using Claude Code. The job must: (1) never hang waiting for interactive input, (2) produce output that a downstream step can parse programmatically and post as inline PR comments, (3) produce identical results regardless of which engineer's local configuration happens to be cached on the CI runner, and (4) never write files or run shell commands — it may only read and search the diff. Which invocation satisfies all four requirements?

options.text: `claude -p "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against CLAUDE.md. Report only bugs and security issues." --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA" --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" --max-turns 15 --bare`
`claude -p "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against CLAUDE.md. Report only bugs and security issues." --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA" --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" --max-turns 15`

`claude -p "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against CLAUDE.md. Report only bugs and security issues." --dangerously-skip-permissions --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA" --max-turns 15`, run this same way for every repository regardless of what the job touches, so it never has to stop for a permission prompt

`claude --headless "Review the diff in /tmp/pr.diff against CLAUDE.md. Report only bugs and security issues." --output-format json --json-schema "$SCHEMA" --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob" --max-turns 15 --bare`

questions.explanationEs: The objective measures 'Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling': the team version of an assisted workflow is the one that runs in the pipeline without depending on a human. A covers all four constraints with the chapter's exact vocabulary: `-p`/`--print` keeps the job from hanging while waiting on input (1); `--output-format json` + `--json-schema` lands validated output in `structured_output`, parseable without regex (2); `--bare` skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP, and local CLAUDE.md files, so the result doesn't depend on what the runner machine happens to have cached (3); and `--allowedTools "Read,Grep,Glob"` applies least privilege — a review job doesn't need `Write` or `Bash` (4).

distractorsEs.B: D7 · The One That Contradicts the Stem. `--bare` is missing. The chapter is explicit: without it, `-p` loads the same configuration as an interactive session and the result depends on the machine — the exact opposite of constraint (3) that the stem declared ('regardless of which engineer's local configuration').
distractorsEs.C: D4 · Self-Incriminating Absolute. 'Regardless of what the job touches' is the self-incriminating phrase, and always running with `--dangerously-skip-permissions` in CI is the chapter's textbook example of this archetype. It also breaks the least privilege in constraint (4): without `--allowedTools`, nothing stops it from touching `Write` or `Bash`.
distractorsEs.D: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect. `--headless` doesn't exist in Claude Code — the chapter names it explicitly as an invented-feature distractor, alongside `--batch` and `CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true`. The only real mechanism for non-interactive mode is `-p` / `--print`.

questions.trap: D is the vocabulary trap: 'headless' sounds exactly like what's needed, but it's a flag the real CLI doesn't have.

questions.objective: Support debugging and operational issue resolution
questions.scenario: Priya vs. Marcus: same repo, same commit, different behavior
questions.stem: Marcus and Priya both have the repository open at the same commit, and a `git diff` confirms their `.claude/settings.json` files are byte-for-byte identical. Yet every time Marcus runs a command matching `Bash(git push:*)`, Claude Code stops and asks him to confirm — Priya's session never prompts for that same command. Which command should Marcus run first to see exactly which permission rule is firing for that command and which file it came from?

options.text: `/status`
`/context`
`/permissions`
Conclude that Marcus is on a less capable Claude model than Priya, and request a model upgrade so it follows the committed settings more reliably.

questions.explanationEs: The objective is 'Support debugging and operational issue resolution,' reading (a): debugging the tool itself. The chapter tabulates this unambiguously: the question 'why does/doesn't it prompt me for this tool?' is answered with `/permissions`, which lists every rule and which file each one comes from. Since the repo's `.claude/settings.json` has already been verified identical, the difference has to come from another source that only `/permissions` exposes in full — for example a `~/.claude/settings.json` or a `.claude/settings.local.json` of Marcus's that adds a rule Priya doesn't have.

distractorsEs.A: D1 · Wrong-Category Control. `/status` is a real, useful command — it shows which settings sources are active overall, including the presence of managed settings — but it doesn't drill down to 'this rule, this file' for a specific tool. It's the adjacent category, not the one the symptom calls for.
distractorsEs.B: D8 · Irrelevant Knob. `/context` is a real view of what occupies the context window, by category and source. It has no causal relationship with whether a permission fires or not — it's the wrong knob for this symptom.
distractorsEs.D: D3 · Model as Security Boundary. Model capability is never the mechanism that determines whether a permission rule gets evaluated: enforcement is deterministic and happens client-side before the model acts (Law 1). A 'more reliable' model doesn't change which settings file got loaded.

questions.trap: A is the subtlest decoy: it's a real command from the same diagnostic family and 'sounds like' the settings command, but the chapter draws a precise line around which question each one answers.

questions.objective: Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling
questions.scenario: Per-team spend visibility for leadership
questions.stem: Castellan Insurance runs Claude Code for 120 engineers and has told its clients, in writing, that prompt content is never persisted outside the session. The VP of Engineering now wants visibility into Claude Code spend broken down by team, across the whole organization, to decide whether to expand the rollout. Which mechanism gives leadership that visibility?

options.text: Have every engineer run `/usage` at the end of each week and report the number in a shared spreadsheet.

Pull team-level spend and adoption from the Claude Code Analytics dashboard, or the Analytics API with an Admin API key scoped to `read:analytics`, which is backed by the same `claude_code.cost.usage` metric available over OpenTelemetry.
Have each engineer document a personal token budget in their `CLAUDE.md` and rely on Claude to stay under it.
Set `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1` so the spend dashboard can be built from the logged prompt and response content.

questions.explanationEs: The objective includes measuring whether the assisted workflow actually helped, and here the piece that matters is per-team cost governance, not individual introspection. The chapter is explicit: `/usage` is 'your session,' not governance; when the stem says 'leadership needs visibility into spend across the team,' `/usage` is a distractor. The answer lives in the Claude Code Analytics dashboard / API (Admin API key, `read:analytics` scope) or in the `claude_code.cost.usage` OTel metric — neither requires reading prompt content, which is exactly the line Castellan Insurance promised not to cross.

distractorsEs.A: D1 · Wrong-Category Control. `/usage` is real and responsible — but from the wrong phase: it's personal introspection of a session, not an organizational governance mechanism. Manually aggregating it in a spreadsheet doesn't turn it into the dashboard the VP asked for.
distractorsEs.C: D6 · Relabeling Without Effect. This is the chapter's textbook example: a token budget written into CLAUDE.md is FinOps vocabulary with zero enforcement — the model reads it as a suggestion (Law 1), no spend number is actually capped, and it doesn't produce the per-team breakdown leadership asked for.
distractorsEs.D: D5 · Optimization That Breaks the Requirement. `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS` would indeed produce a spend dashboard — paying for it with Castellan Insurance's contractual promise that prompt content is never persisted. It's unnecessary besides: `claude_code.cost.usage` already gives per-team spend without touching content — turning it on is a compliance decision, not an observability one.

questions.trap: D is the most dangerous variant: it solves the requested metric, but pays for it with exactly the requirement the stem declared in writing — the same family of trap as the `bypassPermissions` shortcut, wearing a different disguise.
